10467-a-select-collection-of-old-english:
W. Carew Hazlitt edited this eighth volume of Dodsley's old English plays, in the fourth edition of 1874 to 1876. Dodsley first issued the collection in 1744; Hazlitt arranged it by date, revised it, and added notes from all commentators. The volume serves students of early drama and stage history.

Summer's Last Will and Testament by Thomas Nash, The Downfall and Death of Robert Earl of Huntington, Contention between Liberality and Prodigality, and Grim the Collier of Croydon make up the set. Nash's life, from Lowestoft to Cambridge, opens the notes. Readers get rare Elizabethan plays with full scholarly care.
12623-the-life-and-adventures-of-robinso:
Daniel Defoe's Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe, in a London edition of 1808, opens with a life of the author. Defoe, born in London about 1663 to James Foe, a butcher of St. Giles, Cripplegate, and a Protestant dissenter, added De to his name for reasons never explained. Political scribblers accused him of hiding his Englishness, a charge the memoir doubts.

Crusoe's own story follows: shipwreck, island solitude, a canoe made with one labour, goats, grain and Friday, and rescue after years alone. Defoe writes in plain, circumstantial prose, letting work and prayer fill the days. The novel remains the founding English castaway tale, and a portrait of self-reliance under providence.
16183-in-indian-mexico-1908:
Frederick Starr's 1908 narrative, reprinted from the Forbes Chicago edition, records travel and labor among the Indians of Mexico. Starr, an anthropologist, dedicated the book to A. A. Robinson, to whom he owed his Mexican work and whose interest never failed. Contents open with priestly archaeology, then the start of a journey into country where old rites, crafts, and village life still shaped daily existence.

The book mixes road narrative with close observation of peoples, markets, and ceremonies, illustrated with scenes such as the music at Cancuc. Starr writes as a fieldworker and a storyteller at once. Modern readers gain a vivid, if dated, portrait of Mexico's native peoples at the start of the twentieth century.
16748-holinshed-s-chronicles-vol-2-of-6-:
This slice of Holinshed's Chronicles covers William Rufus, or William the Red, second son of William the Conqueror, from his crowning on September 9, 1087. The text, in old spelling, notes the emperor, the French king, the pope, and Malcolm of Scotland in its side notes. Rufus crossed to England with speed before his father's funeral was done.

Rufus won the peers by large gifts, on the counsel of Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, in whom he put all his trust. The slice shows a king buying favor after a father's hard rule. Readers who push through the old spelling get a reign opening in full chronicle style, with dates, gifts, and counsel in one long march.
16877-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
This September 8, 1920 number of Punch, volume 159, leads with rumors of prohibition in Scotland. A food controller freeing rice gets a joke. A Spanish cabinet that has not resigned this week gets one too. A Daily Mail prize for a new men's hat rounds out the lead items. A horse run down by a train, an American ambassador who will not retire, and Mr. Smillie's hopes all get short, dry jokes.

Punch keeps its weekly mix of news jokes and cartoons, aimed at politics, drink, and daily life. The Scotland joke plays on dry laws and southward drift, while the rice joke ties food rules to marriage. The issue is a brisk, funny snapshot of early autumn 1920, best read in short bites for its targets and tone.
17663-mcclure-s-magazine-vol-31-no-1-may:
McClure's Magazine, volume thirty-one, number one, dated May 1908, gathers the magazine's famous mix of fiction, biography, and public affairs. Its contents include The Misadventures of Cassidy by Edward S. Moffat and a life of Mary Baker G. Eddy by Georgine Milmine. In Charge of Trusty by Lucy Pratt adds fiction to the number.

Carl Schurz contributes First Days of the Reconstruction, covering restless foot-loose freedpeople, the Freedmen's Bureau, pickles and patriotism, and the South's hopeless poverty. Readers get a single monthly number of a leading muckraking magazine. The issue suits readers of American magazines and of Reconstruction history.
2108-history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-:
Carlyle follows Frederick after his failed flight, reprieved from death and sent to live at Custrin from November 1730 to February 1732. Chaplain Muller waits on the crown prince, and the young man faces shame, sorrow, and despair. Custrin, a fortress town on the Oder, became Frederick's school in humility and rule.

The volume traces how Frederick bore punishment, learned administration, and slowly regained his father's trust. Carlyle writes through clouds of old Prussian chronicle, yet the human shape of the prince emerges, chastened and watchful. Muller's chaplaincy shows the religious side of punishment, since the prince was urged to repent.
23507-a-short-history-of-pittsburgh-1758:
Samuel Harden Church wrote this short history of Pittsburgh from seventeen fifty eight to nineteen hundred eight, printed at the De Vinne Press in nineteen hundred eight. George Washington, called the first Pittsburgher, fronts the book, with William Pitt, Fort Pitt, Henry Bouquet, Anthony Wayne, and Conestoga wagons in the plates.

Three parts follow: historical, industrial, and intellectual, tracing a frontier fort town into a steel and river city, with canal boats hauled over portage roads and old Pittsburgh views from eighteen seventeen. Church writes with civic pride and a storyteller's ease, pausing on forts, floods, and foundries alike. Readers of city history will find a compact, well pictured survey of how Pittsburgh grew from a fort at the forks to a great industrial town.
23510-the-sheriffs-bluff-1908:
Thomas Nelson Page set this tale in an old colonial county, where court house and jail stand as relics beside the judge and the sheriff. The court house, solemn grey brown brick with mighty columns like a temple of Minerva, might pass for a jail until the real jail is seen. The real jail is a cube of huge stone blocks, its small square openings crossed with great iron bars.

Through those bars one glimpses a second grating and a hint of darkness within, and the sheriff's bluff of the title grows from that grim stage. Page writes with a lawyer's eye for old Virginia law and a storyteller's sense of bluff, nerve, and local pride. Readers who like tales of county courts and bold men will enjoy the slow build toward a confrontation where a sheriff's nerve must match his jail's stone.
23511-the-christmas-peace-1908:
Thomas Nelson Page set this Virginia tale between two old neighbours, Judge Hampden and Colonel Drayton. They were born a month apart on adjoining plantations and lived within a mile of each other for fifty odd years. Both are counted good men, yet to each other they have never been neighbours, passing by on the other side like the Levite in the parable.

The feud runs back to early colonial days, when the families settled on opposite hills and eyed each other across a stream like hostile forts. No one now knows quite how it started. Page builds toward a Christmas truce, where old pride meets the season's call to forgive. Readers who like tales of the old South will find a warm, wistful story of two proud houses and a peace long overdue.
23512-mam-lyddy-s-recognition-1908:
Thomas Nelson Page tells the story of Mam' Lyddy, a Black woman whose work for the Frenches spans her whole lifetime, following her mother and grandmother in the same household role. Her skin was a deep brown, her eyes dark and bright, and her voice could grow fierce when roused, yet her small, solid build carried a dignity far beyond its size. She rocked three generations on her ample bosom.

When Cabell Graeme courts pretty Betty French at the Chateau place, with rivals and obstacles in his path, Mam' Lyddy becomes his valuable ally. Her standing in the house opens doors his suit alone could not. Page writes her with fond, period bound admiration, and modern readers will read the tale through that lens. The story turns on loyalty, recognition, and the quiet power of a woman who knows a family better than it knows itself.
23513-old-jabe-s-marital-experiments-190:
Thomas Nelson Page wrote this comic Virginia tale of Old Jabe, a man of the Meriwether household who never lets anyone forget his long standing there. On that standing he trades. Among its dividends, he claims, are wives, so many that his own count would eclipse Henry the Eighth and Bluebeard.

Jabe was no model hand before the war, and overseers called him slick tongued and lazy, yet he outstayed them all, remaining oily and humorous after slavery ended. Page follows his marital experiments with broad, period humour, as Jabe courts, weds, and wrangles his way through wife after wife. Modern readers will note the tale's old South lens, while enjoying Jabe as a tall tale trickster who talks his way into and out of trouble.
23514-the-long-hillside-a-christmas-hare:
Thomas Nelson Page wrote this Christmas hare hunt in old Virginia as a boyhood memory, opening with a lament that hares grow fewer than in his youth. Old fields and branch bottoms once teemed with them. Boys counted hares their own game, scorned by grown gentlemen who shot partridges over pointers and only picked up a hare in passing.

Traps of hollow gum logs, set by Black trappers and copied by boys wild to imitate, fill the fall and winter scenes. Bruno and Don, the gentlemen's crack pointers, watch from the side. Page writes the long hillside with nostalgia and humour, as boys, dogs, and hares play out a Christmas chase. Readers who like country memory pieces will enjoy the hunt, the dogs, and the vanished boy world it recalls.
23515-the-spectre-in-the-cart-1908:
Thomas Nelson Page framed this ghost tale as a reunion with an old college friend, Stokeman, once hard headed and free of superstition, full of life and scorn for apparitions. Years have tempered his wild spirits into gravity, and the narrator, recalling college days steeped in superstition, wonders what changed him.

Stokeman once held that no ghostly show, however well attested, could not be explained on natural grounds. A notable college instance tested that creed, and the spectre in the cart of the title haunts the tale's close. Page lets dread grow from talk, memory, and a country road at night. Readers who like a ghost story that reasons with its own fear will enjoy this measured, Virginia flavoured haunting.
23516-bred-in-the-bone-1908:
Thomas Nelson Page set this racing tale on the afternoon before the closing day of the old Jockey Club's spring meeting. The next day promised the greatest race ever known on that course. A motley crowd at the white painted gate, agreed on little from God to horse talk except the universal worth of whiskey, now agreed on one more thing. Tomorrow would be a record.

Stable talk, prize money for the great overnight event, and the bred in the bone nature of horses and men drive the tale. Page writes the racecourse with insider ease, from windgalls and blisters to the hopes pinned on a favourite. Readers who like horse stories will enjoy the build to the big race, and the question of whether blood, training, or luck decides the day.
24877-lucy-maud-montgomery-short-stories:
This volume gathers twenty-four of Lucy Maud Montgomery's short stories from 1907 to 1908, in order of first printing. A Millionaire's Proposal leads, with Anna's Love Letters, Aunt Caroline's Silk Dress, The Genesis of the Doughnut Club, Matthew Insists on Puffed Sleeves, and The Revolt of Mary Isabel among them.

One tale climbs a cliff with Lynde, who creeps up a rope hand over hand while her dog fawns on her in joy at her rescue. Montgomery writes with growing confidence about love, work, and Island girls finding their footing. The set gives readers another rich year of her short fiction, between Anne's early triumphs and her later novels.
24895-the-call-of-the-south-1908:
Louis Becke published The Call of the South in London in 1908, a set of pearling and trading tales. The first story opens on a pearling lugger off Callie Harbour, Admiralty Island, where Paul Fremont, a big bronzed diver, lies weak from New Guinea fever under the awning.

Paul later gives his skipper an old octagon fifty-dollar gold piece, taken from a ship sunk off Galveston in the 1860s, to carry to the girl he hopes to marry in Australia. Other tales follow recruiting voyages, where the skipper refuses married men unless their wives come too. Becke writes from island life, with salt detail and a warm eye for its people.
27045-project-gutenberg-1971-2008:
Marie Lebert's Project Gutenberg, 1971-2008, updates her 2005 history to May 2008, with thanks to founder Michael Hart. The overview counts the project's growth: 1,000 books in August 1997, then 5,000 by April 2002, 10,000 by October 2003, and 25,000 by April 2008.

Lebert traces Hart's 1971 bet on free electronic public-domain books, the shared proofreading method, and the move into 55 languages with 40 mirror sites and some 340 new books a month. The article closes with stats and a chronology, recording the oldest digital library as it passed its first quarter century. Lebert notes that the project pioneered free information on the internet, and the article is also available in French.
27501-mcclure-s-magazine-vol-xxxi-no-3-j:
McClure's Magazine for July 1908, volume thirty-one, number three, shows the famous muckraking monthly at work. Its lead article, by Samuel Hopkins Adams, is called Guardians of the Public Health, and it takes up health boards, vital statistics, and the negligence of physicians.

Adams also treats business interests and yellow fever, newspapers and the bubonic plague, and prejudice and the death rate in Charleston. Carl Schurz contributes The Repudiation of Johnson's Policy, on the Fourteenth Amendment and the campaign to destroy a president. Fiction and impressions from Ellen Terry and others fill out a strong number.
27699-mcclure-s-magazine-vol-31-no-2-jun:
McClure's Magazine, volume thirty-one, number two, dated June 1908, opens with Ellen Terry's My First Appearance in America. Its other pieces include The Decree Made Absolute, President Johnson and His War on Congress, The Crystal-Gazer, and Mary Baker G. Eddy: Her Fruits.

Terry recalls first talk of going to America in 1874, when she played in The Wandering Heir, and Dion Boucicault dazzled her with figures. Cautious Charles Reade influenced her against the engagement. When she did go, in 1883, she was thirty-five, with an assured position in her profession. Her first tour came in a set of eight, seven with Henry Irving. The frontispiece shows Augustus Saint-Gaudens, from a painting by Ellen Emmet.
3084-original-short-stories-volume-08:
Clochette opens volume eight, with recollections too old to shake off. The narrator wonders at old recollections that haunt without release, one so old he cannot understand its vivid tenacity, despite many sinister and terrible things seen since. The volume adds The Kiss, The Legion of Honor, The Test, Found on a Drowned Man, The Orphan, The Beggar, and The Rabbit. Later tales include His Avenger, My Uncle Jules, The Model, A Vagabond, The Fishing Hole, The Spasm, In the Wood, Martine, All Over, The Parrot, and A Piece of String.

A vagabond who has spoken to no one for years, almost losing his tongue, faces unfamiliar houses in dismay. The volume shows Maupassant's compassion for outcasts alongside his irony.
31484-the-works-of-robert-louis-stevenso:
Volume eight of the Swanston Edition of the Works of Robert Louis Stevenson, published in London in 1911, the year given as MDCCCCXI, contains The Black Arrow. The edition was printed in twenty-five volumes, with 2,060 copies of this edition in all, of which 2,000 were for sale. The Black Arrow unfolds in five books: The Two Lads, The Moat House, My Lord Foxham, The Disguise, and Crookback.

Stevenson's tale is a Wars of the Roses adventure, full of outlaws, castles, and disguised identities. The Swanston volume presents it in the handsome collected form its publishers intended for Stevenson's readers. For collectors and general readers alike, it offers one of his most exciting historical romances in a well-made edition.
31851-mcclure-s-magazine-vol-xxxi-no-4-a:
McClure's Magazine, volume thirty-one, number four, August 1908, gathers the month's reporting, fiction, and essays under one cover. Its contents open with General Kuropatkin's disclosure of the secret policies of Russia and Carl Schurz's talks with Bismarck. They continue with Margaret Wilson's story The Forehanded Colquhouns.

Later pages carry Ellen Terry's last years with Henry Irving, Willa Sibert Cather's poem The Tavern, Hugo Münsterberg on prohibition and social psychology, and Marie Belloc Lowndes's The Moving Finger Writes. Readers get a full issue of a leading muckraking-era magazine, a snapshot of what educated Americans read in the summer of 1908.
3346-the-wandering-jew-volume-08:
Eugene Sue's serial reaches Book Eight, the third part, the redemption, in this volume. The Wandering Jew's chastisement opens it, with the descendants of the Wandering Jew and the attack. The wolves and the devourers, the return, and the go-between follow, with another secret, the confession, and love. The execution, the Champs-Elysees, and behind the scenes lead to up with the curtain and death.

Redemption, in Sue's scheme, costs as much as chastisement did. Old sins, old agents, and old loves converge on Paris, and the Rennepont inheritance nears its end. By now the stage machinery shows itself plainly, and a long punishment turns toward its close.
3558-memoirs-of-napoleon-bonaparte-volum:
This eighth volume of Bourrienne's memoirs follows Napoleon in 1805, the year of Ulm and Austerlitz. Bourrienne, the emperor's former private secretary, draws on his knowledge of the government and army that won those victories. Austerlitz crowns the year, but Bourrienne keeps his eye on the marches and orders behind the victory.

The narrative moves from the camps on the Channel coast to the march east and the great battle in Moravia, where Napoleon beat a larger allied army. Bourrienne shows the planning, the marching, and the diplomacy that followed victory. The volume suits readers who want 1805, often called Napoleon's finest military year, from a man who knew the machine behind the glory.
3575-recollections-of-the-private-life-o:
Constant's eighth volume looks at Napoleon as host and courtier in his own palaces. He describes receptions, dinners, and levees, where ambassadors, generals, and ladies waited for a word from the emperor. The valet watches how Napoleon received visitors, how he dressed for ceremony, and how quickly a formal evening could turn to blunt talk.

The volume shows the theater of power from backstage. Servants arranged rooms, announced guests, and cleared away the signs of hurry so that majesty could appear effortless. Constant writes with the eye of a man who knew the props. Readers interested in court life will find a close account of how an empire presented itself each night.
3588-essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-volum:
This eighth volume of Montaigne's Essays gathers chapters forty eight through fifty seven of Book One. They treat war horses, ancient customs, Democritus and Heraclitus, the vanity of words, the parsimony of the ancients, a saying of Caesar, vain subtleties, smells, prayers, and age. Montaigne opens the war horse chapter by joking that he has become a grammarian, though he learned no language except by rote.

The mix is typical Montaigne: a learned topic beside a bodily one, a laugh beside a moral. He compares the laughing and weeping philosophers, weighs ancient thrift against modern waste, and ends with age and prayer. The volume suits readers who like his miscellany style, where no subject is too small for reflection.
3908-the-confessions-of-jean-jacques-rou:
Jean Jacques Rousseau begins his eighth book with the long chain of misfortunes deduced from their origin, after a pause at the end of the seventh. Living in the splendid houses of Dupin and La Popliniere in Paris, he meets the young hereditary prince of Saxe-Gotha, Baron de Thun, and Seguy, known for a beautiful edition of Rousseau. At Fontenay, talk turns to Diderot's confinement at Vincennes, and Rousseau defends his friend with an impetuous zeal that is pardoned.

Music lightens the book, as trios composed at Chenonceaux are sung with friends, and Rousseau regrets leaving them at Wootton, where Mademoiselle Davenport may have curled her hair with them. He insists they deserve preservation for good counterpoint. Readers who like Rousseau among the philosophes will find friendship, music, and the first clouds of persecution.
5050-state-of-the-union-addresses-1790-2:
This complete collection gathers every State of the Union address from 1790 to 2008, in chronological order. Washington opens the series on January 8, 1790, followed by his later messages, then Adams, Jefferson, and every president through George W. Bush, with dates and speakers listed in a full contents table.

Read straight through, the collection is a history of America told by its presidents: war and peace, expansion and depression, reform and retrenchment, in the language of each era. Students and citizens get a single primary source for two centuries of national self-description. No other volume in this set covers so much ground in the presidents' own words.
5363-the-inside-of-the-cup-volume-08:
Winston Churchill's Inside of the Cup concludes in its eighth volume with chapters twenty-seven and twenty-eight: Retribution and Light. It opens at the Bishop's House, a comfortable double dwelling of smooth, bright red brick on Waverley Place. The Diocese bought it in the nineties, and it has pointed gables and a tiny, useless porch.

This final volume brings Hodder's story to its close, weighing retribution against the light that follows it. Readers finishing the novel here get the resolution of the rector's long struggle with wealth, faith. His parish completes the struggle, in the last chapters of Churchill's study of conscience.
5372-richard-carvel-volume-08:
Winston Churchill's Richard Carvel concludes in its eighth volume with chapters fifty through fifty-seven. They are Farewell to Gordon's, How an Idle Prophecy Came to Pass, and How the Gardener's Son Fought the Serapis. Discoveries, More Discoveries, The Love of a Maid for a Man, How Good Came Out of Evil, and I Come to My Own Again close the book.

It opens with Richard's misery after Mr Swain's death, lightened by one hope through all his years of servitude: that Dorothy was still free, as every letter from Comyn told him. This final volume brings Richard home at last, through war at sea and discoveries on land, to the love and estate that were his own.
5381-a-modern-chronicle-volume-08:
Winston Churchill's Modern Chronicle concludes in its eighth volume with a chapter in which a mirror is held up. Spring comes to Highlawns, a garden of tender greens: yellow-greens like beech boughs over the old wall, gentle blue-greens like turf. Lake waters run blue and white beneath a cloud-flecked sky.

Honora, sitting on a garden bench, feels the yellow and crimson tulips cannot open wide enough to the sun. For the first time, she believes she can measure her idol. This final volume holds Honora's reckoning, as the mirror of the title shows her, at last, what her modern chronicle has meant.
5395-the-crisis-volume-08:
Winston Churchill, the American novelist, brings The Crisis toward its close in this eighth volume. The story opens after the death of Silas Whipple, as Virginia Carvel sits alone with grief and fear for her father. Questions crowd her mind: where is Clarence, what has he seen, and is the house being watched?

The chapters that follow balance mourning with suspense, as family safety and wartime secrets press on every decision. Virginia must act while danger circles her household and old loyalties are tested. Readers get a tense, emotional stretch of the novel, where personal loss and Civil War intrigue meet in one St. Louis home.
5446-uarda-a-romance-of-ancient-egypt-vo:
An hour later, Ani leaves his father's tomb in rich attire and drives past the witch's cave and the little cottage of Uarda's father in the eighth volume of Georg Ebers's Uarda. Nemu squats on the step in the dwarf's usual place, grinding his teeth when he glimpses a man's white robe beside Uarda through a hedge opening. The pretty child's visitor is not welcome to him.

Jealousy, watching, and household secrets drive the volume, as figures cross paths around the rebuilt hut. Ebers mixes romance with menace in a small Egyptian neighborhood. Readers get a tense, closely observed stretch of the story, where a glance through a hedge carries real danger.
5457-an-egyptian-princess-volume-08:
Sunlight tries to break through thick curtains in a sick-room in the eighth volume of Georg Ebers's An Egyptian Princess. Nebenchari has not left the Egyptian girl's bedside, feeling her pulse at times and spreading sweet-scented ointments on her forehead and chest, then sitting gazing dreamily into space. Nitetis seems to have sunk into deep sleep after an attack.

The volume centers on illness, care, and waiting, with a physician's vigil replacing court ceremony. Ebers slows the romance to the pace of a sickroom, where small gestures carry weight. Readers get a tender, anxious stretch of the story, focused on Nitetis and those watching over her.
5480-cleopatra-volume-08:
Night brings little sleep to Cleopatra in the eighth volume of Georg Ebers's Cleopatra, as memory follows memory and plan is added to plan. The resolve made the day before stands: today she will begin to carry it out, prepared for whatever may happen. Before her work, she grants a second audience to a Roman envoy, while Timagenes exerts all his skill in persuasion and wit.

The volume turns on a queen's resolve and a diplomat's eloquence, with the future of her kingdom at stake. Ebers keeps the tension in council and conversation rather than battle. Readers get a taut, political stretch of the romance, centered on Cleopatra's judgment under pressure.
5490-the-emperor-volume-08:
A story told by Mastor has greatly agitated Pollux and driven him to a mad flight in the eighth volume of Georg Ebers's The Emperor. Mastor's tale concerns events in the steward's rooms during hours when the young artist was helping his parents move household goods into his sister's tiny dwelling. Keraunus, seldom cheerful at the best of times, faces a morning when Sabina comes to call.

The volume untangles household secrets, steward's rooms, and family moves in Roman Alexandria, as a secondhand story sets a young man running. Ebers keeps the intrigue domestic and close. Readers get a suspenseful stretch of the romance, where gossip and misunderstanding carry real consequences.
5515-arachne-volume-08:
Filled with longing, Hermon goes down toward evening to the shore in the eighth volume of Georg Ebers's Arachne. The sun sets, and the riot of color in the western sky seems to mock the torturing anxiety mastering his soul. He does not notice an approaching boat, though travelers bound through Arabia Petraea have landed here for days, stirring the quiet waters.

The volume follows a blind sculptor's anxious wait by the sea, with boats and travelers passing unnoticed. Ebers writes longing against a sunset that offers no comfort. Readers get a melancholy, atmospheric stretch of the romance, where waiting itself becomes the story.
5524-the-bride-of-the-nile-volume-08:
After his interview with Orion, Philippus hurries through town in the eighth volume of Georg Ebers's The Bride of the Nile. He pays so little heed to passers-by and to processions praying loudly for the Nile to rise that he bumps into people and earns shouted abuse. He enters two or three houses, where neither patients nor attendants recognize their usual physician.

The volume follows a distracted doctor through a city praying for the river, with personal trouble drowning out public ritual. Ebers sets private urgency against communal hope. Readers get a troubled, atmospheric stretch of the romance, where a man's mind is elsewhere even as his city begs for water.
5537-a-thorny-path-volume-08:
The slave Argutis waits for Melissa in the antechamber in the eighth volume of Georg Ebers's A Thorny Path, beaming with joy as she approaches, since he plainly brings good news. Before she leaves the house, she learns that her father and Philip have returned and regained their freedom. Argutis kept the joyful tidings from his beloved mistress's ear so he might have the pleasure of bringing them himself.

Melissa hurries back to Johanna to share the news, her delight matching his. The volume turns on homecoming and a servant's proud gift of glad tidings. Readers get a joyful stretch of the romance, where freedom restored becomes a household celebration.
5559-margery-gred-a-tale-of-old-nurember:
Good hope of going forth into the wide world to risk all for lover and brother is not yet fulfilled. This eighth volume of Georg Ebers's Margery, a tale of old Nuremberg, opens in waiting. The maidens must take patience, hard as that seems, and it is worse for Kubbeling, a man used to wandering free. During days of waiting at the forest lodge, he first loses his mirthful humor, then falls sick of a fever.

The volume follows waiting, illness, and delayed adventure, with a free spirit caged by circumstance. Ebers writes patience as its own trial. Readers get a restless stretch of the tale, where tarrying tests everyone, especially the wanderer.
5568-barbara-blomberg-volume-08:
Everything in Barbara's residence remains as when she arrived in the eighth volume of Georg Ebers's Barbara Blomberg, except that the second story has stood empty since the marquise departed. Two horses wait in the stable, the steward works as before, the cook rules the kitchen, and Frau Lamperi tends Barbara's rooms. Yet at Wolf's first visit he must use all his persuasion to stop his miserable friend from moving back to her former home.

The volume follows a woman's unhappiness amid an unchanged household, after a conversation with Charles's messenger left her ill. Ebers writes domestic order against inner distress. Readers get a sad, quiet stretch of the romance, where nothing has changed except Barbara herself.
5910-the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-1:
Chapter twenty-three alone fills this Don Quixote installment, on what befell the knight in the Sierra Morena, one of the rarest adventures in this veracious history. Seeing himself served in a certain way, Quixote tells Sancho that doing good to boors is like throwing water into the sea. Sancho answers that warning will be taken as much as he is a Turk, and warns that chivalry counts for nothing with the Holy Brotherhood.

Readers enter the Sierra Morena, where Quixote's penance and madness take their wildest form. The single chapter favors master and squire dialogue, as Sancho's proverbs meet Quixote's ideals. It suits readers midway through volume one, since the Sierra episode becomes the novel's great wilderness interlude, with Cardenio and penance ahead.
7593-the-caxtons-a-family-picture-volume:
Part eight of The Caxtons lets wonder interrupt domestic life, and Lytton plays the scene straight. A small, delicate figure in white appears in the father's Russell Street drawing room, with dark curls over her shoulders and eyes of unusual size and shine. The household, startled, falls silent for some moments. The figure is the part's mystery, a childlike presence tied to the novel's romantic thread.

The father, as the bolder and wiser of the household, and the better fitted to face eerie things, finds the nerve to speak. That plain courage, set against the strangeness of the visit, gives the scene its charm. Nothing is explained at once, and the part is stronger for it. A scholar's house briefly holds something it cannot account for, and the novel lets it stand.
7622-pelham-volume-08:
Mr. Job Jonson holds knowledge Pelham needs in this part of Pelham, and the scene moves the inquiry forward through talk, manners, and a visitor who knows more than he first says. Over breakfast things, Jonson remarks on the appetite fresh air gives a man. The scene is small, but it matters: a visitor's small talk can hide knowledge worth a fortune. Pelham must listen past the manners to the matter.

The meeting itself is awaited with strain. Jonson keeps his appointment punctually, after the narrator has waited on the rack of expectation for three hours before his arrival. His warm welcome removes any diffidence in so shame-faced a gentleman. The part thus pairs suspense with politeness, and lets a breakfast do the work of a confrontation.
7638-the-disowned-volume-08:
A winter dusk gathers over Crauford's town house in this part of The Disowned, and two schemers weigh a mesh of their own weaving. Their talk turns to plotting and ambition: had inquiry been protracted another week, Bradley hints, Crauford might have been a lord and he a knight. The near-miss gives the scene its edge. Titles were close enough to imagine, and far enough to lose.

The room itself sets that talk in gloom. An expiring fire relieves the closing darkness, and Mr. Bradley sits with his feet on the fender, coaxing warmth into his icy palms. Crauford paces the room with a changeful step. Fate, like a gathering force behind them, labors onward while they plot. The part shows ambition at its coldest: two men in a dark room, counting what a week might have bought.
7647-ernest-maltravers-volume-08:
At Cleveland's full villa in Book Eight of Edward Bulwer Lytton's Ernest Maltravers, Lady Florence Lascelles joins a bright company. Cleveland, wise and kind, thinks thirty a fit age for marriage and hopes Florence may suit Maltravers, whose gifts and temper he trusts. Her odd ways, he thinks, love will tame.

But Lumley Ferrers works the room with smooth talk, hinting that Maltravers loves another, while Florence grows pale and proud. Letters pass, pride flares, and a plain truth gets twisted by gossip. The volume shows how a good match can be undone by one schemer's well-placed word.
7657-kenelm-chillingly-volume-08:
A letter at the breakfast table shakes Sir Peter in Book Eight of Edward Bulwer Lytton's Kenelm Chillingly. He hides his dismay from his wife at the tea urn, while Cecilia and Gordon watch his pale face and guess at bad news. Talk of a failed tenant covers the shock for a time.

The volume moves toward love plainly spoken, as Kenelm weighs how to tell a girl she is a woman to him, not a child, with little time for slow steps. An offer for a picture from a merchant prince also pulls art and trade together. The closing book ties family worry to a lover's choice.
7666-what-will-he-do-with-it-volume-08:
Guy Darrell goes back to a lone life at Fawley in Book Eight of Edward Bulwer Lytton's What Will He Do With It? His try at the social world has failed, and his last hope has fallen like a torch from his own hand. Childless, he fears his line and his fame will die with him.

The volume weighs what lasts: wealth, a lawyer's name, or a book that may live a year or fifty. Caroline Montfort, white with fear, hears how a hidden tie could shame a young woman and wound Darrell himself. Pride, posterity, and a secret past drive these somber chapters.
7679-harold-the-last-of-the-saxon-kings-:
Harold stands bareheaded before widowed Queen Aldyth in Book Eight of Edward Bulwer Lytton's Harold, subtitled Fate. Her lord Gryffyth lies dead, his bard fallen beside him, and she speaks of a queen's robe torn over an aching heart as she prepares to return to her father's land.

Harold, who twice saved the child of his foe, hears her farewell with grief. Later his mother Githa and brother Gurth urge him not to risk himself, since danger to him now means evil to England. Fate, kinship, and duty press the earl toward a choice he cannot dodge.
7699-a-strange-story-volume-08:
Fenwick returns with joy to his philosophical work in the final volume of Edward Bulwer Lytton's A Strange Story. Each link in his chain of thought seems too tight to alter, yet the whole argues against the wonders he himself has seen. To admit phantoms would wreck the book, and the book is himself.

Then Lilian appears in what looks like a bridal robe, calling his name and clasping him in a wife's first frank embrace. Memory floods back, and she thanks his guarding love. The closing volume pits sober system against lived marvel, and lets love answer where reason stalls.
7709-my-novel-volume-08:
Trumpets for enlightenment draw a dry rebuke in Book Eight of Edward Bulwer Lytton's My Novel, where the narrator asks where the march is headed and gets six poor answers. One man cries for the Charter, one for women's rights and social love, one merely hopes his head stays whole.

Amid the satire, Randal returns home to his sister Juliet, who springs to his neck while he smooths her hair and urges more care for her looks. The volume pairs public cant with private feeling, and shows a schemer whose strongest bond is to his own sister.
7722-the-last-of-the-barons-volume-08:
Lady Anne visits the court in Book Eight of Edward Bulwer Lytton's The Last of the Barons, where the last link between kingmaker and king snaps. Warwick has beaten Lancastrians on the frontier, yet Edward lingered at Middleham, chained by a stronger lure than battle, while Hastings halted at York.

Rumors say Edward is held against his will, and Warwick sends Montagu to clear his name. Alwyn later bears a ring to the ramparts, trusting Anne's word to smooth all. The volume shows a great alliance breaking not in open war, but in suspicion, absence, and court whispers.
7744-the-parisians-volume-08:
On May 8 a plebiscite backs the Emperor in Book Eight of Lytton's The Parisians. Seven to eight million votes support him, against a million and a half who include Paris's old throne-shakers. Days later Rameau leaves his printing office and gets a note from two shabby foreigners.

They are members of a long-silent Secret Council of Ten. Thaddeus Loubinsky is tall and martial, Leonardo Raselli small and cat-like, both in shabby gentility. Their summons revives a conspiracy the poet-politician had nearly forgotten. Empire, press, and secret plots collide in this volume.
7908-american-historical-and-literary-cu: Part eight of American Historical and Literary Curiosities by John Jay Smith and John F. Watson, in text form, is just an editor's note and a title page. The editor notes the series is entirely illustrations and page images, with only a few text sections that could be digitized, and urges readers to open the HTML file instead.
8786-the-divine-comedy-by-dante-illustra:
This eighth part of Cary's Inferno covers cantos twenty-three through twenty-eight, still deep in Malebolge among hypocrites, thieves, and sowers of discord. Canto twenty-three moves in silence and solitude, one following the other like minor friars on a road. Dante's thoughts turn to Aesop's fable of mouse and frog, whose chances match his own in origin and end. Fear doubles as he reasons that the demons, foiled through the travellers, will pursue them.

Hypocrites in leaden cloaks, thieves transformed by serpents, and sowers of schism, split and maimed, fill the later cantos. Dante's encounters grow more Florentine and more personal, with old enemies and false counsellors. The part shows fraud's many masks, from pious dress to stolen identity to words that split cities. It is intricate, grotesque, and often darkly funny, and it rewards readers who have learned Dante's moral map.
9321-tales-and-novels-volume-08:
Maria Edgeworth's eighth volume of Tales and Novels concludes Patronage, adds Comic Dramas, and gives Leonora with letters. Patronage resumes at chapter thirty-six, where Alfred's marriage alone could recover Lady Jane's sympathy for Caroline. Caroline left a happy home and Hungerford Castle, where she was adored, to tend Lady Jane in sickness.

Alfred Percy, restorer of her fortune and friend in adversity, would grieve to find sisters quarrelling at his happiest hour. Edgeworth weighs gratitude and affection with her usual wit. The volume shows her range across novel, drama, and letter, lively and moral to the last.
9770-alice-or-the-mysteries-book-08:
Book eight of Edward Bulwer Lytton's Alice, or The Mysteries, opens with a letter from Ernest Maltravers to Frederick Cleveland. Evelyn is free, Maltravers writes, she is in Paris, and he sees her daily. Affections, he confesses, prove stronger than all reasonings on self-rule. Men cannot build a philosophy of indifference while love lives. Fate, he finds, makes fools of the wise.

The book follows Maltravers and Evelyn through Paris, as old vows and new hopes collide. Lytton's prose favors high feeling and moral reflection. A reader gets the eighth book of a Victorian mystery romance, where love undoes a hero's cold philosophy.
a-catalogue-of-rare-and-valuable-books-i:
A Catalogue of Rare and Valuable Books, issued in 1908 by Bernard Quaritch, is a London bookseller's catalogue of the first rank. Quaritch was the era's great dealer in rare books, and this catalogue ranges across the whole market. Its headings include works on America, Australasia, Bibles and theology, bibliography, English literature, European history and literature, and European philology.

Genealogy and heraldry, typography, Ireland, and the occult sciences of alchemy, astrology, folklore, and magic all have their sections too. Each entry offered a copy for sale, with the dealer's description. Such catalogues are now sources in themselves: they record what the rare book world held, and valued, in the Edwardian years.
a-modern-chronicle-volume-08:
Winston Churchill's A Modern Chronicle, volume eight, closes Book Three and the novel in three chapters. In Which a Mirror Is Held Up opens at Highlawns in spring, Eden tinted with tender greens. Honora's life with Hugh Chiltern has reached its country stillness. The Renewal of an Ancient Hospitality gathers the past's claims.

Six letters from a club, and a Paris sitting-room, carry the final chapter: In Which Mr. Erwin Seeks Paris. The chronicle that began with a consul's daughter at Nice ends in the city of her birth's continent, her choices made. Churchill resolves Honora's career — St. Louis, Quicksands, divorce, work, and second love — without punishing her for ambition. The mirror of the first chapter's title is the reader's own society. Eight volumes of manners conclude in acceptance: the modern woman, neither ruined nor canonized, at home in a world she helped to make.
a-select-collection-of-old-english-plays: Robert Dodsley continues his select collection of old English plays in this eighth volume, with notes by W. Carew Hazlitt. Its contents include Summer's Last Will and Testament by Thomas Nashe, printed in 1600. The Downfall and The Death of Robert, Earl of Huntington follow, with Contention between Liberality and Prodigality, and Grim the Collier of Croydon. The Robin Hood earl and Nashe's summer comedy anchor a volume of early English stagecraft.
a-strange-story-volume-08: Edward Bulwer Lytton continues his strange story in this eighth volume as the narrator eagerly returns to his philosophical work, the ambitious hope of his intellectual life. Each link in its chain of reasoning seems so serried that altering one would derange all. Yet the whole reasoning opposes the wonders he himself experienced. Between his being as man and his being as author lies a strange contradiction, for the work was himself before phantoms perplexed his brain.
a-thorny-path-volume-08:
A Thorny Path turns toward relief in Volume 8 of the novel by Georg Ebers, where the slave Argutis waits in an outer room. Ebers lets the man's shining face tell the news before his words can. The ship that carried Melissa's father and brother away from Alexandria has anchored at dawn. Both prisoners won their liberation while still at sea, far from the imperial court that condemned them.

Chapter XXIII follows Melissa as the report fills in, detail by detail. Her father Heron survived the brutal galley service, the heavy rowing labor imposed on condemned men. A reunion with his beloved birds calmed his fury quickly. Her brother Philip returned in miserable health and was carried straight to his bedchamber. Old Dido now nurses him there with devoted attention. Melissa hurries toward the Serapeum quarter first, then turns for home. Gratitude and anxiety travel with her in equal measure.
abdul-baha-some-answered-questions-1908:
Abdu'l-Baha, the son of the founder of the Baha'i faith, gave these talks at table in the years before this book of 1908. Laura Clifford Barney heard them, wrote them down, and turned them into English. The book was the first great Baha'i work to come out in English in the West.

Guests asked him hard points on God, on Christ, on science, and on the ways of the soul. He gives crisp, calm replies, each fit to stand on its own as a short essay. The book is the door through which most first readers step to the Baha'i faith.
alexander-locke-1908:
Samuel Alexander wrote this short study of John Locke for the Philosophical Classics series, and it appeared in 1908. Alexander taught at Manchester and later won fame as a thinker in his own right. His subject was the English thinker whose work shaped modern ideas about knowledge, government, and faith.

Readers get Locke's life in brief, then a clear tour of his main claims. Minds start blank, Alexander explains, and all knowledge grows from sense and reflection. In politics, Locke held that rule rests on consent and that people keep rights no ruler may take. The book stays a neat first map of a thinker who helped found liberal thought.
alice-or-the-mysteries-book-08: Edward Bulwer Lytton gives the eighth book of Alice, or the Mysteries over to a letter from Ernest Maltravers to Frederick Cleveland, written from Paris. Evelyn is free, Maltravers has seen her daily, and he confesses that affection defeats every philosophy of indifference. The epistolary turn lays bare a lover's hopes and the limits of reason against feeling.
american-historical-and-literary-curiosi: John Jay Smith presents an eighth part of American Historical and Literary Curiosities, a series that treats history through reproduced pages and objects. Scanning could only lift a few text sections, a limit the editor's note states plainly while directing readers to the HTML edition. The volume joins a sequence meant to be seen as much as read.
an-egyptian-princess-volume-08:
Georg Ebers brings An Egyptian Princess toward its crisis in Volume 8, set at the Persian court of Cambyses. Ebers keeps the focus close and human here. The Egyptian bride Nitetis lies gravely ill, and the palace waits through the night for the end that her doctors plainly expect.

Chapter VIII stays at the sickbed, where the physician Nebenchari keeps watch and feels the girl's pulse in silence. Six Persian doctors murmur spells under his orders, yet their art can do nothing. Atossa, the king's sister and the patient's friend, slips in to kiss her forehead and is sent away. Kassandane, the blind queen mother, waits in the next room. Grief, rank, and helpless medicine fill a quiet, painful chapter.
andrewes-devotions-vol1-1908:
Volume one of the Devotions of Bishop Andrewes gathers the private prayers of Lancelot Andrewes, Bishop of Winchester and one of the great figures of the early English church. This 1908 edition presents the first part of the devotions he wrote for his own daily use, not for public worship. Andrewes was famed for learning, and his prayers draw deeply on the early church fathers.

The devotions follow set forms for the days and hours, mixing confession, praise, and intercession in dense, ordered language. They show a bishop's inner discipline rather than his public sermons. The volume remains a classic of Anglican spirituality, read for both its craft and its picture of private prayer in the seventeenth-century church.
andreyev-seven-that-were-hanged-1908:
The Seven Who Were Hanged, Leonid Andreyev's story of 1908, reached English in Herman Bernstein's translation of 1909. Five young terrorists who plotted against a minister wait in prison for execution. With them hang two common criminals, a murderer and a horse thief, each facing death in his own way.

Andreyev enters each cell in turn: the brave, the broken, the calm, the terrified. Parents visit, clocks tick, and the state machine moves without haste or hatred. The story made Andreyev famous around the world on its appearance. Tolstoy's circle debated its protest against capital punishment for years. Its quiet, mounting dread has lost none of its force.
angela-foligno-divine-consolations-1908:
The Book of Divine Consolations records the spiritual life of Angela of Foligno, a thirteenth-century Franciscan tertiary and mystic. This 1908 English edition, translated by Mary Steegmann with an introduction by Algar Thorold, brings her book to English readers. After a deep conversion, Angela gave up her former life and set down what she believed God showed her.

Her account moves through stages of penitence, suffering, and intimate visions of Christ's love. It is written as a mystical autobiography, dictated from lived experience rather than argued as theology. Readers meet one of the most intense voices of medieval women's devotion, in a translation that keeps her direct, confessional tone.
aquarian-gospel-of-jesus-the-christ-1908:
Levi Dowling said he read the past from a vast store of all deeds. The Aquarian Gospel of Jesus the Christ came out in 1908. Dowling was a preacher in the States with a love of the East. The book calls its age the Aquarian age, now at its dawn.

The tale fills the lost years of Jesus with trips to India, Tibet, and Greece. Wise men of each land teach him a part of the one truth. His birth, his works, and his death then run in a new dress. The book is a chief text of the New Age line of faith.
arabian-nights-burton-1885-vol-08:
The eighth volume of Burton's Nights, published in 1885, nears the end of Shahrazad's thousand and one nights. Her pardon, when it comes in the frame, will rest on the king's transformed heart. The tales still run the full gamut: high romance, low comedy, pious legend, and sly trickster turns.

Burton's apparatus grows richer as the set proceeds, and volume eight carries his learning lightly over long stretches of story. He translates charms, songs, and riddles that tidier versions drop. The result can daunt new readers, yet it preserves the book as the East knew it. Scholars still cite Burton's notes beside his text. The volume keeps faith with both.
arachne-volume-08:
Sunset finds the blind sculptor Hermon walking down to the shore in Volume 8 of Arachne, by Georg Ebers. Ebers paints the western sky in full color, then sets it against the anxiety that has mastered his hero. Boats land here often with travelers bound through Arabia, and the water has been busy for days, though Hermon barely notices until a familiar shout rings out across it.

He answers with a cry of hope before his weak eyes can make out the man standing in the boat. It is Bias, his freedman, back from an errand carried out well and no longer bound by an oath of silence. Bias reports that Ledscha has sailed away with the Gaul Lutarius toward Paraetonium, on the border with Cyrene. News, loss, and reunion meet on one evening shore.
arrhenius-worlds-making-borns-1908:
Svante Arrhenius was a Swedish chemist who won a Nobel Prize for his work on how salts split in water. His Worlds in the Making, in Borns's 1908 translation, surveys the birth and death of worlds for general readers. It is climate science's first popular classic.

Arrhenius calculates how carbon dioxide in the air traps heat and could warm or cool the whole planet. He also proposes panspermia, the idea that life's seeds drift through space from world to world. His greenhouse figures, rough as they were, started a line of research that runs to today's climate models.
arxiv-2509-00408:
Thi Khanh Linh Ha, Andreas Heinrich Hamel, and Daniel Kostner compute expectiles through fixed point iterations in 2025, with a general convergence proof. Expectiles are statistical summaries like quantiles but built from squared loss, and they serve as risk measures in finance. Each expectile solves a continuous optimization problem.

The first-order condition for that problem yields two fixed point characterizations, both usable as algorithms. One two-sided version is already implemented and widely used in practice. A general convergence proof for these iterations appears to be new, in the authors' account. Firm convergence grounds a tool that risk analysts already rely on for tail-sensitive summaries.
arxiv-2509-00508:
Nhat-Tuong Do-Tran leads five authors in total, with Ngoc-Hoang-Lam Le, Ian Chiu, Po-Tsun Paul Kuo, and Ching-Chun Huang, on ultrasound style transfer. Scans from different devices look different in style, which lowers the accuracy of models trained on one device when used on another.

Do-Tran and his co-authors propose TRUST, a token-driven method that keeps source content while taking on the shared style of a target device. Their module picks suitable target tokens for each source token and optimal ones for the downstream model, guided by a behavior mirror loss, a penalty that matches model behavior. Added prompts help match content to that behavior. Tests beat prior unpaired translation methods on image quality and task scores.
arxiv-2509-00708:
Jingyi Guan, with two co-authors, presents ReWeave for network traffic control after link failures. Internet service networks face such failures often. Older schemes reroute traffic over fragile fixed paths. Others precompute backups for many failure cases at high cost. Both approaches scale poorly as networks grow.

ReWeave gives each link a compact set of backup paths. Those paths use adjacent links only. When a link fails, only its two end routers act. They reroute traffic with SRv6-based detours on the spot. No central controller is needed, and no full path is recomputed. On large backbone networks, peak link use drops sharply. Packet loss stays as low as a protection scheme in most cases. Response speed matches the fastest local schemes.
arxiv-2509-01108:
Vsevolod I. Ivanov examines a 1999 paper on multiobjective programming, a field that seeks good answers when several goals must be balanced at once. The earlier paper, by Osuna-Gomez, Beato-Moreno, and Rufian-Lizana, dealt with a broad form of convexity in such problems. Ivanov reports a flaw in the proofs of its two main theorems.

Because the old proof plan could not be fixed as it stood, Ivanov derives correct proofs by a different route. Along the way he obtains two added theorems for which the older proof scheme does work. The note is a correction to the record: it keeps the field's results on firm ground and shows which claims hold, and under what revised statements they hold.
arxiv-2509-01308:
Turning a plain question into a database query, called text-to-SQL, has improved with large language models, yet complex queries still trip them up. Mattia Tritto, with six co-authors, studies how to pick the best answer when a model makes several tries at test time. Common methods favor the query that runs without error, or the answer given most often.

The team argues outcome reward models, scorers trained to judge whether an output is truly right, can serve as a better test-time guide. Their work, GradeSQL, explores that largely untested use for SQL generation. By scoring the meaning of each candidate query rather than its surface form, the method aims to lift accuracy on hard questions. Better selection could widen safe access to databases for non-expert users.
arxiv-2509-02108:
Brahim Touayouch, Loic Fosse, Geraldine Damnati, and Gwenole Lecorve merge task specific models with a divergence guided method called DivMerge. Model merging via task arithmetic combines fine-tuned models into one multi task model. Interference between tasks grows as more models are merged, hurting results. Their approach uses Jensen-Shannon divergence, a symmetric gap measure between distributions, to steer the merge.

No extra labeled data are needed, and task importance balances automatically. Robustness holds as the task count grows, unlike many prior methods. Comparisons show consistent wins over earlier merging work. The method suits settings where many specialist models already exist and retraining is costly. Divergence guidance keeps each task voice audible in the merged model.
arxiv-2509-02408:
Spyros Angelopoulos, Loris Marchal, Adrien Obrecht, and Bertrand Simon wrote a 2025 computer science paper on memory management for mixture-of-experts language models. Such models activate only some expert subnetworks per token, so the active experts should sit in fast cache memory.

The authors define a new paging problem that captures layered model structure and expert reuse. They prove lower bounds on how well any deterministic or randomised strategy can compete with an ideal one. Those bounds suggest least-recently-used style policies perform well in theory. A layer-aware version of that policy is then proposed. Simulations on synthetic data and real usage traces show it beats classic paging policies, helping large models run within tight memory limits.
arxiv-2509-02708:
Anja Butter and four co-authors wrote a 2025 particle physics paper on unfolding. Unfolding removes detector smearing from data. It recovers the true distributions of particles. Machine learning methods now handle high-dimensional, unbinned data. Most ignore real-world flaws, though.

Real data also hold stray events that do not belong. Finite detector reach and efficiency matter too. The authors extend generative unfolding to cover that full suite of effects. Two variants are offered. One is fully generative. The others mix generative and discriminative steps. Tests use a Gaussian case and a simulated collider dataset. Both handled all effects. The authors call theirs an analysis-ready option for the toolkit.
arxiv-2509-02908:
Santosh Chapagain and 4 co-authors reported a 2025 study on spotting minority stress in social media posts. Minority stress is the extra strain that stigma and unfair treatment place on sexual and gender minority people. It is tied to worse mental and physical health.

The team tested several transformer models, a kind of language software that weighs words in context, on two large sets of Reddit posts. Adding graph links, which encode who talks with whom and how posts connect, improved results across the board. Careful training with those links beat quick zero-shot or few-shot use, where a model gets few or no examples. The best setups noticed markers like hiding one's identity, absorbed stigma, and requests for support.
arxiv-2509-03008:
Bikai Gao, Yuk-Kei Kong, and Yong-Liang Ma asked in 2025 where the mass of protons and neutrons comes from. A fresh measurement of the pulsar PSR J0614-3329, a spinning neutron star, gave it the smallest reliable radius yet for its mass. That tight size sharply limits how dense matter can behave inside such stars.

The authors use a parity doublet model, which splits nucleon mass into parts that do and do not come from a symmetry effect called chiral symmetry breaking. Their matter model then crosses over smoothly into quark matter at higher density. Matching all known pulsar and gravitational wave limits narrowed one key mass parameter greatly. The result suggests most nucleon mass does not come from chiral effects alone.
arxiv-2509-03208:
Pauliina Ilmonen and 4 co-authors developed data-driven models in 2025 for several interest rates at once. The Vasicek model is a classic formula describing how a single rate drifts and jitters over time. Most extensions still handle one rate, assume bell-shaped noise, or both.

Their generalized version models many rates jointly while assuming little about the noise beyond steady increments and fading memory. They give estimators, recipes for recovering unknown parameters from data, and prove those recipes converge to the truth. Limiting distributions describe the remaining uncertainty. Worked examples illustrate the theory. The model is then tested on simulated data, where the truth is known, and on real market data.
arxiv-2509-03408:
Mohammed Amer and 4 co-authors built a multimodal deep learning framework in 2025 for subtyping breast cancer. Molecular subtypes guide personalized treatment and prognosis, and they are better judged from several data kinds at once. Clinics, though, hold different mixes of data for different patients and sites, so rigid fusion designs break easily.

Their loosely coupled framework ingests copy number variation, clinical records, and pathology slide images, and can add or drop modalities with little overhead and no retraining of the rest. A dual representation of whole slide images combines the usual image view with a graph view of tissue structure. That pairing drove significant performance gains. A new fusion strategy added further improvements across combinations of available data, beating leading methods in their comparisons.
arxiv-2509-03708:
Leyna Shackleton argues that twisted quantum doubles do not suffer from the sign problem after all in a 2025 research paper. The sign problem blocks efficient computer simulation of many quantum systems, because negative terms cancel positive ones in the calculation. Some phases of matter, like the double semion model, were widely believed to carry an intrinsic sign problem that no local model could avoid.

Shackleton shows that belief is wrong. The double semion model can be realised in local Hamiltonians free of the sign problem. So can every twisted quantum double phase for a finite group, under stochastic series expansion, a standard simulation method. These models fail the usual stoquastic test for sign freedom, yet still simulate cleanly. No fine-tuning is involved, and exact solvability is not required. Sign-free perturbations around these models also give access to varied topological phase transitions, widening what simulations can explore.
arxiv-2509-04108:
Francisco Marín Sola, writing alone, gives random versions of some classic shape inequalities in a 2025 mathematics paper. Isoperimetric inequalities link a shape's size with its boundary, like the fact that circles enclose the most area for their perimeter. Functional versions extend those links to mathematical functions instead of plain shapes. Sola works with a family called p-concave functions, using random models for them built by earlier researchers.

One result covers a functional form of quantities known as quermassintegrals, with a Sobolev-type inequality falling out as a special case. Another shows the affine Sobolev inequality of Zhang holding on average in this random setting. The random results also recover the older fixed-shape versions, and yield a broader form of Zhang's inequality.
arxiv-2509-04308:
Farshad Amani and two co-authors teach a learning system to dispatch repair crews after earthquakes in a 2025 engineering paper. Restoring power grids fast saves lives, but classic optimization can take minutes to hours per plan. Their framework treats dispatch as a sequence of choices under uncertainty. Transformer networks, a design that tracks long patterns, read the damaged grid's state, while deep reinforcement learning picks adaptive moves. Seismic standards first estimate damage, and many scenarios compress into one impact map.

Dispatch plans then form within seconds when the map arrives. A case study on a large European gas and power network with thousands of buses showed much faster restoration with solution quality kept high. Emergency managers could act sooner.
arxiv-2509-04508:
Biddut Sarker Bijoy and five co-authors train teams of small language models to handle complex app tasks in a 2025 research paper. Multi-agent systems built from small models could rival one big model on cost and speed, but small models struggle to learn long task trajectories, even when specialized by role. Their strategy, ProST, introduces new sub-tasks progressively during each training pass, like a curriculum that adds homework gradually. Tests run inside the AppWorld environment of simulated apps.

Progressive training improved multi-agent effectiveness at every configuration tried. A Pareto analysis, which weighs quality against cost, favored fine-tuned multi-agent systems for the trade-off. Ablations confirmed the strategy cuts sub-task error rates. Small-model teams become a credible budget option.
arxiv-2509-04608:
Can a classic probability result be moved safely between probability spaces in a market with trading costs? Artur Sidorenko asks that question in a solo-authored 2025 paper on the Kabanov conic market model. The model covers many assets with trading costs that scale with the size of each trade. The problem is to get the most utility, meaning the best gain one can expect from wealth.

Sidorenko examines the Skorokhod representation theorem in filtrated probability spaces. The concern is that the theorem may not preserve adaptedness, so a solution found elsewhere may not match the original setting. He shows that, under mild conditions, the Bellman functionals stay consistent across different probability spaces.
arxiv-2509-04808:
Room scheduling for sports camps at the Australian Institute of Sport becomes a test case for quantum annealing in a 2025 paper by Krzysztof Giergiel, lead author with two co-authors. The full problem cannot fit current annealing hardware, so the team build a hybrid method mixing classical heuristics with quantum subroutines.

They improve the problem formulation and add a problem-aware calibration scheme using multi-qubit statistics. Results show the best annealing time matches the device coherence time, while longer anneals perform worse. Performance still degrades as problems grow more connected, clarifying limits of present hardware and routes to extend its usefulness.
arxiv-2509-05108:
Fast simulation of particle detector showers needs training data that span many geometries and angles. Real detector data are too costly to gather at that scale. Peter McKeown, lead author with two co-authors, present LEMURS, a large simulated calorimeter shower dataset, in a 2025 paper. The name is short for a much longer title. It improves on an established challenge dataset with greater statistics and wider incident angles. It also adds multiple detector geometries, including more realistic calorimeters.

The data ship in a standard scientific format, with extra variables beyond the earlier representation. Scale and diversity make the dataset suited to developing foundation models for fast simulation. It already supports a pretrained model released with a standard simulation toolkit. All data and generation code are openly available to anyone.
arxiv-2509-05208:
Asking a language model to write code that draws a picture tests its grasp of the visual world. Yamei Chen, lead author with six co-authors, study symbolic graphics programming in a 2025 paper. The target format is scalable vector graphics, where a program renders into precise visual content.

Their benchmark grades object fidelity, scene fidelity, and composition skills such as attribute binding, spatial relations, and counting. Leading proprietary models far outperform open-source ones, and skill tracks general coding ability. A reinforcement learning method with verifiable rewards, including a check that output renders, lifts a mid-size open model to near the frontier in their tests.
arxiv-2509-05408:
Hidden layers that encode symmetry are studied by Daniel Robbins and Subham Roy in a 2025 mathematical physics paper. These field theories place a theory's symmetries into a companion in higher dimensions, and their algebraic structures sort possible phases of matter.

The authors examine non-abelian symmetries that cannot be undone, and list the Lagrangian algebras tied to a given Drinfeld centre. From the algebras that can condense they pick out gapless protected phases, unusual states on a boundary between order and disorder. More examples show how an anomalous symmetry can be fixed by placing it inside a larger symmetry family.
arxiv-2509-05608:
Attack fingerprints can be shared between company services without sharing the private prompts behind them, Waris Gill, Natalie Isak, and Matthew Dressman propose in a 2025 security paper. Prompt injection is the top risk for language model services, yet compliance walls stop services of one firm from pooling warnings.

Their system, BinaryShield, redacts personal data from a suspect prompt, embeds its meaning, converts that to binary form, and adds a randomised response step for privacy. The resulting fingerprint keeps attack patterns while respecting privacy rules. In evaluations it scored far above a classic hashing baseline, used less storage, and searched far faster than dense embeddings. Cross-service warning without raw prompt sharing is the goal.
arxiv-2509-05708:
Bigger blockchains are safer blockchains, Junjie Hu argues in a solo 2025 paper on Nakamoto-style consensus, the proof-of-work design behind Bitcoin. Classic security models assume attackers coordinate instantly, which flatters the attacker and misstates the real threshold for a private-chain attack.

Hu proposes two more realistic models. A static delay model builds in adversarial communication delay and gives a closed-form security threshold, showing delay slows private chain growth. A dynamic model adds the decay of corruption power and a total delay window. Private attacks stay optimal in both models. The final theorem says large-scale chains offer better security, giving design guidance for consensus protocols.
arxiv-2509-05808:
What happens when people hand their choices in a large group game to agents acting for them? Yu-Wen Chen and two co-authors build that layered setup in a 2025 paper on population games. Classical models assume each person decides directly, yet real settings add managers, platforms, and other proxies between individuals and outcomes.

The authors set out the hierarchy, prove what its equilibria look like, and show when play settles toward them. A second payoff follows: their results give a systematic way to study group games under general convex limits, rules stated as curved constraint sets, without each player knowing the full limits. A navigation example with road capacity limits shows the framework at work in a concrete setting.
arxiv-2509-06608:
Tiny added vectors that steer a language model's reasoning are dissected by Viacheslav Sinii and eight co-authors in a 2025 machine learning paper. Reasoning training improves models, but how it rewires their internal computation is unclear. Steering vectors are small, learnable nudges inserted into the model's residual stream.

Trained with a reinforcement learning objective, these vectors recover much of the gain from full fine-tuning while staying easy to inspect. The last-layer vector behaves like a bias favoring certain first tokens, such as words that start a worked solution. The next layer's vector leaves attention patterns mostly alone and works through later components, boosting process words and structure symbols. The vectors even transfer to sibling models from the same family. The findings offer concrete evidence about what reasoning training changes inside a model.
arxiv-2509-06708:
Clouds made of lumpy, branching particles rather than smooth spheres are added to an exoplanet weather code by Sarah E. Moran and seven co-authors in a 2025 planetary science paper. The open-source Virga code models how particles form and settle in an atmosphere. Evidence from the solar system, dusty disks, and Earth studies says real aerosols often form fractal aggregates.

The team built a simple parametrization for how such aggregates fall and how they scatter light, using a modified mean field theory. As a test case they modeled a planet resembling the cloudy mini-Neptune GJ 1214 b, with potassium chloride clouds made of aggregates, chosen to match earlier studies closely. The new treatment runs faster and covers more conditions than previous fractal models. The authors show how spectra change, note the setup's limits, and offer guidance for future users.
arxiv-2509-06908:
A nearby flare star is watched for seven straight days across many wavelengths by Yuta Notsu and five co-authors in a 2025 stellar astronomy paper. The star, AU Mic, is a young M dwarf famous for frequent flares. X-ray spectra from XMM-Newton are combined with chromospheric line observations and near-ultraviolet and optical continuum data.

Thirty-eight X-ray flares were catalogued. The three largest were followed in detail through their temperature and emission measure histories, and the largest, of the Neupert type, matches the standard picture of thermal coronal flare evolution. Two slower flares are interpreted as larger in size. Hydrogen line flares showed no clear blue or red wing asymmetries, while the biggest flare showed symmetric line broadening synchronized with the continuum brightening. Radiative hydrodynamic models suggest electron beam heating parameters used for M-dwarf flares can reproduce that broadening.
arxiv-2509-07008:
What particle spectra in oxygen-oxygen collisions should look like if nothing interesting happens afterward is calculated by Aleksas Mazeliauskas in a solo 2025 nuclear physics paper. The baseline assumes no final-state interactions, so any measured deviation would signal quenching, the energy loss of fast particles in hot matter. Proton-proton collisions provide the comparison point.

Using next-to-leading order perturbative QCD with current parton distribution and fragmentation functions, Mazeliauskas builds the baseline nuclear modification factor for light hadrons. Uncertainties are large at low transverse momentum, shrink to about five percent in an intermediate range, and grow again at high momentum, where fragmentation functions disagree over isospin assumptions. Swapping oxygen for neon in the initial state, or charged hadrons for neutral pions in the final state, barely changes the factor, which strengthens the baseline's usefulness.
arxiv-2509-07308:
David Oprea and 1 co-author test a new method in 2025 for telling what state an object is in from a photo. State change detection asks, for example, whether a shirt is wet or dry, using language embeddings, numeric summaries of words, to judge the image. The work uses the MIT-States dataset of about 53,000 images, covering 225 nouns and 115 adjectives in roughly a thousand pairings.

Their Basis Vector Metric, or BVM, is compared against six rivals, including cosine similarity and a small neural network. BVM wins the first test, naming the state of each noun class best. A second test, telling adjectives apart for each adjective, gives no conclusive edge over a logistic regression baseline from the dataset's own paper. The authors note clear routes to improve BVM, so the method stays a promising work in progress.
arxiv-2509-07408:
Sushil Kumar and 2 co-authors analyze secret key sharing over free-space optical links in a 2025 paper. Free-space optics sends data on laser beams through air, and continuous-variable quantum key distribution, or CV-QKD, uses quantum states of light to create secret keys. Air turbulence spreads and misaims the beams, and mixed quantum noise further degrades the key exchange between the two users, Alice and Bob.

The system uses multiple inputs and outputs, several beams at each end, and must resist an eavesdropper, Eve, mounting a collective Gaussian attack. The authors derive channel transmissivity formulas and new secret key rate expressions for one-way and two-way protocols they propose. Numerical results confirm the analysis and quantify the gains from multiple beams and from the two-way design. Secure optical links could serve campuses or cities where fiber is impractical.
arxiv-2509-07808:
Gravitational lensing in the distant system JVAS B1938+666 is the focus of a 2025 astrophysics paper by Lei Lei and 9 co-authors. Strong lensing happens when a massive object bends light from a source behind it. The team rebuilds, without assuming a fixed shape, the mass of a dark subhalo, a clump of matter inside a larger galaxy halo.

Both self-interacting dark matter and fuzzy dark matter fit the rebuilt profile better than the standard model. The self-interacting option wins the comparison. The profile shows a dense core about half a kiloparsec across. Results like these test rival ideas about what dark matter is, using a clump that emits no light of its own.
arxiv-2509-08108:
Lan Xiao and 4 co-authors spent time with twenty video makers in Kenya who are blind or deaf, for a 2025 study. Video is a key way to speak and take part in public life. Yet the tools still shut out many makers, most of all where money and bandwidth are scarce. The study follows their real work: tools, blocks, and help from others.

Making a video turns out to be a shared, staged task. Trusted people help at set steps. New AI tools help at others. The makers guard their say over the final cut at each stage. Access fixes must back that control. A single auto tool is not the answer these makers ask for.
arxiv-2509-08208:
Sukmoon Huh's moduli space, built with Dongsun Lim and Sang-Bum Yoo in a 2025 algebraic geometry paper, organises rank-two sheaves on a curve made by gluing. The base curve joins two smooth curves at a single point, and the objects classified are semistable sheaves, a bundle-like notion that tolerates the singular point.

The moduli space is proved irreducible, one connected piece, and birational to a projective bundle over the moduli spaces of stable bundles on each component curve, regardless of polarisation choice. As an application, its virtual Poincaré polynomial is computed, a generating count of its topological features. Explicit descriptions like this turn abstract moduli problems into geometry that can be measured and compared across curve types.
arxiv-2509-08308:
Bohr-type inequalities for a family of harmonic mappings are extended by Molla Basir Ahamed and Taimur Rahman in a 2025 complex analysis paper. The classical Bohr phenomenon bounds how large the tail of a power series can be inside the unit disk. Here the functions are K-quasiconformal, sense-preserving harmonic mappings whose analytic part is subordinate to a convex function.

Parameter-dependent versions and convex combinations are established. Parallel results cover subordinating functions drawn from concave univalent families, including ones with a pole and ones with a prescribed opening angle. Several earlier results fall out as special cases. Bohr radii are precision tools in function theory: they mark exactly where series approximations can be trusted term by term.
arxiv-2509-08408:
Neutral-atom quantum computers linked by light need gates that do not disturb bystander atoms, and Tim Keller with 5 co-authors address that crosstalk problem in a 2025 quantum optics paper. Their platform traps atoms at nanofiber cavities connected by ordinary optical fibers, so photons carry quantum logic between modules while atoms hold the data.
