Inside one cavity, several atoms couple strongly to the same light field, and pairs can be addressed locally or across distant cavities. Local light shifts tune the effective coupling to select the target pair. Crosstalk-free addressing is a scaling requirement: a machine with thousands of qubits cannot have each gate quietly corrupting neighbours it never meant to touch.
arxiv-2509-08608:
Yichao Zhang and 4 co-authors describe HeartStream, a computer cluster chip for future wireless networks, in a 2025 paper. The design packs sixty-four RISC-V cores that share fast memory. It targets AI-enhanced open radio access networks, known as O-RAN, for 5G and 6G systems.

Special instructions handle complex numbers, division, and queued systolic work, where data flows through cores in a steady pattern. Tests show strong speed on wireless tasks and useful AI processing on received signals. Power use stays under one watt in a low setting. The chip fits base station limits on power and delay.
arxiv-2509-08708:
Teresa Portone and 2 co-authors present a method to quantify prediction sensitivity to model-form uncertainty in a 2025 paper. Model-form uncertainty comes from assumptions made when building a physics model. It is widely seen as important, but hard to measure beyond available data.

Parameterized changes, called MFU representations, stand in for altered assumptions. Grouped variance based sensitivity analysis then measures how much each assumption matters. The method works without calibration data, unlike many earlier approaches. If such data exist, they can shape the representation and handle dependence between parameters. Managers can better decide where to spend effort reducing model error.
arxiv-2509-08808:
Mohammad Saqib Hasan and 6 co-authors study open-vocabulary constructs in turning plain language specs into formal language in a 2025 paper. Some phrases are not known in advance, so models lack the knowledge to parse them. An expert can supply the right construct at run time.

Their system, ROLex, stores expert phrases and their formal meanings in a growing lexicon. A retriever and generator learn to find and use the right entries without retraining. Synthetic data and augmentation help train the parser. Tests cover three tasks, from temporal logic to shell commands. The task proves hard, but ROLex improves baselines.
arxiv-2509-09108:
Gregory Moille and 5 co-authors demonstrate chaotic group velocity hopping of an on-chip Kerr soliton in a 2025 paper. Optical microcombs can run in a stable soliton state or in chaotic instability. A single stable soliton showing chaotic behavior is new.

Phase modulation of the synchronization between a soliton and an injected laser drives the effect. The soliton's repetition rate jumps randomly as its group velocity hops. Experiments with a chip integrated, octave spanning microcomb validate the second order Adler equation for synchronization. That equation lets the team predict and trigger the chaotic state. The work links nonlinear dynamics with soliton physics for randomness based uses.
arxiv-2509-09308:
The upgraded Large Hadron Collider will collide so often that particle detectors must timestamp every hit to keep up. Daan Oppenhuis reports tests of a fast timing sensor in a 2025 research paper written alone. The device is an inverse low-gain avalanche detector bonded to a Timepix4 readout chip. Lab tests used radioactive sources; beam tests ran at a CERN facility with a precision telescope.

The sensor showed nearly uniform gain and an efficiency close to perfect. Raw timing resolution started at several hundred picoseconds. After correcting for timewalk and clock effects, the resolution improved to well under half a nanosecond. Grazing-angle measurements revealed how resolution varies with the depth where charge lands. Fast, efficient pixel sensors like this are candidates for the trackers that must survive the high-luminosity collider's flood of collisions.
arxiv-2509-09608:
Hassan Firouzjahi and 1 co-author compute the trispectrum for an extended inflation model in a 2025 cosmology paper. Inflation's earliest phase here runs in an ultra-slow-roll mode, stretched longer than usual, before settling into ordinary slow roll. The trispectrum records how four density ripples correlate, a sharper probe of the early universe than simpler statistics.

A sharpness parameter governs how abruptly the young universe reaches its final attractor behaviour. The authors calculate with two independent methods, the delta-N approach and the in-in formalism, and confirm both agree. Resulting strength measures peak when the changeover is infinitely sharp. Let the transition soften, and much of the signal washes away instead.
arxiv-2509-09708:
Nirmalendu Prakash and 5 co-authors dissect why language models refuse harmful requests in a 2025 interpretability paper. Refusal is a core safety habit in instruction-tuned systems, yet its inner machinery is poorly mapped. Working with two public models and sparse autoencoders trained on their internal activity, the team hunts for feature sets whose removal flips a refusal into compliance.

Their search runs in three stages: locate a refusal direction, greedily shrink the nearby feature set, then fit a model of how surviving features interact. The pipeline surfaces many features that matter for the jailbreak, including spare ones that stay dormant until earlier features are suppressed. Such a map supports finer audits and targeted fixes for safety behaviour.
arxiv-2509-09808:
Judith Massmann and 2 co-authors test a phone-based eye check for small children in a 2025 health technology paper. The red-eye reflex in a flash photo can betray many early visual problems, and doctors read it through the Bruckner test in a clinic. Phones and modern image models now make a home version plausible, which could matter most where specialists are scarce.

Their free app, KidsVisionCheck, runs a neural network trained on pupil images labelled by an eye doctor. On unseen test pictures the model scored about ninety percent accuracy without any specialist hardware. The study also pins down the lighting and distance conditions that give the cleanest input, letting the app coach parents in real time toward a usable screening photo.
arxiv-2509-10008:
Chunxiao Zhou and 2 co-authors test whether a famously symmetric nucleus is secretly a little lopsided in a 2025 nuclear physics paper. Samarium-154 long served as a textbook example of axial symmetry, a nucleus shaped like a symmetric top. Recent work by Otsuka and colleagues hinted at slight triaxiality instead, and gamma-ray measurements of its giant dipole resonance have since backed that hint, making the small effect worth a hard look.

Using a newly proposed theory that blends SU(3) symmetry with the interacting boson picture, the authors model the nucleus as rigidly triaxial. With the ground state placed in one specific symmetry representation, calculated energy levels, transition strengths, and quadrupole moments all match experiment well. The agreement strengthens the case that collective nuclear motion here is ruled by SU(3) symmetry.
arxiv-2509-10108:
Abdulrahman Allam and 3 co-authors tackle a data shortage for Arabic medical chatbots in this 2025 paper. A real set of 20,000 patient-doctor exchanges, gathered earlier from social media, was too small to train models that generalize well. The team used two advanced generative systems to write 80,000 more synthetic question-answer pairs, modeled on the real ones and checked by filtering and manual review.

Five language models, including Mistral and AraGPT2, were fine-tuned on the enlarged corpus. Data from one generator consistently produced higher scores and fewer invented facts than data from the other. The authors conclude that careful synthetic expansion is a practical fix for low-resource medical language tools, and a path to wider Arabic health chatbot coverage.
arxiv-2509-10608:
C. S. Kochanek and 3 co-authors settle the identity of a hidden companion star in this 2025 paper. The system V723 Mon pairs a red giant with a massive unseen partner. One team proposed the partner was a black hole. A later study argued it was instead a hot star spinning so fast that its light smears out and hides in optical spectra.

The authors took an ultraviolet spectrum with the Hubble Space Telescope's STIS instrument. In ultraviolet light the hot companion is far easier to see than in visible light. The new spectrum confirms the stellar companion is really there. The result closes the black hole claim for this system and shows the value of checking candidates in a second wavelength band.
arxiv-2509-10708:
Iman Barati and 2 co-authors present SearchInstruct, a recipe for building training data for language models in narrow fields, in this 2025 paper. Fine-tuning needs instruction and answer pairs that fit a domain, and such pairs are scarce where data are limited. Their method starts from a small set of human-written questions in the target field.

A large language model first expands those seed questions into a larger, varied set. The system then retrieves material from domain sources to ground accurate answers for each new question. Tests report gains in both the variety and quality of the data, and better fine-tuned model performance in the specialty area. The authors also show the method can help edit an existing model's knowledge.
arxiv-2509-11008:
Ala Eddine Bahrouni and Anouar Bahrouni extend a classic tool of analysis in this 2025 mathematics paper. The tool is the concentration-compactness principle. It describes how sequences of functions can split, spread, or stay tight. The authors carry it into Musielak-Orlicz spaces. That is a flexible family of function spaces.

Their version works on bounded and unbounded domains. It covers well-known special cases. Classical Orlicz spaces are included. Variable exponent spaces are included too. So are double phase spaces. One new double phase setting lets exponents depend on the solution itself. The authors pair the principle with variational methods. They then tackle certain quasilinear equations. Those equations carry critical nonlinear terms. The paper proves that solutions exist.
arxiv-2509-11108:
Zhi Chen and Le Zhang present one network that both outlines tissue and predicts disease in ultrasound images in this 2025 paper. Ultrasound is cheap, portable, and safe, so clinics lean on it heavily. AI studies, though, usually treat outlining organs and diagnosing disease as separate jobs, and their models tend to be heavy.

Their network, UltraUPConvNet, joins a UPerNet design with a ConvNeXt backbone to handle both tasks in one efficient frame. It was trained on a large set with more than 9,700 annotations across seven body regions. The authors report state-of-the-art results on some of those data sets at lower computing cost than rivals, and they released the model weights and code in public.
arxiv-2509-11208:
Leon Chlon and three co-authors study a quiet failure mode of transformer models in this 2025 machine learning paper. A model may decide yes or no from a set of evidence passages. Shuffling the passage order can change its answer. The evidence itself stays the same.

The authors model this order sensitivity mathematically. They derive bounds on how much answers scatter under shuffling. They also build decision tools from the theory. One tool is a sufficiency gate. The model answers only when evidence carries enough information. Otherwise it abstains. The team tested thousands of grounded questions from public datasets. In a held-out audit, the gate kept wrong answers near zero. It declined roughly a quarter of the questions.
arxiv-2509-12008:
Yuqing Song and 5 co-authors report a contactless way to control a robot arm in a 2025 paper. They use millimeter-wave radar, which senses distance, speed, and angle without a camera. That choice protects privacy and works in poor light or when objects block the view, problems that trouble camera systems.

Their system recognizes nine hand gestures and turns them into commands for the arm in real time. A behavior tree, a structured way to organize robot actions, links recognition to control in one pipeline. Earlier work often treated those two parts separately. Case studies test how practical and reliable the setup is. The result is hands-free human-robot interaction suited to homes and factories.
arxiv-2509-12308:
A galactic collision can light one galaxy up. It can also shut its partner down. Amir H. Khoram and nine co-authors document that split outcome in 2025. The pair is bound, and it is seen as it was at cosmic noon. One galaxy wears a collisional ring and hosts an active nucleus. The other is its bullet-like companion.

Images and spectra date the first impact. It happened under a hundred million years before the snapshot. The ringed host is bursting with new stars. The bullet has quenched suddenly, with no burst of its own beforehand. The authors blame turbulence and instability driven by the merger. Outflows from the host's black hole may have helped. Those flows could strip the bullet's loose gas.
arxiv-2509-12408:
Yaqing Yang and 5 co-authors present a human-AI workflow for creative problem solving in a 2025 paper. During ideation, people explore many possible directions, a process called divergent thinking. In practice they shift constantly among searching, creating, and evaluating, rather than following a neat linear order.

Existing tools either force rigid step-by-step workflows or allow unguided free-form work. The authors aim for a middle path with three optional aids that users can invoke at any moment. High-level schemas suggest alternative ideas, a risk analysis offers mitigation suggestions, and users can steer system-generated suggestions. Moving back and forth among design actions without friction is meant to preserve creative momentum while adding guidance only when wanted.
arxiv-2509-12508:
Speech recognition built on large language models can transcribe brilliantly and then hallucinate a word that was never said. Keyu An and thirty-seven co-authors present Fun-ASR in 2025, a technical report on a production-grade recognition system that fuses massive data, a large model, language model integration, and reinforcement learning.

The engineering targets daily use: streaming output, robustness to noise, switching between languages mid-sentence, and custom hotwords. On open benchmarks most rival systems look strong, yet they sag on real industry test sets. Fun-ASR claims the top spot on those practical sets, and its code and models are public.
arxiv-2509-12608:
Tamar Ervin and 11 co-authors investigate why magnetic reconnection often fails to start in the near-Sun solar wind in a 2025 paper. Reconnection is a basic process that converts magnetic energy in plasma. Observations from the Parker Solar Probe showed many current sheets near the Sun with no reconnection occurring.

Using probe data from encounters spanning 2020 to 2022, the team tested whether velocity shear, a difference in flow speed across a sheet, suppresses onset. They compared tearing mode growth rates for reconnecting and non-reconnecting periods and found systematically larger rates when reconnection occurred. Most reconnection events sat in slow, non-Alfvenic wind streams. In highly Alfvenic streams, growth was suppressed and reconnection was not seen, matching theoretical expectations.
arxiv-2509-13008:
Somnath Basu and Sachchidanand Prasad prove in 2025 a Reeb-like result for Morse-Bott functions with two critical sheets. Classic Reeb theory ties two peak points to a sphere shape. Here sheets of differing sizes take the place of points.

If a closed smooth shape holds such a function, its size is the sum of sheet sizes plus one. The shape is then homeomorphic to the standard sphere of that size. It need not match smoothly. Like results hold for projective spaces over real, complex, and quaternion numbers. The work widens a classic shape test.
arxiv-2509-13108:
Erik Burman, Janosch Preuss and Tim van Beeck test in 2025 whether wave continuation stays stable when the medium jumps. The task rebuilds a wave field from side data on a space-time wall. In even media, a control rule gives firm stability and best-rate solvers.

Numeric trials suggest the firm picture carries to jump media. Solvers still behave as hoped in the tests run. One cost is clear: jumps make the work far heavier than the even case. More care and compute are needed per solve. The signs support wider use, with price noted.
arxiv-2509-13208:
David Basin, Nate Foster and six co-authors argue in 2025 that network protocols need formal specs, not prose alone. Formal specs give clear docs, test bases, and proof starts. Yet most Internet protocols live in long prose RFCs with code sketches.

Roles of specs differ between network and formal crowds. Recent wins show what formal work can add for safety and fit. Gaps in what each crowd means by a spec are named. Bridge plans close the paper: shared terms, joint cases, and stepwise adoption. Village-wide work is framed as the price of trust.
arxiv-2509-13308:
S. Satheesh-Sheeba and 35 co-authors present VAR-PZ in a 2025 paper on gauging the distance to quasars from how their light flickers. A new survey with the Vera C. Rubin Observatory should find tens of millions of fresh active galactic nuclei, the bright cores of galaxies. There will be no way to take spectra for most of them, so distance must come from photos alone, a route known to be shaky for such cores.

Their trick uses the flicker itself. A quasar's light varies in a random-walk way, and the pace and size of that flicker shift with distance, with the light's color, and with the quasar's glow. Cosmic time stretch plays a part too. By fitting those flicker traits, the team can pin down the distance far more tightly than photos alone allow.
arxiv-2509-13408:
A. Mori, P. Di Matteo and five co-authors decode in 2025 the chemistry of motion-picked halo substructures in the Milky Way. Merged debris should keep motion coherence, yet big mergers scatter integrals and heat the disc into halo-like orbits. Motion samples thus mix intruders.

Gaia and APOGEE data supply motion picks and seven element abundances per star. A mixture model compares chemistry star by star. Sequoia shares roots with the big GSE merger. Heracles, Thamnos, and Helmi streams all hold large GSE plus heated disc shares. GSE-like stars spread widely and taint all samples. No substructure stands as a pure lone origin.
arxiv-2509-13508:
Maksim Penkin and Andrey Krylov build FunKAN in 2025, a functional Kolmogorov-Arnold network for medical image enhancement and segmentation with interpretability. Classic deep nets use complex stacks with limited clarity. Arnold nets flatten images and break spatial structure.

FunKAN generalizes the representation theorem to function spaces. Inner functions learn via Fourier forms over Hermite bases, which keeps spatial life intact. Gibbs ringing suppression in MRI tests the enhancer. U-FunKAN segments ultrasound, histology, and colonoscopy sets for cancers, glands, and polyps. Scores beat Arnold rivals on quality and segment marks. Theory bridges to clinic use.
arxiv-2509-13908:
Priyobrata Mondal, Faizanuddin Ansari, and Swagatam Das tackle intersectional fairness in a 2025 machine learning paper. Bias rarely comes one attribute at a time. It compounds across intersecting traits such as race, gender, and age. Most fairness methods handle single traits. They miss the multiplied disadvantages faced by small subgroups where those traits overlap.

Their framework, APFEx, is the first to pose this fairness problem directly as joint optimization. The search runs over the full combination of sensitive traits. An adaptive optimizer switches among Pareto cone projection, gradient weighting, and exploration moves. Smooth fairness metrics let gradients flow through normally jagged subgroup measures. Convergence to Pareto-optimal trade-offs is guaranteed in theory. On four real datasets, the method cut fairness violations while holding accuracy competitive.
arxiv-2509-14108:
Piotr Majek and Ireneusz Weymann hunt Majorana fingerprints in heat-driven currents in a 2025 condensed matter paper. Their device is a double quantum dot. It is wired to a topological superconducting nanowire and magnetic leads. Majorana modes are exotic boundary states sought for quantum computing. They leave traces in conductance that are hard to separate from other effects. The two-stage Kondo effect and lead-induced exchange fields muddy the picture.

Computing with the renormalization group, the authors map the Seebeck coefficient. That is the voltage a heat gap generates, resolved by spin. The exchange field reshapes its temperature course into a rich, non-monotonic curve. Competition between spin channels drives it. Distinct regimes of spin thermopower emerge from the interplay of Majorana asymmetry and lead polarization. This heat-based transport becomes a sensitive probe for them.
arxiv-2509-14308:
Hülya Karagöz and three co-authors examine two nearby open star clusters, Alessi 36 and Collinder 135, in 2025 using Gaia DR3 data. Open clusters are loose groups of stars born together. A close pair in the sky may be a true binary system or a chance alignment.

Member stars were picked by motion and position, giving a few hundred likely members for each cluster. Both clusters sit at similar distances, a little under three hundred parsecs, and share a young age near forty million years. Their motions across the sky are also close. Orbit calculations show near circular paths around the Galaxy with small wobbles. Together the match in age, distance and motion supports treating the pair as a close binary cluster system.
arxiv-2509-14508:
Akira Matsui and three co-authors model how users spend loyalty points in 2025 using large transaction records from a personal finance app. Digital platforms use complex point systems to keep users. How people value points against cash is hard to observe directly.

The data capture both cash spending and point transactions for the same users. Point use links to demographic traits in the analysis. A natural experiment with a large point grant raised point spending, with no detectable change in cash spending. Shopping styles also connect to how consumers treat points across product areas. Points behave partly like a separate currency in users minds, a fact incentive designers should plan around rather than ignore.
arxiv-2509-14608:
Shashank Shreedhar Bhatt and twelve co-authors argue in 2025 that enterprise AI must enforce participant aware access control. Company assistants are fine tuned on sensitive internal data and joined with retrieval pipelines. That mix can leak confidential material to users who should never see it.

Demonstrated exfiltration attacks exploit current fine tuning and retrieval designs, coaxing assistants to reveal training content. Knowing who is in a conversation, and what each participant may access, is not tracked by default. The authors call for access checks that follow participants across model memory and fetched documents. Without such controls, a helpful internal assistant becomes a search engine over secrets for anyone with a login.
arxiv-2509-14708:
Nguyen Dang Bao Nhi and Eibun Senaha examine a two-Higgs-doublet model in a 2025 particle physics paper. Their version of the model has no built-in scale and allows explicit CP violation, meaning matter and antimatter can behave differently. They study how that violation could coexist with a vanishing electric dipole moment for the electron, a quantity experiments constrain very tightly.

Using the Gildener-Weinberg method, the authors compute the Higgs mass spectrum and couplings at one-loop level. A flatness condition forces the mixing of the known Higgs boson with heavier states to arise only through quantum corrections. Couplings therefore stay close to Standard Model values, matching collider limits. The analysis also finds regions where contributions cancel, letting the electron dipole moment shrink or vanish for specific mass patterns.
arxiv-2509-14808:
Krzysztof Kowalski studies the far edge of a branching random walk with several particle types in a solo 2025 probability paper. In such a walk, particles move, split, and change type across generations. The displacements here can be very large, following distributions with heavy tails rather than thin ones.

Kowalski tracks the asymptotic behavior of the rightmost particle as time grows. He treats both irreducible regimes, where types mix freely, and reducible ones, where they do not. For each setting he identifies the correct normalization, the scaling that keeps the edge position meaningful in the limit.
arxiv-2509-14908:
Clément Cancès, Claire Chainais-Hillairet, and Amélie Dupouy design a finite volume scheme for a moving-boundary oxidation model in a 2025 numerical analysis paper. Their toy model tracks oxygen concentration inside an oxide layer whose width changes over time. Boundary motion is driven by the concentration values at the edges, coupling transport and geometry tightly.

The authors first find an exact condition on the parameters for a unique traveling-wave solution to exist. They also uncover an entropy structure: pick any convex function of the concentration, and it defines a free energy that the flow dissipates, apart from boundary exchanges. Their implicit scheme, built on a moving mesh with Scharfetter-Gummel fluxes, converges unconditionally, preserves the traveling wave exactly, and dissipates all those free energies. Numerical tests show the expected accuracy in time and space.
arxiv-2509-15108:
Anastasiia Mikhno and the CTAO NectarCAM group test a light flasher that calibrates a gamma-ray camera, in a 2025 paper. The camera will sit on the medium telescopes of the Cherenkov Telescope Array site in the north. The flasher sits at the dish center and fires short, even pulses of light across the full focal plane.

Even light lets the team work out each pixel's gain and how well each pixel catches light. It also probes the range over which the camera works well. A test bench measured several flasher units against the design goals. Good calibration sits under every energy value the telescope will later assign to flashes of light in the sky.
arxiv-2509-15208:
Pierre Fernandez and seven co-authors hide a signal in images so that later crops or spins can be gauged and undone, in a 2025 paper. This task is called synchronization: gauge the change made to an image, then reverse it. Their method, SyncSeal, adds such a signal on top of current watermark tools to help them survive edits that change shape.

One network hides the signal with no visible damage. A second network reads back the change that was made. Training cuts the error in that read-back, while a critic network keeps the marked images clean to the eye. Tests across many shape and value changes show the read-back stays sharp. The add-on lifts the toughness of current watermarks.
arxiv-2509-15308:
Andrei Cuceu and the DESI collaboration analyze the three-dimensional shape of Lyman-alpha forest correlations from the instrument's first data release in a 2025 cosmology paper. The forest of absorption lines in distant quasar spectra traces cosmic structure at high redshift. Beyond the standard baryon acoustic oscillation scale, the full shape of the correlations carries extra information.

The analysis measures the Alcock-Paczynski effect, a geometric distortion test, and the growth rate of structure scaled by fluctuation amplitude. Validation runs through two mock sets, data splits, and many analysis variations, all performed blinded before unblinding. The geometric ratio comes out more than twice as tight as the oscillation-only constraint from the same data. Combined with the oscillation measurement, the forest becomes a sharper cosmological ruler.
arxiv-2509-15508:
Xintong Ma, Dong Li, and Howell Tong model counts over time, such as daily case numbers. Their new model adds a twist called hysteresis: the current regime depends on the path taken, not just the present value. Other models with that name lack a true driving factor for the effect. This one builds that factor in.

Counts switch between regimes at set thresholds, and each regime keeps a simple linear form. The team study how to fit both their model and a rival buffered model, and prove the fits behave well for large samples. They build tests to tell the two models apart. On two real series, their model gives clearer stories and better forecasts.
arxiv-2509-15608:
Zheng Wang leads a team that predicts cancer outcomes from tissue slide images. Whole slide images hold fine detail that helps judge a patient's outlook. Yet their traits are noisy, and data can be hard to get. Pathology reports hold rich facts about each patient, but their use beside slides was largely untried.

Their frame, Rasa, first uses a large language model to pull clean, slide linked facts from messy reports. A teacher and student setup then filters the slide traits, guided by those facts. A mixing step boosts both the count and the variety of training cases. Broad tests back the frame. The work shows text reports can sharpen image based forecasts.
arxiv-2509-15808:
Máté Gedeon and Péter Mihajlik simulate talks with several speakers and true to life timing. Who speaks when, and the gaps and overlaps between turns, shape how real a fake talk feels. Past work summed up talk stats as if speakers and turns were independent. That misses the habits each speaker keeps.

Their method gives each speaker a personal spread of timing quirks, held steady across the talk. A Markov chain steers who takes the next turn. A fixed room echo keeps the space real. Pauses and overlaps merge into one gap spread, smoothed by a standard estimator. On a known phone talk set, their fakes match real timing better than a base method.
arxiv-2509-16208:
Many bridges are aging while repair funds stay tight, so knowing how long each bridge will last guides where money goes first. Lu Gao and five co-authors review how service life is predicted for bridges in Texas. Design-build contracts often demand long service life, yet clear rules to meet or check those demands are missing.

The review sums up current practice and recent gains in forecasting wear, inspection, and repair timing. Its guidance covers both standing bridges and new builds. Better life estimates can stretch maintenance funds and keep structures sound for longer. The work speaks to planners who must rank many repair needs.
arxiv-2509-16308:
Weak blasts from giant stars can mimic several kinds of red transients, and a new sky survey will soon find them in large numbers. Andrea Antoni, Yan-Fei Jiang, and Eliot Quataert simulate these low-energy explosions with radiation and fluid physics in one dimension. The blasts may come from mergers, shared envelope events, eruptions, or failed supernovae.

Red giant blasts glow for hundreds of days, longer than common supernova types, while stripped yellow giants fade in tens of days. The team gives formulas for plateau brightness and length. Two vanished-star candidates match failed supernova models at modest energies, which aids telling these events apart.
arxiv-2509-16408:
A flat sheet of electrons on a crystal of strontium titanate can turn superconducting, but only within a dome of charge densities. Sushant Padhye and five co-authors grow the crystal film on a matching base and tune the sheet's density with an ionic liquid gate. The top of their dome reaches a higher transition point than the same sheets on plain crystal bases show.

Across the dome, the transition point scales with length measures in the standard theory's pattern. Shifts in transition width fit a model of extra conduction above the transition. Cleaner film growth may be what lifts the dome here.
arxiv-2509-16608:
Bei You and co-authors read the flicker of a feeding black hole in a 2025 astronomy paper. Gas spirals in as a disk, while a hot cloud above it glows in X-rays. The region is too small to image directly. Delays in the flicker, though, reveal its shape. Some delays come from X-rays bouncing off the disk.

The team measure these delays at the highest X-ray energies yet used. Echo delays show up clearly only in the fastest flicker. Slower delays shift a lot over just a few days. That change tells a story about how matter drifts inward. The work sharpens a tool for mapping space near black holes.
arxiv-2509-16908:
Sixtus Dakurah, working alone, extends heat smoothing to higher-order networks in a 2025 paper. Graphs capture pairwise links, but real networks hold group links too. Simplicial complexes encode those group links as triangles and beyond. Dakurah builds heat kernels that diffuse signals across vertices, edges, and higher pieces in one frame.

Simulations show cleaner signals on both vertices and edges after diffusion. Applied to human brain networks, smoothing cut spurious links. It also boosted coherent anatomical patterns. The method gives neuroscience a tool that respects group-level wiring, not just pairs. That matters since brain regions often act in coordinated groups.
arxiv-2509-17008: Yuri Tschinkel and Zhijia Zhang study group actions on tori in a 2025 math paper. They work in small dimensions. They ask when such an action has a simple rational description that respects the group. That property is called equivariant unirationality. The record gives only a brief statement of the topic. It gives no detail on methods or results. The paper is best read as a focused study of that one question.
arxiv-2509-17208:
Kevin Bachelor, Sanya Murdeshwar, Daniel Sabo, and Razvan Marinescu wrote a 2025 arXiv paper on speeding up molecule simulations. Learned energy models can run coarse simulations fast, but they fail when the molecule wanders into shapes they never saw in training. Making full fine-grained data to cover every shape is far too costly.

Their active learning setup watches a running simulation and flags frames that stray far from known shapes. Those flagged frames go to a costly oracle, and the model retrains on the gaps it just found. Built on the CGSchNet model, the setup was tested on the small protein chignolin. It explored shapes the model had missed and sharply improved a standard score for how well the simulation covers the protein's motion.
arxiv-2509-17408:
Hiroshi Noguchi, writing alone, simulates how patterned domains grow in an active material. His 2025 arXiv study uses active Potts models, where each site holds one of several states and the states flip in a cyclic, driven way. Over long times, waves of finite length emerge, some spiraling and some disordered.

Noguchi starts from a random mix and watches order spread on square and hexagonal lattices with Monte Carlo runs. Cluster size and correlation length first grow by the classic Lifshitz-Allen-Cahn law. Near the natural wavelength, growth saturates, but the rate first surges, lifting the growth exponent for a while. The surge is stronger for disordered waves than for spirals, and stronger still when more states compete. Lattice shape and update rule leave the pattern unchanged, which suggests the effect is robust.
arxiv-2509-17608:
Jungeun Lee, Kyungah Lee, Inseok Hwang, SoHyun Park, and Young-Ho Kim built a story tool for autistic children and their parents. Their 2025 arXiv paper starts from social narratives, short stories that help autistic children read social situations. Tailoring those stories takes parents much time and effort, and the lessons need steady repetition to stick.

Their system, AutiHero, uses generative AI to help parents make personalized stories with several paths. Each story targets a specific behavior of their own child. While reading together, parent and child can explore choices and their consequences inside the tale. A two-week deployment with sixteen child-parent pairs showed parents actively creating, adapting, and reading the stories. Parents also grew more confident in daily behavioral guidance. The work shows AI content creation fitted to a sensitive, real-world setting.
arxiv-2509-18108:
Adam Viktorin and 4 co-authors present EASE, an open toolkit that grows algorithmic fixes with language models in a loop. Their 2025 paper deals with a messy task: using such models to draft code, test it, and learn from faults, in a way folk can repeat. Prompt craft and model wrangling can hide what went right or wrong.

EASE links draft, test, study, and grade steps in one clear loop. Users keep full say on error care and quality checks. More than one model can play split roles, such as drafter, analyst, and grader. The design stays modular, so parts can be swapped by task.
arxiv-2509-18308:
Yixin Zhang and 4 co-authors rethink how blood clots in the lung are outlined on scans, and share their best model. Their 2025 study deals with pulmonary embolism, a clot that can kill if missed. Past work in the area rests on small, mixed data sets with no shared baselines, they find.

The team built a dense-tagged set of hundreds of CT scans, one per patient. Nine known outline models, in flat and 3D forms, were run on that set. A 3D U-Net with a deep encoder stayed a top pick, and 3D beat flat forms across the board. Far clots stayed the hardest to catch.
arxiv-2509-18508:
Optimization routines hunt for the lowest point of a cost curve, and speed near the goal matters. Nazarii Tupitsa presents CaCuTe, a casual cubic-model technique for faster optimization, in this 2025 paper. The core is a plain gradient step with a step size set by the gradient's size and a curvature bound. He proves it converges at a fast local rate.

A check based on cheap curvature probes tells the method when that fast regime holds, with no full curvature matrix needed. That check plugs into cubic-regularized Newton methods, letting each step switch between cubic and gradient moves while keeping global guarantees. A first-order version stays monotone, adapts on its own, and needs no tuned parameters. In tests it posted the lowest run times among rivals. The paper extends the idea to noisy, stochastic settings and to looser smoothness rules.
arxiv-2509-18908:
Shaoshuai Chu and four co-authors design new numerical schemes for equations that govern flows with sharp jumps, such as shock waves. A single fixed method struggles: sharp methods can add fake wiggles near jumps, while safe methods can blur fine detail. Their schemes switch methods by region, guided by a smoothness indicator that flags rough parts of the solution.

In rough zones the scheme uses a second-order method that keeps shocks and contact edges crisp. In smooth zones it switches to a fifth-order method for better accuracy. The indicator also tells contact edges apart from other rough spots, so each gets the limiter that fits it best. Tests on hard example problems show the combined scheme stays both sharp and clean.
arxiv-2509-19108:
Are most sentences we speak truly brand new, never said before in history? Hiram Ring, writing alone, tests that famous claim, tied to Noam Chomsky and retold by Steven Pinker, against large text collections. Modern corpora make the question answerable by counting. Ring used a standard Python language toolkit to split corpora of several genres into sentences and count exact repeats.

Unique sentences did form the majority in many corpora, as the claim suggests. But the share swung widely with genre, and duplicates were never a trivial slice of any corpus. Short, formulaic genres repeat themselves far more than free prose does. Ring's counts give the old claim a needed correction: novelty is common, but how common depends heavily on what kind of language you sample.
arxiv-2509-19208:
Sorting crop plants from weeds in thermal images is a stubborn problem for field phenotyping, the measurement of plant traits at scale. Earl Ranario and four co-authors attack it with synthetic data. In outdoor thermal views, crops and weeds have similar heat signatures and often overlap, so models trained on real images alone struggle. The team generated over a thousand synthetic color images with complex crop-and-weed mixtures, and trained segmentation models on them.

Adding as few as five hand-labeled real field images lifted accuracy further, with relative gains above twenty percent for weeds. A generative translation step converts color images to thermal ones, letting the synthetic training carry across sensors without careful calibration. The full recipe, synthetic data plus a pinch of real labels plus cross-domain translation, significantly boosted performance. The approach promises cheaper training data for hard field conditions.
arxiv-2509-19408:
Lenders predicting who will default face skewed data: defaulters are a small minority, and models trained on raw data can ignore them. Obu-Amoah Ampomah and three co-authors compare ways to rebalance credit data and pick features. They first benchmark classifiers with no resampling, then layer in the Boruta feature selector and a density-based outlier cleaner. Three resampling methods are tested: SMOTE, SMOTE-Tomek, and ADASYN, which all synthesize or trim examples to even the classes.

Classifiers range from naive Bayes and nearest neighbors to four boosting ensembles. On a real credit dataset from a public repository, one combination won clearly: Boruta features, DBSCAN cleaning, SMOTE-Tomek balancing, and gradient boosting. Its F1, G-mean, and both area-under-curve scores topped the field. The authors frame the recipe as a foundation for more resilient credit default systems as borrowing grows worldwide.
arxiv-2509-19708:
Do AI coding tools truly make engineers faster, or do teams just feel faster? Anand Kumar and ten co-authors measured a year of real use at enterprise scale. Three hundred engineers used an in-house platform that writes code and reviews it. Review cycle time fell by about a third over the year.

Engineers rated the review features highly, and most wanted to keep the tool. Use climbed from a few percent in the first month to a peak above four fifths by month six. Top adopters pushed far more code to production. The authors stress measured cohorts over gut feeling, hence their title's move from intuition to evidence. The study is a rare long, large look at AI help in daily software work.
arxiv-2509-19908:
Control systems written as Chen-Fliess series describe outputs through iterated integrals of the inputs. W. Steven Gray and three co-authors cut the cost of computing those series. The integrals are tied together by shuffle products, so naive evaluation repeats work. Lyndon words, a special family of letter strings, index a leaner basis that holds all needed information.

Transducing word bases converts the computation into that lean form. The shuffle algebra on polynomials is isomorphic to a polynomial algebra on Lyndon words, which is the mathematical hinge. Less redundancy means faster, larger simulations of nonlinear systems. Chen-Fliess series appear across control engineering, from robotics to circuits. A basis change is a quiet kind of progress: same answers, fraction of the effort.
arxiv-2509-20008:
Automated penetration testing pits a learning agent against a network it can only partly see. Raphael Simon, Pieter Libin, and Wim Mees evaluate reinforcement learning policies under that partial observability. Hidden state breaks the Markov property that standard methods assume. History aggregation or belief estimation must fill the gap.

The team builds stochastic test scenarios over host networks of varied size, aiming for benchmarks that mirror real complexity. A standard policy optimization method serves as the baseline under study. Robust, transferable policies are the goal: a tester that only works on one toy network helps no defender. Security automation needs agents that stay reliable when scans lie and hosts hide. The study systematizes how observability limits bite.
arxiv-2509-20208:
Parker Glenn, Alfy Samuel, and Daben Liu wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on mixing language models with databases. Declarative query languages can call model-powered functions inside a query. The outputs, though, must obey type rules and match real database values. Existing fixes use many extra model calls to clean up outputs, which slows everything down.

The authors first study how well open models of different sizes can run functions inside an SQL-like language. Small models did surprisingly well as function executors over mixed data sources. They then propose a cheaper way to enforce well-typed outputs. On a multi-hop question dataset, accuracy rose by seven percent. Latency improved by fifty-three percent over comparable methods. The team released its implementation for others to build on.
arxiv-2509-20308:
Testing whether two programs follow a communication protocol takes more than feeding single inputs. Alexander Liggesmeyer, Jose Antonio Zamudio Amaya, and Andreas Zeller introduce language-based protocol testing in a 2025 arXiv paper. A tester must exchange messages that fit the current state of the conversation. Earlier generators rarely covered that full interaction space.

Their approach specifies protocols as interaction grammars. Each grammar element is tagged with the party that must produce it. States, messages, and transitions all become grammar symbols, so one specification can both generate and parse conversations. Extra constraints cover checksums, encodings, and binary formats. The method was built into the FANDANGO test generator. Trials on mail, naming, and file transfer protocols reached high code coverage in the tested implementations.
arxiv-2509-20408:
Generative flow networks learn to build objects step by step, with better objects built more often. Leo Maxime Brunswic and five co-authors extend that idea to teams of agents in a 2025 arXiv paper. Until now, no theory covered several agents generating one object together through joint actions. The paper supplies that missing framework.

The authors propose four algorithms for multi-agent flow networks. Variants cover centralized training, fully independent execution, and a joint design that trains centrally but runs in a decentralized way. Training the joint version rests on a local-global principle: many local networks are trained as one global network. That principle keeps the learning loss manageable and carries over the single-agent guarantees. Experiments showed the framework beating reinforcement learning and sampling-based rivals.
arxiv-2509-21108:
A spoken assistant can be biased by what a question says or by how the voice sounds. Junhyuk Choi and three co-authors separate those channels in VoiceBBQ, a 2025 paper accepted at EMNLP 2025. The dataset is a spoken extension of the BBQ bias benchmark for question answering.

Every text context is converted into controlled voice conditions, keeping scores comparable with the original benchmark. The authors score accuracy, bias, and consistency along each social axis. Testing two spoken language models, they find contrasting architectures. One resists acoustic bias but amplifies gender and accent bias from content; the other behaves differently. The results show that bias audits for voice systems must probe sound and wording independently.
arxiv-2509-21308:
Quantum divergences that respect fast reading limits are defined and compared here. Authorship belongs to Álvaro Yángüez and 2 co-authors. Quantum tasks are limited to steps that can be implemented fast. Standard divergences measure gaps between quantum states without that constraint. The authors define divergences that keep operational meaning under fast readings. They present computational max divergence and computational measured Renyi divergences.

Both new measures are constrained by a family of fast binary readings. They suit state discrimination tasks in the computational setting. The authors prove that one measure coincides with the other in the infinite order limit. For many copies, they define regularized versions. They also establish a one sided computational Stein bound on achievable error rates.
arxiv-2509-21408:
Limits on the interstellar object 3I/ATLAS come from precise position data in a 2025 paper by Richard Cloete, Abraham Loeb, and Peter Vereš. Astrometric data compiled by the Minor Planet Center span May to September 2025. The authors fit a gravity only trajectory and study the residuals. Any extra push beyond gravity must hide inside those residuals.

The residuals imply the non gravitational acceleration is below a very small upper limit. Mass loss rate and outflow speed from JWST data give lower limits on the nucleus mass and diameter. The mass limit is large and the diameter at least several kilometres. Together the bounds describe a heavy, sizeable nucleus with little anomalous acceleration.
arxiv-2509-21508:
Minimal surfaces with isolated singularities are constructed in a 2025 paper by Camillo De Lellis and 2 co-authors. Their objects are stationary and stable varifolds, generalized surfaces used in geometric analysis. The construction gives minimal immersions in a space with a mildly smooth metric. A sequence of catenoidal necks or floating disks converges to one singular flat point.

That limit point has multiplicity two, meaning two sheets meet there. The singularity is isolated, with regular behaviour around it. Varifold theory handles such singular limits where classic surface theory cannot. The authors note the work corrects an earlier version after a colleague flagged a mistake about ambient regularity. The construction adds sharp cases for regularity theory of minimal surfaces.
arxiv-2509-21708:
Chengming Bai, Li Guo, Yunhe Sheng, and You Wang build new algebraic structures in this 2025 mathematics paper. Their starting point is the dynamical Yang-Baxter equation, a rule that first arose in physics. Earlier work reached its solutions through two separate routes, one using matched groups and one using groupoids. The authors aim to join those routes in a single frame.

They define a braided dynamical group, built from a matched pair of dynamical groups with extra conditions. Such a group yields a solution of the equation and a braided groupoid at the same time. The paper then links this idea to relative Rota-Baxter operators, a tool from algebra. It also shows that two further notions, dynamical post-groups and dynamical skew-braces, amount to the same thing.
arxiv-2509-22408:
Lorenzo Nicolodi studies curves in Lie sphere geometry through a classic variational lens. The setting is the bundle of unit tangent directions over the three-sphere, where a contact group acts on all points alike. Nicolodi looks at generic curves that always cross the contact structure, never lying inside it. Using moving frames, he shows each such curve has a natural Lie-invariant length parameter.

In that parameter, four local quantities, the Lie curvatures, fix the curve up to the group action. He then takes the simplest invariant energy, the total Lie arclength. Its critical curves are described fully through their Lie curvatures, using the exterior differential systems approach of Griffiths.
arxiv-2509-23008:
Making a new camera view from one photo is a core world-modeling task. Wenbin Teng and 3 co-authors do it with an autoregressive model, not a diffusion model. Diffusion methods build all views at once by slow denoising. Autoregressive models go step by step, each token based on the tokens before it. Their system, ARSS, follows a set camera path from a single image.

A video tokenizer turns image sequences into discrete tokens. A camera encoder turns the path into 3D position guidance. One module shuffles token order in space while keeping time order, which lifts quality. Tests on public data matched top diffusion methods overall.
arxiv-2509-23108:
Can words alone spark visual imagery, with no picture-like code involved? Morgan McCarty and Jorge Morales test that old cognitive science question with language models. They built fresh items for a classic task held to need pictorial imagery. Subjects imagine letter and shape changes, then name the resulting form. One hundred humans took the task alongside top models.

The best models beat humans by a clear margin. Longer reasoning chains improved model scores further. The authors call the effect artificial phantasia, an emergent imagery that may not be pictorial. They weigh three accounts of how it works. The debate over imagery format reopens with this evidence.
arxiv-2509-23508:
New neutrino data slightly favor one ordering of the neutrino masses over the other. Maria Aguilar and 5 co-authors study what that means for a seesaw model that mixes type I and type II routes to tiny neutrino masses. Their setup adds an extended scalar sector that yields the mix once symmetry breaks. They track two arenas at once: collider searches and rare decays that break lepton flavor rules.

Rare muon decays and same-sign dilepton hunts at the LHC, a classic sign of a doubly charged scalar, are the key tests. Changing the assumed sum of neutrino masses barely moved the decay predictions. One muon decay to three electrons proved the stronger test, pushing the scalar's mass floor past current LHC limits.
arxiv-2509-23608:
Fixing a dull or damaged photo with deep learning can be slow, while lookup tables are fast but rigid. Liubing Hu and 5 co-authors merge the two in FlowLUT. A set of trainable 3D lookup tables, each carrying a different prior, first remaps the image colors. A light network then predicts how to blend those outputs for the scene at hand, keeping the cost flat.

Lookup tables alone cannot restore fine local detail, so an iterative flow matching step rebuilds structure and removes artifacts. The whole model trains under a loss that guards both perceptual and structural fidelity. Tests on three benchmarks show the design works well.
arxiv-2509-23708:
Removing an object from a photo also means erasing its shadow and reflections, or the edit looks fake. Boseong Jeon and 6 co-authors built CrimEdit, one diffusion model that removes, inserts, and moves objects. Removal and insertion share training through task embeddings, and a classifier-free guidance scheme steers both. Guidance strengthens the cleanup of objects and their side effects, and controls how strongly effects are painted in during insertion.

Applying the two task prompts to different regions lets the model move an object in a single denoising pass. Wide experiments show strong removal, controllable insertion effects, and efficient movement, with no extra training stages.
arxiv-2509-23908:
After a disaster, drone base stations must serve the worst-off user, not just the average one. Qingyang Wang and 3 co-authors design a rate-splitting multiple access scheme for a multi-drone network in obstacle-filled terrain. The goal is to maximize the minimum rate among ground users, with drone positions chosen as part of the design. The optimization is non-convex and hard, so they relax the obstacle constraints with penalty terms.

Block coordinate descent and successive convex approximation alternate inside each round, while penalty multipliers update to pull the relaxed problem back to the original. Simulations show a clear lead in minimum rate over benchmark methods.
arxiv-2509-24008:
A video model that samples frames on a fixed schedule wastes attention on moments the question never touches. Haonan Ge and 4 co-authors built FrameMind, which lets the model ask for the views it needs during reasoning. Trained with reinforcement learning, it alternates text reasoning with active perception, pulling targeted frames or clips when it spots a knowledge gap. A sampling scheme exposes it to varied trade-offs between time coverage and spatial detail during training.

A group-relative policy algorithm learns from outcome rewards alone, with no frame-level labels. On MLVU and VideoMME, the method beat existing models, advancing flexible video understanding.
arxiv-2509-24208:
Saber Omidi tackles a control problem: nonlinear predictive control steers fast quadrotors well, but its heavy math blocks real-time use. His fix rewrites the nonlinear dynamics with the state-dependent coefficient method. The hard nonlinear program becomes a sequence of quadratic problems, which are far cheaper to solve.

The controller adds integral action to erase steady tracking error, plus constraints that keep the craft clear of obstacles. A disturbance estimator guards against outside pushes. In simulations, the method matched the tracking accuracy of full nonlinear control while cutting compute cost by over a third. Theory backs the design with stability and ongoing feasibility results.
arxiv-2509-24608:
Clinical prediction models are judged across thresholds, and two curve families compete for that job. Louise AC Millard and 3 co-authors compare decision curve analysis, which weighs net benefit, with cost curves, which weigh loss. They show a decision curve is closely tied to one specific cost curve, the Brier curve, and that reference lines translate between the two spaces.

The pair of tools will always pick the same best model at a fixed threshold, they prove. But scores cannot be compared or averaged across thresholds without extra assumptions. They also propose an upper envelope decision curve, which shows the most net benefit reachable through recalibration.
arxiv-2510-00008:
En-naoui constructs a single functional space meant to hold every classical arithmetic function at once. The Möbius and von Mangoldt functions, Euler's totient, divisor functions, and Dirichlet characters among them. The space, called U, carries a hybrid norm combining a Hilbert-style part, square summability of Dirichlet series coefficients at every point above one. With a Banach part controlling logarithmic averages of partial sums in this paper.

En-naoui proves U is complete, that it continuously embeds all the standard Hilbert spaces of Dirichlet series. And that Dirichlet polynomials are dense in it, so every classical function of sub-exponential growth genuinely belongs. Dirichlet convolution, pointwise multiplication, Möbius inversion, and shift operators all act naturally on the space, giving multiplicative number theory one unified analytic setting. With applications to L-functions and spectral approaches to the Riemann hypothesis outlined for future work.
arxiv-2510-00208:
Tanay Kumar Raktim Bhattacharya wrote this 2025 engineering paper on keeping multi-rotor drones steady in rough air. A drone's attitude, its tilt and heading, must hold despite wind gusts and sensor noise. Nonlinear dynamics and changing parameters make that control problem hard. Bhattacharya compares a robust H-infinity controller against the classical PID controllers used in most products.

The flight model is written in a parameter-varying form that treats uncertainty in a structured way. The robust controller is designed using only gyroscope measurements, with guaranteed performance bounds. In simulations with severe wind from a standard turbulence model, it cut peak attitude errors sharply. It also lowered tracking error while using less actuator effort than PID control. Realistic sensor noise from cheap inertial units was included throughout. The results argue robust control is practical for real multi-rotor missions.
arxiv-2510-00408:
Michelle Jamer and eight colleagues published this 2025 physics paper on Fe3Ga4, a magnetic iron-gallium crystal. Its spins form a helical spiral, caught between ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic ground states. That rivalry produces several sharp transitions as field and temperature change. The team measured how electrical resistance responds to magnetic fields in an aligned single crystal.

At high fields, resistance rose at low temperatures, a cyclotron-like effect of circling charge carriers. At high temperatures it fell instead, which the authors link to electrons scattering off magnons. The striking feature sits at low fields: a large anomalous jump in resistance. They suspect emergent spin fluctuations near the transitions cause that jump. Magnetization data measured alongside help pin down how the spins align in each phase. The material's crowded phase diagram makes it a rich testbed for spiral magnetism.
arxiv-2510-00508:
Yongchao Long and five colleagues published this 2025 paper on stopping language models from ignoring the documents they are given. Retrieval systems feed models source text, yet models still hallucinate answers that contradict it. The team noticed a pattern: responses that copy more of the context hallucinate less. Their model, CopyPasteLLM, is trained to trust and reuse provided text.

Three prompting tricks first generate high-copying example responses automatically. Preference training then teaches the model to favor that copying style. On faithfulness benchmarks, the model beat the best baselines by wide margins. Accuracy gains on one suite ranged from about twelve to twenty-five percent. Remarkably, training used only 365 samples, a fiftieth of the usual data diet. Analysis showed the model recalibrates its reliance on memorized knowledge rather than reading context better. Copying itself becomes built-in evidence of faithfulness.
arxiv-2510-00608:
Stephan Heinemann and seven colleagues published this 2025 space weather paper on seeing the Sun's far side without leaving Earth. Solar wind forecasts start from maps of the Sun's magnetic field. Half that field hides from our single vantage point at any moment. Helioseismology can sense far-side active regions through sound waves crossing the Sun.

The team fed those inferred regions into magnetic maps and reran forecast models. A standard solar wind model improved markedly for the years twenty thirteen and twenty fourteen. Correlation with observed wind rose by up to about fifty percent in their comparison. Error measures dipped slightly, with the best gains near Earth and a forward spacecraft. A three-dimensional heliospheric model showed real structural differences where far-side regions were added. Better far-side maps mean earlier warning of storms headed our way.
arxiv-2510-00908:
Goworek, Macmillan-Scott, and Özyiğit, at the Alan Turing Institute, survey cross-lingual information retrieval with multilingual language models in this 2025 arXiv paper. Cross-lingual retrieval answers a query in one language with documents written in others. The field long treated it as monolingual retrieval plus translation, developing the two halves in isolation. Embedding-based methods and multilingual large language models have now merged them into a single representation problem.

The survey walks the full pipeline: query expansion, ranking, re-ranking, and increasingly direct question answering. It organizes evaluation practices and the resources available to researchers. Persistent obstacles include skewed training data toward a few rich languages and wide linguistic variation that alignment must absorb. The authors argue the stakes are democratic: most digital content sits in a handful of languages. Robust, language-agnostic retrieval is how the rest of the world reaches it.
arxiv-2510-01008:
Ji and Wu prove a Tits alternative for groups acting on visibility spaces in this 2025 arXiv paper on geometric group theory. The Tits alternative says a finitely generated linear group is either almost solvable or contains a free nonabelian subgroup. Researchers have chased the dichotomy for groups acting on spaces. The authors study finitely generated groups acting properly discontinuously on a visibility CAT(0) space with the bounded packing property.

They prove every such group is either almost nilpotent or contains a free subgroup of rank two. The dividing line is the limit set: almost nilpotent corresponds to having at most two limit points on the boundary. As an application, any finitely generated torsion group acting this way must be finite. Such a group has a fixed point. The result extends the Tits tradition from hyperbolic spaces to a class of non-positively curved ones.
arxiv-2510-01208:
Kaushik, Bhattacharya, and Bhattacharyya track a neutron star in a neighboring galaxy that is spinning faster year by year. The pulsar SXP 46.6 feeds on a companion star, and accretion torque steadily shortens its rotation period. A 2017 space telescope observation caught the spin period measurably below its discovery value.

The spin-up rate implies a very strong surface magnetic field once disk geometry is constrained. Pulse shapes in soft and hard X-rays show two hot spots on opposite sides of the star. Spectra gathered by rotation phase vary, revealing how the beam sweeps past Earth. Long-term spin watching turns one pulsar into a laboratory for accretion physics. The Small Magellanic Cloud hosts the system, close enough for detailed X-ray study. Phase-resolved spectra were extracted for the first time here. Disk radius limits ruled out the weaker field solution.
arxiv-2510-01808:
Molina-Hernández and four co-authors optimize drug switching schedules against resistant bacteria in this 2025 paper. Their strategy exploits a side effect called collateral sensitivity. Resistance to one drug can leave bacteria weaker against another drug. Alternating two antibiotics might then drive a population to extinction. The team asks which switching rhythm gives extinction its best chance.

They built a random birth-death model with four bacterial types and two drugs that stop growth. Simulations swept the switching period at doses below full inhibition. Extinction chances rose in steps tied to individual switch events, not smoothly with speed. Very fast switching actually hurt, because resistance never had time to evolve and be exploited. A simple math framework predicted the total odds of wiping out the bacteria well. The strategy demanded strong two-way sensitivity of this kind to work at all.
arxiv-2510-02008:
Davis and Farnsworth probe a family of conjectures about path graph polynomials in this 2025 mathematics note. A 2023 study of tridiagonal matrices noticed something curious about certain polynomials tied to path graphs. Evaluated at the imaginary unit, some of them return Fibonacci numbers. That observation spawned several conjectures about where the roots of these polynomials lie.

The authors take up the root distribution questions directly. They make partial progress toward establishing two of the conjectures. For a third, they exhibit an infinite class of polynomials where the claim fails outright. They also assemble evidence against a fourth conjecture. The note thus sorts the original guesses into plausible, false, and doubtful piles. Its counterexamples are as valuable as its proofs for guiding future work. The interplay between Fibonacci values and root locations remains partly mysterious. Short notes like this one keep conjectural programs honest.
arxiv-2510-02308:
Kohli and co-authors estimate the local flat directions of curved data clouds under heavy noise. Their 2025 mathematics paper improves a basic tool of data analysis. Data often lies near a curved surface called a manifold. The tangent space at each point describes that surface locally. The standard local method struggles when noise is high. Its neighborhood size forces a painful trade-off. Small windows drown in noise, and large windows blur the curve. Their method, LEGO, uses global structure instead. It orthogonalizes gradients of smooth graph vibrations to find tangent directions.

Theory from differential geometry backs the approach. Low vibration gradients align closely with true tangent spaces. Experiments used noisy data up to the maximum tested noise level. LEGO stayed robust where local methods degraded. Sampling density changes also hurt it less. Manifold learning gains a sturdier measuring tool.
arxiv-2510-02408:
Filimonovic, Rutzer, and Wunsch measure what generative AI did to academic output. Their 2025 economics paper studies social and behavioral sciences. The team built a panel of matched authors over four years. Publications ran from 2021 through 2024 in the dataset. AI adoption was flagged by related keywords in titles and abstracts. A difference-in-differences design compared adopters with similar non-adopters. Adopters published notably more papers after taking up the tools. Journal impact factors rose modestly for them as well. Quality did not fall as quantity climbed.

Gains were uneven across the profession. Early career researchers benefited the most. Authors in technically complex subfields also gained strongly. Scholars from non-English speaking countries saw outsized benefits. The tools seem to lower structural barriers in publishing. Wider participation in research may follow from that shift.
arxiv-2510-02508:
Emran reports the first sign of a nitrogen bearing compound on Jupiter moon Europa. His 2025 planetary science paper mines old spacecraft data. The Galileo probe mapped Europa in infrared light decades ago. Reprocessed spectra show an absorption dip near two point two micrometers. That dip matches ammonia bearing materials. Modeling points to ammonia hydrate and ammonium chloride as carriers. The signal maps onto young terrain types on the surface. Microchaos, lineae, and band units all host detections. Those are places where subsurface material recently reached the top.

Ammonia likely rose through effusive cryovolcanism or similar plumbing. Its presence hints at a thinner ice shell below. The hidden ocean may be thicker and more alkaline than thought. Nitrogen is essential for life as we know it. A nitrogen source raises Europa astrobiology stakes. Ocean world missions gain a sharper target list.
arxiv-2510-02708:
Fernandez-Figueroa and co-authors catch galaxy gas flowing both inward and outward around strong absorbers. Their 2025 astronomy paper uses Keck telescope spectra. Seven isolated galaxy and quasar pairs anchor the study. Each pair shows ultra-strong magnesium absorption in quasar light. The team also took spectra straight down each galaxy's barrel. That dual view separates inflow from outflow geometry. Three galaxies showed outflows along the barrel sightline. Five showed inflows, and one showed both at once. Speeds ran into the hundreds of kilometers per second.

Every inflow galaxy sat below the star forming main sequence. Those galaxies may be refilling their gas tanks now. Outflows covered about half the background light on average. Inflows covered a clearly smaller share. Mass flow rates stayed modest in solar masses per year. Ultra-strong absorbers may flag galaxies in the act of feeding. More imaging and metal tracers would confirm the picture.
arxiv-2510-03308:
Lin and colleagues at Columbia University present a 2025 arXiv paper on designing moving mechanisms with image generating models. Engineers often need a linkage, a set of bars and joints, that traces one exact path. The team treats that design task as a picture translation problem. A mechanism drawing goes in, and its motion curve comes out, or the reverse. Drawing speed is coded as color along the path.

The authors built data sets that range from simple four bar linkages to complex eight bar designs. Their shared latent model learned to link each mechanism with the curve it traces. Tests showed it could invent new mechanisms for given curves and forecast curves for new designs. A printed test mechanism traced its planned path in the real world. The work opens a faster, more playful route to machine design, with clear value for robotics.
arxiv-2510-03408:
Acosta and Palacios present a 2025 arXiv paper on photoacoustic imaging when sound waves lose strength in a memory like way. Photoacoustic tomography flashes tissue with light and listens to the sound that heat creates. Rebuilding the starting picture from those sounds is an inverse problem. Here the fading follows a fractional derivative model, which fits how real tissue absorbs sound across frequencies. The authors ask whether the source can still be pinned down uniquely and rebuilt reliably.

They prove uniqueness under a geometric layering condition on the region. Their proof adapts two kinds of Carleman estimates to the fractional setting. They also prove stability, meaning small measurement errors cause only small picture errors. A rebuilding scheme based on a Neumann series completes the package. The tools may serve other wave problems with memory effects, from medical scans to material testing where signals fade as they travel.
arxiv-2510-04008:
Joshi and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on replacing softmax attention so models can read far longer texts. Attention is the core operation of Transformers, but its cost grows quadratically with context length. Even the best GPU implementations stall beyond a few million tokens in a single training pass. The authors design an alternative whose cost grows only linearly with length.

Their method, RACE Attention, swaps the exponential similarity of softmax for a sharpened angular similarity between vectors. Randomized projections and locality-sensitive hashing approximate the attention output without comparing every pair of tokens. Across language modeling and classification tasks, RACE matched or beat strong baselines while using less time and memory. In stress tests it handled twelve million tokens on one high-end GPU. Such reach could open very long documents, codebases, and media to direct attention instead of chunking tricks.
arxiv-2510-04108:
Dakhmouche, Letellier, and Gorji present this 2025 arXiv paper on measuring language model uncertainty with simple linear probes. For multiple-choice generation, the best existing uncertainty method is still the naive top softmax score. Bayesian treatments of huge networks are intractable, which pushed the field toward post-processing tricks. Recent interpretability work suggests much internal processing is nearly linear, and the authors exploit that observation.

Their method, the Bayesian Linear Lens, trains small Bayesian linear models between consecutive layers. Each model predicts a layer's output from the previous layer's output, yielding layer-level posterior distributions. A sparse combination of features from those distributions produces one global uncertainty estimate. Across several language models, the scheme consistently beat state-of-the-art baselines. The authors frame the result as evidence that principled statistics, not architectural complexity, was the missing piece. Reliable uncertainty estimates are a precondition for trusting models in automated decisions.
arxiv-2510-04208:
Bora, Gogoi, and Karmakar present this 2025 arXiv paper on the thermodynamics of a regular black hole bathed in anti-de Sitter space and a fluid of strings. The Hayward solution avoids a central singularity through a regularization scale, and such objects serve as laboratories for quantum gravity effects. The authors add two ingredients: a surrounding string fluid and quantum corrections to the entropy. They then map how the black hole's phases and stability respond.

The Gibbs free energy develops the swallowtail shape characteristic of a first-order transition between small and large black hole phases. String fluid strength, the Hayward scale, and the quantum correction coefficients all shift the critical temperature and phase stability. The authors present the model as a tunable framework for probing how quantum and stringy effects reshape black hole evolution. Such thermodynamic signatures may eventually meet astrophysical observation.
arxiv-2510-04408:
Pei Liu and six coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on how DNA packs inside a virus. Inside bacteriophage P4, a virus that infects bacteria, the genome coils into a spool like liquid crystal. Three kinds of stiffness shape such packing: splay, twist, and bending. Which of twist and bending matters more in tight spaces was unclear. The team combined microscope images, liquid crystal modeling, and knot theory to find out.

Images first showed that the ordered DNA fills three concentric layers inside the virus shell. A model fitted to the measured layer sizes then gave the ratio of bending stiffness to twist stiffness. The ratio came out near zero, at well under one percent. In plain terms, twist stiffness outweighs bending by about a hundred to one. The result reshapes how scientists model genome packing in viruses and cells.
arxiv-2510-04508:
Lili Xie and four coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on recommendation systems that borrow knowledge across domains. A shop may know a user taste in books but not in films, and new users start with no history at all. Borrowing from several source domains can help, yet a weak source can also hurt. Older methods used one reinforcement learning agent to weigh all sources at once. The team split that job among cooperating agents.

In their framework, MARCO, each agent speaks for one source domain and estimates its contribution. Cooperation lets the system assign credit fairly and block harmful transfer from weak sources. A diversity penalty on the joint actions keeps the agents from collapsing into one voice and steadies training. Tests on four benchmark data sets beat leading rival methods. The gains held up across settings, which the authors read as strong generalization. The code was posted in public.
arxiv-2510-04808:
François Dufour and Tomás Prieto Rumeau wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on how simple a good strategy can be in sequential decisions. Markov decision processes model choices made under randomness. A theorem says that for absorbing models with several goals, deterministic stationary strategies suffice. One needs randomized plans to do best. That theorem assumed the state space has no atoms, no points carrying weight.

The authors ask what survives when that assumption is dropped. Their answer is chattering strategies, which switch among deterministic ones by proportions. For measurable state spaces, chattering stationary strategies form a sufficient class. From that result, the theorem falls out for the atomless case. The proofs study extreme points of occupation measures, which record often states and actions occur. Those extreme points turn out to be the chattering strategies, tied to the number of goals. The work firms up the foundations of constrained decision theory.
arxiv-2510-05008:
Tenzan Araki, Joseph F. Goodwin, and Zhenyu Cai tackle quantum error correction in this 2025 arXiv paper. Classical error-correcting codes are cheap and mature, but quantum noise breaks them. Quantum errors include phase flips, which classical codes cannot even describe. Standard quantum codes pay for protection with many extra qubits and complex checks.

Their protocol, H-VEC, upgrades any classical bit-flip code to fight full quantum noise. It adds just one extra qubit and two layers of controlled-Hadamard gates. Classical post-processing then filters the noise into a single error type the old code can fix. Applied to the repetition code, it suppressed errors far more strongly than the classical original. It also beat the surface code while using far fewer qubits.
arxiv-2510-05308:
Matthew De Furio and ten co-authors hunt faint exoplanets with the Webb telescope without wasting time on reference stars in this 2025 arXiv paper. High-contrast imaging usually spends half its time observing a reference star for calibration. Webb's mirrors also drift thermally and suffer small tilt events. Those drifts distort the telescope's point spread function between calibrations.
