At matched approximation quality, the designed circuits use substantially fewer entangling gates than standard QAOA and hardware-efficient ansätze, and the Schwinger circuits need fewer parameters, friendlier for noisy hardware. The block structure also suits distributed quantum computing.
arxiv-2511-23008:
Caponera and colleagues develop mathematics for random fields on a sphere whose values are not single numbers but functions, such as a temperature curve recorded at each point of the globe. Such Hilbert-valued fields, named for the infinite-dimensional spaces their values live in, are used in functional data analysis. But their theory on spheres lagged behind the scalar case.

They extend Schoenberg's theorem to this setting, showing the covariance of such a field is captured by a sequence of operators. They prove a Feldman-Hájek criterion that decides when two such fields produce equivalent probability laws, based on a summability check on those operators. Two families show how the operators control the geometry and the statistics of the field. The families are a bivariate multiquadratic model with a closed-form equivalence region and an infinite-dimensional Legendre-Matérn model with conditions on smoothness and scale.
arxiv-2511-23108:
Hridya P and Choudhary test how electrode shape changes gas breakdown, the moment a gas between two electrodes turns into a conducting plasma under high voltage. The classic rule, Paschen's law, predicts the breakdown voltage from the product of gas pressure and electrode gap alone, with a characteristic minimum. But it says nothing about whether the two electrodes are the same size or different.

Running many argon discharge experiments with symmetric and asymmetric electrode pairs at several spacings, they map Paschen curves for each setup. They find that both the minimum breakdown voltage and the pressure-gap product at which it occurs shift with electrode configuration and gap size. They fit the curves with a new modified empirical formula using variable power-law terms. They explain the shifts through the electric field distributions between unequal electrodes, which concentrate the field differently than the textbook uniform-field picture assumes.
arxiv-2511-23208:
Kim and Lee build a design-based way to estimate causal effects when units adopt a treatment at different times and confounders themselves change over time. This is the staggered-adoption setting, where standard panel methods lean on fragile modeling assumptions. Their framework targets group- and time-specific effects. It proves when those effects are identified. It supplies estimators plus a block bootstrap for uncertainty and for testing whether effects are homogeneous.

To make the design real they introduce Reverse-Time Nested Matching, which pairs units from different adoption cohorts so their covariate histories are comparable at each treatment time, working backward from adoption. Applied to a Korean broadcaster's monthly panel, the method finds that subscribing to Netflix did not significantly change total IPTV viewing time but did reduce video-on-demand usage. There is statistical evidence that the effect varies even inside a single adoption cohort and event times.
arxiv-2511-23308:
Wang and Ma generalize a congruence from number theory, Zhao's 2007 discovery that a triple sum of reciprocals. Taken over all triples adding to an odd prime, matches a Bernoulli number modulo that prime. Later work stretched the identity to more summands and to prime powers with indices coprime to the prime. And this paper pushes it to totals built from several distinct odd primes at once.

Their two main theorems give congruences for the generalized sum when the total is a product of distinct odd primes. And when each prime carries its own power, with the answer governed by the Bernoulli number indexed by the first prime minus three. The proofs extend the earlier prime-power congruence rather than replacing it. So the Zhao identity and its five- and seven-summand descendants all sit inside one family parameterized by the prime factorization of the total.
arxiv-2511-23408:
Garg and colleagues benchmark how well large language models patch security vulnerabilities in one shot, testing models from the GPT family alongside LLaMA. DeepSeek, and Mistral variants on both real disclosed flaws and artificially generated variants of them. Crucially, success is judged by executing proof-of-vulnerability tests, so a patch counts only if it actually stops the exploit. Not if it merely looks similar to a human fix in practice.

The models patch real vulnerabilities noticeably better than artificial ones, even though the artificial cases share the same failure patterns, which exposes a generalization gap beyond previously seen vulnerability types. Patching overlap between models is higher on real flaws, while many artificial cases are fixed by exactly one model. So the authors stress that choosing or combining the right models matters and propose ensembles and prompt tuning as next steps for defenders.
arxiv-2512-00008:
Veeramani Pugazhenthi and co-authors present MOTION, on-device motion recognition with machine learning help. Tiny devices that recognize gestures with low delay are gaining ground in daily interaction. Medical uses, like fall detection and rehabilitation tracking, need fast responses without false alarms.

Running recognition on the device itself avoids network delay and keeps health data private. The system targets efficient tracking of movement on very small hardware. Reliable fall and activity detection could support safer independent living for patients. Fall detection, rehabilitation tracking, and patient supervision are the named medical drivers for fast, low-latency on-device recognition.
arxiv-2512-00108:
Black holes can, in principle, give up energy through magnetic processes near their edges. Bo Zhao, Chao-Hui Wang, and Shao-Wen Wei study energy extraction from Kerr-AdS black holes in a 2025 study. These are rotating black holes in a universe with a negative cosmological constant.

The extraction mechanism they examine is magnetic reconnection, where magnetic field lines break and rejoin, releasing energy. The authors map the parameter regions where extraction can occur and analyze its efficiency and power. Their results add to theoretical work on how the most extreme objects in physics might power energetic outflows. The analysis stays within general relativity, the standard theory of gravity and black holes.
arxiv-2512-00208:
Computer-generated people need to react to others with motion that looks natural over time. Hajra Anwar Beg, Baptiste Chopin, Hao Tang, and Mohamed Daoudi present ReactionMamba in 2025, a framework for generating three-dimensional human reaction motions. The system is built to handle both short and long sequences.

ReactionMamba combines a motion variational autoencoder, which compresses movement efficiently, with Mamba state-space models that decode reactions consistently over time. It can produce brief simple motions and long complex ones, such as dance and martial arts. Animators and game developers could use such tools to populate scenes with believable responsive characters. Reaction generation matters wherever digital characters must respond to a partner's movement. For folks who make games or films, a tool like this can fill a scene with life. The lead cast can then do the scenes that count the most.
arxiv-2512-00408:
At ultra-low bitrates, traditional video codecs collapse into blocky artifacts because they chase pixel accuracy. Lingdong Wang and co-authors propose DiSCo in 2025, a semantic video compression framework. The failure, they argue, comes from a mismatch between pixel fidelity and human perception.

DiSCo transmits only the most meaningful information and relies on generative priors to synthesize the remaining detail. Viewers forgive invented texture more readily than obvious compression damage. If the approach matures, video calls and streaming could stay watchable on connections where today's codecs simply give up. Generative priors know what natural video looks like, which pixel codecs cannot exploit. Ultra-low bitrates matter most on mobile and satellite links.
arxiv-2512-00608:
Feedback can enlarge what a broadcast channel is able to carry, but noise in the feedback path spoils naive schemes. Jacqueline Malayter and co-authors present deep broadcast feedback codes in 2025. Deep learning has renewed interest in codes that use channel output feedback.

In the Gaussian broadcast channel with feedback, capacity can exceed the no-feedback region. Linear analytical codes, though, perform poorly with even small amounts of feedback noise. Learned codes promise robustness where formulas fail, which matters for wireless systems that already feed receiver information back to transmitters. Broadcast channels serve many receivers at once, which is where feedback design gets tricky. Learned codes are found by training, not derived, which suits noisy feedback.
arxiv-2512-00708:
Ming-Hsiu Wu, Ziqian Xie, Shuiwang Ji, and Degui Zhi built a new dataset for drug discovery in a 2025 paper. Models that predict how well a drug candidate binds to a protein are key in early drug hunting. Yet current models often overfit to simplified datasets that miss how real proteins change.

Real proteins carry modifications, such as swapped, added, or missing building blocks, and added phosphate groups. The team rebuilt the widely used DAVIS dataset in a complete, modification-aware form. It adds thousands of kinase-ligand pairs that involve such changes. A harder, more honest test set should show which models truly work.
arxiv-2512-00808:
Wen-Han Zhou, Yun Zhang, Jiamu Huang, and Douglas Lin offer an idea for the flares of Sagittarius A* in a 2025 paper. That object is the supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way. It gives off frequent short flares across many wavelengths, and their origin is still unknown.

The authors suggest the flares come from bodies being torn apart and evaporating near the black hole. Some bodies are loose rubble piles, others solid monoliths, and each kind breaks up in its own way. If the idea holds, flare timing and brightness could reveal what kind of debris drifts near the galactic center.
arxiv-2512-00908:
Xinzhu Chen, Xuesheng Li, Zhongxiang Sun, and Weijie Yu refine how reasoning models are trained in a 2025 paper. A leading method rewards models for answers that can be checked, and it improves reasoning step by step. Recent work ties learning to token entropy, a measure of how unsure the model is at each word.

High-entropy tokens were thought to drive exploration and deserve stronger updates. The authors argue that most of a reasoning chain is made of low-entropy segments instead. Those calm stretches carry stable, reusable structure. Their correctness-aware method shapes advantages around such segments, rewarding right answers. Better credit assignment could make reasoning training steadier.
arxiv-2512-01008:
Zhongbin Guo and five coauthors present LISA-3D in a 2025 computer vision paper. Text-driven 3D reconstruction needs a mask generator that understands open-vocabulary instructions, like segment the red chair, while staying consistent across camera views. Most 2D segmenters wobble when the viewpoint changes.

LISA-3D lifts language-image segmentation into 3D in two stages. It retrofits the instruction-following model LISA with geometry-aware low-rank adapters, then reuses a frozen 3D reconstructor built from SAM. Multi-view consistency keeps the same object masked the same way from every angle. Consistent masks would make text-guided 3D editing and scene building far more reliable.
arxiv-2512-01108:
Gabriel Olin, Lu Chen, Nayesha Gandotra, Maxim Likhachev, and Howie Choset tackle fast interception in a 2025 robotics paper. Catching a fast moving object is hard because the time window is tiny. Sensor noise makes it harder, since the robot only gets incomplete information about where the target really is.

That uncertainty leaves a distribution over possible target states, not one position. Their system plans in belief space, reasoning over that distribution, and does so in real time with kinodynamic limits in mind. Real-time belief planning could help robots catch, block, or dock with fast projectiles and vehicles.
arxiv-2512-01208:
Alper Yıldırım and İbrahim Yücedağ propose a new attention scheme for transformers in a 2025 paper. Standard transformers pay what the authors call a semantic alignment tax. That tax is a heavy optimization cost. The model must organize a chaotic starting state into a coherent geometric map, through slow local gradient diffusion.

They hypothesize that this diffusive learning causes catastrophic rigidity. A model organized that way cannot adapt to novel concepts without destroying its pretrained reasoning. Their alternative moves from vector space diffusion toward a spectral phase-locking scheme with far better scaling. If the idea works, models could keep learning new concepts without full retraining.
arxiv-2512-01308:
Da-Sol Joo studies how heat-driven flow is modeled in fluids. When a fluid is heated from below, it churns in rolls. This setup is called Rayleigh-Benard convection. Models of churn must add the push of warm, light fluid, but no set form is agreed on.

Joo works out an exact solution for a common churn model in a flat layer. In that layer, churn is fed by heat push alone. An exact case gives model builders a firm check. It shows where the model holds and where its terms for heat push need a fix.
arxiv-2512-01408:
Jose Blanchet and co-authors revisit the Merton portfolio problem with robust data-driven rules. Merton's model picks trades over time to balance gain and risk. Fast trading helps only if drift can be trusted. Drift is hard to pin down in real markets.

Volatility can be screened from realized or implied data. The team builds robust rules around that split. Nonlinear Wasserstein projections guard against drift error. Robust picks aim to hold up when market models are wrong, a key need for real funds. Short horizons are the focus, where frequent trading pays only if robust rules keep model error from eating the gains alive.
arxiv-2512-01708:
Ghita Fassy El Fehri, Aurelien Bellet, and Philippe Bastien learn Bayesian network structure with privacy and federation. Data sits split across sites that cannot pool it. Privacy rules bind each site. Communication costs also grow fast with dimension.

Their Fed-Sparse-BNSL method targets linear Gaussian networks. It keeps rigorous privacy guarantees for each party. Sparse structure keeps messages small as dimension grows. Joint learning without raw data sharing serves hospitals and banks that must map links in data they cannot merge. Sparse structure priors do double duty, cutting both message size and the risk of spurious links in small local data sets.
arxiv-2512-01808:
Ibrahim Abdurrahman and co-authors study pair transfer in calcium-zirconium collisions below the Coulomb barrier. Sub-barrier fusion probes how pairing boosts neutron transfer. Past BCS-based sums boosted pair transfer over no-pairing sums. They still missed the observed boost between one- and two-neutron transfer.

The team revisits reaction dynamics for those collision pairs. Better pairing treatment is the goal. Matching the observed boost would validate how pairing acts during brief nuclear contact. That insight feeds models of fusion used for new element synthesis. Calcium and zirconium targets are stable and well mapped, which makes them a clean stage for isolating the pairing effect itself.
arxiv-2512-02008:
Letting a language model think longer at answer time, rather than training it bigger, has become a popular route to better reasoning. Aradhye Agarwal, Ayan Sengupta, and Tanmoy Chakraborty survey in 2025 how to scale this test-time compute, comparing the well-known strategies side by side under identical conditions.

A fair comparison had been missing, and so had an account of how the best strategy shifts with model type and problem difficulty. The authors organize the options for spending extra inference compute and examine when each pays off. Their map helps builders decide where an extra moment of machine thought is worth its cost.
arxiv-2512-02208:
Random graph theory studies networks that grow by chance, and its limit objects capture what huge random networks look like from afar. Pim van der Hoorn, Huck Stepanyants, and Dmitri Krioukov connect in 2025 two kinds of limits: projective limits of probability measures and direct limits of their symmetry groups.

They show the direct limit group is exactly the symmetry group of the limit probability measure. That tidy correspondence lets results travel between the finite approximations and the infinite limit. It supplies machinery for random graph limits, a framework used to model real networks from social graphs to the internet.
arxiv-2512-02508:
Marco Cardia and co-authors study how to judge water quality with machine learning. Clean water matters across farming and food work, from crop irrigation and animal care to food processing plants. As farms go digital, automatic quality checks become a valuable part of daily operations.

The team applies multivariate analysis, which reads many water measures at once rather than one by one. Learned patterns can flag water that drifts out of a safe range. Faster, cheaper checks could help farms and food firms catch problems early, before bad water harms crops, animals, or products. Clean water checks like these guard both farm yield and the food on our plates.
arxiv-2512-02708:
S. Bellotti and a large team update a survey of magnetic fields on stars that host planets. The survey uses spectropolarimetry, which reads magnetic signatures in starlight. Its targets sit on the current list for Ariel, a planned space mission to study exoplanet atmospheres.

Knowing a host star's magnetic field helps interpret the planet data Ariel will gather. Active stars can mimic or mask atmospheric signals. The campaign status report tells mission planners which target stars are well characterized, and which still need observing time before launch. Star data of this kind takes years to build, so a shared status list keeps scarce scope time from waste.
arxiv-2512-02908:
Iryna Zabaikina and Ramon Grima show how missed counts distort the speeds that cell studies report. Single cell tests fail to catch many of the molecules in a sample. That loss adds noise on top of the true, random way genes turn on and off.

Capture loss is often cast as a binomial draw, a clean model of imperfect detection. Till now it was worked out only for plain gene expression, with no gene control in play. The pair extend it to networks where genes switch each other on and off. Missed counts shift the rates a study would infer, and their work shows how to correct that shift. Labs that count cells one by one can use the fix to read truer speeds from noisy data.
arxiv-2512-03008:
Charmed baryons are heavy particles that contain a charm quark. A team led by A. Dávila-Rivera studies how three of them decay by emitting light in this 2025 work. The three particles belong to a family of six in the quark model.

The authors use the constituent quark model, which treats baryons as built from a few heavy quarks. They work out rates for these light-emitting decays. Such rates give tests that lab experiments can check in the future. They also help show whether the quark model describes heavy particles well. Future collider data can test these rates, since charmed baryons decay in ways detectors can record.
arxiv-2512-03108:
A crystal called RuO2 has sparked debate about its magnetism. Shubhankar Paul and seven co-authors add new evidence in this 2025 work. Some call the crystal an altermagnet, a new class of magnetic matter, while other studies find it is a plain paramagnetic metal.

The authors study how heat capacity, the heat a material soaks up, behaves in this crystal. They report a correction linked to Fermi-liquid theory, with a non-smooth form. Such details help settle what kind of metal RuO2 is. The answer matters for future devices that may use such materials. Heat measures at low temperature often expose the true nature of a metal's electrons.
arxiv-2512-03708:
Groups of cooperating agents, from drones to mobile robots, must agree on a shared course of action while their communication network misbehaves. Loaie Solyman, Aamir Ahmad, and Ayman El-Badawy address delays and dropped packets in a 2025 control preprint. Messages arriving late or not at all create errors that offline planning cannot remove.

Their framework joins semi-continuous hidden Markov models, which track the network's random behaviour in real time, with Lyapunov-based model predictive control. The controller balances three aims at once: gentle control effort, small network-induced error, and small error caused by the communication graph itself. An incremental learning routine updates the network model online as conditions change. Simulations across several network layouts show the agents still reach consensus and stay near optimal performance, even as the topology varies.
arxiv-2512-04008:
Differential privacy promises people in a training dataset that a released model cannot identify them, but the public must take that promise on faith. Zoë Ruha Bell and colleagues design a private learning algorithm whose guarantees can be checked cheaply, in a 2025 preprint. Until now, verification cost about as much computing as training itself.

The team works on differentially private stochastic convex optimisation, where the best trade-offs are known. Their method privately minimises a sequence of regularised objectives and leans only on the standard composition bound for privacy accounting. That structure keeps utility near optimal while making the guarantee auditable with far less computation than training. On large datasets the saving is significant. The authors call it the first algorithm of its kind whose verification scales better than training, a property that could make privacy claims publicly testable.
arxiv-2512-04208:
The Webb telescope's little red dots look like young active galactic nuclei, yet refuse to behave like any known class. They show red continua, feeble hot dust, and no detectable X-rays. Hiroya Umeda and colleagues test an alternative reading in a 2025 astrophysics letter. Each dot may be a black hole in a gaseous envelope, glowing like a cool star.

The authors refit energy distributions of some four hundred dots from the COSMOS-Web survey under this envelope model. Blackbody emission at a few thousand kelvin reproduces the optical and near-infrared spectra. Inferred luminosities drop by one to two orders of magnitude versus dust-reddened interpretations. The revision dissolves the tension: the luminosity function, accretion density, and mass function now agree with active nuclei at later times. Host masses, from the ultraviolet excess, leave a modest excess in the black-hole-to-stellar mass ratio.
arxiv-2512-04808:
Puria Radmard, Paul Bays, and Máté Lengyel automate the search for brain-like circuits that make the same mistakes people do. Neuroscience wants recurrent network models whose internal dynamics explain behavior, errors included. Building them has meant slow, hand-guided tuning of architectures and training goals. Their 2025 arXiv paper flips the workflow: train networks to reproduce behavior itself, including its characteristic slips and suboptimal choices.

Real behavior data are too scarce to train such networks directly. A nonparametric generative model first expands the data into a large surrogate set with the same error patterns. Networks trained on that surrogate learn mechanisms that produce human-like successes and failures alike. Those mechanisms then become hypotheses about the brain's own circuits. Automating the hunt could speed theories of working memory, decision making, and the slips that reveal how cognition is wired.
arxiv-2512-04908:
Fang Li, Fei Zuo, Gopal Gupta, and co-authors build a log anomaly detector out of logic itself, using answer set programming. Security teams drown in system logs while threats keep mutating. Machine learning detectors can be opaque and brittle. Answer set programming instead reasons with explicit rules written as logical predicates. Their 2025 arXiv paper encodes security knowledge in that declarative style and tests it on real Linux logs.

The system flagged brute-force attacks, privilege escalations, suspicious bursts of connections from single addresses, and assorted system faults. Rules can be edited as threats evolve, without retraining. Correlating events across lines, a strength of logic, helped connect scattered signs into incidents. Each alert comes with the rule trail that fired it, so analysts can audit the call. Explainable detection suits forensics, where a black box verdict is not enough.
arxiv-2512-05808:
Sushmita Bhattacharya and six co-authors send a drone out to meet sperm whales at the surface. Whales dive long and surface briefly, in hard to predict spots. Their platform couples an autonomous aerial vehicle with model based reinforcement learning: an empirical model of whale diving steers the search, updated by live sensor data from the field.

Three hard problems sit at the core. The drone must track whale clicks acoustically even when several whales call at once. Robots must share decisions across a distributed setup. And faint signals from fish-borne trackers must be processed on board and caught at long range. The team evaluated the system three ways: real rendezvous attempts off Dominica, hardware trials on land, and simulations from recorded whale tracks. Meeting a whale where it surfaces is a proving ground for autonomous field robotics, and a gentler way to study these animals.
arxiv-2512-05908:
Amirkia Rafiei Oskooei, S Selcan Yukcu, Mehmet Cevheri Bozoglan, and Mehmet Aktas find software bugs faster by translating whole codebases into plain language first. In microservice systems, a bug report in words must be matched to code across many repositories. Language models choke on raw code at that scale. Their approach builds summaries at three levels: file, directory, and repository.

Search then happens language to language. A report is first routed to the likely repositories, then localization walks downward through directories to files, leaving an auditable path. On an industrial system with forty six repositories, the method placed the true bug location in its top ten answers for about four of five reports. It beat retrieval baselines and agentic coding assistants by clear margins. The deeper claim: engineered natural language can beat the raw code it describes.
arxiv-2512-06208:
Ho Fung Tsoi, Dylan Rankin, Vladimir Loncar, and Philip Harris speed up neural nets on images where most pixels carry no signal. In such images, a normal network still grinds through every pixel, which wastes time and chip space. Their framework, SparsePixels, keeps only the small set of live pixels and runs the math on those alone.

Because the pixel budget is fixed when the chip is built, the run time stays the same no matter what image comes in. The team tests the idea on images from a neutrino detector, where true events light up a tiny share of the frame. Their sparse net ran many times faster than a plain one, with only a small drop in accuracy and a modest chip footprint. The method suits fast triggers that must decide, in real time, which rare events to keep.
arxiv-2512-06508: P Mchedlov-Petrosyan and L Davydov study a combined equation used to model surface processes where two things happen at once: molecules settle onto and leave a surface, while also spreading along it. The combined form joins the Cahn Hilliard and Allen Cahn equations, classic tools for diffusion driven change. The authors add flow to the mix, plus viscosity, and a memory effect, so the surface recalls its past states as it evolves. They obtain exact solutions and discuss how the applied field, dissipation, and memory act together.
arxiv-2512-07008:
Mark Shattuck counts patterns in Catalan words, strings of positive whole numbers that start at one and never jump by more than one. Such words pair naturally with Dyck paths, the mountain-range walks that combinatorics uses to model everything from bracket matching to tree shapes. Shattuck's goal is the total of several statistics added across every Catalan word of a given length, with proofs that explain the counts rather than merely verifying them.

Two of the statistics, symmetric valleys and a family of generalized valleys, had formulas awaiting exactly this kind of explanation, requested by earlier researchers. A related identity about Catalan numbers also gets its missing combinatorial proof. The method translates each statistic to Dyck paths and counts sets of paths with one or more steps specially marked.
arxiv-2512-07108:
Ashutosh Jayant Dikshit and co-authors schedule the matchmaking of a future quantum internet in orbit. Quantum satellites can share entanglement, the fuel of quantum communication, with ground stations across the globe. But satellites and stations are scarce, passes are brief, and the weather interferes. Their framework assigns satellite-to-station pairings while respecting fidelity thresholds for the entanglement and the losses imposed by air, weather, and background noise.

Relay chains through links between satellites are included, so a station can be reached through more than one hop. The scheduling is posed as an integer optimization that can chase different goals: the highest total distribution rate, or a fairer spread across station pairs, or a balance between them. That flexibility turns the framework into a benchmark against which simpler, hand-made scheduling policies can be judged.
arxiv-2512-07208:
Fei Luo and co-authors fix a drift problem in federated learning, where many clients train a shared model without pooling their data. When each client's data skews differently, locally trained prompts, the small steering vectors used to adapt big models cheaply, warp toward local habits. Fixes that adjust how results are averaged treat the symptom, not the cause. This framework corrects the local training itself, using a picture of the whole data's shape as a guide.

The server rebuilds that global geometric prior from covariance information in a privacy-preserving way and shares it with clients. A calibration layer on each client then aligns local feature distributions with the global shape during training. On a label-skewed image benchmark the method beat the state of the art, and under extreme skew it improved far more over the baseline.
arxiv-2512-07408:
Minju Jeon and co-authors wire beehives into the internet of things, watching both the colony's indoor climate and the weather outside it. Bee populations are falling under habitat loss, pesticides, and climate change, with farm productivity in the balance. Existing smart hives mostly monitor the inside only, cost too much, and scale poorly. WaggleNet's worker nodes are cheap, about fifteen dollars each, and carry sensors for temperature, humidity, light, and position.

Nodes sit inside and around the hives and whisper their readings over LoRa, a long-range, low-power radio. To a master node that relays them through a standard messaging protocol to a cloud server and a phone app. Field tests delivered every packet across more than a hundred meters of clear sight, and nearly as far with obstructions, including from inside wooden hives.
arxiv-2512-07508:
Achyut Tiwari, Bruno Gompf, and Martin Dressel wrote this 2025 physics paper on a layered crystal. The crystal, a form of tantalum sulfide named in the title, hosts competing quantum states. Charge density waves, a Mott insulating state, and superconductivity all contend inside it.

Its shifts between states come with a stubborn metal-insulator transition. The role of coupling between the layers in that shift was unclear. The authors probe the crystal with spectroscopic ellipsometry, which reads how it handles light. They track its response from room warmth down to its frozen insulating state. At room temperature the crystal acts as a natural hyperbolic medium in visible light.  As temperature changes, the metallic patches that carry current change shape. They stretch from discs into needles, and a new middle phase appears on heating. The transition, they conclude, is a three-dimensional percolation process driven between layers.
arxiv-2512-07608:
Jing Wang, Jie Shen, Xing Niu, Tong Zhang, and Jeremy Weiss wrote this 2025 paper on fairness in language models. Their test ground is medical question answering, where a model picks among given options. Fairness here means one thing: similar questions should receive similar treatment.

Their method, Metric-Fair Prompting, changes how the model works through the questions. Instead of solving each item alone, it pairs up questions that look alike. Similarity is measured with standard language embeddings. The prompt then forces a shared routine for both members of a pair. The model pulls out the decisive clinical features and scores each option as a confidence value. A Lipschitz-style rule keeps scores for similar inputs close together. On the MedQA benchmark for United States medical exams, the paired approach beats plain single-item prompting. Fairness-guided reasoning, they show, can raise accuracy on high-stakes questions too.
arxiv-2512-07708:
Quentin Vigneron and Hamed Barzegar wrote this 2025 cosmology paper on the shapes the universe can take. Bianchi and Kantowski-Sachs spacetimes describe universes that expand unevenly by direction. Their kinship with Thurston's catalog of shapes in three dimensions runs deep.

The authors study such universes inside a gravity theory built on Thurston geometries. Shape enters the laws of gravity directly in that framework. They focus on non-tilted solutions filled with a perfect fluid. Shear-free fluid solutions and static vacuum solutions exist for every topology. A second result concerns what a positive cosmological constant does. Nearly all these metrics settle into smooth, even expansion over time.  Recollapse, meanwhile, is impossible whenever the weak energy condition holds. General relativity fails both tests for its most tangled topology. The new framework needs no extra parameters to earn those virtues. Simple inflation in any shape becomes possible.
arxiv-2512-07808:
M. A. Farooq, G. Di Guglielmo, A. Rajagopala, N. Tran, V. A. Chhabria, and A. Arora wrote this 2025 quantum hardware paper. Reading a qubit means turning a faint analog response into a definite classical answer. Neural networks read qubits well, but their hardware versions are heavy and slow.

Slow readout chokes the fast loops that quantum error correction needs. Their accelerator, LUNA, attacks both the size and the latency problems. Simple integrators first compress the incoming signal at minimal hardware cost. The classifier itself is built from look-up tables instead of arithmetic units. LogicNets, networks synthesized directly into table logic, make that possible. A search framework based on differential evolution hunts for the best designs. The payoff is a far smaller chip footprint. Latency drops by about a third, with little or no loss in reading fidelity. LUNA points toward readout that scales with the quantum machines themselves.
arxiv-2512-08008:
Sarah V White, Precious K Sejake, Kshitij Thorat, and a large international team of radio astronomers posted a catalog paper on arXiv in December 2025. It is the fourth paper on the GLEAM four jansky sample, a complete set of the brightest radio galaxies in the southern sky. The team presents an updated multiwavelength version of the catalog for public use.

The update adds many new host galaxy identifications and redshift information, plus optical photometry from the DESI Legacy Surveys. With that legacy dataset, the authors study how these radio bright galaxies behave across wavelengths. They present a new diagram linking radio power, size, and spectral curvature, which acts as a proxy for a source age. The results highlight candidate remnant and restarted radio galaxies, and show the sample spans the full range of infrared colors.
arxiv-2512-08808:
Erik Rye and Dave Levin turn Wikipedia edit records into a twenty year history of IPv6 client addressing. Wikimedia sites log the network address of editors who are not signed in, using it in place of a username. Public data dumps therefore contain timestamped client addresses spanning more than two decades, an accidental time capsule for network research.

The authors extract tens of millions of unique IPv6 addresses used by editors over that period. With them, they trace how common IPv6 use is in countries tied to each Wikimedia language edition. They also track how adoption grew over time and across regions. A further question is how often client devices such as desktops, laptops, and phones used a specific addressing scheme derived from hardware identifiers. The study shows how a public editing archive can reveal long term change in internet addressing practice.
arxiv-2512-09008:
N S Mankoc Borsnik presents a theory that aims to unify all fermion and boson fields, including gravity,. Internal spaces of the fields are described by basis vectors built from products of gamma operators. In a fourteen dimensional setting, the picture is claimed to cover all observed fermions in families and all known bosons, from photons to gravitons.

A key condition is that fields carry nonzero angular momentum only in ordinary four dimensional spacetime. Bosons fall into two orthogonal groups in this description. The author notes that, in the allowed dimensions, the count of internal fermion states across families matches the count of boson states. General properties of massless fields and their interactions are presented, which fix the Lagrangian of the theory. Basis vectors are illustrated in detail for fourteen and six dimensional cases. New results are reported, and open problems in the theory are discussed.
arxiv-2512-09508:
Oskar Fiuk, Emanuel Kieronski, and Vincent Michielini study the difficulty of reasoning in two-variable first-order logic for hierarchically structured data. Two-variable logic is a fragment of logic using only two variable names, known for balancing expressiveness and decidability. Their setting models databases where items are organized by nested classifications and orders.

Their first logic adds a linear order and a chain of equivalence relations, each coarser than the last, like broader categories. They show deciding whether such a structure exists for a statement is complete for nondeterministic exponential time. A weaker variant without the linear order keeps the exponential model property, guaranteeing small witnesses. Their second logic uses a chain of total preorders; its satisfiability problem is also complete for nondeterministic exponential time. It jumps to exponential space once the successor relations of the preorders can be accessed. Using two independent chains makes the problem undecidable.
arxiv-2512-09708:
Eugenio Clerico gives a short geometric proof of a recent result about merging statistical evidence. E-values are a modern tool for combining evidence across experiments, even dependent ones. An e-merging function takes several e-values and returns a single valid e-value; listing all such functions is basic to the theory.

A full description was obtained by Wang through involved arguments. Clerico's note reproves it with a supporting hyperplane argument applied to concave envelopes, a picture from convex geometry that makes the structure visible. He also shows the result holds without assuming the merging function is monotone, an assumption the earlier proof needed. That extension matters because it proves any non-monotone merging rule is dominated by a monotone one, so restricting attention to monotone rules loses no generality. The note is a compact example of geometry simplifying a basic statistical question.
arxiv-2512-10108:
Ali Zahra reviews a method for analyzing driven diffusive systems with several particle species and open boundaries. Such systems model traffic, transport in cells, and other flows where particles enter, move, and leave. The method generalizes the extremal current principle known from single species models. Its engine is the Riemann problem for the hydrodynamic equations, the mathematical description of how sharp initial profiles evolve. The case study is a two species exclusion process on a lattice, where two particle types move in opposite directions and swap places when they meet.

Despite its simplicity, the model shows the key phenomena of its class, including phase separation, where the species sort themselves into distinct regions. The review shows how the Riemann invariants, special combinations of densities that travel cleanly through the system, dictate the macroscopic behavior. Boundary conditions at the open ends select among phases through the extremal current rule.
arxiv-2512-10308:
Vasiliki Stoumpou leads a team building an interpretable tool to choose between two ways of replacing a failing aortic valve. For low to intermediate risk patients with severe aortic stenosis, surgery and the catheter based alternative are both viable, and real choices vary with patient differences and hospital habits. The authors combine prognostic matching, which emulates randomization between comparable patients, counterfactual outcome models, and an optimal policy tree. The tree splits patients into clinically coherent groups and prescribes the treatment with the lower estimated five year mortality for each.

Trained on data from one hospital, the policy was tested on another institution's patients. Applying its prescriptions in counterfactual evaluation cut estimated five year mortality substantially at both hospitals relative to the choices actually made. The authors describe the framework as the first transparent, data driven recommender for this choice.
arxiv-2512-10908:
K Hari, Subhajit Barman, and Dawood Kothawala give the twin paradox a quantum retelling. In Einstein's classic puzzle, one twin travels and returns younger than the stay-at-home sibling. The authors replace the twins with quantum detectors, small systems that click when they absorb energy from a quantum field. And couple both to the same field as their worldlines diverge and reunite.

The detectors' transition rates and the entanglement that builds between them carry the memory of the trip. The sharpest finding is that the turns leave marks. Changes in direction of acceleration leave distinctive imprints on both the responses and the entanglement. These features have no classical counterpart. The authors note these effects might matter in black hole spacetimes, where detectors on different trajectories probe the field near the horizon. The ten-page paper keeps the model simple so the imprint stays visible.
arxiv-2512-11108:
Jonathan Kamp, Roos Bakker, and Dominique Blok show that tools explaining language model decisions carry hidden biases of their own. Feature attribution methods highlight which words drove a prediction, yet different methods give very different explanations for the same input. Users who notice may distrust the tools, while others may trust them too much.

The authors organise these biases with three general measures covering which words get credited and where in the text credit falls. They tested two transformer models first on a controlled artificial task, then on a natural causal relation task. Models that scored high on word based bias scored low on position bias, and vice versa. Odd or anomalous explanations were also more likely to be biased. The work argues explanation quality must be audited, not assumed.
arxiv-2512-11908:
Heng Zhang and co-authors survey safe learning for robots that must touch the world. Contact rich tasks, like assembly or handling soft goods, carry real risk of damage while a robot explores or performs. Learning based control promises skill, but safety remains the bottleneck for real deployment.

The survey sorts methods into safe exploration and safe execution. Tools reviewed include constrained reinforcement learning, risk aware tuning, uncertainty modeling, control barrier functions, and predictive safety shields. A special thread follows big foundation models, vision language and vision language action systems, which let users state safety rules in words but bring new failure modes. Gaps and next steps close the review.
arxiv-2512-12108:
Dashti A Ali and co-authors present a faster way to mine CT scans for shape features with topological data analysis. Topology based features, counting holes and loops at many scales, can sharpen diagnosis models. The standard route builds a cubical complex over the full 3D scan, which is slow and can underperform at high resolution.

Their patch based method builds the topology from local patches instead. Across data sets it beat both the cubical method and classic radiomic features. Gains averaged 7.2 percent in accuracy, 3.6 in AUC, 8.0 in specificity, and 7.2 in F1 score, with lower compute time as well. A Python package, Patch-TDA, ships for clinical teams.
arxiv-2512-12408:
Antar Bandyopadhyay and Kunal Joshi generalize de-preferential random graph models in a 2025 math paper. Random graph models grow networks step by step. In preferential models, busy nodes attract more links; de-preferential versions reverse that pull. Bandyopadhyay and Sen introduced one such family in 2025, and this work extends it further.

The authors find limit formulas for the degree of a fixed vertex and for the overall degree distribution. Under an inverse power law rule, both grow much more slowly than under the simple inverse rule studied before. For the linear case, adding a shift parameter changes nothing: the results stay exactly the same.
arxiv-2512-12508:
Jinfan Zhou and four co-authors use video foundation models to augment training data in space and time in a 2025 paper. Standard augmentation flips or crops images, a narrow kind of variety. Their method takes an image data set and generates realistic clips that vary camera viewpoint and scene motion, using off the shelf video diffusion models.

Adding those clips as extra training data gave steady gains when labels are scarce, as in drone imagery. They offer practical guidelines on picking a generation setup, moving labels onto synthetic frames, and handling disocclusion, where new views reveal unlabeled areas. Experiments on COCO subsets and drone data sets show the method widens the data spread along axes older methods miss.
arxiv-2512-12608:
Hong Su proposes a human inspired learning framework for large language models in a 2025 paper. Models excel at common patterns in large corpora but falter on rare or unseen cases, like niche hardware faults, since such cases are sparse in training data. They also lean on implicit memory inside their weights, so they act as intuition driven predictors rather than method learners.

Obvious Record stores cause result pairs as explicit symbolic memory, enabling learning from even single encounters. Maximum-Entropy Method Discovery keeps methods that differ most in meaning, preserving diverse strategies that next token training overlooks. On a benchmark of 60 question solution pairs, the entropy guided approach covered unseen questions better and held greater internal diversity than a random baseline.
arxiv-2512-13108:
Juedong Yang, Yuan Li, Wuhong Zhang, and Lixiang Chen detect the rotational Doppler effect using sunlight. The effect shifts light frequency in proportion to the spin speed of an object and the light's orbital angular momentum. Until now, detection relied almost wholly on laser sources.

The team collected sunlight, fed it into the lab, and shaped it into a partly coherent probe. In dim conditions, where noise beat the signal at each single wavelength, adding signals across wavelengths boosted the strength a lot. That let them measure spin speeds accurately. The work points toward passive remote sensing powered by daylight.
arxiv-2512-13208:
Giusi Capobianco and Angelina Zheng examine a tropical version of Martens' theorem for metric graphs. In tropical geometry, curves become graphs with lengths on their edges. The question is whether a classical bound on special divisors carries over, measured through a Brill-Noether rank.

They revisit a known counterexample built from a chain of cycles and generalize it to a new class, Martens-special trees of cycles, where the claim also fails. Those are not the only failures, they note. But they prove the claim does hold for all metric graphs under a stricter assumption on degree in the rank. The result maps where the tropical analogue stands.
arxiv-2512-13508:
A team led by A. Behring studies a small gap between heavy quarks and their antiparticles in high-energy physics. Their 2025 paper works in the variable flavor number scheme, a way to count heavy quarks in a proton. The gap is linked to three-loop terms in quantum chromodynamics, the theory of the strong force.

The authors compute the three-loop heavy-flavor terms for both plain and spin-based cases. They track how the terms change with the energy scale used in the math. The gap is small next to the sum of quark and antiquark shares, but it is not zero. That matters for precise tests of proton structure.
arxiv-2512-13608:
Felix J. Dorfner and co-authors build DBT-DINO, the first foundation model for digital breast tomosynthesis, a 3D form of breast imaging. No such model existed for this scan type, though it is used in breast cancer screening. They train with self-supervised DINOv2 methods on a very large data set.

Training used over 25 million slices from 487,975 scan volumes and 27,990 patients. On breast density classification, the model reached 0.79 accuracy, beating DINOv2 at 0.73 and DenseNet-121 at 0.74. On 5-year cancer risk, it reached an AUROC of 0.78. Gains on lesion detection were mixed, and the authors say local detection needs more work.
arxiv-2512-13708:
Kaiming Luo tackles the inverse problem of finding a hidden interaction network from steady states alone. When time traces are not available, only equilibrium data remain. His frame asks when one interaction operator can fit equilibrium limits from many varied perturbations at once.

Luo stands for the unknown operator as a trainable object in a variational, physics-informed ansatz. Training cuts steady-state residuals across experiments. In the affine case, stacked equilibrium equations give clear conditions for unique recovery, tied to the rank of a compatibility matrix. Synthetic tests on pairwise, directed, weighted, and higher-order systems match that picture. More varied steady states sharpen the split between candidate structures, under the stated premises.
arxiv-2512-13908:
Emma Rosenfeld, Craig Gidney, and a large Google team report a lab test of magic state cultivation on a superconducting quantum processor. Fault-tolerant quantum computing needs non-Clifford gates, which are costly in most error correction schemes. Cultivation is cheaper than distillation for preparing the magic states those gates consume.

The team carries out cultivation, including code-switching into a surface code, on the processor. They also develop a fault-tolerant measurement protocol to bound the magic state's fidelity. Cultivation cut the error by a factor of 40, reaching a state fidelity of 0.9999, while retaining 8% of attempts. The authors say the result establishes cultivation in the lab as a workable answer to a major cost in fault-tolerant quantum computing.
arxiv-2512-14008:
Shufan Li and co-authors present Sparse-LaViDa, a framework to speed up multimodal discrete diffusion language models. Masked discrete diffusion models perform well on image understanding, generation, and editing. Their inference is slow because every sampling step processes many redundant masked tokens.

Sparse-LaViDa cuts unneeded masked tokens at each step. Special register tokens hold compact forms for the truncated tokens, preserving output quality. A custom attention mask makes training match the truncated sampling procedure, keeping the two consistent. Built on the LaViDa-O model, it achieves up to a 2x speedup across text-to-image generation, image editing, and math reasoning. Quality is maintained across those diverse tasks, the authors report.
arxiv-2512-14208:
Mierk Schwabe, Lorenzo Pastori, Valentina Sarandrea, and Veronika Eyring test quantum machine learning for climate modeling in a 2025 paper. Earth system models predict climate change, and cloud cover is one hard part that is often handled by simple physics based schemes.

The team trains a quantum neural network to predict cloud cover as part of such a model. It matches a classical neural network with the same number of free parameters and beats the traditional scheme. They also compare how each network learns. For their case, the quantum network learned more consistent relationships than the classical one. The work tests whether quantum models could earn a place inside hybrid climate models.
arxiv-2512-14308:
Simon Kucharsky and four coauthors improve fast Bayesian model choice with self consistency in a 2025 paper. Fast methods train neural nets on fake data to give quick estimates. But those nets can act in odd ways when real data fall far outside the range they were trained on.

That risk is high for model choice, where some candidate models are bound to be wrong. Across two fake and two real case studies, methods that work through parameter posteriors beat methods that directly guess model scores. Self consistency training helps a lot when the likelihood is known, even when the model is badly wrong. Gains are smaller and less steady when exact likelihoods are not at hand.
arxiv-2512-14408:
Cagla Ozkan and five co-authors tackle a practical problem in quantum communication: running a quantum key distribution channel on the same city-scale fiber network as ordinary data traffic. Their setting uses dense wavelength multiplexing, where many channels share one fiber at different wavelengths. The quantum channel's secret key rate must be balanced against lost classical capacity.

Placement and spacing of the quantum channel decide the trade-off. Putting it at the band edge, with a guard band of 100 to 150 gigahertz, more than doubled the secret key rate in their tests. The cost was a capacity loss of about three percent, roughly half the loss seen with a band-center placement.
arxiv-2512-14508:
Myung-Chul Jung and Nojoon Myoung design a spin qubit in a single sheet of graphene, the one-atom-thick form of carbon prized for keeping spins coherent. Stretching the sheet into a tiny bubble creates a pseudo-magnetic field that traps electrons into a pair of quantum dots. Gate voltages tune how the two dots share their energy levels.

Adding Rashba spin-orbit coupling and a Zeeman field lets electricity steer the spin itself. Simulations found two working regimes, one preserving spin and one flipping it, each visible as a gap when the dots are detuned. Time-domain runs showed the expected Rabi oscillations, evidence that the spin can be controlled coherently.
arxiv-2512-14708:
Deep learning systems for physiological signal monitoring usually have fixed shapes and burn energy at a constant rate. SGEMAS, a self-growing ephemeral multi-agent system, takes the opposite approach, treating intelligence as a dynamic thermodynamic process.

Its architecture couples structural plasticity, meaning agents are born and die as needed, to a variational free energy objective, so the system evolves to cut prediction error while staying extremely sparse. The target is unsupervised online anomaly detection that adapts as signals change. For monitoring that must run continuously, a system that grows and shrinks with the data offers a different balance of accuracy and cost.
arxiv-2512-14808:
Julian Shapiro reports three faint dwarf galaxies near the spiral galaxy M101, about 6.7 million parsecs away. Each one looks quiet, with little or no new star birth. They may be backsplash galaxies, small systems that once passed through a bigger host, lost gas there, and were thrown back out.

The three are very dim, with absolute brightness from -7.3 to -8.1 magnitudes, and half light sizes of about 110 to 140 parsecs. Their distances come from subtle brightness patterns in older survey images. None shows up in ultraviolet data, which fits a quiet past. Views from space telescopes are still needed to confirm the backsplash story, since one could instead be a satellite of NGC 5585.
arxiv-2512-14908:
Turja Kundu and a coauthor present ATLAS, a graph learning system built to scale where message passing networks stall. Graph neural networks shine when linked nodes share labels, called homophily, but they falter when links join unlike nodes. Their step by step message passing also grows costly on huge graphs.

ATLAS skips message passing and instead turns community structure into features at several scales. The authors prove a trade off: finer communities carry more label information but also more entropy, so middle scales often predict best. A modularity guided search picks the useful scales, which feed a simple classifier. Across 13 benchmarks, including graphs with millions of nodes, ATLAS matched or beat rivals. It gained up to 20 points over GCN on heterophilic data and 12 points over plain MLPs on homophilic data.
arxiv-2512-15008:
Sandeep Neela presents the Stock Pattern Assistant, a tool that reads stock price history in a strict, explainable way. Many chart tools lean on platform specific rules, and predictive models rarely explain themselves. In settings that demand audits, that opacity is a real problem.

SPA pulls steady upward or downward runs out of daily price data, then links public events to those runs through a symmetric time window. Its explanations are factual and historical, with guardrails on what they may claim. The author tests it on four stocks, AAPL, NVDA, SCHW, and PGR, spanning calm and jumpy markets. The runs it finds stay stable, and ablation tests show each part of the pipeline adds clarity. SPA does not forecast or give trading signals; it offers a reproducible view of past price structure for analysts and risk reviews.
arxiv-2512-15308:
Basil Ell introduces graph pattern based association rules for labeled multigraphs in a 2025 paper. Association rules state that one pattern tends to come with another, and graphs such as RDF data need versions that respect links and direction. The framework supports both growing a graph and judging how plausible a graph is.

Rules are evaluated under no repeated anything semantics, which lets the shape of a graph count more fully than in older formalisms. Ell defines a probability space and derives confidence, lift, leverage, and conviction for these rules. The paper also shows how those measures relate to their classic itemset versions and when their key properties carry over.
arxiv-2512-16108:
Wendong Bi and six co-authors build a chatty music recommender in their arXiv paper, posted in 2025. Recommending songs in conversation needs both deep music knowledge and good judgment about user taste. Systems also need outside tools, like search and recommendation services, but calling them for everything is slow and costly.

Their framework, WeMusic-Agent, teaches a language model to store music knowledge inside itself and to learn when a tool call is truly needed. The resulting model was pretrained on 50 billion tokens of music-related text. The team also built a benchmark from real WeChat Listen data, scoring relevance, personalization, and diversity. On real-world tests, WeMusic-Agent improved significantly over existing models, balancing built-in knowledge with tool use.
arxiv-2512-16208:
Angel Chandro-Gomez leads a large team in simulating dead galaxies in their arXiv paper from 2025, accepted by a leading astronomy journal. The James Webb Space Telescope found many massive galaxies that had already stopped forming stars when the universe was young, at redshift 2 and beyond. Their existence strains galaxy formation models.

The team studies these massive quenched galaxies inside COLIBRE, a new cosmological simulation suite with updated feedback physics. Counts and mass distributions in the flagship simulation broadly match the latest observations, once observational uncertainty is modeled. The simulated galaxies formed over about 0.5 to 1.5 billion years, then shut down within about 0.6 billion years after strong starbursts. They also hold far less dust and molecular gas than similar star-forming galaxies, matching the scarce data available.
arxiv-2512-17008:
Junbo Li and coauthors present turn-PPO, a variant of Proximal Policy Optimization for training language model agents over many turns. The popular GRPO method wobbles on long-horizon agent tasks, where credit for a win must be split across many steps.

The team first shows plain PPO already beats GRPO in stability for multi-turn work. turn-PPO then recasts the task at turn level, not token level, so advantage scores attach to whole replies. On WebShop and Sokoban, turn-PPO beat the baselines with and without long reasoning traces. The fix is simple: match the training unit to the unit the agent actually chooses.
arxiv-2512-17208:
Yu-Peng E, Chun-Chun Zhu, and Yu-Xiao Liu examine how thick branes vibrate in a modified theory of gravity known as f(R) gravity. A brane is a sheet-like object in a space with extra dimensions. When it is disturbed, it rings at special rates called quasinormal modes, much like a struck bell.

The authors solve the wave equation for these shakes in three separate ways and check that the answers agree. They find that the shape of the barrier in the effective potential, a kind of energy wall, controls the pattern of rates. The real parts of the rates rise in near even steps. That pattern suggests the trapped states act like echoes bouncing between two barriers.
arxiv-2512-17508:
Silke Johanndeiter, Jonas Finke, and Justus Heuer compare three flavors of a policy meant to steady wind power income. A two-way Contract for Difference pays a wind farm when market prices fall below a set strike price, and claws money back when prices soar. Governments across Europe lean on such deals, yet the fine print varies, and each variant spreads risk in its own way.

The team derives ideal strike prices on paper, then replays 36 market futures in an energy model. Every design cut price swings for both shoppers and investors by a lot. Shopper prices barely differed across designs. A capacity-based design calmed investor profits most, but it also dulls the price signals that steer farms to build where the grid needs them. That trade-off is the paper's warning.
arxiv-2512-17608:
Jérémy Itier, Gilles Renversez, and Frédéric Zolla speed up the math of light bouncing off materials that change under the light itself. In a nonlinear material, the scattered beam reshapes the material, which reshapes the scattering, so standard solvers loop round and round until the answer stops moving. Each loop is slow.

Their perturbative method treats the nonlinearity as a small correction built up in steps, with no loop back to the start. They test it on a nonlinear slab and a nonlinear crystal, lit by a tilted plane wave of any polarization. Against their own earlier rigorous solver, the new method matched accuracy while cutting compute time. Optics designers modeling switches and limiters gain a far cheaper tool.
arxiv-2512-17708:
Nils Wittek and three co-authors survey three decades of speakers shrunk onto silicon chips. MEMS speakers, built like computer chips, promise earbuds and phones a smaller, more exact sound source than the classic coil-and-cone. The review sorts the field by how the chips make sound: moving a membrane directly, beaming ultrasound, or heating air in rapid pulses.

Across work from 1990 to 2026, one family leads: piezoelectric chips that flex a membrane in the audible band itself. Their rise rests on shrinking size and sipping power. Full-range sound, deep bass from a speck of silicon, remains the open challenge. The authors name the designs most likely to crack it and the hurdles still in the way.
arxiv-2512-17908:
Ananta R. Bhattarai and Helge Rhodin improve depth maps guessed from a single photo. Top models like Depth Anything V2 often slip on real scenes that differ from their training photos. Their method, Re-Depth Anything, refines a depth map at test time with no labels at all.

The trick is to relight the guessed scene and check whether the new shading makes sense to a large image model. Only part of the depth model is adjusted, which keeps the fix stable. On standard tests the refined maps beat the base model by a wide margin, and paired with a newer base model they set the best scores yet.
arxiv-2512-18108:
Yurou Liu, Tiger Lu, and Malena Rice explain a rare double: the twin stars of WASP-94 each host a hot Jupiter, a giant planet hugging its star. One planet crosses its star every 4 days on a tilted path, while its sibling circles in just 2 days without crossing. Few twin systems offer such a matched pair for testing how planets form.

Computer runs show both giants could have arrived by the same tilted fall, called Kozai migration, mirrored in each star. A distant pull slowly tips a far orbit until the planet dives close and settles. Future Gaia star mapping may reveal more twin planet homes, including cold giant pairs that could become such doubles.
arxiv-2512-18308:
Hao Chen leads a five author team building a new family of sponge like surfaces with a twist. These minimal surfaces repeat in all three directions and split space into two maze like halves. In their family, named gyrating H'-T, the two halves do not mirror each other: one follows the quartz net, the other its dual net.

A six step screw motion reveals the built in handedness. At one end of the dial the shape nears a saddle tower, and at the other a wavy sheet form. The team first shaped the surfaces on a computer, then proved the family truly exists with a torus based method. Such tunable chiral templates could steer light in new photonic materials.
arxiv-2512-18408:
Shohini Sen, Suchismita Banerjee, and Bikas K. Chakrabarti compare ways of measuring inequality across very different systems. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, runs computer simulations of two wealth-exchange models and two earthquake models. In each one they compute standard inequality scores, including the Gini, Pietra, and Kolkata indices.

The striking result is how alike the scores behave. In both the wealth and earthquake models, the Gini and Kolkata indices meet near 0.86 at the right settings, a value tied to the edge of critical behavior. A related ratio stays just above one, as theory predicts. The match suggests that money trading and fault lines share hidden statistical patterns.
arxiv-2512-18508:
Barak Or examines a quiet statistical trap inside Kalman filter tracking, the validation gate. Trackers only accept measurements whose normalized innovation squared falls below a threshold, discarding the rest as implausible. His paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, shows this sensible filter changes the very statistics engineers later compute from the accepted data.

Under standard linear-Gaussian assumptions, he derives exact first and second moments of the innovation once ellipsoidal gating is applied. Gating shrinks the innovation covariance by a fixed, dimension-dependent amount. He then shows nearest-neighbor association acts as a second selection step with its own unavoidable energy contraction. Closed-form results for the two-dimensional case measure the combined effect. The lesson: after gating, nominal innovation statistics can never be fully preserved.
arxiv-2512-18608:
Prabigya Acharya and Liza Shrestha ask whether small language models can mask personal information in conversation as well as giant frontier models do. Masking such details is essential for private chat systems. Frontier models do it well but raise data handling worries and cost far more. The pair fine tune two lightweight models, T5-small and Mistral-Instruct-v0.3, on AI4Privacy benchmark data.

Their datasets cover 24 standardized categories in several label variants, and both small models match frontier level performance. Normalizing labels improves results for every architecture. Mistral scores higher on F1 and recall and is more robust across information types, but it generates answers slowly. T5 is less robust on messy chat text, yet its outputs are structured and cheap to run. That tradeoff led the authors to deploy T5 in a live Discord bot, where tests on real messages show performance drops on informal input.
arxiv-2512-18708:
Hai-Feng Wang and a large international team map the Milky Way's bulge, the dense ball of stars at our galaxy's center, to learn how it formed. Their conference summary, posted to arXiv in December 2025, combines RR Lyrae variable stars from OGLE-IV with giant stars from APOGEE and Gaia. Different data sets trace the same structure from different angles.

Orbit calculations for 1,879 RR Lyrae stars split them into central bulge, inner bulge, and stray halo or disk members. The inner bulge moves like a bar, while central stars rotate more slowly. Chemistry from 28,188 APOGEE stars confirms the split and shows two chemical families, pointing to separate formation paths. The team concludes the inner bulge is a pseudo-bulge grown from disk instability, and the whole bulge looks boxy rather than X-shaped.
arxiv-2512-18808: Emmanuel Opshtein works in symplectic geometry, the math behind classical physics and its quantum version. His short paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, concerns prequantization bundles, the structures used to pass from classical pictures to quantum ones. He shows these bundles carry built-in barriers of Legendrian type. Removing them is what blocks long cylinders from embedding over Legendrian submanifolds, so one concrete example pins down a sharp limit.
arxiv-2512-19308:
Ferhat Taş recasts the evolution of three-dimensional shapes as the motion of a spinor field. In his framework the spinor is the main variable, and the geometry of the manifold is read off its size, through a conformal change of metric. A heat flow driven by the squared Dirac operator moves the spinor.

Away from the points where the spinor vanishes, the system is parabolic and well behaved. At those nodal points the induced metric degenerates, while the spinor itself stays bounded. Taş argues that geometric singularities should be read as nodal transitions of the spinor, not as blow-ups. The metric's motion is purely conformal, with extra gradient terms.
arxiv-2512-19708:
Vladislav Kozhukhov studies a classic problem in the mechanics of soft solids. His material is a rubber-like solid that also flows a bit. It cannot be squeezed to a smaller volume. The math for it uses a Gordon-Schowalter derivative, a way to track spin in a deforming body. The family of such rules has one free parameter. He looks at simple shear, under both steady push and random speed.

With a steady push, extra normal stresses show up. That matches the Poynting effect found before for this material. For the random case, the shear rate hangs on a normally spread random value. He builds an exact solution with a method due to Lomakin. The spread of the stress parts depends a lot on which tracking rule is picked. That is a warning for anyone modeling such solids.
arxiv-2512-19808:
Eyal Walach and Efrat Shimshoni map the phases of a superconducting ladder drowned in disorder. The model is a two-legged array of Josephson junctions. Josephson energy and charging energy are of like size. Values vary widely along the legs, but a strict symmetry swaps the two legs. They work in the strong-disorder limit. Their tool is a real-space renormalization group built for such mess.

Three phases ruled by disorder show up. A disordered superconductor sits on one side. A disordered insulator sits on the other. Between them lies a Bose glass phase. The insulating side maps to an XY spin chain in a spin-glass phase. The result muddies the textbook tale of the superconductor-insulator shift. Even in this plain ladder, disorder and quantum effects open an extra phase.
arxiv-2512-20008:
Tuo Wu and five co-authors chart a path from equations to learning for a wireless bargain. Weak devices cannot run their workloads alone. Over-the-air computation lets the air itself do the arithmetic. But run times are unsure. The team models them with gamma-distributed workloads. That turns resource allocation into a hard nonlinear problem.

For one user, two classic methods give near-closed-form answers. They are block coordinate descent and majorization-minimization. Both carry proof-backed promises. Many-user cases defeat exact methods, through clashes and contention. So a deep Q-network learns the allocation policy by trial in its setting. Tests back the handoff. Gains grow as edge server density rises. The pair of methods is pitched as fit for next-generation systems.
arxiv-2512-20108:
Yuntong Gu and four co-authors map the radio spectrum the Bayesian way. Spectrum cartography rebuilds how signal strength varies over space. It backs monitoring and situational awareness. Satellite sensing gives data that are sparse, noisy, and coarsely quantized. Two tasks are coupled: rebuild the map from scraps, and choose where to sense next on a tight budget. Past methods treat the two apart.

Their frame, Generative Spectrum Cartography, treats them as one problem. Recovery is posed as Bayesian inference under a learned diffusion prior. Closed-form updates fold into the reverse diffusion steps. Sampling then stays true to the measures, with no costly gradient guidance. The samples also gauge where the map is least sure. That guides the pick of new sensing spots. Tests on fake maps and a satellite scenario beat baselines.
arxiv-2512-20308:
Maxime Poli and a large team introduce SpidR, a model that learns the sound units of speech without any text or labels. Textless spoken language models need semantic units drawn straight from audio. SpidR trains on raw waveforms with masked prediction, self-distillation, and online clustering, with student layers predicting assignments taken from teacher layers.

That objective steadies the clustering and yields better codebooks than earlier approaches. SpidR beats wav2vec 2.0, HuBERT, WavLM, and DinoSR on spoken language modelling benchmarks. The authors also show that unit-quality scores reliably predict language modelling performance across models and layers. Training takes about a day on sixteen graphics processors rather than a week, and the code and checkpoints are openly released.
arxiv-2512-20408:
Lorenzo Schiavon and co-authors model how a person's job shapes unhealthy behaviour. Smoking, poor nutrition, alcohol misuse, and inactivity drive chronic disease worldwide, and occupation plausibly channels all four. The team uses Italy's PASSI surveillance data, which records health behaviour alongside free-text job descriptions.

Structural topic modelling first clusters those job texts into latent occupational groups. The groups then set mixture weights in a multivariate ordered probit model, letting covariate effects differ by occupation and drift over time. Non-local spike-and-slab priors keep the model interpretable and select variables. A sequential Monte Carlo updater refreshes everything as new survey waves arrive. Public health planners gain a live map of which work contexts amplify which risks.
arxiv-2512-20508:
Kiyan Naderi and Noema Nicolussi study vibration-like operators on graphs whose edges have lengths and weights. Their Laplacians live on finite metric graphs endowed with generalized densities, measures of finite mass. The approach unifies discrete graph Laplacians, Kirchhoff Laplacians, and Dirichlet-to-Neumann operators under one roof.

The main question is spectral optimization: which density makes an eigenvalue as small as possible? Unlike domains and manifolds, a minimizer for the k-th eigenvalue provably exists, while maximization turns out to be meaningless here. The first optimal eigenvalue admits a transparent geometric characterization through the resistance metric. Higher optimal eigenvalues obey a Weyl law, linking their growth to the graph's geometry. The results guide how to distribute mass on a network to tune its spectrum.
arxiv-2512-20608:
Julian Gass and Michael Levin design an entanglement probe that reveals a topological fingerprint. The chiral central charge captures 2D quantum phases with a twist, but pulling it from a ground-state wave state is tricky. Their probe takes powers of reduced density matrices arranged in a particular geometry, producing a two-setting quantity.

The construction generalizes the modular commutator, an earlier probe for the same charge. For free-fermion ground states and string-net models, the authors compute it exactly. In both cases it lands on a universal value fixed by the chiral central charge. At integer parameters it becomes a mean value of permutations on a replica system, so computer runs, and perhaps tests, can measure it directly.
arxiv-2512-20708: János Kollár and Wenhao Ou prove a modification theorem for singular complex spaces. Orbifolds are spaces that look locally like quotients by finite groups, and many complex analytic spaces are almost orbifolds except at their worst points. The authors show that every compact complex analytic space admits a bimeromorphic orbifold modification. The new space agrees with the original exactly on the region where the original was already a locally trivial orbifold. Only the singular locus is genuinely changed.
arxiv-2512-20908:
Kaiyuan Liu and six co-authors trace where a distilled model's sentences actually come from. In reasoning distillation, a big teacher model writes out solution paths and a small student trains on them. Whether the student truly absorbs the teacher's habits, or slips back to its old style on new problems, was unclear.

For every sentence the distilled model produced, the team compared probabilities from the teacher, the original student, and the distilled model. Sorting sentences by those comparisons showed genuine teacher-born behavior appearing in fresh test settings. The same tracing suggests which training examples to keep: those where teacher and student diverge most instructively.
arxiv-2512-21008:
Lichao Wu, Ahmad-Reza Sadeghi, and three co-authors show that the safety training of mixture-of-experts language models lives in a surprisingly small place. Safety research has concentrated on dense models, leaving the sparse, routed architecture unexamined. Their attack framework, GateBreaker, profiles which experts the gating network routes harmful inputs to, locates the safety structure inside those experts, and disables it at inference time, with no retraining.

Safety turns out to concentrate in roughly three percent of the neurons in the targeted layers. Silencing them raised the average attack success rate across eight current aligned models from about seven percent to about sixty-five percent, and the same neurons transferred within model families.
