The findings tell model builders that sparse routing concentrates both capability and vulnerability, and defenses must be designed for that structure.
arxiv-2512-21208:
Ronald Katende builds one dashboard for the ways learning systems wobble. A learning process carries representations, parameters, and update variables. Its stability asks how disturbances, in the inputs, the starting point, or the update rule, amplify or die along a training path. The Learning Stability Profile collects directional sensitivity operators for that question, channel by channel. It gives one object to bound, not scattered papers.

A Lyapunov criterion controls the profile. Under assumptions, an incremental energy forces uniform or exponentially decaying bounds on the linearized dynamics. The label is honest: the criterion suffices, but no converse is claimed. The scheme specializes, giving spectral bounds for feedforward nets and step-size rules for residual designs. It gives mean-square contraction for stochastic gradient methods, and generalized Jacobians for nonsmooth systems from ReLU networks to recurrent models. Theorists gain a language where design, optimization, noise, and nonsmoothness stop needing split theories.
arxiv-2512-22008:
A photonic nanojet, the narrow intense beam formed behind a microscale dielectric particle, has long lacked a shared definition, making published dimensions hard to compare. Mirza Karamehmedović, Kristoffer Linder-Steinlein, and Jesper Glückstad propose a definition that is physically interpretable and quantifiable, resolving the confusion in how nanojet size and quality are measured.

Their framework uses an optimal mass transport metric to score nanojet quality. Building on that metric, they develop a steering method that moves the nanojet with phase-only illumination modulation, needing no opto-mechanical intervention. The redefinition is meant as a design paradigm: once quality has a principled measure, illumination patterns can be optimized against it rather than tuned by eye.
arxiv-2512-22108:
Pavel A. Andreev examines the symmetric Heisenberg exchange interaction, one of the main forces aligning spins in magnetic materials. Its partner, the antisymmetric Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction, has a known Keffer form that accounts for the nonmagnetic ion sitting between two magnetic ions shifting off the line joining them. Andreev asks whether that same shift also changes the symmetric interaction's strength.

He argues it does: the exchange constant gains a second term that depends on the ligand shift. That term adds a piece with one spatial derivative of the spin density to the energy. Andreev derives the matching contribution to the Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation, works out how spin wave frequencies change, and discusses new spin torques, noncollinear order, and spin currents in multiferroics.
arxiv-2512-22208:
Pu Zhao and twenty co-authors introduce the Moxin family of open-source language models, built around the Moxin 7B base model. Proprietary systems like GPT-4 dominate attention, while open models such as LLaMA and Mistral spread through easy customization. Moxin follows the Model Openness Framework, sharing not just weights but training data, code, and implementation details for full transparency.

Three variants extend the base model: Moxin-VLM for vision and language, Moxin-VLA for vision, language, and action, and Moxin-Chinese for Chinese capability. The team trained everything with open-source systems and open data, and reports strong results across their evaluations. Models, data, and code are all released to support a healthier open ecosystem.
arxiv-2512-22808:
Libo Zhang and a twelve-author team address a gap in motion generation: producing a person's physical reaction to what they themselves are seeing. Their starting point is data. Existing datasets pair reaction motion with video that does not line up in space. Moving reactions were matched to fixed-camera footage. So the team built the Human Reaction Dataset with properly aligned egocentric video and reaction motion.

On that data they train EgoReAct, described as the first autoregressive system that generates three-dimensionally aligned human reactions from a first-person video stream in real time. Motion is first compressed by a vector-quantized autoencoder, then a generative transformer predicts reactions while using depth estimates and head movement to stay grounded in the scene. Experiments show stronger realism, spatial consistency, and speed than earlier methods, while each frame is generated strictly from past input.
arxiv-2512-23108:
Henry Adams, Alexandre Karassev, and Ziga Virk prove that two ways of thickening data in topological data analysis capture the same shape information. Analysts summarize a metric space's shape with Vietoris-Rips and Čech complexes, built from balls around points. Their metric thickenings are continuous cousins of the same ideas, and a natural bijection maps each complex onto its thickening.

The main theorem says that bijection is a homotopy equivalence whenever the space is a finite-dimensional Polish metric space, so complexes and thickenings agree on all holes, loops, and voids. Riemannian manifolds are a leading example. The result extends to Vietoris complexes of any bounded cover, with the Čech case included. The authors also show that for compact metrizable spaces the thickening is strongly locally contractible, a property useful for further theory. Users can thus move between discrete and continuous models without losing topological information.
arxiv-2512-23708:
Milosz Matraszek, Wojciech Jankowski, and Jan Behrends extend quantum geometry to systems that leak. In closed quantum systems, the quantum geometric tensor limits how strongly observables can respond, giving bounds on conductivities and optical weights. Real devices are open and often described by non-Hermitian Hamiltonians, where those closed-system bounds need not hold.

The authors identify unique bounds on the geometric tensor for non-Hermitian systems, and from it bounds on response correlators, conductivity tensors, and optical weights. Topological systems carrying non-Hermitian Chern numbers showcase the results. They also show the constraints arise naturally in open systems governed by Lindblad dynamics, the standard description of a quantum system coupled to an environment. The work aims at experiments, where openness is the rule rather than the exception.
arxiv-2512-23808:
The Xiaomi LLM-Core Team releases MiMo-Audio, an audio language model built on the bet that made GPT-3 famous: scale up next-token prediction and few-shot learning emerges. Audio models usually need task-specific fine-tuning for each job, while people pick up new listening tasks from a handful of examples. The team pretrained on more than one hundred million hours of audio.

At that scale, few-shot ability appeared across diverse audio tasks. The base model set open-source records on speech intelligence and audio understanding benchmarks. It generalized to tasks missing from its training data, including voice conversion, style transfer, and speech editing, besides continuing speech in realistic talk-show and debate formats. An instruction-tuned version matched or beat closed-source models on several spoken dialogue and text-to-speech tests. Checkpoints and the evaluation suite are public.
arxiv-2512-24108:
Soumyadeep Halder, Hari Sadhan Ghosh, Axel Pelster, and B Prasanna Venkatesh propose a test for ultracold atomic gases. A dipolar condensate can form several phases. It may be a free-flowing superfluid. It may form isolated droplets. Or it may become a supersolid, part crystal and part superfluid. Telling these phases apart is valuable.

Their probe tilts the polarization direction slightly. An external magnetic field can do this. A superfluid answers with an undamped scissors-mode oscillation. That motion is a classic superfluid signature. Droplet and supersolid states oscillate too. Their motion damps, though, as close frequencies interfere. The damping rate tracks how rigid each phase is. A larger tilt deforms those states for good. That mirrors the elastic-to-plastic change in ordinary solids.
arxiv-2512-24208:
Rohit Kumar Meena, Akhil Tayal, Andrei Gloskovskii, and Mukul Gupta grow thin films of Fe4N. The compound is an anti-perovskite with attractive traits. It shows high magnetization and chemical stability. Its coercivity is low and its Curie temperature high. Spintronic and magnetic storage devices could use it. The problem is the growth window. The pure phase forms only in a narrow band of temperature and nitrogen content.

Slight nitrogen shortage produces iron impurities. Slight excess produces a different nitride phase. The authors show that palladium doping widens the window. Analysis places palladium atoms on corner iron sites. Magnetization drops only slightly with doping. The drop stays nominal up to thirteen atomic percent. Structural and electronic properties change little as well. Pd doping thus looks like a practical route to easier Fe4N growth.
arxiv-2601-00508:
Simon Rudkin and Wanling Rudkin introduce ballmapper, a Stata package for a visualization method from topological data analysis. The Ball Mapper method covers a multi-dimensional point cloud with balls of one chosen radius, producing a graph that shows the data's full shape without shrinking it down to fewer dimensions. That avoids the information loss of standard reduction techniques.

Graphs from the method can be colored by extra variables, model residuals, or values inside the data, which helps users spot structure and outliers. The underlying method is already used in finance, economics, geography, medicine, and chemistry. By packaging it for Stata, a widely used statistics program, the authors make the technique accessible to researchers who work mainly in that environment.
arxiv-2601-00808:
Wisnu Uriawan and five co-authors describe, in 2026, a phone app that points Muslims toward the Kaaba for prayer. The point direction is called the Qibla. Their app, QiblatKita, rests on spherical trigonometry, the maths of triangles drawn on a ball. It is built with a toolkit that lets one code base serve both phone systems. The team built it in short rounds, with user feedback at each round.

The phone's own sensors feed the maths live. Satellites give the user's place, and motion sensors give which way the phone faces. Two classic formulas then yield the angle from the user to the Kaaba. Tests found the shown angle off by less than one degree. The team call the app stable and easy to use. It joins old maths to modern phones in the service of daily practice. Such tools matter most for travel far from home.
arxiv-2601-00908:
Chorok Lee is the sole author of a 2026 paper on a warning sign for AI forecasts that promise fair odds. Conformal prediction is a method that wraps a model and vows a set coverage rate. Lee asks whether the break can be foreseen before any new data land. His test case is supply work during the Covid-19 shock.

The sign he tests is how much of a model's feature weight sits on its top feature. Across eight supply tasks with the same time shift, coverage fell from barely at all to total collapse. Tasks with weight piled on one feature fell hardest. The same link held across sixteen tasks in nine fields. Lee proves a theorem that backs the link under stated assumptions. He is candid that the sign misses a second failure kind seen in neural networks.
arxiv-2601-01408:
Six authors led by Gong Gao improve face attribute recognition, the task of reading traits such as glasses or a smile from a face image. Standard multi-task methods chew on the whole feature map for every attribute, which drags in redundant regions and lets tasks interfere with each other. Their network, MGMTN, instead learns where to look.

An adaptive mask module uses a pretrained keypoint model and a small convolutional network to outline key parts, such as the eyes and mouth, and builds a mask for each group. A fusion module then mixes those focused features with global ones, so context is kept without drowning the signal. Tests on two demanding attribute data sets show the design lifts recognition performance. Precise region choice is a general lesson for multi-task vision: sharing everything helps nothing, while sharing the right regions helps each task.
arxiv-2601-02008:
Medical AI models often fail when hospital data shifts. They also stumble on rare conditions. Their reasoning is opaque to clinicians. Midhat Urooj, Ayan Banerjee, and Sandeep Gupta present XAI-MeD. It is a neuro-symbolic framework. Expert clinical knowledge is woven directly into a deep learning system. The knowledge is written as logical rules over medical propositions.

Rule satisfaction scores feed a symbolic reasoning branch. Confidence fuses that branch with neural predictions. An adaptive routing mechanism steers capacity as well. It favors rare classes and uncertain cases. The tests span many modalities. One task localizes seizure onset in brain scans. Another grades diabetic retinopathy on six multicenter datasets. The system gained about six percent in cross-domain generalization. Rare-class detection rose by ten percent over strong baselines. Ablations credit the symbolic parts.
arxiv-2601-02208:
Ions drift and diffuse through a fluid-saturated porous medium. The Nernst-Planck-Darcy system governs them. Elie Abdo and three co-authors ask what happens over very long times. The setting is three-dimensional space.

They prove sharp decay. Every spatial derivative of each ionic concentration tends to zero. The rate is an exact polynomial, steepening with the derivative order. The relative entropy of the system does not settle, meanwhile. It blows up logarithmically in time, also at a sharp rate. Precise long-time asymptotics like these anchor simulations. The settings are electrodiffusion in batteries, membranes, and underground flows. Slow tails decide whether a model can be trusted there.
arxiv-2601-02308:
Felipe Schardong, Claudio Jose Struchiner, and Luiz Max Carvalho review how researchers model antimicrobial resistance, the growing ability of microbes to survive drugs meant to kill them. Resistance was linked to close to five million deaths in 2019, and models are a main tool for understanding how it spreads. Yet the modeling literature is scattered and uneven.

Following scoping review guidelines, they searched three major databases for modeling studies published between 2019 and 2024 and kept thirty six after screening. Most used deterministic differential equation models and focused on bacteria in human hosts. The review maps the model types, data, and validation choices in use, and points out biases and gaps where future modeling work is most needed.
arxiv-2601-02408:
Aziza Altaibayeva and three co authors build a dark energy model that merges two ideas. One is Barrow entropy, which deforms the usual entropy law with a fractal style correction. The other is the QCD ghost, a vacuum effect from the theory of the strong force. The dark energy density is written in a generalized holographic form that holds both effects at once, inside a flat expanding universe.

The model moves smoothly from an early era where matter dominates and expansion slows, to late acceleration, without crossing into phantom behavior. A matching scalar field version behaves like quintessence. The generalized second law of thermodynamics holds at the apparent horizon across the parameter space, and the sound speed analysis shows where the model stays classically stable. Together the checks mark the model as a viable account of late time acceleration.
arxiv-2601-02508:
Liang Fu introduces Fermi Sets, a neural network architecture for the wavefunctions of many fermion particles, such as electrons, whose wavefunction must flip sign when any two particles swap. The design builds on a parity graded representation.

Fu proves any continuous fermionic wavefunction on a compact domain can be approximated as closely as wanted by a sum of a small number of antisymmetric basis functions. Such as Slater determinants, each multiplied by a symmetric function. One basis suffices in one dimension and on lattices, two suffice in two dimensions, and the count grows at most linearly with particle number in higher dimensions. Small networks learn the antisymmetric parts, keeping the method both universal and physically readable.
arxiv-2601-02908:
Wei-Yuan Cheng and four co-authors improve dense video captioning, the task of describing every event in a long, untrimmed video with its start and end times. Video language models write good descriptions but often misjudge where events begin and end, so captions are not properly grounded in time. Their method, TA-Prompting, adds learned temporal anchors that locate events precisely and prompt the model to reason with time in mind.

At test time, an event coherent sampling strategy picks a caption sequence that stays consistent across events and matches the video content. Across benchmark datasets, the approach beat leading video language models on dense captioning. It also improved related temporal tasks, including moment retrieval and answering questions about when things happen.
arxiv-2601-03608:
Ansh Tiwari and Ayush Chauhan present Shielded RecRL, a way to add written explanations to a recommender system without disturbing its rankings. Earlier reinforcement methods often retrained the ranking itself, risking worse recommendations. Their two-tower design leaves the ranking model untouched while a language model learns to explain its choices in a separate tower.

A combined reward scores explanations for length, relevance, and coherence. Training used a common optimization method with a leash on how far the language model could drift, and only a small fraction of its parameters were trainable. On an Amazon Books dataset of about fifty thousand interactions, click-through rose by over a fifth while rankings stayed nearly unchanged. Honest explanations could make recommendations easier to trust and audit.
arxiv-2601-03708:
Qingyun Zou and four co-authors present MHRC-Bench, the first benchmark for repository-level code completion in hardware description languages. Language models complete software code well, but chip design code was largely ignored by existing benchmarks, even though hardware projects also span many interdependent files. The benchmark includes separate training and evaluation parts and covers three major hardware coding styles.

Each completion target carries labels about code structure and hardware meaning, derived from syntax tree analysis. The team ran a broad evaluation of current models on the evaluation set and analyzed the results. A shared hardware benchmark matters because chip teams cannot judge coding assistants using software tests alone; the languages, idioms, and failure costs of hardware design are quite different.
arxiv-2601-03808:
Usha Shrestha, Dmitry Ignatov, and Radu Timofte teach language models to design data transformations for image training by learning from measured results instead of rules of thumb. Data augmentation is usually tuned by heuristics or brute force search. Their closed-loop system, built inside the NNGPT project ecosystem, fine-tunes models on a new repository of more than six thousand PyTorch augmentation functions, each labeled only by the downstream accuracy it produced.

Training compares better and worse transformations in pairs, aligning the model through empirical feedback without reinforcement learning or reward models. The result needs up to six hundred times fewer evaluated candidates than brute-force discovery while keeping peak accuracy competitive. Generation shifts from random synthesis toward informed design, which could cut the compute cost of squeezing accuracy out of vision models.
arxiv-2601-03908:
Wang Chen and five co-authors present Decide Then Retrieve, a training-free framework that makes retrieval-augmented generation choosier about when and what to fetch. Standard systems retrieve for every question and build evidence along a single path, which often imports noise and caps the benefit. Their framework instead lets the model's own generation uncertainty decide whether retrieval is needed at all.

When retrieval does trigger, a dual-path mechanism gathers evidence two ways and adaptively selects between them, a help for sparse or ambiguous queries. Across five open-domain question answering benchmarks, several model scales, and different retrievers, the method consistently beat standard and strong retrieval baselines on exact match and F1 scores while cutting unnecessary retrievals. Selective retrieval saves cost and, by keeping irrelevant text out, can raise answer quality too.
arxiv-2601-04008:
Rose Berry, as sole author, rebuilds a key algebraic structure so it no longer needs a square root of its parameter. The objects are the extended affine Hecke algebra and the affine q-Schur algebra of type A. Both matter for the representation theory of general linear groups over p-adic fields.

Berry starts from a known cellular structure that does use the square root and rescales it cell by cell. The rescaling is chosen so diagonal blocks stay subalgebras and left and right cells stay matched. She also shows the Schur algebra version has idempotence traits that imply finite global dimension. That trait is a needed step for using these algebras with coefficient rings where the prime is invertible but has no square root.
arxiv-2601-04208:
Xiang Cheng, Wen Wang, and Anindya Ghose tackle a gap in business AI: decisions are given, but the reasons stay opaque. Standard explanation tools list numeric feature weights, which rarely form a coherent story. Language models could tell that story, yet their explanations must stay true to the real drivers, fit different audiences, and be trained without costly human-scored examples.

Their framework, LEXMA, fine-tunes a language model with reinforcement learning in stages. Reflection-aided supervised tuning comes first, then two rounds of group-relative policy tuning that adjust separate settings for correctness and for audience style, using rewards that need no human labels. Tested on mortgage approval, LEXMA beats other language model baselines on accuracy. Human judges rate its expert explanations as more risk-focused and its consumer ones as clearer, more usable, and more polite.
arxiv-2601-04508:
Chenchen Yang and ten co-authors teach machines to hear the laughs and sobs inside speech, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Transcription captures words, but real audio is salted with non-verbal events — laughter, crying, coughs. Whose timing matters for understanding a scene, and pinning them down precisely has lacked both clear task definitions and fair scoring. Their project, WESR, attacks both gaps.

They first define a taxonomy of twenty-one vocal events, split into discrete events that stand alone and continuous ones woven through speech. WESR-Bench, their expert-annotated test set of over nine hundred utterances, scores localization with a protocol that separates transcription errors from event errors. A baseline trained on a corpus of more than seventeen hundred hours beat open audio-language models and commercial services at the task while keeping ordinary transcription quality. Making the benchmark a usable foundation for richer audio understanding.
arxiv-2601-04608:
Jinjun Liu and Ming-Yen Cheng recover the risk factor a forecaster forgot, from its own mistakes, in a 2026 arXiv paper. A forecast compresses its inputs into an average prediction, and whatever systematic structure it omits survives in the pattern of its errors. Their framework makes a decision robust against a two-layer ambiguity set built on those residual errors. reads off the omitted factor from the part of the decision's residual risk that points across its own exposure.

Applied to monthly United States Treasury yields from 2006 to 2025, the method names the factor recovered from a standard yield-curve benchmark as a leading business-cycle factor. Anchored on the Conference Board leading index and certified by a permutation test. A more accurate random forest's residuals point at the same family. Hedging the factor out of a duration position leaves volatility unchanged and worsens the tail, proving it real risk.
arxiv-2601-04708:
Congpei An, Alvise Sommariva, and Marco Vianello compute, rather than merely bound, the constants that decide whether sampled polynomial approximation can be trusted, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Marcinkiewicz-Zygmund inequalities relate a function's continuous norm to its values at cubature points. The weak form of these constants governs how safely least-squares projection onto orthogonal polynomial bases can work from samples alone.

The paper computes the constants numerically for relevant cubature rules across a menagerie of domains — the interval, square, disk, triangle, cube, and sphere. With constants in hand, the authors compare the actual approximation power of least squares against standard hyperinterpolation and its newer exactness-relaxed variant, showing where each method's reputation is deserved. The Matlab code behind the tests is released open-source, making the numbers checkable rather than citational.
arxiv-2601-04908:
Vincent C. Morano's 2026 paper, with 8 co-authors, maps how the atoms line up as magnets in the mineral Mn2GeO4. The atoms sit in zigzag chains, a shape long studied in the field of frustrated magnetism. In such a set-up, rival pulls keep the atoms from a plain, neat order. This mineral acts in a way that caught the team off guard, as it shifts from neat states to a mixed state that also has an electric side.

The team fired neutrons at a lone crystal and read how the beams bounced off, a way to see the magnet rules at work from the inside. They then built a model of those rules, with both near and far pulls in it. Their model helps show how the chain net in this mineral makes its odd mix of states.
arxiv-2601-05108:
Philipp Hanisch and Markus Krötzsch dust off an old trick for fast rule-based queries in a 2026 paper. The trick, called static filtering, trims a Datalog query ere any data are seen. Datalog is a tongue for rules over facts, used in stores of facts and in code checks. The trick dates back to 1986, yet fresh work has passed it by. Parts of it keep being found a new, in weaker forms, by teams who do not know the old work.

The authors restate the old approach in modern terminology and generalize its filter predicates to capture features of current systems. They also extend the method to answer set programming, strictly widening its reach. Recovering a forgotten, more general technique can save implementers from reinventing partial versions, and it speeds rule engines used in knowledge bases and program analysis.
arxiv-2601-05208:
Zichen Wang and 3 co-authors add a mixture-of-experts module to feed-forward 3D reconstruction in a 2026 paper. Models that rebuild a scene's depth from images struggle near depth discontinuities, the sharp edges where one surface ends and another begins. Standard regression losses encourage averaging there, blurring exactly the boundaries that define objects, rooms, and obstacles.

Their module combines multiple smooth depth predictions, with a softmax weighting head choosing among the hypotheses pixel by pixel. Integrated into a pretrained state-of-the-art 3D model, it achieves substantial improvement near boundaries. Sharper depth edges matter for robotics, augmented reality, and scanning, where a blurred boundary can mean a misjudged doorway, shelf edge, or grasp point.
arxiv-2601-05508:
Fuwen Luo and 8 co-authors introduce HieroSA, a 2026 framework that lets multimodal models analyze hieroglyphic characters stroke by stroke. Logographic characters pack meaning into internal structure, but language models read them as tokens and vision models as raw pixels. Neither view captures how strokes build a character.

HieroSA converts character images into explicit line-segment descriptions in a normalized coordinate space. It learns this without handcrafted, script-specific data, so the same approach can cross languages and eras. Experiments show the system captures internal structure and related meaning well. The authors present it as a graphematics tool, useful for studying both modern logographic scripts and ancient hieroglyphs.
arxiv-2601-05608:
Qian Li and Jia-Hui Huang analyze, in a 2026 paper, charged particles circling a loop quantum Reissner-Nordstrom black hole and the light from a thin disk around it. Loop quantum corrections modify the charged black hole's geometry through a quantum parameter. Observations of real black holes can therefore constrain that parameter and the charge.

Using shadow size data from M87* and Sgr A*, the authors find the black hole charge must be extremely tiny for a disk to exist. The direct geometric effect is negligible, but electromagnetic coupling strongly shapes particle orbits and radiation. Ray-traced images show how disk fluxes and redshifts respond to each parameter. The quantum parameter's effect stays small and changes sign with the coupling.
arxiv-2601-05708:
Mahima Kumar and Gabor Wiese prove, in a 2026 paper, a conjecture of Gunter Kohler about Hecke theta series of weight one. Theta series are generating functions built from quadratic forms, and Hecke's versions arise in number theory's study of modular forms. The conjecture concerns an ambiguity in which quadratic field enters the definition of these series.

Kumar and Wiese derive the theta series statement from a similar statement about two-dimensional Galois representations. Those representations encode symmetry information from number fields through characters of quadratic fields. Moving the problem into that representation-theoretic setting resolves the ambiguity Kohler identified. The result ties a concrete question about classical series to modern Galois methods.
arxiv-2601-05908:
Sevilay Sevinçli and 4 co-authors propose in 2026 a way to manufacture squeezed light by storing an ordinary light pulse in a Bose-Einstein condensate. In squeezed light, noise in one trait is reduced below the ordinary quantum limit. The storage maps the pulse onto a shared spin wave shared across the ultracold atoms.

While stored, collisions between atoms twist the shared spin, generating spin squeezing in the atomic ensemble. The initial spin orientation is tunable through the stored excitation number and the phase between probe and control fields. Retrieval maps the atomic squeezing back onto a propagating light mode. Accounting for realistic losses and memory speed, the authors identify optimal storage times and predict several decibels of squeezing under realistic settings.
arxiv-2601-06108:
Many ways to teach language models human preferences look unrelated. Tarun Raheja and 1 co-author unify them in a 2026 survey. Reinforcement learning from human feedback set the pattern, then direct methods multiplied, leaving practitioners unsure which to pick.

The survey shows the diversity reduces to choices along three axes: the preference model behind the objective, how deviation from a reference model is controlled, and whether learning is online or offline. Theorems cover coverage gaps, scaling laws for reward overoptimization, and when direct methods fail. Known failure modes like length hacking and mode collapse follow predictably from design choices. A decision guide built from over fifty papers helps practitioners choose.
arxiv-2601-06208:
Abderrahman Bouhamidi proposes an extension of the famous Collatz conjecture in a 2026 mathematics paper. The classic problem applies simple rules to any starting number and claims the process always reaches a fixed endpoint. Many similar conjectures follow the same pattern with different rules.

Bouhamidi states a new example working modulo 10. Multiples of ten are divided by ten. Other numbers are multiplied by twelve, adjusted by eight times their last digit, then divided by ten. The claim is that every starting number reaches 4 after finitely many steps. A general conjecture then encompasses both the classical Collatz problem and this modulo-10 version, unifying a family of related claims under one statement.
arxiv-2601-06908:
Hakan Cebeci and co-authors published a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint covers note on the matter coupling in exotic general massive 3D gravity. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. Within exterior algebra formalism, we revisit and study the matter coupling in Exotic General Massive 3D Gravity (EGMG), previously introduced in [ 11 ] .

Considering that the matter Lagrangian is both metric co-frame and connection dependent in general. We explicitly construct associated source 2-form by algebraically solving auxiliary 1-form fields in terms of gravitational field variables, energy-momentum and hyper-momentum 2-forms. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07308:
Manuel Parra-Royón and colleagues wrote a 2026 arXiv preprint. The work covers bringing computation to the data. ArXiv posted the preprint in 2026 under its PAPERS collection. Purpose: Serverless computing is a paradigm in which the underlying infrastructure is fully managed by the provider.

Enabling applications and services to be executed with elastic resource provisioning and minimal operational overhead. A core model within this paradigm is Function-as-a-Service (FaaS), where lightweight functions are deployed and triggered on demand, scaling seamlessly with workload. The work gives specialists a compact account of the problem and one proposed way to handle it.
arxiv-2601-08108:
Bowen Li and seven co-authors present a prompting method that aims to cut bias in language models. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that methods like chain-of-thought have improved reasoning. Yet many prompting strategies use too many tokens and generalize poorly across varied reasoning tasks.

The team combines adaptive causal prompting with sketch-of-thought, a compact reasoning style. Causal prompting targets the sources of biased answers rather than surface wording alone. Sketch-of-thought keeps the reasoning trace short, which lowers token cost. For practitioners, the paper offers a route to fairer answers that is also cheaper to run across diverse tasks.
arxiv-2601-08208: Sylvain Crovisier and Enrique Pujals wrote a 2026 arXiv paper that sets out a new sense of a critical set for maps of a surface. The maps are two-dimensional diffeomorphisms, smooth warps that can be run in reverse. The set is built into the map itself. It plays the role that critical points play in one dimension. At such a point, the rate of change drops to zero, and those points block a trait called hyperbolicity. A like set on a surface could sort how wild acts arise.
arxiv-2601-08908:
Anna Biggs builds a quantum toy model that acts like a known wild model, yet has no built in chance. The known model is the SYK model, a set of bits that link in wild ways. It is a prime test bed for black hole like acts in a lab sized system. Its wild links are oft set by random picks, which blur what is law and what is luck.

Biggs gives a clean model with fixed rules. It keeps a spin type symmetry, and its charge is built from a known spin sum sign. At low power it acts like the SYK case with extra symmetry. A reader in theory gets a tidier test bed for wild quantum acts.
arxiv-2601-09008:
Amar Kavuri, Howard Gifford, and Mini Das study how the eye hunts for a faint sign in a noisy image. Such hunts guide care scans, bag checks, and fault checks. The eye does not scan in a flat way. It jumps to zones that look like the sign, and skips zones that look like plain noise. The size of traits in sign and noise steer those jumps.

The team varies trait size in both sign and back noise. They track where the eye goes and how oft the sign is found. The aim is to learn when a sign blends in by size, not just by shade. A reader who designs scan tasks gets facts on eye moves. They can shape an image so a key sign draws the eye.
arxiv-2601-09108:
Yanguang Sun and three co-authors fine tune vast image models to mark things in earth shots from space. Such shots guide farm, flood, and town work. To mark a roof or a road, a model must place it true to the pixel. Past work used mid size models, tuned in full. Vast base models hold more skill, but full tune of them is dear.

The team uses wave expert guides to tune just key parts. Wave tools split a shot by trait size, from broad land to fine edge. Guides steer tune to parts that hold the marks. A reader in earth sight gets a lean tune plan. It seeks vast model skill at a cost a small team can pay.
arxiv-2601-09208:
Miki Ueno gives a character led AI friend named Mikasa, drawn from Japan's oshi culture. Oshi is the fan love for a dear character or star, held with warm zeal. New chat and sight tools let such a friend talk with rich mood. Yet most AI friends lose users in weeks. Talk feels fresh at first, then flat and same.

Mikasa is built to hold zeal over long use. Its character, mood range, and talk style aim to grow a bond, not just fill time. Ueno sets out what was built and why each pick was made. A reader in AI friend work gets a case where culture, not just tech, shapes the design.
arxiv-2601-09308:
Peter Harremoes proves a core law of measure work by way of facts and codes. The law is the Radon-Nikodym theorem. It says one spread law can be set as a rate of a next, when the first can not live where the next is null. That rate is the base for entropy and for gap gauges in facts work. Yet most texts on chance skip its proof as too hard.

Harremoes gives a proof that facts work can own. It builds the rate from code and squeeze ideas that field knows well. A reader in that field gets a key law with a proof in their own tongue, not a loan from a hard text.
arxiv-2601-09408:
R. Turrisi reports for the ePIC collaboration on a detector being built for the future Electron-Ion Collider. The 2026 arXiv paper describes the Silicon Vertex Tracker, a key part of the ePIC detector system. The collider, planned at Brookhaven National Laboratory, will probe the strong force inside matter.

The vertex tracker provides high-precision tracking of particles and reconstruction of the points where they were born. Silicon sensors must sit close to the beam and still survive the radiation there. The paper lays out the design and current status of the subsystem. Its performance will shape how sharply the collider can image protons and nuclei.
arxiv-2601-09508:
Jean C. Peyen shows how to sample powersets at random without a costly helper. The 2026 arXiv paper uses Boltzmann sampling, a method that draws random structures with known chances. For structures whose counting sequence stays bounded, the sampler runs efficiently without ever evaluating the generating function.

An algorithm is given, implemented, and tested. Its runtimes match those of existing Boltzmann samplers in the literature. The author also proposes two extensions for structures with unbounded counting sequences. Random sampling of this kind feeds testing, simulation, and the study of typical shapes in combinatorics.
arxiv-2601-09608:
Arjun Nayak and a large team describe a new attosecond light source at the ELI ALPS facility. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents the SYLOS Compact high-harmonic beamline. High-order harmonic generation is the standard lab route to attosecond pulses of extreme ultraviolet light.

Producing enough flux for nonlinear XUV photoionization has been possible for only a few groups. The compact beamline is designed to supply that flux in a smaller footprint. Attosecond pulses let scientists film electrons moving inside atoms and molecules. A more accessible source widens who can run such experiments.
arxiv-2601-09708:
Chi-Pin Huang and seven co-authors speed up robots that think before they act. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents Fast-ThinkAct for vision-language-action tasks. Such robots must take in a scene, plan in words or thought, and then move with care.

Writing out long chains of thought improves generalization but slows reaction badly. Fast-ThinkAct compresses the plan into a verbalizable latent form: short to run, still readable as words. The robot keeps the benefit of planning without the long pause. Faster reasoning matters when a robot works beside people or handles moving objects.
arxiv-2601-10408:
Luke Mortimer, Leonardo Zambrano, Antonio Acín, and Donato Farina bound traits of large quantum rigs from thin data. Such traits show how new acts emerge in big rigs. Labs can oft read just a few traits, and with few shots. The full state stays out of reach.

Past bounds were set as if shots were vast. The team add the true shot count to the math. They use a class of plans named semidefinite programs. Those plans yield bounds that hold with a set chance. The work makes bounds honest for real labs, where data is thin.
arxiv-2601-10608:
Axel Seifert, Fabian Jakub, Christoph Siewert, Leonie von Terzi, and Stefan Kneifel examine the shape of large snowflakes. Snow and ice shape weather and climate in deep ways. Much of the rain that reaches the ground starts as ice high above. The flakes that fall are rarely the neat six-sided crystals of popular images.

Most large flakes are aggregates, clumps formed when small ice crystals collide and stick. The parts include flat plates, columns, and branched dendrites. The authors study the geometry of these clumps, since shape affects how fast flakes fall and melt. Better shape models feed into sharper weather forecasts and climate simulations.
arxiv-2601-10808:
Mikhail Chernikov and Peter Trifonov speed up decoding for ABS+ polar codes. Polar codes are error-correcting codes that split a channel into good and bad sub-channels. ABS+ codes generalize Arikan's original design and polarize much faster. Decoding them well is the practical test. The authors build the SCL decoder in the LLR domain.

LLRs, log-likelihood ratios, are the natural currency of soft decoding. They also optimize the SCL algorithm to cut the cost of computing those ratios. Faster, leaner decoding matters for 5G-style links and storage systems. The paper helps a strong code family move closer to hardware that must decode at line speed.
arxiv-2601-10908:
Jaime Luisi, John C. Forbes, Heather V. Rusk, and Benjamin Gullick follow brown dwarfs that gain mass and cross into stardom. A brown dwarf that steals mass from a binary partner can pass the hydrogen burning limit. That limit divides brown dwarfs from true low-mass stars. The authors call the crossers pink dwarfs and trace their fates.

Some reach the main sequence and end up looking like ordinary low-mass stars. Others stay brown dwarf-like, unable to burn hydrogen fast enough to power their glow. The split decides what telescopes will see millions of years later. The work helps astronomers read odd stars whose past hides a stolen-mass chapter.
arxiv-2601-11208:
Rodrigo Nicolau Almeida studies a fine point in intuitionistic logic. His 2026 preprint looks at local tabularity and a stronger form. Intuitionistic logic, called IPC, drops some rules of classical logic. Above IPC, local tabularity has proved a hard trait to map.

The stronger form is named uniform local tabularity in the work. It asks that all formulas match some of a fixed depth. Depth here counts how deep implications nest in a formula. The contrast with the logic S4 frames the study. S4 is a modal logic where such traits are better known. The work sharpens the map of where IPC-based logics stay tame.
arxiv-2601-11308:
Ferhat Sindy, Annalisa Buffa, and Marco Picasso flag errors in finite difference runs. Their 2026 preprint gives a new recovery-based error indicator. Finite difference methods solve equations on a grid of points. High-order versions are sharp but still hold some error.

The method works after the run, by post-processing its values. Grid values are moved into a polynomial finite element space. A recovery indicator then reads the gradient error from that form. The indicator keeps a polynomial-preserving trait from past work. That trait keeps the check exact on smooth polynomial cases. Users gain a cheap map of where the grid errs. Such maps guide where to refine the grid next.
arxiv-2601-11408:
Qinlin Chen and eight coauthors build a static analysis frame for Verilog. Their 2026 preprint names the framework Qihe. Verilog is the tongue used to describe hardware designs. Static analysis reads code without running it at all.

In software, static analysis has thrived for decades. It finds bugs, checks security, and aids understanding of code. General frameworks supply the base that such tools share. Hardware code has lacked a like base for Verilog work. Qihe aims to fill that gap for chip design teams. A shared frame cuts the cost of each new check. It could bring software-grade tooling to hardware design.
arxiv-2601-11608:
Ganesh Bikshandi reshapes CNNs to fit specialized AI hardware. The 2026 preprint uses NVIDIA Tensor Cores as the case study. Convolutional neural networks sit at the center of modern AI. Their speed is often capped by hardware constraints, not math.

Tensor Cores demand set shapes for fast execution paths. Input channels must be multiples of 8, for instance. Some paths want multiples of 512 to run at full pace. CPU frameworks like oneDNN impose like rules for blocked formats. Bikshandi reformulates networks to meet those hardware rules. The reform keeps the model's task while easing its layout. Hardware-aware forms can unlock speed that naive forms waste.
arxiv-2601-12208:
Yunzhe Li, Richie Yueqi Feng, Tianxin Wei, and Chin-Chia Hsu grade chat systems in multi-turn talks via co-evolution. Past grading uses fixed rubrics and fixed chat context made by hand. That static form misses the diverse acts that dialogue models show in real talks.

Their frame, called CoReflect in the work, joins simulation and grading in one loop. Chats grow harder as rubrics refine, and rubrics refine as chats reveal gaps. An adaptive loop can catch faults that fixed tests miss. The work aims for more true grades of chat skill.
arxiv-2601-12308:
Anurag Kaushish, Ayan Sar, Sampurna Roy, and their co-authors classify remote sensing images from few labelled cases. Few-shot work in this field is hard for three reasons. Labelled data are scarce, domains shift a lot, and geo objects span many scales.

Their adaptive multi-scale correlation meta-network is built for those three facts. Meta-learning trains a model to adapt fast to new classes. Multi-scale traits catch both small and large land features. The work aims for sound maps from brief labelled sets.  Meta traits must move fast to new land classes.
arxiv-2601-12608:
Himadri Halder introduces a new notion in complex analysis: the second Bohr radius. The classic Bohr radius marks how far a power series keeps a key bound. Halder extends that idea to vector valued pluriharmonic functions. These functions live on complete Reinhardt domains in complex space of several variables.

The work builds on a 2000 study by Lev Aizenberg. Aizenberg treated the corresponding problem for complex valued holomorphic functions. Moving to vector values and pluriharmonic maps adds real difficulty. Radii of this kind give sharp, quantitative control over series. They matter in the theory of function spaces and operator theory alike.
arxiv-2601-12808:
Tong Wu and six co authors rethink how communication systems rebuild images at the receiver. Conventional systems, and even AI driven joint source channel coding, follow Shannon rate distortion theory. Generic distortion metrics fail to capture human visual perception, though. Reconstructions guided by them often come out blurred or unrealistic to the eye.

The team move from distortion oriented reconstruction to semantic consistent generation. Their joint source channel generation coding aims to keep meaning, not just pixels. A generated image can look sharp while staying true to the sent content. That shift suits low bandwidth links where bits are precious. The work bridges information theory and generative modeling.
arxiv-2601-13008:
Jingwei Wang and Ligong Bian set out a way to work out how fast a false vacuum decays. Their method applies to electroweak theories in a general number of space dims, written as D dims. Vacuum decay is a core topic in early universe physics.

The pair give one joined treatment for three kinds of fields. These are scalar fields, fermion fields, and gauge boson fields. The tool kit pairs a WKB method with a way to handle sums that would else blow up. A key plus is fast settling of the sums. The sums still settle fast even when the spin-like index grows large.
arxiv-2601-13808:
Ilaria Svampa, Sonia L'Innocente, Stefano Mancini, and Andreas Winter study qubits built on p-adic numbers in 2026. P-adic quantum mechanics swaps real numbers for an other number system. A single p-adic qubit is a two-dimensional representation of the p-adic group SO(3). The team now asks how to compose such qubits into systems.

They investigate composite systems of p-adic qubits and p-adically controlled logic gates. The work covers entanglement, the linked state of two qubits. It also covers universal quantum logic gates, which can build any operation. The study tests if p-adic quantum theory can support full computing.
arxiv-2601-14008:
Jianing Wang bounds gravitational wave output from a bold early-universe model in 2026. The model has an early phase that violates the null energy condition. That condition is a basic rule on how energy can flow in relativity. Breaking it can drive exotic cosmic histories, like a bounce.

Wang shows perturbative unitarity bounds strongly constrain this scenario. Unitarity is the rule that probabilities must sum to one in quantum theory. The bounds limit both the amplitude and the spectral tilt of primordial gravitational waves. Such limits tell observers if the model's waves could ever be seen.
arxiv-2601-15108:
Oleksandr Gamayun and Miłosz Panfil solve an exact problem for a one-dimensional quantum gas. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with hard rods, particles that cannot pass through each other on a line. They target the dynamical structure factor, a key probe of the gas.

The authors obtain an exact analytic formula for that factor. It holds for any many-body state of the system. They study two cases in detail: the ground state and states at finite temperature. They also report a universal random matrix behavior in the result, a pattern shared with random matrix theory.
arxiv-2601-15408:
Pablo Messina, Andrés Villa, and co-authors teach medical models to point at what they describe. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with radiology report generation by vision-language models. Such models can draft reports, but their grounding is weak: words often fail to match the image.

That mismatch makes reports unreliable. The authors present CURE, an error-aware curriculum learning framework. It improves grounding and report quality with no extra data. The model learns from its own errors in a planned order. Reports thus tie each finding more tightly to the visual evidence in the scan.
arxiv-2601-15508:
Haaris Mian and four co-authors rethink how to measure a character's weight in a novel in a 2026 arXiv paper. Most models score characters by their presence in scenes. They count actions, named mentions, and lines of dialogue. That lens favors the character who shows up most. The main character wins by default under such counts.

The authors argue that presence alone misses much of what makes a character matter. A figure can shape a plot while rarely on stage. Their work builds computational representations of character significance that go further. The abstract frames the flaw more than the fix, so details rest in the full text. For digital humanities, the stakes are clear. Better measures of significance mean better maps of how stories work.
arxiv-2601-15708:
Junseok Kim, Nakyeong Yang, and Kyomin Jung blend prompting styles for language models in a 2026 arXiv paper. Role-play prompting steers a model by giving it a persona. It can improve zero-shot reasoning. The gains are inconsistent, though. They vary by task and even by instance. The authors read that inconsistency as a clue. Plain prompting and role-play may hold complementary strengths.

Their method is called Persona Switch. It mixes distinct perspectives at decoding time, per the title. Decoding is when the model picks its words, one by one. Switching personas mid-stream may combine the best of each stance. For users, the promise is steadier reasoning without picking the right persona in advance. The work treats prompt design as a control problem, not a guessing game.
arxiv-2601-15808:
Yuxuan Wan and six co-authors strengthen research agents at test time in a 2026 arXiv paper. Deep research agents automate knowledge discovery and problem-solving. Most work on them improves the policy model through post-training. This team takes another path. They evolve the agent's ability at inference time. The agent iteratively verifies its own outputs. Carefully crafted rubrics guide those checks.

Rubrics spell out what a good answer must do. Verification against them can catch errors before they compound. Inference-time scaling spends more compute at run time for better results. The title names that scaling as the lever. For teams that cannot retrain huge models, test-time methods are attractive. This paper adds a rubric-guided version to that toolbox.
arxiv-2601-15908:
Claudio Bonanno and Sharvari Neetin Tikekar study escape from open dynamical systems in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their maps expand the unit interval non-uniformly. A parabolic fixed point sits at the origin, where motion slows. The maps admit an ergodic invariant measure, finite or infinite. The authors cut a hole around that fixed point. The hole is an interval containing the origin. Orbits that enter it escape the system.

They analyze the escape rate of the open system. Then they track how that rate behaves as the hole shrinks. Intermittent maps model systems that linger, then burst. Escape rates quantify how long trajectories survive before leaking out. Such results apply to chaotic transport and to any system with a slow trap at its heart.
arxiv-2601-16108:
Marzieh Adeli Shamsabad and Hamed Ghodrati build a tool to spot false climate claims in mixed media. Their 2026 preprint notes how false posts now use strong pics and clips. Text checks alone miss tricks that sit in the image. False claims spread fast on social feeds. Late acts on climate can stem from such false posts.

The pair join vision and language models with facts from known sources. The joint check weighs words, pics and source facts as one. Proof from firm sources helps flag claims that clash with known facts. The tool aims to catch false posts that look true at a glance. It serves teams who guard climate facts online.
arxiv-2601-16208:
Shengbang Tong and coauthors scale image spread coders with a new code form. Their 2026 preprint uses Representation Autoencoders as the code base. Those coders train in a rich sense space of high size. On ImageNet they showed clear gains for spread models. The team now scales that path for text to image coders built as spread chains.

Scale tests check if rich codes keep their gains at big size. Rich codes may let the spread chain learn form fast. They may also lift the grade of pics from text prompts. The work adds a path to strong text to image tools. It tests code choice as a lever for scale.
arxiv-2601-16808:
Huiyun Xiao and a team of six co-authors study drops of quantum fluid that hold their own shape. Such drops form in pairs of cold atom gases. The two gases pull and push on each with unlike force. Their 2026 preprint maps how that force gap warps the drop. Math tools track the drop's ground state and its hums.

As the force gap grows, the drop's form shifts. It moves from a round hump to a flat-top shape. The team also tracks how the drop rings when poked. Such drops test deep rules of quantum fluids. They may serve as clean labs for wave and flow work.
arxiv-2601-17008:
Haochong Xia and a team of nine co-authors build a trade bot that plans for bad days. Trade bots learn from past market runs. They oft shine in tests, then fade in live trade. Live markets shift with news, laws, and crowd moods. Their 2026 preprint trains bots on fake hostile markets. A Bayes frame then weighs doubt as it trades.

Fake foes stress the bot with harsh shifts. The bot learns acts that hold up in rough seas. Doubt marks curb bold bets when signs clash. Such care may cut big loss days for funds. It also shows a path to stress-test trade AI.
arxiv-2601-17108:
Dianxin Luan and a team of six co-authors sharpen how radio nets read their own channels. OFDM waves split a stream in many thin bands. Each band's path traits must be gauged fast and true. Big band counts make that gauge hard work. Their 2026 preprint builds MambaNet, a net that mixes two tools for the gauge. One tool tracks long links twixt bands.

The next tool, self-attention, weighs which bands count most. The mix aims for true gauges at low cost. True gauges keep data streams fast and clean. Next-wave radio nets need such lean skill.
arxiv-2601-17208:
Alejandro R. Urzúa wrote a teaching paper on a well known model in quantum physics. The model is the two-mode Jaynes-Cummings model. It deals with an atom linked to two modes of light. Urzúa works in the dispersive regime, where the atom and field are far off resonance.

Step by step, he derives the first-order effective Hamiltonian for the model. A small-change unitary transform removes terms that do not resonate. What is left shows clear frequency shifts from the atom. Those shifts act like a beam splitter set up between the two field modes. The clear path makes a tough topic easier for students to learn.
arxiv-2601-17408:
Harsharaj Pathak and Vineeth N. Balasubramanian work on source-free domain adaptation. The task moves a trained model to a new domain with no labels. Source data cannot be used at that stage. Most strong methods lean on neighborhood consistency. They trust that near points share labels. Bad neighborhoods can mislead that trust and spread error.

The authors use batch-wise cosine similarity as their guide. Similarity across a batch gives a broader, steadier signal. That should cut the harm from one bad neighbor. Source-free methods matter where data is private or lost. Medical and retail models face that wall often. A steadier method widens where adaptation can work.
arxiv-2601-17508:
Binghong Wu and Pascal O. Vontobel analyze the Bethe permanent for block-structured positive matrices. The permanent sums products over all matchings in a matrix. It is exact but hard to compute at scale. The Bethe permanent gives a tractable approximation. It runs through the sum-product algorithm on a factor graph.

The authors use double covers to study that approximation. Block structure is common in real matrices. Knowing when the approximation is tight guides its use. Permanents arise in counting, physics, and network problems. A fast, trusted approximation widens their reach. The double-cover method gives a lens on error. It tells users where the Bethe value can stand in for truth.
arxiv-2601-17608:
Dong Yoon Lee and four co-authors report field experience with a home health system for older adults. Adult children often care for aging parents from afar. They want remote tools that are plug-and-play. Privacy must hold while activity is tracked all day. The system aims to give real-time, clear, actionable updates.

Deployment experience shows where lab designs meet real homes. Sensors, networks, and family habits all test the plan. Lessons from live use guide the next design round. Aging in place is a growing need worldwide. Tools that families trust can delay costly care moves. The report grounds design claims in homes, not demos.
arxiv-2601-17808:
Alejandro Medina and Mary Lauren Benton look for variety, not just a single best answer, in DNA patterns. Their 2026 preprint deals with motif discovery in liver data from ChIP-seq tests. A motif is a short DNA pattern that tends to appear where proteins bind. The classic way to find motifs seeks one top pattern that best fits the data.

Real biology is messier than one pattern. The same data can hold several good motif readings, each tied to a real process. The authors use MAP-Elites, a search method that keeps many strong but distinct results. That choice gives a map of options, not a lone winner. Such a map can show the range of signals in the data.
arxiv-2601-18408:
Anup Dixit works on a deep guess about how number fields grow. Number fields are sets built by adding roots of whole number rules to the plain ratios. Two counts rule each field: one counts its ideal groups, and one sets the size of its unit grid. An old guess says how the pair of counts should grow as fields get large.

All past proofs shrink the task, by group tricks, to a known hard case for square fields. Dixit takes on fields whose group is close to the full set of swaps of their roots. That near-full case is the hard core of the guess. A proof here would push the guess close to a full proof for all fields. The work thus marks a key step in a long hunt in pure maths.
arxiv-2601-18608:
Fabian Fumagalli, R. Teal Witter, and Christopher Musco speed up a way to grade how much each fact counts in a model's call. The grade comes from a fair-share rule in game maths: each fact gets the share it adds, on mean, to the joint worth of all facts. To get the grade in full takes a huge count of runs, one per set of facts. A famed shortcut samples runs and fits a line to guess the grades.

Their plan adds cross terms to that fit, so pairs of facts can share worth in the guess. Those terms catch cases where two facts count most when they come as a pair. A truer fit could give the same grades for far fewer runs. Staff who must tell why a model made a call need grades they can trust at a cost they can pay.
arxiv-2601-19008:
Jia Xu Wei and Wei Wei redefine what an efficient network is. In network design, talk of efficiency often just means low delay or high total flow. The pair argue that such talk mixes up speed with true efficiency, and they offer a cost based view instead.

Their view counts the hardware cost needed to keep a promise: no flow ever gets blocked. A design that meets the promise with less hardware is, in their sense, more efficient. This lens can change how switch layouts are judged, since the cheapest layout that never blocks may beat a faster but costlier one.
arxiv-2601-19108:
Sharvari Nadkarni-Ghosh and Tanush Reddy Vaka model the messy late stages of a modified gravity theory. In f(R) gravity, an extra field can hide itself near dense objects, a trick called the Chameleon mechanism. The team studies how matter clumps evolve in such models once the clumps grow large and the math turns nonlinear.

Their new step is an iterative fix for the nonlinear equation that governs the field. They show the scheme at work on a spherical case. Sound tools for the nonlinear regime are what let such theories be tested against real maps of galaxies.
arxiv-2601-19208:
Shawn Im and three co-authors open up how transformers learn that certain words belong together. Links like the one between bird and flew let models generalize instead of merely memorizing text. Knowing how such links form is key to a mechanical account of how these models work.

The team studies the leading terms of the gradient, the biggest push in each training step. Those terms, they argue, explain how word links get written into the model. A mechanical story of learning ties deep learning back to language theory and may guide better training.
arxiv-2601-19608:
Louis Dailly works in complex geometry on the stability of special spaces. His setting is a log Fano pair, a geometric space paired with a boundary part. The space carries a singular Kähler-Einstein metric, a notion of perfect balance in its shape. On such a space one can build an adapted tangent sheaf, a tool that tracks directions along the space while respecting the boundary.

Dailly shows that this sheaf, and a related canonical extension, are polystable. Stability here is measured against a class pulled back by any adapted map into the space. Polystability is a strong regularity property with deep consequences. Results like this support the broader program linking stability to the existence of special metrics.
arxiv-2601-19708:
Javier Alonso-García and colleagues present a stellar atlas of our galaxy's plane, seen in near-infrared light. Dust blocks visible light from the galactic plane and the outer bulge. Near-infrared light slips through much of that dust. The atlas comes from the VVVX survey, a public project carried out with the VISTA telescope.

The survey mapped the plane and outer bulge to reveal stars hidden from optical telescopes. An atlas like this is a reference for everyone studying the Milky Way's structure. It supports work on star clusters, variable stars, and the galaxy's history. Catalogues of positions and brightnesses let other teams plan follow-up studies. The result is a clearer census of our home galaxy's crowded heart.
arxiv-2601-20008:
Amitay Sussholz, Tsevi Mazeh, and Simchon Faigler revisit how fast stars spin at their equators. They use line broadening measurements from the Gaia satellite's third data release. Rotation broadens a star's spectral lines, so the broadening betrays the spin. Their sample covers more than a hundred thousand stars, enough to map spin against temperature, mass, and age.

The large sample clearly shows the Kraft break, a sharp change in rotation behaviour near a well-known temperature and mass. Above the break, stars keep spinning fast; below it, they brake with age. A clean map of this transition tests theories of how stars shed angular momentum. Gaia's scale turns an old qualitative picture into precise demographics.
arxiv-2601-20808:
Yifei Li and Glennys Farrar ask how well we truly know the matter around us in space. Their 2026 paper concerns the local large scale structure of the universe. That structure is the map of galaxies and dark matter near the Milky Way. Many studies need this map as a baseline. It feeds models of cosmic ray sources and forecasts of dark matter signals.

The authors compare two sources for that map. One is CosmicFlows, a well-known catalog built from galaxy motions. The other is Biteau's galaxy catalog with cloning, a method that fills gaps by copying known structure. The paper weighs how far the two agree. Gaps between them mark where our knowledge of the nearby universe is still soft. The work matters for any study that starts from the local map.
arxiv-2601-21408:
Xinan He and ten co-authors build a detector for fake videos made by the newest generators. Tools like Veo and Wan now make clips so clean that the old giveaways are gone. Gross errors in meaning and flicker across frames no longer betray a fake.

The team hunts subtler traces instead. Their method reads how a clip sits on the learned manifold of real video, layer by layer. It also tracks tiny wobbles across time that humans miss. Finding reliable traces matters for news, courts, and platforms that must tell real footage from synthetic clips.
arxiv-2601-21508:
Johannes Bertram, Luciano Dyballa, T. Anderson Keller, Savik Kinger, and Steven W. Zucker open up a foundation model of brain activity and inspect its parts. Such models fit visual brain responses well, but their inner workings are opaque. That opacity limits what they can teach about the brain itself.

The authors probe the model the way a physiologist probes real neurons. They test each unit's response over time to controlled stimuli. The check asks how neural the model truly is, unit by unit. Answers could turn these models from mere predictors into tools for understanding vision.
arxiv-2601-21808:
Jörg Weissmüller studies how solute atoms cross the boundary between two crystals. The setting involves two solid solution phases that share an interface, with atoms sitting in the gaps of each crystal's structure. Inside each phase, atoms move fast by diffusion, so each side stays internally balanced.

The 2026 paper derives a rate equation for the thermally activated transfer across that interface. Treating each phase as an ensemble of particles, statistical mechanics predicts how many atoms occupy the transition states at equilibrium. Rates of this kind govern real processes in alloys. These range from aging and hardening to corrosion. A firm equation helps connect atomic jumps to changes engineers can measure.
arxiv-2601-22108:
Shuqi Ke and Giulia Fanti ask whether a little verified feedback can steer a very expensive process. Foundation models are pretrained with fixed proxy goals, such as predicting the next token. Those proxies can waste compute on skills that downstream users never need.

Their 2026 preprint introduces value-based pretraining with downstream feedback. A small amount of verified information about the goal guides where the pretraining effort goes, measured by value rather than by the proxy alone. If steering works, the huge cost of pretraining could be aimed better. It could target capabilities people actually want. It would not be spread evenly over everything a model might ever be asked to do.
arxiv-2601-22208:
Evelien Riddell and co-authors probe where language models fail as cloud troubleshooters. Root cause analysis finds the true source of failures in complex software systems. Modern cloud systems are highly distributed and interdependent, so faults propagate across many hops and symptoms appear far from their causes.

Recent models promise help, but the authors' title names what they found: models get stalled, biased, and confused on these tasks. Their 2026 preprint uncovers specific reasoning failures in cloud-based root cause analysis. Naming the failure modes matters for operators. They must decide how much to trust an AI copilot during an outage. Wrong guidance then wastes the scarcest resource, which is time.
arxiv-2601-22308:
Javier Carnerero-Cano, Luis Muñoz-González, Phillippa Spencer, and Emil Lupu test whether sneaky data attacks can fool regression models. Such models predict a number, and they run plants, labs, and works of all kinds. Their 2026 preprint notes that attack studies often assume powers no real foe would have.

The team craft attacks that stay hidden yet still bend the output. They then check whether known guards can catch them. The result is a sterner, more real test of model safety. It helps owners of key systems judge their true risk. Guards can then be built to match.
arxiv-2601-22408:
Shrey Goel and Pranam Chatterjee design peptide chains by a path that stays in safe chemical ground. Peptides are short chains of amino acids, used as drugs and probes. Their 2026 preprint notes that the space of chains is discrete and tightly ruled, and many mid-steps are not sound.

Old generative tools follow fixed spoil-and-fix paths that can cross poor ground. Their method, built on Schrödinger bridge matching, seeks the least-action path instead. Paths that stay sound yield chains more likely to work in the lab. The work could cut wasted synthesis. It suits drug and materials design.
arxiv-2601-22708:
Haonan He and a large team sort the sprawling family of LoRA variants into one map, with code and tests. LoRA tunes big models by training small add-on matrices, a cheap and strong trick. Their 2026 preprint notes that the flood of variants has fragmented the field.

Their taxonomy, review, shared codebase, and head-to-head tests give users a way to choose. A clear map ends much duplicated effort. It also shows which tweaks truly help. The work is a service to every team that fine-tunes. Order, here, is the contribution.
arxiv-2601-23008:
Saak Gabriyelyan, Alexander V. Osipov, and Evgenii Reznichenko revisit a classic property of topological vector spaces. A Baire space is one where countable intersections of open dense sets stay dense, a mark of completeness-like strength. Earlier results tied this property to a condition called property (K).

Other work showed every sequentially complete Fréchet–Urysohn locally convex space is Baire. The authors examine which Baire-type properties such spaces hold more broadly. These questions sit in functional analysis, the theory behind much of modern applied mathematics. Baire-type properties measure how rich a space's topology is, and they underpin many existence arguments in analysis.
arxiv-2601-23208:
Arie Wortsman, Federica Gerace, Bruno Loureiro, and Yue M. Lu analyze masked self-supervised learning with random matrix theory. Masked training, foundational for transformers, hides parts of the input and predicts them. Training mixes many masking patterns, creating a joint, matrix-valued predictor rather than a single estimator.

That object encodes how coordinates condition on one another, posing new analytical challenges. Random matrix tools are well suited to such large, structured objects. Theory of this kind explains why masked pretraining works as well as it does. How coordinates condition on one another is encoded in that matrix-valued predictor, the new object the theory must handle.
arxiv-2602-00008: He Wang and colleagues test whether rating first or writing first changes consumer scores. Across three trials and a large second data study, rating first pushed scores apart: high quality service scored higher, low quality scored lower. The authors trace this split through feeling based shortcuts and mental effort, and they find fun products show it more than useful ones. Data from Yelp and Letterboxd match the pattern, with Yelp scores spread wide and Letterboxd scores bunched.
arxiv-2602-01008: Yang Xiao and co-authors tune speech models for tongues with little data, where full tuning costs too much and tends to overfit. Layers adapt in a U shape: first and last layers hold tongue traits and need much tuning, mid layers hold shared sense and need little. Their DAMA plan hands out tuning room by layer job, starts it with a singular value trick, and locks a mid-layer base. On 18 low-data tongues, it matched or beat the best scores with far fewer tuned weights.
arxiv-2602-01308: Hengjie Cao and co-authors blame deep-net train wobbles on growing singularities in weight space. Singular spikes grow with each slope step and sync ever tighter with layer outputs, loosening slope-norm caps and raising the odds of sharp loss blowups. They dub that feedback loop the curse of singularities. Their Parametric Singularity Smoothing plan irons out weight singular spectra in a light, bendy way. Tests across data sets, net forms, and tuners show it calms trains, revives dead trains, and lifts both speed and broad scores.
arxiv-2602-01708: Langyuan Cui and colleagues improve information seeking where language models lack facts they need. Methods assume simplifications that degrade worst case performance, a flaw in high stakes settings. The authors use Twenty Questions to test information seeking. They formalize its adversarial counterpart, Strategic Language Search, as a two player zero sum game in extensive form. Their Game of Thought uses game theory to approximate a Nash equilibrium strategy for the restricted game. Tests show it improves worst case performance over direct prompting and heuristic guided search across all settings.
arxiv-2602-01808: Jiaming Liu and colleagues study how independent fission product yields change with energy, crucial for advanced nuclear energy but served only by sparse and imperfect experimental data. They bring a prior informed by physics models into Bayesian machine learning, where the posterior after learning generated data from fission models serves as the informative prior. Cumulative fission yields enter as a physical constraint through a conversion matrix, adding energy dependence information. The work shows truly Bayesian machine learning that uses comprehensive physics knowledge to exploit sparse but expensive nuclear data.
arxiv-2602-02008: Tuyen Nguyen and colleagues ask whether quantum ones can beat classical ones under symmetry. They study symmetry in the quantum model, the analog. Three findings emerge. First, an exponential gap between the two on permutation sets. Second, lower bounds for quantum matching limits up to constants for most cases, with possible gains under skewed orbits. Third, a tolerance gap where quantum ones succeed at noise levels defeating rivals. Together, these findings show when an edge emerges.
arxiv-2602-02108: Wenhao Li and colleagues present OOMB, a memory-efficient system. Long-context training is choked by GPU memory load, with activations as culprits since footprints grow with length. OOMB uses a chunk-recurrent frame with on-the-fly recomputation, holding memory at O(1) and shifting load to the KV cache. OOMB adds a paged manager. Async CPU offloading hides lag, and sparse attention cuts compute. Each extra 10K tokens adds a mere 10MB. Lets Qwen two point five 7B train with a 4M-token context on one GPU.
arxiv-2602-02408:
Jiaxing Qiu and 4 co-authors let people explain their reasoning when fixing a vision-language model, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Model editing corrects errors in a pretrained model without disturbing unrelated behavior. Earlier editors handled simple facts, not tasks where a person must reason about an image.

Their editor, ReasonEdit, stores human explanations in a codebook of facts. At inference time it retrieves only the relevant entries, using a new embedding method that balances connections across image and text, inspired by network science. Across four vision-language models and several question-answering datasets built on rationales, ReasonEdit reached the best editing performance reported. Edits generalized better when reasoning was included. The work suggests explanations are not just documentation; they are usable repair material.
arxiv-2602-02608:
Khandro K. Chokyi and 1 co-author reconstruct a bouncing universe driven by a phantom scalar field coupled to the Gauss-Bonnet term, in a 2026 arXiv paper. A bounce replaces the big bang singularity with a contraction that turns around into expansion. The coupling to the Gauss-Bonnet invariant, a curvature correction from higher-dimensional gravity, shapes the dynamics.

Using a chosen scale-factor form, the authors reconstruct the scalar potential and find a smooth well centered at the bounce. Energy density, pressure, and the equation of state show the energy-condition violation a bounce requires. Bulk viscosity proves decisive: the viscous model stays smooth with a healthy sound speed, while the non-viscous model diverges at the bounce and stays unstable afterward. Fits to supernova data give an excellent reduced chi-squared. Derived inflation observables land inside the Planck satellite's confidence contours, keeping the scenario observationally alive.
arxiv-2602-02708:
Punya Syon Pandey and 1 co-author recast binary classification as reinforcement learning and beat supervised fine-tuning by huge margins, in results posted to arXiv in 2026. Classification tasks like toxicity detection and factuality checks usually train by supervised fine-tuning, which struggles under label noise, class imbalance, and sparse supervision.

BinaryPPO adapts proximal policy tuning to static data sets, with no online back-and-forth needed.
