A confidence-weighted reward penalizes uncertain or incorrect predictions, pushing the model toward robust choice policies rather than rote labels. Across eight domain-specific benchmarks and several model architectures, accuracy rose by forty to sixty percentage points, reaching up to ninety-nine percent. The analysis dissects how reward shaping, advantage scaling, and policy stability each play a part. Confidence-based reward design, the authors argue, is a robust general alternative to supervised training for yes-no choices.
arxiv-2602-02908:
Binxu Wang and 2 co-authors explain a puzzle about diffusion models in a 2026 paper. Models trained on separate, non-overlapping data subsets often generate strikingly similar images from the same starting noise. The authors trace much of that similarity to shared Gaussian statistics across the subsets.

They build a random matrix theory framework for the linear case. It quantifies how finite datasets shape the learned denoiser's average behavior and its variation. Limited data, they show, shrinks low-variance directions and pulls samples toward the dataset mean. Three factors drive disagreement between splits. Tests on larger network architectures in a non-memorization regime matched the theory's predictions, giving a baseline for judging reproducibility in diffusion training.
arxiv-2602-03208:
Searching only the slow-changing parts of an image model's starting noise is proposed by Jinyan Ye, leading 6 other authors. Test-time scaling aligns made images with downstream goals without retraining. Optimizing the full initial noise is inefficient, because many search directions barely influence the final image, wasting computation on dimensions the output process largely ignores during sampling from the initial state.

The authors trace that inefficiency to spectral bias. Sensitivity to initial perturbations diminishes rapidly as frequency increases. Their system, Spectral Evolution Search, runs gradient-free evolutionary search inside a low-frequency subspace only. A spectral scaling prediction, derived from perturbation motion, explains impact differences across frequencies. Tests advanced the trade-off frontier between output quality and computational cost, beating strong earlier methods under equal budgets.
arxiv-2602-03308:
Walkers that avoid each other's future paths can fall into rhythm, according to A. Schmaus, working with 2 colleagues, in a letter on random walks. Self-avoiding walks interact with their own past. Their mutual future-avoiding variant has stochastically driven walkers avoiding each other's planned future trajectories, a setup arising naturally in conceptual models of shared mobility where vehicles reserve routes ahead through a network.

Periodic behavior emerges spontaneously in such systems. Periodic and unstructured motion coexist, a first example of chimera-style behavior for non-oscillatory paths on networks. The authors analytically describe and predict the onset of structure. A self-amplifying coupling to periodic components of the stochastic drivers drives the transition. For shared mobility, these states imply stable coexistence between flexible and line-based transport.
arxiv-2602-03608:
Shoppers increasingly ask a language model what to buy, and the model's shortlist decides who gets seen. Haibo Jin and 3 co-authors present CORE in a 2026 paper, a method for controlling output rankings inside such generative search engines. Because the model's interaction with the search engine is a black box, CORE works on the retrieved content itself.

The method appends crafted optimization text to search results in three styles: plain strings, reasoning passages, and review-like text. To test it, the authors build ProductBench, covering 15 categories with 200 products each. Across four search-capable models, CORE promotes target products into the top five over 90 percent of the time. It beats rival manipulation methods while keeping the text fluent.
arxiv-2602-03908:
City canyons break GPS, so Kuo-Yi Chao and 2 co-authors let vehicles localize together. Their 2026 paper fuses point clouds from car sensors with data shared by other vehicles and by roadside infrastructure at intersections. A registration-based mapping algorithm aligns these clouds to pin down each vehicle's position.

The sensors involved include LiDAR and stereo cameras on cars, plus fixed units watching the junction. Sharing views around corners and past obstructions steadies the position estimate where satellite signals bounce or vanish. Tests in GPS-noisy urban scenes show clear gains in accuracy and robustness over going it alone.
arxiv-2602-04208:
A robot unsure of what it sees should look again before acting. Hyeonbeom Choi and 5 co-authors build that instinct into SCALE, an inference strategy for vision-language-action models, in a 2026 paper. Existing test-time scaling needs extra training, verifiers, and repeated passes, which deployment cannot afford.

SCALE conditions both perception and action on the model's own uncertainty in a single forward pass. High uncertainty widens exploration in seeing and doing; confidence narrows both to efficient exploitation. The idea borrows from active inference theory in neuroscience. Adaptive looking promises robots that hesitate productively instead of committing to a misread scene.
arxiv-2602-04308:
Real transport is rarely optimal; it balances cost against disorder. Riccardo Piombo and 3 co-authors build a statistical mechanics of sub-optimal transport in a 2026 paper. Their model couples entropy and cost through an ensemble of weighted bipartite graphs, interpolating between dense entropic and sparse cost-driven structures.

A mean-field theory now explains the crossover that simulations had only shown. Local fluctuations in the constraint multipliers shrink away at large scale, reducing the model to an effective single-site problem. Statistical mechanics has long solved optimal transport at zero temperature; this work extends its reach to the messy intermediate regimes where real logistics lives.
arxiv-2602-04508:
Measuring how fast a surface spins can be done with light, because rotation shifts the light's frequency. Javier Navarro and 4 co-authors build a quantum version of that idea in a 2026 paper on rotational Doppler metrology, the science of precise measurement.

Their protocol uses squeezed and displaced swirling light beams as probes. The beams strike a rough rotating metal disc, and homodyne detection reads the shift. Analysis using Fisher information, a measure of how much data reveal a parameter, shows ideal Heisenberg scaling. That is the best precision quantum theory allows. Noise weakens that advantage. Still, careful energy allocation kept the quantum strategy ahead of its classical rival.
arxiv-2602-04608:
Maya Janvier, Julien Salomon, and Etienne Meunier stabilize long simulations from neural differential equations in a 2026 paper. These models learn the rules of change for physical systems, but errors can grow until long-term predictions diverge.

Training on long unrolled trajectories helps yet costs too much. Instead, the authors regularize the model's Jacobian, the matrix describing how outputs respond to inputs, through its directional derivatives during training. One version uses known dynamics; another approximates derivatives by finite differences when dynamics are unknown. Both cost far less than long rollouts. Across several ordinary and partial differential equations, long-term stability improved. The approach opens a path toward training such models for large systems.
arxiv-2602-04908:
Chika Maduabuchi and Jindong Wang wrote this 2026 paper on flow matching, a method for training generative models such as image generators. These models learn a field of directions that carries noise toward realistic samples. Training usually treats each time step on its own, which makes the learning signal noisy and sampling wasteful.

Their fix, Temporal Pair Consistency, ties together the model's predictions at two paired time steps along the same path. It changes only the training estimator, not the model, the path, or the sampler. The authors prove this coupling lowers gradient variance while keeping the original goal intact. In image tests on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, the method produced better samples at the same or lower cost, and it also fits modern pipelines such as rectified flow.
arxiv-2602-05008:
Wide binary stars that pair a hot subdwarf with a normal companion star carry clues about how stars trade mass. Francisco Molina and 3 co-authors measured 32 such systems in this 2026 astronomy paper, the first in a series. Pinning down their long orbits takes years of high-resolution spectra, so few systems have full solutions.

Spectra from the HERMES and UVES instruments gave velocity curves for both stars in each pair, and fitting Kepler orbits to both curves at once yielded the orbital parameters. Separate modeling produced the atmospheres of the cooler companions. The team also built a second sample by cross-matching a Gaia catalog with subdwarf catalogs. Comparing both samples with theory tests current ideas about how these binaries form and evolve.
arxiv-2602-05108:
Substorms in Earth's magnetotail release stored energy and light up the aurora, but what sets them off is still debated. Ping Zhu and 4 co-authors test one candidate trigger in this 2026 space physics paper. The trigger is ballooning instability, where plasma pressure balloons outward against curved magnetic field lines, followed by the formation of plasmoids.

The team picked THEMIS satellite events where craft and ground auroral cameras watched the same onset. Starting states inferred from the satellite data fed magnetohydrodynamic simulations, whose growth they set against the seen fields and flows. They also tracked the field-aligned currents at the simulation's Earthward edge. They mapped them along field lines to the ionosphere, and matched growth rates, dominant scales, and brightness against the true auroral patterns. The study is a step toward a coupled magnetotail-ionosphere model of substorm onset.
arxiv-2602-05408:
Rich-media search results compete on looks as much as text, and Zihao Guo and 7 co-authors build a re-ranker around user satisfaction in this 2026 information retrieval paper, accepted at CIKM 2026. Standard re-rankers model intent thinly and ignore side information such as how a result's cover image strikes the eye.

The framework opens with a query planner that reads the session's chain of refinements and splits the need into complementary sub-queries, widening intent coverage. A vision-language evaluator then scores visual signals for each candidate, and an LLM re-ranker weighs everything against stated principles covering relevance, quality, information gain, novelty, and visual presentation. Multi-task reinforcement learning adapts both the evaluator and the re-ranker to the setting. The system is deployed in a large industrial search engine, where the authors report substantial gains in online engagement and satisfaction.
arxiv-2602-05508:
Robot cameras that build maps as they move often drift off course over long trips, especially when the camera is not calibrated ahead of time. Zhuang Xiong, Chen Zhang, Qingshan Xu, and Wenbing Tao present VGGT-Motion, a monocular SLAM system built for kilometer-scale routes. It draws on 3D vision foundation models, but adds motion awareness to fight the scale drift that plagues long sequences.

The system first builds submaps guided by optical flow, which trims repeated static views and wraps turns into stable local pieces. An anchor-driven method then aligns submaps directly, giving dense matching and loop closure without costly feature searches. A light pose graph step enforces global consistency with cost that grows only linearly. In experiments, the system improved both accuracy and speed over rivals.
arxiv-2602-05608:
A robot rolling through a dense crowd often freezes, unable to find a safe move, a failure known as the freezing robot problem. Yufei Zhu, Shih-Min Yang, Martin Magnusson, and Allan Wang present HiCrowd, a framework that treats crowd motion as guidance instead of pure obstacle. The robot aligns itself with pedestrian flows that head in a compatible direction, rather than fighting through gaps.

A high-level reinforcement learning policy picks a follow point that ties the robot to a suitable group of walkers. A low-level predictive controller then tracks that point with short-horizon planning for safety. Tests replay recorded human paths and also run live simulations where people react to the robot. HiCrowd beat reactive and learning-based baselines on efficiency and safety, with fewer freezing episodes. Real deployments in a public museum and at Expo 2025 in Osaka worked without retraining.
arxiv-2602-05808:
Radio telescopes can spot star forming galaxies that dust hides from optical views, but only deep data reach the faint sources of the early universe. Varadaraj and 12 co-authors present three radio sources at redshifts between about five and five and a half, confirmed spectroscopically. They were found in the MIGHTEE survey field and followed up with space telescope photometry and spectroscopy.

Candidates were picked by fitting their spectral energy distributions across Hubble, JWST, and ground based data. The hydrogen alpha line, measured with JWST slitless spectroscopy, confirmed the distances. Star formation rates from three independent tracers broadly agree, and all three galaxies sit on or above the star forming main sequence for their era, after a recent burst. Their extended shapes show no dominant point source, so an active black hole is unlikely to rule their light.
arxiv-2602-06108:
Quantum machines come in two flavors: analog simulators that mimic matter, and digital computers that run controlled steps. Andrei Vrajitoarea and 4 co-authors merged the two in one device. They tied the lattice landscape of a synthetic material to a single control qubit, so the material evolved under two layouts at once.

The setup guided photons into states where solid-like and fluid-like phases coexist in superposition. Adding disorder slowly pinned the photons into a shared cat state, and an echo trick kept that fragile state coherent longer. The work points toward machines that entangle computers with matter itself for sensing and materials studies.
arxiv-2602-06508:
Training robot policies by reinforcement learning in the real world is costly and risky. Xiaokang Liu and 4 co-authors present World-VLA-Loop, a closed loop where a video world model and a vision-language-action policy improve each other. World models can stand in for reality, but they follow actions imprecisely, especially near success, and lack reward signals.

The team first curated a data set mixing successes with near-successes to sharpen action-outcome alignment. Their state-aware world model then predicts both future frames and binary rewards from shared latents, coupling reward to generation. As the policy improves, its fresh rollouts retrain the world model, keeping simulator and policy in step. Tests across simulation settings supported the loop.
arxiv-2602-06808:
Liu Liu, Limin Xu, and Zhenyi Zhu build a faster way to simulate quantum waves whose behavior is uncertain. The semiclassical Schrödinger equation is hard to solve because its solutions oscillate rapidly in space, and uncertainty in the inputs adds further fast oscillations in random space. Standard methods need large bases to capture both kinds of wiggles.

The authors adapt two robust low-rank integrators to this regime, evolving the solution on a small, moving subspace rather than a huge fixed basis. In experiments the method beat the standard stochastic Galerkin approach on efficiency, reaching high accuracy with a remarkably small rank that stayed stable as the semiclassical parameter shrank. Rank growth, they find, comes mainly from the randomness and smoothness of the potential, a practical clue for high-dimensional uncertainty quantification.
arxiv-2602-06908:
Thomas Cridge and two co-authors track a small but now visible effect in our picture of the proton's insides. Parton distributions say how the proton's momentum splits among its parts, and years of data plus better theory have shrunk their error bars. Effects once safely ignored now rival those bars in size, and quantum electrodynamics is one of them.

This proceedings paper looks past the headline QED change to side effects that can shift the shape and size of a combined QCD-plus-QED fit against a QCD-only fit. After lining up fits from several world groups, the authors zoom in on NNPDF4.0, where the QED effect is largest, so finer effects can be seen. As precision keeps climbing, they argue, these side effects will matter more.
arxiv-2602-07008:
Ruoyu Chen and ten co-authors want models that decide for the right reasons, not merely land on right answers. Plain training gives only class labels. A model can then score high by leaning on shortcut links rather than the evidence it should use. Human hints, like boxes around key parts or target screen elements, can rein it in, but lining up model evidence with human hints is hard.

Their training signal comes from subset-selection attribution, which picks compact regions that back a decision. If the model's top evidence drifts far from the human hint region, the loss penalizes that drift. It nudges evidence toward the hinted regions, without blanketing all outside regions. Tests on image sorting and on click decisions in GUI agents show gains in both score and in how well evidence lines up with human hints.
arxiv-2602-07308:
The ICAP method ranks cognitive engagement from passive through active and constructive to interactive, with deeper engagement promising better learning.  Sutapa Dey Tithi and six co-authors build a tutoring system that adaptively scaffolds engagement by choosing between guided worked cases and buggy cases that students must fix.

Comparing Bayesian Knowledge Tracing and deep reinforcement learning against a non-adaptive baseline in a logic tutor, an experiment with 113 students finds both adaptive policies improving posttest results. Knowledge tracing helps low prior-knowledge students most.  Tutor builders get evidence that adapting the kind of example, not just its difficulty, moves learning.
arxiv-2602-07408:
Predicting how genes respond to chemical perturbations in bulk cells is central to drug discovery, yet most work targets genetic perturbations in single cells.  Hyomin Kim and eight co-authors close that gap with a benchmark and a multi-agent method.

LINCSQA tests prediction of target gene regulation under complex chemical perturbations. PBio-Agent sequences tasks by difficulty and refines knowledge iteratively, exploiting the insight that genes hit by the same perturbation share causal structure, so confident predictions can guide harder ones.  Drug discovery teams get both a testbed for bulk-cell chemical perturbation and an agent design that reasons about biology rather than memorizing it.
arxiv-2602-07808:
Climate disasters cost trillions, but their effect on the gap between men's and women's paid work is far from simple. Jheelum Sarkar models household labor decisions and tests them against data from 151 countries between 1995 and 2019, covering droughts and extreme wet conditions.

The gender gap in paid labor traces a U-shape with drought and an inverted U-shape with excess wetness. It is driven mainly by employment gaps in the drought case and unemployment gaps in the wet case. Patterns vary with national context: high disaster-displacement risk countries see gaps shrink in wet extremes, while moderate-risk economies see gaps widen in droughts. Policymakers get evidence that climate adaptation must account for gendered labor responses, not assume a uniform effect.
arxiv-2602-07908:
Quantum gravity in an growing cosmos raises a subtle question: do physical forecasts depend on the gauge chosen for gravitons? Dražen Glavan and three co-authors test this for one-loop fixes to the field equation of a massless scalar in de Sitter space, including fixes from sources and observers.

Varying the graviton carrier across a one-knob family of gauges, they compute the gauge-tied pieces of the effective self-mass. They show the pieces cancel once every diagram class is gathered, including fixes to outer mode functions that play a new role compared with flat space. The cancel supports building genuinely gauge-independent cosmological observables from quantum-corrected equations, a reassuring result for quantum gravity in curved spacetime.
arxiv-2602-08008:
Brain tumors called gliomas invade nearby tissue in ways shaped by tissue structure and treatment, and chance in that process matters for prognosis. Martina Conte and two co-authors build a random multi-scale model that follows tumor growth and spread while accounting for treatment steps.

Starting from single cell motion, shaped by tissue mix and anti-crowding effects, they derive large-scale random rules for cell density and tissue change. Numeric tests then compare treatment plans against shown and newly proposed clinical criteria. Oncologists and math biologists gain a model that treats treatment uncertainty as part of the biology, not as an afterthought.
arxiv-2602-08108:
Goodness-of-fit tests falter when data are cut or clipped, because standard free-form gauges may not exist, behave wildly, or converge too slowly for reliable tuning. Juan Carlos Escanciano and Jacobo de Uña-Álvarez build an omnibus approach around a regular, Neyman-orthogonal score process pooled over a matching kernel Hilbert space ball.

The final maximum-mean-gap-type stat has a handy square form, with key values from a scale bootstrap holding nuisance gauges fixed. Theory shows validity under the null and local alternatives, with concrete builds for left-clipped right-cut data, current-status data, and random double truncation. Statisticians working with partially observed data gain a systematic test that sidesteps the usual estimator headaches.
arxiv-2602-08208:
People in conversation gradually adopt shared conventions, shortening messages while growing more accurate and consistent. Cameron R. Jones and three co-authors test whether language models do the same in a multimodal communication game, and whether humans and models can align with each other.

Both humans and models form conventions in same-type pairs, improving accuracy and consistency while shortening turns. Mixed human-AI pairs fail, however, and prompting models to mimic human surface behavior matches message length but not accuracy or lexical overlap. The authors conclude alignment needs shared interpretive biases about meaning, not just mimicry of past turns. The study matters for anyone designing AI conversational partners that must genuinely coordinate, not merely imitate.
arxiv-2602-08608: The dynamical Mordell-Lang conjecture asks when an orbit under a map returns to a given set infinitely often. Junyi Xie and two co-authors prove that conjecture for split products: one factor an affine curve, the other a projective curve, over the algebraic closure of the rationals. Their arXiv paper states the result in a single sentence, but the proof behind it settles the conjecture for this split product case.
arxiv-2602-08708:
Planning with STRIPS operators is famously hard, but the boundary between hard and easy remains fuzzy for the tiniest operators. Stefan Edelkamp and four co-authors investigate STRIPS with one precondition and one effect per operator, a case where NP-completeness is still unknown. Their arXiv paper builds on Bylander's classic results for larger operators.

Bylander showed plan existence is PSPACE-complete with two preconditions and two effects, even for ground literals. The authors probe the one-and-one case with SAT solvers on small instances, a literal graph construction, and a mapping to Petri nets. Readers get intermediate results on a small-solution hypothesis that could reshape understanding of minimal planning complexity.
arxiv-2602-08808:
Step-by-step how-to procedures are a core language-model skill, yet measuring procedural validity at scale on real tasks remains understudied. Yapei Chang and three co-authors introduce How2Everything, a framework for evaluating and improving goal-conditioned procedure generation. Their arXiv paper mines 351 thousand procedures from 980 thousand web pages across fourteen topics.

From that pool, a seven-thousand-example benchmark balances topics for evaluation, while a scoring protocol uses a language-model judge to flag critical failures that would block the goal. Distilling a frontier judge into an open eight-billion-parameter model reaches 80.5 percent agreement with humans. Reinforcement learning with the scorer as reward improves benchmark scores by over ten points across three models without regressions elsewhere. Readers get a closed loop from web mining to evaluated improvement.
arxiv-2602-09008:
Time-series data keeps growing, straining storage and compute, and condensing it into a small synthetic set is one remedy. Sijia Peng and seven co-authors present ShapeCond, a condensation framework guided by shapelets, the short local patterns that distinguish one series class from another. Most prior methods, built for images, miss such temporal structure.

ShapeCond's synthesis cost does not grow with sequence length, so longer series bring bigger speedups. It runs 29 times faster than the prior best method CondTSC, and up to 10,000 times faster than naive shapelet use on a 3,000-step Sleep data set. By preserving critical local patterns, it also improves downstream accuracy and beats all prior time-series condensation methods. Code is public.
arxiv-2602-09208:
Alexandra Sokolova and two co-authors revisit three landmark clinic trials through a unified Bayesian lens linking priors, step-by-step tuning, and choice theory. In ECMO, the verdict of treatment edge proves tough across priors. In CALGB 49907, forecast-odds watch halted sign-up at 633 patients instead of 1,800. In I-SPY 2, adaptive picking moved nine of 23 arms to Phase III.

Those cases drive exact backward induction for two-arm binary trials, where Beta-Binomial pairing gives closed-form moves with no number crunching, extended to covariate-tuned logistic fitting via Pólya-Gamma boost. Sim runs reveal a strain: best Bayesian designs slash hoped samples to 14 to 26 per arm but lose power. A tuned variant brings back power while keeping savings, a trade-off mapped for rare-disease and child settings.
arxiv-2602-09608:
Token systems, spread-out systems using code-based tokens for value and rights, have grown complex as reward designs expand blockchain beyond simple trades. Samela Kivilo and four co-authors note that current research treats use cases, plans, or solo aspects like rule and rewards, but offers little in-practice end-to-end design guidance. Their 2026 paper presents the Token Economy Design Method to fill that gap.

TEDM joins stepwise design rules across rewards, rule, and token rules, derived from repeat quality-based joining of prior work and refined through a co-designed case. Early test runs through the Currynomics case study, a system running the Redcurry coin backed by real estate, plus expert talks. The method is offered as reusable guidance for looking at basic needs of token systems, with focus on socio-tech context and early design stages.
arxiv-2602-09908:
A Latin square fills a grid so each symbol appears once in every row and column, and two orthogonal squares layered together fill each cell with a fresh pair. A 2026 paper led by Diane M. Donovan, with two co-authors, studies pairs that are maximal, meaning no further cell can be filled without breaking the rules. The question is how few filled cells such a pair can possibly have.

The authors prove the count is at least one third of the square of the order, settling a conjecture from an earlier paper by the same team. For orders of twenty-one or more, that bound is exact, and the pattern reaching it is unique up to reordering rows, columns, and symbols. The result pins down the sparsest possible maximal pair and closes a gap in the design theory.
arxiv-2602-10008:
Three-dimensional frustrated magnets are hard to simulate, since the sign problem and large system sizes block straightforward methods. A 2026 paper by Rajah P. Nutakki and Filippo Vicentini maps ground-state phases for spin models on a body-centered cubic lattice, computed with neural quantum states. For the antiferromagnetic first- and second-neighbor model, they find a direct first-order transition between Néel and collinear ordered phases at a critical ratio matching earlier studies.

In a tetragonally distorted variant proposed for a real copper vanadate material, no quantum paramagnetic ground state appears. A first-order transition between Néel and chain phases takes its place. The distorted model therefore fails to reproduce that material's low-temperature magnetism, and further effects must be added to explain the experiments.
arxiv-2602-10108:
Altermagnetism is usually tied to spin-split bands in bulk matter, but a crystal surface breaks more symmetry than its bulk. A 2026 paper led by Valentin Leeb, with three co-authors, defines the symmetry rules for altermagnetism at the surface of conventional antiferromagnets and shows how it can be topologically shielded. A minimal model covers one trivial and two topological examples.

Spin spectral density, measurable by spin- and angle-resolved photoemission, can show d-wave-like altermagnetic character on the surface even while the full band structure stays spin-matched. The topological model describes the Dirac semimetal CuMnAs as an existing example. Crystal surfaces thus emerge as a platform for robust, symmetry-driven magnetism beyond bulk labels.
arxiv-2602-10208:
IceCube's detection of TeV neutrinos from nearby NGC 1068 raised a puzzle. The neutrino flux far exceeds what gamma-ray observations allow, suggesting neutrinos form near the black hole where dense radiation hides gamma rays. A 2026 paper from the IceCube Collaboration searches for more such sources using muon neutrinos whose interactions start inside the detector, recorded between 2011 and 2021.

The search covers fourteen southern-sky Seyfert galaxies from the Swift BAT survey, guided by disk-corona model links between keV X-rays and TeV neutrinos. A collective search finds an excess of about seven events, inconsistent with background at the three-sigma level. The paper presents this as new independent evidence that Seyfert galaxies feed the extragalactic high-energy neutrino flux.
arxiv-2602-10408:
Normalization layers are standard in transformers. A 2026 paper led by Andrei Kanavalau, with two co-authors, develops TaperNorm, a gated approach to removing normalization from pre-norm transformers. The method starts from standard RMSNorm or LayerNorm and tapers gradually to learned sample-independent linear maps or affine maps. When the gate hits zero, per-token statistics stop in tapered layers, and the maps fold into adjacent linear projections.

Internal normalization tapers in tested settings with only small validation-loss increases. Final normalization has a distinct role: it anchors the pre-logit scale. Growing the last hidden state's radius does not directly cut loss; removing it lets loss fall by inflating logit magnitudes. A fixed-target scale loss offers an alternative anchor and enables norm-free ablations. In a key-value-cached decoding benchmark, tapering internal norms lifts throughput by about fourteen percent, or eighteen percent after folding.
arxiv-2602-10508:
Salma J. Ahmed and two co-authors make medical segmentation models easier to diagnose in a 2026 paper. Modern models segment scans well but remain opaque, so failures are hard to explain and dataset shifts are hard to trace. Clinicians and teams need to know what a model learned, not just how it scores.

Their system, Med-SegLens, decomposes activations from two segmentation systems into clear latent traits using sparse autoencoders. Across healthy, adult, pediatric, and sub-Saharan African glioma cohorts, a stable shared backbone emerges, while dataset shift traces to population-exact traits. The paper shows those traits act as causal bottlenecks for failures, and targeted latent interventions can correct errors without retraining.
arxiv-2602-10608:
Jiangrong Ouyang and two co-authors bring Bayesian inference to contextual bandit policies in a 2026 paper. Policy inference matters whenever a system must judge which decision rule works best, yet finite samples make doubt hard to quantify honestly. Standard tools can understate how little is really known.

The authors use tested likelihood to build a Bayesian method for jointly analyzing multiple bandit policies in small samples. The approach stays robust when data are scarce and gives exact doubt measures for policy value testing. It also supports flexible policy comparisons with full doubt quantification. Monte Carlo simulations and an application to adolescent body mass index data show the method.
arxiv-2602-10908:
Masataka Yoneda and six co-authors present an ultra-fast soft pattern matcher for trillion-scale text in a 2026 paper. SoftMatcha 2 searches trillion-scale natural language corpora in under three-tenths of a second while allowing meaning variations through substitution, insertion, and deletion. Suffix-array string matching scales with corpus size, while vector word models supply meaning bend.

Two algorithmic ideas tame the combinatorial explosion from meaning relaxation: dynamic corpus-aware pruning and fast exact lookup through a disk-aware design. Theory analysis shows the method mitigates exponential growth in search space. Empirically, on a corpus of over a trillion tokens, it attains much lower search latency than current methods. That gives teams a useful tool for soft search at web scale.
arxiv-2602-11308:
Seniority sorts nuclear states by how many nucleons sit unpaired. Chong Qi, writing alone, reviews partial conservation of seniority in semi-magic nuclei. Exact conservation holds for single-j systems with small j, but higher orbitals let residual forces mix seniority states.

Surprisingly, some states at j of nine-halves and above stay solvable even when symmetry should break. Two states with seniority four remain unmixed under any contact, a fact backed by proofs, numerics, and tests across five regions of the nuclear chart. Symbolic shell-model extensions are also covered, showing how partial conservation guides wave-function and symmetry studies.
arxiv-2602-11408:
Mamba2's expanded state helps time building but saturates bandwidth at use. Michael Menezes and Anastasios Kyrillidis offer GHOST, a grouped pruning frame that approximates balanced cutting using only forward-pass stats. Standard pruning fails here: unstructured thinness leaves signals dense, size selection ignores runtime motion, and gradient methods cost too much.

By jointly measuring controllability and observability, GHOST rivals gradient-based fidelity without backpropagation. On models from one-hundred-thirty million to two point seven billion settings, halving state dimension costs about one perplexity point on WikiText-2. Code is released, offering a practical compression route for state-space models in deployment.
arxiv-2602-11708:
Crypto markets show strong momentum and volatility that shifts with regime. That mix tempts systematic traders and punishes naive ones. Duc Bui and one co-author propose AdaptiveTrend, a framework that pairs trend-following on six-hour intervals with monthly portfolio construction. Its long-short split is uneven, 70 to 30, grounded in the upward drift of crypto markets.

Three tools drive it: a trailing stop tied to intraday volatility, Sharpe-based asset picks with market-size filtering, and the uneven split. Backtests out of sample across more than 150 pairs over three years show strong results. The Sharpe ratio tops two, the worst drawdown stays near 13 percent, and the Calmar ratio tops three. Those marks beat trend-following and buy-and-hold benchmarks. Checks across bull, bear, and sideways markets suggest the edge survives changing conditions rather than depending on one lucky regime.
arxiv-2602-11808:
Agentic language-model inference with long contexts is increasingly limited by memory bandwidth rather than raw compute. SwiGLU feedforward blocks, whose large weights exceed cache capacity, become a major yet under-optimized bottleneck. Zixi Zhang and three co-authors propose DeepFusionKernel, a deeply fused kernel that cuts high-bandwidth memory traffic and boosts cache reuse.

Integrated with SGLang and paired with a kernel scheduler, the kernel delivers speedups of about 13 percent on H100 hardware and about 10 percent on A100 hardware. Gains hold consistently across generation lengths, and the design adapts to diverse models, inference configurations, and hardware platforms. For long-context agents, fusing kernels to move less data proves as valuable as faster arithmetic.
arxiv-2602-11908:
Language models remain prone to factual errors that erode trust and limit adoption in high-risk settings. Holding back when trust is low helps, but binary all-or-nothing abstention discards valuable long-form information. Shani Goren and two co-authors introduce Selective Abstraction, a method that lets models trade detail for reliability by trimming uncertain content. Responses are split into atomic claims, each stating a single fact, and uncertain atoms are replaced with vaguer versions.

The method is defined by choosy risk and breadth, and tested with a pipeline that treats risk as factual correctness and measures breadth by retained information. Across six open-source models on two fact-check benchmarks, atom-wise SA beats existing baselines in test after test, improving the risk-breadth curve area by about 28 percent over claim removal. Reducing detail, the work shows, can boost accuracy and reliability while preserving most of the meaning.
arxiv-2602-12108:
Language models still receive their memory as a fixed, hand-engineered context window, even though the databases and retrieval systems around them are mature. Xiaoyuan Liu and six co-authors give the model itself the tools to manage its own state, in a design they call StateLM.

The model learns to prune context, index documents, and take notes through an internal reasoning loop, escaping the fixed-window limit. On long-document question answering it beats standard models at every scale tested. On a chat memory task it gains 10 to 20 percent absolute accuracy. On a deep-research benchmark it reaches up to 52 percent accuracy, where standard counterparts sit near 5 percent. Reasoning becomes a stateful process the model itself manages.
arxiv-2602-12308:
Thin rings pose a puzzle: full two-dimensional equations should simplify to motion around a circle, but the reduction must stay faithful. Jean-Pierre Magnot works alone here, building a geometric frame for equations on thin annuli in the plane. Special inner products yield bases fitted to the thin shape, supporting stable approximations of Galerkin type.

A general reduction theorem shows solutions tending to effective one-dimensional motion on the limiting circle. Beyond that limit, small transverse correctors and cell problems capture spread and averaged effects in different directions. The frame covers integrable models, dispersive systems, and non-integrable cases with loss, forcing, or rapid oscillation, and proves stability under changes of order and geometry.
arxiv-2602-12808:
Emergency departments on tourist islands face sharp seasonal swings, and staffing them well depends on forecasting arrivals. Paride Crisafulli and five co-authors study the reference hospital in Palma de Mallorca, asking which outside factors actually help predict visits. They build models from tourism, weather, calendar, and demographic variables alone, testing random forests, support vector machines, and neural networks.

Calendar data and resident plus tourist population counts proved statistically significant, while weather added no further gain. Time-series models won for short horizons under a week, but for fortnight or month horizons, simpler models using only outside variables matched them. The lesson for planners is to choose predictors carefully: well-picked outside variables can carry long-range forecasts without extra complexity.
arxiv-2602-12908:
Poisson shape and its wilder cousins gain structure from bialgebras, and this paper builds that theory for tidy pre-Poisson algebras. Hongliang Li and Qinxiu Sun prove matches among matched pairs, Manin triples, phase spaces of Poisson algebras, and pre-Poisson bialgebras. Studying coboundary cases leads plainly to a pre-Poisson Yang-Baxter formula.

Even answers of that formula yield coboundary bialgebras, and even uneven answers can make them, prompting quasi-triangular and split-form variants. Answers with a fixed skew-symmetric part give quasi-triangular bialgebras, clear as linked Rota-Baxter tools with weights. A final link ties square Rota-Baxter pre-Poisson algebras with split-form bialgebras, closing a tidy algebra picture.
arxiv-2602-13208:
Monkeypox, a viral disease related to smallpox, has become a global threat, most of all in African countries, as smallpox vaccination ended and incidental immunity faded. Mine Yurtoğlu and five co-authors model its spread with the Atangana-Baleanu operator, a fractional calculus tool with a Mittag-Leffler kernel, and tune three controls: vaccination, treatment, and quarantine. The goal is to reduce exposed and infected numbers at minimum cost.

For the controlled model, the authors prove existence and uniqueness of answers, calm, and sensitivity, then solve the optimal system numerically with an Adams-type predictor-corrector method. Mock runs test single, double, and triple control strategies separately. The most strong strategy, the results show, is applying vaccination, treatment, and quarantine jointly, a finding that supports combined intervention over any single measure alone.
arxiv-2602-13308:
Labeling medical images takes costly expert time, so active learning tries to pick only the most useful cases for annotation. Standard picks rely on model uncertainty alone, ignoring whether the model looks at the right anatomy, a gap that matters for clinical trust. This framework adds a second test: it compares the model's attention maps with radiologist-marked regions and favors cases where the model looks in the wrong place.

Using just 570 chosen samples, the method beat random sampling on three expert-labeled sets covering brain tumors and chest X-rays, reaching 77.22 percent accuracy on BraTS. Attention maps confirmed the trained models focused on diagnostically relevant regions, pairing data efficiency with interpretability. Ifrat Ikhtear Uddin leads the work with four co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13608:
Spontaneous oscillations, systems that sway without an external periodic drive, show rich physics such as phase-locking and sync. This paper reports a new route to magnetic spontaneous sway via parametric pumping. A pump tone excites traveling spin waves in a yttrium iron garnet delay line, and four-wave mixing splits the pump mode into two free-phase magnon modes. One is a spontaneous mode near twice the pump wave number, and the other is an idler near zero wave number.

That mechanism reliably generates ultrasharp spin wave motion tunable by pump and magnetic field. The spontaneous mode phase-locks to a probe tone like an auto-oscillator. The motion also yields a high-gain magnetic parametric booster reaching 40 decibels, opening routes to nonlinear spin physics and new magnetic devices. Yi Li leads the work with twelve co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13708:
Local symmetries are often treated as harmless extra structure that physics can leave implicit, working up to sameness without pausing over invariance. But in some settings, shape-change invariance or gauge invariance becomes a pressing practical concern, and philosophy discussions of sophistication have paid little attention to when and why. Surveying textbook general relativity and gauge theory, this paper identifies the settings where symmetry must be handled explicitly, such as straight-line cases, an initial-value setup, or a Hamiltonian 3+1 formalism.

The paper proposes background-relative sophistication as a working test marking just where symmetry can stay implicit and where it must be made explicit. Quantum and subsystem settings raise a further difficulty, since superposition and gluing force symmetry into view even for theories that pass the test. Henrique Gomes is the sole author.
arxiv-2602-13808:
Checking language-model smart contracts from natural-language specs needs more than reading the output code. This framework parses contract text into set schemas, generates Solidity code, and performs auto quality checks through compilation and security checks, using CrewAI-style agent teams with step-by-step refinement. The pipeline produces set artifacts with full origin metadata. Quality is measured across five areas: functional completeness, variable truth, state-machine correctness, business-logic truth, and code quality, combined into single scores.

Paired testing against ground-truth implementations measures alignment and identifies steady error modes such as logic omissions and state transition inconsistencies. The result is a reproducible benchmark for empirical research on smart contract synthesis quality, supporting extensions to formal checks and rule checks. Abhinav Goel leads the work with three co-authors.
arxiv-2602-14108:
Luigi Ciceri and three co-authors present a 2026 arXiv study of fluid flow through and around porous bodies. Flows in free and porous regions obey different physics, and models must generalize across shapes and boundary settings. The team tests two physics-informed learners: PointNets and a geometry-aware neural operator.

Both enforce incompressible Navier-Stokes equations in free flow and a Darcy-Forchheimer extension in porous zones, within one loss, conditioned on shape and material traits. Data came from OpenFOAM runs on ducts with porous blocks and on windbreak scenes with trees and buildings. Errors in velocity and pressure stayed low on seen and unseen shapes, with wakes reproduced well, though sharp interfaces and steep gradients proved hardest.
arxiv-2602-14508:
Partha Ghose, writing alone, clears a 2026 arXiv puzzle in classical optics: Bell-like states with no quantum mechanics. Old twist optics uses a two-size complex Hilbert space of Jones vectors, so tensor-product motion for two-part non-split acts already exists classically. For random light fields, with no pre-set outcomes assumed before detection, tuned two-beam twist states can show Bell-CHSH links of quantum strength.

The same bench offers a tunable, low-cost test bed for stress-testing Bell, CHSH, and context witnesses under noise, coarse binning, and picky sampling. Another build uses outside conical refraction, where built crossing conical-refraction rings mimic the crossing send cones of spontaneous parametric down-conversion. A self-contained category form treats the build-and-tune line as a single morphism in an operational process theory.
arxiv-2602-14608:
In some magnets, electron spins split apart even with no net magnetism. Muskan, with Subhadeep Bandyopadhyay and Sayantika Bhowal as co-authors, asks why copper fluoride breaks the usual pattern. Most related fluorides show flat, planar splitting, while copper fluoride shows a bulk form.

The authors trace the change to shifts of the fluorine ions out of their symmetric spots. Those shifts add a new plane of uneven magnetization and a new term in the magnetic octupole. That term sets an extra direction for the splitting. The work points to pressure or shape change as a way to steer spin splitting.
arxiv-2602-14708:
T. Shaska and I. Kotsireas give data fabrics a firm math base, in place of ad-hoc builds that strain to keep order, track roots, and grow. They model sets, labels, maps, rules, and tools as one linked net, where a link can join many nodes at once. Sets act as points and maps act as arrows in this view, so joining data and learning across sites gains clear rules.

The net is then placed in a rich algebraic setting that adds more structure. Data work thus gains a tongue precise enough to prove things about, not just to hope for.
arxiv-2602-14808:
Metin Gurses and Yaghoub Heydarzade extend a theorem on FLRW cosmology from generic metric gravity to scalar-vector-tensor theories. Earlier work showed that, without matter, field equations built from curvature and its derivatives reduce in FLRW spacetime to Einstein equations with an effective perfect-fluid source.

The new result covers a broad class of theories whose action holds arbitrary scalar and vector fields with derivatives at any order. It proves the metric equations still take Einstein form under FLRW symmetry. Cosmic expansion thus hides a wide family of gravity theories behind one familiar shape. Cosmology gains a universality result for symmetric spacetimes.
arxiv-2602-15008:
Dmitriev and colleagues sharpen the theory of sampling with discrete diffusion models, a family with striking empirical success but incomplete foundations. They study score-based discrete diffusion under a continuous-time Markov chain view, with a focus on leaping-based samplers. Sharp convergence guarantees are given for reaching accuracy in KL divergence under both uniform and masking noising processes.

For uniform diffusion, the leaping sampler drops linear dependence on vocabulary size and gains a matching lower bound showing linear dependence on ambient dimension cannot be avoided in general. For masking diffusion, a modified sampler adapts to low-dimensional structure. Its rate follows a quantity called effective total correlation. That quantity can stay sublinear or constant for structured data such as hidden Markov models, images, and random graphs. No boundedness or smoothness assumptions beyond score entropy loss control are needed.
arxiv-2602-15408:
Raujouan and colleagues give exact formulas of stepwise fixed minus Gauss bend sheets of spinning, also known as stepwise saddle-like sheets. They build Bäcklund maps that again have exact formulas and are new cases of non-spinning stepwise saddle-like sheets.

In the work, for stepwise fixed Gauss bend round webs, they give spin-proof steady groups of flat links. They give terms on them so that the Bäcklund maps keep repeat, that is, have ring shape. The new sheets push the known spinning cases into non-spinning ground while holding exact forms. The repeat terms guard the mapped sheets close up into loops.
arxiv-2602-15608:
Atalla and colleagues give robots a friction switch. Friction drives all land locomotion, yet robots usually treat it as fixed by surface and material. Ultrasonic lubrication changes that: resonant structures excited at ultrasonic frequencies let a contact flip between grip and slip on demand. The team builds two modules, a cylindrical one for tube-like spaces and a flat plate for outer surfaces, and fits them into bio-inspired crawlers modelled on inchworms and wasp ovipositors.

Both crawlers move both ways with efficiency above 90 percent, near perfect for their design. Friction tests show large reductions across rigid, soft, granular, and tissue surfaces, dry and wet, and across roughness levels. The work establishes ultrasonic lubrication as a practical active friction control, one that could simplify robot design while raising locomotion efficiency.
arxiv-2602-15908:
Bani-Ata and Alhuraiji give a short, explicit, elementary construction of the Lie algebras of type G2 over fields of characteristic 2. The algebras have dimension 14. The work aims to lay out that construction in full, with no hidden steps and no appeal to tools beyond the basics.

It counts as elementary because it uses little more than naive linear algebra notions. No heavy machinery is called in. The plain route makes the characteristic-2 case of G2 open to readers with only basic linear algebra at hand. They get a concrete account of the 14-dimensional algebra, built step by step from simple notions, rather than a terse claim that such an algebra exists.
arxiv-2602-16308:
Markus Rueggeberg and coauthors propose marker-free robot spotting and six-dimensional pose finding for multi-agent SLAM. Merging position history and maps from other watchers is often challenged by matching. Loop closure spotting between sensory inputs of other agents is easily harmed by sensory mix-ups, or when views differ a lot. Direct mutual viewing among robots connects partial SLAM graphs well.

That viewing often relies on tuned arrays of marker arrays, which badly limit viewing range and often fail under sharp lighting such as glare. Using recent gains in deep-learning-based 6D pose finding, the authors feature marker-free pose finding within a spread-out multi-robot SLAM system. They show benefit to mutual position accuracy among the robotic team. The solution is tested on data recorded in a test field campaign on a planet-like similar environment.
arxiv-2602-16508:
Owen Hearder leads two coauthors on a fully discrete finite element method for a stochastic heat equation. It carries nonlinear finite-rank space-coloured multiplicative noise and admits a unique nonnegative solution from nonnegative initial data. The new method pairs mass-lumped finite elements with a Lie-Trotter splitting strategy.

The discretization preserves nonnegativity at the discrete level and is shown to converge under suitable smoothness conditions. A rigorous convergence analysis shows mass lumping secures sign while operator splitting separates fixed and random dynamics. Numerical experiments confirm the rates and the preservation of sign, and further examples outside the theory probe the method's range and limits.
arxiv-2602-16708:
Nils Palumbo and co-authors present a formal runtime enforcement approach for agentic system security. Agentic systems face serious attack risks, and prior defenses are often too coarse and lack formal correctness guarantees. The new method lets users state intended policy in Datalog and enforces it at runtime by building event graphs.

When an agent is about to act, such as calling a tool, the system checks the action against policy in light of current state and past events. The action is then blocked or allowed accordingly. The approach is implemented and tested across multiple benchmarks, showing merit in real-world settings. It marks a step toward agentic systems that are provably safe and secure.
arxiv-2602-16908:
G. Laskaris and co-authors apply multi-objective tuning and quantum hybridization to equivariant deep learning interatomic potentials. Allegro is a machine learning potential model predicting atomic traits in molecules with E(3) equivariant neural networks. Training it trades accuracy against inference time, so the team tunes hyperparameters for both goals. They also build two variants: one with added classical layers, and one with quantum-classical hybrid layers.

All models are tested on QM9, rMD17-aspirin, rMD17-benzene, and a self-made copper-lithium set. Both variants beat Allegro in force prediction accuracy across multiple sets. The classical variant consistently improves over baseline, while the hybrid variant achieves the best force accuracy on the copper-lithium set, beating the classical variant by about thirteen percent. It also stays competitive elsewhere despite hyperparameters transferred with no set-specific tuning.
arxiv-2602-17008:
Swapnil Saha and co-authors study covert multi-hop message passing in wireless networks where an adversary employs a cyclostationary detector to reveal hidden transmissions. The covert route employs direct sequence spread spectrum signals to ensure either maximum end-to-end covertness or minimum latency, under quality-of-service and link budget constraints.

Optimal bandwidth, transmit power, and spreading gain for each hop jointly satisfy reliability and either rate or hiding needs. The paper shows equivalence between the covertness and the detection signal-to-noise-ratio gain-based widest-path versions, enabling fast route computation. Numerical tests in a realistic three-dimensional environment illustrate three findings. End-to-end latency increases exponentially with the hiding requirement. Latency increase is super-linear with packet size. Cycle and energy detectors impose different latency behavior as a function of message length and hiding requirement.
arxiv-2602-17108:
Anton Dzega led a five-author team asking whether large multimodal models show personality-like traits that a projective psychology test can reveal. The Thematic Apperception Test, a classic tool for surfacing unconscious aspects of personality, asks subjects to tell stories about ambiguous images. Here the models play two roles: subject models that spin stories from test images, and evaluator models that score those stories with the SCORS-G scale.

Evaluators proved strong at reading the stories, matching human experts closely. All models grasped interpersonal dynamics and the sense of self well, but consistently failed to perceive and regulate aggression. Larger and newer model families outperformed smaller, older ones across the scale. The study suggests projective testing can expose structured strengths and blind spots in model behavior.
arxiv-2602-17508:
Pranay Jain led a six-author team on Pareto optimal benchmarking of AI models on ARM Cortex processors for sustainable embedded systems. The work offers a hands-on benchmarking frame for tuning AI models on ARM Cortex chips, M0-plus, M4, and M7, for energy use, accuracy, and resource use in embedded systems. Through an automated test bench, the team weighs key performance indicators to spot the best chip-model pairings.

The study finds a near-linear link between floating-point operations and inference time, a trusty gauge of compute demand. Pareto analysis weighs energy use against model accuracy, so apps meet performance needs without giving up sustainability. The M7 chip suits short inference cycles best, while M4 saves more energy on longer jobs. M0-plus, weaker on complex models, still fits simpler tasks. The work steers builders toward energy-thrifty AI systems that still perform well in real use.
arxiv-2602-17808:
Nathan Ng and team present SwapLess, a system for adaptive, multi-tenant TPU-CPU collaborative inference on memory-constrained Edge TPUs. On-device AI accelerators serve IoT uses where links are weak and safety matters. Yet limited on-chip memory forces runtimes to swap model segments between host and accelerator memory at high cost. Naive CPU-accelerator partitioning can worsen latency by overloading the CPU or cutting swapping too little.

SwapLess uses an analytic queueing model. It captures partition-dependent CPU and TPU service times plus swapping overheads across workload mixes and request rates. It adjusts the partition point and CPU core allocation online cheaply to minimize end-to-end response time. Tests on Edge TPU platforms show mean latency reduced by up to roughly two thirds for single-tenant workloads. Multi-tenant workloads improve by up to roughly three quarters against the default Edge TPU compiler.
arxiv-2602-17908:
Mingzhang Zhu and team present WHED, a wearable hand exoskeleton for natural demonstration collection. Scalable dexterous learning stalls on collecting natural, faithful demonstrations of multi-finger hands, hindered by blocking, complex hand motion and contact-rich interactions. WHED is designed for in-the-wild demonstration capture. It follows wear-first operation and a pose-proof thumb coupling. That coupling keeps thumb movement natural and maintains a consistent correspondence with the degrees of freedom of the target robot thumb.

WHED brings together a linkage-driven finger interface offering passive fit, a modified passive hand with robust sensing, and a sensing and power module. An end-to-end data pipeline aligns joint encoders, AR-based tip pose and wrist-mounted views, supporting time alignment and replay. Feasibility tests on grasping and manipulation sequences spanning precision pinch and full-hand enclosure grasps show a match between collected demos and replays.
arxiv-2602-18108:
A large team led by S. Filomeno confirms a new planet, TOI-5734b, circling a fairly young K-type star. Their 2026 paper joins light curves from the TESS space telescope with speed measures from the HARPS-N spectrograph. The star is a few hundred million years old, which makes the system a useful case for how young planets form and change.

Careful joint modeling, with flexible math to separate star spots and flares from planet signals, pins down the planet's size, mass, and orbit. It circles its star in about six days, with a size near twice Earth's and a mass near nine times Earth's. Its density sits close to Earth's, which points to a mostly rocky body whose first light air layer is nearly gone. The team flags the planet as a good target for air studies with ground and space telescopes.
arxiv-2602-18508:
Gabriel Faria and Arnaldo Candido Junior make Neural Turing Machines parallel. Their 2026 paper introduces P-NTM, a simpler version changing the core steps of the original design for efficient scan-based execution.

The team tests the model on a synthetic benchmark of algorithm problems covering state tracking, memorization and arithmetic, solved with autoregressive decoding. They compare it against a revisited stable build of standard NTM, plus conventional recurrent and attention models. Despite simplifying, the model works across lengths like the original, solving all problems, including unseen lengths, with perfect accuracy. Parallel execution of P-NTM also improves training speed, running up to ten times faster than the standard NTM. The work contributes toward efficient neural models able to express broad algorithms.
arxiv-2602-18708:
Quantum-safe cryptography makes messages much larger, and on tiny wireless devices the radio, not the maths, may eat the battery. Tao Liu, with two co-authors, measures the energy cost of post-quantum key establishment on Bluetooth Low Energy hardware in 2026, separating the cost of computing from the cost of sending.

Large post-quantum payloads fragment, keep the radio on longer, and add transmission overhead, so communication often dominates the total energy, outrunning the cryptographic work itself. Earlier work had optimised computation while largely ignoring that traffic cost. The practical message is that quantum-resilient pairing needs protocol settings and lower-layer design chosen together, a point that should shape future personal-area-network standards.
arxiv-2602-19008:
Why do language agents fail at tasks they can solve? Wilson Y. Lee, writing alone in 2026, argues many such failures are reliability failures, not capability failures. They arise from stochastic drift away from a task's solution structure.

Every well-defined tool-use task carries a canonical solution path. It is a convergent set of tool calls shared by successful runs. Success depends on staying within that path's operating envelope. A natural experiment holds model capability and task difficulty fixed. It analyses trajectories from a tool-use benchmark. Successful runs adhere more closely to the canonical path than failed runs. The gap is zero through the first half of trajectories. That rules out early-branching selection bias. Each off-canonical call raises the chance the following call is also off-canonical by over a fifth. A simple monitor restarting the weakest runs by mid-trajectory adherence lifts success rates.
arxiv-2602-19108:
Robots entering burning buildings need to sense heat, not just see flames. Anton R. Wagner, with three co-authors, gives them that sense in 2026 through real-time thermal radiation fields. Depth and thermal images are registered into a three-dimensional point cloud. Each point carries a temperature value.

Fires are identified from that cloud. The Stefan-Boltzmann law then approximates radiation in empty space. A continuous thermal field covers the whole environment. Navigation embeds thermal constraints into the cost map. Paths stay collision-free and thermally safe. Tests on a Boston Dynamics Spot robot confirm the approach. Hazardous regions are avoided while goals are still reached. Search-and-rescue, firefighting, and hazardous response all stand to benefit.
arxiv-2602-19208:
Training large language models with verifiable rewards has sharpened their reasoning, but two habits waste effort. Giving every problem the same number of trial runs ignores a key fact. Some problems vary far more than others. The usual policy shape also weakens learning signals for answers the model already trusts. Yangyi Fang and eight colleagues argue both habits hold training back.

Its answer, DynaMO, works on two fronts at once. At the problem level it derives a rollout plan from measured variance, spending more trials where they teach the most. At the update level it adjusts the advantage signal so confident correct actions still teach, without letting oversized updates destabilize the model. The result is a principled scheme for spending training compute where it counts.
arxiv-2602-19308:
A robot searching open country for a named object cannot rely on a map it does not have. Hardik Shah and eight co-authors present WildOS, a system that searches outdoors for objects named in plain words. It builds a sparse navigation graph as spatial memory. ExploRFM, a vision module, scores the graph's frontier points, predicting traversability, visual frontiers, and similarity to the target object in image space.

A particle-filter method also gives a rough location for the target beyond the robot's depth range, so planning can aim at distant goals. Closed-loop field tests across off-road and urban terrain show WildOS beating purely geometric and purely vision-based baselines on efficiency and autonomy. The paper points to vision foundation models as a way to make open-world robot behavior both semantically informed and geometrically grounded.
arxiv-2602-19408:
Genomic analyses often store and traverse k-mers, short DNA substrings, and compact representations matter. Sankardeep Chakraborty and five co-authors study spectrum-preserving string sets, collections of strings whose k-mer spectrum matches the input. Existing methods such as Unitigs, Eulertigs, and Matchtigs model the task as a path cover on the de Bruijn graph.

The paper extends that framework from paths to branching structures called necklace covers, combining cycles with tree-like attachments known as pendants. A greedy algorithm builds a necklace cover with guaranteed optimality in total size under certain conditions. On real genomic data, the minimum necklace cover beats Eulertigs and matches Masked Superstrings on compression, while keeping the k-mer spectrum exact.
arxiv-2602-19508:
Aritra Bhattacharya and two co-authors show that the Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomial matrix for a Hecke algebra splits into a product of matrices. The setting is the Hecke algebra of a Coxeter system whose Weyl group belongs to a symmetrizable Kac-Moody algebra, over Laurent polynomials in q. Each factor matrix has entries that are polynomials in q with nonnegative coefficients.

The factorization uses a hybrid basis defined by Grojnowski and Haiman, with intermediate matrices giving transitions between bases for nested subsets. Equivalently, the coefficients come from a natural restriction map to parabolic Hecke algebras. Following Grojnowski-Haiman ideas, the paper also gives a geometric proof that the coefficients are positive, linking algebra to geometry.
arxiv-2602-19608:
Looting at dig sites threatens cultural heritage, yet watching thousands of far-flung places is hard to staff. Girmaw Abebe Tadesse and nine co-authors build a satellite-based pipeline that spots looted sites from space. It uses PlanetScope monthly mosaics at 4.7 meters per pixel, plus a hand-checked set of 1,943 sites in Afghanistan, 898 looted and 1,045 kept safe, with images from 2016 to 2023 and site-footprint masks.

The team tests two routes. End-to-end CNN sorters train on raw color patches, while older machine learning trains on hand-built spectral and texture traits plus embeddings from remote-sensing foundation models. ImageNet-pretrained CNNs with spatial masking score F1 0.926, well ahead of the best older setup at 0.710. Readers get a public code base and a test that looting marks are tightly local, so masking matters more than fancy embeddings.
arxiv-2602-19708:
Small, specialised image sets often lack examples of rare classes, and synthetic images can fill those gaps. A 2026 arXiv paper by Hoyoung Kim and four co-authors introduces ChimeraLoRA, a way to adapt a pretrained diffusion model with small low-rank adapters for few-shot synthesis.

An adapter trained on a single image keeps fine detail but gives little variety, while one trained on a whole class gives variety but blurs detail. ChimeraLoRA splits the job: a shared adapter carries class-level meaning, strengthened by preserving bounding boxes in training, while per-image adapters carry specific traits, mixed at generation time. Across varied data sets the synthetic images stay diverse, detailed, and close to the real few-shot distribution, lifting later classification accuracy.
arxiv-2602-20308:
Raphaël Maire studies how nucleation unfolds in active fluids whose large-scale fluctuations are strongly suppressed. In typical active fluids, nucleation often looks equilibrium-like, but hyperuniform fluids depart sharply from that picture. This 2026 paper tracks the full density field through a few key collective variables. The governing object turns out to be a nonequilibrium quasipotential, not the reversible work of formation.

Because large-scale fluctuations are reduced, nucleation odds no longer split cleanly into surface and volume parts. Once capillary waves are taken into account, the detailed balance fails outright, and that failure traces back to nonreciprocal dynamics. The framework extends beyond the hyperuniform case and can help spot nonequilibrium signs in ordinary active fluids as well. The study thus reframes nucleation as a genuinely nonequilibrium process when large-scale fluctuations are tamed.
arxiv-2602-20408:
Ideas sampled independently from people tend to be more diverse than ideas sampled independently from language models, raising fears that heavy reliance could homogenize invention. Yuting Deng and two co-authors trace the gap to two mechanisms from cognitive psychology. At the individual level, models fixate like people do, letting early outputs constrain later ideas. At the collective level, models merge knowledge into one distribution instead of partitioning it the way human populations do.

Across four studies, the authors test prompting fixes for each mechanism separately. Chain-of-thought prompting cuts fixation by encouraging structured reasoning, though only in models, not people. Ordinary personas, rather than creative entrepreneurs such as Steve Jobs, improve knowledge partitioning by anchoring generation in distinct regions of meaning. Combined, the two fixes yield the highest idea diversity, beating humans, and offer a practical path for human-AI teamwork that keeps invention diverse.
arxiv-2602-21008:
The Council of Giants is a ring of galaxies in the Local Universe whose existence needs explaining. Edward Olex, Alexander Knebe, Noam Libeskind, Stefan Gottlober, and Dmitry Makarov test whether such rings arise in standard cosmology in this 2026 arXiv paper, the second part of the HINORA series. They apply their ring-finding code to dark-matter-only simulations with random and constrained initial conditions, selecting regions that match the Local Group and Volume.

After checking that simulated regions match the observed mass function and density, the search finds Council-like rings to be rather unusual. The observed ring sits more than two and a half standard deviations from expectations for massive-galaxy distributions. It may be a rare chance arrangement, or a sign of intermediate-scale physics that dark-matter-only simulations miss.
arxiv-2602-21308:
Spotting compounds in liquid blends from IR spectra is a choke point for auto chem work, because peak shifts and widening defeat naive data-driven methods. Yannah Melle, Thanh Nguyen, Jeffrey Lopez, and Daniel Schwalbe-Koda show a method-based path can do it in this 2026 arXiv paper, for mock and lab blend spectra alike.

Tested on over forty-four thousand mock liquid-phase spectra, the method reaches up to ninety percent hit rate on binary and ternary blends. It resists spectral nudges, and its ceiling comes from near-same spectra that at root limit sharpness. A blind lab study spots nearly all samples right, giving tools and data for auto chem labs.
arxiv-2602-21408:
Nick Polson and one co-author propose Generative Bayesian Computation with Implicit Quantile Networks. It is a scalable rival to Gaussian process surrogates for emulating costly computer experiments. Gaussian processes are the default tool. But cubic cost, stationarity assumptions, and Gaussian predictions limit their reach.

Their method learns the full conditional quantile function from input-output pairs. One forward pass per quantile level then yields draws from the predictive distribution. Across 14 benchmarks it beats Gaussian-process methods on jump processes by 11 to 26 percent in CRPS. It gains 14 percent on a ten-dimensional Friedman function. It scales linearly to 90,000 training points where dense Gaussian processes fail. Gaussian processes keep an edge only on smooth surfaces, where their smoothness prior regularizes well.
arxiv-2602-22008:
When air churns in a heated tank, tiny solid particles do not simply spread at random; a temperature gradient can herd them into clusters. E. Elmakies and four co-authors test this effect, called turbulent thermal diffusion, in lab tanks stirred by one or two oscillating grids. They track air motion and particle positions with a laser imaging system, and map temperature with a probe carrying a dozen thermocouples.

The measurements show large particle clusters forming near the coldest average temperatures, just as theory predicts for this drift effect. The drift speed, which points against the temperature gradient, depends on particle inertia and flow strength in the ways tested. The experiments give a concrete, measured picture of how heat gradients sort dust-like particles in turbulent air.
arxiv-2602-22108:
Imagine one fast machine and endless slow ones, with jobs arriving over time and no knowledge of what comes next. John Jeang and Vladimir Podolskii study this one-fast-many-slow scheduling problem, asking how much an online scheduler must lose against an offline rival that sees the future. They treat three commitment styles: instant, eventual, and never-committing with restarts.

Earlier work pinned the instant case at a competitive ratio of two and bracketed the other two cases. This paper delivers tight bounds for the setting, giving exact or near-exact limits on the overhead each style must pay. The results map how much freedom to delay or revise decisions is worth when tasks keep arriving.
arxiv-2602-22208:
Video world models can simulate a game world from one player's view, but real environments teem with interacting agents. Georgy Savva and eight co-authors introduce Solaris, a multiplayer video world model that simulates consistent views for many players at once. They first built a data system for robust, automated, continuous collection of synchronized multi-player video and actions in games like Minecraft.

From that system they gathered millions of multiplayer frames and built an evaluation suite covering movement, memory, grounding, building, and view consistency. Training proceeds in stages from single-player to multiplayer modeling, mixing several training regimes. Solaris points toward game worlds that stay coherent no matter how many players share them.
arxiv-2602-22408:
Humans learn abstract rules from sparse examples with remarkable flexibility, but the mind strategies behind that skill are little mapped. Caroline Ahn and six co-authors introduce CogARC, a human-adapted subset of the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus, originally built to benchmark AI. Across two experiments, hundreds of participants solved dozens of abstract visual problems, inferring rules from few examples to transform test inputs.

Behavior was recorded at high time resolution, tracking example viewing, edit sequences, and multi-attempt tries. Participants mostly succeeded, with high accuracy in both experiments, though scores varied by problem. The corpus gives mind researchers a close record of how people actually crack abstract puzzles, not just whether they do.
arxiv-2602-22908:
Liangwei Wang and four co-authors ease reading scientific papers where tables and text intertwine. Data tables carry central meaning, but that meaning is co-built with surrounding prose through narrative interplay, taxing readers. A formative study mapped linking mechanisms, multi-level alignments, mention types, and a layered model of reader intents.

TableTale, the resulting augmented reading interface, weaves tables into text at paragraph, sentence, and mention levels. It builds a document-level linking schema automatically and renders cascading visual cues that unfold as readers move through the text. A within-subject study with 24 participants found lower cognitive workload and faster reading, promising better paper reading and future interface design.
arxiv-2602-23408:
Yuchun Feng and seven co-authors dissect action space design for imitation-based robotic manipulation policies. The action space, how a policy's outputs are represented, plays a pivotal role in learning, shaping the optimization landscape. Yet while data and model scaling have drawn heavy attention, action space choices have rested on ad-hoc heuristics or legacy designs, leaving policy design philosophy murky.

The team runs a large, systematic empirical study: over 13,000 real-world rollouts on a bimanual robot and evaluation of over 500 trained models across four scenarios. They split the design space along temporal and spatial axes and test absolute versus delta representations and joint-space versus task-space parameterizations. Results show predicting delta actions consistently improves performance, while joint-space representations favor control stability and task-space representations favor generalization, giving complementary strengths.
arxiv-2602-24008:
Kazuya Fujimoto and four co-authors give the first exact microscopic derivation of anomalous current fluctuations, described by the M-Wright function, in quantum many-body dynamics. The 2026 paper addresses a gap. Anomalous fluctuations had been derived exactly in a classical automaton and seen in varied classical systems. The quantum derivation remained elusive.

The authors analyze the integrated spin current in a one-dimensional Fermi-Hubbard model with infinitely strong repulsion between particles. In that strongly interacting quantum setting they derive the M-Wright form exactly, capturing a universal aspect of one-dimensional many-body transport.
