The result lays groundwork for exploring anomalous integrated currents across a broad class of quantum many-body systems. In short, the result opens a new line of study.
arxiv-2602-24208:
Yasaman Haghighi and Alexandre Alahi present SenCache, a sensitivity-aware caching framework that accelerates diffusion model inference without retraining. The 2026 paper notes that diffusion video generation is expensive because it requires many sequential denoising steps.

SenCache formalizes caching error by analyzing how sensitive model outputs are to perturbations in denoising inputs, and shows that sensitivity predicts caching error well. A dynamic policy then adaptively selects caching timesteps for each sample, replacing fixed heuristics with a principled, sample-specific rule. The framework explains why some earlier heuristics partly work. Tests on three video generation models show better visual quality than existing caching methods under similar compute budgets.
arxiv-2603-00308: Li and colleagues use megahertz surface acoustic waves to drive a silicone oil film over obstacles, a new route to coating by ultrasound. Tests show tiny waves in a piezoelectric base push oil films to climb and cross obstacles. Ultrasonic forcing, surface tension, and gravity decide whether coating succeeds. Their simple two-dimensional model folds obstacle shape into the film-evolution equation, with a new account of streaming over uneven bases. Despite its simplifications, the model matches tests in quality, suggesting it captures the key physics.
arxiv-2603-01008: Marcus and three colleagues count fixed points of cellular automata on random sparse graphs, where large systems flip between a frozen phase and a fluctuating phase. They compute the first two moments of the fixed-point count. These stay finite except at transitions where they turn singular in several forms. Fixed points cluster by near-agreement, with one cluster in the frozen phase and possibly many far-apart clusters in the fluctuating phase. The frozen-phase count distribution is fully calculated.
arxiv-2603-01108: Ashraf and six colleagues introduce GroundedSurg, the first benchmark that asks models to find one specific surgical tool from a spoken-style description, not just every tool of a class. Each item pairs an image with language targeting a single instrument, plus box and point grounding labels, spanning eye, laparoscopic, robotic, and open surgery. Tests reveal large gaps in modern segmentation and vision-language models, underscoring the need for clinically grounded reasoning in surgical AI.
arxiv-2603-01208: Yüksek and Golfinopoulos test whether the SPARC tokamak, built for positive triangularity, can run negative-triangularity plasmas. From over 600 equilibria spanning triangularity and elongation within coil and wall limits, they find moderate negative-triangularity double-null plasmas workable at a reduced 8-tesla point. The current is 2.1 mega-amperes. Volume drops about 43 percent and connection lengths shrink about 40 percent against the baseline design, while one shaping coil needs five and a half times more current. Yet all equilibria pass stability checks with margin.
arxiv-2603-01508:
Tony Rost asks a forward-looking question in this 2026 work: could a country cope if AI systems might one day merit moral concern? Science now tests AI designs against leading theories of mind, and none yet counts as a strong case. Still, Rost argues that even a credible chance calls for early planning.

He builds a Sentience Readiness Index that scores nations across six weighted areas. The index covers thirty-one jurisdictions and uses expert scoring with language-model help and repeat review. No place earns more than a partly prepared grade, and the top score still sits below half marks. Research settings score best everywhere, while job-level readiness scores worst, which Rost reads as a clear gap to close.
arxiv-2603-01608:
Wenye Lin and Kai Han improve the reasoning of large language models without erasing what they already know. Their 2026 work targets a known trade-off: extra training boosts thought, but it can wipe prior skills. Past work credits fresh on-policy data, yet the pair find a second, overlooked cause.

They show that a hidden regularizing effect sits inside a popular preference method reward estimate. Their method, SPoT, first fixes wrong steps in training traces with tiny edits from an expert oracle. Those near-native traces then train the model with a simple right-or-wrong score per trace. With just a few thousand fixed math pairs, a mid-size model gains clear accuracy in brief training. Gains hold on both familiar and new task types.
arxiv-2603-01808:
Kaiming Cui, Guang-Yao Xiao, Fabo Feng, and colleagues map where brown dwarfs are scarce between planets and stars. Their 2026 study joins radial velocity and astrometry data to build one large sample of wide-orbit companions. Brown dwarfs sit at the blurry border of planets and stars, so their scarcity pattern tests how each class forms.

The sample holds fifty-five giant planets, brown dwarfs, and low-mass stellar companions around sun-like stars. A rigorous count finds a clear brown dwarf desert near a set mass, with no sign it ends out to wide orbits. A new population of giant planets and light brown dwarfs also appears past the water-ice line. Metal and orbit trends point to two distinct formation routes for the groups. A combined population model reproduces the desert, which backs the dual formation view.
arxiv-2603-02008:
Faisal Mohamed, Catherine Ji, Benjamin Eysenbach, and Glen Berseth teach agents to explore with no outside rewards at all. Their 2026 work argues that good exploration tracks not just visited places, but how the agent represents the world. Temporal representations capture what a state implies about the future across many possible tasks.

Their method guides exploration toward states whose future outcomes are hard to predict. Temporal contrastive learning supplies those representations without full state reconstruction costs. The agent thus seeks states that add the most to its knowledge of the environment. Tests span locomotion, manipulation, and embodied tasks with complex exploratory behavior emerging. Such behavior usually needs hand-crafted extrinsic rewards, which this simpler time-based strategy avoids entirely.
arxiv-2603-02208:
Valentin Lacombe, Valentin Quesnel, and Damien Sileo build a data factory for reasoning in this 2026 paper. Training on tasks with checked answers can stretch what language models can reason about. Old task makers use fixed puzzles, so their data lacks breadth at scale. Their suite, Reasoning Core, makes fresh symbolic tasks on demand.

Tasks span planning, logic with equality, grammar rules, cause chains, and equation sets. Each task pairs with a solver that checks answers with full rigor. Task hardness can be dialed up or down for staged training. Solved traces can also be kept as teaching examples for models. Mixing this data into training lifted later reasoning and kept language skill intact. Even top models found the tasks hard with no examples.
arxiv-2603-02308:
Akshat Pandey, Aditya Mahadevan, A Alan Middleton, and Daniel Fisher study a disordered magnet at low temperature in this 2026 paper. Their model is the two-dimensional random-bond Ising model, a grid of spins with random link strengths. Frustration drives a switch between magnetic and nonmagnetic phases as temperature falls. A zero-temperature fixed point controls that switch and borders a spin glass phase.

The authors explain the point through a step-by-step rebuilding of the ground state. Each step adds frustration to a calm starting model until the target is reached. A mapping turns heat behavior into spectral traits of a linked quantum matrix. Disorder in that spectrum grows without bound along the flow. One exponent ties the spectral gap to system size and the spin stiffness at the fixed point.
arxiv-2603-02408:
Tobias Meier, Claire Marie Guimond, Raymond Pierrehumbert, and colleagues model the inside of a lava world in this 2026 paper. K2-141 b is a rocky planet with a magma ocean on its dayside. Extreme starlight couples its interior, air, and surface evolution. The team runs two-dimensional convection models that track volatile gases with tracers.

With a strong outer lid, mantle upwellings rise under the hottest and coldest points. Downwellings sink near the day-night borders, recycling crust in a one-sided tectonic style. The magma ocean runs a few hundred kilometers deep across models. Steady nightside volcanoes build a basalt crust and slowly drain mantle gases. Over a billion years, outgassing could reach tens of bars. Nightside eruptions stay too faint for current telescopes to detect.
arxiv-2603-02608:
Pavan Adroja and Sujoy Chakraborty wrote this 2026 mathematics paper on the Brauer group of certain moduli spaces. A moduli space is a space whose points stand for whole families of geometric objects. Their setting is a compact Riemann surface, a smooth closed curve, of genus at least three.

The authors compute the Brauer groups for spaces of stable parabolic connections and Higgs bundles. They also prove an equality for the related PGL case, matching a stack with the smooth part of its coarse space. The Brauer group measures whether a universal bundle can exist, so these results settle a basic structural question for these spaces.
arxiv-2603-02908:
Qi Zhang, Yifei Wang, Xiaohan Wang, and colleagues forecast whether fine-tuning a language model will help or hurt other skills. Their 2026 paper uses sparse autoencoders, tools that split a model's internal activity into cleaner features. Extra training shifts those features, and the shifts can spill into unrelated domains in poorly understood ways.

Their score, STS, finds which feature directions move during fine-tuning and matches those moves against target domains before any training happens. Across many models and domains, the score predicted real performance changes with strong correlation. An early extension to reinforcement learning is also reported. Because the features are interpretable, the score can guide training choices rather than merely warn about them after the fact.
arxiv-2603-03208:
Tracy Beck, Stephane Guilloteau, Gail Schaefer, and colleagues watch a young triple star system flare as two of its stars swing closest together. T Tauri South's close pair passed periastron in March 2023, and the ALMA telescope imaged the system before, during, and after. Their 2026 paper resolves the pair directly in the sharpest epochs.

Millimeter brightness rose as the passage heated the primary's disk and the surrounding dust, likely because the close approach triggered extra accretion onto the stars. Extended emission near the pair also changed shape and brightened, hinting at magnetic interaction or gravitational disruption of the disks. Around the northern star, a compact dust disk shows a shallow gap and a crescent of excess emission moving at orbital speed.
arxiv-2603-03308:
Adi Simhi and four colleagues study how a conversation's past can trap a language model. Earlier answers, even hallucinated ones, seem to steer later replies toward repeating the same stance. Their 2026 framework, History-Echoes, measures that pull in two ways at once: as probabilities over conversation states, and as geometry inside the model's hidden representations.

Three model families and six datasets cover varied behaviors, from errors to safety refusals. The two measures track each other closely. Persistence turns out to be a geometric trap: gaps in the model's inner space confine where its trajectory can go next. The finding links what a model does on the surface to the shape of its internal state, and the team's code is public.
arxiv-2603-03408:
G Alencar and three colleagues study black holes in a lower-dimensional version of Gauss-Bonnet gravity, an extension of general relativity with higher-curvature terms. They add quintessence, an exotic matter proposed to drive cosmic acceleration, and take the theory's limit down to three spacetime dimensions. Their 2026 paper finds exact solutions that extend the known BTZ black hole with both new ingredients.

Each solution has a single horizon that shrinks as the quintessence strength grows, plus a curvature singularity at the center whenever quintessence is present. Stable circular light orbits appear only for phantom-like quintessence, the most extreme kind. Heat calculations show the holes are stable and, as they evaporate, settle into remnants whose size quintessence controls, preventing complete evaporation. Every physical quantity also depends on the Gauss-Bonnet coupling strength.
arxiv-2603-03508:
Project Polyglot, led by Shiza Fatimah and Nicholas Kluge Corrêa, trains a Hindi language model from zero instead of borrowing one. Giant multilingual models leave low-resource languages behind, and earlier Hindi models quietly extended those opaque foundations. Their 2026 model, LilMoo, is a compact model of well under a billion parameters, built through a fully transparent and reproducible pipeline designed for limited computing budgets.

The training corpus, GigaLekh, was filtered by rules and by a language model acting as judge, then strengthened with curated English data. Recipe experiments explore how small models learn best under such constraints. Across broad evaluation suites, LilMoo consistently beats similarly sized multilingual rivals from the Qwen families. The team argues that careful language-specific pretraining can rival giant multilingual models at this scale.
arxiv-2603-04008: Audrito and others present the eXchange Calculus and its FCPP implementation for aggregate programming at the far edge. The paper gently presents the calculus and its C++ library, developed mainly at the University of Turin, home to Stefano Berardi's research on logical foundations. FCPP programs are essentially typed lambda terms, and the library has driven far-edge rover code, with aerial vehicles planned next.
arxiv-2603-04308: Kaliaperumal reproduces a known transformer quantization failure and extends it at systems level. For BERT base on QNLI, global W8A8 quantization drops accuracy from 89.66 percent in full precision by more than 35 points. Activations grow heavy tailed with depth, kurtosis reaching 271 in late layers. Mixed precision nearly restores baseline accuracy, while percentile calibration fails to recover it. Large channels thus carry structured signal, not rare noise, so channel aware precision beats scalar clipping. The study thus warns that blunt cutoffs miss real signal.
arxiv-2603-04508: Fischer and Yu probe dark matter with ultra-faint dwarf galaxies, the most dark dominated systems known. If dark matter self interacts, dwarf halos evolve gravothermally toward diverse density profiles. Idealised high resolution SIDM simulations of a Milky Way like system are compared with observed dwarfs. Most dwarfs show high central densities, meaning halos passed peak core expansion and entered collapse, with central density still rising. Collapse depth varies across satellites, and tidal stripping speeds evolution for close pericentre dwarfs, explaining the observed diversity.
arxiv-2603-04608: Gao and colleagues recover joint clusters across views with KRAFTY. Many datasets describe the same entities from complementary angles, like brain scans over time. Clustering each view alone misses shared structure, and each view mixes joint clusters, showing only part of the picture. KRAFTY models this setting in a space of enough dimension that each joint cluster fills its own orthogonal subspace. A sharp scree plot drop then marks the true joint cluster count, easing model choice. Simulations show KRAFTY wins when joint clusters outnumber per-view cluster sums.
arxiv-2603-05008: Tom Gustafsson and the rest of the team offer guidance on working out new Nitsche finite element methods holding same-value and inequality constraints on the unknown mechanical amount. They cast the problem in steadied finite element form built on the saddle point setup, with a Lagrange multiplier setting the constraint. The Nitsche method then appears in a general least form for nonlinear finite element methods, letting plain build with auto slope-finding. This stretches the method beyond classical edge holding, checked with solid mechanics setups and number settling evidence.
arxiv-2603-05108: Yichen Cai and team offer GaussTwin, a real-time digital twin mixing Cosserat rod physics with position-based dynamics for simulation. It adds Gaussian splatting for rendering and visual fix. Gaussians anchored to real primitives update coherently under photometric error and splitting masks, giving stable guess-fix while keeping real trueness. Tests in simulation and with a Franka Research 3 robot show raised tracking accuracy and toughness over shape-matching and rigid-only older models. The twin also lets push-based planning happen.
arxiv-2603-05208: Alexandra Weinberger and Ji Zeng ask when complete graph drawings must contain many pairwise disjoint curves. They prove disjoint curves are unavoidable under either of two rules: adjacent curves, sharing an endpoint, never cross, or non-adjacent curves cross at most once. Conversely, they construct drawings where adjacent curves cross exactly once and non-adjacent curves cross once or twice, so no two curves are disjoint. They also analyze how disjoint curves emerge without those assumptions and characterize the plane structures each rule guarantees.
arxiv-2603-05308: Qiao Jin and team present Med-V1, small three-billion-setting evidence-attribution models. Frontier models cost too much. Trained on synthetic data, Med-V1 beats its base models on five benchmarks, matches GPT-5 with good accounts. A case study quantifies hallucinations across citation instructions, finding format affects validity, with GPT-5 making more claims at GPT-4o-like hallucination rates. A second case study finds Med-V1 spotting high-stakes clinical-guideline misattributions, revealing negative health impacts. Med-V1 offers a lean, lightweight frontier-model alternative for biomedical evidence attribution.
arxiv-2603-05408: John Cullinan and Elisabeth Young study the Fourier close fit of the sign function by Krawtchouk polynomials. They give number evidence that the close fit's Gibbs phenomenon differs from the classical Gibbs constant, in contrast to other orthogonal polynomial families. They also show the close fit's steepness at zero is bounded by outright proving the limit of the derivative at zero equals log 4. This also contrasts with classical orthogonal polynomial approximations, where steepness has been shown unbounded as degree lifts.
arxiv-2603-05808: Fang and team study two linked groups of shapes tied to genus 0 stable maps into the Lagrangian Grassmann space. They construct a closing up in the style of Kausz for the space of even tables and describe its two-way geometry in full. The same closing up then appears as a checking fiber, in general place, inside a Kontsevich space. That modular reading yields results for the shape of pointed-conic spaces in the Lagrangian Grassmann space. Similar closings up for orthogonal Grassmann spaces are also given.
arxiv-2603-06608: Panda and colleagues present the Two-Bridge Map Suite, an intermediate StarCraft II benchmark between full game and mini-games, where full-game space makes rewards sparse but mini-game agents saturate. By disabling resource collection, base building, fog-of-war, and other economy mechanics, the environment isolates long-range navigation and micro-combat as two tactical skills. Experiments show agents learning maneuvering and engagement without full-game costs. Two-Bridge ships as a lightweight Gym-compatible wrapper on PySC2, with maps, wrappers, and reference scripts open-sourced.
arxiv-2603-06808: Barker and colleagues study rate-induced tipping when a habitat moves with environmental change, using a scalar reaction-diffusion equation for a localized habitat shifting between two asymptotic locations. The system admits three steady states at each location: a stable extinction state, an unstable pulse edge state giving an Allee effect, and a stable populated pulse at carrying capacity. Simulations identify a critical displacement, beyond which a critical movement rate exists. Faster than that rate, an initially thriving population goes extinct because the habitat moves too rapidly.
arxiv-2603-07108: Pathak and colleagues offer deep models for outbreak forecasts across space and time that carry honest doubt. Point outlooks alone hide doubt, so their methods sample full outlook spreads instead. That gives best- and worst-case outlooks for public health planning. The light models build doubt in from the start through an added noise step. Tests on low-rate outbreak data show true, solid out-of-sample outlooks.
arxiv-2603-07408: Fatima and colleagues run the first physical testbed study of the Internet of Mirrors, a network of smart mirrors spanning home, professional and hub tiers. They compare four plans for placing computation across the tiers under real Wi-Fi and 5G networks. No single plan wins everywhere; the best choice hinges on network, proximity and shared load. Sending classification upward cuts latency and consumer load but adds network overhead that grows with payload size and hop count.
arxiv-2603-07508: Sinai builds external subsets of nonstandard models of arithmetic mostly from internal sets. If an ultraproduct of prime finite fields contains a copy of the algebraic reals, then either that copy or its algebraic closure can be built by these methods. No copy of the full real field inside such an ultraproduct can ever be built this way. Yet the methods do yield a hyperreal field, or else an algebraically closed field at least as large as the continuum.
arxiv-2603-07608: Bouzeraib and Zidi add an extra non-abelian gauge symmetry to the left-right symmetric model, plus one generation of vector-like fermions. New self-dual scalars break the symmetry and mix vector-like with chiral fermions. The model explains tiny neutrino masses: first- and second-generation masses follow the standard left-right seesaw, while the third generation follows a new seesaw involving vector-like neutrinos. Collider data then bound the extra charged gauge boson and its neutral partner.
arxiv-2603-07708: Ranjan and colleagues present VoiceSHIELD-Small, a lightweight real-time model that transcribes speech and flags harmful content in one step. Traditional pipelines convert speech to text then filter, adding delay and discarding audio cues. Built on a Whisper-small encoder with mean pooling and a classification head, it classifies audio in about a tenth of a second on mid-tier graphics cards. Tests on a balanced clip set show very high accuracy with few missed harmful inputs.
arxiv-2603-08008: Dai and colleagues extract the universal small-x dipole scattering amplitude from a global analysis built on a physics-led network. They impose no prior MV-type parametrization. The network supplies a smooth surrogate for the amplitude, whose rapidity curve follows the Balitsky-Kovchegov evolution law. Deep Inelastic Scattering data on total and charm cross sections, exclusive J/psi photoproduction, and a positivity rule constrain its shape. The final single amplitude covers all fitted data in one framework, easing the tension between total and charm channels that rigid fits suffer.
arxiv-2603-08508: Goulas and colleagues test two ways to scrub lingering starlight speckles behind a pyramid wavefront sensor. Non-common path flaws escape the main sensor yet stain the sky image, capping how faint a companion can be found. One fix cuts leftover starlight by a factor of 20 for bright stars, while a dark-hole loop cuts it by a factor of 200.
arxiv-2603-08908: Brown and colleagues measure masses of neutron-rich ytterbium nuclei for the first time. Six new measurements isolate a strikingly strong proton-neutron link in the hole-hole quadrant below lead-208. The signal rivals those at doubly magic nuclei and shape transitions, while current mean-field models miss the anomaly, and the results benchmark models toward a key r-process waiting point.
arxiv-2603-09108: Yuheng Wang and colleagues build a search tool that finds past skin cancer cases from a query pairing a lesion photo with written descriptors. Their transformer framework learns layered query features and aligns them with candidate images at both global and local levels. Local alignment pools key regions through several spatial attention masks, while global alignment adds whole-image semantic guidance. A weighted score favors clinically salient local evidence, and tests on Derm7pt beat prior methods.
arxiv-2603-09608: Kazım Yavuz Ekşi studies why magnetar spin periods cluster in a narrow band, alongside those of X-ray dim isolated neutron stars. The current samples hold 30 magnetars and 8 of the isolated stars, with periods spanning roughly a third of a second to about thirteen seconds. Using a point-likelihood technique under a steady-state population and a general braking law, Ekşi constrains the final periods tightly for braking index above two. Magnetars end near twelve seconds, while birth periods stay largely unconstrained.
arxiv-2603-09908: Syed Izzat Ullah and Jose Baca introduce NanoBench, a flight data set for the tiny Crazyflie nano quadrotor. Heavier drone benchmarks miss the actuator level signals that nano craft need, where odd airflow and small motors break standard models. NanoBench holds many flights with motion capture truth, raw sensor data, controller internals and motor commands, all time aligned. Set protocols cover system identification, control testing and onboard state estimation.
arxiv-2603-10008: Ahmed Khaled Khamis describes a system for sorting Arabic medical texts into many distinct categories for the AbjadMed task. His main model fine tunes AraBERTv2 with hybrid pooling and multi sample dropout. Benchmarks against multilingual encoders and large causal decoders show the specialised bidirectional encoder wins clearly. Decoders trained to predict the next token, he argues, form sequence biased embeddings that blur the fine boundaries this task needs.
arxiv-2603-10108: Rishi Acharya and coauthors show that a bulk plasmon can create electron hole pairs in a non equilibrium Fermi liquid. Collective modes are usually seen as channels that merely drain excitation energy through Landau damping. Under strong optical photo doping of EuCd2As2, time resolved photoemission shows plasmons moving energy from a flat bulk band into empty surface states. That transfer stabilises a long lived feature matching a Mahan exciton.
arxiv-2603-10208: Ho-Sang Chan and coauthors simulate a strongly relativistic tidal disruption event and find general relativistic effects surprisingly weak. A Sun like star passing close to a million solar mass black hole was expected to shed orbital energy fast and form a disk promptly. Their relativistic hydrodynamics run instead shows debris staying highly eccentric, pooled near apocenter, with shocks rather than accretion powering the event. Early precession driven shocks fade within about a week.
arxiv-2603-10408: Tianshuo Xu and co-authors introduce Motion Forcing, a framework that steadies video generation when scenes grow complex, with collisions or dense traffic. Video models must juggle visual quality, physical consistency, and controllability, and that balance often breaks. The key move splits physical reasoning from visual synthesis in three stages: sparse point anchors for dynamics, depth maps for shape, then rendered appearance. Masked point recovery in training forces the model to infer missing paths from latent physical laws, not mere pattern matching. Driving, physics, and robotics tests support the design.
arxiv-2603-10508: Sai Li, Cheng Liu, and Jincheng Guo investigate nearly two dozen candidate luminous blue variables in M31 and M33, studying eight in detail. Spectra show broad hydrogen and helium lines, rich iron emission, and clear changes over time, all in line with known luminous blue variables. Low outflow speeds from P Cygni profiles joined the classification criteria. Fitting energy distributions gave temperatures, luminosities, and starting masses well above the Sun's. One source is confirmed, four rate as high-probability candidates, and three await more data.
arxiv-2603-10808: Linghao Zhang argues for nurture-first agent development, in which expert AI agents are grown through conversation rather than built in one code or prompt phase. Domain expertise is tacit, personal, and always shifting, so a finished build phase fits it badly. The proposal starts agents with minimal scaffolding and grows them through structured talk with practitioners, periodically turning scattered dialogue knowledge into reusable assets. A three-layer design sorts knowledge by how fast it changes. A finance research agent case study shows the idea at work.
arxiv-2603-11208: Tal Schwartzman and coauthors prepare ground states by approximating imaginary-time evolution, which exponentially suppresses unwanted higher-energy states, using purely unitary multi-copy protocols. Their circuits run several copies of the system under real-time evolution and controlled-SWAP operations. One family is a tree design with provable polynomial-depth convergence but fast-growing width; the other is a compact hedge design with polynomial width, supported by numerics. Mid-circuit post-selection can speed convergence at practical success rates, and circuit volume can be traded against measurement shot counts.
arxiv-2603-11308: Mario Sayde and coauthors rebuild PCA for heavy-tailed data. PCA relies on second moments, which fail under infinite variance and impulsive noise. Their model treats data as a random positive rescaling of a Gaussian vector, capturing multivariate t and stable laws. They define PCA through a logarithmic loss that stays defined when moments do not exist. Under that loss, the heavy-tailed parts coincide with PCA of the Gaussian covariance below. They estimate that covariance with robust methods and beat PCA on denoising tasks.
arxiv-2603-11408: Dai and co-authors test whether richer news sentiment can help predict weekly moves in WTI crude oil futures. Simple positive or negative scores miss much of what energy news carries. The team uses large language models to score five traits in each story, from relevance to uncertainty. News from 2020 to 2025 feeds a weekly model. Pairing GPT-4o with FinBERT works best, and the intensity and uncertainty scores prove most useful.
arxiv-2603-11608: Li and Bernacki present a level-set framework for modeling grain growth in polycrystals, built for high fidelity. Full-field methods struggle when boundary energies vary sharply across a sample. Their framework extends an earlier form that was checked on a single triple junction case. It tracks growth driven by capillarity, with boundary energies that depend on disorientation. Against three established models, it gives the most energy-consistent grain statistics and angle patterns. Accuracy and robustness hold across the full range of energy variation.
arxiv-2603-11808: Bi and co-authors present a framework that mines open-source agent repositories to harvest skills for LLM agents. General models know much but often lack the step-by-step craft real workflows need. The pipeline scans repository structure, finds skills by dense retrieval, and rewrites them into the standard SKILL.md format. It draws visualization and teaching skills from systems like TheoremExplainAgent and Code2Video, both built on Manim. With security checks and scoring, the authors report 40% gains in knowledge transfer for agent-made teaching content.
arxiv-2603-11908: König and Messing build witnesses for fixpoint games played on lattices. A witness can certify that the least fixpoint of a function sits above, or not below, a given bound, and yields game strategies. A Galois connection links a logic universe, where the witness lives, to a behaviour universe, where the function is defined. They treat primal and dual games, showing witnesses and winning strategies convert both ways. Case studies cover bisimilarity formulas and lower bounds on termination odds for Markov chains.
arxiv-2603-12508: Antony, Cao, Wang, and Huang present ELLA, a social robot that supports early language growth at home. ELLA uses generative AI to hold adaptive conversations with preschoolers through interactive storytelling. Parents pick the language targets, and the robot scaffolds dialogue around them. The team interviewed parents and educators, then refined the robot through twelve in-home design workshops. ELLA was then deployed with ten children for eight days. The authors report how children engaged with the robot and draw design lessons for home language robots.
arxiv-2603-12608: Bo Pan and co-authors build a deep research system that keeps people inside the search loop. Current tools run from query to report on their own, which leaves users passive. A formative study found weak points in process visibility, steering, and context handling. Their InterDeepResearch sorts context into information, actions, and sessions. That structure trims context and lets users trace evidence back across steps. Benchmark scores rival top systems, and a user study backed the joint approach.
arxiv-2603-12808: Pengfei Liu and co-authors build a large reasoning model that handles many molecular tasks at once. The model routes each task to a fitting specialist for prediction or inference. It learns from chain-of-thought traces and from rewards tied to molecule facts. Tasks span description, generation, naming, property checks, and reaction calls, 10 in all. It beat more than 20 rival models, both general and task-specific. One case study drafts and screens a brain drug lead end to end.
arxiv-2603-12908: MoniJesu Wonders James and co-authors present GoalSwarm, a decentralized team of drones that hunts objects named in open words. Heavy perception models strain onboard compute, and coordination across agents is complex. Each drone projects depth views into a shared, light 2D semantic map. A Bayesian value map fuses detection confidence into goal relevance per pixel. Frontier scoring, cost-utility bidding, and spacing penalties then split the search. Zero-shot detection from SAM3 needs no task-specific training.
arxiv-2603-13008: Georges Abboudeh and co-authors ask whether supernovae drive turbulence in the solar neighborhood. They compare hydrogen line-of-sight velocities near the Sun with 1 kpc simulations. Two drivers were tested: supernova feedback and imposed large-scale forcing. Synthetic sky maps let the runs face the data on equal terms. Supernova-driven runs fell well short of the observed velocity spread. Strong large-scale forcing matched both the median spread and the full distribution shape.
arxiv-2603-13208: Hayyim Pulido-Hernández and Jorge L. Cervantes-Cota test how spatial curvature affects limits on neutrino mass. Their joint analysis uses CMB, BAO, and supernova data from recent major surveys. A symmetric extension lets the effective neutrino mass take negative values, which softens prior bias near zero. Adding curvature shifts the posterior and eases the tension with the terrestrial lower limit. The most flexible model eases tension further but weakens the precision of the mass estimate. Bounds, they conclude, hinge on boundary effects and geometric degeneracies.
arxiv-2603-13408: S. R. Pinto and P. P. Avelino derive a Lagrangian identity for p-branes and trace what it means for mass. The identity links a Nambu-Goto p-brane Lagrangian to the trace of its energy-momentum tensor, for any gravitational field. For point particles it reduces to the standard on-shell relation. In nonminimally coupled scalar-tensor gravity, cosmic string loops can gain or lose rest mass as the universe evolves. The team extends the result to closed p-branes in higher-dimensional spacetimes.
arxiv-2603-13908: Abdelmeguid and Hasan build a small neural predictor for power use in GTernal robots at the Georgia Tech Robotarium. Past power readings predict future use far better than motion data alone, with a lag-one correlation of 0.95. Their 7,041-parameter network reaches an R2 of 0.90 on held-out motion patterns. On seven real robots in a collision avoidance task, it scores 0.87 with no retraining. Each prediction takes 224 microseconds, fast enough for real-time control.
arxiv-2603-14808: Ung, Mahajan and Reichman benchmark constrained-path Monte Carlo on the triangular-lattice Hubbard model. Symmetry-adapted trial wavefunctions drive the accuracy gains here. Away from half-filling, symmetry-keeping free-electron trials stay within about 1% of exact results. Exact diagonalization and DMRG runs supply the reference values. At half-filling, frustration in mid to strong coupling breaks simple trials. Symmetry-projected trials restore matching accuracy there. Cost grows only polynomially with system size under projection. Frustrated ground-state contests gain a practical tool, they conclude.
arxiv-2603-14908: Gao and co-authors train closed-loop driving policies in pseudo-simulation with PerlAD. Imitation policies stumble when open-loop training meets real driving demands. Reinforcement learning fixes goals but rendering worlds cost too much. PerlAD builds a vector-space pseudo-simulation from offline driving data. A prediction world model makes nearby agents react to the ego plan. A split planner pairs imitation for lateral paths with RL for speed. Bench2Drive scores top prior end-to-end RL results, they report. Rendering gaps vanish in the loop.
arxiv-2603-15108: Tian and co-authors present BodyGuards, a framework where several robots escort a human operator through unknown, hostile ground. Communication is limited, so the robots cannot stay in constant contact. The operator follows a dynamic plan that keeps a local map with marked risk zones. Robots mix frontier exploration with planned return trips to share news and spot threats. Coordination protocols tie exploration and information sharing together. In human-in-the-loop simulations and hardware tests, the method cut operator risk and mission time versus baselines.
arxiv-2603-15408: Wang and co-authors present TrinityGuard, a safety evaluation and monitoring framework for language-model multi-agent systems. The framework rests on OWASP guidance and a three-tier taxonomy of twenty risk types. Tiers cover single agents, agent-to-agent links, and whole-system hazards. An abstraction layer adapts it to varied system shapes. Curated attack probes produce per-risk reports, while monitor agents watch run traces and raise live alerts. Case studies show it works across representative multi-agent setups.
arxiv-2603-15608: Lee and co-authors test whether today's quantum processors can simulate quantum materials with real accuracy. They run a superconducting processor with up to 50 qubits. A quantum-classical workflow computes dynamical structure factors for the material KCuF3. The team compares the spectra with neutron-scattering measurements from the lab. Circuit depth and fidelity shape how close the match is. They also simulate a gapped XXZ chain linked to CsCoX3 compounds.
arxiv-2603-15808: Heaton and co-authors push axion hunts into the keV mass range with SACLA. Axions were proposed to explain CP symmetry in quantum chromodynamics. The team runs a light-shining-through-wall setup at the SACLA X-ray laser. Laue crystal Bormann effects boost the search reach. Bounds on the axion-photon coupling improve by over tenfold. Sensitivity spans masses up to about 22 eV. In a narrow band near 3.47 keV, reach touches the QCD axion line. Those lab limits now lead that mass range.
arxiv-2603-16308: Trybus studies spatial logics built on affine geometry and regions. Most prior work treats the flat real plane. His long-term aim is a family of such logics over spaces of growing dimension. First he shows that logics of distinct dimensions have distinct theories. He then takes up the three-dimensional case. Its logic can describe a full coordinate frame. In the end, each region satisfies an affine complete formula.
arxiv-2603-16408: Curien, Hu, and Qian study critical self-similar Markov trees. These random decorated trees generalize the fragmentation tree. Earlier work set the critical case aside. The authors borrow tools from branching random walk. A recent result by Aïdékon, Hu, and Shi anchors the method. They construct the critical trees and compute their fractal dimension. Spinal decomposition then yields their harmonic and length measures.
arxiv-2603-16508: Xiao and Zhang hunt nearby primordial black holes by geometry alone. A close evaporation burst would bend the gamma-ray wavefront. That bend shifts arrival delays between spacecraft in a telling way. Their method joins imaging positions with multi-spacecraft timing. Applied to Swift short bursts, no clear bend appears yet. The tightest event already probes distance near 1.2 AU. Future wide-field detectors could reach far deeper into space.
arxiv-2603-16708: Zweig, Zhang, Knowles, and Azizi let lineage trees steer trajectory inference. The task fills in paths between observed time points of a changing system. Earlier methods used smooth geometry alone to set the metric. Many systems also carry discrete, directed rules for allowed transitions. Their Finsler metric folds lineage knowledge into the geometry. Interpolation then respects both shape and lineage. Tests on synthetic and real data improved over geometry-only priors. The gain matters most in developmental biology, where lineage trees are known.
arxiv-2603-16908: Qian and co-authors present 4I-SIM, a microscope method that joins super resolution with optical sectioning. Structured illumination microscopy blurs thick samples, because out of focus light creates artifacts. Four beam interference adds extra orders, widening lateral support and filling the axial missing cone. The authors report lateral resolution of 103 nm and axial resolution of 336 nm. That is nearly twice the lateral sharpness of the 2D method, with much better sectioning. Tests on thick fixed and live samples show detail such as mitochondrial changes under high glucose stress.
arxiv-2603-17608: Raßhofer and Frey show how local composition can freeze droplet growth in active emulsions. In passive blends, droplets merge and grow without control. Their system swaps molecules between two species that diffuse at unlike speeds. When the fast species builds up inside droplets, gradients push back against more inflow. That balance pins droplet size, they show with sharp-interface theory and simulations. No interaction asymmetry is needed.
arxiv-2603-17708: Brumer and Kramer find number fields that host no good abelian varieties at all. They extend tools from Fontaine, Abrashkin, and Schoof into clear criteria. The tests decide when every abelian variety over a field must face bad reduction somewhere. Under the generalized Riemann hypothesis, they count 24,744 such fields. The fields span many degrees, up to degree 16. The result maps where smooth arithmetic geometry cannot live.
arxiv-2603-18008: Huang and co-authors present TherapyGym, a framework that tests and trains therapy chatbots on fidelity and safety. Fidelity uses the Cognitive Therapy Rating Scale, scored over multi-turn sessions by an automated pipeline. Safety uses labels for therapy risks, such as missed signs of harm or abuse. A bench of 116 dialogues with expert ratings helps audit the LLM judges. Training with these rewards raised mean fidelity scores sharply in their tests.
arxiv-2603-18308: Kulkarni, Poulakakis, and Huang build state tracking for legged robots that uses body senses alone. Joint traces hold rich clues about how the robot moves and where it goes. Past learned models treat noise as Gaussian, a claim that can break with thin training data. Their method states noise as set claims, with no fixed shape assumed. A clear scheme feeds those claims into a Gaussian filter, and tests on two real quadruped sets stay on track.
arxiv-2603-18908: Gorbett and Jana test whether one language model's inner states can be read by another model's output head. They learn a simple linear map between the late hidden states of separately trained models. Mapped states keep much of the target model's choice edges and confidence in tests. At times, the map even lets one model speak through the other's head with no fine-tuning. Success tracks shared token sets and source model size. Maps from strong to weak models work best.
arxiv-2603-19008: Chang and co-authors improve search for systems that must pick among rival options. Plain retrieval often brings back broad background that cannot split the choices. Their method first forms a quick working guess from the question and options. It then writes three targeted searches. One seeks support for the guess. One seeks marks that split it from rivals. One checks key clues in the question. Tests on medical question sets show steady gains. The generator can confirm or drop its first guess on the found proof.
arxiv-2603-19108: Safta and Najm examine how to build Karhunen-Loeve expansions for random processes with care. The method breaks a covariance operator into modes through an integral equation. On a grid, that task becomes a matrix eigen problem. They show it matches a scaled singular value split of the sample matrix. That link gives one path for model-based and data-driven builds. Known kernel cases serve as checks in one dimension. Tests in two and three dimensions show how grid, rule, and sample choices trade off.
arxiv-2603-19208: Hoffreumon and Woods argue that quantum theory built on real numbers cannot be ruled out by tests. An earlier study claimed a network test could falsify the real version but not the standard one. They show that claim rests on an assumption no test can check. The key split is between math rules for sources and what can be seen in data. Once source freedom is set by what is seen, both theories match. This holds for all finite network and step-by-step setups.
arxiv-2603-19308: Wang and co-authors help self-driving cars share what they sense, even when their gear and models differ. Mixed feature types make fusion hard, and pairwise translators do not scale. Their GT-Space builds one shared feature space from ground-truth labels. Each agent then needs just one adapter to map its features into that space. A fusion network trains with contrastive loss across many sensor mixes. On two simulated sets and one real set, detection beats the baselines. Robustness holds across the mixes tested.
arxiv-2603-19408: Pal and Powell study how spin ice relaxes after a magnetic field quench near the Kasteleyn transition. They run Monte Carlo simulations and lean on dynamic scaling theory. The decay of magnetization and monopole density is tracked over time. A simple model of free strings of flipped spins fits the data well. It matches both the relaxation and the spread of string lengths near the point. Wider scaling forms cover states with more monopoles. Farther from the point, the scaling picture breaks down in a clear way.
arxiv-2603-19508: Mahraj and co-authors test MgSnN2 as a low-cost, non-toxic material for solar cells. They use density functional theory and efficiency-limit calculations. The crystal has an orthorhombic form with a bandgap of 2.45 electron volts. A two-micron film reaches 13.17 percent efficiency in the model at room temperature. A multi-junction tandem design lifts that figure to 22.42 percent. Adding cation disorder shrinks the bandgap, which may suit solar use even better.
arxiv-2603-19608: Hu and co-authors present FB-CLIP, a zero-shot tool that finds small flaws in images. Such flaws are hard to spot in industry and medicine, and labelled examples are rare. CLIP-style models mix object and background, which blurs the search. FB-CLIP builds richer text cues from three views of its text side. On the image side, it splits foreground from background and damps the background down. A consistency rule pulls image traits toward normal or abnormal text anchors. Tests show sharp pinpointing in cluttered scenes.
arxiv-2603-19908: García and co-authors build a theory of composable lingos for protocol dialects. Dialects harden network protocols with light security, and the lingo is their key part. Attackers cannot speak the lingo, and its talk keeps changing, making a moving target. The authors use formal patterns, generic system transforms with strong guarantees. They give patterns that make single lingos stronger and compose several into one. A further pattern turns any chosen lingo and protocol into a full dialect.
arxiv-2603-20008: van de Bruck, Burgess, and Smith ask if QCD axions survive in models that relax the vacuum energy. Yoga models let a field slowly lower the cosmological constant. The same relaxation damps other slow physics, set by the relaxon mass scale. Fast collider physics stays untouched, but light scalars in cosmology change a lot. For the QCD axion, the vacuum potential gets suppressed. Matter effects can then dominate and push the axion from its usual minimum. The standard mass and coupling link breaks, landing in ruled out territory.
arxiv-2603-20308: Bansal and Gangwani present Reason-to-Transmit, a framework for cooperative perception among vehicles. Agents must share sensor data over tight vehicle-to-everything bandwidth. Older methods use fixed rules to choose what to send. Their module weighs scene context, neighbor information gaps, and budget for each region. Any communication beat no communication by about 58% average precision. Their method gained most under heavy occlusion, nearing oracle scores. It also held up under packet drops of up to 50%.
arxiv-2603-20508: Roytburg and co-authors study whether strong reasoning models write traces that weaker models can follow. Chains of thought now feed monitoring and distillation between models. Cooperation across capability tiers needs such traces to stay legible. They call this goal weak-to-strong legibility. Weak monitors may become a standard, affordable safety scaffold. Current legibility metrics, they note, reward shortness over thoroughness. That misses what oversight actually needs from a trace. Their work frames how legibility should be measured instead.
arxiv-2603-20708: Zhang and co-authors use event cameras to clean images blurred by air turbulence. Standard methods need many frames, which adds delay and data load. Event sensors track fast change with microsecond timing. The team found turbulence events flip polarity near sharp image edges. Moving objects instead form smooth tubes in space and time. Their EHETM method uses both cues in two modules. It beat prior tools on two real datasets they built. Data load fell by about 77 percent.
arxiv-2603-20808: Wang and co-authors find that multimodal language models lose visual skill in their middle layers. Language driven training, they argue, trades visual fidelity for text output. Compared with the input features, mid layer features lose global and patch level structure. Their fix is predictive regularization, called PRe. It forces mid layer features to predict the initial visual features. This keeps core visual traits alive inside the model. Broad tests showed vision language scores rose when this decay was curbed.
arxiv-2603-20908: Fichera and co-authors propose Bayesian scattering as a simple baseline for uncertainty in image tasks. Complex deep learning methods dominate this area, yet no clear, principled baseline exists. Their method pairs the wavelet scattering transform with a simple probabilistic head. Scattering features come from geometry, not training, so they resist overfitting the training data. This helps the uncertainty stay sensible when the data shifts a lot. They test medical images across hospitals, wealth maps across countries, and molecule search. Results suggest the method is a solid first baseline.
arxiv-2603-21008: Przybyłek and Siedlecki settle questions on phaseless polynomial interpolation. Earlier work showed a polynomial over the rationals can be recovered from few points, but only with exponential time methods. With more points, recovery runs in polynomial time. They prove three results. Recovery from slightly fewer than twice the degree bound stays polynomial time. Recovery from a smaller point set, scaled by any constant factor below one, is NP-Complete. And evaluation points that admit a unique solution can be chosen in polynomial time.
arxiv-2603-21308: Faza and co-authors recast interval uncertainty propagation as a direct regression task for neural network surrogates. In robust design, engineers need bounds on a system's output when the inputs are known only within intervals. The standard route solves costly optimization problems. Surrogates inside that loop still need many calls. Their approach predicts the output bounds in one step. They test plain propagation through standard networks, bound propagation methods such as IBP and CROWN, and interval neural networks. The methods run much faster while the bounds stay accurate.
arxiv-2603-21808: Yang and co-authors read lips in Mandarin without the cascade that most Chinese systems rely on. Mandarin tones make visual speech recognition hard, so older systems pass through pinyin first. Errors then pile up between stages, and inference slows. Their design learns phoneme, viseme, and text targets jointly in one multitask setup. A semantic-guided contrastive loss aligns the feature streams over time. Features can switch on at inference as needed, trading speed for accuracy. On public datasets, the method beat prior systems, the authors report.
arxiv-2603-21908: Zhang and co-authors cut energy use in neural network inference on edge devices by tuning chip speeds around sparsity. Voltage and frequency scaling at the whole-model level is too coarse, while per-operator scaling loses time in switching delays. Their SparseDVFS system uses operator sparsity to guide frequency choice. An offline model maps sparsity to the best speed set for CPU, GPU, and memory. A runtime step groups operators into blocks to spread switching costs. A single governor then coordinates the parts. Tests gained 78 percent in energy efficiency.
arxiv-2603-22208: Kendall and co-authors build a model to catch hidden bleeding in ICU patients. Internal bleeding may not show clear signs, yet late treatment can be catastrophic. Clinicians watch vital sign trends for warning patterns. Their Bayesian regime switching model reads vitals and labs over time. It gives a probability for the patient's hidden physiological state at each moment. The data behind it covers 33,924 real ICU stays at Mayo Clinic. A new sampling routine learns the state probabilities and handles pre-admission changes.
arxiv-2603-22308: Todorov shows that the complex numbers hide tiny infinitesimals inside them. The complex field contains non-Archimedean subfields, and those hold non-zero infinitesimals. The claim rests on an old algebra theorem by Steinitz, which Todorov walks through in detail. The result surprises, since the complex field is built from the reals. The reals were defined in the 1800s in part to banish infinitesimals from calculus. Todorov argues that infinitesimals still simplify the language of analysis. He links the point to Colombeau generalized functions.
arxiv-2603-22708: Zhang and co-authors present SysInsight, a system that tunes database settings by reading source code. Modern database systems expose hundreds of knobs that shape performance. Manuals give generic advice, the authors argue, while the code holds the real control logic. SysInsight mixes static code analysis with language model reasoning. It extracts tuning insights, then turns them into checked rules via rule mining. In tests it finds the best setup 7.11 times faster than the top baseline. Performance also improves by 19.9 percent.
arxiv-2603-22808: Vepakomma introduces PolyVeil, a protocol for private Boolean sums across many clients. Each client hides its bits as permutation matrices inside the Birkhoff polytope. The server gets perfect simulation-based security. A separate aggregator faces a hard inference problem based on permanents. Two variants differ in what the aggregator sees: full matrices or one scalar. Analysis shows a deep tension between the two privacy goals. Hardness needs the full view, while strong differential privacy needs the scalar view. The protocol needs no public-key setup and gives exact totals.
arxiv-2603-23208: Bergam, Deng, and Hsu prove new bounds on the sample complexity of multi-group learning. Their algorithm extends the one-inclusion graph method with a generalized form of bipartite matching. In the group-realizable setting, a matching lower bound shows their log n over n rate cannot be improved in general. A relaxed version of the goal yields more. When the test group is picked without seeing the sample, their method reaches the optimal 1 over n rate.
arxiv-2603-23408: Hanna and three co-authors build GeoSANE, a foundry that learns geospatial skill from model weights, not data. Remote sensing now has many foundation models, each strong in one corner. Their strengths stay split rather than merged. GeoSANE distills many models into one shared representation. Given a target design, it generates weights ready for fine-tuning. The models serve classification, segmentation, and detection across sensing modes. On ten datasets and GEO-Bench, they beat models trained from scratch. They top pruning and distillation routes for light networks.
arxiv-2603-24108: Blondel and co-authors bring Aitchison geometry to uncertainty estimates in hyperspectral image unmixing. Unmixing finds the share of each material in every pixel, but most tools give only point estimates. Users then cannot tell how much to trust the shares. The authors use compositional geometry to build simplex-valued Gaussian process priors. They link this geometry to constrained sampling methods already in use. They also propose diagnostics that respect the sum constraints on abundance vectors. Tests use both real and simulated data.
arxiv-2603-24508: Williams and co-authors present a multi-GPU version of the BIT1 particle-in-cell Monte Carlo code for plasma physics. Such simulations struggle on heterogeneous supercomputers due to data movement and synchronisation costs. Their portable MPI plus OpenMP design runs on both Nvidia and AMD accelerators, using target tasks with explicit dependencies to overlap computation and communication. Persistent device memory, a compact data layout, and pinned host memory improve transfer efficiency. Using openPMD and ADIOS2 for I/O, they scale to 16,000 GPUs on Frontier with strong gains.
arxiv-2603-24708: Park proves Hamilton decompositions for the directed 3-torus for every m at least three. The torus is the product of three directed m-cycles, and splits into three arc-disjoint Hamilton cycles. The proof reduces the problem to m-step return maps on a layer section. For odd m, five Kempe swaps give return maps conjugate to the standard odometer. For even m, a sign-product invariant blocks that route, so a low-layer witness and finite splice analysis finish the job. A Lean 4 formalisation accompanies it.
arxiv-2603-25408: Keskin and Baştürk sort eclipsing binary stars with deep learning, straight from their light curves. Big sky surveys like Kepler, TESS, and Gaia pour out more light curves than people can grade by hand. An eclipsing pair dims in a rhythm set by its orbit and shapes. The study trains machine learning methods to read that curve shape and assign a class. The aim is fast, accurate sorting of huge survey hauls. Such automation helps astronomers spend their time on the odd cases.
arxiv-2603-25508: Tachikawa, Tsuji, and Watanabe track what a special wall does to fermion wave packets. The Maldacena-Ludwig boundary turns plain excitations into exotic ones with fractional charge. The setup echoes fermion-monopole scattering and the multi-channel Kondo effect. They write the outgoing state for a scattered pair in explicit form. Its charge density piles up in one spot and sums to a finite fractional value. The mean particle count, though, blows up as the packet shrinks to a point.
arxiv-2603-26008: Bhosale and co-authors present FairLLaVA, a fine-tuning method that curbs demographic bias in medical vision-language models. Such models can write uneven diagnostic text for different patient groups. FairLLaVA cuts the mutual information between target attributes in the model's representations. This pushes the representations to ignore demographic traits. The method works as a light plug-in with low-rank adapters. It fits many model designs. On chest X-ray reports and skin image questions, group gaps shrink, the authors report. Clinical scores and text quality both improve.
arxiv-2603-26308: Ain, Temizel, and Jawed propose D-GATNet, a graph model that flags ADHD from brain scans. The model uses dynamic functional connectivity, built by sliding a window over fMRI data. Brain regions form graph nodes, and link strengths form the edges. A graph attention network reads spatial links, while convolution and temporal attention read change over time. Attention weights show which regions and time spans drive each call, keeping the model open to inspection.
arxiv-2603-26508: Gadouleau and Johnson extend the semiring of discrete dynamical systems to partial transformations. In the original semiring, finite transformations add by acting on disjoint sets and multiply by acting in parallel. The authors widen the frame to formal sums over any semiring, then focus on binary coefficients. They study injective partial maps, which split into sums of chains and cycles. For sums of cycles over the binary field, they give a compact account of every solution to the division problem, then extend it to all injective cases.
arxiv-2603-26608: Collins and co-authors test two fixes for timing errors in gaze-and-pinch control for virtual reality. Users often pinch just before their gaze lands, or after it leaves a target. A sticky rule adds a time buffer, while a magnetic rule pulls selection toward nearby targets. Nine users tried both against a baseline on a Samsung Galaxy XR headset. Speed and throughput held steady, yet errors fell and user habits shifted in clear ways. Magnetic selection led users to trade precision for speed, an offloading effect.
arxiv-2603-26708: Bernal-Alvarado and Delepine derive fractional epidemic dynamics from a quantum field theory model of contagion. Classic compartment models assume well-mixed, local spread, yet real outbreaks show bursts and long-range links. Fractional operators are often added by hand to mimic those traits. Mapping the spread process through the Doi-Peliti formalism, the authors compute a one-loop correction beyond mean field. Integrating out a shifting host vacuum yields coupled space-time fractional equations. In the anomalous regime, Lévy flight super-spreading and temporal avalanches follow.
arxiv-2603-26808: AlMasri studies resurgence in holomorphic quantum mechanics, using the quartic anharmonic oscillator as the test case. Working in the Bargmann picture of bosonic operators, the work shows the energy series is Borel summable only after crossing the Stokes line. An instanton acts as a shift of coherent states. It links perturbative terms to non-perturbative sectors. The author computes the first seven energy levels to sixth order. The results match the classic Bender-Wu values.
arxiv-2603-27008: Soni introduces RASPRef, a framework that improves prompts for large reasoning models without human labels. Reasoning models are strong on math and multi-hop questions, yet their scores swing with prompt wording. RASPRef retrieves examples and past reasoning traces to guide prompt edits. Signals like multi-sample consistency, verifier feedback, and self-critique drive the loop. The prompt itself, not the model output, is the optimization target. On GSM8K-style tasks, retrieval-guided prompts beat a static baseline. The author also discusses how retrieval quality shapes the gains.
arxiv-2603-27308: Li and co-authors map code clones across the Eclipse industrial IoT open-source ecosystem. They gathered 90 release versions from 15 Eclipse IIoT projects. The NiCad tool plus a custom module measured clone spread and evolution. Clones touched 16.3 percent of all code lines, nearly double the usual open-source share. Most clone pairs arose between commits rather than within one commit. Clone counts stayed stable across versions in most projects. Only 0.17 percent of clones were ever changed together. Cross-project clones were common, especially in Java projects.
arxiv-2603-27508: Xue and co-authors test speech tools on talk recorded after exercise. Hard breathing and weak voice support strain transcription. Their bench compares speech models under one shared protocol. FunASR proves toughest off the shelf, at 14.57 percent word error. Fine-tuning helps several CTC-based models a lot. Whisper adapts in an unstable way. Non-fluent speakers prove harder than fluent ones. The study gives a first map of this failure zone.
arxiv-2603-27608: Blum and Shamir introduce domain wall fermions for lattice QCD study. Quarks live in four dims plus a thin fifth direction. Exact chiral symmetry returns as that direction grows unbounded. The effective operator then meets the Ginsparg-Wilson relation. Finite depth leaves a small symmetry residue. Spectral traits of the Wilson kernel control that residue. Variants such as Möbius fermions improve the tradeoff. These notes form a chapter of the Lattice QCD at 50 years book.
arxiv-2603-27708: Chen and co-authors detect replay attacks on nonlinear plants. Attackers replay old sensor data while injecting bad signals. Linear cases are well studied; nonlinear ones are not. An innovation-based detector alone may miss such attacks. A watermark design then strengthens the watch. Two indices weigh detection gain against control loss. Incremental gains of the plant feed both indices. An explicit optimization balances the trade-off.
arxiv-2603-28108: Bassanini and five co-authors present VERITAS, a framework that turns archival scans into rich, searchable text. Plain OCR gives flat text with no structure or meaning attached. VERITAS runs four stages, from preprocessing to semantic enrichment, under a schema that tells it what to extract. On a 1,600-page Renaissance chronicle of Milan, it cut word errors by 67.6% versus a commercial OCR tool. A question-answering layer over the output shows the text supports real historical research.
arxiv-2603-28208: Garland and co-authors untangle the links among active galactic nuclei, galaxy bars, and bulges. Bars can drive gas inward, feeding both black holes and bulge growth, so the true driver is unclear. Using DESI Legacy Survey data for nearby galaxies, they control for mass, color, and bulge size. The AGN share still climbs with bar strength at fixed bulge size. It also climbs with bulge size at fixed bar strength. Both traits matter on their own.
arxiv-2603-28808: Kawalec analytically continues the Euler prime product for complex s with real part above one half, assuming the Riemann Hypothesis. The continuation holds except for the pole at s equal to one. Kawalec introduces a new factor into the Euler product to achieve it. He also discusses how to recover Mertens's third theorem at s equal to one. The same technique may continue other similar Euler products. A simple Pari/GP script computes the product and checks the calculations numerically.
arxiv-2604-00208: Liu and six colleagues show that alignment metrics, similarity analysis, kernel methods, linear regression track activity readings rather than hidden feature content. When systems encode more feature types than neurons through compression, in superposition, these metrics follow projection Gram matrices instead of latent feature sets. Two networks with same feature content can look less alike than networks sharing part of their feature set. Training supervised TopK sparse autoencoders built for solvable compressed sensing brings back alignment on regained latents, extending to unsupervised and ready-made vision and language models.
arxiv-2604-00308: Wu and six colleagues test whether voice features predict decline in chronic heart failure, tracking 32 patients for 2 months with daily voice recordings. From 21,863 recordings, vowel features track health closely, and time-series voice features beat standard-care measures, reaching about 83 percent sensitivity and 78 percent specificity, against 78 and 57 percent for standard care. Warning signs include delayed energy shift, low energy variability, higher shimmer variability, slower speaking, and greater formant variability. Voice monitoring offers a non-invasive early-warning route for proactive, personalized care.
arxiv-2604-00408: Wu and colleagues build a theory for scalable fluid antenna systems, antennas that can shift their aperture to form different views of the signal space. Fixed arrays have static observation entropy, but shifting apertures need a theory beyond standard identifiability analysis. Their observation-entropy framework joins three jobs: setting identifiability limits, finding processing bottlenecks, and guiding design. For setups with mutual coupling suppressed, they rank compressed, extended, and jointly stacked designs by capacity, and show that two-step processing done in stages hits an information bottleneck.
arxiv-2604-00808: Sun, Wang, and Chen study a way to spot potassium-40 geoneutrinos, tiny particles from decay deep inside Earth that hint at what Earth is made of. They use neutrino-electron scattering in a Cherenkov liquid scintillator. Solar background is cut by an angle cut tuned for the job. Finding them in a potassium-rich energy band takes 6.9 kiloton-years, while ruling out a uniform spread across Earth takes over 27 kiloton-years.
arxiv-2604-01008: Ou-Yang and team study D to VV decays with the factorization-assisted topological-amplitude approach, with D for D0, D+, Ds+ and V for rho, K*, omega, phi. They express nonfactorizable contributions as a set of parameters fitted to all data, extracting ten parameters tied to the C and E cases from 36 points. A large strong phase in the longitudinal E amplitude destructively interferes with the C component, giving f-parallel above f-L against naive factorization predictions. Their predictions for 28 decay modes match current data.
arxiv-2604-01108: Jamshidi and colleagues introduce Adversarial Moral Stress Testing, a test suite for judging AI models under multi-round chats. One-shot benchmarks with overall scores miss rare failures and decay, so AMST applies stress changes and spread-aware scores that track swing, tail risk and drift across rounds. Tests on several models reveal varied hardiness and decay patterns hidden from one-shot rules. Toughness rests on steady scores and rare-case handling rather than mean scores alone, and AMST gives a model-free route to toughness testing and watch.
arxiv-2604-01208: Shende and Zhou link a noncompact surface with no closed edge to the sum of Fukaya categories of its symmetric powers. They build covers with bar-resolution combinatorics to show this link extends to an open two-dimensional topological field theory. No Lagrangian or holomorphic disk needs naming. In particular, the construction recovers Rouquier and Manion's extension of Heegaard-Floer theory down to an interval.
arxiv-2604-01308: Amusat and colleagues design a machine-learning-aided method for sizing and running industrial energy systems. Cheap low-detail models and costly high-detail models often disagree, hiding where performance is lost between layout and operation. Their online multi-resolution optimizer estimates the best performance a chosen layout can reach while sparing costly high-fidelity runs. On a pilot plant supplying a 1 megawatt heat load, it shrinks the layout-to-operation gap by up to 42 percent against a rule-based controller and cuts high-fidelity runs by 34 percent.
arxiv-2604-01608: Xu and colleagues ask when squeezing a multi-agent workflow for data science into a single skill pays off. Multi-agent setups spread control across stages, tools and checks, and distilling them can cut costs but muddle which parts cross over. On the same causal tasks, adding pipeline guidance lifted method-choice utility by 19.6 points yet hurt numerical accuracy. The authors trace this flip to a rank mismatch called Behavior-Outcome Freedom. AdaSkill keeps resources, drops orchestration, and inherits guidance when a calibrated rule over that mismatch allows it.
arxiv-2604-01708: Li and colleagues built OpenGo, a robot dog that swaps skills on the fly as scenes and spoken tasks change. A custom skill library lets users add skills and checks each one on its own, while a dispatcher picks the right skill from task prompts or plain speech. A self-learning loop tunes skills from finished jobs and human notes, and the system runs on Unitree's Go2 dog. Through Feishu messaging, people with no training can steer the dog with simple spoken guidance.
arxiv-2604-01808: Kolodziejczyk and Sun show that over weak base theory RCA0-star, cohesive Ramsey for pairs implies exponential closure of cut I0-1, the intersection of all Sigma0-1-definable cuts. This yields non-elementary proof speedup over RCA0-star alone for Pi-1 sentences, and unprovability of cohesive Ramsey in RCA0-star plus CAC. RCA0-star plus stable Ramsey for pairs is polynomially simulated by RCA0-star for universal Pi0-3 proofs. Yet stable Ramsey also implies a nontrivial property of I0-1, closure under functions of quasipolynomial growth.
arxiv-2604-02008: Wong, Li, Wu and Zhou align proxy models for black-box detection of machine generated text with kNNProxy, without training. Zero shot detectors avoid training, but assume a proxy matches the unknown source model. Earlier fixes fine-tune the proxy or query APIs, raising cost. kNNProxy builds a small datastore once from a target reflective corpus. Nearest neighbor evidence shapes token predictions blended with the proxy output. A mixture extension routes each input to a domain matched store.
arxiv-2604-02508: Somathilake and Diagne extend performance-barrier event-triggered control, a scheme that spaces out control updates while keeping performance on track, to systems where only outputs are measured. They build a dynamic barrier paired with a fast-converging observer for boundary control of a class of two-by-two linear hyperbolic equations. The design guarantees a minimum gap between updates and global exponential stability in simulations.
arxiv-2604-02608: Nadaf tests whether function vectors, directions in activation space extracted from demonstration examples, both steer a model and decode through its output layer. Across 12 tasks, six models and 4,032 directed pairs, steering routinely succeeds where the logit lens fails to decode the right answer at any layer, while the reverse is nearly empty. Function vectors thus encode computational instructions, not answer directions, and nonlinear probes recover only part of the gap.
arxiv-2604-02808: Xu, Wang and Niu define cross-modality clothing-change person re-identification, matching pedestrians across both visible-infrared modality gaps and outfit changes in long-term surveillance. Prior work tackles one gap at a time, so they build the SYSU-CMCC benchmark with identities in both domains and distinct outfits. Their progressive identity alignment network disentangles identity cues from clothing factors and aligns prototypes across modalities.
arxiv-2604-03208: Zhang and colleagues tackle long-horizon robot planning, where prediction errors compound and naive search explodes with the horizon. Their HWM system learns world models at several time scales in one latent space, letting long-horizon predictions set subgoals for short-horizon control without task-specific rewards. On a real Franka arm, pick-and-place from one goal image succeeded 70 percent of the time, versus zero for single-level planning.
arxiv-2604-03508: Mao, Pickard, and Chen tackle finding same-degree polynomial moving systems, which model higher-order networked systems from nature to robots. They adopt low-rank tensor splits, including tensor train, layered Tucker, and standard multi-way forms, to shrink the setting space. Rather than finding the full system tensor, their framework learns factor tensors directly from time-series data with back-and-forth least-squares methods.
arxiv-2604-03908: Md Arafat Habib and team built an agentic AI system for running 6G radio access nets. A super agent built on a Hierarchical Online Decision Transformer directs slice shares, app orchestration, and self-healing agents, fed by an agentic search module. The system beat three leading rivals on throughput, delay, and energy use. It also screened operator intents at slice and KPI levels with 88.5 percent right calls, and self-healing won back 90 percent of prior speed after breaks.
arxiv-2604-04208: Muhammad Rizwan Awan and team built a graph-assisted retrieval framework for defect reasoning in laser powder bed fusion, using Ti6Al4V as a case study. Papers were turned into a structured form, with links between parameters, mechanisms, and defects stored in an evidence-linked knowledge graph. Semantic and graph-based retrieval plus a lightweight agent reasoning layer build interpretable defect pathways. Evaluation showed accuracy and recall both at 0.9667, proving it finds relevant defect evidence effectively.
arxiv-2604-04408: Barua, Dalui and Desai probe anisotropy with galaxy clusters and supernovae. Using Lambda-CDM and Padé cosmography, they study H0 shifts by direction from galaxy clusters and Pantheon supernovae. Since H0 trades off against supernova brightness, the team also uses galaxy cluster scaling rules with Cepheid calibration. Cluster-based and Cepheid-based H0 shifts differ by at most one sigma, showing the same result across methods. Across all combinations, they find a steady two-sigma drift from isotropy, with peak H0 gaps mostly lining up with the CMB dipole.
arxiv-2604-04608: Qiu, Zhao and Qu ask which physical features stably tell AI-generated images from natural ones across datasets. Deepfake detectors often overfit to single models, so the team surveys 15 physical features across over 20 datasets from GANs and diffusion. A new selection algorithm picks five core features, including Laplacian variance, Sobel statistics and residual noise variance. The features become text values joined with captions to guide image-text learning in CLIP. Tests reach state-of-the-art performance on Genimage benchmarks, with accuracy of 99.8 percent on Wukong and SDv1.4.
arxiv-2604-04808: Raman, Milani and Fang tackle concept choice for reinforcement learning policies, a task done by hand at high expert cost. Their key move views concept choice as state abstraction: a concept matters for decisions when dropping it would blur states that need different actions. The Decision-Relevant Selection algorithm picks a subset of concepts so that states sharing a concept profile share the same best action, keeping decision structure intact. It comes with performance bounds, recovers hand picked concept sets, and matches or beats their performance.
