arxiv-2604-05108: Madabushi and three co-authors develop differentiable invariant sets for hybrid limit cycles, for legged robots. For hybrid systems with behavior, the invariant set containing the limit cycle offers a way to study robustness. Computing these sets is expensive, especially for systems such as legged robots. The authors extend methods for overapproximating reachable sets using embeddings. They compute a set around the trajectory of a bipedal robot model. Their approach computes a reachable set around the flow, catalogs guard-surface intersections, and passes them through the reset map.
arxiv-2604-05408: Datta investigates a quantum version of the Mpemba effect inside a strongly interacting one-dimensional Bose gas. In this effect, a system farther from equilibrium settles faster than one nearer it. After a sudden expansion of its confining box, density differences between regions show the relaxation order of ground and excited symmetry sectors reversing over time. The effect depends on the chosen observable and dynamics rather than holding as a universal law.
arxiv-2604-06008: Shahnawaz and three colleagues build a WhatsApp chatbot for menstrual health education in Pakistan. Cultural taboos and thin curricula leave women there few trusted sources. Built with campus women, the bot uses retrieval-augmented generation. It supports Roman Urdu and draws on an expert-curated knowledge base. A two-week deployment with 13 participants yielded 403 messages. Users challenged taboos and pressed concerns dismissed as normal. Their 2026 study showed tensions around trust, validation, and the bot's gendered persona.
arxiv-2604-06208: Faiz and seven colleagues extract breast cancer phenotypes from messy oncology notes with a language-model framework, then compare it against classical ontology methods. These notes hold chemo outcomes, biomarkers, tumor location, size, and growth patterns that structured record fields often miss, since oncologists prefer writing in natural language. The language-model approach matches ontology-based accuracy on breast cancer phenotypes, and once trained it adapts readily to other cancers through fine-tuning.
arxiv-2604-06508: Teo and four colleagues train a neural network on Doppler backscattering data to forecast DIII-D's first edge localized mode crash. Edge localized modes expel heat and particles beyond the transport barrier, threatening the divertor and plasma-facing parts, so forecasting aids mitigation. Adapted from DeepHit, it reads 50 milliseconds of spectra and predicts crash odds in set windows. On DIII-D shots, it reliably flags the first mode 100 milliseconds before it occurs, a proof of concept for pre-crash mitigation. Future work expands shots and hardens it against noise.
arxiv-2604-06908: Roy and three colleagues bring a quantum relative alpha-entropy building on Umegaki entropy beyond f-class. Most quantum divergences borrow structure from classical ones or Renyi builds, hiding shape effects. The new measure shows bent shape yielding broad Petz-Renyi shape above one, matching known sub-one shape. It adds under tensor products, stays unitary-fixed, and depends only on shape, not sizes. With Nussbaum-Szkola cases, the authors match it with plain alpha-entropy, framing quantum telling apart.
arxiv-2604-07008: Öttinger offers a solo paper that rebuilds gravity as a gauge theory built from freely falling frames. A freely falling frame is a small lab in free fall where gravity seems to vanish. The paper argues such frames point to a local Lorentz gauge rule with a flat backdrop frame. From shifts between these frames, the author builds gauge fields in the style of Yang Mills theory. He gives frame rules for an exact black hole answer, and works out a full Hamiltonian form.
arxiv-2604-07408: Agrawal, Erturk, and Louis count successive vertex orderings of connected graphs, where each vertex after the first has an earlier neighbor. Such orderings model growth that stays connected as vertices join one by one. They derive a count by inclusion-exclusion over independent sets, using two counting parameters, one defined by a self-referential rule. No regularity or symmetry is assumed. A counting polynomial over independent sets encodes the count at minus one, with its rates of change giving orderings where k later vertices precede all their neighbors.
arxiv-2604-07708: De Pas, Dipierro, and Valdinoci develop a Fredholm alternative for a general class of nonlocal operators. Their mixed-order fractional elliptic operator extends classical second-order elliptic cases with measured coefficients, building on Trudinger's treatment. It weighs the fraction gradient's order over a measure that may be continuous, discrete, or mixed. Its factors may depend on that order, may be unbounded or discontinuous, and may break homogeneity. A working framework supports the main results, which rest on custom analysis of the right function spaces.
arxiv-2604-07908: Ramaschi, Paolone, and Leva present part two of a study on game-theoretic control of electric vehicle charging stations. The method, SG-ADMM, steers drivers' goals toward the station optimum through incentive design while dispatching power in a distributed way. It sits inside a layered energy management system, with the station as Stackelberg leader trading power for incentives and vehicles as followers tuning charging curves. Tests in a large-scale station benchmark the method against decentralized, centralized, and uncontrolled approaches, showing cost-effective, fair, efficient use of vehicle flexibility.
arxiv-2604-08108: Arzhantsev, Galt, and Staroletov prove that items of fixed finite order in the linked part of a maximal torus normalizer form a simple pattern. In a maximal torus normalizer of a semisimple group, items of fixed finite order form either an empty set or a disjoint union of few irreducible subvarieties. Each subvariety's dimension equals the fixed-vector subspace dimension for the matching Weyl group element action. Each one is a torus orbit on the part by twisting, tying the sorting to torus orbits.
arxiv-2604-08508: John Zhang and sixteen colleagues steer a pretrained whole body control policy at test time with a sample based planner, letting legged robots handle large heavy objects with whole body skill. On a Spot quadruped in the real world, the method uprighted a tire beyond the robot's nominal lift. It also dragged a barrier larger and taller than the robot, with no extra tuning. The same approach also opens doors and pushes tables for humanoids in simulation.
arxiv-2604-08708: Chen and four colleagues measure uncertainty in multi agent language model systems with MATU, a tensor split method. Single turn uncertainty tools miss cascading reasoning uncertainty, varied message paths, and diverse layouts, so MATU represents full reasoning paths as embedding grids across runs in a higher order tensor. Splitting the tensor separates distinct uncertainty sources, giving a whole reliability measure that works across agent structures and tasks.
arxiv-2604-09008: Li, Wang, and Sun argue that English as a second or foreign language should be treated as its own linguistic system, not as faulty standard English. That shift calls for knowledge-rich representations, so they survey existing resources, expose their limits, and propose a construction-based design. Grounded in constructivist theories, the design treats grammatical constructions as the basic units and maps form to meaning. The result is a gold-standard resource of 1643 annotated sentences, tested in a pilot study of the Linguistic Niche Hypothesis for second language acquisition.
arxiv-2604-09108: Tanboga offers a plain guide to reading randomized trials, warning that the riskiest error is mixing a p-value above 0.05 with no effect. The review gives a rule-based system sorting trial results into six groups: positive, imprecise, neutral, inconclusive, negative, and harmful. Sorting rests mainly on where the confidence range sits against the smallest medical gap that matters, plus Bayesian posterior probabilities. The point is that underpowered, inconclusive, negative, and neutral are four verdicts of their own, not the same thing as failure.
arxiv-2604-09308: Sun, Zhang, and Meng present CACM, constraint-aware corrective memory for language-based drug discovery agents. Reliable success depends not on any single action but on whether the final set jointly meets protocol requirements like size, diversity, binding quality, and fitness. Existing systems rely on long raw history and vague self-reflection, making failure finding imprecise and planner states noisy. CACM adds protocol auditing and a checker that localize violations and suggest remedies, improving success by about 36 percent over baseline.
arxiv-2604-09408: Trinh and colleagues present HiL-Bench, asking whether agents know when to ask for help. Frontier coding agents solve complex tasks with full context but collapse when specs are incomplete. The bottleneck is judgment, not capability: knowing when to act alone and when to ask. Each task holds human-validated blockers surfacing only through exploration, and Ask-F1 balances question precision against blocker recall. Tests across coding and text-to-SQL domains show no frontier model recovers more than a fraction of full-information performance.
arxiv-2604-09708: Ramírez and Tassieri present i-Rheo-Tempo, a quadrature-free method deriving the shear relaxation modulus from dynamic tests. Frequency-to-time shift in linear viscoelasticity suffers from finite bandwidth, discrete sampling, and noise. Through a second-derivative form for complex viscosity and a stepwise spectrum guess, the method reduces to a local-slope formula from spectra. It avoids curve fitting and preset spectra. Tests span mock models, polymer melts, elastomers, comb polymers, and microrheology data across nearly nine decades, with rebuilt moduli matching other tests.
arxiv-2604-10408: Wiggins asks whether symplectic shape ideas can shed light on chemical reaction paths. Near an index one saddle, normal forms map the gates, walls, and bath motions that steer passage. For plain saddle models, the math picks out natural area scales at the reactive pinch point. Anharmonic Eckart Morse style cases get matching width scales from high order local forms. Two number trials back the view that bath edge bias can stall reaction for a long spell.
arxiv-2604-10508: Arimbur asks how many retries language models need to fix their own code. Single shot tests hide the repair loop, where error notes feed back for another try. Across seven models and two test sets, repair lifts scores for every model tried. Gains run 5 to 17 points on HumanEval and 16 to 30 points on MBPP, mostly in round one and two. Logic slips prove hardest to mend, while syntax and name slips yield far more often.
arxiv-2604-10608: Farhan and Koehler improve customizable route planning for large road networks. Planners must answer millions of queries under changing costs like travel time, fuel, and tolls. Building on Customizable Tree Labeling, they introduce leaner ways to store and rebuild path information. Several variants trade memory against query speed. A batch strategy shares path data across queries to cut repeated work. Tests on 13 real road networks show their methods clearly beat the current state of the art.
arxiv-2604-10808: Barbagli and three colleagues model tripartite hyperevents in scientific collaboration networks. There, teams of actors, lists of prior works, and sets of labels jointly drive output. Existing multi-part methods, they note, fail to scale to current dataset sizes while testing rival ideas about output drivers. Applying relational hyperevent models to dynamic three-part hypergraphs, they model events linking any number of actors, cited works, and keywords. They test and adjust for links within and between each set.
arxiv-2604-11008: Tominaga and Onishi develop LCS.jl, a single-source, multi-platform Julia model for turbulent particle-laden flows. Few multiphase turbulence models are highly optimized for graphics processors, now mainstream in high-performance computing. Validation shows fluid and particle statistics agreeing well with prior studies. A graphics-processor-native particle communication method based on prefix-scan cuts communication cost from 78 percent to 10 percent of total run time. The model matches a Fortran implementation on many-process runs. On graphics processors, strong scaling efficiency stays above 85 percent up to 256 units.
arxiv-2604-11308: Okada and Singh propose a radiative Dirac neutrino mass model stabilized by a non-invertible fusion rule from Z3 by Z3-prime gauging. The symmetry blocks tree-level Yukawa couplings, so neutrino masses arise only at one loop through exotic fermions and inert scalars. The framework fits current oscillation data and offers a dark matter candidate: a bosonic singlet with compatible relic density, while the fermionic option is disfavored by suppressed annihilation. Flavor-violating effects stay well below present bounds.
arxiv-2604-11708: Krishnan, Donghoon Kim, and Hokeun Kim present ACT, Automated CPS Testing, to help open-source teams check robot-linked software lacking thorough testing. With many volunteers writing separate CPS modules, tests on robotic platforms are often missing, so serious faults stay hidden. ACT fills that gap with automated, steady checks of community code on its robots, linked to open-source infrastructure such as GitHub. They built an early version and ran a case study on a public CPS with an educational robot platform, showing what it can do.
arxiv-2604-12008: Chaudhary and seven colleagues compute surface plasmon resonance in the continuum of metal clusters with a TDDFT approach. For unusual plasmon metals like aluminium and indium, the peak sits above the ionisation potential, so it must enter the quantum description. With Al13- as standard, exact treatment of that range captures a broad UV surface plasmon. In Al clusters, the spectra evolve from discrete features in Al6 to a surface plasmon in larger clusters in the deep UV.
arxiv-2604-12108: Ziftci, Liu, Greene, and Dalloro introduce Auto-Diagnose, a tool using language models to diagnose integration test failures, a slow task given massive, unstructured logs. It analyses failure logs, summarises them with key lines, and posts findings in Critique, Google's code review system, for timely assistance. An evaluation on 71 real failures showed 90.14 percent accuracy on root cause. After deployment across 52,635 failing tests, users rated it Not helpful in only 5.8 percent of cases, ranking it 14th among 370 Critique tools, with interviews confirming usefulness and accuracy's role in perception and adoption.
arxiv-2604-12208: Hua and eight colleagues find end-to-end driving systems lean too hard on local scene understanding while underusing global navigation input, so planning correlates weakly with navigation. Their Sequential Navigation Guidance framework encodes navigation paths for long-term trajectories plus turn-by-turn cues for real-time choices, with a matching question-answering dataset. Their fused model leads the field through precise navigation modeling, needing no extra perception losses.
arxiv-2604-12708: Eric Ngondiep builds a second-order two-step method for the two-dimensional Gray-Scott model. Stage one is explicit, while stage two is implicit. Space derivatives use a Galerkin finite element form with a spectral basis. Errors that grow in stage one shrink in stage two. The method computes solutions efficiently and accurately. Theory shows unconditional stability and second-order time accuracy. Spatial convergence reaches order q, with q at least two. Numerical examples confirm the theory and show efficiency.
arxiv-2604-13108: Jin tests whether formal architecture descriptors cut the roaming AI coding agents do when searching codebases. In controlled trials, architecture context cuts navigation steps by 33 to 44 percent, and an auto-generated descriptor hits 100 percent accuracy against 80 percent blind. A field study across 7,012 sessions shows 52 percent less variance, and format matters for failure: JSON fails atomically while YAML silently corrupts half of errors. Jin proposes intent.lisp, an S-expression descriptor, with the open-source Forge toolkit.
arxiv-2604-13308: Vakhnovskyi presents the first full threat model for Internet-connected controlled-environment farming. The United States counts this sector as critical infrastructure yet leaves it without mandatory cyber rules. Applying STRIDE, MITRE ATT&CK for industrial control, and zone-and-conduit analysis, he studies a platform running in more than 30 commercial facilities. He catalogues 123 threats and names five novel attack classes aimed at AI-driven controls and crop biology. He recommends defense in depth with Security Level 2 as the floor.
arxiv-2604-13608: Kashif and four colleagues explore designs of hybrid quantum neural networks for diagnosing chronic kidney disease. They test 625 combinations of data encoding, circuit layout, measurement choice, and shot count. All models use ten-fold cross-validation on a curated clinical dataset. Compact circuits with suitable encodings give the best balance of accuracy, robustness, and efficiency. One strong pairing is IQP encoding with ring entanglement, and it needs no large parameter count.
arxiv-2604-14608: Hachisu and Kato bound nova ejecta mass by nuclear-burning energy balance. White dwarfs run six-tenths to 1.38 solar masses, and accretion rates one hundred-billionth to three ten-millionths solar masses per year. These maxima cap ejection for individual novae. Schaefer inferred ejecta-to-accreted ratios of 26 for U Sco and 540 for T CrB from orbital period changes, implying shrinking dwarfs. The energy argument caps the ratio below three for near-maximum dwarfs. Burning cannot expel Schaefer's masses, and common-envelope friction barely lifts the cap.
arxiv-2604-14708: Jana and Das model how winds blowing off a magnetized, viscous accretion disk change the flow spiraling into a spinning black hole. Their model uses mainly toroidal magnetic fields with synchrotron radiation as the chief cooling channel. The inflow rate falls inward as a power of radius, and the global flow admits standing shocks. Winds cut disk luminosity sharply and shift shock radius, compression, and strength. Beyond a critical wind strength steady shocks vanish altogether, a threshold lowered by stronger viscosity and angular-momentum loss.
arxiv-2604-14808: Xiao and six others recast language-model unlearning as an asymmetric two-task problem with retention primary and forgetting auxiliary. Their retention-prioritized gradient synthesis separates task-specific gradient extraction from conflict-aware combination. They adapt PCGrad to settle gradient conflicts and add SAGO, a new synthesis method with tighter alignment to the retain gradient. On WMDP Bio, target-model MMLU scores climbed from 44.6 percent naive to 94.0 percent with PCGrad and 96.0 percent with SAGO, while forgetting strength held steady. Reshaping gradient geometry, they conclude, beats merely rebalancing losses.
arxiv-2604-15008: Ponge joins semiclassical analysis with noncommutative geometry in a book that proves semiclassical Weyl laws and new forms of Connes's integration formula for broad noncommutative manifolds. His method drops limits on regularity and dimension and swaps a strict Tauberian rule for a weaker spectral one that holds more widely. He gives checks that are easy to use in real cases, a need Connes raised in an online talk. Closed manifolds and quantum tori show the laws at work, and the torus case settles a conjecture of McDonald and Ponge.
arxiv-2604-15208: Renu and colleagues trace how bars steer quenching in 12 nearby barred galaxies with star-forming discs but quiet centers. Central spectra show leftover emission from ongoing star formation or LINER-like activity, hinting at varied ionization. Ultraviolet-optical color maps show discs that are star-forming and blue while bulges and bars run redder and older, flipping at the bar end. Black hole masses sit below the kinetic-feedback threshold, supporting bars as the main quenching driver at a stage just before full central shutdown.
arxiv-2604-15808: Moukheiber, Yeung, Xue, Helbling, Zhao, and Chen offer SGMRI-VQA, a 41,307-pair test of multi-frame, pinned thought on volume MRI. It is built from eye-doc marks in fastMRI+ brain and knee. Each pair holds a doc-lined trail with frame-tagged box spots. From spotting to placing to counting, sorting, and captioning, asking what, where, and across which frames. Tuning Qwen3-VL-8B with box watch beats no-shot baselines on grounding, showing space watch aids grounded clinic thought.
arxiv-2604-16208: Cusati and Brown survey 280 experienced software engineering researchers about why the field struggles to accumulate knowledge despite booming output. Respondents point to a tension between rising productivity and weak tools for synthesising results, tracking claims, and building shared understanding over time. The authors diagnose four linked breakdowns, isolated papers, lost context, untracked claim changes, and incentives favouring novelty over consolidation, and frame these as barriers to long-term progress.
arxiv-2604-16508: Jaramillo Quiceno presents two Heisenberg algebras deformed by a diagonal Lorentzian metric. The family unifies those q-deformed cases, including q-hbar, new q-Heisenberg and q-generalized forms. Using Sylvester's inertia theorem, he links metric sign to deformation size. He then builds a q-Dirac operator from the deformed wave part. Its square gives the Klein-Gordon form. The result relates to his quadratic q-Dirac operator and bridges space-time shape with q-deformed quantum theory.
arxiv-2604-16608: Breiner and Dees show harmonic-map orders from surfaces into Euclidean buildings are discrete. In buildings of type W, orders take the form m over k, where k divides the size of W. This generalizes the Gromov and Schoen order gap to two-dimensional domains. The proof analyzes homogeneous maps into Euclidean buildings, then a related spherical billiards problem.
arxiv-2604-16708: Ma and colleagues build beam prediction and tracking models for mmWave links via KD. Channels vary rapidly, and noise from nearby objects makes beam training hard. Cameras and radars capture rich scenes, aiding lean beam control. A teacher network of convolutional networks and loop units guesses current and future beams from past reads. A compact student then learns the teacher's skill through distillation. Radar and image use beats single rivals, and the student tops 96 percent Top scores with far lower cost and far fewer parameters.
arxiv-2604-17308: Zhang and colleagues introduce SkillFlow, a benchmark asking whether AI agents can discover, repair, and carry skills across tasks instead of merely using supplied ones. Its 166 tasks span 20 families under a shared workflow, with agents starting skill-less and patching their library from experience as they proceed. Lifelong learning lifted one leading model by about eight points, yet heavy skill use did not always help, exposing a gap between using skills and using them well.
arxiv-2604-17808: Tong and eight colleagues present MORPH, reformulating ZKP kernels for AI-ASIC execution. ZKP provers stay costly because MSM and NTTs dominate runtime. MORPH's Big-T complexity exposes bottlenecks and layout costs ignored by Big-O. MORPH's MXU-centric extended-RNS lazy reduction recasts high-precision modular arithmetic as dense low-precision GEMMs without carry chains, and unified-sharding layout-stationary TPU Pippenger MSM with optimized 3/5-step NTT avoids on-TPU shuffles. TPUv6e8 with MORPH reaches up to 10x higher NTT throughput and comparable MSM throughput versus GZKP.
arxiv-2604-18108: Arribillaga, Moreno-Ternero, and Neme study how to split the proceeds of a joint venture organized as a hierarchy. Each participant also has individual needs to meet. They describe a set of need-adjusted geometric rules in which surplus revenue bubbles upward through the ranks. They add a serial rule that shares each person's surplus equally with everyone above them.
arxiv-2604-18208: Kriegler, Beleznai, and Gelautz tackle pose estimation for symmetric objects, whose orientation ambiguities confuse deep networks. Current fixes rely on custom losses, network designs, or shape-blind metrics. The authors instead rework the rotation representation itself, tweaking trigonometric identities by each object's degrees of symmetry. Their SARR code gives canonical poses on two standard data sets, letting a plain convolutional network beat the state of the art under a shape-aware distance.
arxiv-2604-18308: Martynov presents a teaching module on images and communication, taught at the University of Birmingham since 2021. The module covers applied optics with focus on imaging, lasers, and classical and quantum signals. Students meet theory and lab work side by side through tools such as telescopes, adaptive optics, laser cutters, optical tweezers, interferometers, atomic clocks, coatings, cables, fibers, frequency combs, and quantum key sharing. The notes survey basics and devices in one single course.
arxiv-2604-18408: Ochoa and Salort study function spaces and potential theory in the Orlicz setting. They generalize Bessel and Lizorkin-Triebel spaces to Orlicz spaces, recovering classical results such as the Calderón-type coincidence of integer-order Bessel-Orlicz spaces with Orlicz-Sobolev spaces. Inclusion results cover fractional orders, and a Strauss-type lemma holds for potential spaces. Certain Orlicz-Lizorkin-Triebel spaces match Bessel-Orlicz spaces, with a useful atomic decomposition provided.
arxiv-2604-18508: Khalighinejad, Thirukovalluru, Oh, and Dhingra argue that document-as-image representations fall short for scientific retrieval. Drawn-page vectors lead recent models and benchmarks, yet research evidence spreads across text, tables, and figures. Their ArXivDoc benchmark builds from LaTeX sources, opening tidy parts for set queries. Weighing text-only, image-based, and mixed views shows image-only views always lose, text wins even for figure queries via captions and context, and woven text-plus-image beats image-only without special training.
arxiv-2604-18608: Aiello and three colleagues write a physicist-friendly primer on the simplest Hamiltonian for the radical-pair mechanism, the leading microscopic idea for magnetic sensing in living things. They give a full analytic solution in the singlet-triplet basis. They also give a bright-dark split of the spin mixing that makes old features clear. In this view, the low-field effect comes from coherence between bright and dark parts, and zero field acts by phase locking rather than by stronger mixing alone.
arxiv-2604-18808: Singh and four colleagues compare synthetic oxygen-VI absorption in galaxy groups from the SIMBA and TNG50 simulations against COS-IGrM observations. They select 14 galaxy groups from each simulation and create 90,000 synthetic spectra per group. Oxygen-VI covering fractions in TNG50 and SIMBA are both systematically lower than observed, at about 21 percent and about 6 percent versus 44 percent. In TNG50, strong absorbers sit near star forming galaxies, suggesting a link to stellar feedback, while SIMBA shows no comparable trend. Differences may arise from feedback models and resolution effects.
arxiv-2604-20108: Leditto and three colleagues build quantum routines for sync gauging and no lock proof in the simplicial Kuramoto model of high order linked oscillators. High order nets with multiway links show joint motion missed by pair models, but their state sets swell fast with link order. Under plain data use and shape rules, the authors work out full gate costs and find poly quantum edge for sync gauging. No lock proof gains super poly edge over old tools, moving quantum tools from shape study to twist filled motion checks.
arxiv-2604-20208: Mazouz, Laurenti, and Lahijanian study safety checks for random systems in shifting settings with moving obstacles. They give fixed and varying barrier certificates that bound from below the chance of staying safe over a set time span. The varying form uses Bellman optimality ideas to catch time structure, giving tighter bounds than current best methods. Keeping certificates in polynomial form turns the varying build into a convex sum-of-squares program, and tests on nonlinear systems with moving obstacles show tight, scalable guarantees.
arxiv-2604-20508: Gonzalez-Rosa and five colleagues compare two models of charged-current neutrino events that knock out a single pion, testing them against T2K, MINERvA, and MiniBooNE measurements. The SuSAv2 model, a superscaling approach, draws single-nucleon structure functions from the ANL-Osaka DCC model, separating positive, negative, and neutral pion outcomes. The RDWIA model, a relativistic distorted-wave impulse approximation, uses the Ghent group Hybrid model for the boson-pion-nucleon vertex. Neutrino energies span hundreds of MeV to roughly 20 GeV, and targets are mainly carbon-12.
arxiv-2604-20808: Amelotte and Gorchakov give models, built as homotopy orbit spaces of moment-angle shapes, for classifying spaces of right-angled Coxeter groups' coabelian subgroups. Those extend the models for a Coxeter group and its commutator subgroup. This matches the groups' cohomology to the Borel equivariant cohomology of abelian group actions on cubical parts. They then define equivariant formality for these actions, which yields a graph test. It tells when a coabelian subgroup's cohomology is free as a module over the quotient.
arxiv-2604-21208: Moises Acero and three colleagues track photon entanglement in two cavities linked by an optical fiber, watching N photons hop between chambers under repeated projective measurements. They compute transition and return probabilities and judge the prized N00N state by fidelity and phase sensitivity, with entanglement entropy for the two-cavity split. They also test a single cavity coupled to one qubit. In every case, entanglement hinges on the monitoring protocol, which can thus steer it for applications.
arxiv-2604-21308: Wenjie Fu and seven colleagues benchmark contextual integrity in enterprise AI agents, which must use internal context without leaking sensitive details. Their CI-Work benchmark simulates workflows across five information-flow directions and checks whether agents convey essentials while withholding sensitive context under dense retrieval. Frontier models fail often, with violation rates from about 16 to 51 percent and leakage up to about 27 percent. Higher task utility correlates with more violations, and neither larger size nor deeper reasoning fixes the problem.
arxiv-2604-21708: Pelkner, Hallatschek, and Raeth work toward hybrid kinetic and drift-kinetic plasma simulations in six-dimensional Vlasov codes. Fully kinetic two-species plasmas are hard to simulate because electron and ion dynamics move on very different scales. Their implicit method couples kinetic ions with massless, drift-kinetic electrons in the BSL6D code, capturing ion-scale zonal flows. They prove second-order time-splitting convergence and analyse interpolation errors for steep tokamak edge gradients.
arxiv-2604-21908: Kremer and Dupuis show that peaked quantum circuits, which concentrate output on a single bitstring, can be simulated classically despite claims of heuristic quantum advantage. Recent work on Quantinuum's 56-qubit H2 processor estimated classical runtimes of years for the largest cases. The authors contract the tensor network, exploiting mirrored structure and cancelling both halves into a Matrix Product Operator. Unswapping avoids the obfuscated permutation by reducing bond dimension. The circuit contracts in about one hour on a single GPU, roughly half the quantum runtime.
arxiv-2604-22208: Huynh, Bao, Yang and Zytoon build a machine-learning solver for high-dimensional partial differential equations. Such equations link a quantity to its rates of change. Classical methods struggle as dimensions grow. The team extends the finite expression method, which approximates solutions from a small set of analytic formulas. Their version draws its formula pool from shallow neural networks initialised by TransNet. Tests suggest it handles several hard high-dimensional cases well.
arxiv-2604-22608: Ryczkowski surveys recent SMEFT work: its new tools, results, and phenomenology. The survey sits inside Effective Field Theory, a way to probe heavy new physics through its faint indirect effects. That heaviness is the lesson of the LHC, where no new particles have turned up, leaving such physics far above the electroweak scale. The hunt matters because the Standard Model, for all its success with fundamental interactions, leaves matter-antimatter asymmetry, dark matter, and dark energy unexplained.
arxiv-2604-22708: Chen and six colleagues offer TraceElephant, a benchmark for tracing blame when teams of language-model agents fail, using complete execution records rather than outputs alone. Existing benchmarks hide inputs and context that debuggers actually rely on, so many failure causes stay invisible. Their tests show full traces lift attribution accuracy by up to 76 percent over partial records.
arxiv-2604-22808: Jin presents FreqFormer, a video diffusion transformer design that splits token features by frequency instead of applying one attention shortcut everywhere. Dense attention handles compressed low frequencies carrying layout and coarse motion. Block-sparse attention covers middle bands, and sliding windows cover high-frequency texture and detail. A routing network shifts compute from structure early to detail late. In simulations up to one million tokens, the design sharply cuts attention work and memory traffic against dense attention.
arxiv-2604-23308: Hedman and seven colleagues introduce CODA, a diffusion trajectory maker adding to offline multi-agent learning data. Sampling tuned to the current joint policy, it makes mock runs tracking changing behaviours, enabling joint learning static datasets block. Earlier diffusion top-ups fail for coordination because its datasets stay fixed while policies change; CODA copies on-policy learning instead. Usable with any algorithm and layerable onto model-free and model-based pipelines, CODA fixes coordination pathologies in polynomial games and scores strongly on MaMuJoCo.
arxiv-2604-23608: Angstmann and Gebbie challenge the habit of modelling markets as if time were one shared, continuous clock across all assets. Real markets are asynchronous and event-driven, with random gaps between events, so they revisit no-arbitrage and option pricing for discrete event systems. Their central suggestion is that non-unique continuum limits point to a deeper form of market incompleteness, with effective completeness re-emerging only at longer horizons.
arxiv-2604-23808: Sandoval extends a model of turning bird flocks with active torques that inject rotational energy, as real birds do when turning under threat. The torques speed up and sharpen information transfer during turns and render the flock non-reciprocal. The continuum limit yields a non-reciprocal modified Korteweg-de Vries equation with dissipation, in which transfer speed depends on turning rate, matching the need for faster signalling in faster turns.
arxiv-2604-24108: Cavalleri, Colli, and Rocca study distributed optimal control for a nonisothermal Caginalp-type phase-field model of tumor growth under thermal therapy. The system couples a possibly viscous Cahn-Hilliard equation for healthy and tumor phases with heat balance and nutrient reaction-diffusion equations, including chemotaxis and active transport. Hyperthermia serves as the control variable. The authors introduce a tracking-type cost, prove optimal controls exist, differentiate the control-to-state map, and derive first-order conditions through a variational inequality in the adjoint variables.
arxiv-2604-24908: Brady and nine colleagues present the first uniform lens-modeling analysis across eight doubly imaged quasars. The data come from Hubble multi-band observations. Using the open-source Lenstronomy framework with a pipeline tailored for doubles, they reconstruct the lensing systems. Modeled Einstein radii agree with literature values on average, while image separations differ from Gaia measurements by only 3.6 milliarcseconds root-mean-square. A strong correlation links Fermat potential precision to host arc surface brightness, so arc brightness chiefly drives mass model precision in doubles.
arxiv-2604-25208: Singh and five colleagues present a deep-learning framework for radiometric normalization of lunar mosaics, built mainly from Chandrayaan-2 Terrain Mapping Camera and SELENE data. Uneven lighting, sensor traits and capture conditions leave seams and tonal breaks across orbital images. Their adversarial network, with a U-Net generator and PatchGAN discriminator, maps conventional mosaics to a consistent LROC reference. Patch training with overlap-aware inference keeps structure continuous across tiles. Tests show steady gains over traditional histogram methods on similarity, signal and error measures.
arxiv-2604-25508: Eisele and three colleagues propose Dyna-style Safety Augmented Reinforcement Learning, learning a scalable safety filter and a control policy from an uncertainty-aware dynamics model, with minimal domain knowledge. Safety in reinforcement learning training remains open. Safety filters promise safe exploration, but suit high-dimensional unknown dynamics poorly. The filter avoids failures and high uncertainty regions, so better models expand safe states, reducing conservatism. Dyna-SAuR works on goal-reaching CartPole and MuJoCo Walker, reducing failures versus state-of-the-art methods by 2 orders of magnitude.
arxiv-2604-25608: Mangeleer and three colleagues test how far satellite observations can go in detecting coastal hypoxia in the Black Sea. Summer stratification blocks renewal of bottom oxygen used up by respiration. They frame the task as a Bayesian inverse problem linking surface observations to full three-dimensional physical and biogeochemical states. A deep generative neural network trained on numerical model outputs approximates the true posterior of sea states. Accurate estimation reaches only the mixed layer, and in summer the method detects 38 percent of hypoxic events with a precision of 47 percent.
arxiv-2604-25708: Maciejunes and three colleagues compare four ways of measuring to classify three families of quantum circuits, using only polynomial resources. Z-basis-only readings beat multi-basis and classical-shadow approaches at every qubit count and classifier tested. A nearest-neighbor plan nearly matches them. Under Z-only readings, a random forest tops out at 0.91 accuracy with four to five qubits. All plans collapse to near chance above about 12 qubits under a quadratic shot budget, suggesting the signal lives in local Z links.
arxiv-2604-25808: Lailey and four colleagues present a unified quantum random walk model for internal crystal effects in dynamical diffraction. Dynamical diffraction theory underpins precise neutron and X-ray experiments, but real crystals carry deformations and defects that degrade interferometers and resist conventional modeling. A quantum information model has shown agreement for ideal crystals and some imperfections. The new model extends it to a broad range of internal effects, including temperature gradients, the Talbot effect, and angled or miscut crystals. It offers a flexible framework for next-generation neutron interferometers and optics.
arxiv-2604-26108: Pouillon and eight colleagues add hybrid exchange-correlation functionals to the SIESTA code. The code pairs exact exchange with local atomic orbitals. Gaussian fits to them allow closed-form four-centre electron repulsion integrals. The code's real-space grid and sparse-matrix gear join screening with a closed-form force form. Benchmarks on semiconductors, insulators, and two-dimensional samples show HSE06 raising band gaps clearly over a standard method, close to higher-level theory and tests.
arxiv-2604-26208: Kota Yoshioka studies whether moduli spaces of stable sheaves on an elliptic ruled surface with a nef anticanonical bundle are actually nonempty. Such moduli questions ask whether the geometric objects being classified genuinely occur under the stated conditions, rather than forming an empty formal space. The note takes up that existence question in this ruled-surface setting, where the anticanonical bundle's nefness constrains which stable sheaves can occur.
arxiv-2604-26408: Rahman and Uysal compared photonics and electronics routes to terahertz communication for future 6G networks. Terahertz links promise huge bandwidth for holograms and immersive reality, but each hardware path carries distinct flaws. Electronics builds on mature chips yet suffer phase noise, offsets, and chain nonlinearities, while photonics offers pure tunable carriers but adds laser and mixer noise. The review models both paths, derives signal-quality formulas, and maps how each flaw shapes link performance.
arxiv-2604-26708: Shuryak and Zahed give a unified account of heavy hybrid hadrons from a constituent-gluon picture inside the Born-Oppenheimer framework. The gluonic excitation acts as a moving quasiparticle whose mass comes from instanton effects, and a simple variational derivation yields the Born-Oppenheimer potentials. The main focus is light-front wave functions for hybrid systems, namely the ccg and qqqg cases, built with variational methods plus computer solutions of the Schrödinger equation in momentum form. These wave functions yield gluon parton distributions for these systems.
arxiv-2604-27308: Anantha, Levato, and Price propose BoostLoRA, a gradient-boosting framework that grows effective rank by merging minimal adapters trained on the model's errors. Ultra-low-parameter adapters sit in fixed low-rank spaces that cap performance. A ROTATE SVD basis strategy assigns each round to a right-angle space, so total effective rank grows linearly with rounds each staying ultra-low-rank. After merging, adapters are discarded, leaving zero run-time extra cost. On Qwen2.5-3B it reaches 89.1 percent on GSM8K and about 69 percent on MATH-500.
arxiv-2604-27408: Rose and five colleagues propose a framework for personalizing dynamical cancer models when patient data are scarce. That need matters for medical digital twins, virtual disease copies updated from patient measurements over time. Their method splits parameters into a shared part, estimated once across patients, and a personal part that updates as new data arrive. The shared part captures population structure and supplies a starting point, enabling personalization. On synthetic data from setups like logistic growth with tuned treatments, parameter splitting improves calibration in limited-data settings.
arxiv-2604-27708: Adedeji, Tchakounte, and Yusuff propose a Pan-African, culturally contextualized plan for ethical AI education in primary and high schools. African youth must prepare for AI-mediated labor markets without importing curricula built for other tongues, cultures, and political settings. The plan sets six guiding principles and four curriculum domains, five ethical competencies, and staged progression from lower primary to upper school. It maps global AI-ethics principles onto Ubuntu-shaped relational ethics and plans validation via a Delphi study, teacher surveys, and classroom pilots.
arxiv-2604-27908: Jia and Lu chase sharper toughness rules for spanning k-trees, which cap links at k per vertex and touch every vertex. Win showed in 1989 that toughness of at least one over k minus two forces a tree. Liu, Fan, and Shu gave a tight 2025 spectral rule. Jia and Lu fill that gap. They prove a size floor guaranteeing the tree at a toughness level set by t. They add spectral-radius and signless-Laplacian tests. At t equal to one, it returns.
arxiv-2604-28008: Valet and Vukadinovic show that magnetic states in three-dimensional objects can be stored far more compactly than on regular grids. Thin, high-gradient regions such as domain walls sit beside nearly uniform domains, and a tensor-train format exploits that uneven pattern while keeping errors under control. On flux-closure shapes in soft magnets, the stored size grows far more slowly than dense grids require, pointing toward faster magnetic solvers.
arxiv-2605-00308:
Santiago Badia and Kishore Nori study a hidden ingredient in neural methods for partial differential equations: the numerical quadrature behind the training loss. These methods train a network by minimizing a residual, and the residual must be estimated at sample points. Errors at that stage can quietly cap the final accuracy, whatever the network's power.

The authors first split the total error into approximation, quadrature, and optimization parts, with an estimate of how quadrature error infects the result. Guided by that analysis, they propose an adaptive composite quadrature that refines points where the error indicator runs high, rebuilding the grid only when needed. On benchmark problems, the approach narrowed the gap between training and reference losses, used points more efficiently, and beat fixed quadrature strategies on accuracy.
arxiv-2605-00408:
Zhenhua Ning and 5 co-authors replace hand-written rules with a learned policy for a core chore in 3D Gaussian Splatting, the fast rendering method that builds scenes from millions of soft blobs. Deciding where to add or remove blobs has relied on heuristic density control. Refined rules still cannot adapt to every scene's geometry, the authors argue.

Their framework, LeGS, recasts density control as a policy network trained by reinforcement learning. A reward grounded in sensitivity analysis measures each blob's marginal contribution to reconstruction quality, and a closed-form shortcut keeps that reward cheap to compute even for huge scenes. On three standard datasets of indoor and outdoor scenes, LeGS beat leading methods, striking a better balance between image quality and efficiency. The work suggests learned control can retire a whole family of brittle hand-tuned rules.
arxiv-2605-00508:
András Formanek and 5 co-authors compare methods for judging how well drug molecules cross membranes, using a dataset built for the purpose. Their set holds 143 drug and candidate molecules, each tested in lab membrane assays against six different model membranes. Knowing passive permeability matters early in drug development, when most candidates will fail.

The team tests a range of descriptors and regression models, from plain linear regression to a modern deep learning model. The central tension is accuracy against how easy a model is to read, since black-box models are hard for chemists to trust or learn from. With so few molecules, expert-designed descriptors based on chemistry and physics beat deep learning. The authors describe the study as the widest joint modeling of several organ membranes to date, and it maps how permeability profiles differ from membrane to membrane.
arxiv-2605-00608:
M. Yu. Piotrovich, S. D. Buliga, and T. M. Natsvlishvili select red quasars, a dust-reddened type of active galaxy core, from the SDSS DR16 catalog. Using a color cut, they find 733 candidates, about four percent of their starting sample. For each object they then estimate radiative efficiency, black hole spin, viewing angle, and a revised mass for the central supermassive black hole.

Estimates under three models show many objects with retrograde spin, where the black hole rotates against its disk. The authors suggest those may be very young objects or products of mergers. Spin also rises strongly with mass, which leads them to argue the sample likely mixes Seyfert galaxies and narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies fed mainly by disk accretion.
arxiv-2605-00708:
Bruce Rushing and 4 co-authors stratify glaucoma patients by where their disease is heading, not just how bad it is today. Clinicians managing this chronic eye disease need to spot who will progress, from sparse, irregularly sampled health records. Their architecture pairs deep kernel learning with a Gaussian process back end, whose kernel is built by a transformer over embeddings of the clinical record produced by a medical language model.

The model sorts patients into three clinically distinct subgroups. Its sharpest finding is a decoupling: one high-risk group is worsening steadily while still seeing better, on average, than a second group whose vision is stably poor. A severity-only tool would rank those groups backwards. By learning trajectory risk rather than current state, the system can flag quietly deteriorating patients for targeted intervention. The authors offer it as decision support for glaucoma care.
arxiv-2605-00908:
Alcides Toledo Espinosa and four co-authors compare convolutional and transformer detectors for early weed detection in tomato plantations. Models tested include a recent YOLO nano variant on the convolutional side, and RT-DETR Large and RF-DETR Medium on the transformer side. Evaluation on a ground-based weed dataset covers six weed classes plus unidentified plants, using precision, recall, average precision, speed, and statistical tests.

Results show a clear trade-off. Convolutional detectors reach high performance at lower computational cost, while transformer approaches capture global context better at higher resource demand. The authors frame the findings as practical criteria for choosing models in precision agriculture, where both accuracy and field-ready efficiency matter.
arxiv-2605-01208:
Haowen Hu and five co-authors present Faithful-Agent, a framework that makes mobile GUI agents act on screen evidence rather than memorized shortcuts. Vision-language GUI agents interact strongly, yet often behave unfaithfully by ignoring displayed evidence or user instructions. Their two-stage pipeline first applies faithfulness-oriented supervised tuning to instill abstention under evidence perturbations. That teaches the agent to hold back when evidence does not support an action.

A second reinforcement finetuning stage uses a guided advantage estimator built on GRPO, with anchor-based and variance-adaptive tempering. That keeps the guided edge from collapsing under sparse rewards. A thought-action consistency reward further aligns reasoning with actions. Trap success rises dramatically over the baseline while general instruction-following performance is preserved.
arxiv-2605-01708:
Yipin Guo and Siddharth Joshi squeeze the memory cache that must cross machines before a language model can answer. Modern serving splits the work: one machine reads the prompt, another writes the reply, and the key-value cache built in the first step has to travel, which throttles long and agentic jobs.

SplitZip compresses that cache losslessly on the graphics card itself, bit for bit. It exploits a quirk of the cached numbers: their exponents repeat heavily, so frequent exponents get short fixed codes while rare ones escape through a sparse side stream of positions and values. A pre-tuned codebook of the top exponents skips any counting pass. Compression and decompression run several times faster than prior lossless tools on real cache tensors. End-to-end tests show faster transfers, quicker first tokens, and more requests served, for both standard and small-format caches.
arxiv-2605-01808:
Roberto Casadio, Andrea Giusti, Alexander Kamenshchik, and Jorge Ovalle follow a collapsing star past the point where gentle singularities form inside it. Schwarzschild black holes are the expected end state of collapse, and integrable curvature singularities, wild but tame enough to integrate through, can appear on the way.

In the interior, the inner horizon then vanishes in a transition the authors call Minkowski breaking, after which all matter falls to the central singularity. That picture cries out for quantum treatment of the last stages. The paper adds two semiclassical lenses: an approximation for the energy-momentum content, and the Madelung reading of the matter as a quantum fluid. The quantum potential inside the Raychaudhuri equation, the law that focuses infalling paths, turns strongly against the collapse after the breaking, pushing back against the Schwarzschild end. The result sharpens a candidate story for how quantum effects enter gravitational collapse.
arxiv-2605-01908:
Renu Bala and colleagues study how cold rubidium atoms change the width and shift of a mercury clock transition. The transition they examine is the one used for precise timing in mercury. They model collisions from very cold to one kelvin, using a potential built from long-range forces between the atoms.

Full quantum scattering results are compared with a semi-classical method. The team shows how line shape depends on the reduced mass of the pair and on scattering lengths in the ground and excited states. Resonances in both states cause large changes when the isotope mix changes. Inelastic collisions may also matter and could push the behaviour toward a universal pattern.
arxiv-2605-02008:
F Mavoa and colleagues study how the early universe could have made more matter than antimatter inside a modified gravity theory. The theory couples a scalar field to nonmetricity, a measure of how lengths change under transport. They test two forms of that coupling and track the baryon-to-entropy ratio as the universe expands, assuming power-law growth of the scale factor.

In the first model, the ratio falls steadily as the expansion parameter rises, and the observed tiny asymmetry is matched without fine tuning for a narrow range of that parameter. The second model is explored across its parameter space in the full paper. Both cases link the matter excess to gravity itself, rather than to particle physics alone.
arxiv-2605-02208:
Tsunefumi Mizuno and colleagues test a hadronic account of a candidate PeVatron, a source that may accelerate cosmic rays above a peta-electronvolt. The source, LHAASO J1912+1014u, overlaps a H.E.S.S. source, and identifying the particle species needs data across wavelengths. The team analyses fifteen years of Fermi-LAT gamma-ray data and carbon monoxide data from the FUGIN survey.

By improving the diffuse emission model, they cut large residuals near the source in a key energy band. A significant excess above background appears, likely tied to the LHAASO source, with a hard spectrum. Gas templates at a matching velocity reproduce the excess well. That fit supports a hadronic picture, where protons striking gas make the gamma rays.
arxiv-2605-02408:
Songnan Gu, Hao Jiang, Chongjun Ouyang, Dian Fan, Yuanwei Liu, and Arumugam Nallanathan join over-the-air computing with a segmented waveguide pinching-antenna system, called SWAN. Over-the-air methods add up signals from many users during transmission itself. That saves time and bandwidth. Pinching antennas sit along a waveguide to shape coverage. Splitting the waveguide into segments adds control.

Three uplink designs are given: segment selection, segment joining without phase shifters, and joining with phase shifters. For each, simple algorithms tune antenna placement and per-segment phase shifts. In tests, both selection and joining beat a standard pinching system on computing error. Phase control by segment improves joining further, showing the value of the split design.
arxiv-2605-02508:
Jelena Kovačević-Dojčinović and two co-authors study iron emission lines in the spectra of type 1 active galactic nuclei, the bright centers of galaxies. Iron emission there is strong and complex, and its source region is still not well understood. The team uses a large sample of spectra and a flexible template that splits the optical iron lines into groups.

Lines are sorted by atomic traits into groups that behave in consistent or inconsistent ways, with one group split further by region within the broad-line zone. Tracking these groups along the quasar main sequence, the authors find a tight inverse link between iron line strength and line width. That link, they argue, may be a basic relation behind the main sequence itself, driven mainly by one line group.
arxiv-2605-02608:
Kevin Guan, Happy Buzaaba, and Christiane Fellbaum compare sentence parsers across languages with very different amounts of training data. Dependency parsing marks how words in a sentence relate grammatically. Transformer models lead in languages with large treebanks, but whether they beat simpler designs when data are scarce was poorly understood. The study covers twelve diverse languages, with a focus on low-resource African languages.

Four parsers are tested, from a bidirectional LSTM design to large pretrained transformers. The simpler LSTM parser wins consistently in low-resource settings, and transformers regain their lead only as training data grow. The crossover sits in the range typical for under-resourced treebanks. Morphological complexity also predicts part of the transformer shortfall. The practical advice: build syntax tools for scarce languages on the simpler design for now.
arxiv-2605-02908:
Bumjun Kim and Albert No uncover a surprising driver of memorization in Stable Diffusion, the text-to-image model known for sometimes reproducing its training images. Text enters the model as embeddings from a CLIP encoder, split by token type: start, prompt, end, and padding tokens. Which of these actually steer a memorized output was the open question.

In memorized cases, the prompt embeddings contribute surprisingly little. Padding embeddings matter far more, because the default pad token duplicates the end token, the one embedding directly optimized in CLIP training. That duplication quietly amplifies the end token's influence and drives the model to over-rely on it. Two simple fixes at run time follow: changing the pad token and masking part of the end embedding. Both are cheap mitigations.
arxiv-2605-03408:
Akshat Singh Jaswal, Ashish Baghel, and Paras Chopra study whether language models can discover complete reinforcement learning interfaces from raw simulator state. Building observation mappings and reward functions by hand is a major cost for each new task, and past automation fixed the observations and designed rewards only.

Their LIMEN framework evolves executable interface programs with language model guidance, refining them with policy training feedback and only a trajectory-level success signal. Across gridworld, locomotion, and manipulation domains, evolving observations and rewards together found working interfaces, while optimizing either part alone failed badly on at least one domain.
arxiv-2605-03508:
N. Grasser, I. A. G. Snellen, S. de Regt, D. González Picos, Y. Zhang, T. Stolker, S. Gandhi, R. Landman, P. Mollière, and N. F. Allard measure carbon isotope ratios in the young ROXs 12 star and its companion. Isotope ratios in atmospheres may trace how substellar objects formed, and systems where both host and companion can be measured are rare tests.

High-resolution spectra show water, both carbon monoxide isotopologues, and hydrogen fluoride in both objects. The companion's isotope ratio came out lower than the star's, a measurable but not decisive contrast, alongside a well-measured carbon-to-oxygen ratio for the companion. Such paired chemistry constrains super-Jupiter formation paths.
arxiv-2605-03608:
Matthew Adeoye, Simon E. F. Spencer, and Xavier Didelot build a Bayesian model for epidemics where several strains of one pathogen spread across space and time together. Understanding such multi-type pathogens requires accounting for how strains interact across geography. The authors build a joint state-space model for all strains, with biology-informed links between their epidemic states.

Several copula models capture the dependence structure between strains, and a fast Markov chain Monte Carlo scheme fits the models. Bridge and importance sampling support model comparison in high dimensions. On simulated data the epidemics and parameters were recovered correctly. The team also fits monthly meningococcal disease data from twenty-six European countries, and releases an R package.
arxiv-2605-03808:
Chandan Singh and six co-authors introduce Agentic-imodels, an automated research loop that evolves data-science tools to be interpretable by artificial intelligence agents rather than by humans. Agentic data science systems increasingly analyze and fit data autonomously, yet they still use statistical tools designed for human readers. The loop develops a library of scikit-learn-compatible regressors for tabular data.

The evolved models are optimized for predictive performance and for a new interpretability metric graded by language models. The metric tests whether a model's string representation can be simulated by a model reader. The reader answers questions about the model's behavior. The evolved regressors improved both scores, generalized to new datasets and tests, and raised downstream performance of several agent systems on the BLADE benchmark.
arxiv-2605-04108:
Chamani Shiranthika, Hadi Hadizadeh, and Parvaneh Saeedi propose MuCALD-SplitFed, a framework for medical image segmentation across sites that cannot share raw data. Federated learning combines model updates instead of data, and split federated learning further divides the model between clients and a server. Real clinical teams, however, work on different tasks at different sites. Standard setups handle that poorly, and with privacy vulnerabilities.

Their multi-task split-federated framework joins causal representation learning with latent diffusion. In experiments it improved results while a baseline split-federated method failed to converge. The approach also reduced information leakage at split points. It blunted reconstruction-based and membership inference attacks. It outperformed state-of-the-art personalized and multi-task federated learning methods.
arxiv-2605-04308:
Kaustubh Pethkar and three co-authors propose a way to add new knowledge to a language model without retraining its weights, which can erase old knowledge and cannot easily be undone. They ask whether large weight updates are really needed for a small amount of new material.

They model text generation as a Markov process over tokens, where the model's memory is a transition table. Adding knowledge then means extending that table while keeping old transitions intact, which protects what was learned before. They prove a bound on how many samples are needed to learn each new token's behaviour through a dictionary mapping.
arxiv-2605-05008:
Jiayu Weng and Alec Kirkley present a fast, principled way to divide a map into regions that share similar behaviour over time, a task called regionalization. Older methods use static snapshots or force spatial continuity with ad hoc penalties, and most time-series clustering ignores space altogether. Their approach uses the minimum description length principle from information theory instead.

The method jointly finds a spatial partition and a set of representative time patterns, called drivers, that best compress the full dataset. Its running time grows gently with dataset size. Tests recovered planted regions in synthetic data and found meaningful patterns in large air quality and vegetation records.
arxiv-2605-05508:
Benchmarks say what a model did, not why it did it. Isabelle Lee and six co-authors argue that rigorous interpretation should count as evaluation in its own right. Understanding a behavior's cause can matter as much as measuring the behavior, and good explanation meets scientific standards: claims that can fail, be repeated, and predict.

They outline three evaluative uses of interpretability. It can find the root cause of unwanted behavior, expose subtly broken mechanisms behind outputs, and flag weaknesses before failures appear. Trusted this way, interpretation becomes a richer check on models than surface scores alone.
arxiv-2605-05608:
Periodically driven quantum systems can host topological phases with no static counterpart. Xin Shen, Bing Lu, and Yan-Qing Zhu show how to spot those phases by watching a wave packet drift. They develop a Floquet perturbation theory that describes the packet's center-of-mass motion in an extended Hilbert space.

Applied to the driven Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model, the motion shows trembling oscillations at several frequencies. Their makeup and phase encode the band structure directly. At a topological transition, new low-frequency modes and phase shifts appear, giving experimenters a practical detection protocol for both weak and strong driving.
arxiv-2605-05808:
Every learning algorithm is quietly shaped by its loss function. Lena Helgerth and Andreas Christmann survey one family: ratio-based losses. Classification losses usually depend on the margin between output and prediction, while regression losses depend on their difference; ratio-based losses instead depend on their quotient.

The survey places these losses inside the standard machinery of risk, hypothesis spaces, and probability measures. Ratio losses behave differently under scaling and outliers, which recommends them for particular data regimes. The authors organize what is known about their statistical properties so practitioners can choose deliberately rather than by habit.
arxiv-2605-05908:
Labels in real datasets are wrong in structured ways: a cat is called a dog, not a refrigerator. Frederik Schäfer, Luis Mandl, Lars Kälber, and Tim Ricken build a classification head designed for exactly that semantically proximal noise. Their Bayesian header can sit atop any feature extractor and constrains both the mean and spread of its weights through spectral normalization.

The bi-Lipschitz constraint promotes calibrated uncertainty and stops noise from amplifying through the head. Applied to vision transformers, the resulting model separates genuine ambiguity from label corruption. Robustness, here, is engineered into the last layer.
arxiv-2605-06308:
Marc Boubnovski Martell and six co-authors estimate the confidence of black box reasoning models from the shape of their reasoning traces. Safe use of chain of thought systems through text only interfaces needs reliable confidence, yet the standard self consistency baseline costs scale linearly with samples and ignores trace geometry. Their score embeds a reasoning trace as a sliding window trajectory and measures how it converges toward external answer anchors.

No logits, hidden states, or trained calibrators are required, so the method works through plain text access. Fused with coverage and verbalized confidence channels, it beat self consistency at double the sample count in all six tested settings. Geometry carried independent signal in nearly every configuration, and swapping the judge model barely moved the geometry scores. Median discrimination reached well above the baseline across medical and science benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-06408:
Bernardo Taveira and four co-authors present a GPU method for building large 3D Voronoi diagrams and their weighted form, power diagrams. These diagrams split space around points and matter in fields including mesh-based neural rendering. Building them for huge point sets has stayed costly, and GPU methods often assume evenly spread points.

Their algorithm builds each cell by clipping an initial volume against planes from nearby points. A directional culling rule and a hierarchical search find those neighbors efficiently under varied distributions. Performance matches leading Delaunay methods on smaller problems and scales more robustly to large, uneven point sets.
arxiv-2605-06608:
Kateryna Husar and one co-author design medical trials that must pay to measure patient covariates before treatment. Trials usually assume useful outcome-linked traits are known and free, but rich data taken before treatment are costly, forcing a trade-off between sharpness and budget. Their DARTS method treats covariate buying as a step-by-step choice inside the trial design itself.

A budgeted Thompson sampler learns across batches which traits predict outcomes best, and chosen traits drive fresh random splits plus regression to cut effect-estimate variance. Theory shows adaptive selection preserves randomization soundness and nominal coverage, with a near-optimal risk bound for the buying layer. In tests DARTS focuses spending on useful features and nears oracle gains.
arxiv-2605-06708:
Lv Tang, Tianyi Zheng, Yang Liu, Bo Li, and Xingyu Li explain when compressing text into an image helps or hurts a vision-language model. Rendering text visually can cut token counts many-fold, yet savings do not predict downstream quality: some tasks match the text path, others collapse, and the compression ratio does not tell which. They reframe the question using measure transport.

Text and visual tokens become probability measures, and the vision encoder's cost splits into a precision cost from grouping within patches and a coverage cost from splitting across patches. Both are measurable without labels. A routing rule chooses the visual path per input, and a foveation step re-encodes costly regions at higher resolution, improving average scores while using fewer tokens.
arxiv-2605-06908:
Ziming Li and four co-authors show that extra test-time computation helps or harms language model agents depending on direction, not just amount. Adaptive methods gate extra rollouts by confidence or uncertainty, assuming the signal's meaning is fixed. The authors demonstrate the same signal predicts benefit in one environment and harm in another, even with the task unchanged. Uncertainty can mark states where comparison helps, or states where intervention cannot.

Their DIAL method learns the utility direction of state features separately for each environment and model backbone, trained from counterfactual exploration that does not presuppose the signal's meaning. Across six environments and three backbones it achieves a stronger success-versus-cost trade-off than fixed-direction gates.
arxiv-2605-07208:
Jianrong Ding and three co-authors forecast the future impact of research papers, a task where language models judge poorly. True impact takes years to appear, so they use impact prediction for human-written manuscripts as a testable stand-in. Frontier models, they find, cannot reliably tell high-impact papers from ordinary ones using text alone.

Their FAME framework tracks how scientific topics move over time in a latent space shaped by paper text and knowledge flow. On thousands of papers from three fast-moving fields, it beat leading model evaluators at forecasting impact. Feeding its signals back into language models also improved their forecasts, supporting trajectory-aware evaluation.
arxiv-2605-07308:
Xiaoqi Li and seven co-authors add touch sensing to vision-language-action robot models without wrecking their pretrained skill. Contact-rich tasks need tactile feedback, but injecting a new sense during fine-tuning can disrupt earlier capabilities, and slow inference limits real-time reaction. Their AT-VLA injects touch only at the right times and places.

A second, fast tactile stream handles high-frequency physical interaction while the slower visual-language stream reasons about the scene. Together they close the control loop in a fraction of a second. Real-world experiments on contact-rich manipulation validate the design, showing robots can exploit touch feedback while keeping their pretrained strengths.
arxiv-2605-07508:
Matthias Knopf and twelve co-authors measure the fine time structure of particle beams at two medical accelerator facilities. Such knowledge is needed to avoid pulse pileup in detector tests. Beam timing details are rarely supplied by the sites and hard to measure. The team used a silicon carbide sensor with a fast readout to resolve arrivals in under a billionth of a second.

The readings show a rhythm at the machines' radio frequencies, tied to how particles are extracted, for both beam types. That structure lets teams estimate pileup amounts directly and set design constraints for future readout electronics. The work stresses beam timing checks for precise instrument building.
arxiv-2605-07708:
Julius Bohm and two co-authors propose a topological pump that runs itself. In a Thouless pump, particles are transported in exact quantized amounts as external parameters are cycled by hand. Their version replaces the external control with a quantum spin in a static magnetic field, whose Larmor precession performs the control cycle for fermions on a one-dimensional lattice.

In some energy eigenstates of the combined system, the fermions are transported with topological quantization as hoped. In others, the fermions push back on the spin and distort its cycle enough to disrupt the flow. Numerically, though, they find a critical magnetic field above which the autonomous pump works robustly, suggesting topological protection and self-operation can coexist in a kind of quantum motor.
arxiv-2605-07908:
Fabio Cuzzolin surveys statistical inference with belief functions, a framework for reasoning under uncertainty when data are too scarce to pin down a probability distribution. Belief functions are popular exactly in that regime, where learning a full distribution cannot be done. Any argument built on them begins with inference: learning a belief measure from the data actually available.

The survey focuses on that first step, drawing beliefs from statistical data, and reviews the most key work in the area. It sorts a spread-out literature for readers who want to adopt the framework or compare its methods against other approaches.
arxiv-2605-08108:
Ioannis Emmanouil writes a short note on lim-one groups. These groups measure how far a module sits from its completion. For a shrinking chain of submodules, the lim-one group is the cokernel of the map into the completion. The note asks if every lim-one group arises in that way.

Emmanouil proves that it does. The form is canonical and functorial. Any inverse sequence of modules admits a map from a chain sequence that matches on lim-one. The proof uses Quillen's small object argument, as recast by Eklof and Trlifaj. It also uses a construction of Salce that gives enough projectives.
arxiv-2605-08408:
Binghang Lu, Runyu Zhang, Changhong Mou, Na Li, and coauthors enforce the physics in a neural PDE solver instead of merely penalizing violations. Standard physics-informed networks mix residuals, data mismatch, and boundary losses with hand-chosen weights, which often yields ill-conditioning and constraints satisfied only loosely.

AdamFLIP recasts training as an equality-constrained optimization problem. Constraint residuals are treated as the output of a controlled system, and the Lagrange multiplier becomes a feedback signal that drives them toward stable linear contraction. Adam-style moment adaptation then tunes that feedback. The hard-constraint framing aims at solutions that respect the governing equations by construction rather than by bargaining among loss weights.
arxiv-2605-08608:
Zheng Wang and nine coauthors clean up noisy speech with a language model while stopping it from inventing words. Under heavy noise, such enhancers can output smooth speech that says the wrong thing. Their system, L3-SE, learns conditioning signals that stay stable in noise by copying two clean targets at once: one for sound quality, one for word content.

A high fidelity audio codec built from layered speech features feeds the generator with clean tokens. Tests show fewer invented words and stronger content faithfulness than earlier language model enhancers, especially in low signal and echoing rooms, while sound quality stays competitive. Speech technology gains reliability where noise is worst.
arxiv-2605-08708:
Simón Paiva-Ortega and three coauthors say the way a test reads its signal sets the fade time it finds. Two dimensional light tests read line widths as coherence times. Yet the same deep acts can look unlike through unlike readouts. Their frame splits two kinds of readout. One reads the field that the sample emits. One reads counts of excited states, like light given off or current.

Field reads keep the old link to coherence time. Count reads mix in how excited states spread out. That mix gives a longer fade time in effect. One shared model proves the split. Line width is part trait of the sample, part trait of the test.
arxiv-2605-08808:
Ziyao He and five coauthors describe three dimensional scenes in words while keeping objects precisely located, using attention that respects curved geometry. Flat embedding spaces struggle to hold both fine local detail and the branching hierarchies of indoor scenes, so captions end up vague or misplaced. Their curvature aware framework runs self attention in an oblique space for long range links and cross attention in a hyperbolic Lorentz space for hierarchical relations.

Theory shows the two curvatures complement each other, steadying features while preserving hierarchy. On two standard scene captioning benchmarks, the method sets new highs for both localization accuracy and descriptive richness. Robotics and augmented reality gain scene narration that knows where things are and how they group.
arxiv-2605-08908:
Ayushi Agarwal, Anannya Mathur, and Preeti Ranjan Panda manage the shared cache memory contested by processor cores and hardware accelerators in modern chips. Accelerators carry strict deadlines, and naive sharing can wreck core performance, while existing bypass methods were designed around processor access patterns that accelerators do not follow. Their LERN method clusters past behavior to predict accelerator reuse at the shared cache.

The HyDRA strategy then trades reuse against deadline pressure when deciding which accesses to bypass. Across varied workloads and accelerator setups, system performance rises significantly and accelerator deadline misses fall. Heterogeneous chip design gains cache policy that respects both throughput and the hard timing promises accelerators must keep.
arxiv-2605-09408:
Porcedda and three colleagues tackle link prediction, guessing missing or future links between nodes in a graph. It is a core problem in network science with uses from fraud detection to drug-target interaction in biomedicine. Prediction stays hard for graphs enriched with edge direction and node attributes, since graph deep learning research has mostly covered undirected graphs without fully using node attributes.

Their GravityGraphSAGE pairs a modified GraphSAGE backbone for node embeddings with a gravity-inspired decoder, the first GraphSAGE backbone used for directed link prediction. On PubMed, Cora, Citeseer, and 16 real-world graphs from Netzschleuder, the model beats state-of-the-art graph deep learning link prediction methods. Further evidence links output quality to graph characteristics, suggesting the framework scales well as data complexity grows.
arxiv-2605-09608:
Wang and eleven colleagues explain and control forgetting in continual post training of large language models. Sequential updates should add new knowledge, skills, and behaviors, yet they often erode earlier capabilities. Existing fixes use sequential fine tuning, replay, regularization, or merging, but give little guidance on when a new update helps or harms.
