The authors study the problem through task geometry, representing each task by its parameter update.

Their central finding is that forgetting is an integration failure relative to state. It arises when task covariance geometries clash with the evolving model state's geometry. Updates transfer when they stay compatible with the state shaped by earlier updates, and interfere when geometry conflict runs high. Their data free merging method, GCWM, builds a shared Wasserstein metric from Gaussian barycenters and gates correction by geometry conflict. It beats data free baselines on Qwen3 models without replay data.
arxiv-2605-09808:
Suh and three colleagues ask how to judge a user simulator, a fake user used to train chat assistants. The test that matters is how well the assistant performs with real people afterwards. They hold everything fixed except the simulator. Assistants are trained by reinforcement learning against a range from a language model told to act as a user to one trained on real human chats from WildChat. A study with 283 people plus the WildBench test set provides the verdict.

Training against the role-playing model left the assistant statistically tied with its starting point, winning about fifty-one percent of comparisons. Training against the fine-tuned simulator gave clear gains, about fifty-eight percent over the starting assistant. Making role-players more lifelike helped but never closed the gap. Bigger role-playing models added nothing, while the fine-tuned simulator's gains carried over to new test partners.
arxiv-2605-10108:
Stepanov and three colleagues unify two language tasks that are usually run apart: finding named entities in text and extracting relations between them, the two steps behind building knowledge graphs. Their system, GLiNER-Relex, extends the GLiNER framework so one model does both jobs at once, instead of needing separate models for each.

A shared bidirectional transformer encoder represents text together with entity-type and relation-type labels, which lets the model extract arbitrary types specified at run time, even types never seen in training. Entity pairs are scored against relation embeddings by a dedicated module. Tests on CoNLL04, DocRED, FewRel and CrossRE show competitive results against specialised extractors and large language models, with GLiNER's trademark efficiency intact and code released openly.
arxiv-2605-10408:
Prasun Saurabh and four colleagues automate a bottleneck in robot testing: judging whether a robot did its task well. Old assessment relies on task-specific symbolic oracles, which give pass-or-fail verdicts with no quality measure, plus slow, subjective human inspection of robot behavior. Their 2026 paper proposes VISOR, a vision-language-model-based test oracle that rates task correctness and quality by itself.

VISOR also rates its own doubt during assessments, since vision-language models are inherently unsure. The authors tested it with two models, GPT and Gemini, across four robotic tasks on over 1,000 videos. Gemini caught more correct performances, scoring higher recall, while GPT made fewer false positive calls, scoring higher precision. Both models, however, showed low correlation between doubt and correctness, so doubt cannot yet serve as a correctness predictor.
arxiv-2605-10608:
Ryan Mickler argues that Jack Littlewood-Richardson coefficients are versions of certain novel polynomials, showing hidden structure in these numbers. For the triple of partitions (21, 21, 321), he proves the matching polynomial is stable under a group. It is identified as the automorphism group of the Johnson graph on 6 elements taken 3 at a time. The investigation continues a project on these numbers, motivated by the Stanley guess that the numerator of one such number is a non-negative polynomial.

Mickler guesses that the polynomials split on certain hyperplanes. This follows from fit relations between polynomials for next-door triples in the Young graph. From this follows the guess that the difference of next-door such numbers divides by the shared hook length. This is shown for two triples differing by a single box move. The work culminates in a guess exposing hidden structure across these numbers.
arxiv-2605-10708:
Elin Ranjan Das and co-authors present a hybrid spring-qubit form of linear mix of Hamiltonian runs for solving linear ordinary rate equations. Math error bounds cover the two ways of getting close for ideal kernel-state setup, with super-fast closing in for Schwartz-class kernels and slower closing in under stronger strip-analytic guesses.

The finite squeezed-Fock kernel state captures the required non-Gaussian nature, with cutoff size as the measure of the oracle's non-Gaussian stock. A product-formula bound gives the Trotter steps needed for a given error, and a nudge bound shows that near-ideal oracle build only slightly perturbs the post-pick chance. In heat-equation benchmarks, the Law-Eberly protocol tops 99.9 percent, while a tuned 30-layer route tops 99.6 percent, with a much more compact oracle account than a matrix-product-state qubit build at matched quality.
arxiv-2605-11008:
Yonatan Sverdlov, Benjamin Friedman, Snir Hordan, and Nadav Dym analyze when canonization generalizes as well as built-in invariance. Canonization maps symmetric data to a standard form before a plain model runs, and group averaging offers a similar shortcut, but how well these tricks learn from samples has stayed murky.

Bounding covering numbers, the team proves a ranking: canonized models rank at best equal to invariant and group-averaged models, at worst equal to plain baselines. Whether a canonization hits the good or the bad end depends on its smoothness. Applied to point clouds, alphabetical sorting grows exponentially with dimension while Hilbert-curve canonization grows polynomially, formally justifying Hilbert serialization's practical success. Practitioners get theory for choosing canonizations wisely.
arxiv-2605-11708: Liu and four others study wrinkling of thin elastic sheets with two round holes. The Lamé setup, ring wrinkles in an annular sheet, is the wrinkling model, giving long-distance transfer. With multiple holes, they combine models and tests on two-hole sheets. The pre-buckled state is solved in bipolar grids, giving the wrinkling threshold by hole distance. Near-threshold wrinkling and links are checked against video of plastic sheets floating on liquid. Balance breaking shapes wrinkle starts, aim and extent, backing a mechanosensing match.
arxiv-2605-12208: Julian Rodemann and three colleagues skip the parameter posterior and target predictions. Bayesian inference usually works out parameter values, yet predictions matter more than parameters in practice. Their Self-Supervised Laplace Approximation measures doubt by training again on data the model itself predicts. If the model rates its own data highly, doubt is low, and vice versa. The method is sampling-free, letting varied priors serve as prior tests. A cheaper variant avoids costly repeat training, and tests from linear models to neural networks show better tuning than Laplace methods.
arxiv-2605-12308: Sevinchan and ten colleagues build an early-warning system for abrupt shifts in dynamical systems. Standard warning signs fail with scarce data and correlated noise. Deep classifiers rarely extrapolate beyond their training mix. Their TipPFN framework learns in context from a synthetic generator built on classic bifurcation patterns. It can judge closeness to a tipping point from contexts of many sizes, and detects unseen tipping regimes and real cases in both in-context and zero-shot modes.
arxiv-2605-12808: Zhang and Branson benchmark agents on neuroscience data reuse. Neuroscience data are fragmented across labs and formats, and reuse demands manual effort. Flexible formats are rarely self-explanatory, while datasets demand documentation few labs sustain. Given data, code and paper, agents reformat data to train a neural decoder. The team pairs outcome metrics with a rubric scored by two evaluators. Agents succeed on subtasks but rarely produce an error-free solution, and judges are unreliable.
arxiv-2605-12908: Awano and Suzuki study weak-to-strong generalisation, where a strong model is fine-tuned on a weaker specialist's outputs as a path to aligning superhuman AI. They work in reward-model learning with two-layer networks, where the strong model's pretrained representations sit in low-dimensional subspaces. They prove the strong model efficiently learns the target task, eliciting pretrained knowledge while retaining general capabilities. Weak-to-strong training also preserves off-target features, where standard fine-tuning causes catastrophic forgetting when features correlate.
arxiv-2605-13108: Jabbar and four co-authors tackle face presentation attack detection, spotting spoofed faces from prints, replays, masks, makeup and occlusions. Motion cues discriminate well but explicit optical flow costs too much for real-time use. Their dual-branch teacher fuses RGB appearance cues with colourwheel-encoded flow to model micro-motions and temporal consistency. A distillation step transfers that motion-aware knowledge to a lightweight RGB-only student, which matches or beats the teacher while running at 52 frames per second on a Jetson Orin Nano.
arxiv-2605-13608: Adam Bartoš and three colleagues view ultrametric spaces as two-sorted frames of points and a set of gaps in order. They show the class of all finite two-sorted ultrametric spaces with such maps is Fraïssé, with limit the counting ratio Urysohn ultrametric space U. That space covers all counting ultrametric spaces, and its Cauchy closure covers all split ultrametric spaces. They also map the self-map group of U as a mixed product of order-keeping pairings and rigid maps.
arxiv-2605-13908: Al-Badawi and three co-authors derive an exact black hole solution in higher-order curvature gravity. They wed a ModMax sector to quintessence dark energy. For purely charged cases they probe heat traits and their geometry, testing if the hole holds firm and where its phases shift. In this sector ModMax acts like plain Maxwell theory up to a rescale of charge. Bends in heat curvature line up with heat capacity hitting zero.
arxiv-2605-14008: Hilbert studies kernel density estimation as a rule for Bayesian predictive inference, where each predictive distribution for the next observation is specified from past data. He examines two kernel-based rules, the classic estimator and a recursive version built for online problems, and shows both converge weakly almost surely. That convergence opens new Bayesian readings of kernel density estimation, though the classic rule lands on a compactly supported measure while the recursive one does not.
arxiv-2605-14108: Doshi and Shah evaluate a two-tier edge-cloud cascade for automated diabetic retinopathy screening. Diabetic retinopathy ranks among the top preventable causes of blindness, and automated screening can stretch scarce specialist capacity. Cloud deep learning grades well but demands image upload and steady connectivity. Tier one runs a lightweight MobileNetV3-small model on-device to triage referable versus non-referable cases. Tier two runs a RETFound-DINOv2 model in the cloud for severity grading, but only on images tier one flags.
arxiv-2605-14208: Erdem and seven co-authors study the long-ignored close binary V486 Carinae with satellite photometry, high-dispersion spectrometry and ground-based photometry. Smooth wave-like light variations hint at a near-contact system, yet shallow eclipses make confident parametrization challenging. The team finds masses of 2.1 and 0.4 solar masses, radii of 3.20 and 1.48 solar radii, and temperatures near 10000 and 6200 kelvin for the two stars, at a distance near 162 parsecs. New times of minima, including recent TESS observations, are examined with the O'Connell effect.
arxiv-2605-14308: Zhang and four co-authors train a neural-network method on N-body simulations for stripping times of stream stars from phase-space coordinates. The stream comes from a dwarf's disruption, with wraps stripped during pericentric passages. SEGUE, APOGEE and LAMOST spectroscopy plus Gaia astrometry and StarHorse distances identify members. The method finds a metallicity gradient with stripping time, linear with slope near a third of a dex per Gyr. M 54, Terzan 7, Terzan 8 and Arp 2 look bound to it, while Pal 12, Whiting 1 and NGC 2419 were stripped about 1, 1, and 2 Gyr ago.
arxiv-2605-14608: Oszmian and Lesiuk study effective ranks for the canonical polyadic decomposition of electron repulsion integrals, a core object in quantum chemistry. They show, in math and in numbers, that this rank cannot in general grow linearly with system size. A lower bound near the square of the atomic orbital count, divided by a log power, is derived under mild threshold conditions. A subquadratic growth is not ruled out, but a universal linear link is.
arxiv-2605-14708: Chen, Zhao, Shu, Liu, Yu and Zhou present StyleTextGen, a framework for generating scene text that copies a reference style across languages and writing systems. A dual-branch style encoder models style in messy real scenes, a style consistency loss keeps characters coherent, and a mask-guided inference step aligns generated text with the reference. A new bilingual benchmark, StyleText-CE, covers monolingual and cross-lingual settings, with claimed state-of-the-art style consistency.
arxiv-2605-14808: Roming and team propose SuperADD, a training-free anomaly segmentation pipeline for industrial inspection that works across object classes. Models must stay robust when training and deployment data differ, for example under varying light. The pipeline builds on SuperAD with a DINOv3 backbone, overlapping patch processing, light-based augmentations, better memory-bank sampling, and iterative morphological closing. One shared design and setting set serves all classes, with segmentation F1 scores above sixty percent reported.
arxiv-2605-15008: Chon-Fai Kam reviews the Majorana stellar picture, which maps a pure spin state to points on a sphere, with entanglement as the guiding thread. The star pattern's degeneracy stays fixed under stochastic local operations and classical communication. Integer partitions then label families of symmetric multi-qubit states. The permanent of the stars' Gram matrix supplies what the pattern omits, yielding concurrence, three-tangle, and a Berry-phase term in closed form. Limits of the geometry for computing are also pinned down.
arxiv-2605-15108: Connor Douglas, Joel Persson, and Foster Provost study how to design logging policies for off-policy evaluation. It values a target policy from data gathered under a different policy. Accuracy hinges on the logging policy, through a reward-coverage tradeoff. Favoring high-reward actions cuts variance but may miss signal on actions the target would take. The authors characterize optimal logging policies when the target and rewards are known, unknown, or partially known. They distill practical design principles for firms choosing among candidate recommenders.
arxiv-2605-15308: Jiachen Jiang, Huminhao Zhu, and Zhihui Zhu offer SMCEvolve, a principled framework for LLM-driven program evolution toward scientific discovery. Old systems offer no design rules for their parts and no convergence guarantee. Reframing search as sampling from a reward-tilted distribution with a stepwise Monte Carlo sampler yields three principled mechanisms: live parent redrawing, mutation mixes with approval, and auto settling control. A finite-sample analysis bounds the LLM-call budget, and benchmarks show wins over state-of-the-art evolving systems with fewer calls.
arxiv-2605-15408: T. Ferreira and colleagues show that two very different kinds of light beam share the same second-order statistics. Any cylindrically symmetric beam carrying orbital angular momentum has a covariance matrix fixed by its spread, its momentum spread, and its twist number, matching that of a twisted Gaussian Schell-model beam. The match holds for Laguerre-Gaussian, Bessel-Gaussian, and perfect vortex beams, so the well-known propagation tools for the second kind apply directly to the first.
arxiv-2605-15908: Yanhao Ge and four colleagues propose RaPD, size-free pixel diffusion in a Neural Image Field latent space. Natural images are smooth, yet most models draw them on grids, blocking size-free output. Prior neural fields add smoothness only at decode time via interpolation, leaving the latent space gridded. RaPD bridges this gap with Semantic Representation Guidance for learning generation-ready latents and a Coordinate-Queried Attention Renderer for scale-aware output at chosen coordinates. One denoised latent renders at any size by changing query points alone, keeping cost fixed.
arxiv-2605-16008: Eugenia Moris and thirteen colleagues automate plaque counting, the standard readout of virus infectivity, from laboratory plate images. Their workflow pairs a well-finding model with a plaque-detecting model, both derived from the Segment Anything Model, and computes plaque-forming units per milliliter in a web platform. On held-out plates of Mayaro, Coxsackievirus B3, and Vaccinia viruses, counts agreed strongly with manual annotations and four independent experts.
arxiv-2605-16108: Visser and five colleagues develop weighting methods for marginal association between paired outcomes in clustered data. When subgroup composition within clusters shapes outcome distributions, ignoring it can bias association estimates. Their pair-based weights come from within-cluster resampling and extend standard cluster weighting to paired subgroups. In simulations the weights cut bias, and an application to NHANES oral-health data found strong evidence of informative subgroup size for filled-surface outcomes.
arxiv-2605-16208: Lee, Kim, and Do present QSurv, a large-scale deep learning tool for survival models over time with no time steps and no strict shape rules. Training such models is hard because the needed integral has no closed form. QSurv nears the total hazard with Gauss-Legendre quadrature, for fast end-to-end training by standard backprop. Time-tuned low-rank tuning lets general nets track shifting hazards, and tests show strong guesses with sharper instant hazard values.
arxiv-2605-16708: Li and colleagues adapt a beta-TCVAE model, a kind of variational autoencoder that learns separate latent factors, to split nonlinear brain signals in fMRI data. Standard independent component analysis assumes linear mixing, which fails against the brain's nonlinear dynamics. Their model recovers real nonlinear spatial parts, including the default mode network and other core connectivity networks. Checks of functional network links show the learned structure captures coherent, clear brain patterns.
arxiv-2605-17108: Gaudreault and Mao build a recurrent network that keeps the memory strengths of older sequence models without their step-by-step bottleneck. Their Parallel Recursive LSTM merges token states through a balanced tree instead of marching left to right, so parallel depth grows like a logarithm rather than like sequence length. The design keeps nonlinear gated memory while dodging attention's quadratic cost. It solves more formal-language tasks than standard rivals and stretches better to longer sequences.
arxiv-2605-17808: Chenguang Wang and Tianshu Yu build a theory for data-free sampling from unnormalized targets via Wasserstein gradient flows. For f-divergence objectives, the velocity field splits into a score term and a divergence-chosen weight. That split shows f-divergence drifts share a target but differ in repair effort across under-covered regions. A regional-response theory plus a compression-elasticity identity links divergence choice to transport geometry. The framework extends to Log-Variance divergence, with kernel and flow implementations sampling in one step on Gaussian-mixture tests.
arxiv-2605-18108: Borhan Ahmadi's 2026 paper swaps the usual ideal microwave drive for a finite quantum battery in a demanding qubit control test. The test is echo-refocused geometric Landau-Zener interference, driven by one quantized bosonic mode. At finite photon counts the coupling splits the path into photon-resolved sectors, so the run is no longer one classical device but a set of linked quantum paths. The result is lost contrast, warped fringe patterns, and clear back-action on the battery.
arxiv-2605-18208: S. Rajendran's 2026 paper studies how erbium spins in calcium tungstate lose their spin order at millikelvin cold, read out via a small superconducting resonator. At high field, where phonon emission runs fast, decay times grow a lot as more spins are excited. The rise tracks a squared tanh law with temperature, the mark of a phonon bottleneck, where freed phonons cannot leave fast enough. The result matters for quantum gear that uses rare-earth spin groups as steady resources.
arxiv-2605-18308: In their 2026 paper, Sergey Kitaev and Ryan Martin determine how far an arbitrary graph can sit from two hereditary families, word-representable graphs and poset comparability graphs. The maximum edit distance reaches one eighth of n squared for word-representable graphs and five thirty-seconds of n squared for comparability graphs, ignoring lower-order terms. They also map the full edit-distance function across all edge densities, including k-word-representable graphs.
arxiv-2605-18808: João Paulo Cavalcante Presa and Sávio Salvarino Teles de Oliveira map literary features inside two instruction-tuned language models. Using sparse autoencoders, they find naming gates for affect, a cluster of eleven first-person features, style modulators, and emotions built only by combining features. A five-model judge panel over twenty-seven emotion types gives Llama full coverage. Gemma reaches twenty-three of twenty-seven, with adoration as the lone strict failure. Chance, they argue, cannot explain that coverage.
arxiv-2605-18908: Yinbo Yu and six colleagues offer a data-free backdoor detector probing only a model's prediction head with random latent inputs. Backdoored models concentrate responses on the target class under such probes, a unified signature avoiding trigger reconstruction. HTell builds architecture-aware probes, feeds them into the head, and reads class response statistics. On a benchmark of over six thousand backdoored and seven hundred clean models it reaches 99.03 percent true positives at 2.11 percent false positives. It runs over thirty thousand times faster than gradient-based rivals.
arxiv-2605-19808: Nawani and Semino introduce nb-UiO-FF, a partly reactive force field for UiO-66, the most studied metal organic framework, prized for tolerating many point defects. Node ligand reactivity enters through a Morse potential plus dummy atoms mimicking the uneven charge of zirconium nodes. The field reproduces structures of UiO-66 and UiO-67 and stability with defects, plus behaviour when filled with dimethylformamide or ethanol. Defect and binding energies sit near density functional values. Molecular dynamics then traces early solvothermal node ligand binding, including UiO-66 like motifs.
arxiv-2605-19908: Kulumba and colleagues ask where authorship signal emerges in encoders. Models tuned with the same encoder, data and loss can differ four fold by scoring mechanism alone. Style features like word length, punctuation density and function word frequency are readable at every layer, including in a control encoder, so readability does not explain the gap. Causal intervention shows the scorer decides where signal consolidates: mean pooling forces early consolidation, while late interaction defers it. Gradient structure and training dynamics confirm distinct learning trajectories per scorer.
arxiv-2605-20508: Aritra Banerjee and Sara Algeri tackle spotting a faint new signal against a poorly known background. They argue that mapping that background in full is not needed. Estimating a single number, called the compensator, is enough to absorb the background ignorance. That number also carries its doubt into the signal estimate and sets how cautious the answer is.
arxiv-2605-20608: Binghan Wu and five colleagues propose HANA, a hierarchical agent-native design for highly autonomous networks. Current operations rely on rigid scripts that struggle with unusual conditions. Their framework pairs a dual-driven orchestrator with specialist executive agents and a shared public memory for domain knowledge. Agent self-awareness links strategic planning with fast fault recovery, and a 5G core trial cut mean repair time by 86 percent while holding throughput under congestion.
arxiv-2605-20708: Chao Xu and eleven colleagues rethink how information flows across layers in diffusion transformers, the backbone of modern visual generation. The residual stream, which carries built-up information across layers, was inherited unchanged from the first transformer. Their analysis along depth and denoising time finds three symptoms: growing forward magnitudes, sharp backward gradient decay, and block-wise redundancy. They propose diffusion-adaptive routing, a drop-in replacement that aggregates past sublayer outputs in a learned, time-aware way.
arxiv-2605-21008: Zhihan Guo and ten colleagues survey audio reasoning in multimodal foundation models. Reasoning defines modern foundation models, yet its growth in audio remains limited. Audio poses distinct challenges from text and vision, being continuous, temporally dense, and rich in linguistic, paralinguistic, and environmental information at several time scales. Audio models must therefore match acoustic signals with the distinct semantic space of large language models while preserving fine-grained detail.
arxiv-2605-21108: John-Joseph Brady, Nikolas Nüsken, and Yunpeng Li speed up training for deep state space models, which track hidden states behind noisy time-series data. Older methods train in sequence and scale poorly on modern hardware. Their parallel variational Monte Carlo method bridges auto-encoding and sequential Monte Carlo approaches. On benchmarks it matches or beats the best prior results while training ten times faster than the fastest rival Monte Carlo method.
arxiv-2605-21408: Kexin Xie, Ryan Lekivetz, and Xinwei Deng study nearly balanced two-level designs with treatment cardinality constraints, applied to prompt engineering. Modern designs often limit the number of included factors per treatment, common in simulation, AI tuning, and system verification. They study two-level designs where the design matrix has constant row sums equal to k, closely related to balanced incomplete block designs, though exact block structure is unavailable for many practical combinations.
arxiv-2605-21508: Julio César Jaramillo Quiceno constructs metric-deformed gauge theories based on a q-Dirac operator. The operator arises from a deformed D'Alembertian, with parameter q tied to metric values. Making metric values spacetime-dependent fields, he defines a deformed derivative. The field strength gains new terms from inverse square-root slopes, zero for constant metrics. He writes gauge-invariant actions for deformed Yang-Mills theory and lightly coupled matter.
arxiv-2605-22108: Yuxiao Che and Rikkert Frederix present MAcNLOPS matching for ZZ pair production at the Large Hadron Collider, in a MadGraph5_aMC@NLO plus Pythia8 setup. From a standard MC@NLO event sample, negative H events are removed and compensated by a veto on the first shower emission of S events. Validation against MC@NLO for radiation-sensitive and diboson observables shows agreement except for a small power-suppressed part at very low transverse momentum. The method removes all negative H weights at negligible extra cost, leaving negative S weights unchanged.
arxiv-2605-22208: Kailin Zhuang and co-authors present EvoIR-Agent, a self-evolving image restoration agent driven by experience. Multimodal agents pick tools and removal orders flexibly, yet zero-shot planning fails without experience. Training-based methods embed experience but cannot handle new tools, while training-free methods store it explicitly yet still waste trials. EvoIR-Agent formulates experience components, builds a hierarchical pool for coarse-to-fine guidance. It leads on full-reference metrics with a Pareto-optimal balance, running 61 percent more efficiently than state-of-the-art methods.
arxiv-2605-22408: Signing studies deterministic reiterated homogenisation of non-stationary Navier-Stokes type equations. The setting is fixed domains whose coefficients vary rapidly and periodically. One convergence theorem is proved, plus a corrector result. From these, the author derives a large-scale model. The work thus passes from fine-scale varying coefficients to a large-scale model through fresh homogenisation. The large-scale model captures the mean behaviour.
arxiv-2605-22708: Džavoronok studies the Manickam Miklós Singhi property for graphs and hypergraphs, building new regular graph families with the property from the two uniform case. He then maps regimes where Erdős Rényi random graphs gain the property with high probability. Finally, he extends a matching based sufficient condition to higher uniformities through pseudo matchings and adds a blowout construction that lifts lower uniformity examples into higher uniformity hypergraphs with the property. The paper thus broadens both the examples and the random theory of the property.
arxiv-2605-22908: Cônsoli, Vijayvargia, and Erten propose layered quantum spin-orbital models for studying fractionalization and unconventional symmetry breaking together. Piling N layers of a square-lattice system with Kitaev-type interactions, coupled by Ising interactions, they map the low-energy physics onto N-component Fermi Hubbard models on a pi-flux lattice. Near equal all-to-all interlayer coupling an emergent SU(N) symmetry appears. For N equal to 3, mean-field theory reveals intertwined orders and magnetic fragmentation.
arxiv-2605-23108: Bansal constrains AI code reviewers through philosophical dispositions, style lenses from schools such as Pyrrhonist Skepticism, Navya-Nyaya logic, Diogenes' Cynicism, and Confucian ethics. Expert reviewer agents give uniform findings no matter the analysis type needed. Each lens is defined by what it refuses to do, carries a self-monitoring failure mode, and is run in sequence by role rules. On 50 pull requests across 7 repos, the system matched human readers 46 percent. It found unique findings at 75 percent. It gave no author false positives among 601 findings.
arxiv-2605-23608: Rizzi and Piazza study the optimal transport problem within linear square optimal control systems. They establish soundness of the Monge problem and analyze regularity of the final optimal transport map, extending results for costs at or above zero. They also study displacement interpolation of measures and derive general interpolation inequalities for entropy functionals. The analysis is motivated by these systems as natural model spaces for comparison theory in sub-Riemannian geometry.
arxiv-2605-23708: Nauck and colleagues propose learning stability landscapes for synchronization networks, beyond scalar per-node indices. They pioneer graph-to-image prediction: learning image-like landscapes as per-node targets from topology. They release two datasets of 10,000 graphs at 20 and 100 nodes with per-node labels, from an oscillator model of power grid synchronization. A graph neural network encodes topology and a decoder renders per-node images, learned end-to-end, generalizing to realistic power grids. Stability landscapes prove learnable from topology, opening avenues beyond scalar indices in biology and power grids.
arxiv-2605-23808: Guzman presents AGDES, a tool for Automatic Generation of Dependent Event Sequences. Each event sequence is either the output word of a deterministic finite automaton. It can also be the output word of a deterministic finite automaton called transducer, which reads events from one or more input sequences and gives an output sequence.
arxiv-2605-23908: Sam Earle and colleagues replay Picbreeder, the collaborative human experiment where users bred images by evolving small neural networks, with frontier vision language models in place of people. Clear qualitative gaps separate model output from the human baseline. The team measures those gaps through lineage complexity and visual and semantic novelty. Probing causes, they test added exploratory noise, diversity between agents, and narrative memory of past choices. They hunt the ingredients that let unguided search stay open ended and fruitful.
arxiv-2605-24208: Hathaway, Kagan, and Jones study self-assignment in emergency departments, where physicians pick cases from a shared pool. Across five departments and nearly one and a half million visits, batching, taking several patients at once, proves common and tracks longer stays, even after accounting for acuity, physician effects, and congestion. A queueing model plus experiments with 203 workers and 73 physicians show batching persists even when it cuts the batcher's own payoff. The authors call this the personal productivity bias and suggest redesigning the assignment interface rather than pay alone.
arxiv-2605-24608: Gustavo Angulo develops a lattice-theoretic framework for deep convolutional architectures, including CNNs, ResNets, and encoder-decoder nets like UNet. The main tool is MMBB representation theory for translation-invariant maps, applied layer by layer. The key finding recasts the standard pipeline as a cross-lattice device. Convolution acts as erosion, ReLU as a lattice-join closing, and max-pooling as dilation, composing into a morphological opening in neither lattice. Since the composed layer is not idempotent, depth adds genuine power. Three idempotent opening designs are identified and characterized.
arxiv-2605-25108: Sergey A. Denisov shows that a nonlinear Fourier transform for the group SU(1,1) can fail to converge at individual points, even for square-summable coefficients. That failure overturns the classical pointwise behavior expected for polynomials orthogonal on the unit circle, at least for measures in the Szegő class. The paper also singles out special cases where pointwise convergence does survive. It draws a sharper line between the settings where the transform behaves and where it breaks down.
arxiv-2605-25308: Xiaoyang Lyu and colleagues steady video models' frame-by-frame 3D geometry from one moving camera. Strong single-image models drift badly over time, as their depth scale and shift wander with internal feature statistics. The team traces the fault to those statistics and adds Dynamic Feature Normalization, a small module that steadies them in streaming video. Tuning only that module, about 2 percent of extra weights, with the backbone frozen preserves single-image accuracy. Across four benchmarks it removes temporal artifacts and beats prior streaming methods by up to 14 percent.
arxiv-2605-25508: Qishi Zhan, Liang He, Minxuan Hu, and Ziheng Chen study where pruning damage lands at high sparsity and whether repair can recover it. They introduce Relative Repairability, a diagnostic weighing raw damage from pruning with residual damage after variance-matching repair, using only unlabeled tuning data. On CIFAR10 and CIFAR100 with ResNet and VGG variants, it is not always dominant. It helps most near a recoverability transition, where standard priors lose reliability but recovery has not collapsed. There it beats ERK mid-band and LAMP near the top.
arxiv-2605-25708: Mandalika tackles task-incremental learning across visual domains without forgetting earlier ones or knowing the task at test time. Existing methods route tasks from visual features alone, leaving CLIP text space unused. His CMAP routes tasks in text space with frozen CLIP prototypes, by cosine similarity. It adds multi-prototype confidence and cross-modal gating for the text encoder. On MTIL, CMAP beats the prior best by 5, nearly 4 and 3 points on Transfer, Average and Last. It needs two and a half million trainable parameters and no outside data.
arxiv-2605-26108: Huang and five colleagues align few-step image generators with human taste by reward-tilted distribution matching. Few-step diffusion models run fast, yet matching taste stays hard. Their RTDMD framework splits the task in two. First, ambient-consistent matching works step by step, with a steadying term tracking the shifting generator. Second, joint optimisation pairs matching with reward gains. The split follows from closing in on a reward-tilted teacher distribution, which breaks into those two terms. Results improve taste match without slowing few-step sampling.
arxiv-2605-26408: Valentina V. Kuskova, Dmitry Zaytsev, and Michael Coppedge argue that boiling each causal link to one number discards the real finding. Nonlinear models learn an effect that shifts with regime and size, so the trio formalize function-valued causal influence for additive, splittable designs. With Neural Additive Vector Autoregression, they estimate response curves via Individual Conditional Expectation plots. Synthetic trials show edges with matching scalar scores can rise, jump at a threshold, level off, or flip sign. A democratic-development study finds regime-specific patterns that score views miss.
arxiv-2605-26708: Meiting Song and eleven others demonstrate a hybrid laser that steadies light for atomic clocks and quantum tools. Fast state control exposes noise at high offset frequencies that cavity locks alone cannot tame, while miniaturization also matters. Their design pairs a cryogenic silicon cavity's stability with an integrated Brillouin laser's high-frequency quieting. Noise falls across more than seven decades. It reaches sub-hertz linewidth, confirmed by sub-hertz spectroscopy on a strontium lattice clock, with record-low noise at 698 nanometers.
arxiv-2605-26908: Luttermann, Möller, and Gehrke revisit the basics of spotting commutative factors in factor graphs. A commutative factor is one whose outputs stay the same when inputs to a subset of arguments are permuted. They show the leading algorithm rests on a theorem mistakenly read as sufficient when it only gives a necessary condition, so the algorithm can return wrong results. They prove a corrected necessary test, present a fixed algorithm that keeps its speed and stays correct, and add a second algorithm with tighter worst-case bounds.
arxiv-2605-27008: Bénard and Zhang study a walk on a manifold driven by a measure on twice-differentiable diffeomorphisms. When the measure has support, meets gap and pinching, and sits weakly close to a volume-preserving measure, the manifold carries a unique atomless measure. This measure has Frostman dimension and equals volume in the volume-preserving setting. Every n-step distribution converges to that measure unless its start lies in an invariant set. It covers expanding walks on surfaces, Zariski-dense walks on tori and quotients, and sphere walks.
arxiv-2605-27108: Vigna-Brummer and four co-authors quantify liquid flow between a soap film and a vertical meniscus. This coupling governs film drainage and stability and sets bubble and foam lifetimes. Flux per contact length follows a known scaling law in film height and meniscus radius, but its dimensionless factor resisted measurement because interface flows are uneven. By placing a solid plate into a soap film and mixing tests, models, and theory, the authors measure the flux coefficient three ways and find it constant across the range.
arxiv-2605-27308: Pranav Jain and colleagues present PINNsur, a mesh-free way to solve partial differential equations on curved surfaces. The method learns surface normals with a neural field, then projects operators from three-dimensional space onto the surface. It suits every orientable surface, and the authors add a simple empirical test of whether such solvers converge.
arxiv-2605-27708: Bokang Hou and colleagues test perturbative and mixed quantum-classical methods for hot exciton cooling in semiconductor nanocrystals against full quantum runs. Bare cadmium selenide shows ultrafast early decay then slower cooling, while the core-shell system runs mostly on the slower component. The mapping approach to surface hopping gives the most consistent match with test dynamics and equilibrium populations.
arxiv-2605-27808: Wang and colleagues fix a blind spot in shrinking speech-recognition models for deployment: rare words such as names and numbers get little weight during compression. Their label-free method, TARQ, rebalances calibration toward the vocabulary's tail and corrects the leftover error consistently. Across eight model backbones and six datasets it improved rare-word accuracy without harming overall word error.
arxiv-2605-28008: Matsutani and colleagues study when short reasoning traces help or hurt model training. They sort chain-of-thought into explicit, composed, and implicit forms and test each with care. Merged traces gain most from repeats, silent traces drift toward rote recall, and coarse traces need more data. Later reward training, they show, unpacks shrunken steps.
arxiv-2605-28408: Konstantin Kovalyov proposes a natural axiomatization of Büchi arithmetic. It covers natural numbers with sums, plus a function giving the greatest power of a fixed base that goes into each number. He reads numbers as sets with repeats via base expansions, using a set-building schema kept to bounded claims. Full proof comes from the Büchi-Bruyère theorem, tying what can be defined here to spotting by finite machines. The theory can be settled by machine, and a structure is automatic when it fits inside it.
arxiv-2605-28608: Vernon Barger reads the B-lattice flavor framework as a compositeness hierarchy for fermion generations. All three generations are elementary chiral fields, while third-generation Yukawa couplings are undressed, while lighter generations gain couplings through chains of spin-zero subconstituents counted by a Z9 discrete gauge symmetry. The lattice yields mixing parameterizations, a seesaw benchmark near 51 millielectronvolts, an axion mass window near 7 to 12 microelectronvolts, and a tan-beta prediction near 10 to 16, all from two parameters. Generation-dependent Peccei-Quinn charges lift the axion-photon coupling from suppression.
arxiv-2605-28808: Andrea Celotto and eight colleagues present in situ microwave noise metrology for nonlinear cryogenic quantum devices. Active quantum devices work in cryo-electronic setups, and all figures of merit must be expressed at their port planes. Their setup swaps in a tunable noise source for the device under test, since placing the source at the device input affects whether calibration splits from device traits. It combines Planck readings with a varying heat stage and short-open-load-reciprocal scattering calibration, referring noise and signal values to the same reference planes.
arxiv-2605-28908: Jacob Erickson argues conversational agents should face fiduciary care, like the duty a lawyer, surgeon, or investment manager owes a client. Conversational agents now sit inside users' most private lives, with access to troves of sensitive user data. Much AI alignment literature focuses on matching user goals with agents acting for them. But Erickson says this may overlook a new normative baseline. As systems designed to feel and interact human-like, agents deserve matching care for their capabilities. And fiduciary design could unify trust and accountability.
arxiv-2605-29108: Yujia Guo and colleagues build an expert-augmented scoring framework for multi-step synthetic route evaluation. A DeepSets model trained on tree edit distance between reference and machine-generated routes is fine-tuned with expert evaluations, yielding quantitative scores and qualitative categories of Good, Plausible, and Bad. The system reaches correlations above three-quarters for category prediction and about 60 percent top-1 ranking accuracy for score prediction. That beats the previous baseline near 18 percent, showing expert knowledge plus machine learning beats proxy patent routes.
arxiv-2605-29208: Gary Wolfman describes libhmm, a C++20 library for hidden Markov model estimation. It fills two gaps: no zero-dependency C++ HMM library, and moment approximations in the Baum-Welch emission M-step. The library gives correct maximum likelihood estimators for sixteen scalar emissions. These include ECME for Student-t, Newton-Raphson for four more, and von Mises for circular data. Forward-backward and Viterbi calculations run in log-space, with SIMD acceleration. Version 4 adds multivariate observations with three emission families, plus Python bindings, and benchmarks on seven datasets.
arxiv-2605-29708: Zhibo Zhang and four colleagues test a common hunch about safety in mixture-of-experts language models and find it wanting. Routing, they show, tracks topic more than safety, and safety conduct can shift with scant change to the model's own routing path. Their probe tool, RASET, hunts safety-critical experts with a contrast test, then tunes just those experts while leaving routing intact. Across five open-weight expert models it reached a high-quality bypass rate near one half, far above the best rival method.
arxiv-2605-29808: Damian L. Corzi and seven colleagues build high-resolution X-ray microtomography on cheap commercial CMOS sensors as direct detectors. A microfocus source in cone-beam layout yields absorption contrast from the sensor's fine detail and phase contrast from shifting the object-to-sensor gap. A flat-field correction counters radiation wear during long runs. Voxel sizes reach a few microns, with detail down to about ten microns in magnified phase mode and about twenty otherwise. Phase contrast reveals soft tissue edges that absorption contrast alone struggles to show.
arxiv-2605-30208: Chris Adams and 30 co-authors describe RADAR, Meta's system for automating low-risk code review. Code per human-landed diff more than doubled, while timely review shares fell. RADAR classifies diffs by authorship and source, applies gates, heuristics, a Diff Risk Score, LLM review and validation before landing qualifying changes. Across 535 thousand diffs, relaxing the threshold raised the pass rate, reverts ran at a third of non-RADAR diffs, incidents at one in fifty, and close time fell sharply. Risk-aware automation can cut review bottlenecks without compromising production safety.
arxiv-2605-30308: Mohit Verma and five co-authors describe a metadata-first approach repurposing write-time table statistics for data quality observability without scanning data. Modern formats such as Apache Iceberg record timestamps, counts, value bounds, and null counts when writing. At LinkedIn across 200,000+ Iceberg tables, this satisfies about 60% of quality rules at zero compute cost and cuts profiling use by around 50%. Counters and sketches can raise coverage to close to 90% of rules, and they propose storing sketches in Puffin sidecar files.
arxiv-2605-30508: Aaron Kim and six co-authors present the ARISTO Hand, a tendon-driven robot hand joining active distal hyperextension to a hybrid fingertip-sensing design. Active hyperextension enables controlled fingertip engagement past standard flexion limits, lifting pull-out force nearly threefold for object thicknesses of 1 to 20 millimeters. The rigid nail-mounted sensor gives reliable force readings during edge contacts, where estimation weakens near kinematic singularities. They validate the design through a multi-stage SD card extraction and insertion task.
arxiv-2605-30608: Suresh and colleagues bridge spoken words and co-speech gestures with semantic motion anchors, plain labels capturing a gesture's form and communicative intent. Direct matching of transcripts with flowing motion embeddings stresses low-level movement too much and misses what gestures mean. Their method cuts three-dimensional gestures into body-hand units, writes them up as set notes, and grounds them in the transcript for extra contrast training. On BEAT2, text-to-gesture search lifts clearly over a direct baseline, and users prefer the retrieved gestures for new ones.
arxiv-2605-30708: Cool and colleagues study behavior in Lenia, a system of emergent patterns in active media, by blinding creatures to parts of their world. Beside infotaxis, the usual drive toward rich regions, they find beings avoid information-free regions, a behavior they term agnosiophobia. Mapping each being's sense for set occlusions and reading results through dynamic systems, they observe beings changing heading to preserve their morphology. The work begins a roadmap for understanding how emergent agents' habits mix with the informational, not only solid, topography of their world.
arxiv-2605-30808: Gao and Yang propose DPPrefSyn, generating private synthetic preference data for large language model alignment. Post-training on real preference data raises privacy concerns, as datasets contain sensitive prompts and judgments. DPPrefSyn is grounded in the Bradley-Terry model and pairwise preference geometry. It first learns a preference model from private data, then uses it with public prompts to synthesize data. It exploits shared linear structure across reward models to capture varied preferences, and uses private component analysis. Tests show DPPrefSyn achieves competitive alignment performance under strong privacy guarantees.
arxiv-2605-30908: Fuller, Español, and Kilmer derive bounds on the Kronecker rank of block-structured matrices. Building on a tensor framework, they show the rank equals the span dimension of blocks, and likewise for a permuted matrix whose structures swap. They prove this equality by a direct dimension argument and by an explicit isomorphism to a tensor unfolding. The results turn patterns like Toeplitz, Hankel, banded, or sparse forms into computable upper bounds, and link sparsity in one matrix to sparsity in the other. Numeric tests confirm the theory.
arxiv-2605-31008: Van Kempen and colleagues study galaxy change versus place in the nearby cosmos, against a baseline volume to the Nexus structure around Abell 4038. They measure quenched fraction and star making rate versus stellar mass and group halo mass; quenched fraction rises with stellar mass, with extra halo link for group systems. The Nexus differs clearly, matching varied infall past and early handling. Star-forming galaxies' specific star formation rate falls strongly with stellar mass, with extra suppression in group halos.
arxiv-2605-31108: Swinnen and Tuytelaars give a stepwise learning approach tuning models to shifting data, letting models forget and using it. Their model mixes a task head with a masked coder head, learning LoRA units. Each unit fits its domain, causing loss on other domains. At use, test-time training finds which units match the input, so the model recalls the domain. The scheme suits video streams, where samples are linked and shifts are gradual. They show the method on action tagging and meaning splitting.
arxiv-2605-31308: Nian and colleagues turn agent trajectories into shared decision landscapes with TraceGraph. Benchmarks record rich rollouts yet score them by pass rate alone, hiding where models diverge. For each task, TraceGraph graphs states seen in pooled rollouts before model identity enters, then overlays productive cores and trap regions. Rollouts are summarised by access, trap exposure and repair. A recovery pipeline aware of traps, built for SWE-bench, lifts resolved rates on fired states, showing how failure regions can guide improvement.
arxiv-2605-31508: Zhao and colleagues build temporal consistency into video object-centric learning as model design rather than an added loss. Slots track objects across frames, and the standard Slot-Slot Contrastive loss enforces their match but needs one-to-one correspondence across frames. The team instead splits slot channels into static and dynamic parts and rebuilds target features by fusing static channels from current slots with dynamic channels from target slots. Consistency then emerges from plain reconstruction error alone, with gains on video object discovery and recognition.

arxiv-2606-04308:
Sophia Liu and co-authors argue in 2026 for creative reading, a different goal for the software now being built to help people read. Current reading aids treat reading as information transfer, summarizing and filtering on the reader's behalf, which quietly takes over the interpretive work itself.

Drawing on literary theory, studies of scholarly sensemaking, and creativity support research, they propose tools that help readers produce their own readings and grow as readers in the process. Their provocation-oriented design space values keeping several readings alive rather than collapsing a text into one digest. For scholarship especially, they note, deciding what a text implies is the work, not a chore before it. The paper is a position piece inviting designers to build for transformation, not just throughput.
arxiv-2606-05008:
Jie Huang and co-authors present M3Eval in this 2026 arXiv paper, a benchmark for testing memory in multi-modal models that watch long videos. Existing benchmarks stress perception and reasoning, but they rarely check what a model retains, how faithfully it keeps information, or how memory holds up under interference. M3Eval builds its tasks from cognitive psychology so that separate aspects of memory can be isolated and measured.

Running representative multi-modal models through the benchmark exposed consistent weaknesses. Models struggled to keep separate representations when processing parallel video streams, and their interference patterns differed substantially from those seen in human memory. They also grounded remembered sources more reliably in space than in time, and showed limited symbolic memory. The authors offer the benchmark as a resource for designing stronger memory mechanisms.
arxiv-2606-05108:
Mete Şeref Ahunbay, Weiqiang Zheng, and Tao Lin analyze learning dynamics in first-price auctions in this 2026 arXiv paper. In a first-price auction the highest bidder wins and pays their own bid, and in markets like online advertising the bidders are algorithms that adjust bids across rounds. The authors ask what emerges when every buyer in a discretized, complete-information first-price auction learns by gradient ascent.

They show that, in time average, the outcome is almost the efficient outcome of the second-price auction, where the winner pays the second-highest bid. The proof brings two innovations to the analysis of gradient ascent in games. First, a potential-function argument shows some strategies vanish, and under stated conditions it can be applied repeatedly, like iteratively eliminating dominated strategies. Second, a class of cubic potential functions classifies quadratic strategy modifications against which gradient ascent incurs no regret.
arxiv-2606-05308:
Abhishek Divekar presents PRECISE in this 2026 arXiv extended abstract, a framework for statistically reliable evaluation of ranking systems that mixes human labels with model judgments. Human evaluation is expensive, so small labeled sets give wide confidence intervals, while raw model-as-judge scores carry biases.

Prediction-powered inference offers a middle path: use a gold set to measure and correct the judge's bias, yielding estimates that are unbiased whatever the judge's error profile. PRECISE extends that idea to hierarchical metrics like Precision@K, where annotations are per document but the metric is per query. On the ESCI benchmark, augmenting just 30 human annotations with Claude 3 Sonnet judgments reduced the standard error of Precision@4 estimates from 4.45 to 3.50, a 21 percent relative reduction. In a production system the framework picked the best of three system variants from 100 human labels and two hours of annotation, and a later A/B test confirmed the ranking.
arxiv-2606-05608:
Cao argues that AI agents change what software itself is in a 2026 arXiv paper. For fifty years, engineers wrote decision logic into fixed code by hand. In agentic software, a large language model does the reasoning at run time. Code becomes a tool the agent writes, uses, and throws away. Cao draws a sharp line between the two forms: fixed logic carried by code versus logic made fresh by the agent.

The paper traces three eras of delivery, from licensed software to cloud services to agents as a service. Each era shifted more work away from the user, and the agent era shifts decision making itself. Cao names a new field, Agentic Engineering, centered on agent systems rather than source code. Benchmark evidence shows both the power and the current limits of the approach. A four-stage road map toward self-evolving agent systems closes the argument.
arxiv-2606-05808:
Graham revisits the link between black hole mass and stellar speed spread in a 2026 arXiv paper. The famous relation ties a galaxy's central black hole to how fast its stars swirl. Graham argues one line for all galaxies hides split histories. His sample holds one hundred thirty-seven galaxies with measured bar strengths and careful shape classes. A new Bayesian regression code, scope, handles lopsided errors and treats both axes symmetrically.

Primeval dust-poor S0 galaxies follow a shallow slope: mass grows with speed spread raised to a power near three. Massive ellipticals, built by dry mergers that erase discs, follow a far steeper slope near eight. Gas-rich and gas-poor assembly paths split cleanly in the diagram. Using one blended relation under-predicts the heaviest black holes. Those giants drive the nanohertz gravitational wave background, so forecasts shift with them. Morphology, Graham concludes, belongs inside the scaling law.
arxiv-2606-06308:
Yongqiang Yu, Tian Huang, and Yipeng Yang calibrate cheap motion sensors with pure linear algebra in this 2026 arXiv paper. Triaxial MEMS accelerometers, the tiny chips that sense acceleration in phones and robots, suffer from bias, scale errors, and axes that are not quite perpendicular. Standard calibration needs costly reference rigs or slow nonlinear optimization. Their method needs only a platform reporting its own orientation, like a turntable, robot arm, or inertial unit.

The approach packs all sensor errors into one combined error matrix. Bias and the gravity vector are estimated jointly, which quietly absorbs any platform misalignment. A matrix decomposition then splits out the scale, skew, and rotation corrections. The whole problem becomes a constrained least squares solved in closed form, with no iteration. Five oriented measurements suffice in principle, and a recursive version recalibrates online. On a robot mounted sensor, precision from twenty four orientations rivaled full self calibration.
arxiv-2606-06708:
Web browsing agents drown in their own observations. Gaur and Lane diagnose that problem in this 2026 arXiv paper, a position piece rather than an experiment report. At every step, a typical agent swallows the full page structure, often tens of thousands of tokens, and its reasoning slowly degrades long before a long task ends.

Their fix, called Signal-Driven Observation, splits looking from acting. A separate helper call reads the whole page but returns only the parts that matter for the task, and a light signal detector decides when a fresh look is needed at all. Signals include a changed web address, newly visible buttons, a failed action, or an outside browser event. The authors list open problems the design raises, including errors that leave no structural trace, and they urge the field to treat how agents observe as a core design choice.
arxiv-2606-06808:
Nanopore sequencers read DNA by watching electrical levels shift as a strand slides through a tiny hole, but the strand moves unevenly. McBain and Viterbo analyze how much information survives that messiness in this 2026 arXiv paper. Each base may produce a random number of samples, a duplication effect, and several bases sit in the pore at once, smearing the signal between neighbors.

The authors split the channel's information rate into two readable parts. One comes from the memory of a cleaner auxiliary channel. The other is a penalty for not knowing where each base's samples begin and end. They study the penalty with a soft alignment tool from time series analysis, proving strong stability results for it. A final lower bound ties the rate to how far the signal jumps between levels. That gives a geometric way to compare pore designs. The bound stays tight at real noise levels.
arxiv-2606-07108:
Reasoning models often keep thinking long after the answer is settled, wasting compute on easy problems. Tengyao Tu and co-authors give them a sense of difficulty in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their framework, DyCon, controls reasoning depth dynamically without any retraining. The key discovery is that problem difficulty changes during the reasoning itself. That difficulty is written plainly in the model's step level embeddings.

DyCon reads those embeddings as reasoning unfolds. When the remaining problem looks easy, it trims redundant steps. When difficulty rises, it lets the model keep working. Twelve benchmarks covered math reasoning, general questions, and coding. Models from four to thirty two billion parameters all benefited. Redundant reasoning steps dropped significantly while accuracy held steady. Earlier fixes relied on static difficulty guesses or task specific training. Overthinking becomes a measurable signal, not a fixed budget choice.
arxiv-2606-07408:
Mateusz Gienieczko, Muñoz, Murlak, and Paperman show how to answer queries over streaming documents as early as possible, in this 2026 arXiv paper. JSON or XML files cannot be parsed into memory, so systems process them as streams. Earliest answering returns each node the moment it is guaranteed an answer, regardless of how the document continues, and discards nodes the moment they cannot qualify. Path-only queries are easy, but practical languages support filters drawing on information anywhere in the document.

Filters force nodes to wait in memory until content settles their fate. The authors prove this waiting can be managed for all unary queries in monadic second-order logic, a language for tree properties. Their method gives constant update time per streamed element, provided answers are delivered through an iterator rather than one by one. The result pins down which query languages admit earliest streaming evaluation at bounded cost.
arxiv-2606-07608:
Akeret fine-tunes a speech recognizer for Swiss German and questions whether the field's published scores mean anything, in this 2026 arXiv study. Swiss German dialects differ from the Standard German of broadcast subtitles, which served as training labels across nearly 1,400 hours of speech. 16 training runs compared adapter tuning against fine-tuning of the largest Whisper model, investigating hallucination causes. The best model scored a word error rate near 26 percent on a held-out test of all dialects.

A harmonized analysis separating real errors from valid stylistic variation cut the content error rate to under 14 percent. Bias correction suggested the rate is a third of the headline number. Worse, Akeret shows benchmark contamination: a model self-trained on the test set, with no Swiss German training, beats every published system on it. Reported state-of-the-art results are inflated, and the paper's disjoint baseline is offered as the trustworthy reference.
arxiv-2606-07908:
Martnishn reports that controlling each layer's derivatives makes networks generalise more steadily, in this 2026 arXiv paper, the series' second. The networks, built on his ChainzRule design, use cubic polynomial layers plus a penalty, DREG, that watches each layer's Jacobian, the matrix of local sensitivities, during the forward pass. This paper asks whether the design holds up across data regimes.

On the Pima Diabetes dataset, the networks performed strongly with little data and kept an accuracy advantage from five percent to full data. Their gradient tail ratios stayed near one point zero one, against up to one point zero nine for ReLU networks, a sign of stable gradients. On the SST-5 sentiment benchmark the method matched or beat rivals in frozen-embedding and BERT fine-tuning regimes, outperforming prior BERT baselines despite much less data. He argues derivative control builds in a bias toward smooth representations that travels across domains.
arxiv-2606-08108:
Mehdi Ouslim builds a fast stand-in for the optics simulations used to design Bragg reflectors, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A distributed Bragg reflector stacks alternating layers of gallium arsenide and aluminium gallium arsenide to reflect a chosen wavelength band. Computing its reflectance spectrum with the transfer matrix method is accurate but slow when designers want to sweep layer counts and thicknesses.

Ouslim generated fifteen hundred transfer-matrix simulations across the design space. Each spectrum was compressed with principal component analysis, keeping twenty-six components with over ninety-nine point nine percent of the variance. A Gaussian process surrogate was fitted per component. On held-out tests it was about seventy times faster than the full simulation, answering in about four milliseconds. Its accuracy trails a random forest baseline, but its uncertainty bands are trustworthy: the ninety-five percent band covered about ninety-nine percent of test residuals.
arxiv-2606-08308:
Florindo and Misturini propose a way to predict how well a neural network will perform on unseen data, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Generalization, that performance on new examples, is usually estimated with held-out test data, and predicting it without such data is a fundamental challenge. Training follows heavy-tailed, non-Gaussian dynamics, meaning occasional very large jumps that trace complex paths through weight space. The authors measure that complexity through the Fourier fractal dimension of the weight variations.

Their measure comes from analyzing the underlying stochastic equations in the frequency domain, capturing the learning process's geometric complexity in one metric. The authors also add a custom Fourier-based optimizer that controls this fractal dimension during training. In evaluations on the CIFAR-10, SVHN, and MNIST image datasets, the measure matched actual generalization closely.
arxiv-2606-08408:
Diandaru, Hanif, and Al Ghiffari teach diffusion language models to rewrite text in place, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Activation steering, nudging a model's internal activations, was developed for ordinary autoregressive models. Diffusion language models generate text differently, by refining a whole sequence at once. That creates a new problem: modifying an existing text in place so it expresses a different concept while staying recognizably the same text. Their mechanism, TimpaTeks, performs this in-place modification by steering the model's activations as it refines the text.

Experiments cover sentiment changes on movie reviews from the IMDB dataset and a built dataset. The authors report that TimpaTeks makes in-place steering feasible, lowering sentence perplexity, a measure of fluency, while retaining the original sentence structure. It is also cheaper than prompt-based steering for such models.
arxiv-2606-08708:
Qiming Li and colleagues fix a credit assignment flaw in training vision-language models, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards improves the reasoning of large vision-language models. But existing methods rely on trajectory-level outcome rewards: the whole answer is judged, and every token receives the identical learning signal. That coarse assignment mismatches multimodal reasoning, where only a sparse subset of tokens is grounded in visual evidence. These pivotal perceptual tokens receive weak supervision.

Their method, PRPO, is a token-level framework that identifies and reinforces pivotal perceptual tokens in long reasoning trajectories. It introduces a robust visual dependency measure scoring how much each token depends on the image. Advantages are then reshaped at the token level, amplifying learning on those tokens.
arxiv-2606-08808:
Sossan surveys the jobs energy storage can do across a power grid, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Storage systems, above all batteries, can charge when electricity is plentiful and discharge when it is scarce. Because solar and wind output swings with the weather, grid operators need that flexibility at many time scales, from seconds-long frequency support to seasonal shifting. The paper builds a taxonomy of storage applications by grid level, ownership, and purpose.

An installation can stack several services, and stacking is what makes the investment pay. Sossan stresses that technology, size, and location must be chosen together, then managed through scheduling and real-time control. He discusses regulation with attention to Switzerland, where solar capacity may reach thirty gigawatts by 2040, nearly double the country's hydropower capacity. It closes with the Swiss STORE project, where four academic and thirteen industrial partners test storage across five application domains.
arxiv-2606-09108:
Walter and colleagues teach a neural network to answer, for any robot body, whether a pose is reachable, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Reachability underlies robot design, but workspaces are slow to compute, imprecise, or redone per morphology. Their system, RAM, is a morphology-conditioned implicit neural representation: given a body description and a target pose, it predicts reachability, accounting for self-collisions, on bodies it never saw. Training data came from forward kinematics, the cheap geometry of joint angles.

The training set is huge: 30 billion samples. RAM reached an F1 score of 86 percent, beating the baseline by 14 percent, with nanosecond answers, three orders of magnitude faster. Because the surrogate is differentiable, gradient-based optimization through it sped morphology design tenfold and trajectory optimization a hundredfold. The authors publish the dataset with the model. The pitch is a reusable reachability engine: a new robot's workspace comes almost free.
arxiv-2606-09308:
Tingfei Li and Runyu Chen study how energy moves between two quantum systems joined by a random coupling in this 2026 arXiv paper. When a hotter system touches a colder one, energy flows until both settle at the same temperature. Modelling that flow is hard because the interaction usually has a complicated, specific form.

The authors instead treat the coupling as a Gaussian random matrix, a table of random numbers with a bell-shaped distribution. That choice makes a systematic perturbation expansion possible, in which answers are built order by order in the coupling strength. In the limit of large systems, they derive explicit formulas for the energy transfer rate and the heat conductance up to second order. The formulas are worked out for four different densities of states, including Gaussian and semicircular profiles, and checked against numerical simulations at several coupling strengths.
arxiv-2606-09408:
Srravya Chandhiramowuli, Ding Wang, and Alex Taylor present an ethnographic study of data work organised around repair in this 2026 arXiv paper. Data work means the human labour of labelling, checking, and building the datasets that train artificial intelligence systems. It is usually low-paid and tightly controlled. The authors ask whether it could instead redress harms, and follow one initiative trying to do so.

The case is Tattle Civic Tech in India, which builds datasets for online safety systems together with people most affected by online harms. Contributors were paid an equal hourly rate roughly ten times the Indian industry norm, and leftover funds were shared out as extra compensation. The study traces real tensions over fair reward and collective control of the datasets. The authors argue that repairing data work means resetting accountability, putting affected people, not the datasets, at the centre.
arxiv-2606-09708:
Sabhyata Gupta and Luis Santos propose a cold-atom setup that mimics chiral magnetic dynamics in this 2026 arXiv paper. The chiral magnetic effect is a current that flows along a magnetic field when left- and right-handed particles are out of balance. It is prized as a probe of quark-gluon plasma, yet hard to compute head-on.

Their analog route uses ultracold atoms in an optical superlattice, a grid of light with two spacings. In a set limit, the massive Schwinger model maps onto the Rice-Mele model, a standard chain with staggered traits. The fermion mass and a topological angle become knobs on the lattice. Two quench plans then drive the vector current: one feeds chirality in, one lets it relax. Runs with true lab settings and noise showed a clear mass link in both plans. The signal held up under flaws.
arxiv-2606-09908:
Hussain and colleagues build a test for a neglected privacy risk in language models, in a 2026 arXiv paper on AI safety. The risk is interdependent privacy, where one person's data gets exposed through someone else's information, without consent. Earlier tests mostly cover risks to the individual user alone. Their benchmark, IDP-Bench, grounds shared-privacy scenarios in Contextual Integrity, which judges sharing by social norms.

The team evaluated eight open-source language models across three levels of privacy reasoning, scored by two model judges. Recognition of co-ownership was strong, with six of eight models scoring above ninety percent on that skill. Weaker spots persisted elsewhere: seven of eight models scored below seventy-four percent at spotting secondary subjects, the extra people affected by a disclosure. Judging whether sharing was appropriate also lagged, and smaller models declined further while prompt wording swung results, showing the skill is fragile.
arxiv-2606-10008:
Dillon extends a popular machine learning toolkit so brain-inspired networks can run on reconfigurable hardware, in a 2026 arXiv paper on computing. Spiking neural networks pass information as discrete spikes and keep internal state over time, suiting low-latency temporal tasks. Many scientific systems, though, rely on synchronous FPGAs, field-programmable chips, rather than special neuromorphic processors. His extension targets the hls4ml toolkit, which converts trained models into FPGA firmware through high-level synthesis.

The new workflow deploys spiking networks trained in PyTorch in a clock-driven way. A dense quantized network trained on the Heidelberg Spiking Digits dataset reached inference latencies of about thirty-four microseconds per input. Dillon validates the generated design through software comparisons, simulation, synthesis, and chip-tool reports. The work opens hls4ml to neuromorphic computing, streamlining how spiking models are optimized and deployed for real-time inference in experiments.
arxiv-2606-10208:
Qiu and his team review what happens when foundation models are put inside robots meant to care for patients and older adults, in a 2026 arXiv paper on healthcare robotics. Demand for care is growing rapidly as more people grow old, and foundation models promise more flexible talk and tailored help. Care settings, however, demand reliability, workflow compatibility, and accountable human oversight. This Perspective surveys the field across design features, user experience, and evidence for care-related outcomes, asking whether embodied systems translate technical advances into clinical impact.

Current systems most often use such models as conversational and reasoning layers inside voice-centered, socially assistive robots, while multi-sense grounding and physical autonomy remain limited. Tests report positive ease of use and interest, but failures persist, including made-up answers and chat breakdowns. The authors argue future work needs care-specific standards, autonomy with oversight, and genuine workflow fit.
arxiv-2606-10408:
Bartusek, Liu, and Malavolta work on succinct proofs for quantum claims in this 2026 arXiv paper in cryptography. A succinct argument lets a prover convince a verifier that a claim holds with very little communication, and QMA is the class of problems whose proofs are quantum states. Earlier QMA systems all rested on learning with errors, a highly structured hardness premise. This construction instead uses an oblivious state preparation protocol and collapsing hash functions, a quantum version of collision resistance.

The work proceeds in two steps. First comes a round-efficient argument needing only the state preparation assumption. Then a compiler compresses any long protocol so communication grows with the number of rounds, not the first message sizes. Combined, they give the first classically verifiable succinct argument for QMA without learning with errors. The compiler may also serve other quantum protocols.
arxiv-2606-10708:
Ihle, Zink, and Menth give a network traffic generator a pulse in this 2026 arXiv paper on computer networks. P4TG is an open-source, hardware-accelerated generator on Intel Tofino chips, producing up to 4 terabits per second. Like most generators it mainly emits constant bit rate, but real traffic surges: flash crowds spike, and attacks pulse on and off. The authors add a data-plane mechanism shaping time-varying patterns at full rate, covering burst-load and attack-like profiles.

They evaluate shaping accuracy across resolutions and periods, and show uses such as zero-loss throughput determination and buffer measurement. Microburst attacks overload UDP receivers and switch buffers and degrade TCP throughput on shared links, while staying invisible to rate monitoring, which sees only the tame average. The work lets engineers rehearse bursty failures, the attackers' favourite trick, at scale.
arxiv-2606-10908:
Vojtěch Staněk and colleagues find a training trick for voice deepfake detection in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their countermeasure for speaker-verification spoofing takes a reference recording of the claimed speaker as an extra input. Oddly, the trained model learns to ignore the reference almost entirely, yet training with it still helps.

They turn the quirk into a method, Reference-Augmented Training: the reference channel acts as a training-time regularizer, and at test time it can be replaced by zeros. The result is a state-of-the-art equal error rate of 2.57 percent on the ASVspoof 5 benchmark from a single detector, beating large ensembles.
arxiv-2606-11008:
Zhao, Aichelin, and Bratkovskaya question a shortcut in cluster physics in this 2026 arXiv paper. Models of light nuclei and hypernuclei formed in heavy-ion collisions often assume each cluster's wavefunction is a simple Gaussian bell matched to its measured size. Comparing true Schrödinger-equation solutions with those Gaussian stand-ins at the same root-mean-square radius, the authors find the real distributions are significantly broader.

The microscopic wavefunctions show pronounced non-Gaussian structure the shortcut erases. The team also explores production routes for four-body clusters with a phenomenological two-body force, offering a mechanism that may explain why models undercount such clusters against experiment. The moral: yields computed with Gaussian clusters rest on too narrow a shape.
arxiv-2606-11208:
