Hossain and three co-authors introduce BioDivergence in a 2026 arXiv paper, a benchmark for a subtle failure in biomedical analysis. Two study abstracts seem to contradict each other, yet both can be locally right: different cohorts, geographies, protocols, subtypes, or settings explain the divergence. Existing benchmarks force such pairs into flat entailment labels, overstating disagreement and hiding context that systems need.

BioDivergence scores four targets per claim pair: the conflict type from a six-class taxonomy, the axes from a thirteen-axis ontology, the dominant confounder, and a reconciliation explanation. The released benchmark holds 11,865 claim pairs across five domains, split with zero article overlap. That strictness matters: the fine-tuned reference model dropped about twelve F1 points on the article-disjoint version, exposing memorization. On the full 842-example test set, Mistral-7B-Instruct reached 0.5523 accuracy and 0.3894 contextual F1. Version 1.0 reliably supports two conflict classes and nine of thirteen axes.
arxiv-2606-11908:
L Moscadelli leads a seventeen-author team tracing winds from newborn massive stars in this 2026 arXiv paper, part of the POETS survey. Protostars accrete through disks, and magnetohydrodynamic disk winds, gas flung out along magnetic field lines, may remove the angular momentum blocking accretion. Earlier water maser observations hinted at such winds near two massive young stars.

Using the NOEMA interferometer and archived ALMA data, the team mapped the same tracers around both objects at scales of hundreds of astronomical units. Around the first star, emissions from sulphur-bearing molecules line up along the known radio jet, with a velocity gradient across it. Position-velocity plots of the sulphur monoxide lines match Keplerian rotation, the pattern of a rotating disk wind. The second, much more massive star shows consistent behaviour. Together with maser data at smaller scales, the results support disk winds as the common launching mechanism.
arxiv-2606-12008:
Arjen Simons and four colleagues make thematic maps adapt to any screen in this 2026 arXiv paper. Thematic maps colour or size regions, such as countries, by a statistic. They must keep each data-carrying element readable while keeping geographic context, and today they must also respond fluidly to phones, tablets and desktops. The authors introduce the first framework computing such responsive maps efficiently.

Its core is the layout guide, a combinatorial structure encoding each element's visual requirements plus the context as relative positions. Their map arranger algorithm converts any display container into a suitable layout guide. It is stable and consistent: a small change in container produces only a small change in layout, and the same container always yields the same guide. Designers supply a reference layout and ordering constraints, then instantiate the guide as concrete styles such as cartograms.
arxiv-2606-12208:
Jonata Soares and co-authors redo the statistics of a cold atom gas under a stricter accounting rule, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A Bose gas is a crowd of particles that can pile into one quantum state, forming a condensate at low temperature. Most theory uses the grand-canonical ensemble, letting particle number fluctuate. Trapped lab gases hold a fixed number, the canonical ensemble, where number is pinned. Weak two-particle interactions then perturb the thermodynamics, needing fresh calculation.

The authors derive a recursion formula for the canonical partition function, the master quantity behind all properties. Its diagrams match the grand-canonical ones, but the counting rules differ. Resumming the recursion, needed because the raw form can turn negative at low temperature, yields ground-state occupancy statistics through its cumulants, measures of spread and shape. They apply it to a gas with contact interactions in a box trap, matching experiments.
arxiv-2606-12408:
Bertou and co-authors turn dark matter non-detections into a thermometer for the infant universe, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Freeze-in dark matter never reaches thermal equilibrium; it trickles into existence through feeble interactions in the hot early universe. Recent DAMIC-M and PandaX results excluded the standard freeze-in story for masses between three megaelectronvolts and one gigaelectronvolt, in models with an extra ultralight force carrier. The authors ask what survives at stronger couplings.

The reheating temperature, how hot the universe got after inflation, becomes the key variable. Below the electroweak scale, production is Boltzmann-suppressed, but stronger couplings can compensate exactly. The right abundance then emerges while dodging the electron-scattering bounds, and the scenarios sit within reach of current experiments. A hybrid variant adds a second source: a small share of inflaton decays seeding dark matter directly. That seed significantly reshapes predictions across wide parameter regions.
arxiv-2606-12708:
Buzaaba and a large team present AfriSUD, the first large set of syntactically annotated treebanks for African languages, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A treebank is a set of sentences marked up with grammatical structure, here the dependency links between words. African languages hold nearly a third of the world's linguistic diversity yet lack such resources, which blocks grammar-aware language technology.

AfriSUD covers 9 languages, including Hausa, Wolof, Yoruba, Swahili, and isiXhosa, spanning 3 language families and roughly 192,000 annotated tokens verified by native speakers. The languages feature agglutination, where words are built by stringing meaningful pieces together, and tone that changes word identity. Benchmarking parsers, encoders, and large language models, the team finds a clear syntax gap. Models identify dependency attachments, which word governs which, far better than they label the relations between words. Labelling errors cluster in serial verb constructions, tense-aspect-mood auxiliaries, and possessives.
arxiv-2606-12808:
Tomar and Peddireddy introduce SymQNet, a learned controller that makes adaptive quantum-device calibration faster, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Hamiltonian learning estimates a quantum processor's couplings and fields from measurements, and adaptive designs choose each next experiment using the current Bayesian posterior. Recomputing that choice after every update can take seconds, which dominates runtime across shots.

SymQNet amortises the decision. A reinforcement-learning policy is trained to map the posterior belief state, system graph, and measurement history to the next experiment. So online selection becomes one forward pass while Bayesian feedback is retained. At 5 qubits, decision latency falls by a factor of 47.1 against Fisher-information search and 72.6 against 2-step Bayesian active learning by disagreement. At 12 qubits, a simulated step takes 1.02 seconds with SymQNet versus 13.27 seconds for the 2-step baseline. The authors conclude that learned acquisition makes adaptive Hamiltonian learning practical for low-latency workloads.
arxiv-2606-13108:
Zhang and the PaddlePaddle team at Baidu present PP-OCRv6, a lightweight optical character recognition system spanning 1.5 million to 34.5 million parameters, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Vision-language models achieve general results but suffer hallucination, imprecise localisation, and prohibitive cost on OCR tasks. PP-OCRv6 redesigns its backbone and detection and recognition necks around a MetaFormer-style building block with structural reparameterisation, decoupling spatial token mixing from channel mixing.

On the team's in-house benchmarks, the medium tier achieves 83.2 percent recognition accuracy and 86.2 percent detection Hmean, outperforming the PP-OCRv5 server model by 5.1 and 4.6 percentage points respectively. The authors report that it surpasses Qwen3-VL-235B, GPT-5.5, and Gemini-3.1-Pro on these OCR benchmarks with orders of magnitude fewer parameters, and that the tiny tier runs 3.9 times faster than the mobile model on an Intel Xeon CPU while maintaining comparable accuracy.
arxiv-2606-13208:
Peng and colleagues propose PWOA, an improved whale optimisation algorithm for deploying UAV relay communications, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A drone relay's position, altitude, transmit power, and bandwidth must be tuned jointly, a non-convex, constrained problem that traps swarm optimisers in poor local optima.

PWOA adds 3 mechanisms matched to those failure modes. A Good Nodes Set initialisation spreads the population across the search space. A polynomial schedule for the convergence factor prolongs exploration and sharpens exploitation. A stagnation-triggered pinhole-imaging opposition-based learning operator, paired with a Gaussian local search, escapes local optima while refining the leader. On a 5-dimensional UAV relay problem with 5 inequality constraints, PWOA was run with population 30 over 500 iterations and 30 runs. It attained the lowest mean and standard deviation among the whale, sine cosine, and particle swarm methods. It cut the mean by 1.4 to 18.5 percent and the standard deviation by 15 to 87 percent.
arxiv-2606-13708:
Li presents Tiara in this 2026 arXiv paper, a programmable instruction set for remote memory access. Remote direct memory access lets one machine read another's memory in one round trip, the primitive for disaggregated memory. The performance breaks when the needed address depends on data that must first be read remotely, a pattern the author calls the indirection wall. Indirection is everywhere: graph traversals chase pointers, address translation walks page tables, and disaggregated inference resolves paged caches through lookup tables. Each level costs another round trip.

Tiara runs programs on the memory-side network card, resolving indirection locally and collapsing multi-trip chains into one round trip. The instruction set is compact and verifiable, in the spirit of kernel packet-filter programs. An FPGA prototype demonstrates it. The work matters because data centres are disaggregating memory and compute, and pointer-chasing workloads suffer most when every hop crosses the network.
arxiv-2606-13808:
Sahu and colleagues at Cohere Labs argue that cultural knowledge in large language models is lost during training, long before anyone prompts the model. They call this the culture funnel. Earlier fixes mostly act at inference time, assuming the knowledge is already inside the model. Their 2026 arXiv paper tags data from pretraining, fine-tuning, alignment, and reasoning stages with cultural markers, such as place and topic, to track where those signals go.

Explicit cultural signals drop sharply during post-training, when data favor reasoning tasks and a few dominant regions. Adding more languages widens geographic spread, yet representation stays unbalanced. Their tags also prove useful, lifting scores on downstream cultural benchmarks. The team released the tagged collection, holding five point six million samples, for public use. Fairer cultural coverage, they argue, must be built into data pipelines from the start, not patched on later through prompting.
arxiv-2606-13908:
Zahed reviews how quantum effects break the apparent symmetries of the strong force and build most visible mass. Quantum chromodynamics governs quarks and gluons. Two anomalies drive the story. The axial anomaly ties quark handedness to gluon field topology, solving the U(1)A problem about one meson's surprising mass. The trace anomaly breaks scale symmetry and generates the QCD scale. His 2026 arXiv paper unifies these themes.

The review covers anomalous Ward identities, instantons, and topological susceptibility, the vacuum's response to topological charge. It explains the large mass of the eta-prime meson and how most hadron mass comes from gluon energy rather than quark masses. Polarized scattering experiments and the proton spin problem show the same physics in measurements. Recent work links vacuum topology, the flavor-singlet axial charge, and topological screening. The aim is one perspective joining vacuum structure and hadron properties across regimes.
arxiv-2606-14108:
Bae and Lee argue numbers should enter neural networks already wearing their structure, not as broken character strings. Tokenizers split numbers into arbitrary fragments, erasing the additive and multiplicative relations defining them. Their 2026 arXiv paper introduces Adelic operation-preserved embeddings. Each number is encoded by combining its real value with its modular signatures, p-adic expansions across primes, from algebraic number theory. The embedding preserves addition and multiplication by design, training-free.

The representation drops into existing models without task-specific retraining. On the benchmarks, Transformers with the embeddings beat baselines on every task. The standout was the first-ever perfect accuracy on the Weaving Pattern task, where large commercial models have stumbled. The authors frame this as a principled attack on the long-standing number problem in AI: embed the structure of objects, not just the language describing them.
arxiv-2606-14208:
Misumi shows a complex-valued cousin of entropy knows which way time flows, before any measurement. Pseudo entropy generalizes entanglement entropy using a transition matrix between two states, not one density matrix. His 2026 arXiv paper studies real-time pseudo entropy for a subsystem whose initial pure state evolves unitarily over time. Its short-time behavior is governed by correlations between the physical Hamiltonian and the modular Hamiltonian of the reduced state.

The split is clean: the initial imaginary response is controlled by the symmetrized covariance of the two Hamiltonians, with a minus sign; the real response by their commutator. So the imaginary part is no artifact: it is a time-oriented response tying microscopic evolution to coarse graining. He derives an all-order expression in a Schmidt-diagonal model, recovers thermal pseudo entropy as a special case, and confirms the response in two-qubit and transverse-field Ising chain models.
arxiv-2606-14408:
Chahat Kaushik, Kumar, and Samanta demonstrate a 2026 arXiv scheme for quantum sensing, using quantum effects to measure tiny physical changes. Their setup builds on Hong-Ou-Mandel interference, where two photons entering a device together behave in ways that reveal small delays. Older sensing schemes place a sample in one arm, leaving them open to loss and misalignment.

Instead, the team tunes the exchange symmetry of an entangled photon pair, shifting it smoothly between bosonic bunching and fermionic antibunching behavior by adding a geometric phase to the pump beam. The interference signal swings with a steady width that does not depend on photon bandwidth. Using a birefringent crystal in the pump beam, they measure temperature-driven optical changes with resolution near one part in a million across a wide range.
arxiv-2606-14508:
Hidalgo and Schleicher examine whether tidally locked planets can keep protective magnetic fields in a 2026 arXiv study. Planets in the habitable zones of small M dwarf stars often lock one face toward the star, slowing their rotation. Since rotation powers the internal dynamo that generates a magnetic shield, locking may weaken atmospheric protection.

Their framework couples the stellar wind with two dynamo models and a tidal spin-down model, testing a modern-Earth-like interior against a faster, less dissipative early Earth. Tidal locking acted as a severe negative feedback in both models, and the dipolar field often collapsed before locking finished. Only early M dwarfs hosting an early-Earth-like planet offered strong protection odds near the outer habitable edge, while mid-to-late M dwarfs saw shielding fall to essentially zero.
arxiv-2606-14908:
Bhavsar, Bala, and Santra optimize how quantum networks purify entanglement in a 2026 arXiv paper. Entanglement distillation upgrades weak entangled pairs into stronger ones. Parties use local operations plus classical messages. Fresh pairs arrive only by chance, across a set of quantum memories. The question is sequencing: when to generate, when to distill, and which pairs to combine.

The authors cast the task as a Markov decision problem. A value iteration algorithm then finds the policy minimizing the expected wait for a target fidelity. The best policy beat greedy, nested, and pumping baselines. Waiting time fell as generation odds and memory count rose, as expected. Oddly, it moved non-monotonically with starting fidelity at a fixed fidelity gap. The optimal policy's edge over baselines also shifted by regime. The work shows decision theory can design distillation schedules systematically.
arxiv-2606-15108:
Kong and coauthors use time-varying drive as a resource to sharpen frequency estimation in a 2026 study. Quantum metrology measures frequencies with oscillators, but static encoding limits how precision scales. Changing the Hamiltonian or adding feedback can help, at the cost of complexity. The authors instead modulate the oscillator's own frequency over time.

For a modulation profile and its time integral, quantum Fisher information grows with the square of that integral. The gain comes from a changed phase accumulation mechanism in the driven oscillator. Judged under fixed energy and evolution-time budgets, the advantage over static baselines is genuine. Linear, quadratic, and exponential modulation profiles all confirm the universal scaling law. The scheme needs no prior knowledge of the unknown frequency and no extra energy overhead. It offers a simple, open-loop route to better continuous-variable quantum sensors.
arxiv-2606-15308:
Liu and coauthors attack the routing logic of multimodal model cascades in a 2026 machine learning security paper. Cascades save money by letting a cheap model answer first, escalating only when it sounds unsure. That confidence signal decides who pays for the expensive model. The authors show an attacker can game it with a doctored image border. Their Forced Deferral Attack trains a border trigger that flattens the weak model's confidence. Triggered queries then get routed to the strong model more often.

The attack needs no knowledge of which uncertainty metric the cascade uses. It beat image-perturbation and prompt-injection baselines across datasets and model families. It survived preprocessing defenses in their tests. Answers stay answerable; only the billing changes. The provider absorbs compute costs the cascade was built to avoid. The work exposes confidence-based routing as an attack surface. Designing routing that resists manipulation remains a problem.
arxiv-2606-15808:
Wen and colleagues recast quantum channels, the noise processes of open quantum systems, as trainable building blocks for quantum machine learning in 2026. Variational quantum learning normally restricts itself to unitary operations and treats channels as damage. Their framework instead makes the channels themselves learnable, grounded in open-system dynamics.

The outputs of a channel-enhanced model form a structured superposition of functional components. Each is governed by an effective observable whose spectrum training can modulate, something unitary models cannot do, since their spectra stay fixed. Unitary models survive as a special case of the framework. The training geometry also grows richer, with ensemble-averaged gradients and extra directions from the Kraus operators. Experiments with trainable amplitude-damping and phase-damping channels on classification tasks confirm better training dynamics and predictions. Dissipation, long the enemy of quantum computing, becomes a design resource here.
arxiv-2606-16008:
Biglin studies, in a 2026 mathematics paper, when a cloud of particles that stick together on a line finally settles down. The pressureless Euler system tracks a mass distribution and its velocity with no internal pressure pushing particles apart. In sticky particle solutions, mass that collides stays joined for all later times. A known projection formula builds such a solution from starting data, but settling was not fully understood.

Biglin gives a necessary and sufficient condition, readable from the initial condition alone, for that solution to reach equilibrium. The argument also pins down exactly what the equilibrium looks like and gives a formula for the collapse time when settling occurs. Worked examples track the distance to equilibrium over time in detail. The result sharpens a model first proposed by Zeldovich for large structure formation, and it clarifies long-run behavior for related crowd and dust models.
arxiv-2606-16208:
Xu and colleagues present ATHENA in 2026, a method for choosing which robot demonstrations are worth training on. Influence functions estimate how much each demonstration affects task outcomes. Scaling them to billion-parameter vision-language-action models hits computational and multitask bottlenecks. ATHENA is built for that scale, across 50 jointly trained tasks.

Two tricks cut the cost. Kronecker structure in linear-layer gradients reduces projection cost sharply, and a rank-r Random Truncated Approximation replaces dense Hessian inversion, giving about a 313.4 times speedup in the reported figures. Global and local influence scores then balance curation across tasks. On RoboTwin 2.0 and real-robot tests, ATHENA matches or beats full-data fine-tuning using only half the demonstrations in simulation. Real-robot tasks need about two thirds of the data for the same effect.
arxiv-2606-16308:
Bonari and co-authors run a physics-informed sensitivity analysis in 2026 on their digital twin of a full-scale test bridge in Munich. The two-span, mixed steel-concrete bridge at the University of the Bundeswehr Munich has a detailed finite element model that acts as a virtual replica. Sensitivity analysis asks which structural parameters drive the model's response most. Knowing that guides both simpler models and smarter sensor placement.

The team applies generalized polynomial chaos expansion, a method that propagates parameter uncertainty through the model, and reads influence from Sobol indices. Material properties and connection details turn out to significantly impact the bridge's vibration characteristics, per the report. Other parameters show negligible influence on the dynamic response. Those can be fixed or dropped, simplifying the model without losing accuracy. The framework pairs the physics-based replica with advanced uncertainty quantification to sharpen structural health assessment.
arxiv-2606-16408:
Yeo and co-authors introduce MUNI in 2026, a single diffusion framework that can generate any mix of modalities from any other mix. Earlier media generators lean on large language models, need text-paired training data, or freeze a latent space first and fit a prior afterward. MUNI instead trains per-format encoders, expressive decoders, and one shared flow-based prior together, under a single objective.

The shared latent is the meeting point, judged by three criteria: predictivity, coherence, and minimality. Standard rules from multimodal variational inference fall short once a learned prior enters, the authors show. Their fixes are non-mixture mixing, target-detached self-reconstruction, and prior learning on leave-one-out latents. On PolyMNIST-Quadrant-Labels and an image-text-audio setup, MUNI keeps conditional generation competitive while substantially improving unconditional coherence, per the report.
arxiv-2606-16708:
Adrian and colleagues ask how central banks should handle risk around their forecasts in a 2026 paper. Banks have long used two tools side by side. Scenario analysis tells stories about possible futures but gives them no odds. Forecast distributions give odds, often shown as fan charts, but little story.

The authors place both tools in one frame by treating each scenario as a forecast density tied to set conditions, and the fan chart as a reference distribution. Their Scenario Synthesis then weights the scenarios so the weighted mix matches that reference. Committees gain a practical, repeatable way to check whether their scenario set spans the real risks before they set policy under deep uncertainty. The paper also traces how the two traditions grew apart since the late nineteen-sixties. Its verdict is that scenarios and distributions are complements, not rivals, when judging growth and inflation risk.
arxiv-2606-16908:
Mohamed, Shang and Vazirgiannis make diffusion language models cheaper to run in a 2026 paper on adaptive sampling. Diffusion models generate text by unmasking tokens over many reverse steps, and standard samplers fix the step count in advance. That wastes passes on positions that settled early and sometimes locks in shaky tokens too soon.

Their sampler, LESS, treats each token's commitment as a stopping decision made online. A masked position can unmask only when three stability tests agree. The top prediction must be confident. The same token must persist across recent steps. The predictive distribution must barely change between steps, as measured by Jensen-Shannon divergence. No training is needed and any diffusion model can use it. Across seven benchmarks in knowledge, math and code, and three open diffusion models, LESS raises average accuracy over strong adaptive rivals. It also uses far fewer reverse steps than fixed-budget decoding, cutting latency.
arxiv-2606-17008:
Abdollahi and Javadi review uncertainty in Cepheid distance measurements in a 2026 astronomy paper. Cepheid variable stars obey a period-luminosity relation: brighter Cepheids pulse more slowly. That relation anchors the cosmic distance ladder and the measured expansion rate of the universe, so its errors matter far beyond the stars themselves.

The review separates systematic errors, which more data cannot shrink, from statistical ones. Calibration offsets, metal content effects, blending with neighbors, extinction and parallax biases head the systematic list. On the statistical side, photon noise, intrinsic scatter and phase sampling dominate, with random-phase error growing as telescopes like the James Webb gather single-epoch snapshots. A recently proposed cross-filter correction earns special attention: it recovers mean brightness from one epoch by exploiting how residuals correlate between filters. The method cuts infrared scatter by more than a quarter, worth roughly a tenfold increase in time sampling.
arxiv-2606-17408:
Dai and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper asking a basic question about generative robot policies: where should action generation begin? Such policies usually start from a plain Gaussian noise source that knows nothing about the robot's current state. The generator must then haul samples all the way from uninformed noise to sensible actions, and the authors propose fixing the starting point instead of the generator, which stays untouched.

Their learnable source prior, LeaP, swaps the standard source for a diagonal Gaussian shaped by the robot's own body sensing. A small network predicts both its mean and a state-dependent variance for each action chunk. On fifteen simulated manipulation tasks, LeaP beat four baselines by wide margins in average success. It helped both flow-matching and diffusion-bridge generators, used fewer parameters, converged faster, and led in real-world deployment too.
arxiv-2606-17508:
Hapuarachchi presents a 2026 arXiv paper on predicting what a concurrent Go program does next, where the honest answer is a distribution, not a single step. Schedulers interleave goroutines differently on every run, so one trace prefix can legitimately continue in several ways. Training a model against one recorded outcome teaches it to guess a random draw, and this work instead turns that nondeterminism into the training signal for the model to learn from directly.

Each program is run many times, and the observed next events are pooled into an empirical distribution per prefix. A mid-size model is fine-tuned to match those distributions, using fewer than a thousand traces from real production bugs. It beat a large commercial model used zero-shot on held-out predictions from systems such as Kubernetes and etcd. Calibration also improved over plain cross-entropy training at equal accuracy.
arxiv-2606-17608:
Liu and Montreuil present a 2026 arXiv paper on a two-echelon delivery system for hyperconnected city logistics, built around a three-tier hub network in the Physical Internet style. Standardised containers swap quickly between vehicles at gateway, local, and access hubs, cutting handling time. The study asks how to route services and containers jointly while sharing vehicles across firms and repositioning them between hubs as demand shifts through the day.

A multi-period integer program joins path-based vehicle planning with arc-based container routing in one model. A decomposition heuristic with capacity-aware flow assignment splits big cases by echelon and region so real cities stay solvable. In an Atlanta case study at full market share, the system cut emissions by nearly half and total costs by a sixth versus single-echelon delivery. Vehicle repositioning lowered costs further still.
arxiv-2606-18008:
Gu and colleagues speed up a core tool for explaining what vision models look at, in a 2026 paper. Visual attribution ranks the regions of an image by how much each drives the model's decision. Done faithfully, it becomes a search over ordered subsets of regions, and even greedy search is costly, since every step rescores all remaining candidates against the model.

Their algorithm, PhaseWin, reshapes greedy selection into phases: screen candidates globally, prune the weak ones adaptively, then refine inside local windows. The reorganization preserves the ranking behavior that makes greedy search trustworthy while slashing the number of model evaluations. The authors analyze the method under a monotone evidence model, giving conditions for its faithfulness. For teams auditing vision and vision-language systems, cheaper faithful attribution means explanations can run at production scale.
arxiv-2606-18108:
Estévez and colleagues let astronomers query a sky-survey database in plain words instead of code, in a 2026 paper. Their target is ALeRCE, a community broker that classifies events for the Zwicky Transient Facility and the coming Rubin Observatory. The system turns natural language questions into executable SQL through in-context learning, with a dataset of one hundred ten hand-built question and query pairs for development and testing.

Generation runs in four steps: link the question to the schema, classify the query type, decompose the prompt, and self-correct the draft. That pipeline beat direct one-shot inference across thirteen language models tested, and self-correction steadily cut execution errors. The strongest models included recent Claude, Gemini, and GPT releases. The authors see the work as a step toward observatory archives that any astronomer can interrogate conversationally.
arxiv-2606-18308:
Meng and colleagues argue that safe multi-agent learning for physical systems fails when its three hard parts are bolted naively, in a 2026 paper. Networked cyber-physical systems force agents to mix discrete and continuous actions, respect hard safety limits during training, and obey physics. The authors prove a three-way coupling lemma: each feature injects bias into the others in a cycle that defeats off-the-shelf combinations.

Their framework, Trident, co-designs one component per leak. A corrected gradient estimator shrinks the bias of relaxed discrete choices, a Lyapunov-constrained trust-region update keeps every iterate feasible, and a physics-informed critic decomposes value rather than reward. Theory gives convergence to a constrained Nash equilibrium, with violations growing only as the square root of training length. On drone edge computing, intersection management, and a strategy-game variant, violations fell by over ninety-five percent against a baseline.
arxiv-2606-18508:
Abaskohi and colleagues present MCompassRAG, a retrieval framework that uses topic metadata to steer document search, in a 2026 natural language processing paper. Retrieval faces a granularity bind: small chunks are precise but multiply search cost, while large chunks mix topics inside one representation and make similarity scores noisy, a problem for deep research.

MCompassRAG enriches each coarse chunk's representation with topic-level signals living in the same embedding space. It then trains a student retriever by distillation from a language model teacher, so no model calls are needed at query time. Across six retrieval benchmarks it improved information efficiency by more than eight percent on average over the strongest efficient baselines while running at several times lower latency than model-based rivals. Ablations showed the metadata selection policy and the abstraction module are necessary. The authors flag dependence on the quality of the topic model as the main limitation.
arxiv-2606-18608:
Shimasue, Hotokezaka, and Beniamini offer a single explanation for an apparent gap between ordinary pulsars and magnetars in the distribution of neutron star magnetic fields, in a 2026 astrophysics paper. Pulsars usually show fields around a trillion gauss and magnetars fields a hundred to a thousand times stronger, with few objects in between.

Their analytic argument rests on magnetic inclination: the angle between a star's magnetic and spin axes shrinks over time. The alignment timescale falls with the square of the field strength, so strongly magnetized stars align fast. Aligned pulsars beam their radio emission away from most sightlines and vanish from surveys, carving the observed gap, while magnetars are found through isotropic X-ray bursts and are barely affected. Correcting for beaming and luminosity, the authors reconstruct a single continuous birth distribution, such as a log-uniform one, shared by both populations.
arxiv-2606-18908:
Jolicoeur warns that gravitational lensing corrupts a measuring stick when surveys push to high redshift, in a 2026 cosmology paper. The turnover scale of the matter power spectrum, set by matter-radiation equality, works as a ruler independent of baryon acoustic oscillations. Stacking redshift bins should sharpen it. That motivates measuring it with spectroscopic surveys such as Euclid and MegaMapper.

The problem is that lensing magnification adds a correction to the galaxy power spectrum monopole. It distorts its shape, and shifts the turnover. Using mock surveys, Jolicoeur forecasts the bias grows with redshift. It is modest for a Euclid-like survey, but several times the uncertainty for a MegaMapper-like one. There, the turnover vanishes beyond a redshift of three point seven. Keeping the bias below one standard deviation caps the MegaMapper range near redshift two point nine. So the lensing correction must be modeled in any turnover measurement.
arxiv-2606-19008:
Wang gives explicit constructions for Ramanujan-type congruences in a 2026 number theory paper. Such a congruence says that one subsequence of a counting sequence is always divisible by a prime, in a shifted pattern. Ramanujan found the classic cases for the partition function. Since then many methods have proved such results, but a unified explicit approach has remained a clear goal.

The author builds modular forms directly to establish these congruences for a broad class of generating functions. The class covers eta-quotients, weakly holomorphic modular forms, and mock modular forms. As applications, the explicit method recovers known congruences in a single framework. It also yields new explicit congruences and new non-congruence results, which show where such patterns fail. The value is constructive. Rather than proving existence alone, the work exhibits the forms that make each congruence work for combinatorial and arithmetic functions.
arxiv-2606-19108:
Zha and colleagues present JourneyFormer in 2026, a sequence model for search ranking at Airbnb. Sequence models infer guest intent from past browsing and booking behavior. Deployment is hard in practice, though. Guest sequences are long, exploratory, and complex, while booking labels, the signal that matters most, are sparse. Design choices on data and modeling must balance ranking quality with scale and serving cost.

JourneyFormer encodes the full guest journey for ranking. The paper details key choices on which guest events to keep, how to embed item identities, and how to handle long histories and sparse labels. Those choices were tested in production, not just offline. The deployed system shows sequence modeling can work at Airbnb scale when data selection and model design are tuned together. The account gives ranking teams a practical playbook for turning guest histories into better search order without losing scalability.
arxiv-2606-19208:
Nair and colleagues study bisections of a local Lie groupoid in a 2026 mathematics paper. Lie algebroids are the infinitesimal counterparts of Lie groupoids, but not every algebroid integrates to a global groupoid. The obstruction is global and tied to monodromy groups. Local groupoids, whose structure maps exist only near the unit section, avoid that block. Every Lie algebroid admits such a local integration, making local objects a key bridge in the theory.

The local Lie group formed by admissible bisections of a local Lie groupoid over a compact manifold is examined. It relates that group to the Lie algebra of sections of the associated Lie algebroid, the infinitesimal shadow of the construction. The authors also prove a transfer result. If a local Lie groupoid is globalizable, then its associated local Lie group of bisections is globalizable too. That link passes global structure to the bisection group.
arxiv-2606-19408:
Yoshimoto and colleagues present FlexLAM in 2026, a latent action model with variable-length codes. Latent actions give a compact interface between action-free video and downstream decision-making. Existing models force every transition through a fixed-capacity bottleneck. Tight codes can discard cues needed for action alignment. Loose codes keep extra variation that must be resolved when alignment labels are scarce or narrow.

FlexLAM replaces fixed capacity with variable-length latent actions trained by nested dropout. The codes are prefix-valid. They capture compact transition structure first and add detail only when needed. A single FlexLAM matches or beats separately trained fixed-capacity models at every token budget tested, under scarce-label supervision and a stress test. It also improves transition reconstruction on egocentric video. Budgets can be adjusted at inference time without retraining. Variable-length codes look like a drop-in upgrade for latent action models.
arxiv-2606-19508:
Troy Yang sharpens modular data assimilation for fluid flow equations in 2026. Data assimilation blends model forecasts with fresh observations to track a moving system. The target equations are the Navier-Stokes equations, which govern viscous fluid motion.

Yang pairs a second-order backward differentiation scheme, BDF2, with a two-step nudging method. A forecast step advances the flow, then an analysis step nudges the state toward observed values. When the observation operator is a projection, the analysis step turns explicit in closed form. That explicit step keeps the stability feel of an implicit step at lower cost. Stability and error estimates come with full proofs. Numerical tests find accuracy on par with standard fully coupled assimilation. Computational cost and complexity drop sharply at the same time, a gain for weather-style forecasting codes.
arxiv-2606-19608:
Alexander Balinsky and Yarema Prykarpatskyy tackle a Grothendieck-type question about subspaces of Banach spaces in 2026. A Banach space is a complete normed space of functions or vectors. Their subspaces sit inside Lp spaces, the standard homes for functions measured by power integrals.

Take a closed linear subspace that also embeds continuously into a higher Lq space, with q above p. Balinsky and Prykarpatskyy prove such a subspace must be finite dimensional. They bound its dimension by an explicit estimate built from gamma functions and an embedding constant. The bound holds along a ladder of exponents that doubles the gap from two at each step. Certain subspaces made of continuous functions on the domain must also be finite dimensional. Results of this kind limit how nice an infinite function space can be inside two norms at once.
arxiv-2606-19708:
Yumeng Wu and Jie Xiao realise affine bases geometrically through the Kronecker quiver in 2026. Quantised enveloping algebras carry two famed bases: the PBW basis and Lusztig's canonical basis. The Kronecker quiver, two vertices joined by two arrows, is the test case.

Flag sheaf complexes over strata of representation varieties realise PBW elements. The pair describe the simple parts inside restrictions of those complexes to smaller strata. Comparison with Lusztig's simple perverse sheaves follows from that description. A purity result then re-proves that Lusztig's sheaves form a basis of the composition algebra. Transition coefficients between the two bases turn out to be local system multiplicities. The change-of-basis matrix is upper triangular with ones on the diagonal. Coefficient polynomials also show positivity in this case.
arxiv-2606-19808:
Sajib Acharjee, Dawei Zhou, and Liqing Zhang study when extra reasoning checks pay off in 2026. Test-time reasoning can rescue wrong answers, waste compute on right ones, or flip right answers to wrong. The question is deployment allocation, not verifier design.

SeVRA, their serving-layer controller, keeps a frozen solver's first answer or calls active verification. Recoverability-aware gates train on logged intervention outcomes from the serving stream. On MATH500, selective checking edges out always verifying on accuracy. Post-generation tokens drop by about a quarter, and harmful flips halve. A longer first solve, though, matches selective recovery with fewer total tokens. Transferred to GSM8K, the selective policy checks only three percent of items yet lifts accuracy. The deployment rule follows: tune the first budget first, then add selective recovery where audits matter.
arxiv-2606-20108:
Pengwei Wang, José Morano, Qian Wan, and Hrvoje Bogunović present EFIQA, a method for judging the quality of fundus photographs used to screen for eye disease. Their 2026 paper targets two flaws of standard graders. Such graders inherit the labeling habits of their training set, and they give a bare score with no map of where an image is degraded. EFIQA instead learns what healthy retinal anatomy should look like, using blood-vessel structure as prior knowledge, and needs no quality labels.

First, an anomaly detector trained by masked inpainting learns to fill in missing vasculature, flagging regions where vessels should appear. That knowledge is distilled into a small adapter on a frozen foundation model, which outputs precise spatial quality maps. On external datasets with different grading rules, the label-free system beat supervised rivals on accuracy and explainability. Clinics could use such maps to retake bad photographs on the spot.
arxiv-2606-20308:
Yuanle Yao, Xiang-Dong Li, and Xiao-Jie Xu report candidate X-ray pulsations from an ultraluminous X-ray source in the galaxy NGC 7456. Their 2026 paper analyzes a 2023 XMM-Newton observation of the source known as ULX-1. Such sources shine brighter than the Eddington limit for stellar-mass objects, and their nature is debated. Coherent pulsations would settle the question in favor of a neutron star, as they did for other ultraluminous pulsars.

Three independent timing methods, including accelerated searches and an orbital-demodulation analysis, point to a signal near 0.22 hertz. Its drift during the observation suggests rapid spin-up from accretion torque. The implied surface magnetic field spans ten to the twelfth to ten to the fourteenth gauss. The authors present the signal as candidate evidence only: a neutron star is the likely host, but independent data must confirm it.
arxiv-2606-20408:
Hanwool Lee, Dasol Choi, Bokyeong Kim, Seung Geun Kim, and Haon Park red-team language model agents running a simulated nuclear plant. Their 2026 paper presents NRT-Bench, where a five-role operator team backed by language models runs a plant with six critical safety functions. Adversaries inject messages over four channels in multi-turn sessions. Harm is objective: a run ends the moment any safety function is lost, blamed on the causing message.

Under a fixed-attack paired-replay protocol, adaptive attacks pushed all four frontier operator models past a safety limit in 8.7 to 12.1 percent of sessions. The models looked equally robust in aggregate, yet their failures barely overlapped: of 149 sessions, none defeated all four, while a third defeated at least one. Vulnerabilities are nearly disjoint across models, not nested. Added guardrails helped or hurt depending on the model, so ensemble diversity may matter more than any single score.
arxiv-2606-20608:
Md Zabirul Islam, Md Motaleb Hossen Manik, and Ge Wang generate pedagogical videos from a course corpus with a structured blueprint. Their 2026 paper notes that text-to-video systems make fluent clips but rarely encode pedagogical content knowledge: prerequisite-aware sequencing, learner-adaptive depth, and sustained engagement.

CourseBlueprint takes a topic and a learner persona and produces a structured teaching blueprint in a single forward pass over an undergraduate biomedical imaging corpus of 23 lectures and 1,116 slides. Typed intermediate representations replace ad-hoc prompt chaining. The blueprint then drives video generation with the course's own content as ground truth. Generated lessons inherit a syllabus instead of improvising one.
arxiv-2606-20708:
Liang Chen tests whether simulated customers behave like real buyers in a solo 2026 study of language model user simulators. Such simulators now support agent benchmarks and training. Most checks ask whether they talk like humans. Those checks use paid participants with assigned goals. Chen argues that setup has a blind spot. When a goal is assigned, willingness to buy is fixed from outside. Real users have hidden, fading motivation.

Chen defines decision fidelity as matching real decision dynamics. The testbed holds 2,790 production chats between a sales agent and real customers. Of those, 793 have verified payment outcomes. A teacher-forced probe keeps context and measurement fixed. Findings point to a systematic gap: simulated customers rarely walk away as real ones do. That gap matters because training on eager fake buyers can produce sales agents that misread hesitation and push at the wrong moment.
arxiv-2606-20908:
Youssef Hakiki and Samy Tindel explore a new strategy in 2026 toward an Itô-Stratonovich formula for rough sheets, surfaces of irregular paths in two parameters. Planar integration for rough paths has long been cumbersome. Mixed terms create overlapping integrals. Earlier work built a large structure with dozens of elements to handle them.

Elementary Taylor expansions are used in a more fundamental way. That simple trick, they claim, streamlines the algebra of planar integration greatly. The method is illustrated in a specialized rough Young framework. The classical change-of-variable formula is extended to paths with asymmetric regularity in the two directions. Simpler foundations could widen use of rough path theory in fields such as finance and physics, where two-parameter noise appears.
arxiv-2606-21008:
David Nordfors introduces the Metanym Game in a solo 2026 paper, a self-contained benchmark where language models compete in a word game and rate each other. Structural intelligence is measured against cognitive science constructs. No content is given in advance. Contestants create all of it, producing analogies that can be checked sentence by sentence. With no fixed test set, leakage into training is resisted by construction.

In the council-of-peers design, contestants also rate each other's creations. A spectral method reads the ratings matrix. One decomposition yields competence as both generator and judge of true statements at once. Consistency serves as the yardstick for subjective criteria. Factual ratings correlate strongly with an established benchmark. Peer-based scoring without a golden key could matter as benchmarks saturate: if models judge each other reliably, evaluation can scale with the models themselves.
arxiv-2606-21308:
Denis Fatkhiev and five colleagues built a quantum key distribution system in 2026 on two photonic chips made of different materials. Quantum key distribution lets two parties share secret keys with security grounded in physics, since eavesdropping leaves detectable errors. Their transmitter chip in indium phosphide generates the states, while a silicon nitride chip decodes them with low loss, combining strengths neither platform has alone.

The system runs the three-state time-bin BB84 protocol with one decoy state, encoding bits in early and late time slots. The design removes the long transmitter delay line that interferometric time-bin schemes usually need, and the basis choice ratio can be tuned. Key rates are checked under a finite-key security analysis against coherent attacks, showing secure operation over metropolitan and intercity fiber distances.
arxiv-2606-21408:
Sujith Pulikodan and seven colleagues release the Vaani Benchmark in 2026, an inclusive test set for Hindi speech recognition gathered from 104 districts across India. Existing Hindi benchmarks cover few regions and speaker types, so systems can look strong while failing many real users. Vaani records spontaneous speech prompted by images, captured in everyday acoustic conditions from diverse demographic groups.

Each clip carries three independent transcriptions, allowing multi-reference scoring that tolerates spelling and word-choice variants instead of marking them wrong. That design makes evaluation more robust and realistic for a language with wide regional and dialect variation. The team benchmarks a range of open and proprietary recognition systems on the data, giving developers a fairer picture of how their models serve Hindi speakers nationwide.
arxiv-2606-22208:
Hakam and colleagues demonstrate, in 2026, steady control over the random phase dynamics of an injection-locked spin-torque nano-oscillator. These nanoscale magnetic devices fluctuate thermally, so their phase jumps at random between states. Under second-harmonic injection locking, a vortex-based device settles into two phase attractors separated by half a cycle and hops between them.

A weak radio-frequency signal at the free-running frequency tunes the jump rates without calming the fluctuations. Each attractor's occupation share can be programmed from the unbiased limit toward zero or one. The signal's phase selects which attractor is favoured, and its strength sets the size of the imbalance. A phase-reduced quasipotential model accounts for the observations in numbers. The authors propose such devices as hardware primitives for probabilistic computing, Ising machines, and brain-inspired designs.
arxiv-2606-22608:
Wentao Che, Esteban Garcés Arias, Asim Niaz, Andreas Bender, and Enrique Jiménez build a reading machine for cuneiform in this 2026 paper. Of roughly half a million excavated clay tablets, only a small fraction has been analysed, because reading the wedge-shaped signs takes years of training. Computer vision could help, but it needs large annotated datasets to learn from.

The team use the largest annotated cuneiform dataset to date. They evaluate a Deformable DETR detection model at two class levels, one hundred seventy-three and one hundred six. Their pipeline adds automatic tablet-side extraction, heuristic line grouping, and n-gram-based textual similarity checks. It improves on prior work by up to roughly a third on standard detection metrics. Run over nearly eighty-eight thousand tablet fragments from the Electronic Babylonian Library, it produced almost three million sign detections, a scalable foundation for corpus-wide analysis.
arxiv-2606-22708:
Yichen Xu gives language-model agents a grip on musical structure in this 2026 paper. Generative music systems now produce impressive audio from text prompts. But audio is hard to inspect, edit, or diagnose as structure, so an agent cannot easily tell what it made or how to fix it.

His framework, Libretto, works in symbolic music instead. A grammar built for language models spells out onset slots, voices, and bar-level organization. Each piece is then scored in a corpus-calibrated statistical space along six axes: rhythm, harmony, melody, texture, form, and variation. Those measurements support retrieval of similar pieces, diagnosis of weaknesses, and copy-risk control. An agent can revise its own output iteratively against the scores. Across gap filling, full-piece generation, gradual morphing, and educational tasks, Libretto turns a raw token sequence into a measurable, editable object.
arxiv-2606-22808:
O. V. Kaptsov develops exact solutions for coupled wave equations in this 2026 paper. The systems are nonlinear Schrödinger equations in three space dimensions plus time, describing several interacting wave components held in a transverse trap, a potential that confines them sideways. Exact solutions in such high-dimensional systems are rare and valuable as benchmarks.

The core result is a lifting lemma. If the transverse phase functions are harmonic and the trapping potential exactly cancels the squared phase gradient, the full system reduces to a closed one-dimensional integrable hierarchy. Every solution of the simpler system then lifts to an exact solution of the full one. Kaptsov applies this to four systems. They include the Gross-Pitaevskii equation, where vortex lattice breathers keep finite density at their cores, and a spinor condensate, where a rogue wave briefly amplifies one channel's density ninefold.
arxiv-2606-22908:
Bo Yang shows that pure lambda calculus needs no extra machinery for cyclic data in this 2026 paper, published in PACMPL. Writing cyclic or infinite structures normally takes an added recursion construct or a fixed-point combinator. Sharing repeated work, as memoization does, normally takes an impure cache, which breaks the purity of the calculus.

Yang applies tabling, a standard method for solving least-fixpoint equations, to weak-head reduction. The new semantics keeps each term's standard lazy meaning. A term that reaches finitely many distinct states comes out as a finite graph, possibly cyclic, and that graph is sound regardless of reduction order. His interpreter does dynamic programming on its own, sharing repeated subproblems with no memo table. It also detects an unproductive loop in finite time, where naive evaluation would spin forever. Finally, Yang writes a bootstrap compiler, itself a pure lambda term, that compiles its own source.
arxiv-2606-23108:
Bechir Dardouri, Kaïs Zhioua, and Yassine Msaddak build a medical question-answering system that reasons over a knowledge graph in a 2026 paper. Clinical language models that answer from memory can hallucinate, inventing fluent but baseless guidance. The team's system serves a fertility assistant backed by a medical graph of about seven hundred thousand nodes. Answers must follow verifiable paths through that graph, step by step. A distance oracle precomputes exact graph distances, giving sub-millisecond feasibility checks and simple path listings.

Dardouri and colleagues add a lightweight neural search heuristic that works only inside the corridor the oracle allows. Candidate paths are scored for overlap, length, and source quality, then packed into compact prompts. The hybrid beat text-only retrieval and single-part baselines on the speed and recall balance. It also lowered time to first token and reduced hallucinations judged by clinicians, while keeping explanations clear.
arxiv-2606-23208:
Leona Hennig and Marius Lindauer tune energy-frugal neural networks with automated machine learning in a 2026 paper. Deep learning extracts complex patterns but burns much computation, raising environmental and resource concerns. Deep shift networks replace heavy operations with cheap shifts, cutting inference cost. They remain poorly understood and rarely optimized well. The authors apply multi-objective hyperparameter optimization, balancing accuracy against energy use. A multi-fidelity method tests cheap approximations first, then promotes promising designs.

Hennig and Lindauer find configurations that beat default shift networks on both loss and emissions at once. Performance rose by about twenty percent while emissions sometimes fell by more than sixty percent. Quantized versions showed the largest energy savings, with surprising model-specific trade-offs between accuracy and emissions. The study maps how to design such networks for low-resource image classification.
arxiv-2606-23308:
A. O. Sboychakov predicts superconductivity in strongly twisted bilayer graphene in a 2026 condensed matter paper. Twisted bilayer graphene became famous at a magic small angle, where it superconducts. This paper looks at the opposite corner: large twist angles with a small superlattice cell. There, the two layers' electronic states hybridize near matching momentum points and open a gap in the spectrum. Light doping then adds carriers with a large density of states. Sboychakov shows that the screened Coulomb repulsion between electrons is enough to stabilize a superconducting state in that setting.

Sboychakov finds the superconducting order parameter has d-wave symmetry, like the cuprate superconductors. Applying a bias voltage raises the predicted transition temperature. For realistic model parameters, the transition can reach several hundred millikelvin. That is cold, but within reach of standard cryogenics. The result widens the map of where graphene-based superconductivity might hide.
arxiv-2606-23408:
Yves Achdou and Qing Tang build numerical methods for heterogeneous agent models in a 2026 paper in computational economics. Such models track many unlike households or firms at once, each planning over time. Epstein-Zin utility, a flexible preference form, lets the model split risk aversion from the wish to shift spending across time. Solving the model means solving a Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation. The authors replace it with a grid-based version and give two iterative algorithms. One fits agents who prefer late resolution of uncertainty. The other fits those who prefer early resolution.

Achdou and Tang prove both algorithms converge. That proof also shows solutions of the grid problem exist. For the late resolution case, they add error bounds that compare the grid solution with the true one. Tests of the methods give macroeconomists a firmer base for computing with this model class.
arxiv-2606-23508:
Fengbo Yuan and colleagues build an atomic-scale theory of ferroelectricity in ultrathin films in a 2026 condensed matter paper. Ferroelectric materials hold a switchable electric polarization, prized for future memory devices. Textbook macroscopic theory says that polarization must fade as films grow thinner. Experiments defy that prediction for certain materials, notably hafnia-based and bismuth-based oxides, which stay robustly ferroelectric at a few atomic layers. The authors develop a framework that explains the survival from the atomic scale up.

Yuan and colleagues focus on the film's termination layers, the atomic sheets at its surfaces, and their work functions. Robust ferroelectricity arises from two effects they name self-polarizing behavior and the switchable role of the termination layer, both tied to the material's characteristic structure. The theory also shows why top electrodes matter for holding polarization in such thin films. The framework is meant to guide device design.
arxiv-2606-24808:
Zidu Liu and Florian Marquardt use a large language model to discover new quantum error correcting codes. Quantum hardware errs constantly, so scalable machines need codes that correct errors cheaply. Quantum LDPC codes promise sparse checks, a finite encoding rate, and growing distance. Designing them is a hard discrete search problem. Their framework, structured concept evolution, pairs the language model with an algebraic mutation grammar. It searches for lifted product code families, a class of CSS codes.

The model never designs from first principles. It evolves structured concepts: algebraic specifications paired with programs that realise them. Mutations act at several levels, changing the group algebra, the protograph geometry, or the base space. The search found diverse competitive families. Some are abelian; others rest on non abelian groups beyond standard designs like bivariate bicycle codes. Performance is characterised under code capacity depolarising noise with standard decoding.
arxiv-2606-24908:
Sagar Mandal settles a number theory problem about when Fibonacci numbers can equal values of Nathanson's totient function. Nathanson's function counts the nonempty subsets of the numbers up to m whose elements share no factor with m. A recent paper by Chatterjee, Mandal, and Mohan asked for all solutions when a Fibonacci number equals that count. The equation mixes exponential growth on one side with delicate counting on the other, a classic hard shape.

Mandal proves the complete solution list has just three entries: the index and modulus pairs one one, two one, and three two. No larger Fibonacci number ever hits the totient value. The proof leans on lower bounds for linear forms in logarithms, due to Matveev. A Baker Davenport reduction, in the Dujella Pethő form, then cuts the search down to checkable size. The result closes the question posed in the earlier paper.
arxiv-2606-25008:
Yizhou Liu and Jeff Gore argue, in a position paper, that the exponents in neural scaling laws are explained and the coefficients are where the action is. Scaling laws describe pretraining loss falling as a power law in time, model size, and compute. The authors claim the exponents come from generic mechanisms. A one third time scaling follows from the strong nonlinearity of softmax. Inverse width scaling follows from representational superposition. Inverse depth scaling follows from ensemble averaging across transformer layers.

Current large language models therefore sit in one universality class with fixed exponents. Coefficients are another matter: they are sensitive to data and architecture, and they fix practical quantities like optimal model shape and the compute optimal frontier. Understanding coefficients is thus the key to near term performance gains. Liu and Gore aim the field's theory effort at the part of the scaling law that engineers can change.
arxiv-2606-25108:
AI systems are moving from advising doctors to prescribing medication on their own. Eileanor LaRocco and six colleagues examine what safe AI prescribing would require, as United States bills and a Utah pilot already let AI prescribe. Clearance today leans on average performance scores. The authors say three things are missing. A confidence score for each single prediction. A split between not knowing and true clinical doubt. And a clear record at decision time, so blame can be shared fairly.

A survey of 136 prescribing doctors in the United States tests the stance. Doctors would not allow AI prescribing without a route that hands hard cases to a human. Faced with doubt in the case itself, they wanted a summary of competing options; faced with gaps in the model's knowledge, they preferred it to abstain. They took on extra blame only when the record let them judge for themselves.
arxiv-2606-25208:
The Theo Jansen linkage, famous from walking sculptures, turns rotation into a stepping gait through a web of bars and pins. Jichao Wang asks how the leg degrades in service, relaxing the ideal pin assumption of an earlier durability study. His forward dynamic model gives each revolute joint a real clearance, with a damped contact force law and friction, and couples it to wear through a feedback loop.

Wear grows the clearance each cycle, and the larger clearance feeds back into the dynamics as harder impacts. Ignoring clearance understates the load badly. The peak force at the load bearing pin roughly doubles. It quadruples again when two loaded joints carry clearance at once. Single wear paths are erratic and can even flip which design looks better, so Wang compares designs statistically. Across sixteen randomised starting phases, the gait and durability optimised joint is robustly the longer lived.
arxiv-2606-25308:
Software logs can reveal how students regulate their own learning, down to how long they sit idle before starting a session. Jordan Gutterman and colleagues study that pause, called delayed start, in 2026 using practice data from seven hundred eleven seventh graders. They ask whether delay habits during maths practice predict standardised test results in other subjects too. Mixture modelling also splits students into behavioural subgroups so the measure can be applied in real classrooms.

Delays during maths predicted later scores in both maths and English, a cross subject signal. Students who typically began within five minutes, about a fifth of the group, grew more than average in both subjects. Another fifth, averaging over thirteen minutes of delay, trended in the opposite direction. The authors argue session level behaviour adds a content free engagement measure beside usage and progress data.
arxiv-2606-25508:
Pathology slides are huge, and labelling every pixel of tissue type needs scarce expert time, so weak labels are attractive. Hualong Zhang and colleagues present a segmentation framework in 2026 that learns from image level labels only. Standard heat map seeds follow stain appearance instead of true tissue shape, so a causal module intervenes counterfactually on feature factors to suppress misleading context. A second stage then merges fine structural detail with global meaning from a frozen foundation model.

Cross path gating lets local structure decide how much global meaning enters, protecting boundary sharpness. A further loss term adjusts its pressure according to prediction uncertainty, softening the effect of noisy seed labels. On two public tissue datasets the combined system reached state of the art weakly supervised results, according to the authors' experiments.
arxiv-2606-26308:
Nnamdi Ekwe-Ekwe, a solo author, prices serverless computing across the big three clouds. Functions-as-a-Service lets developers rent code execution by the sip, with no servers to manage. A decade of feature growth made each provider's pricing its own maze. His Priceless study maps the current features and their price models first. Example workloads then run the same jobs on AWS Lambda, Azure Functions, and Google Cloud Functions for a fair comparison.

Price gaps yawn in two directions. Providers charge markedly different totals for equivalent work. Regions inside one provider differ too, so the same function costs more in one city than another. AWS comes out cheapest overall in his tests. Microsoft Azure comes out most expensive. Shoppers who assume serverless pricing is uniform leave money on the table in both directions.
arxiv-2606-27008:
Chakraborty and Dutkay study when the Fourier transform keeps lengths exactly on regions that stretch without bound. The Fourier transform rewrites a signal as a mix of wave patterns. Plancherel's identity says total energy is the same before and after that rewrite. For bounded regions this balance can fail, so pairs of special regions are needed. The authors describe a class of such pairs in flat space of any dimension. Their regions repeat under shifts from a full-rank lattice, a regular grid of points.

Restricted to those paired regions, the transform becomes an isometric isomorphism, meaning a perfect length-keeping match between two function spaces. That gives the Plancherel identity directly on unbounded sets, where naive energy sums would diverge. They also give a clean test for when energy balance survives on infinite regions.
arxiv-2606-27308: This paper studies universal Lichnerowicz lifting of near-horizon soft modes. The studying studies. Their studying is universal Lichnerowicz lifting. The modes are near-horizon soft. It is gravity. The studying is of. The soft modes are near-horizon. The Lichnerowicz lifting is universal.
arxiv-2606-27708:
Fashion retrieval needs a vision-language encoder tuned to clothing. Tuning brings a trade-off. Gains on fashion data can cost the base model's broad generalisation. Siqiao Xue and Chunxue Xu present ZooClaw-FashionSigLIP2 in 2026 to resolve that trade-off. The model is a fashion-specialised version of SigLIP2-base. Its recipe has two steps.

First comes full fine-tuning on curated fashion data, with knowledge distillation from the base model. Then WiSE-FT blends the tuned model back with the base model. The recipe beat LoRA tuning, larger billion-parameter backbones, and outside training data. Under fair evaluation, the model led on every benchmark in the suite. The authors also release ZooClaw-Fashion, a new fashion retrieval benchmark. A quality analysis of common benchmarks accompanies it. That analysis exposes structural biases in public ground truth and mitigates them. Weights and evaluation artifacts are open-sourced.
arxiv-2606-28308:
Luis Leal, writing alone, asks a question game theory usually glosses over. Many two-player zero-sum games have not one Nash equilibrium but a whole convex set of them, all worth the same game value yet prescribing different behavior. Solvers are guaranteed to reach some equilibrium, and are often treated as interchangeable.

Leal tests six exactly solvable games, including Kuhn poker, and finds the algorithm, not the random seed, decides which equilibrium a solver picks. Regularized methods select the maximum-entropy equilibrium, while regret-averaging methods drift toward lower-entropy edges on asymmetric games. A randomized ensemble of one hundred eighty asymmetric games confirmed the split. In Kuhn poker the maximum-entropy choice also hedged better against flawed opponents, though elsewhere no member dominated.
arxiv-2606-28508:
Lokesh Rasabathina and colleagues compare two ways of growing the gold-cobalt-gold films used in spin-selectivity experiments. Chirality-induced spin selectivity lets chiral molecules filter electron spin at gold surfaces, and a companion effect can magnetize nearby films. Whether the base layer's grain steers these effects was unclear, so the team grew films by molecular beam epitaxy and by sputtering.

Films grown by epitaxy showed sharper interfaces and tidier crystal alignment, yet microscopy found locally smooth gold regions fit for peptides to land on in both kinds. After exposing the films to helical peptides, tunneling spectroscopy showed a similar strength of the effect in both. Large-scale magnetic measurements told a different story: only sputtered films showed slight coercivity gains and slower domain walls. The small-scale signatures look robust. The large-scale responses depend on how the film was made.
arxiv-2606-28708:
Dawon Ahn, Audrey Der, and Evangelos E. Papalexakis present AnTenA, a demonstration system that explains the hidden patterns inside tensors, multi-way data cubes such as users by items by time. Analysts usually explain the co-clustered patterns a decomposition extracts by leaning on labels or side metadata, which may be wrong, stale, or simply absent, especially for narrative human data.

AnTenA instead asks large language models to explain the patterns, using a mix of task-agnostic and task-specific prompts aimed at the stories people tell. To check whether the explanations hold up, the evaluation runs forward and backward inference tasks, predicting data from explanations and explanations from data. The system is available as a public demo, positioning language-model knowledge as a substitute narrator where metadata cannot be trusted.
arxiv-2606-29108:
Zhu, Li, Li, Shen, Li, Chen and Pei present Symbolon, a system that learns how to rewrite programs so that symbolic execution, a powerful but slow analysis technique, scales better. Symbolic execution explores program paths with symbolic inputs to find bugs, but it suffers path explosion and hard constraints. Earlier fixes transformed programs rigidly, sometimes borrowing compiler optimisations designed for normal execution that misalign with symbolic goals.

Symbolon instead treats transformation discovery as a search over program representations. It learns transformations cheaply offline on small programs, distils them into a reusable library of skills for agents, and lets an agent apply them in context on repository-level targets. Symbolon improved the KLEE engine across sixteen search strategies on thirty-two real programs, raising line coverage about three and two thirds times on average. Applied to the Linux kernel, it uncovered twenty-one new bugs, all reported to maintainers.
arxiv-2606-29508:
Alves leads a large team testing whether feedback from massive stars shapes gas filaments in the Ophiuchus star-forming complex. Feedback should organize filaments into radial ones, pointing away from the stars, and tangential ones, running across that direction. Radial filaments should also carry gas flowing lengthwise away from the stars. The team studies the filament called B44, a candidate radial case.

They combine three-dimensional dust maps built from Gaia data with radial velocities from carbon monoxide observations. That pairing breaks a long-standing ambiguity between position on the sky and motion along the line of sight. Both gas tracers show flow running along B44 away from the Upper Scorpius massive stars. The flow speeds up along the filament, at a rate matching accelerations seen in nearby star cluster chains. A shock appears at the wind-facing head, and assembly took about three million years.
arxiv-2606-29608:
Elías-Chávez leads a large team presenting a deep X-ray spectral analysis of active galactic nuclei in the Lockman-SpReSO project. Active galactic nuclei, or AGNs, are the bright centres of galaxies powered by accreting black holes. The sample comes from far-infrared selected sources in the Lockman Hole field.

The team characterizes ninety-four AGNs across a wide redshift range, using absorbed power-law, reflection, and soft excess components to model each spectrum. They estimate intrinsic column densities, rest-frame luminosities, and iron line strengths. An advanced model handles Compton-thick candidates, the most heavily obscured nuclei. The obscured fraction rises toward higher redshifts, and three Compton-thick candidates emerge. Soft excess emission appears in ten AGNs. The authors also detect the X-ray Baldwin effect and a strong link between torus width, dust covering factor, and luminosity. That link supports the receding torus scenario.
arxiv-2606-29908:
Chen and twelve colleagues propose SWAM, a world action model for robot navigation from camera images. A world model predicts how the scene will look after moving, and older planners separate choosing a goal from generating the path, which costs time and can mismatch actions with predicted views.

Given a start image and a goal image, SWAM generates in one pass both the intermediate depth-augmented views and the action trajectory, keeping the two consistent. It learns from depth pseudo-labels during training but needs only an ordinary colour camera when running. A refinement module aligns motion with visual cues, and a scale loss steadies predictions over different distances. In experiments SWAM beats leading two-stage planners in success rate, accuracy, and speed, and generalises to unseen places.
arxiv-2606-30008:
Hongbin Cui, Jiahuan Li, and Xiaowei Xu prove a rigidity result for weighted surfaces. A hypersurface is alpha-stationary when it is a critical point of an energy functional. That functional is the Euler-Dierkes-Huisken functional, introduced by Dierkes and Huisken. It weights each surface point by distance from the origin. The question echoes the classic Bernstein problem about flatness.

Cui and colleagues consider smooth, complete, connected, embedded hypersurfaces through the origin. They prove every such alpha-stationary hypersurface is a linear hyperplane. This holds whenever the exponent alpha is positive. No genuinely curved example exists under those conditions, in any dimension. The zero exponent case recovers ordinary minimal surface theory. Euler's early work on curves with least moment of inertia inspired the functional. Their theorem extends flatness to the whole weighted family.
arxiv-2606-30108:
Sebastian Aas, Elias Stenhede, and Arian Ranjbar turn a clinician's diameter line into a full three-dimensional tumor mask. RECIST measurements summarize lesions with simple two-dimensional diameters. Those lines cannot capture a lesion's true shape or extent. Their model, LETT-NeXt, was built for a CVPR 2026 segmentation competition. It predicts volumetric masks from CT scans plus RECIST markers.

LETT-NeXt first crops a region centered on the RECIST marker. The RECIST line and its endpoints become two extra prompt channels. These are concatenated with the CT input for the network. A compact encoder-decoder then predicts the lesion mask. Prompt-aware component selection and adaptive zoom refine the output at inference. Validation scores are strong on overlap and surface measures alike. Hidden test scores land somewhat lower but remain competitive. CPU inference takes only seconds per case with modest memory.
arxiv-2606-30208:
George Andrews and Mohamed El Bachraoui study a power series built from partitions whose parts come in two colors. Each part may appear in red or blue, with the smallest part restricted to one color. The same series generates counts of strictly concave compositions. Odd and even companion series accompany the main one. The authors pin down their terms in several ways.

For the main series, the terms are determined modulo four completely. That yields a full criterion for Ramanujan-type arithmetic progressions among them. The even companion gets a direct overpartition interpretation of its coefficients. Half those terms count each of two natural partition families. The odd companion, after eta normalization, shows a quintic self-similarity. Its coefficients vanish in exact patterns and change sign infinitely often. A coefficient can be nonzero only under a representability condition. That condition involves a specific quadratic form in two variables.
arxiv-2606-30608:
Mohamed El Amine Boudjoghra, Ivan Laptev and Angela Dai present UnfoldArt, a system that rebuilds articulated 3D objects from a single text prompt or image. Articulated objects, things with moving parts like drawers and laptops, are vital for robotics and virtual worlds. Rebuilding them is hard because hinges, hidden surfaces and inner structure cannot be seen in one still view, and training data is scarce.

UnfoldArt lets software agents debate the answer. High-level agents reason about meaning and motion using vision-language and video models.
