Orwell and later dystopians read this fierce, flawed prophecy with care.
lowell-mars-abode-of-life-1908:
Percival Lowell made his case to the broad public in this book of 1908. It sums up his years of work on Mars for the lay reader. The theme is plain in the title: Mars is a home for life.

He walks from the white caps at the poles to the dark belts that shift with the seasons. Each sign, he holds, points to air, water, plants, and at last to minds at work. The book is the full habit plea for the red world, in Lowell's best public voice. It marks the peak of the Mars craze in print for lay readers.
maeterlinck-blue-bird-1908:
Maurice Maeterlinck wrote The Blue Bird in 1908, a fairy play for the stage. Two children, Tyltyl and Mytyl, set out to find the Blue Bird of Happiness. A fairy sends them through strange lands on Christmas Eve. They visit the past, the future, and the homes of night and joy.

Along the way, their dog, cat, and household objects come to life and speak. Each land teaches them something about what happiness is. At the end, the bird they sought was at home all along. The play charmed audiences around the world. Its gentle lesson still suits family reading and school stages today.
margery-gred-a-tale-of-old-nuremberg-vol:
Volume eight of Margery opens in delay and disappointment. The maidens hoped to ride into the wide world for their lover and brother. That hope is not to be yet, and patience is hard. Their guide Kubbeling, a born wanderer, loses his mirth at the forest lodge.

Then Kubbeling falls sick of a fever and lies abed two weeks. He had never needed healing beyond his cattle-leech's art. The household awaits his tidings with much fear. Doctor Holzschuher, once a steadfast friend, gives no sign at all. Ebers slows the tale into suspense and waiting. Love and loyalty are tested by sickness and silence.
mcclure-s-magazine-vol-31-no-1-may-1908:
McClure's Magazine for May 1908 opens volume thirty one. A full contents page lists tales, lives, and reports for the month. Georgine Milmine writes on Mary Baker G. Eddy in this issue.

Carl Schurz tells of the first days of Reconstruction in the South. He treats the Freedmen's Bureau, Johnson's haste, and the South's deep want. Fiction comes from Edward S. Moffat, Lucy Pratt, and James Barnes. George Kennan reports on poverty and unrest in Russia, and Ellen Terry writes on stage plays. A play piece on Olivia and Faust at the Lyceum adds stage talk. Tales and reports share the issue in the McClure mix of that era.
medela-chymica-or-an-account-of-the-vert: Christopher Packe wrote Medela Chymica, dated 1708 in the record. Its title promises an account of the virtues and uses of chemical medicines. It also promises cures for chronic and stubborn diseases. The hosted sample for this entry is garbled scan text with no readable passage. Only broken marks and letter scraps can be made out in it. This note stays with the title, the author, and the year for that reason.
medical-and-alchemical-recipes-manuscrip: Denis de la Fontaine is named as author of Medical and Alchemical Recipes, a manuscript dated 1608. The record calls it one volume, with drawings, in a small octavo size. The hosted sample for this entry is garbled scan text throughout. No readable recipe or passage can be made out in it. This note stays with the title, the author, and the year for that reason. The contents cannot be described from the sample held here.
memoirs-of-napoleon-bonaparte-volume-08: Volume eight, etext 3558, continues Bourrienne's account of his master Napoleon. The head note pairs its title with the year 1805. Eleventh edition, English language, and Widger as producer are also listed there. Readers of the sample, however, meet only Gutenberg boilerplate from top to end. Not one line of the secretary's narrative is included. Any summary of this volume would have to come from outside the sample, so none is offered.
munro-palaeolithic-man-1908:
Robert Munro, a Scots doctor and digger, gave these talks on stone age man and the Terramara sites in 1908. The Terramara are mound sites in Italy, built by folk of the bronze age. Munro had dug lake dwells in Scotland and knew both themes at first hand.

He joins the deep stone age of France to the lake and mound homes of a later Europe. Tools, homes, and graves show how life grew from camp to town in slow steps. The book forms a bridge from man's first times to the prehistory of Europe as a whole.
my-novel-volume-08:
Edward Bulwer-Lytton's eighth book opens with a blast at loud progress. Trumpets and drums hail the March of Enlightenment, he writes. Yet light is noiseless, so why does this march clatter? He asks where Enlightenment is marching to at all.

Six loud fans would give six poor answers, he wagers. One slave cries for the Charter's seven points. One young French type wants free love and no prejudice. One plain rich man hopes for less and fears his errand boy. The chapter mocks cant about progress from all sides. Lytton's satire cuts reformers and snobs alike with a cool, amused hand.
nicoll-three-voyages-of-a-naturalist-190:
Michael Nicoll sailed the world to study birds and beasts, and met a monster on the way. Three Voyages of a Naturalist, printed in 1908, gathers his trips as a ship's naturalist. Nicoll was a trained observer with a name in the science of his day.

Off Brazil in 1905, from the yacht Valhalla, he and a mate watched a great sea serpent at close range. He tells the sighting with a field man's care for size, shape, and motion. Rupert Gould and others weighed the report as one of the best of its kind. The monster sits at the heart of a fine travel book.
ocean-of-story-kathasaritsagara-tawney-1:
The eighth volume of The Ocean of Story, in Penzer's edition of Tawney's Somadeva from 1924, nears the Kathasaritsagara's final books. The hero's marriages, wars, and wanderings among the Vidyadharas gather force here. Around him the tale streams still run thick with merchants, demons, and clever queens.

Penzer, by now deep in his ten-volume labor, annotates with a comparativist's full toolkit. Tawney's English stays lucid even where the Sanskrit delights in compounds and wordplay. The result serves two readers at once: the one lost in story, and the one tracing stories across the world. Volume eight rewards both. Its tales of the Vetala, the vampire riddler, are a set favorite.
openalex-w1599923008:
Ana Pilar Betrán, Ahmet Gülmezoglu, and co-authors wrote this review. It appeared in Reproductive Health in the year 2015. In 1985 the WHO set a guide rate for caesarean births. Rates above that guide lacked justification, the WHO said. World rates have climbed for three decades since then.

The team searched four databases for population level studies. Thousands of citations narrowed to eight included studies. Most linked higher caesarean rates to lower death rates. That link held only up to a modest threshold rate. After adjusting for wealth factors, the link weakened or vanished. Rates above the threshold brought no further gains, they report.
openalex-w2088190208:
Brian Lehmann, Joshua Bauer, Johanna Schafer and colleagues tested drug pairs for a breast cancer subtype. Their paper appeared in Breast Cancer Research in 2014. The subtype lacks three common drug targets. One group within it carries the androgen receptor. Those cancers often carry a key gene mutation.

The mutation switches on a growth pathway called PI3K. The team checked mutation rates in patient samples. Mutations were far more common in receptor-positive cases. They treated cancer cells with pathway blockers. Adding an androgen blocker strengthened the effect. Mouse tumour tests showed the same added benefit. The pair may suit patients whom chemotherapy fails. Targeted trials are the next step.
openalex-w2122737708:
Ricardo Esper, Roberto Nordaby, Jorge Vilariño, and colleagues published this review in Cardiovascular Diabetology in 2006. They give a full account of endothelial dysfunction, a failure of the thin cell layer that lines all blood vessels. That layer, the endothelium, helps control vessel widening, clotting, and swelling.

The review explains how the healthy endothelium senses physical and chemical signals and releases substances that keep balance. It then shows how heart risk factors and oxidative stress damage that control and start vessel disease. The authors also cover ways to test endothelial health, which rest largely on how much vessels widen in response to nitric oxide.
openalex-w2124463708:
Gisela De La Rosa, Jorge Donado, Alvaro Restrepo, and colleagues published this trial in Critical Care in 2008. They asked whether tight control of blood sugar with insulin helps very sick patients in a mixed medical and surgical intensive care unit. Earlier trials in single-type units had shown benefits, but mixed units were untested.

About five hundred patients were assigned by chance to tight or standard sugar control. Death rates after twenty-eight days did not differ in a meaningful way between the groups. Infection rates in the unit also showed no clear difference. Low blood sugar was much more common under tight control, so the stricter plan carried a real added risk here.
openalex-w2136326608:
América Mederos, Zully Ramos, and Georgget Banchero published this short report in Parasites and Vectors in 2014. They give the first report from Uruguay of worm resistance to monepantel, a sheep deworming drug. On two farms, egg counts in dung failed to fall after routine treatment, and lambs died from the blood-feeding worm Haemonchus contortus.

The team ran a standard egg count reduction test on both farms. Treated lambs were compared with untreated controls about a week after dosing. Egg counts barely fell on the first farm and fell only partly on the second. The resistant worms belonged to the Haemonchus group. The drug showed poor efficacy on both farms.
openalex-w2145617208:
Humberto Lara, Vanesa Ayala-Nunez, Liliana Ixtepan-Turrent, and Cristina Rodríguez-Padilla published this study in the Journal of Nanobiotechnology in 2010. Silver nanoparticles were already known to block HIV at doses that do not harm cells. The team set out to learn exactly how the particles attack the virus.

Using a panel of lab assays, they found the particles act mainly at an early stage. They bind to a coat protein on the virus and block its grip on the CD4 receptor of immune cells. That stops binding, fusion, and infection for free virus and virus passed between cells. The effect held across lab strains, patient isolates, and drug-resistant strains, and later stages were also inhibited.
openalex-w2151276208:
Lilian Bahia-Oliveira, Jeffrey Jones, Juliana Azevedo-Silva, and colleagues published this survey in Emerging Infectious Diseases in 2003. Reports of eye disease consistent with toxoplasmosis prompted a study in northern Rio de Janeiro state, Brazil. They measured how common Toxoplasma gondii infection was and what raised the risk.

Blood from more than fourteen hundred people was tested in 1997 to 1999. Infection was extremely common and rose steeply with age. After age adjustment, about eighty-four in a hundred people in the poorest group carried the parasite. Rates fell to about sixty-two in the middle group and twenty-three in the richest. The pattern points to waterborne spread hitting poorer households hardest.
openalex-w2161205508:
Kostas Tsigaridis, Nikos Daskalakis, Maria Kanakidou, and colleagues published this evaluation in Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics in 2014. The AeroCom project compared how global models simulate organic aerosol, tiny carbon-rich particles floating in the lower air. Such particles affect climate and health, yet models build them in very different ways.

Thirty-one global models joined the comparison. Their recipes varied hugely, from two to sixty-two particle species, with wide gaps in emissions and aging chemistry. Spread between models grew since earlier rounds, driven by more complex formation schemes and new, uncertain sources. Modeled particle amounts at different heights differed by more than tenfold between models. The authors flag that vertical spread as needing its own dedicated study.
openalex-w2762984108:
Derek P. Tittensor, Tyler D. Eddy, and Heike K. Lotze lead a large team presenting the Fish-MIP protocol in Geoscientific Model Development in 2018. Fish-MIP is the Fisheries and Marine Ecosystem Model Intercomparison Project. Climate science long ago learned to compare rival models side by side. Ocean models of fish and ecosystems had never had a shared comparison routine, despite rapid human-driven change at sea.

The protocol sets common rules so different marine models run the same future scenarios. Comparing outputs measures how much models disagree and where they agree. It also tests models against historical data and sharpens their development. Food security, biodiversity, and marine industries all depend on believable ocean projections. Fish-MIP belongs to a wider cross-sector network of climate impact modelers. Its ensemble approach aims to give decision-makers projections with honestly stated uncertainty.
openalex-w2776096008:
Rodrigo E. González-Reyes, Mauricio O. Nava-Mesa, and Karina Vargas-Sánchez, with colleagues, reviewed astrocytes in Alzheimer's disease in Frontiers in Molecular Neuroscience in 2017. Astrocytes are the brain's star-shaped support cells. Dementia affects over forty-six million people worldwide, and Alzheimer's causes most cases. Research long centered on neurons, but astrocytes shape inflammation and oxidative stress in the diseased brain.

The review gathers evidence on how astrocytes join the disease process. Reactive astrocytes feed the chronic inflammation seen around Alzheimer's lesions. They also handle, and sometimes worsen, oxidative damage from reactive molecules. Genetic risk factors like the APOE ε4 variant act partly through these cells. Viewing Alzheimer's through astrocytes widens the search for treatments beyond neurons. The authors map where this perspective is solid and where it needs testing.
openalex-w3004400108:
Lucía DeSoto, Maxime Cailleret, Frank Sterck, and colleagues published this study in Nature Communications in 2020. It links how well a tree bounces back from drought to its risk of dying later. Severe droughts cut forest growth and can trigger widespread tree death.

Most trees face several droughts in a lifetime, so recovery strength may decide long-term survival. Earlier work had hinted that weak recovery raises death risk, but proof was thin. The authors use growth records to measure resilience, meaning how fully a tree resumes its functions after a dry shock. They report that low growth resilience goes with higher future mortality risk. The finding could sharpen forest management under a changing climate.
openalex-w3122792808:
Diana Zeballos Rivas, Marinalda Lopez Jaldin, Blanca Nina Canaviri, and colleagues published this study in PLoS ONE in 2021. It surveys social media exposure and COVID-19 behavior in La Paz, Bolivia. The design is cross-sectional, taking one snapshot of the city's residents during the epidemic.

Social media spread information fast during the pandemic and could promote preventive behavior, yet the pathway was unclear. The authors set out to trace the links among media exposure, how risky people judged the virus, and what they actually did. Attitudes toward the measures were part of the chain as well. Local data of this kind help health officials decide whether social channels deserve trust as a tool for outbreak messaging.
openalex-w4220924308: Abdurro'uf, Katherine Accetta, Conny Aerts, and the Sloan Digital Sky Survey collaboration announce the survey's seventeenth data release. It completes the release of data from the MaNGA, MaStar, and APOGEE-2 survey programmes, and appeared in The Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series in 2022. The preserved sample holds only the publisher's citation page and author list. It has no readable abstract, so the release's contents cannot be detailed from it here.
openalex-w7204201608:
Railson Carneiro Amaral led a Portuguese-language systematic review, published in Brazil in 2026, on periodic eye injections of VEGF inhibitors for age-related macular degeneration. In the neovascular form of the disease, abnormal blood vessels grow under the macula, leaking fluid and blood and threatening central vision. Drugs that block the growth factor VEGF are injected into the eye to quiet those vessels. The review followed standard guidelines across three databases for the last ten years of studies.

The main agents reduced neovascular activity and preserved or improved visual acuity. A treat-and-extend schedule, which lengthens intervals when the eye stays quiet, gave favorable visual results with fewer visits. Longer-acting agents promised wider spacing still. The review weighs efficacy, safety, and treatment burden together.
openalex-w7204550808:
Gabriella da Silva Vizotto led a Portuguese-language review, in Brazil in 2026, on how social class shapes child development. Working qualitatively from two sources and papers released between 2020 and 2025. The team identified the social and economic factors that most directly influence growth, among them family income, housing problems, and access to health care.

Unequal access to schooling greatly affected school results, socialization, and future opportunities, the review finds. Children in vulnerable situations tended to show more difficulty with attention, memory, language, and emotional self-regulation, and the work reports strong effects on cognitive and emotional results. Social disparities compromise integral child development, the authors conclude, reinforcing the case for public policies that promote equity from the first years of life.
openalex-w7206191808:
Roseli Ferreira da Silva and four colleagues study how tutors experience competency-based training in Brazilian family health residencies. Three multiprofessional residency programs organize their teaching plans around integrated curricula, where subjects are joined together and learning is judged by real abilities rather than topics covered. The authors ran focus groups with twenty-three tutors and sorted what they said into themes.

Tutors described curricula that link theory with practice, mix professions, and use active learning methods, all fitted to the needs of Brazil's public health system. Daily tensions remain, though: keeping the written plan and actual teaching in line takes joint planning between tutors and preceptors, ongoing staff education, and thoughtful management. The study gives residency leaders an inside view of what makes this kind of curriculum hold together.
openalex-w7212426108:
Lorena Lavagnoli Ravagnani leads a team that counts cases of diabetes in pregnancy at a health group in Cascavel, Brazil. The group read charts from 2023 to 2025 at a joint health pact in the west of Parana state. In this form of diabetes, blood sugar first climbs while a child is in the womb, and can harm both mother and child. The team logged age, weight, sugar tests, and the births that came next.

Out of more than four thousand charts, about one in seven women had the disease. The women were, on the whole, in their late twenties and heavy by weight norms. Fasting sugar sat just past the safe line. High blood strain and a slow thyroid were the most seen side ills. Most women with the disease took insulin for the rest of the term. The counts give the pact a clear view of the load it holds.
openalex-w7213304208:
Alexandre Augusto Cesar Ferro Alves leads a team that built a lock-room game to teach med students how to take a case tale. The theme is the world of Harry Potter: spells, clues, and a ticking clock. To take a case tale well is a core skill. It is the talk in which a sick soul tells what ails them, and the healer sorts the tale. Class drills of it can feel flat, so a game was the bid to wake it up.

In the room, squads crack tasks that stand in for the steps of a good tale: ask, hear, note, and sort. Each lock that springs marks a step done right. The build is set out for schools to copy: cheap props, clear rules, and a debrief to tie the fun back to the wards.
openalex-w7213403208:
João Emmanuel de Sousa Lopes leads a large team reporting on health education tools built through university outreach. Their 2026 article describes materials made with communities in Brazil. Topics ranged from cancer care and shock warning signs to diabetes, nutrition, and lack of exercise.

The team produced folders, booklets, leaflets, and digital items reached by QR code. Activities took place in basic health units, schools, public spaces, and science events. A practical model guided how each tool was developed. The report presents outreach as a two-way link between university and community. Such tools, the authors argue, can support health promotion where people already live and learn.
openalex-w7214040608:
Romário Silva Ribeiro and Rozineide Iraci Pereira da Silva critically analyse teacher training rules in Brazilian professional and technological schooling. Their 2026 documentary study reads the federal institutes law, national guidelines, and official plans. Content analysis follows Bardin's three stages.

Expansion after the 2008 federal institutes law raised demands on teachers sharply. Many degree-holding teachers lack pedagogical training, while the law expects integrated curriculum and teaching across many levels. That mismatch is the structural contradiction of the title. Normative omissions on pedagogical formation leave the gap unclosed, they argue. Institutional policy, as written, asks more of teachers than it prepares them to deliver.
openalex-w7214124008:
Osenilda Francisca de Castro and Delner do Carmo Azevedo assess the Maria da Penha Law, nearly twenty years on. Brazil's 2006 law protects women in domestic and family violence. Their 2026 qualitative, bibliographic and documentary study uses doctrine, legislation, and official statistics from public security and family law bodies.

The law built one of the world's most advanced legal frameworks against gender violence, they argue. Recent laws made femicide an autonomous, heinous crime and widened electronic monitoring of aggressors. Yet 2025 and 2026 data show record femicide levels, fed by under-reporting, uneven local protection networks, and failed urgent protective measures. Effectiveness now depends on investment and reach, they conclude, more than on new rules.
openalex-w7220907508:
Ana Belle Barcelos Faria, Denison Melo de Aguiar, and Felipe Matheus de Assis Saraiva examine who controls ticket sales for the Parintins Folk Festival, in a 2026 law article. One company dominates sales for the famous festival, and the authors ask how far free enterprise can go when it shuts local people out of their own celebration.

Using case study and legal sources, they argue that business at the festival must respect the social function of free enterprise, consumer defense, and the constitutional right of access to culture. Concentrated sales, they conclude, can exclude the local community, which justifies state action to widen access. The paper frames a folk festival as a test of cultural rights.
original-short-stories-volume-08:
Seventeen short pieces make volume eight of Maupassant's Original Short Stories the largest in this run. It contains two of his most retold tales: My Uncle Jules and A Piece of String. The contents range over beggars, orphans, rabbits, fishing holes, and a parrot. The English translation is by McMaster, Henderson, and others.

The volume opens with Clochette, a narrator's confession that one memory will not leave him. As a boy of ten or twelve he knew Mother Bellflower, an old seamstress who came every Thursday to mend linen at his parents' country house. Decades of sinister sights since have not dimmed her face. Maupassant builds the tale on that haunting, moving from a child's-eye household to the sorrow the grown man finally understands.
osler-alabama-student-1908:
An Alabama Student, printed in 1908, collects William Osler's biographical essays on doctors and scientists. The title piece tells of a young medical man from Alabama. Around it stand lives of other figures Osler admired. He wrote such essays for years, as medicine's chief memorialist.

Each life mixes facts, character, and the feel of a working career. Osler hunts down letters, dates, and small human details with care. His aim was to give young doctors models worth following. The essays read as gracefully as short fiction. They also preserve figures who might else be forgotten. The volume shows his love of the profession's past.
pelham-volume-08:
Volume 8 of Pelham opens the final act with a detective's bargain. Mr. Job Jonson calls on Pelham and offers to unmask the real murderers of Sir John Tyrrell. He is sure Thornton and Dawson are guilty, but the work is dangerous, and his little family must be provided for.

Jonson produces a ready-drawn bond: three hundred a year if, within three days, his information brings the true criminals to punishment. Pelham signs with pleasure. The last volume trades on such seedy, comic machinery to clear the innocent and close Lytton's tale of fashion and crime.
perkins-discourse-damned-art-english-160:
William Perkins, the great Puritan theologian of Cambridge, wrote his Discourse of the Damned Art of Witchcraft late in life, and it appeared in 1608. Perkins sets out witchcraft so far as Scripture reveals it, no further and no less. His becomes the most influential English Reformed demonology of the age.

He defines the witch by her covenant with the devil. Good and bad witches alike fall under his condemnation, a hard point against village healers. His verdicts are measured in tone and severe in effect. Generations of English ministers preached Perkins on this subject. The book shows Puritan theology giving the witch trial its most respectable English foundation.
plaw-110-176-2008: How long the head of the Internal Revenue Service serves is clarified by Public Law 110-176. Approved on January 4, 2008, the act gives the Commissioner a five year term. Terms run back to back from a first term that began on November 13, 1997. A person named mid term serves only the rest of that term. The President may remove the Commissioner at will, and may name the same person again.
plaw-110-177-2008:
Guarding the people who run federal courts is the aim of Public Law 110-177, the Court Security Improvement Act of 2007. Congress approved it on January 7, 2008. Its purpose line names judges, prosecutors, witnesses, victims, and their families.

The first part shown deals with who sets guard needs for the courts. The Marshals Service must consult the Judicial Conference on an ongoing basis. Their talks cover staffing, program goals, and how guard funds are split. The topics run from court buildings to threats made against judges. Final say stays with the Marshals Service.
plaw-110-178-2008:
Merging two Capitol area police forces is carried out by Public Law 110-178, approved on January 7, 2008. Its long short title calls it the U.S. Capitol Police and Library of Congress Police Merger Implementation Act of 2007.

On a set transfer date, each Library of Congress Police employee moves to the Capitol Police. The Chief of the Capitol Police decides who becomes a sworn member and who becomes a civilian worker. For sworn posts, the Chief must certify in writing that the employee meets set tests. One test looks ahead to pension rights after the move.
plaw-110-179-2008:
Cheating to get disaster aid draws a new crime under Public Law 110-179, approved on January 7, 2008. Its short title is the Emergency and Disaster Assistance Fraud Penalty Enhancement Act of 2007. The act adds a section to chapter 47 of title 18.

The crime covers a person who knowingly hides a key fact, or makes a false claim, in a matter tied to disaster aid. The aid must link to a major disaster or emergency declared under the Stafford Act. Fraud tied to contracts for goods or services after such a declaration counts as well. The sample cuts off mid section.
plaw-110-181-2008:
Authorizing the armed forces for fiscal year 2008 is the work of Public Law 110-181, the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2008. Congress approved it on January 28, 2008. The act enacts an earlier enrolled bill, with some changes noted at its head.

Those changes touch court rules on seizing property in some judgments against Iraq. They also touch lapsed powers to pay bonuses and special pays to service members. The act has three parts, for the Defense Department, for building projects, and for Energy Department security work. A joint statement from the earlier bill counts as part of its history.
plaw-110-182-2008: Fifteen more days for a spy law is all that Public Law 110-182 provides. Approved on January 31, 2008, the act extends the Protect America Act of 2007. It does so by changing one number in that law, from 180 days to 195 days. No other text appears in the act. That short span is the whole change made by this act.
plaw-110-183-2008:
Marking two hundred years since the ban on the slave trade is the purpose behind Public Law 110-183. Approved on February 5, 2008, the act sets up the Commission on the Abolition of the Transatlantic Slave Trade.

The findings trace the ban's history. President Thomas Jefferson signed the ban bill on March 2, 1807, and it took effect on January 1, 1808. A law of 1820 then made slave trading a form of piracy for United States citizens. The act says the trade seized, bought, and shipped Africans, mostly from West and Central Africa, to the Americas. The sample ends in the findings.
plaw-110-184-2008: Taft, California has a renamed post office under Public Law 110-184, approved on February 6, 2008. The site at 427 North Street is now the Larry S. Pierce Post Office. Any mention of that site in a law, map, rule, or other federal record now counts as a mention of the site under its new name.
plaw-110-185-2008:
Boosting a weak economy is the stated goal of Public Law 110-185, the Economic Stimulus Act of 2008. Congress approved it on February 13, 2008. The act works through tax rebates, business tax breaks, and higher loan limits.

The first title gives 2008 recovery rebates to individuals. It also raises the amount firms may write off at once for some gear, and adds a special allowance for gear bought in 2008. A second title raises, for a time, the loan limits for Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and the Federal Housing Administration. A third title marks the whole act as an emergency measure.
plaw-110-186-2008:
Small firms run by veterans and reservists get expanded help under Public Law 110-186, approved on February 14, 2008. Its short title is long, the Military Reservist and Veteran Small Business Reauthorization and Opportunity Act of 2008.

The contents list starts with more funds for the Office of Veterans Business Development. It adds a joint agency task force, makes a veterans business advice panel permanent, and calls for more outreach centers. A study must find gaps in where those centers sit. Later parts cover loans for reservists, some with no collateral, and loan priority.
plaw-110-187-2008:
Phone numbers on the federal do-not-call list no longer expire under Public Law 110-187, the Do-Not-Call Improvement Act of 2007. Approved on February 15, 2008, the act bars the automatic removal of a listed number. A number leaves the list only at the owner's request, or under the act's cleanup rule.

The trade agency must check the list on a regular basis and drop numbers that were cut off and given to someone else, or that are not valid. It must also report to Congress within nine months on steps to make the list more accurate.
plaw-110-188-2008: Fees that fund the do-not-call list are kept going by Public Law 110-188, the Do-Not-Call Registry Fee Extension Act of 2007. Approved on February 15, 2008, the act lets the trade agency charge each year for access to the list. The yearly fee is the lesser of $54 for each area code used, or $14,850 for all area codes. No fee is charged for the first five area codes a person uses.
plaw-110-189-2008:
Child deaths in and around cars are the target of Public Law 110-189, approved on February 28, 2008. It is the Cameron Gulbransen Kids Transportation Safety Act of 2007, also called the K.T. Safety Act of 2007. The act orders new safety rules for light motor vehicles.

The first rule topic shown is power windows. Within eighteen months, the transport chief must start weighing a rule that windows reverse on their own when blocked. That change could keep children from being trapped or killed. A final call is due within thirty months, with a public report if no rule is set.
plaw-110-190-2008: Airport funds get a short extension from Public Law 110-190, the Airport and Airway Extension Act of 2008. Approved on February 28, 2008, the act moves the end date for fuel and ticket taxes from February 29, 2008 to June 30, 2008. It also moves the power to spend from the airport trust fund from March 1, 2008 to July 1, 2008. Both changes took effect on March 1, 2008.
plaw-110-191-2008: Trade benefits for Andean goods run longer under Public Law 110-191, the Andean Trade Preference Extension Act of 2008. Approved on February 29, 2008, the act moves the program end date from February 29, 2008 to December 31, 2008. It also stretches the time spans that govern how some clothing goods are treated. In a side change, two end dates for customs user fees move from December 13, 2014 to December 27, 2014.
plaw-110-192-2008: Minting certain one dollar coins through 2008 is kept alive by Public Law 110-192, approved on February 29, 2008. The act says a clause of the coin law, as it stood before Public Law 110-82, stays in effect. It does so despite a change made by section 3 of that 2007 law. The clause stays until a second change, in section 2 of the same law, takes effect.
plaw-110-193-2008: Wording fixes to the federal pesticide law make up Public Law 110-193, approved on March 6, 2008. The act makes what it calls technical corrections to the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act. Much of the text swaps the word waiver for exemption, for fees on minor use pesticide requests. It also changes the year 2008 to 2012 in one fee part. The changes took effect on October 1, 2007.
plaw-110-194-2008: East Hampstead, New Hampshire honors an Army captain in Public Law 110-194, approved on March 11, 2008. The post office at 59 Colby Corner is designated the Captain Jonathan D. Grassbaugh Post Office. Under the second part, federal records that mention that site are read as using the Grassbaugh name. The act's own heading adds the word Building, though the name it sets does not.
plaw-110-195-2008: Memory of a postal worker killed on duty shapes Public Law 110-195, approved on March 12, 2008. The Southpark Station in Alexandria, Louisiana is designated the John 'Marty' Thiels Southpark Station. The title states the honor is for Thiels, who was killed in the line of duty on October 4, 2007. Later mentions of the station in federal records are read under the Thiels name.
plaw-110-196-2008:
Farm programs near their end date get a few more weeks from Public Law 110-196, approved on March 14, 2008. The act extends programs under the Farm Security and Rural Investment Act of 2002. It also suspends older permanent price support powers past that date, per its title.

The programs keep running, as they stood on September 30, 2007, until April 18, 2008. Three conservation programs are named with yearly funding levels. They cover farmland protection, ground and surface water, and wildlife habitat. A short list of laws is left out of the extension. Each keeps its stated yearly level during the added weeks.
plaw-110-197-2008: John W. McCarter of Illinois joined the Smithsonian board under Public Law 110-197, approved on March 14, 2008. The joint resolution filled a vacancy in the group of regents who are not members of Congress. The seat had opened when the term of Walter E. Massey of Georgia ended. McCarter's term runs six years from the day the resolution took effect.
plaw-110-198-2008: One more month for college aid programs comes from Public Law 110-198, the Higher Education Extension Act of 2008. Approved on March 24, 2008, the act moves an end date in the 2005 extension law from March 31, 2008 to April 30, 2008. A guard clause adds that nothing here trims the funds or time spans set by two other laws. Those laws are the 2005 reconciliation act and the College Cost Reduction and Access Act.
plaw-110-199-2008:
Helping people leaving prison avoid a return to crime is the aim of Public Law 110-199. Its full title is the Second Chance Act of 2007: Community Safety Through Recidivism Prevention. Congress approved it on April 9, 2008.

The act renews a grant program for offender reentry in the 1968 crime control law. The contents list renews state and local demo projects for adults and youth. It also improves live-in drug treatment for state offenders. New ideas in the list include reentry courts for state, tribal, and local use. The sample ends within that list.
plaw-110-200-2008: Seven more days for farm programs come from Public Law 110-200, approved on April 18, 2008. The act amends Public Law 110-196, the short farm extension passed a month earlier. It moves the end date in two places, from April 18, 2008 to April 25, 2008. The change took effect on April 18 itself. Nothing else in the earlier act is altered by this brief text.
plaw-110-201-2008: Judgeships on the Superior Court of the District of Columbia are the subject of Public Law 110-201. Approved on April 18, 2008, the act carries a title about keeping the court's current judgeships. Its one operative line changes a number in the District code. The count in the court's composition section rises from fifty-eight to sixty-one. That single word swap is the whole law.
plaw-110-202-2008:
Falls among older adults draw federal action in Public Law 110-202, the Safety of Seniors Act of 2007. Congress approved it on April 23, 2008. The act directs the health chief to expand research and related work on elder falls. It amends the Public Health Service Act.

The health chief may back a national teaching campaign, run by a nonprofit group with skill in injury prevention work. The lessons target older adults, their families, and health care providers. Grants may fund state level groups that run local versions. The sample ends as a research part begins.
plaw-110-203-2008: One hundred years of the Army Reserve are marked by Public Law 110-203, approved on April 23, 2008. The joint resolution congratulates the force on its centennial, marked that same day. Its opening clauses trace the start to a 1905 message from President Theodore Roosevelt. A draft bill from War Secretary William Howard Taft and General Leonard Wood followed that year. Congress then set up the first federal reserve force in a law signed on April 23, 1908. The sample ends among those history clauses.
plaw-110-204-2008:
Testing newborns for hidden disorders is strengthened by Public Law 110-204, the Newborn Screening Saves Lives Act of 2007. Congress approved it on April 24, 2008. The act amends the Public Health Service Act and sets up grant programs.

Grants go to groups that help state and local health agencies screen, counsel, and care for babies at risk. Other grants train health workers and lab staff in screening and in new tests. Teaching programs for parents and support groups are covered too, at reading levels they can use. The sample ends as a tracking system is described.
plaw-110-205-2008: Another week for farm programs is granted by Public Law 110-205, approved on April 25, 2008. The act amends Public Law 110-196 as already amended once before. It moves the end date in two places, from April 25, 2008 to May 2, 2008. The change took effect on April 25 itself. The text is a date swap and nothing more.
plaw-110-206-2008:
Brain injury programs are reshaped by Public Law 110-206, the Traumatic Brain Injury Act of 2008. Congress approved it on April 28, 2008. The act promises, in its purpose line, to expand and improve such programs. It amends part J of the Public Health Service Act.

Early parts mostly move and renumber sections, sorting rape prevention, brain injury prevention, and registries into a new order. A later part shifts a data source for prevention work, from hospitals and trauma centers to hospitals and emergency departments. The national program heading gains the word surveillance. The sample ends mid grant text.
plaw-110-207-2008: Spouses and siblings of Purple Heart holders may join their order as associate members under Public Law 110-207. Approved on April 30, 2008, the act is called the Purple Heart Family Equity Act of 2007. It revises the federal charter of the Military Order of the Purple Heart. The change is one line. Where the charter listed parents and lineal descendants, it now lists parents, spouse, siblings, and lineal descendants.
plaw-110-208-2008: Two more weeks for farm programs come from Public Law 110-208, approved on May 2, 2008. The act amends Public Law 110-196 as amended by the two prior short extensions. It moves the end date in two places, from May 2, 2008 to May 16, 2008. The text gives an effective date of April 25, 2008, a week before its own approval. The act is a date swap and nothing more.
plaw-110-209-2008:
Awarding a congressional gold medal to Daw Aung San Suu Kyi is the act taken by Public Law 110-209. Congress approved it on May 6, 2008. The title cites her brave, steady work for peace, nonviolence, human rights, and democracy in Burma.

The findings tell her story from her birth in Rangoon in 1945. She called for free elections in 1988 and helped form the National League for Democracy. The league won most votes in an open election, which the ruling junta voided. She stayed under house arrest for years, won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1991, and gave its money to a health and schooling fund.
plaw-110-210-2008: Port Jervis, New York sees its post office renamed by Public Law 110-210, approved on May 7, 2008. The Postal Service site at 20 Sussex Street is designated the E. Arthur Gray Post Office Building. Section two then treats later mentions of that site, in any federal law or record, as mentions of it by the Gray name.
plaw-110-211-2008: Elizabeth City honors a doctor in Public Law 110-211, approved on May 7, 2008. The post office at 1704 Weeksville Road in North Carolina is designated the Dr. Clifford Bell Jones, Sr. Post Office. Later federal maps, rules, and records that point to that site are read as pointing to it by the Jones name instead.
plaw-110-212-2008: Lula, Georgia has a post office named for a private in Public Law 110-212, approved on May 7, 2008. The site at 5815 McLeod Street is designated the Private Johnathon Millican Lula Post Office. The second part of the act reads later mentions of that site, across federal records, as mentions under the Millican name.
plaw-110-213-2008: Waco, Texas honors an Army private first class in Public Law 110-213, approved on May 7, 2008. The post office at 424 Clay Avenue is designated the Army PFC Juan Alonso Covarrubias Post Office Building. Any later mention of that Texas site in a federal law, map, or record counts as a mention by the Covarrubias name.
plaw-110-214-2008: Goldsboro names a post office building in Public Law 110-214, approved on May 7, 2008. The site at 3100 Cashwell Drive in North Carolina is designated the John Henry Wooten, Sr. Post Office Building. The act's second part ties the name to later use, so federal records that cite that site cite the Wooten name.
plaw-110-215-2008: Cleveland, Georgia honors a sergeant in Public Law 110-215, approved on May 7, 2008. The post office at 116 Helen Highway is designated the Sgt. Jason Harkins Post Office Building. From approval on, federal laws, maps, and records that mention that site are understood to mean the building by the Harkins name. The act changes the name only, and nothing about mail service there.
plaw-110-216-2008: Fort Worth, Texas honors a master sergeant in Public Law 110-216, approved on May 7, 2008. The Postal Service site at 3701 Altamesa Boulevard is designated the Master Sergeant Kenneth N. Mack Post Office Building. The act's second part deems later mentions of that site, in federal laws and records alike, to be mentions under the Mack name.
plaw-110-217-2008: Lebanon, Missouri gives a carrier annex a personal name in Public Law 110-217, approved on May 7, 2008. The Postal Service site at 701 East Copeland Drive is designated the Steve W. Allee Carrier Annex. References to that site in United States laws, maps, and records are then treated as references to the annex by the Allee name.
plaw-110-218-2008: Lithonia, Georgia honors an Army specialist through Public Law 110-218, approved on May 7, 2008. The post office at 3035 Stone Mountain Street is designated the Specialist Jamaal RaShard Addison Post Office Building. Its references part reads any later citation of that Georgia site, in a law or other record, as a citation of the Addison building.
plaw-110-219-2008: Roanoke Rapids honors a judge in Public Law 110-219, approved on May 7, 2008. The Postal Service site at 725 Roanoke Avenue in North Carolina is designated the Judge Richard B. Allsbrook Post Office. After approval, a mention of that site in federal papers, maps, or rules counts as a mention of the post office under the Allsbrook name.
plaw-110-220-2008: Lakewood, Colorado names a post office building in Public Law 110-220, approved on May 7, 2008. The site at 10799 West Alameda Avenue is designated the Felix Sparks Post Office Building. Section two of the short act then ties that name to later use. Federal laws, maps, and documents that cite the site are taken to cite the Sparks building.
plaw-110-221-2008: Louisville honors its fallen service members in Public Law 110-221, approved on May 7, 2008. The post office at 3050 Hunsinger Lane in Kentucky is designated the Iraq and Afghanistan Fallen Military Heroes of Louisville Memorial Post Office Building. The title states the honor is for local men and women who died in service during Operation Enduring Freedom and Operation Iraqi Freedom. Federal records citing the site then cite that memorial name.
plaw-110-222-2008: Derby, Kansas honors a sergeant in Public Law 110-222, approved on May 7, 2008. The Postal Service site at 201 West Greenway Street is designated the Sergeant Jamie O. Maugans Post Office Building. The short act's second part makes the name govern later use. A citation of that site in a federal law, map, or paper means the Maugans building.
plaw-110-223-2008: Beaverton, Oregon names a post office for a major in Public Law 110-223, approved on May 7, 2008. The site at 3800 SW. 185th Avenue is designated the Major Arthur Chin Post Office Building. Later mentions of the site in United States laws, maps, regulations, and records are deemed mentions of the building under the Chin name.
plaw-110-224-2008: Chagrin Falls, Ohio honors a sergeant in Public Law 110-224, approved on May 7, 2008. The post office at 160 East Washington Street is designated the Sgt. Michael M. Kashkoush Post Office Building. Under part two, federal records that refer to that site refer to it by the Kashkoush name from approval onward. The name is the only change the act makes.
plaw-110-225-2008: Indianapolis names a post office for Julia M. Carson in Public Law 110-225, approved on May 7, 2008. The site at 2650 Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Street is designated the Julia M. Carson Post Office Building. The act then provides that references to that site in federal laws, maps, and records are references to the Carson building.
plaw-110-226-2008: Gloucester, Virginia honors a congresswoman in Public Law 110-226, approved on May 7, 2008. The post office at 6892 Main Street is designated the Congresswoman Jo Ann S. Davis Post Office. The second section ties future use to that honor. Any federal law, map, or record that mentions the site is read as naming the Davis post office.
plaw-110-227-2008:
Keeping federal student loans within reach is the purpose of Public Law 110-227, approved on May 7, 2008. Its heading in the text calls it the Ensuring Continued Access to Student Loans Act of 2008. Oddly, its first section says this title, not this act, may be cited by that name.

The part shown raises loan limits under the Stafford loan program in the Higher Education Act. Graduate and professional students may borrow the base amount plus added sums, the text states. One added sum is given for coursework tied to teaching paths. The sample cuts off deep inside the limit rules, with exceptions still being spelled out.
plaw-110-228-2008:
Longer leases on tribal land are allowed by Public Law 110-228, approved on May 8, 2008. The land belongs to the Mashantucket Pequot (Western) Tribe. Leases are made for the tribe by its tribal corporation, under a 1934 law.

A lease may now carry an option to renew for up to two added terms. Each added term may run up to twenty-five years, with only tribal council approval needed. The United States is not liable for any loss from such a renewal. No gaming may be run on land leased with such an option.
plaw-110-229-2008:
Dozens of land and park items are bundled in Public Law 110-229, the Consolidated Natural Resources Act of 2008. Congress approved it on May 8, 2008. The act covers programs in the Interior Department, the Forest Service, and the Energy Department.

The contents list opens with Forest Service items, such as the Wild Sky Wilderness. It names a trail in Oregon's Willamette forest for Jim Weaver, a former House member. Land bureau items cover two light stations and a Nevada National Guard land transfer. Park Service items start with joint deals to guard park resources. The sample ends within the contents list.
plaw-110-230-2008: College programs get a further month from Public Law 110-230, approved on May 13, 2008. The act extends programs under the Higher Education Act of 1965 for a time. It changes a date in the 2005 extension law, from April 30, 2008 to May 31, 2008. The change counts as if it took effect on April 30, 2008. A guard clause keeps in place the funds and time spans set by the 2005 reconciliation act and the College Cost Reduction and Access Act.
plaw-110-231-2008: Farm programs get their last short bridge from Public Law 110-231, approved on May 18, 2008. The act amends Public Law 110-196 as amended three times before. The end date now reads the earlier of May 23, 2008, or the day the Food, Conservation, and Energy Act of 2008 is enacted. That new farm law is named in both places where the date is changed.
plaw-110-232-2008:
Adding oil to the national reserve is paused by Public Law 110-232, approved on May 19, 2008. Its short title is the Strategic Petroleum Reserve Fill Suspension and Consumer Protection Act of 2008. The pause runs from enactment through the end of 2008.

Two cabinet chiefs must halt buying oil for the reserve. The Interior chief stops the royalty in kind route, and the Energy chief stops all other routes. Buying may restart in 2008 only after the President tells Congress one fact. The average oil price for the most recent ninety days must be seventy-five dollars a barrel or less.
plaw-110-233-2008:
Genetic bias in health cover and jobs is barred by Public Law 110-233, approved on May 21, 2008. It is the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act of 2008. Congress set the ban out in titles on each of those two fields.

The health title amends pension, health, tax, and Social Security laws, and adds privacy and secrecy rules. The jobs title defines key terms and then sets practice rules. They bind employers, job agencies, labor groups, and training programs. Other parts cover how genetic facts must be kept secret, and what a wronged person may do. The sample shows the contents list.
plaw-110-234-2008:
Farm policy for five years is set by Public Law 110-234, the Food, Conservation, and Energy Act of 2008. Congress approved it on May 22, 2008. Its purpose line keeps farm programs going through fiscal year 2012.

The contents list opens with commodity programs. They cover direct payments and extra payments that rise when crop prices fall. Rules follow for base acres, payment yields, and planting freedom. One new path lets growers choose a revenue based program instead. Loan help for crops comes next, with loan rates and terms. The sample ends inside that first title.
plaw-110-235-2008: Small business programs run about ten months longer under Public Law 110-235, approved on May 23, 2008. The act extends programs under the Small Business Act and the Small Business Investment Act of 1958. It changes one date wherever it appears in a 2006 extension law. May 23, 2008 becomes March 20, 2009. The change took effect on May 22, 2008, the day before approval.
plaw-110-236-2008:
Settling a land suit between a tribe and a county is carried out by Public Law 110-236. Congress approved it on May 27, 2008. The act ratifies a transfer of part of the Jicarilla Apache Reservation to Rio Arriba County, New Mexico.

The opening definitions set the scene. A settlement deal was signed by the nation's president and the county board chair in May 2003, and approved by the Interior Department that June. It settled a suit filed in state court in October 1987. Land added to the reservation in 1988, known locally as the Theis Ranch, is also defined. The sample ends among the definitions.
plaw-110-237-2008: Funding figures in the newborn screening law are corrected by Public Law 110-237, approved on May 27, 2008. The act makes technical corrections to the Newborn Screening Saves Lives Act of 2007, passed weeks earlier in this same slice of laws. It restates the grant funding levels year by year. For each grant group, the level starts in fiscal year 2009 and rises in small steps through fiscal year 2013. A second part restates smaller sums for judging how well the screening work performs. Later fixes shift years in an advisory panel's rules from 2007 to 2008.
plaw-110-238-2008: College programs get another month from Public Law 110-238, approved on May 30, 2008. The act extends programs under the Higher Education Act of 1965 for a time. It changes the date in the 2005 extension law from May 31, 2008 to June 30, 2008. A guard clause protects funds and time spans set by three other laws. The third law named is the student loan act passed earlier that May.
plaw-110-239-2008: Father's Day joins the list of days when flag display is urged, under Public Law 110-239. Approved on June 3, 2008, the act amends title 4 of the United States Code, the part on the flag. It adds one short entry after Flag Day, June 14. The new entry reads Father's Day, third Sunday in June. That single insertion is the whole act.
plaw-110-240-2008:
Missing children are the concern of Public Law 110-240, the Protecting Our Children Comes First Act of 2007. Congress approved it on June 3, 2008. The act provides funds under the Missing Children's Assistance Act, per its purpose line.

New findings open the act. Each year, thousands of children are taken from a parent with legal custody, in ways that put them in grave danger. Many face harm or sexual exploitation, and parents and local police often lack the means for wide searches. Children are moved from place to place, so levels of police must work together. The sample ends within the findings.
plaw-110-241-2008:
Card receipts that still showed an expiry date drew hundreds of suits, and Public Law 110-241 responds. It is the Credit and Debit Card Receipt Clarification Act of 2007, approved on June 3, 2008. The act clarifies a term in the Fair Credit Reporting Act.

The findings recount a 2003 law meant to cut identity theft. Shops had to print no more than the last five digits of a card number, and no expiry date, on receipts. Many shops thought cutting the number was enough. Suits then called the printed date a willful breach, though none claimed harm to a shopper's identity, the act states.
plaw-110-242-2008: Year labels in a visa rule for some Iraqis are corrected by Public Law 110-242, approved on June 3, 2008. The act makes technical corrections to the defense law for fiscal year 2008. That law grants special immigrant status to certain Iraqis. Phrases that counted years from the act's passage are swapped for plain fiscal years. The span becomes fiscal years 2008 through 2012, with later parts running into 2013. A second part gives power to convert petitions during a changeover period, though the sample cuts off there.
plaw-110-243-2008:
Fish that move across Arctic waters should be managed by agreement, says Public Law 110-243. The joint resolution, approved on June 3, 2008, directs the United States to open talks with other nations. The goal is a deal on migratory and cross boundary fish stocks in the Arctic Ocean.

The opening clauses give the reasons. Valuable fish stocks have fallen across the world, and warming seas may push fish into Arctic waters that were once too cold. Fishing already goes on in named Arctic seas, yet data on the stocks is thin. Native towns on the coast depend on small scale fishing to live, the text adds.
plaw-110-244-2008:
Fixing a giant highway law takes a law of its own, Public Law 110-244. It is the SAFETEA-LU Technical Corrections Act of 2008, approved on June 6, 2008. The act corrects the Safe, Accountable, Flexible, Efficient Transportation Equity Act: A Legacy for Users.

The contents list for highway fixes runs long. Items cover magnetic levitation trains, key national projects, and facilities that cut truck idling. Other items fix road names, project lists, and research funds. One item defines a repeat intoxicated driver law, and one takes funds back. The sample shows only part of the long contents list.
plaw-110-245-2008:
Tax help for service members is gathered in Public Law 110-245, approved on June 17, 2008. Its short title is the Heroes Earnings Assistance and Relief Tax Act of 2008. The act amended the Internal Revenue Code of 1986.

The contents list for the military title runs through many breaks. It gives the 2008 recovery rebate to military families and lets combat pay count as earned income for a tax credit. Other items cover home loan bonds for veterans and pay for survivors. Rules on retirement plan payouts for people called to active duty are listed too. The sample ends within that list.
plaw-110-246-2008:
A second farm act with the same name appears as Public Law 110-246, approved on June 18, 2008. It is again the Food, Conservation, and Energy Act of 2008. This version speaks of farm and other programs of the Department of Agriculture, kept going through fiscal year 2012.

Its contents list matches the first act's list from the title on commodity programs onward. Direct payments, payments that rise as prices fall, base acres, and loan help all appear again. Two early items set this act apart. One covers an explanatory statement, and one repeals a duplicative enactment. The sample ends inside the first title.
plaw-110-247-2008:
Surplus federal food should go to hungry people, under Public Law 110-247. It is the Federal Food Donation Act of 2008, approved on June 20, 2008. The act works through contracts that agencies sign for the supply, service, or sale of food.

The stated purpose is to urge agencies and their contractors to give excess food away, as far as is practical and safe. The donees are nonprofit groups that aid people with shaky access to enough safe, healthy food. Excess food is food an agency does not need and would otherwise throw out. The sample ends as a rule writing duty begins.
plaw-110-248-2008: State and local buyers may use federal price lists for safety gear under Public Law 110-248. Approved on June 26, 2008, the Local Preparedness Acquisition Act amends title 40 of the United States Code. It adds a group of goods to the lists such buyers may use. The group covers alarm and signal systems and systems that run buildings. It also covers firefighting and rescue gear, police and security gear, marine craft, and special work clothing, plus related services.
plaw-110-249-2008: Four lots near the International Center may be leased to private hands under Public Law 110-249. Approved on June 26, 2008, the act amends the International Center Act. The lots are District of Columbia tax lots 803 through 806, within the center area. They may be leased or subleased to a group that is not a foreign government or a world body. One guard applies. The Secretary keeps the right to approve who moves in and what use is made of the land.
plaw-110-250-2008: Mutual aid deals around the capital are reformed in wording by Public Law 110-250, approved on June 26, 2008. The act amends a part of the Intelligence Reform and Terrorism Prevention Act of 2004 on the National Capital Region. One change widens a key term to cover any town, agency, authority, or body in the region that can sue or be sued in its own name. Other changes drop two named transit and airport bodies from one clause. They also add agents next to employees in a third clause.
plaw-110-251-2008:
Service members seeking citizenship get a shortcut on fingerprints under Public Law 110-251. It is the Kendell Frederick Citizenship Assistance Act, approved on June 26, 2008. Its purpose line promises help for armed forces members who seek United States citizenship.

The homeland security chief must reuse prints given at enlistment, or with a status filing, for background checks on a citizenship plea. Set tests apply. The person must qualify for citizenship through service, and must have been printed by the Defense Department at enlistment. The plea must also come within twenty-four months of enlistment. The sample ends within those tests.
plaw-110-252-2008:
Extra spending for the year ending September 30, 2008 is granted by Public Law 110-252. It is the Supplemental Appropriations Act, 2008, approved on June 30, 2008. The opening line of the bill names military building, veterans affairs, and related agencies.

The first title covers military building, veterans, foreign affairs, and other security matters. Its first chapter adds large sums for a food aid grant program, in two parts. One part is open at once, and one opens on October 1, 2008. A justice chapter then adds funds for an inspector general's office and for legal work. The sample ends inside that chapter.
plaw-110-253-2008: Airport taxes get three more months from Public Law 110-253, the Federal Aviation Administration Extension Act of 2008. Approved on June 30, 2008, the act moves the end date for fuel and ticket taxes from June 30, 2008 to September 30, 2008. It moves the power to spend from the airport trust fund from July 1, 2008 to October 1, 2008. The tax changes took effect on July 1, 2008.
plaw-110-254-2008: A federal charter for Korean War veterans is granted by Public Law 110-254, approved on June 30, 2008. The act adds a new chapter to title 36 for the Korean War Veterans Association, Incorporated. The group is a nonprofit body formed under New York law. Its charter chapter lists parts on purpose, membership, and its governing body. It also covers powers, limits, records, and a yearly report. One part makes tax exempt status a condition of the charter itself.
plaw-110-255-2008:
Diesel cleanup projects may be accepted in legal settlements under Public Law 110-255, approved on June 30, 2008. The act lets the head of the Environmental Protection Agency accept such projects. They form part of a deal over claimed breaches of environmental law.

Four tests apply. The project must guard health or nature, and must relate to the claimed breach. It must not be work the defendant had to do anyway. It must not fund agency staff or its own operations. In the deal papers, the defendant must certify, under penalty of law, that it would have done a like valued project of another kind.
plaw-110-256-2008: College programs get a further month from Public Law 110-256, approved on June 30, 2008. The act extends programs under the Higher Education Act of 1965 for a time. It changes the date in the 2005 extension law from June 30, 2008 to July 31, 2008. A guard clause protects funds and time spans set by three other laws. Those laws cover tax based aid changes, college cost cuts, and student loan access.
plaw-110-257-2008:
Members of the African National Congress gain relief from old terror labels under Public Law 110-257. Congress approved the act on July 1, 2008. One part adds the group's name to an exemption list in a 2008 spending law.

A second part lets the Secretary of State, or the homeland security chief, waive set entry bars for a person. The waiver covers acts done with the group while fighting apartheid rule in South Africa. Each chief must consult the other top officials first. Congress adds that the power should be used at once, where fitting, for past and present South African officials. A third part starts on clearing names from government data lists.
plaw-110-258-2008: Four names are added to a voting rights law's honor roll by Public Law 110-258, approved on July 1, 2008. The act revises the short title of the 2006 voting rights renewal act. After Coretta Scott King, the title now adds Cesar E. Chavez, Barbara C. Jordan, William C. Velasquez, and Dr. Hector P. Garcia. They join Fannie Lou Hamer and Rosa Parks, who were already named. Matching changes are made in the Voting Rights Act itself. A final clause keeps old dates tied to the 2006 act as first passed.
plaw-110-259-2008:
A Capitol artist dead for over a century is honored by Public Law 110-259, approved on July 1, 2008. The act awards a congressional gold medal, after his death, to Constantino Brumidi. Findings trace a life that began in Rome in 1805.

Brumidi became a United States citizen and, from 1855, painted rooms across the Capitol. His peak work was The Apotheosis of Washington, finished in 1865 in the eye of the dome. He placed Crispus Attucks at the center of a Boston Massacre scene in 1871. He began the Rotunda frieze at age seventy-two and died in 1880, months after a fall from a scaffold.
plaw-110-260-2008:
Honoring a Senate pioneer is the work of Public Law 110-260, approved on July 1, 2008. Its short title is the Edward William Brooke III Congressional Gold Medal Act. The title cites his unmatched, lasting service to the nation.

The findings say Brooke was the first African American elected by popular vote to the Senate. He served two terms, from 1967 to 1979. Before that, he chaired the Boston Finance Commission and fought graft there. In 1962 he became the first African American state attorney general in the country, in Massachusetts. He won in a strongly Democratic state, as a Republican. The sample ends within the findings.
plaw-110-261-2008:
Wiretap rules for foreign spying are rewritten by Public Law 110-261, approved on July 10, 2008. It is the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act of 1978 Amendments Act of 2008, or the FISA Amendments Act of 2008.

The contents list for the first title adds steps for gaining foreign intelligence from some persons outside the country. It names court orders, their filing with Congress, and rules for using what is gathered. Other items cover physical searches, emergency tracing devices, and the special court for such cases. A second title covers protections for phone and internet firms. The sample ends within the contents list.
plaw-110-262-2008: Brooklyn's bankruptcy courthouse takes a judge's name in Public Law 110-262, approved on July 15, 2008. The courthouse at 271 Cadman Plaza East in New York is designated the Conrad B. Duberstein United States Bankruptcy Courthouse. Later references to that courthouse in federal laws, maps, and records are deemed references to it by the Duberstein name.
plaw-110-263-2008:
An Arkansas lock and dam takes an engineer's name in Public Law 110-263, approved on July 15, 2008. Lock and Dam No. 5 of the McClellan-Kerr Arkansas River Navigation System, near Redfield, is redesignated for Colonel Charles D. Maynard.

The findings praise a long career. Maynard served as an engineer officer in World War II and later oversaw the huge Arkansas River Project build of the early 1960s. As Little Rock district engineer for three years, he led work on thirteen locks and dams. He served twenty-one years on the state waterways panel, named by three governors.
plaw-110-264-2008: Murrieta, California names a Border Patrol station for two men in Public Law 110-264. Approved on July 15, 2008, the act covers the station at 25762 Madison Avenue. It is designated the Theodore L. Newton, Jr. and George F. Azrak Border Patrol Station. Federal laws and records that cite the station then cite it under both names, per the act's second part.
plaw-110-265-2008: Lorena, Texas honors a Marine gunnery sergeant in Public Law 110-265, approved on July 15, 2008. The post office at 1190 Lorena Road is designated the Marine Gunnery Sgt. John D. Fry Post Office Building. The act then deems a mention of that site, in any federal law or record, to be a mention of the Fry building.
plaw-110-266-2008: Port Angeles names its federal building in Public Law 110-266, approved on July 15, 2008. The building stands at 138 West First Street in Washington, an address given in the act's text though not in its title. It is designated the Richard B. Anderson Federal Building. References to that building in federal laws, maps, and other records are read as references under the Anderson name.
plaw-110-267-2008: El Monte, California names a post office building in Public Law 110-267, approved on July 15, 2008. The Postal Service site at 11151 Valley Boulevard is designated the Marisol Heredia Post Office Building. Part two of the act reads later mentions of that site, across federal records, as mentions of the building by the Heredia name.
plaw-110-268-2008: Brooksville, Florida is the site renamed by Public Law 110-268, approved on July 15, 2008. The post office at 19101 Cortez Boulevard is designated the Cody Grater Post Office Building. From then on, a federal law, map, or record that points to that site is taken to point to the Grater building instead. The act makes that name change only.
plaw-110-269-2008: St. Louis honors William 'Bill' Clay in Public Law 110-269, approved on July 15, 2008. The post office at 11001 Dunklin Drive in Missouri is designated the William 'Bill' Clay Post Office Building. The second part ties later use to the honor, so federal records citing that site cite the Clay name. No other change is made by the text.
plaw-110-270-2008: Ionia, Michigan names a post office building in Public Law 110-270, approved on July 15, 2008. The site at 117 North Kidd Street is designated the Alonzo Woodruff Post Office Building. The act's references part then treats a citation of that site, in a federal law or other record, as a citation of the Woodruff building.
plaw-110-271-2008: Humble, Texas honors a whole group in Public Law 110-271, approved on July 15, 2008. The post office at 7231 FM 1960 is designated the Texas Military Veterans Post Office. Unlike most naming acts in this run, the honor names no single person. Later federal mentions of the site are read as mentions of the post office under that group name.
plaw-110-272-2008: Brockton, Massachusetts names a building for Rocky Marciano in Public Law 110-272. Approved on July 15, 2008, the act covers the post office at 120 Commercial Street. It is designated the Rocky Marciano Post Office Building. A mention of that site in a federal law, map, regulation, or record is then deemed a mention of the Marciano building.
plaw-110-273-2008:
Keeping the capital's water agency free of outside control is the point of Public Law 110-273. Approved on July 15, 2008, it is the District of Columbia Water and Sewer Authority Independence Preservation Act, per its first section.

One part states that the city finance chief's power, under a 2005 law, does not reach the water agency's staff. That change counts as if it sat in the 2005 law from the start. A second part heads a new home rule part for bodies with their own financial, staff, and buying power. The sample ends there.
plaw-110-274-2008: Travel costs for a levee safety panel are clarified by Public Law 110-274, approved on July 15, 2008. The act amends the Water Resources Development Act of 2007. Title and text agree that the point is the Army chief's power to repay travel costs of Committee on Levee Safety members. The change is one phrase. Words tying repayment to funds given ahead of time become a simpler test, subject to whether funds are on hand.
plaw-110-275-2008:
Medicare patients and providers are the focus of Public Law 110-275, approved on July 15, 2008. It is the Medicare Improvements for Patients and Providers Act of 2008. Its purpose line promises wider access to preventive and mental health care, stronger aid for low income users, and care kept open in rural areas.

The contents list opens with user gains. It improves cover for preventive services and ends unequal copay rates for outpatient mental health care. It also limits how Medicare plans and drug plans may be sold. Low income parts extend a qualifying person program. The sample ends within those parts.
plaw-110-276-2008: Mayaguez, Puerto Rico names its customhouse in Public Law 110-276, approved on July 15, 2008. The building at 31 Gonzalez Clemente Avenue is designated the Rafael Martinez Nadal United States Customhouse Building. Later references to that building in federal laws, maps, and records are deemed references to it under the Nadal name. The act is a naming act only.
plaw-110-277-2008:
A silver dollar for disabled veterans is ordered by Public Law 110-277, approved on July 17, 2008. It is the American Veterans Disabled for Life Commemorative Coin Act. The Treasury chief must mint the coins for veterans disabled for life in service.

The findings honor service from World War II beaches to the deserts of the Middle East. They note Congress cleared a memorial to such veterans in 2000. A fee added to the coin price would help build that memorial. The terms shown cap the minting at a set number of one dollar coins. The sample ends as the coin's weight is given.
plaw-110-278-2008: Gas cans sold for home use must resist child opening under Public Law 110-278. Approved on July 17, 2008, the Children's Gasoline Burn Prevention Act sets the rule as one of the product safety agency. Six months after approval, each can made on or after that date for sale in this country must meet a named test standard for its closure. If the standards body later changes that standard, the change joins the rule unless the agency objects in time.
plaw-110-279-2008:
Senate restaurant workers keep some federal benefits after a move to a private firm, under Public Law 110-279. Congress approved it on July 17, 2008. The act covers staff whose work shifts when the Senate Restaurants are run by contract.

The part shown defines who counts. A covered person works for the Architect of the Capitol in the restaurants on the day the act passed. That person then becomes a worker of the private firm on the transfer date. For two of the benefits, the person must file a choice ahead of that date. The sample ends within the definitions, at the contract term.
plaw-110-280-2008: Ship air pollution rules from a world treaty are put into United States law by Public Law 110-280. Approved on July 21, 2008, the Maritime Pollution Prevention Act of 2008 amends the Act to Prevent Pollution from Ships. Its aim, per the purpose line, is to carry out Annex VI of the MARPOL treaty. The changes shown are definitions. The head of the environment agency is defined. The word emission joins the list of key terms. Navigable waters is said to include the territorial sea and internal waters of this country.
plaw-110-281-2008: A wildlife group's board grows under Public Law 110-281, approved on July 21, 2008. It is the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation Establishment Act Amendment of 2008. The title states its single aim, a larger board for the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation. The act strikes one paragraph and replaces it. The board shall have thirty directors, named under a later part of the act. Each director must be a United States citizen.
plaw-110-282-2008:
A stretch of road in Orchard Park, New York takes a newsman's name in Public Law 110-282. Approved on July 23, 2008, the act designates part of United States Route 20A as the Timothy J. Russert Highway.

The findings tell his path. Russert was born in Buffalo in 1950 and earned law and other degrees in Ohio. He worked for a senator and a governor, then joined NBC in 1984. In 1991 he began hosting Meet the Press, and became its longest serving host. The act lists many honors, among them dozens of honorary degrees. The sample ends among the awards.
plaw-110-283-2008:
Internet phone services must offer full 911 service under Public Law 110-283, approved on July 23, 2008. It is the New and Emerging Technologies 911 Improvement Act of 2008, or NET 911 Improvement Act. Its purpose line backs a shift to a national internet based emergency network.

Each web based voice provider must give its users 911 and enhanced 911 service, under the rules of the communications agency. A provider may claim access, on fair terms, to the lines and links it needs to do so. That right holds only for meeting the 911 duty itself. The text also backs better access for people with disabilities.
plaw-110-284-2008: Toledo, Ohio names its courthouse for two men in Public Law 110-284, approved on July 23, 2008. The courthouse at 1716 Spielbusch Avenue is designated the James M. Ashley and Thomas W.L. Ashley United States Courthouse. Later references to that courthouse in federal laws, maps, and records are deemed references to it under both Ashley names.
plaw-110-285-2008:
Childhood cancer is the target of Public Law 110-285, approved on July 29, 2008. It is the Caroline Pryce Walker Conquer Childhood Cancer Act of 2008. Its purpose line promises better research and care, facts for families, a national registry, and wider public awareness.

The findings are stark. Cancer kills more children than any other disease, the act states. Over twelve thousand young people are found to have it each year, and about twenty-three hundred die. Most childhood cancers strike the blood, brain, bone, or lymph system. In most cases the disease has already spread when found.
plaw-110-286-2008:
Sanctions on Burma's rulers and a ban on its gems form Public Law 110-286, approved on July 29, 2008. It is the Tom Lantos Block Burmese JADE Act of 2008. JADE stands for the Junta's Anti-Democratic Efforts, in the act's own title.

The findings recall protests that began in August 2007. Hundreds of thousands of citizens, monks, and students marched in peace. They sought freedom for political prisoners, among them Aung San Suu Kyi, and talks toward shared rule. The regime answered with force, the act states. About two hundred people were reported killed, and over two thousand were held or beaten.
plaw-110-287-2008: Import limits on Burma are renewed by Public Law 110-287, a joint resolution approved on July 29, 2008. Congress approves the renewal of limits in the Burmese Freedom and Democracy Act of 2003. The text counts as a renewal resolution under that act. Two side items ride along.
