The particles were made by a flash-combustion method and checked with infrared spectroscopy and microscopy before cells were exposed.

Against MCF-7 breast cancer cells, the plain cobalt ferrite particles killed half the cells at a concentration of 144 micrograms per milliliter. Even a tenth of that dose pushed cells into programmed death and froze the cell cycle at two checkpoints. In mice carrying Ehrlich ascites tumors, treatment cut tumor volume by forty-four percent and reduced tumor cells, while blood counts and liver and kidney function improved and tissue looked healthier. The drug cisplatin was more potent per microgram in the dish, a gap the authors acknowledge while presenting the particles as an adjunct for nanotherapy.
pmc-13219808:
Ke-Jun Liu and colleagues test starting lung cancer patients on a low dose of dacomitinib in a 2026 study. Dacomitinib beats older drugs for cancers carrying an EGFR exon 21 mutation, but the forty-five milligram dose causes severe side effects, and many patients cannot stay on it. The question was whether starting low keeps the benefit while trimming the harm.

Thirty-one patients with advanced cancer who began dacomitinib at fifteen or thirty milligrams were compared with thirty-five patients on first-generation EGFR drugs. Tumors shrank in 67.7 percent of the low-dose group, more than in the comparison group, and median time before the cancer progressed reached 14.2 months, favoring dacomitinib. The fifteen and thirty milligram starters fared alike, but severe rash struck a third of the thirty milligram group and nobody on fifteen. The authors present proactive low dosing as a strategy and support for dose-optimization trials.
pmc-13222408:
Jun Li and colleagues test two variants in the RANK gene for links to type 2 diabetes in postmenopausal women, in a 2026 study from Xinjiang, China. Two hundred Han Chinese women attended one hospital between October 2024 and March 2025. Glucose testing split them into 105 women with diabetes and 95 with normal tolerance, and gene variants were read by mass spectrometry.

One variant, rs3018362, differed in frequency between the groups and stayed independently associated with diabetes in regression analysis. The second variant related to blood fat and insulin resistance measures within the normal group. RANK is better known for bone biology, so the finding connects two conditions that often travel together after menopause.
pmc-13224008:
Ian V. Soares and co-authors develop a 2026 accounting method that assigns cloud computing emissions to the country where services are used, not only where data centres sit. Standard practice charges emissions to the host country, which hides cross-border demand. The team applied their approach to Germany, Ireland, and the Netherlands over the years 2017 to 2022.

Cloud activity was split into domestic use, exports, and imports using electricity and emissions data for data centres and networks. Germany's footprint was mostly domestic, at about three quarters of its total. Ireland looked very different, with most of its hosted computing serving foreign users. Such figures can sit beside territorial inventories when governments plan climate and infrastructure policy.
pmc-13229108:
Alejandro E. Camacho, David A. Dana, and Mikhail Matz reply a 2026 response to critics of their proposal for ecological replacement of Caribbean corals, importing hardier species from elsewhere as local reefs collapse. Two commentaries had warned the idea could spread pathogens, might fail, and should be a last resort only. The authors agree replacement is a last resort, yet argue that stance supports starting careful research now rather than at the brink.

Rearing introduced corals from larvae in near-sterile conditions, then quarantining them, could cut pathogen risk. Some Pacific corals already survive in the Caribbean, one patch sheltering nineteen native invertebrate species. Waiting until Caribbean species are ecologically extinct, they warn, would leave no time for the staged, democratically informed testing they propose.
pmc-13230608:
Mohammed A Taha and colleagues show in 2026 how waste iron can be turned into a stronger magnetic composite material. Powder from waste iron mixed with silicon and niobium was milled with rising amounts of activated carbon, then pressed and heated. Heating triggered reactions inside the material that formed new hard phases in place.

With carbon added, one iron niobium phase faded and hard ceramic phases took its place. The richest carbon mix gained large rises in hardness, strength, stiffness, and heat expansion control over the base material. Magnetic strength eased down gradually as carbon rose, yet the material stayed magnetic. Using waste iron this way could lower cost and resource use for parts needing strength plus magnetic response.
pmc-13231008:
Yingfen Jiang and colleagues test in 2026 whether grinding purple wheat bran very fine makes healthier bread without ruining it. Purple bran is rich in fiber and purple pigments tied to lower diabetes risk, yet coarse bran can tear dough structure. The team made coarse, fine, and superfine powders and baked breads with each at three loading levels.

Finer grinding freed more of the purple pigments for measurement and eased the harm to dough. Bread with the highest superfine loading carried far more pigment than matching coarse bread. Antioxidant strength also rose several fold over plain bread in lab tests. Taste acceptance held up, which supports using superfine bran to lift fiber and antioxidant content in daily staples.
pmc-13231608:
Sara Becker and colleagues survey in 2026 how doctors and hospital managers in Germany judge the ethics of case-based hospital pay. Payment by diagnosis group rewards short stays and high case counts, which can squeeze time with each patient. An online survey in two federal states asked both groups about pressure, moral conflict, and care quality.

Doctors reported moral conflict far more often than managers did, and they also felt patient focus slipping more sharply. Time pressure linked to the payment system weighed on both groups, though managers stressed efficiency and coordination gains more. Both sides backed quality indicators to guard standards. Reform, the authors argue, should weigh ethical strain alongside savings when payment rules are reset.
pmc-13231808:
Malfrid A Nummedal and colleagues track in 2026 how Norway routes sudden illness from first contact care into specialist care. Registry data covered every citizen from 2012 to 2021, linking doctor visits to hospital contacts within ten hours. That short gap marked a referral from primary care into acute specialist services.

More than twelve million acute specialist contacts were counted over the decade. Contacts that followed a primary care visit rose in rate by close to a fifth, driven by the out-of-hours service. Referrals after regular doctor visits stayed flat across the same years. Most specialist contacts still arrived with no primary care visit first. Service organization, not population change, best explains the steady shift.
pmc-13232608:
Bechir S Naffeti and colleagues model in 2026 what a future vaccine against herpes simplex virus type 1 could prevent in the United States. The virus causes cold sores, genital herpes, and rare severe newborn infections, and several vaccine candidates are in development. Their model starts infant vaccination in 2030 with a vaccine that works in most children and protects for life.

By 2075, new mouth and genital infections fall by roughly half in the model, with tens of millions of cases avoided in total. Adding a teen catch-up round deepens the cuts, most of all for genital disease. Protection that fades after fifteen years delivers only about a third of the lifelong benefit. Each prevented case also gets cheaper in vaccine terms over time.
pmc-13232808:
Jaewon Seol and colleagues forecast in 2026 how climate change will squeeze four Korean spicebush relatives that survive from a warmer ancient age. Ensemble models combined six methods to map fit habitat for each Lindera species under three climate paths. Temperature swing across seasons and growing-season rain mattered most in the models.

Fit habitat slid north and uphill in every path, with southern and central Korea losing the most ground. Even the widest-ranging species lost about four fifths of its fit habitat. The narrowest species lost over nine tenths and ranked most at risk. Overlap between species shrank as each moved its own way, so refuges that stay stable deserve first protection.
pmc-13232908:
Stanley C. Jordan and co-authors report a 2026 case series on kidney transplant care for highly sensitized patients. Such patients carry strong antibodies against donor tissue and face high risks of rejection. They also suffer side effects from standard calcineurin inhibitor drugs, leaving few safe alternatives. The series covers four sensitized patients switched to a drug pair that avoids calcineurin inhibitors.

Two patients received clazakizumab, which blocks interleukin-6, and two received tocilizumab against its receptor. All four moved from calcineurin inhibitors to CTLA4-Ig. Kidney function improved, donor-specific antibodies largely disappeared, and no new antibodies formed over more than six years of follow-up. Immune cell patterns also shifted in ways suggesting calmer immunity, though the authors treat that part cautiously.
pmc-13233008:
Pranavsingh Dhunnoo and colleagues published a 2026 futures study on adding an artificial intelligence assistant to virtual consultations for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, a long-term lung condition. Rather than guess at side effects, the team used a Futures Wheel workshop, a structured method that maps first and later consequences of a change across eight areas of life and care.

Two patients and two health professionals who had helped design the tool took part, after a pilot session with public contributors. Patients expected the assistant to deepen their involvement and confidence in remote visits. Professionals expected help with communication and a better read on patients' emotional well-being. The paper also shares practical advice for running such workshops with new health technology.
pmc-13234008:
Nibras Soubh and colleagues published a 2026 evaluation of vision-capable language models reading electrocardiogram images. Six leading generalist models, plus two ECG-specialized ones, were tested on seventy real patient ECG tracings stripped of identifiers. Each model had to answer nine standard questions about rhythm, conduction blocks, intervals, extra beats, and signs of ischemia, judged against expert consensus.

Generalist accuracy was mediocre, with balanced scores between about fifty and sixty-two percent. The best model was also by far the slowest. Sensitivity for atrial fibrillation was dismal, at best catching one of nine cases, and detection of conduction delays and interval prolongation was likewise poor. The authors warn that today's general-purpose vision models are nowhere near safe for independent ECG interpretation.
pmc-13234108: Gianmauro Palombelli and co-authors issued a 2026 correction notice in Scientific Reports. The notice is a correction only, repairing the author names on their earlier article about brain imaging in Wistar-Kyoto rats under chronic stress as a model of treatment-resistant depression. Every listed author's name had been printed in reversed order, surname first. The corrected byline gives each name in proper order, and the original article has been corrected. No findings, data, or conclusions of the study were altered.
pmc-13234908:
Nidhi Sunhare and Padamjeet Panchal described in 2026 a rare variation in a small forearm muscle that straightens the index finger. The muscle, extensor indicis proprius, is usually considered one of the most predictable in the forearm. During routine dissection of a female cadaver aged about fifty-five, they found the muscle split into two fleshy parts. A tendon ran between the two parts and also attached to the wrist joint capsule.

The second belly stretched several centimetres across the back of the hand before becoming tendon again and attaching normally. The authors link the pattern to incomplete regression of developing muscle tissue before birth. Extra muscle tissue could crowd its tight tunnel, raising risk of inflammation, lag in finger extension, or hand pain. Surgeons planning tendon transfers or decompression should watch for this anatomy to avoid injury.
pmc-13236508:
Ling Meng and colleagues profiled in 2026 how a medicinal balloon flower plant responds to heat stress at the gene level. Seedlings were exposed to forty-degree heat for up to forty-eight hours while physiology and gene activity were tracked. Protective enzyme activities rose strongly under heat in the measurements. Damage markers spiked early, then eased as the response developed.

More than one thousand genes changed consistently across all heat time points compared with unstressed plants. Small regulatory RNAs also shifted, with dozens responding to heat and targeting many genes. The ones building the plant's prized saponin compounds responded unevenly, with early pathway steps mostly quieted. One growth hormone pathway gene was jointly targeted by two small RNAs yet rose in activity. The authors describe a redistribution of chemistry between saponin and growth pathways under heat.
pmc-13236808:
Alistair Benford and Per Kristian Lehre proved a general runtime bound in 2026 for a coevolutionary algorithm, a method that trains game players against each other, on impartial combinatorial games. Such self-play methods can cycle without improving, so theory is needed to show when an optimal strategy will be found. Their result counts simulated games for a simple distribution-based algorithm.

The bound applies to any impartial combinatorial game, meaning games where both players share the same legal moves. For many games the bound grows only polynomially or near-polynomially with the number of positions. The authors then work through Nim, Chomp, Silver Dollar, and Turning Turtles as examples. They present the result as a first step toward a full theory of coevolution on games.
pmc-13239408:
Yashodani Pillay and a large team present a 2026 prospective study of mothers and newborns after hospital delivery in Uganda. The group followed families for six weeks after discharge from two regional referral hospitals to count deaths, readmissions, and care seeking.

More than seven thousand women delivered during the study period, and most mothers and babies left hospital alive. About three percent of mothers and four percent of newborns were readmitted, usually for suspected infection. A third of newborn deaths happened after discharge. Caesarean birth, losing a baby, and household food insecurity raised readmission risk, while routine postnatal visits were strikingly rare.
pmc-13240308:
Yamin Chen and a large team run a full safety battery on a Chinese medicinal fig root in a 2026 toxicology study. Roots of this Ficus pandurata variety flavour soups and medicinal diets across south-eastern China, and developers wanted evidence before wider use in foods and herbal products.

Rats and mice received a water extract powder in single-dose, genetic damage, pregnancy, and ninety-day feeding tests. Even the highest acute dose caused no deaths or clear harm. Tests for mutation and chromosome damage came back negative. The ninety-day study set safe daily levels that translate to large amounts of raw root. The authors present the results as support for food development.
pmc-13240408:
Guochun Lou and co-authors question whether the amount of stomach bacteria seen under the microscope matches inflammation severity in a 2026 Chinese study. Pathologists routinely grade Helicobacter pylori density alongside inflammation in stomach biopsies, assuming more bacteria means angrier tissue.

Nearly seventeen hundred untreated patients contributed more than two thousand biopsy samples from 2022 and 2023. Overall, high bacterial density showed no reliable link with marked neutrophil inflammation, the sign of active damage. One narrow subgroup showed an inverse link that vanished when multiple sites were combined, which the authors read as sampling chance. Older patients had less severe inflammation in the lower stomach. Density grading, they conclude, should not stand in for activity.
pmc-13241008:
Francois D. Rouleau and colleagues report a 2026 study predicting drug resistance in a fungal pathogen that cannot be grown in the lab. Pneumocystis jirovecii causes dangerous pneumonia in people with weakened immunity. Antifolate drugs remain central to treatment, yet testing mutations directly in this fungus is impossible.

The team produced the fungal enzyme inside baker yeast and scanned nearly every possible single change to it. Readings of enzyme function fed a machine learning model with structural features. Function data proved the strongest predictor of resistance. Mutations that blocked the drug still had to keep the enzyme working, which limited their options. The framework extends to predicting resistance against the main treatment drug.
pmc-13241508:
Kim and colleagues at Pusan National University trace how a tumor signal remakes natural killer cells in ovarian cancer. Epithelial ovarian tumors are often cold, with few immune cells inside. The team focused on growth differentiation factor 15, a stress protein tied to poor outlook. They asked how it interacts with a chemical-sensing receptor pathway in killer cells.

Tumor-derived Gdf15 boosted aryl hydrocarbon receptor signaling inside natural killer cells, especially after chemotherapy and at relapse. Killer cells first fought tumors low in the protein, yet long signaling pushed them toward exhaustion. Their surveillance markers faded and tumors resisted attack. Mouse transplant and chemical exposure models echoed the clinical pattern, marking the axis as a warning sign for progression.
pmc-13241608:
Negret and colleagues in Colombia comment on trial evidence for JULIETA, a portable bioimpedance device for breast screening support. The letter stresses that the device cannot diagnose cancer or replace mammography. Its proposed role is triage: flagging which women should reach imaging sooner. Several authors work for the company developing the device.

The underlying multicenter study tested the device against mammography in four Colombian cities. It covered six hundred seventy-three breasts from four hundred sixty-nine women. The algorithm reached moderate sensitivity and specificity, with a negative predictive value above eighty percent. The device is painless, radiation-free, and quick, though the letter calls for validation beyond urban diagnostic centers.
pmc-13241808:
Iqbal and Osman in Dhaka report a young electrician whose lens clouded months after a high-voltage shock. The 21-year-old took current through his face from a power line, taking extensive burns. Five months later his left eye blurred more and more. Exams found flower-shaped cloudy spots typical of electric cataract.

Lens surgery with an implant proceeded without complications. Imaging then checked the back of the eye: retinal layers, nerve fibers, and optic capillaries all proved intact. His visual field tested normal. Vision reached perfect sharpness and held through twelve months, backing the guarded outlook.

pmc-13270608:

pmc-13270708:

Those with higher remaining activity tend toward vasculitis, inflammation of the blood vessels.
pmc-13271108:

pmc-13271508:

pmc-13271608:

pmc-13272208:

pmc-13272308:

pmc-13272508:

Earlier work pointed to this extract, so the team followed its activity step by step.

pmc-13273508:
Mouyuan Sun and a large team reviewed metal ions in peripheral nerve growth and repair in a 2026 article. Artificial nerve guides exist but work far worse, as their network meta-analysis confirms.

pmc-13274008:

pmc-13274608:

pmc-13275508:

A single collapsed fork formed a one-ended break repaired by recombination, without restarting copying. That second route produced small deletions and insertions, showing how fork geometry shapes repair accuracy.
pmc-13276308:

pmc-13276508:

pmc-13276608:

pmc-13276808:
Niels Jig Jansen and Lars Ingmar Veldhuis wrote a 2026 systematic review, meaning a study that gathers prior studies, on early warning scores in poorer countries. pmc-13277008:

Powered brushing alone cleaned little of the gap surface. Cleaning from both sides raised results sharply for both tools. The authors note the work was done in a model, not in mouths, so real-world results may differ.
pmc-13277108:

Absence of pain was more useful for ruling a fracture out than its presence was for ruling one in. The authors caution that pain should not drive imaging choices by itself in this group.
pmc-13278408:

Holm oak roots carved winding, branching grooves, olive roots made shallow straight marks, and grapevine roots made linear-to-round engravings, often with cracking nearby. Marks grew stronger with deeper and longer burial. Root marks may serve as signatures of the plants around a burial, aiding readings of fossils and secondary burials.
pmc-13278908:

pmc-13279408:

pmc-13279908:

pmc-13280108:

pmc-13282708:

Linking those lists to patient outcomes usually means manual data merging and gene-by-gene survival checks, which limits scale and repeatability.

It joins gene expression tables with clinical data, then runs survival curve and log-rank analyses across all genes in one pass, covering overall and progression-free survival. The updated version adds configurable grouping strategies, options for missing values, multi-group analysis, and richer reporting for sensitivity checks. pmc-13283208:

pmc-13283308:

pmc-13283908:

Lab tests confirmed the parasite species, and she regained full movement afterward.
pmc-13284108:

pmc-13284508:

pmc-13285608:

pmc-13285908:

pmc-13286008:

pmc-13286308:

pmc-13286808:

pmc-13286908:

pmc-13287008:

pmc-13287208:

pmc-13287508:

pmc-13288108:

pmc-13288608:

pmc-13288708:

pmc-13288908:

pmc-13289308:

pmc-13289408:

pmc-13289608:

pmc-13289708:

Weak splitters favored ions gaining nothing extra, while strong splitters favored ions gaining a lot.
pmc-13290108:
Drug resistance in the malaria parasite among pregnant women in Bobo-Dioulasso, Burkina Faso, is measured by Mamoudou Cissé and colleagues in a 2026 study. They focused on sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine, a drug still used to protect pregnant women from malaria.

Blood spots were collected from October to December 2022 from 288 women attending care in pregnancy who had not taken the drug. Among 172 confirmed infections, the Pfdhfr triple mutant form appeared in 33.7% of cases and the Pfdhps A437G change in 82.7%, while two other worrying changes were absent. Carrying the triple form and being further along in pregnancy each predicted anaemia in the mother. The authors say the drug still seems usable in pregnancy but checks must continue.
pmc-13290608:
Pairing brain stimulation with light-based brain watching could personalize stroke rehabilitation, Yuzhe Zou and colleagues conclude in a 2026 systematic review. After stroke, the two brain halves compete unevenly, and magnetic stimulation guided by near-infrared light readings offers a closed loop to correct it.

Searching four databases, the team found nine studies of the combined approach in post-stroke hemiplegia. Six of nine intervention studies reported significant motor gains, and effective stimulation raised activity in motor areas on the stroke side, rebalanced the halves, and strengthened connectivity. In two-thirds of studies, those brain changes tracked the clinical gains. Zou and colleagues rate the evidence only moderate to low, citing tiny samples, mixed protocols, and bias risk in non-randomized work, and they call the mechanism support preliminary.
pmc-13290908:
Three patients with stubborn anti-NMDAR encephalitis improved after under-the-skin ofatumumab, Yekai Ma and colleagues present in a case series from 2026. Their severe psychiatric and cognitive symptoms had persisted despite steroids, intravenous immunoglobulin, and long-term mycophenolate, leaving few options.

Each patient received subcutaneous ofatumumab at 20 mg per dose while B cells, antibody levels, imaging, and function scores were tracked. All three improved markedly in psychiatric symptoms, cognition, and brain scans, and their CD20-positive B cells crashed to extremely low levels. Side effects were slight: one patient had mild bone pain and a low fever, and no severe events occurred. Ma and colleagues present the drug as a fast, tolerable option when standard immune therapy fails this brain inflammation.
pmc-13291008:
Arman Abroumand Gholami and colleagues write a 2026 letter on a study of loneliness in older adults. The study covered older Iranian adults with heart disease. It found loneliness and social support rising together. That odd link drew the writers’ close attention.

Four concerns shape the letter. Shared survey methods may have inflated the link. Subgroup patterns clash with the main trend. Test tools may work poorly where literacy is low. A one-time survey cannot show which factor comes first. The writers urge studies that track people over time. Measures beyond self-report would also help. Social health in aging needs that firmer base.
pmc-13291108:
Brain networks at rest after spinal cord injury are mapped with a light-based scanning method in a 2026 study led by Ying Zou. Twenty-one patients with spinal cord injury were compared with 23 healthy adults using functional near-infrared spectroscopy, a tool that tracks blood signals linked to brain activity across sensorimotor and frontal areas.

Links between the two sides of the sensorimotor cortex ran weaker in patients on both blood signals tracked, and one frontal-to-motor link also fell. Weaker side-to-side links went with poorer sensory and motor scores on standard injury scales. The authors suggest that this weakened link could serve as a marker of sensorimotor trouble, while stressing that the frontal finding is early and needs more work.
pmc-13291308:
Fruit peel waste can brew silver particles that clean dye water. Abdulrahman Sani Aliero leads a 2026 study comparing two peels. Factory dyes resist normal water treatment. Silver particles can speed dye breakdown as catalysts.

Banana and pineapple peels both made working particles. Banana peel held far more plant phenols. Pineapple particles still came out smaller in size. Both types showed the expected crystal form and round shape. Light tests confirmed particle formation in each brew. Direct side-by-side data under one protocol was the gap filled. Peel choice trades size against plant chemistry. Such waste reuse cuts cost and trash at once.
pmc-13291708:
Surgery on a child’s hand is never only about function. Joseph Salem-Hernández leads a 2026 review of congenital hand differences and beauty norms. Born hand traits range from joined fingers to missing bones. Surgical writing has mapped technique in fine detail.

The look and culture behind operating went unexamined. A five-fingered, even hand acts as a hidden ideal. That ideal is cultural, not neutral, the authors argue. Parental worry over looks and stigma drives early surgery. Choices often come before a child can speak. Disability scholars frame the critique used here. Clinics are urged to name the aesthetic stakes aloud.
pmc-13291808:
Konstantin L Makridis, Linda C Laux, and Angela M Kaindl report a 2026 case paper on cenobamate in two children with Dravet syndrome. The syndrome stems from SCN1A gene variants, and classic sodium-channel blockers usually make it worse, so cenobamate's mixed record drew interest. Reports in children range from no response to clear worsening.

A 7-year-old girl on valproate, clobazam, and cannabidiol saw her total seizure burden fall by 80 percent on added cenobamate. When doctors tapered the drug, seizures surged back; restoring the dose ended her convulsive seizures from October 2025. A 17-year-old boy stopped seizing on just 50 mg per day, apart from one episode after a missed dose. The authors urge controlled studies rather than routine use.
pmc-13292008:
Vysakh Ramachandran and Davit A Potoyan derive rules for how protein-RNA droplets organize inside, in a 2026 study. Cells form membraneless droplets whose insides can layer like tiny onions or hollow into vesicles. What sets that pattern was unclear. Large simulations varied how proteins attract each other and RNA. They also varied protein amounts, chain length, and droplet density.

Those knobs swept droplets through uniform, layered, two-phase, and vesicle shapes. Hollow vesicles formed on their own from mixed starts, with no flow or strong charge needed. The authors explain the pattern with a soap-like packing idea borrowed from amphiphile science. A protein-RNA complex acts like a single-chain soap whose shape factor is set by domain proportions. That factor predicts whether micelles, cylinders, vesicles, or inverse phases appear. The grammar links sequence choices to droplet forms that modelers can now design.
pmc-13292308:
Zeynep Ozturk Yalcin and co-authors audit a 2026 clinic question: how much kidney-toxic medication baggage do chronic kidney disease patients carry when starting SGLT2 inhibitors? The observational study ran in a university nephrology clinic from September 2022 to February 2023. A clinical pharmacist reviewed the medicines of 72 newly prescribed patients, scoring drug problems and nephrotoxic load.

The review found 69 drug-related problems, led by wrong treatment duration, drugs without an indication, and untreated symptoms. Doctors accepted 85.5 percent of the pharmacist's recommendations. Patients took a median of two nephrotoxic drugs each, yet no overt toxic events surfaced, and burden did not track with estimated kidney failure risk. The authors present real-world baseline data and ask for prospective studies of pharmacist review.
pmc-13292508:
Rekha Chotaliya and colleagues compare a 2026 case-control look at the eye surface of people taking antidepressants, drugs known to unsettle the tear film. Seventy-two users and seventy matched controls aged 20 to 40 underwent tear breakup and Schirmer tests, symptom scoring, surface staining, and impression cytology that counts mucus-making goblet cells. The drug mix spanned SSRI, SNRI, and tricyclic types.

Users had roughly half the goblet cell density of controls, 183 against 366 cells per square millimeter in the readings, plus weaker tear stability and wetting. Symptom scores more than doubled, and corneal staining odds ran thirteen times higher. Goblet cell counts tracked with both tear breakup time and Schirmer results. No drug class stood out as worse. The authors advise routine eye monitoring for patients on antidepressants.
pmc-13293808:
Yongpeng Li and co-authors compare, in a 2026 brain imaging study, resting brain patterns in people with bothersome tinnitus, non-bothersome tinnitus, and no tinnitus. Why the same ringing distresses some people and not others may lie in brain networks, not the ear alone.

Groups held 61, 52, and 50 people, scanned at rest and compared on local activity and links from hearing regions. The bothersome group showed stronger links between hearing areas and a frontal-limbic cluster than the non-bothersome group, yet matched controls. Local synchrony in a frontal area ran lower in the non-bothersome group than in both others. Imaging did not track symptom scores.
pmc-13294108:
Grant Maxie walks readers inside peer review at a vet lab journal in a 2026 editorial. The journal prints work on lab tests for animal disease and runs papers through the SageTrack system. Maxie sums up tips shared at the 2025 AAVLD annual meeting best practice talks.

Good reviewers judge the science and help authors say it more clearly. New reviewers can train online or co-review with a senior peer after checking with the editor. The journal tracks skills, past reviews, and declines so no one is swamped. AI tools for reviewers get frank talk as norms shift.
pmc-13294308:
Lucas Henrique da Silva e Silva and a large team report the first complete mitochondrial genomes for two Amazon ticks in a 2026 study from Pará, Brazil. Amblyomma humerale and Amblyomma geayi matter for public and veterinary health because their genus, with about 138 species, spreads many disease agents. Full circular genomes were assembled and gene order was charted.

Each molecule held 37 functional units: 13 protein-coding genes, 22 transfer RNAs, and two ribosomal RNAs, plus control regions. Family trees built from all 13 protein genes kept the genus as one clean branch, placing the two species in separate subgenus groups. Complete references sharpen species identification and outbreak tracing.
pmc-13294908:
Yuefeng Zhang and Zhenbin Wang test a shared belief about catalyst surfaces in a 2026 study. Gaps where oxygen atoms are missing are often praised for making oxide catalysts work. Yet how long such gaps last under real working volts and acid levels was not clear.

Their frame works out the cost of forming a gap across acid and voltage ranges. They ran it on 19 catalysts used to take in or give off oxygen in fuel cells and splitters. Gaps that look cheap to form at rest grew costly at work, past set marks. Lasting surface gaps thus seem rare in use.
pmc-13295408:
Elena Stefanel and colleagues present a step-by-step calibration method for electrical hand therapy in a 2026 study. Stimulating many forearm channels to bend fingers in a coordinated way is hard to tune for each person. Their framework first maps single finger moves, then blends them into full gestures.

Thirteen volunteers took part in mapping sessions over a forearm grid for eight separate finger actions. Ten achieved at least six movements, and three achieved every target motion, though thumb and outer finger lifts were hardest to isolate. In a smaller second group, blended settings produced seven recognisable gestures with movement sizes matching the intended patterns.
pmc-13295708:
Tingting Chen and colleagues track brain development of emotional self-control in a 2026 study. Stopping a response amid emotional distraction grows harder or easier as prefrontal networks mature. Light-based brain recording watched the forehead while teenagers and young adults played an emotional conflict game.

Twenty-six adolescents aged 13 to 16 and thirty adults aged 18 to 22 took part. Both groups slowed on mismatched trials, showing the emotional conflict effect clearly. Teenage brains leaned on the right forehead area alone, while adults spread activity across both sides. The authors read the shift as a move from backup effort toward a better joined, more efficient network.
pmc-13295908:
Timothy O Jenkins and co-authors present a 2026 protocol for finding a breathing-muscle training load that ventilated patients can accept. Weak diaphragms prolong time on breathing machines, but heavy training loads can distress patients and may miss the diaphragm itself.

Forty hard-to-wean patients with tracheostomies will try four load levels in random order on a training device. Sensors will record diaphragm and neck muscle activity, while patients rate breathlessness and discomfort at each level. Mixing those measures should pinpoint a load that works the diaphragm without needless distress. Results will appear in journals and at meetings.
pmc-13296008:
Joana Vieira dos Santos and colleagues adapt a scale of illegitimate tasks for a Portuguese public university, in a 2026 study. Illegitimate tasks are jobs that feel needless or beneath a role, and they wound professional pride. The Bern scale that gauges them has held up in several tongues. The team translated it with care for the bureaucratic culture of a university and surveyed 601 staff and faculty.

Checks on the data tested whether the scale's shape held in the new setting and how steadily it scored. The work sits inside a theory that ties self-worth to stress: threats to pride stir harm across mind, body, and behavior, while stronger pride guards well-being. A sound local version lets the university spot where pointless tasks pile up and chip at staff.
pmc-13296108:
Felix Muehlensiepen and co-authors survey, in 2026, digital tool use among palliative care staff in Brandenburg, Germany. Such tools could help reach rural families, but routine uptake was little known, so 152 doctors, nurses and other professionals answered questions on use, skills and attitudes.

Email and record systems were common, while video visits, apps and wearables stayed rare. Doctors scored highest on digital literacy, nurses were most positive overall, and inpatient and urban staff used tools more. Staff praised flexibility but blamed weak infrastructure and families' low digital skills. The authors urge investment in both.
pmc-13296708:
Maria Cândida de Carvalho Furtado and colleagues connect play patterns with screen time in very young children in a 2026 Brazilian study. Mothers of 278 children aged up to three years, drawn from all five national regions, completed online questionnaires. The analysis asked which family and play features accompanied screen use within recommended limits.

Children who played with other children were more likely to stay within the guidelines. Body-based exploratory play and homemade toys also lined up with healthier screen habits. Living with both parents mattered as well. The authors suggest that routine child-health visits should ask about play and family setup, and that encouraging varied play may itself curb screen time.
pmc-13297108:
Bulat I. Yalaev and colleagues replicate genetic links to type 1 diabetes and its eye and kidney complications in a 2026 study. Earlier candidate findings conflict, so independent checks matter. The cohort held 618 people, most of them diabetes patients treated at a Moscow endocrinology centre, with seventeen variants compared across groups.

One variant in a growth-factor receptor gene roughly doubled diabetes risk in this sample, while another in a collagen gene lowered it. A further variant tracked kidney complications, and two variants in one gene tracked eye disease. The authors present the markers as candidates for risk stratification, pending confirmation in larger independent cohorts.
pmc-13297408:
Adding a probiotic strain to a standard antibiotic did not clearly improve recovery from a common hospital gut infection, reports a 2026 Japanese cohort study led by Yota Yamada. The work concerns non-severe Clostridioides difficile infection treated with metronidazole at a single center.

Records covered April 2015 to March 2025, and 53 eligible patients were split between antibiotic alone (27 people) and antibiotic plus Clostridium butyricum MIYAIRI 588 (26 people). Cure rates were 51.9% and 69.2%, a gap that was not statistically significant at p = 0.196. Recurrence stayed rare in both groups, and adjusted analysis found no independent link between the probiotic and cure. The authors call the result hypothesis-generating only.
pmc-13298008:
Standard hormone-blocking pills still help breast cancer patients who inherited BRCA mutations, finds a 2026 Turkish Oncology Group study led by Mustafa Seyyar. The multicenter cohort followed 121 people with hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative metastatic disease treated with CDK4/6 inhibitors plus endocrine therapy.

Treatment delivered meaningful benefit across the group. Outcomes hinted at a split by mutation type, with BRCA1 carriers showing numerically longer time without progression than BRCA2 carriers, although the gap was not statistically significant. Because trials enrolled few such patients, the authors call for research on biomarker-guided choices and on how best to sequence these drugs against PARP inhibitors.
pmc-13298208:
Nicole Mckeever and colleagues describe sinus findings in patients preparing for sinus floor elevation before dental implants, in a 2026 retrospective study from an English dental institute. Cone-beam scans covered 26 maxillary sinuses in 20 patients. Thickening beyond a set threshold counted as pathological, and reviewers noted its shape, location, drainage opening status, and nearby dental disease.

Most sinuses showed mucosal thickening, most often polypoid in form and wrapping around the sinus walls. A minority with heavy thickening had a blocked drainage opening. Incidental findings included root-tip disease and implants breaching the sinus floor. The authors urge wide scans and joint planning with ear, nose, and throat specialists.
pmc-13298308:
Zishan Jiao and colleagues assess the safety of a tea-fermenting fungus strain for possible food use, in a 2026 toxicology study. Aspergillus cristatus drives Fu brick tea fermentation, yet strain-level safety data remain limited. Their strain, CCNH008, underwent acute and ninety-day feeding studies in rodents, plus a recovery period and several genotoxicity tests.

No deaths, clinical signs, or treatment-related tissue changes appeared at the doses tested, and body weight, blood measures, and organ weights stayed unaffected. Mutation and chromosome damage assays were negative throughout. The authors conclude the strain shows no evidence of oral toxicity or genotoxicity, supporting further food application work.
pmc-13298908:
Adding fluorine atoms stiffens layered cadmium crystals in unexpected ways, report Maciej Ptak and colleagues in a 2026 solid-state study. They examined difluorinated hybrid compounds pairing organic cations with cadmium chloride, bromide, or a mixed halide layer.

Swapping halides introduced positional disorder in both the organic and inorganic parts of the structure. Heat measurements showed unusually large entropy changes at the phase transition, pointing to combined cation ordering, hydrogen bond reshuffling, and slab distortion. Fluorine atoms sat at strikingly short distances from each other, though calculations showed these contacts were forced by packing rather than attractive. Light emission shifted with halide choice and rigidity, suggesting tuning knobs for optical materials.
pmc-13299508:
A home-built pancreas aid gave Brazilians with type 1 sugar disease firmer grip on their blood sugar. Gabriella Lopes Ventura and her team show that in a 2026 survey. They set 62 users of the open Android aid, built from a sugar probe, a phone bridge, and a plain pump, next to 309 non-users.

Users held their sugar in the goal band 78.5% of the time. Their long-run mark, HbA1c, fell from 7.3% to 6.5% once the aid was in place. Users told of fewer bad low-sugar spells and a life that felt more free than that of non-users. Close to a fourth of users still missed the goal share the field aims for, and time spent too low ran past guide marks. The team back the cheap aid as a way to widen reach where funds are thin.
pmc-13300308:
Two silkworm strains raised on artificial feed differ inside the gut, and Shengxiang Zhang and colleagues tied those differences to growth in a 2026 study. They sequenced gut microbes and profiled blood chemicals in Youshi No. 1 and Guangshi No. 1 larvae, two strains bred for life on man-made diets.

The strains carried distinct gut microbe mixes and distinct metabolic profiles. One compound, L-valine, stood out: it tracked with growth and matched levels of the gut bacterium Bacillus. Feeding tests backed the link, since adding L-valine or Bacillus improved several body measures in Youshi No. 1 stock. The results offer levers for breeding and feeding diet-adapted silkworms.
pmc-13300708:
Screening newborns only helps if families return for care, and Umma A. Ibrahim and colleagues report a 2026 implementation study from Kano, Nigeria. At Aminu Kano Teaching Hospital, two sequential cohorts tested whether sickle cell screening could link babies into full care before three months of age. A family-centered communication plan was added after a weak first round.

In the first period, 277 newborns enrolled but only 46.5 percent arrived early, though babies with sickle cell disease did better at 72.8 percent. After staff adopted structured family outreach and tracking, early enrollment jumped to 91.7 percent among sixty more babies. Cheap communication fixes, the authors conclude, can close the follow-up gap.
pmc-13300908:
Painful spasms pointed one woman's doctors toward two overlapping autoimmune diseases, Hajar Hanane and colleagues describe in a 2026 case report.
