Her history also held optic neuritis and stubborn hiccups.

Brain and spine imaging fit neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, yet aquaporin-4 and MOG antibodies both came back negative, making the case seronegative. Immunosuppressive treatment brought clinical improvement. The authors warn that paroxysmal tonic spasms in a Sjögren's patient should trigger a search for NMOSD, since early therapy can spare lasting nerve damage.
pmc-13301008:
Bianca Oana Bucatos and co-authors analyze what predicts social cognitive outcomes in teenagers with schizophrenia in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Seventy-three adolescents with the illness and fifty-eight healthy controls took a mind reading test from photographs of eyes, an empathy questionnaire, and symptom ratings. The team genotyped the metabolism gene CYP2D6, sorting participants into normal and reduced metabolizers, then layered the predictors hierarchically.

Patients scored lower on both measures. Reduced metabolizers performed worse on mind reading and carried heavier negative symptoms. The mind reading model explained nearly eighty-nine percent of the variation, with metabolism status predicting independently alongside intelligence and negative symptoms. Empathy behaved differently: the gene effect there ran entirely through negative symptom severity. The authors describe a double dissociation, mind reading as a stable trait like anchor and empathy as state dependent, and they back metabolism aware treatment planning.
pmc-13302208:
Domenico Albano and colleagues evaluate, in a 2026 study, whether an artificial intelligence fracture detector changed night-shift accuracy for orthopaedic doctors working without an on-site radiologist. Missed fractures are a known emergency department risk, especially for tricky bones. The hospital introduced a commercial tool partway through the study window.

Records covered nearly twenty-nine thousand patients imaged between September 2024 and June 2025. Recall rates for possible missed injuries were already low before the tool arrived and dipped only slightly afterwards. Fracture-related recalls and changes to patient management likewise shifted by tiny, non-significant amounts. The authors conclude the tool brought no measurable improvement in this setting, though baseline performance left little room to gain.
pmc-13302908:
A lung-on-a-chip scaled for the smallest babies lifts blood oxygen without battering the blood, Yu Tao and colleagues report in a 2026 device study. Their microfluidic oxygenator copies the alveolar-capillary barrier's geometry to spread flow evenly and avoid shear hotspots. Bench tests pushed blood through single layers and an eight-layer stack.

One layer raised oxygen saturation from 64.7 to 96.5 percent at eight milliliters per minute. Six hours of circulation left blood largely intact, with most damage blamed on the pump rather than the device. The stacked version primed with only about 5.6 milliliters and modest pressure drops, pointing toward pumpless support and artificial-uterus systems for extremely preterm infants.
pmc-13303008:
Studies of dementia care networks measure them in wildly mixed ways, Noelle E. Carlozzi and colleagues conclude in a 2026 scoping review. Sifting over fourteen thousand papers yielded 197 studies that defined or measured the unpaid care webs around people with dementia: kin, friends, and others who help. The team listed the tools used and the facts most often gathered.

Only nineteen studies used a tested, standard tool; the rest made up their own, and thirteen standard tools saw use once or twice each. Seven facts came up again and again, led by whether a backup helper exists and how much help each person gives. The authors call for shared, tested measures.
pmc-13303708:
Miguel A. Galindo-Campos leads a 2026 study hunting blood markers that show who gains from immune checkpoint drugs in small cell lung cancer. Chemotherapy plus these drugs is now standard care, yet survival gains stay modest and no good selection test exists.

Patients from eight centers joined three treatment cohorts covering chemotherapy alone or with two classes of checkpoint drugs. Blood immune cells sampled before care and again before the second cycle were sorted and measured. Six cell groups changed early in ways tied to longer survival, including growing killer T cell sets. Early blood shifts may guide fairer patient selection.
pmc-13304708:
Y. Eugene Chen writes a 2026 commentary on a single molecule that works two bile acid receptors at once to protect the heart. Restoring blood flow after a heart blockage saves muscle, yet the returning flow itself triggers fresh damage.

One receptor, TGR5, calms inflammation and supports heart defense when switched on. The other, FXR, has been tied to heart cell death in this setting. The highlighted compound activates the first while blocking the second, a pairing found through computer screening rather than luck. Hitting two linked targets may succeed where single-target drugs failed in past trials.
pmc-13305308:
Shiqiao Wang, Hongming Hou, and co-authors review, in a 2026 paper, how six common phthalate plasticizers poison zebrafish, a stand-in for aquatic wildlife. These plastic softeners leach freely from products, disrupt hormones, and accumulate in waterways. Most lab tests, the authors note, use single chemicals at unrealistically high doses.

Comparing the six priority compounds, the review finds long, water-repelling chains far more toxic than short ones. Two mid-length phthalates hit the heart and nervous system hardest, while two others slashed reproduction at concentrations measured in parts per billion. Alarmingly, pollution hotspots in the real world already reach those effect levels. The authors urge future testing on chronic low-dose mixtures and harm passed to offspring, arguing current assessments understate the ecological risk.
pmc-13306108:
Ayman Elbehiry proposed tailoring tiny drug carriers to bacterial behaviour in drug-resistant Acinetobacter infection in a 2026 review. The pathogen, resistant to carbapenem drugs, kills many patients and leaves few treatment choices in hospital care.

Standard drugs miss how bacteria hide in films, slow their metabolism, pump drugs out or reshape outer membranes, the authors argue. Poor tissue reach and uneven drug levels add further failure. Nano-sized carriers can spread drugs better, release them slowly and enter restricted sites, so matching carrier design to the dominant bacterial state could sharpen treatment precision.
pmc-13307308:
Jingfan Zhang uncovered new building genes for scleric acid, a bacterial natural product, in a 2026 study. The compound weakly blocks a cancer-linked enzyme and was first found by waking a silent gene cluster from Streptomyces sclerotialus in a host strain.

Deleting gene sclG with CRISPR tools proved its enzyme essential for making the compound in reported tests. Long-read genome sequencing redrew cluster borders and found two extra genes, sclC and sclK, likely feeding starting materials. Gene activity scans after removing a repressor gene clarified how the cluster is switched on.
pmc-13307408:
Guojun Liang and co-authors study in 2026 why immune cells inside liver tumours often help the cancer instead of fighting it, and they focus on an enzyme called XOR. Using single cell data and tumour samples, they found far less XOR in tumour linked macrophages than expected.

Loss of XOR upset cholesterol balance and pushed those cells toward a state that weakens killer T cells, in part through higher PD-L1. A resveratrol based compound named Res616 bound and steadied XOR, which restored balance and revived T cell attack. In mice, Res616 plus anti-PD-L1 care slowed tumour growth more than either approach alone would suggest.
pmc-13307508:
Xiaofeng Zhang and co-authors present in 2026 DSHformer, a lean model that reads wearable sensor signals to name human actions for health, sport, and home care. Two faults drive the design: shifts in user or sensor place hurt broad use, and full attention grows too costly on long signal streams.

The model packs channel and time traits into small patches, aligns traits to learned class prototypes, and uses hashing based attention that keeps like signals grouped. Scores on five public data sets ran from 88.5 percent up to 98.6 percent across the sets tested here. Tests that removed parts one by one showed each part added value to the whole.
pmc-13307808:
Jiying Yin and colleagues uncover in 2026 how bovine viral diarrhea virus builds tiny bridges between cells to spread unseen. The viral protein NS5A binds a host protein called CKAP2 inside cattle cells. That contact switches on a growth signalling pathway, which drives construction of tunneling nanotubes.

Viruses then travel through the tubes straight into neighbouring cells, dodging antibodies outside. Blocking the host protein or the signalling pathway cut bridge formation sharply and hindered viral multiplication in their experiments. Direct cell-to-cell spread is a known route to the persistent infections that plague herds. The authors present CKAP2 and its pathway as drug or vaccine targets. Protecting cattle health also protects food supply stability, they note, which gives the mechanism practical weight.
pmc-13307908:
Xucheng Zheng and colleagues tune goose diets in 2026, asking how the starch-to-fat ratio interacts with lower protein levels. Three hundred sixty male geese ate diets with two protein levels and three energy ratios. Low-protein feeding is common but can leave birds depositing excess fat when energy balance goes wrong.

A lower starch-to-fat ratio increased body fat, raised liver cholesterol, and drained liver glycogen stores. Protein level mainly shifted liver enzyme activity tied to energy sensing, while the ratio drove wider glucose and fat metabolism effects. A middle ratio preserved the healthy unsaturated fat profile of breast meat better than the lowest ratio. The authors advise against letting the ratio fall too far in low-protein diets. Matching energy structure to protein level, they argue, protects both bird metabolism and meat quality.
pmc-13308608:
A 2026 report by Jinyoung Park and co-authors covers a fully biodegradable pressure sensor that sits in the knee and reports joint load for osteoarthritis care. Most built in sensors need a second surgery to take them out, while body models give only rough guesses of true load.

Their single ended design uses one electrode and body safe parts, and it kept working for more than two months in tests. Bench runs that mimicked the body tracked skull pressure and knee motion well, and implants in rabbits proved safe and true during natural moves. Load feedback could let rehab plans fit each knee and guard healing cartilage from overload harm.
pmc-13308908:
Anna Jolliff and co-authors give in 2026 a step by step guide to forming a lived experience panel. Such a panel groups patients and caregivers who advise research from first idea to final share. Wide range in the panel is the goal, so teams must reach past their own known circles to find it.

Steps run from joint groundwork with trusted town partners, through shared flyers and a smart interest form, to picks that chase the widest spread of lives. Channel yields, timelines, and member tales show what worked in their own build of a panel. Snags span vague role briefs and the strain of picking for spread. Ties built early pay off in trust and reach.
pmc-13310208:
Stephen P Robertson and co-authors describe a gene-guided prescribing pilot built with a Māori tribal community in a 2026 article. Indigenous communities are often left out of genomic medicine research and may hold distinct cultural views on genetic data. The pilot ran on a platform shaped by Māori ethical frameworks.

Community talks held face to face guided the design, with study stories rooted in tribal history to support joining. Genome data for 148 Māori participants were checked for variants in CYP2C19, a gene that changes how many drugs are processed, and matched against a year of prescriptions. About 7 percent were predicted poor metabolizers and 11 percent rapid ones in the pilot counts. The authors offer the process as proof of principle for tribal-led precision care.
pmc-13310408:
Angelique Cheryl and co-authors hunt for blood and marrow parcel markers of multiple myeloma in a 2026 study. Myeloma is a cancer of plasma cells in bone marrow that still lacks a cure. Diagnosis needs a marrow biopsy, an invasive test patients repeat over the disease course.

Parcels shed by cells, called extracellular vesicles, were gathered from blood and marrow fluid of 33 patients and 12 healthy donors. Protein cargo was profiled by mass measurement, and learning models built signatures for early stage, active disease, and relapse states. Scoring tests judged how cleanly the signatures separated the states. The authors present parcel proteins as a possible needle-free liquid biopsy for staging and tracking.
pmc-13310908:
Rui Yan and colleagues review brain imaging in sepsis linked brain harm in a 2026 paper. Sepsis can cloud the brain without direct brain infection, a state tied to death and lasting memory loss. Causes span vessel harm, barrier leaks, swelling, and signal imbalance, which end in nerve and support cell injury.

New scan tools can show those harms early and may sort patients by outlook. Work joins clinic scans with lab proof to define scan types for each cause. Clear scan types could point to drug targets and guide trial choice. Shared scan rules are still needed before routine use.
pmc-13311008:
Christina L. M. Khodadad and colleagues check germs on crops grown in a space station growth system in a 2026 study. Long space trips need fresh food grown with little mass, and a mist and water root system called XROOTS was tested in orbit. Returned lettuce, mustard, wheat, radish, tomato, and pea samples were checked for food safety.

Counts on root unit surfaces fell after cleaning, and leaf tips held fewer germs than roots or wicks. Tomato fruit and pea pods held the lowest counts. All screens for foodborne pathogens came back negative. Gene reading showed low leaf diversity and richer root communities, much like past space greens.
pmc-13311108:
Jean Marc Haurand led a 2026 study on whether vein congestion or low heart output drives kidney harm after heart dye tests. Dye linked kidney injury is common and harmful, and kidney filtering depends on pressure balance. Vein backup cannot be offset by the kidney, unlike low flow, so its role was tested.

Records covered 3,126 cases with heart dye and pressure checks at one center. Kidney injury hit about one fifth overall. Congested patients faced clearly higher risk than controls, while low output patients showed only a weak trend. After full adjustment, congestion alone stayed linked to injury. Vein pressure checks may refine risk sorting.
pmc-13311208:
Leila Aghazadeh and co-authors test diet adds for sperm quality in Moghani rams in a 2026 study. Male fertility drives sheep output, and oxidative stress can harm sperm DNA, motion, and life. Nano selenium and a fat aiding lysophospholipid were fed to boost antioxidant guards in the testis.

Rams on the paired diet showed better sperm making steps, taller lining, and more support and hormone cells in tubules. Index scores for tubule growth and sperm release rose. Total sperm count, living share, and intact DNA share all climbed with the adds. Diet based antioxidant plans may lift ram breeding value.
pmc-13311308:
In Tae Moon and co-authors describe a 2026 case of repeated ventricular fibrillation tied to Graves' disease, a thyroid condition. Wild heart rhythms are known with thyroid overactivity, but this deadly rhythm is rare.

A 33-year-old woman arrived after a fibrillation arrest. Her Graves' disease was poorly controlled despite thyroid drugs. She needed intensive care with a heart-lung machine, a ventilator, and kidney support, and received an implanted defibrillator. Two months later the device saved her when fibrillation struck again. Radioactive iodine treatment later steadied her rhythm and thyroid. The case supports device use when control stays poor.
pmc-13311708:
Veronika Whitesell Skrivankova and co-authors build risk models for unnatural death after self-harm in South Africa in a 2026 study. Repeat self-harm is common, and services cannot reach everyone at once.

Insurance claims and death records covered 6846 people aged ten and over who left hospital alive after self-harm care from 2011 to 2021. Models predicted death from suicide or accident within one to three years. Final models used age, sex, care details, past mental health drug use, and some past diagnoses. The tools aim to steer scarce prevention effort toward those at highest risk.
pmc-13311808:
Muneera A. Alajlan and co-authors test seaweed-based gels as scaffolds for dental stem cells in a 2026 lab study. Young teeth with dead pulp are hard to treat because standard root work cannot restore living tissue.

Five gel mixes were built from kappa-carrageenan, gelatin, or both, and compared with cells grown without gel. The gels differed in structure, breakdown, swelling, and stiffness. Stem cells from the tooth root tip stayed alive in all mixes. Gelatin-bearing gels supported longer-term growth and bone-like differentiation signs. The work moves regenerative root treatment a step closer by tuning the scaffold recipe.
pmc-13312108:
Wenyu Luo and colleagues describe a 2026 artificial intelligence model that predicts early recurrence after surgery for stage II or III colorectal cancer. Patients at this stage still face a real risk of the cancer returning soon after surgery, and current staging sorts that risk poorly.

The model reads two kinds of whole-slide images, standard hematoxylin-eosin stains and Ki-67 stains, for 362 patients from two medical centers. Among several image encoders tested, the combined model reached an area under the curve of 0.902 in the outside validation group and split patients into clearly different risk groups. Heat maps suggested high-risk calls drew on invasive tumor fronts, while low-risk calls leaned on immune cell areas and fibrous tissue. The authors see promise for personal follow-up planning.
pmc-13312808:
Maija Finnholm and colleagues test, in a 2026 retrospective study, how well a veterinarian's hands can judge injury to the supraspinous ligament that runs along a horse's spine. Back pain is common in horses and its cause is hard to pin down; diagnosis of this ligament usually leans on ultrasound. Nobody had formally checked palpation, the simple feel of the back, as a diagnostic tool.

Records from 126 horses brought to a university teaching hospital for back problems held both a written palpation finding and an ultrasound scan from the same visit. Comparing the two, palpation proved highly sensitive but less specific: it rarely missed signs the scan confirmed, especially swelling over the thoracic spine, though it also flagged some healthy tissue. The authors advise treating a positive feel as a prompt for ultrasound rather than an answer on its own.
pmc-13313308:
Bothaina AL-Awady and colleagues test, in a 2026 laboratory study, whether astaxanthin, a red carotenoid pigment, can make breast cancer cells more vulnerable to radiation. Radiotherapy works but carries heavy side effects, so sensitizers that lower the needed dose are prized. Working with MCF7 breast cancer cells, the team combined the pigment with ionizing radiation. They measured survival, programmed cell death, cell cycle position, and markers of spread.

Radiation alone did limited damage. Adding the pigment cut the dose needed for the killing effect roughly tenfold. Death markers rose, with caspase-3 activity up by 16 percent in the reported assays. Cell growth and the division phase shrank by over 40 percent in treated cells. Two enzymes tied to metastasis fell by about a quarter and a third. Unusually, the antioxidant pigment acted as an oxidant inside cancer cells, stalling them in radiation-sensitive phases. The authors back study toward clinical use.
pmc-13314108:
Vitor Barbosa Fialho Martins and colleagues ask, in a 2026 study, whether genetically mixed Swiss mice can judge pig vaccine quality as well as standard laboratory strains. Porcine circovirus 2 causes heavy losses in swine production, and vaccine testing usually relies on uniform inbred mice, even though outbred animals better mirror the variety of real immune systems. One hundred eight young female mice from three backgrounds received recombinant vaccines against two virus genotypes or plain water, with doses on days zero and fourteen and antibody measurement at day twenty-eight.

Every vaccinated mouse seroconverted, while all controls stayed negative. Antibody titers ran high across groups, spanning 1:25,600 to 1:102,400 in the reported dilutions, and no statistically significant difference separated outbred Swiss mice from the two inbred strains. The authors conclude that Swiss mice mount responses equivalent to the traditional models and can serve in immunogenicity and quality-control testing for these vaccines.
pmc-13314908:
Mathilde Pelletier Visa and co-workers ask knee patients what helps or blocks app-based rehab at home, in work published in 2026. People with knee osteoarthritis often drop exercise once clinic therapy ends, and phone health tools might keep them moving.

The team ran deep interviews in a French rehab clinic with 26 adults aged 40 years or more with doctor-proven disease, of whom a share of 61.5 percent were women as given in the report. Chats ran a median of about 40 minutes, as timed in the report, and were coded by two analysts working apart. Five themes arose, the first being that a clinician blessing is a must before patients trust an app. The findings tell designers that tech alone will not carry home rehab; human backing must lead.
pmc-13315508:
Yihan Wang, Zeyao Zhang, and Xuefeng Shi review in 2026 how egg quality shapes whether poultry eggs hatch. Shell traits and inner traits together form the base for embryo growth, acting through gas exchange, water balance, germ defense, and food supply for the chick.

Shell thickness, strength, and pore layout set protection and breathing room, while shell color and translucency hint at inner structure. Inside, the yolk share, albumen freshness, and albumen chemistry feed and steady the embryo. Storage time, storage heat, and incubation settings further shift the outcome. The review sums up these links and offers ways to raise hatch rates.
pmc-13315808:
Almien Smit and Vidya Lalloo surveyed in 2026 how emergency medicine doctors in South Africa learn, comparing free open online resources with textbooks and journals. Open access medical education has changed learning worldwide, but its use in South Africa was little studied.

Doctors and trainees at two Gauteng universities answered an online survey from October 2023 to December 2024. Fifty-five replies came in, mostly from trainees. Every respondent used blogs, nearly all used podcasts, and most used social media, while textbooks and journals stayed popular for deep learning at 89 percent. Named favorites included EMCrit. Barriers and quality views were also gathered.
pmc-13316208:
Yu He and colleagues built a biomimetic nanoplatform in 2026 to guard kidneys against calcium oxalate crystal damage, a chronic disease with no targeted therapy yet. Crystal deposits bring oxidative stress, neutrophil invasion, and tube cell injury, so the design pairs reactive oxygen cleanup with a block on neutrophil trap release.

Black phosphorus sheets loaded with DNase I were wrapped in neutrophil membrane fitted with a CD44 targeting peptide. The coating steers particles to inflamed kidney tissue, copying how neutrophils home there. Together the parts aim to cut crystal deposition and the injury that follows.
pmc-13316308:
Mandefro Abere Tegegne and fellow researchers offer a 2026 study of family planning among women in Ethiopia, where use and unmet need differ sharply by zone. Standard models can miss curved effects and place patterns, so the team used a geo-additive method that handles both.

The study drew on survey records for 7,484 women of childbearing age gathered by the PMA2020 project. Place alone explained most of the spread in contraceptive use and much of the spread in unmet need across zones. Schooling, wealth, fewer children, and more clinic visits linked with higher use, while wanting children and private care linked with unmet need. Programs, the authors argue, should be shaped zone by zone.
pmc-13317408:
Longcha Liu and colleagues present, in 2026, interview research on how men in nursing reach leadership roles in China. Nursing has long been a female-dominated profession, yet more men now hold senior posts. Understanding their routes upward may help hospitals build fairer leadership pipelines.

Ten senior nurses at a high-level hospital in China took part in long, partly scripted talks, analysed in seven steps. Four themes emerged: early career planning, strong clinical skill, good mentor support and skill at handling a gendered workplace. Subthemes covered setting leadership intent early, proving skill when crises hit, handling stereotypes about male nurses and balancing visibility with standing in female-majority teams. The authors urge formal mentor schemes and early planning support.
pmc-13319008:
Hongyu Huang and colleagues give a 2026 case report of reversible bone marrow disease caused by sodium valproate in a child with epilepsy. A nine-year-old boy developed low counts across all blood lines after six months on the drug. His haemoglobin was 77 g/L, and platelets were 83 × 109/L at presentation. Marrow testing confirmed myelodysplastic syndrome.

Doctors cut his valproate dose to 250 mg per day and added lacosamide. Within three months his blood counts returned to normal. A repeat marrow exam showed the abnormal features had cleared. Seizure control held without relapse through the reported period. The authors stress the dose-dependent nature of this rare harm. They urge regular blood monitoring for children on valproate.
pmc-13319408:
Martina Gaia Di Donna and co-authors report a 2026 study of blood vessel response in the brain among people with Alzheimer disease. Weak vessel response may add to memory loss, and its links to blood markers and gene type were tested here. The group held 64 patients with spinal fluid proof of the disease plus 28 healthy peers of like age.

A breath hold test with sound wave checks gauged how well brain vessels widened. Response was weaker in both patient gene groups than in healthy peers, with no gap between gene types. In one gene group only, weaker response tracked with a higher blood marker of disease and with more vessel harm on scans. Vessel checks may flag early harm in that group.
pmc-13319708:
Somia Gul and co-authors test old drugs for new use against monkeypox in a 2026 computer based study. The virus spreads from animals to people and belongs to a family close to the smallpox virus. Drugs cleared for smallpox may thus fit its proteins too, and reusing known drugs could speed up the search for care.

A cleared smallpox drug served as the yardstick while 38 cleared drugs from four drug classes were docked in software against key virus proteins. Several drugs bound more strongly than the yardstick in these tests. Motion checks on the best pairs held steady over time, which supports them as leads. Lab and animal proof must come before any clinical use.
pmc-13320008:
Jack Dowie and co-authors trial a new way to put patient values at the center of care choices in a 2026 study. Health value sets for shared measures are now built by averaging public tastes, which can drown out what one patient holds dear. Their method builds a full value set for each person first, then can pool those sets for public use when needed.

Choice heavy questions were swapped for scale based ones so the task fits inside a real clinic visit. A workbook tool walks the patient through rating health states on a common five part scale with calm help from the clinician. The clinician then adds likely states for each care option, and the match guides a joint call.
pmc-13320508:
Yuhuai Wang and colleagues introduce a new cancer drug candidate in a 2026 report. The compound, BGC1201, blocks SHP2, a protein that helps many tumours grow, and was built by a fragment based design method. Early lab checks looked at strength, heart safety signals, and effects across tumour cell types.

BGC1201 blocked its target at very low doses and slowed growth in 12 of 14 tumour cell lines while sparing normal vessel cells. In mice carrying human lung, pancreas, and gullet tumours, oral doses slowed tumour growth in a dose linked way. Tests in rats showed the drug was absorbed and cleared by several routes, supporting further study.
pmc-13320708:
Lara Bettenhäuser-Hartung and colleagues report, in 2026, failure rates for nearly a thousand small orthodontic screws used to pull the upper teeth backward. The screws, placed between tooth roots, anchor a fully customised lingual brace system for correcting class II bite problems in teenagers and adults. Reliable anchorage without extra appliances is the attraction.

One specialist practice placed 958 screws between 2015 and 2025 in 283 patients, following a strict insertion protocol shared by eight clinicians. Only fourteen screws were lost early, a failure rate the authors compare favourably with screws placed in the palate. Clinician experience did not significantly affect loss. The oldest patient group, over forty-five, showed the highest loss rate. The authors credit protocol discipline for the low failures.
pmc-13320808:
Aditya Hemendra Bhatt and Somashekhar Marutirao Nimbalkar draw lessons for the Global South in a 2026 article on advanced practice nursing for newborns. Specialist nurses have long anchored newborn intensive care in the United States, but staff shortages, duty hour limits, and burnout now press units hard. A clinical report from the American Academy of Pediatrics sets out role guidance.

The authors argue that training, licensing, and certification must line up with the babies a nurse actually serves, above all in high need units. Poorer countries face parallel shortages, and world guidance urges skill based training and supportive supervision. India's new neonatal nurse practitioner residency is offered as one emerging model for building that workforce.
pmc-13321008:
Weijian Ye and a large team study immune cells in heart failure caused by pressure overload in a 2026 article. About 55.5 million people worldwide live with heart failure, and high blood pressure is a major driver. Under lasting pressure the heart first thickens to cope, then remodels in harmful ways. Past work focused mostly on heart muscle cells themselves.

The authors centre on macrophages, immune cells whose role shifts across disease stages, and on a signal they release called SPP1. Their framing treats the heart as a multi-cell organ where fibroblasts, vessel cells, and immune cells jointly shape decline. Pinpointing a macrophage specific driver could open treatment paths beyond muscle centred drugs.
pmc-13321908:
Malik Jessen and colleagues survey collarbone hardware removal practice among German-speaking shoulder surgeons in a 2026 study. Removing plates after clavicle fracture healing is routine, yet choices on reasons, timing, imaging, and return to sport vary widely. A web survey went to members of the regional shoulder and elbow society, and 198 surgeons completed it.

Irritation, at 90.9 percent, and patient preference, at 87.9 percent, were the most chosen reasons for removal, while infection led absolute reasons. Most surgeons favoured late removal, with 38.9 percent waiting over 18 months and many judging timing by X-ray healing. X-rays were near universal, while CT was used far less often.
pmc-13322908:
Mwangala Nalisa, Thifhelimbilu Emmanuel Luvhengo and Petrina Kapewangolo review how surgery itself may affect cancer spread, in a 2026 article on the period around operations. Removing a tumour remains central to cure, yet that window brings tissue injury, inflammation and stress responses that can shift how spread develops.

Mechanisms covered include immune suppression, tumour cells entering the blood, shifts in cell character, dormant cells waking, neutrophil traps and changes in gut microbes. The authors also discuss building patient strength before surgery and team-based preparation. Counter-moves range from drug treatment around surgery and immune support to less invasive operations and treatments aimed at the tumour setting.
pmc-13323408:
Mohamed A Elshimy, Ahmed M Farrag and Gamal M Abdalla compare two revision operations for stubborn bile reflux after a sleeve jejunal bypass, in a 2026 prospective study. Forty patients whose reflux resisted medical therapy were converted either to Roux-en-Y gastric bypass or back to sleeve gastrectomy.

The bypass group, with 22 patients, had longer operations and hospital stays than the 18-patient sleeve group. Every bypass patient saw bile reflux fully resolve, while reflux persisted in a share of sleeve patients reported as 27.8 percent of that group. Reflux disease scores improved after bypass but worsened after sleeve revision, and weight control also favoured bypass over twelve months of follow-up.
pmc-13323808:
Chaofeng Niu and co-authors compared the burden and quality of care for nonrheumatic valvular heart disease in Asia with the global picture. Their 2026 study drew on Global Burden of Disease 2021 data from 1990 to 2021, tracking incidence, deaths, and disability-adjusted life years, and projected trends to 2050 with time-series and Bayesian models. A quality-of-care index built by principal component analysis rounded out the comparison.

Incidence grew faster in Asia than globally, even as age-standardized mortality and disability rates declined. Men showed higher incidence, while older women bore greater mortality and disability, a persistent sex and age disparity. Quality of care improved substantially over three decades, but projections point to slowing gains and a possible plateau under current strategies. The authors argue that prevention and management must improve if Asia is to keep pace with its rising case load.
pmc-13324308:
Djamel Tahir and co-authors survey tick-borne pathogens in dogs across France, in a 2026 multicentre participatory study run from December 2022 to December 2023. Clinics, owners and labs together collected ticks and blood from 82 dogs seen at 41 practices in 34 departments.

The 165 ticks collected were led by Dermacentor reticulatus, followed by Ixodes ricinus and Rhipicephalus sanguineus in the reported shares. DNA screening found Borrelia garinii and Babesia canis canis in five dogs each, and antibody tests flagged Ehrlichia in one dog and Anaplasma in three, with several infected dogs showing no symptoms. Ticks carried further pathogens. The authors cast dogs as sentinels for human tick risk.
pmc-13325908:
Mahak Jain and colleagues test a stain meant to separate Ewing sarcoma from look-alike neuroendocrine tumors in a 2026 pathology study. Both cancers form sheets of small round cells that can fool the microscope.

Staining for Nkx2.2 covered 60 cases: 17 Ewing sarcomas, 34 neuroendocrine tumors, and nine others. The marker caught 88.2 percent of Ewing cases but also lit up in many other tumors, giving a specificity of just 53.4 percent overall. Gut and pancreas neuroendocrine tumors stained often, while most lung ones stayed negative. Pleomorphic sarcoma and melanoma also stained in the small extra set. The authors advise using the stain only within a wider panel.
pmc-13327608:
Huidi Cui and team review how fiber gel webs could change eye drug delivery. Their 2026 paper notes that eye build and workings make drug delivery oddly hard, and that usual routes, drops, shots into the eye, and body-wide drugs, each hit distinct limits. Fiber gels, mainly self-built protein-based and plant-fiber-based webs, can be tuned for exact physical and chemical traits, giving steady release and better body fit.

The payoff is large: steady release stretches useful treatment time up to threefold while cutting shot counts, lowering risks like inner eye infection and retina harm from frequent eye shots. Lab-stage wins show in age-linked macular decay, cornea inflammation, and uveitis, with promise for smart contact lenses. The team warns that clinic use hangs on large-scale making and strict long-term safety checks before these webs can reshape care for sight-threatening disease.
pmc-13331908:
Siqi Yang-Fu and colleagues review a 2026 puzzle in dog cognition research: why touchscreens remain rare despite their clear strengths. Screens let tests run in a standard way, cut the influence of the person running the test, and improve data quality. Yet a sweep of the dog literature found only fourteen touchscreen studies in the whole indexed record, even as dog cognition work keeps growing.

The authors sort the barriers into three groups. Technical hurdles include the need for skills from more than one field. Practical hurdles include high cost and long training times for dogs. A third group concerns the dog's own senses and view of the world, which shape what screen tasks can fairly ask. They propose open-source tools, joint work across labs, and screens better matched to dogs.
pmc-13332008:
Salman Siddiqui and colleagues map 2026 epidemiology and burden of eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis in England. Data on this rare vessel inflammation disease have been thin. The team mined a large English primary-care record set for patients diagnosed between 2006 and early 2019 with at least a year of prior data. They tracked how often the disease arose, how common it was, and what followed: other illnesses, deaths, treatments, and clinical outcomes.

The new-case group held 486 people and the prevalent group 729, with incidence near three cases per million person-years. Nearly all new cases carried at least one other condition, and about eight in ten had asthma recorded. The study gives health services a firmer picture of a rare disease that often travels with asthma and other illness, and it sets a baseline for judging future treatments.
pmc-13332408:
Stefania Corti and colleagues review evidence in 2026 that the protein TDP-43, the hallmark deposit of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, also builds up outside the brain and spinal cord. ALS has long been framed as a disease of motor neurons alone, but that picture is widening.

The altered, phosphorylated form of TDP-43 has been found in patients' skeletal muscle and in the small nerve bundles running through muscle, with a distinct spread pattern and molecular profile. The review weighs why muscle cells may be vulnerable, covering failed transport along nerve fibers and broken protein cleanup systems. Muscle biopsy detection of the deposits looks promising for earlier diagnosis. The authors argue ALS is better seen as a whole-body TDP-43 proteinopathy, a shift that could open new treatment angles.
pmc-13333108:
Ali K Hasan and colleagues report a 2026 case of silver-induced contact dermatitis from heart monitoring electrodes. Twelve-lead electrocardiography ranks among the most common and essential hospital investigations worldwide. The patient was a 57-year-old man in the cardiac intensive care unit needing continuous heart monitoring, who developed multiple well-defined red annular lesions across the chest after exposure to silver-containing electrodes. The pattern pointed to contact dermatitis from the electrode silver.

He received mixed-field care for heart failure, obstructive uropathy, and the skin reaction before transfer to a better-equipped national cardiac center for his acute cardiac illness. Skin reactions to silver electrodes are rarely reported, the authors note. The case stresses thorough history-taking and routine skin examination in daily practice, especially when new rashes appear under monitoring devices. It also urges care teams to weigh device materials when rashes defy other explanations.
pmc-13333508:
Mahendra Gawali, Hsiang-Chen Wang, and Arvind Mukundan open a Research Topic in a 2026 editorial on machine learning for biomedical diagnosis and disease detection. Cancer caught late frames the collection: algorithms that read scans, signals, and lab panels promise faster, personal detection than unaided review.

The editorial tours contributions spanning medical imaging, wearable data, and biomanufacturing. One group classified endoscopic ultrasound images from 219 patients, pairing deep learning with radiomic features to reach an AUC of 0.95. Another sorted 1,498 diabetic patients by microvascular complication risk, with gradient boosting on top and blood markers such as urea, fibrinogen, and D-dimer among the signals. Lung cancer work on 197 surgical patients combined spectral CT radiomics with deep learning to predict tumor spread through air spaces, logistic regression leading at an AUC of 0.918, while a colon cancer team modelled CT scans from 247 patients. The editors frame the set as data science and healthcare meeting.
pmc-13333708:
Nicholas D. Thomson, Brooklyn A. Worthen, and Jessica J. James authored a 2026 study of psychopathy traits and suicide risk among adults injured by violence. Suicide risk is hard to predict in this group, and the authors asked whether specific trait facets matter more than the overall score.

Participants were 458 violently injured adults, mostly men with an average age near 33, recruited at a city trauma center in the United States. They completed measures of psychopathic traits, suicide risk, post-traumatic stress, and substance use. Overall psychopathy tracked with higher suicide risk even after accounting for trauma symptoms and substance use. Only the Lifestyle facet, covering impulsive and unstable behavior, predicted risk on its own. Screening for that facet could sharpen risk assessment in trauma care.
pmc-13334808:
Madeleine Thès and co-authors ran the COLT-ICU study, reported in 2026, of lung transplant recipients admitted to intensive care with COVID-19 pneumonia. Transplant patients face high risk from the virus, yet ICU outcomes for this group were barely documented.

All nine accredited adult lung transplant centers in France contributed cases from March 2020 to December 2022. Of 84 patients, 39 died in the ICU, a mortality of 46.4 percent in this cohort. Being more than 30 months past transplant and needing intubation each independently predicted death. Among intubated patients, mortality hit 59 percent whether intubation came first-line or after noninvasive support failed, and rose to 80 percent when intubation followed five or more days of trying alternatives. The data sharpen risk conversations with transplant families.
pmc-13335108:
Hui Zhu and colleagues report 2026 in-womb natural killer cell therapy for unclear-cause repeat pregnancy failure. Unclear-cause repeat pregnancy loss and repeat embryo implant failure represent significant clinical challenges in human reproduction. The study reports promising birth outcomes of fifteen patients with these conditions related to uterine natural killer cell abnormalities, treated with induced CD49a-positive womb-lining-like natural killer cells from the patients' own blood. Ongoing pregnancies and live births came about in eighty percent, twelve of fifteen patients, after two cycles of therapy.

No serious treatment-linked side effects showed up among all participants. These findings point to a need for further clinical studies testing this cell treatment in repeat pregnancy loss and implant failure tied to uterine natural killer cell disorders. Implant failure meant no clinical pregnancy after at least two embryo transfers.
pmc-13335408:
Mari Morimoto and colleagues report a 2026 case of severe low prothrombin linked to vitamin K lack during long cefazolin therapy in a kidney patient. A 73-year-old man on maintenance dialysis for end-stage kidney disease from diabetic kidney damage was hospitalized for pus-filled ankle tendon infection and treated with the drug. During hospitalization, he had persistent anorexia and recurrent gut bleeding. On a day without treatment, he developed an under-skin bruise around the artery-vein fistula.

Despite no blood thinner use, clotting times were much longer. Lab findings showed reduced activity of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors and a much higher vitamin K absence protein level, indicating vitamin K lack. IV vitamin K and switching the antibiotic from the drug to ampicillin followed.
pmc-13336108:
Xuedong Qiang and co-authors built an information encryption system driven by how liquid metal wets surfaces in a 2026 engineering study. Standard optical and electronic encryption can fall to analysis because materials respond predictably; a fluid metal's shifting surface is harder to clone.

Their system joins an inclinometer sensor exploiting liquid metal's dynamic wetting, a 3D motion platform, and a probe-driven transmission mechanism. Machine control and fluid dynamics together encode information physically across several modes. Tests encrypted and decrypted images and text with high precision and steadiness. Four separate settings guard the code, and decoding tolerates deviations only below 0.02 percent. The authors frame it as a materials-driven route to flexible, high-security storage.
pmc-13336408:
Wenhui Li and co-authors built a tandem catalyst that turns carbon dioxide and hydrogen into gasoline in a 2026 catalysis study. Existing oxide-zeolite pairs activate hydrogen weakly and waste much of the carbon as methane or carbon monoxide.

Their system pairs gallium zirconium oxide with gallium-substituted ZSM-5 zeolite. The optimized version converted 17.2 percent of CO2 with 83.2 percent selectivity to gasoline-range hydrocarbons at 320 degrees Celsius and 3 megapascals, keeping methane below 1 percent and CO at 11.7 percent in the reported product mix. It ran 400 hours without significant deactivation. Tuning calcination gave the oxide the right mix of gallium-hydrogen coverage and oxygen vacancies, while gallium in the zeolite softened its acidity toward making fuel-range molecules.
pmc-13336508:
Xingyi Li and colleagues present 2026 STransformer, a joined deep learning model for reading tissue variety from space-aware many-type and many-omics data. Gains in space-aware tech now allow many data types to be read at once within a tissue slice, keeping key space context. Yet current computing paths lack the freedom to handle both space-aware many-type and many-omics data at once.

STransformer takes in a full range of space data with ease. By catching short-range cell links and tissue-wide meaning patterns at once, it pulls out strong readings to split complex tissue variety with care. Tests across varied species, tissue types, and data types show its wide range. For space-aware many-type data, STransformer marks complex body structures in the human cortex, finds disease paths in Alzheimer's disease, and tracks changing growth paths.
pmc-13336908:
Changxu Nie and co-authors test silencing a microglial gene to clear amyloid in Alzheimer's models in a 2026 study. The mouse gene Lilrb4a rises in brain immune cells in disease models and links to APOE signaling. In 5xFAD mice carrying human APOE4, deleting the gene or blocking it with antisense strands cut cortical plaque load.

Amyloid clogging of brain vessels also eased, without any change in amyloid production. Gene data pointed to PPAR-linked metabolic programs switching on a pro-clearance state, with calmer inflammatory signals. In cell tests, PPAR-gamma activation copied the improved uptake and breakdown of amyloid. The checkpoint could be druggable for APOE4 carriers, who face high Alzheimer's risk.
pmc-13337108:
Tingting Zhan and a large team watch single binding events live to skip washing steps in a 2026 biosensor study. Counting single molecules gives precise marker measures, but endpoint tests are slow and plagued by stray binding. Their chip carries a microlens array that magnifies scattering from gold particle labels under an ordinary microscope.

Each event's motion fingerprint separates true target binding from stray sticking, enabling wash-free digital sensing with low-magnification optics. For cardiac troponin I, a heart attack marker, the limit reached 0.051 pg per milliliter with validation in undiluted serum samples in the reported work. A compact, portable setup delivering lab-grade answers at the bedside is the goal.
pmc-13337408:
Liyan Song and colleagues trace how a rhubarb compound fights fatty liver inflammation in a 2026 study. Rhein, an anthraquinone from traditional rhubarb medicine, eased metabolic steatohepatitis in earlier hints, but its mechanism was murky. The team combined network pharmacology and docking with mouse and cell validation.

In mice fed a choline-deficient high-fat diet, rhein improved liver fat, inflammation, and injury in step with dose, without changing body-wide lipid levels. It raised fat-burning genes such as Acadl and Cpt1a while quieting inflammatory cytokines in the reported tests. Docking flagged the growth receptor EGFR as a core target, and cell work confirmed rhein switches it on, firing a pathway that coordinates metabolism and inflammation.
pmc-13337508:
Wei Zheng and co-authors study how AI scoring can shrink academics' sense of their own worth in a 2026 survey study. In metric-heavy Chinese higher education, AI-based scoring increasingly judges faculty work. The authors name the feeling algorithmic relative devaluation: a sense that one's work counts for less beside AI-set standards.

A three-wave survey of 448 faculty members found that AI visibility and benchmark intensity raised that feeling, while explainability lowered it. The feeling pushed both adaptive and defensive career reshaping and lowered how lasting people judged their careers. Adaptive moves restored that judgment; defensive ones eroded it further. Governance rules played a mixed role, softening visibility's harm yet sharpening benchmark pressure in the model results.
pmc-13337808:
Nazik M. Nurelhuda leads a 2026 systematic review of business training inside public health degrees. Shifting health needs, tight resources, and changing jobs have pushed calls for entrepreneurial skills. Such skills might help graduates innovate and build varied careers.

Eight databases were searched for work from 2000 to May 2025, plus a scan of master's program pages. Only three peer-reviewed studies met the entry rules, showing a small and mixed evidence base. Programs that mention this training were also mapped. The thin record suggests universities speak about enterprise more often than they study whether the teaching works.
pmc-13339008:
Bradley Lonergan and colleagues reviewed advance care planning in 2026 for people with advancing Parkinson disease. As complications such as falls and cognitive decline grow, reliance on health and social care rises, yet planning for future care often starts only after crises hit. Advance care planning lets patients, caregivers, and clinicians record wishes on future care, wills, powers of attorney, and advance statements.

Basic palliative care can be woven into Parkinson care from diagnosis through end of life, tailored to disease stage. Starting planning earlier gives patients a stronger voice in later decisions. The review urges services to normalise early conversations rather than waiting for decline to force them.
pmc-13339108:
Sai A. Nagaratnam and colleagues describe orthostatic myoclonus, a jerking disorder of standing, in a 2026 hospital cohort. Irregular leg bursts while upright cause unsteadiness and falls, yet its features were poorly charted. Records came from Westmead Hospital for 2007 to 2023.

Forty-two people, average age 74 years, were included as reported. Muscle recordings measured burst length, timing, and rhythm with a custom program. Bursts lasted 77 to 90 ms across leg muscles as reported, strongest and most synced in the front shin muscle. Only 12 percent showed any rhythm. Most, 79 percent in the count, had another nerve disorder alongside.
pmc-13340208:
Chapter 5 of a 2026 reference work on fish lesions turns to the blood-forming and lymphoid system, with Wes Baumgartner heading the author group. Fish lack bone marrow and lymph nodes, so blood cell production sits mainly in the kidney and spleen, while the thymus matures T cells.

The chapter contrasts fish organs with their mammalian counterparts and explains primary and secondary lymphoid tissues. It describes how the front kidney supports B cell formation and how mucosa-linked lymphoid tissue adds immune cover. Knowing this anatomy gives fish pathologists a baseline for judging growths and losses in these tissues.
pmc-13340708:
Money worries linger for living liver donors even decades later, according to a 2026 single-center survey by Piper Stacey and colleagues. The center performed 402 donor operations over 24 years, and 129 past donors answered a 2024 phone survey about life after donation.

Twenty-four donors reported financial harm, most often lost wages, with a median 10 weeks off work. Travel, lodging, and follow-up care added costs, and six donors struggled to get life insurance. Thirty-four had medical complications such as hernias. Yet 98.4% said they would donate again and 93.7% would recommend it, a gap the authors say counseling and support programs should address.
pmc-13343708:
Hilde Erdal and co-authors examine care given before hospital admission for severe pregnancy sickness in Norway, in a 2026 analysis of the SUKK-P cohort. Women with hyperemesis gravidarum need fast, fitting treatment to protect mother and fetus, so the team charted what help arrived before 214 women reached hospital care.

Most women, 89 percent, had already sought care, and 88 percent had taken anti-nausea drugs, yet 42 percent received sick leave before anyone offered medication. Symptom scores at admission were severe, daily life was heavily disrupted, and nearly all felt low or depressed, with half reporting thoughts of ending the pregnancy. Faster drug treatment, the authors argue, should come before work leave.
pmc-13344008:
Grayson Barnes and colleagues probed the copper importer YcnJ in 2026 in Bacillus subtilis. Copper is a key enzyme cofactor for cell breathing in most aerobic organisms but toxic in excess. Most copper enzymes sit within or outside the cell wall, yet proper copper loading often needs copper import into the cytosol. YcnJ had been tipped as a copper importer, but its biology was poorly mapped.

Under copper starvation, YcnJ proved key for aerobic growth by backing Qox, the main breathing menaquinol oxidase. YcnJ function needs a copper binding site in an outside CopC domain plus a second putative site in its transmembrane CopD domain. The work clarifies bacterial copper handling with implications for breathing and metal balance.
pmc-13344208:
Madeline Pence and colleagues tested scan timing in 2026 for pregnancies with edge or membrane cord insertion, where abnormal cord insertion into the placenta has been linked to slow fetal growth. Some guidance backs third trimester growth checks, yet best timing was unclear. The look back cohort covered singleton pregnancies diagnosed with isolated edge or membrane insertion before 24 weeks at a single centre from September 2021 to May 2025.

Outcomes were slow fetal growth, defined as estimated fetal weight or belly size below the tenth percentile, plus low amniotic fluid. Among 248 edge insertion patients, 710 scans at or after 24 weeks found eight slow growth cases, about 3 percent. Before 32 weeks, four cases were found with a number needed to scan of about 37, though half resolved on follow up. After 32 weeks the number needed to scan was about 81 with all cases persisting.
pmc-13345808:
Ping Cheng, Shuang Liu, and Qinwen Shen present a refined laparoscopic technique for the most dangerous form of cesarean scar pregnancy in 2026. A 35-year-old with two prior cesareans bled from a pregnancy lodged in her scar, classed type IIIb with a thin wall under 3 millimeters and a sac of 66 millimeters.

Surgeons briefly tied both uterine arteries with absorbable thread, freed adhesions, cut the mass out in one block with a small safety margin, and rebuilt the uterus in layers. Total blood loss held at 100 milliliters, frozen sections confirmed full removal, and anatomy stayed intact. Eighteen months later she conceived naturally and reached the second trimester smoothly, backing the method's fertility promise.
pmc-13346008:
Ryan Reagans and Zaibo Li lay out a diagnostic approach to chest-center tissue sampling in 2026. The mediastinum packs thymus, lymph, germ cell, and soft tissues into one space. That mix breeds a wide range of harmless and deadly lumps. Needle sampling through airway or gut ultrasound scopes now reaches every corner with little invasion.

Scant samples and look-alike cells still trip diagnosis, so the review pairs cell appearance with add-on tests: stains that pin lineage, flow cytometry for lymphoma, and gene sequencing for treatment targets. Digital imaging and AI tools are joining the kit. Classic traps, such as thymic tumors mimicking spread cancer, get named, with a stepwise workflow to dodge them.
pmc-13347208:
Erika N. Dreikorn and colleagues report five years of genomic care inside a family medicine clinic, in a cohort study from 2026. Chart review covered 1,602 new patients seen at the UPMC clinic from 2019 to 2024 for family history checks, counselling, and clinician review, in person and by telemedicine.

Testing was ordered for 1,174 patients, a share of 73 percent, with 1,360 tests in total and a completion rate of 83.4 percent across the period. Panel tests made up 71 percent of orders, and most tests matched the main referral reason while some came from extra findings at intake. Growth let the clinic add staff and settle into a two-visit model.
pmc-13347708:
Andrew J. Perciaccante and colleagues squeeze three kinds of molecular data from one tiny vesicle sample, in a methods study from 2026. Small vesicles shed by cells carry proteins, fats, and small molecules that mirror cell state, yet material is scarce. So stepwise extraction pulls each class in turn from the same ten million vesicles for mass-based reading.

Repeated fragmentation scans deepened small-molecule coverage while nanoflow protein runs added depth, giving repeatable profiles across all three classes from a single draw. Plasma vesicles cleaned by three routes gave distinct profiles that exposed yield against purity trade-offs for each route. One-sample multi-reading saves precious material for marker hunting and therapy work.
pmc-13348508:
McClatchey and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how patients and staff view psychologists based in primary care, the front-line general practice setting. Psychologists there can target habits that drive long-term illness and support people in managing their own health, and a national body urges routine embedding, but practice lags behind. The team searched four databases for English-language studies since 2010 and added finds from reference lists and citation tracking.

Seventy-two studies qualified. Patients and primary care staff spoke well of the setup, crediting it with wider and better access to care, stronger patient skills, and lower workload and stress for practice staff. They also credited it with better quality of care and chances for staff growth. Psychologists were satisfied too, yet flagged heavy role demands, organizational friction, and training needs. The authors offer practical steps for rollout and point to where further study is needed.
pmc-13349508:
Masahiro Hisaoka and colleagues count new heart failure after ablation. Their cohort study appeared in 2026. It covers atrial fibrillation patients with normal heart squeeze. A total of 480 patients took part. All had ejection fraction at or above 50 percent. None had prior heart failure. All had first ablations for the rhythm fault. Follow-up ran a median of 70 months. Rhythm return and new failure were both tracked. Landmark and time-varying models did the judging.

New failure struck 18 patients in total. That share is 3.75 percent of the group. The rate is low yet worth guarding against. Age over 75 years was the steady predictor. Early rhythm return did not forecast failure. Return after the final ablation told a different story. Its hazard ratio was 4.028 in the time model. Lasting rhythm control is thus backed.
pmc-13349708:
Haneul Jung and co-authors charted in 2026 malaria diagnosis in South Korea from 2021 to 2025, using samples sent to the national disease control agency. Home-grown and imported malaria differ in species, source, and control needs. Yet referral paths shape what national data truly show.

The agency took in 2,508 malaria-positive samples, sorted by private versus public and military referral routes and confirmed by microscopy or gene detection. Home cases were overwhelmingly Plasmodium vivax at 96.2 percent. Imported cases were mainly falciparum, with ovale and mixed infections also seen. Parasite levels gauged from PCR thresholds added clinical detail. The review helps Korea aim elimination and traveller advice by species and route.
pmc-13350008:
Meng Zhu and colleagues reviewed 20 years of ultrasound practice for testicular lumps in children in a 2026 study from West China Hospital. Records covered 84 lumps in 79 patients aged up to 18, scanned between 2004 and 2023, and the analysis used the 2022 WHO tumour classification.

Ultrasound finds these rare lumps reliably, but telling harmless from malignant ones by image alone is unsettled. Statistical models compared image traits between the two groups across all lumps, primary tumours, and pre-teen cases. Clear image clues would help surgeons spare healthy tissue in benign cases while acting fast on cancers, a balance that matters greatly in children.
pmc-13351708:
Liqin Ke, Shuxian Li, and Guohong Zhu review gut and airway microbes in asthma and allergic disease in 2026. Both illnesses involve immune imbalance, weak surface barriers, and wide variation between patients. Microbes in the gut and airways may shape onset, flare risk, and course through a two-way gut-lung link.

The review draws on recent English-language work on early-life colonisation, disturbed microbe balance, and microbe-made chemicals. Evidence links early gut seeding and airway imbalance to allergy risk and flare patterns, though strength varies by topic. Microbe-based treatments are covered as an emerging option. The authors stress careful reading, since much of the field rests on links rather than proven cause.
pmc-13352508:
Francesca Ramacciotti leads a 2026 study of light-heated woven mats that lift polymer coatings off layered films without harming layers below. Removing an insoluble top coat is hard when it chemically resembles what sits beneath. A plant-derived electrospun mat loaded with melanin particles turns light into heat right at the contact surface.

Careful solvent loading plus light heating tuned the interface temperature, tracked by thermal cameras and probes. As proof of concept, a tough cross-linked alkyd coat was lifted from acrylic or alkyd layers beneath. Imaging, chemical checks, and stiffness mapping judged selectivity. The reusable mat approach may help art conservation and recycling tasks that need gentle, local heating.
pmc-13354308:
Nader Aghakhani and others wrote a 2026 guide for healthcare staff on preventing and managing collective trauma. Shared catastrophes such as terrorism, mass violence, earthquakes, and pandemics can overwhelm a society's coping stock, leaving wounds that echo across generations. Chronic stressors can produce similar damage over time.

Drawing on Jungian ideas of the collective unconscious, the guide explains how shared myths and patterns carry trauma forward, and it sets out useful steps for staff who support affected groups. The letter speaks straight to doctors facing communities in distress. It offers language and strategies for care that addresses the group wound, not only single symptoms.
pmc-13354808:
Jorge Hoegl led a 2026 multicentre study of routine endoscopy in staging locally advanced cervical cancer in Venezuela. Cystoscopy and rectosigmoidoscopy are traditionally used to check whether cancer has invaded bladder or bowel, but their added value with modern imaging is debated, mainly in low- and middle-income settings. The team asked whether routine scopes still change staging or care.

In 233 people with stage IB3 to IVB disease, all underwent medical check, magnetic resonance imaging, and routine endoscopy. The primary outcome was confirmation of mucosal spread. The study gives oncology teams in resource-limited settings evidence on when endoscopy adds information beyond imaging, and when it can safely be omitted.
pmc-13355008:
Prerana Roth and co-authors present a 2026 clinical case of a 34-year-old man in South Carolina with a spreading rash and burning pain in his legs. The rash began on his arm and spread over weeks across his body. A skin biopsy was taken, and the case is posed as a quiz before the answer is given: lepromatous leprosy, also called Hansen's disease.

He was treated for two years with a three-drug course and later retreated, and most spots healed with scars. New painful lumps then arose during care, which proved to be a type 2 immune reaction to the illness. He was given steroids and thalidomide. The case stresses early finding to stop nerve damage.
pmc-13355908:
Mohammed N Taha and Moath Al-Shudifat report a 2026 case of a 62-year-old severely malnourished woman whose large fluid sac around the heart was the first sign of mixed connective tissue disease. This rare immune disease blends features of lupus, scleroderma, and muscle inflammation. She came in with lasting nausea and vomiting, and a scan for gut symptoms found the fluid by chance.

Heart ultrasound showed early pressure danger signs, and about a liter of clear fluid was drained, with no infection or cancer found. Swollen sausage-like fingers prompted antibody tests, which confirmed the disease pattern. She improved with drainage and nutrition support and left with team follow-up. The case warns against blaming such fluid on nutrition alone.
pmc-13358508:
Ananya Kommuri and co-authors present a 2026 study of safety reports for two heart valve repair devices. MitraClip and PASCAL fix a leaky mitral valve through a tube in a blood vessel, with no open-heart surgery. The team mined a United States database of device problem reports to compare the two.

From 2022 to 2025 they gathered 518 reports and sorted the problems into 13 types. Device parts breaking or coming loose were the most common reports. Real-world reports like these cannot prove which device is safer, but they show regulators and doctors which faults to watch for as use of these devices grows.
pmc-13359008:
Katharina Busch and co-authors track gaming disorder in teenagers in a 2026 study. Gaming disorder means play that a teen cannot control and that harms daily life. The team followed 3,358 German adolescents with yearly surveys from 2019 to 2024, spanning the COVID-19 pandemic years.

The share with the disorder doubled from 2.9 percent in 2019 to 6.5 percent in 2023, then fell to 3.9 percent in 2024, still above pre-pandemic levels. Boys were affected more than girls in most years. The study also weighs risk factors for new and lasting cases, giving schools and parents a firmer picture of the trend.
pmc-13360108:
Alina Crenguța Nicolae led a 2026 review on why many cancers stop responding to drug treatment. The review centers on P-glycoprotein, a pump in the cell wall that pushes cancer drugs back out of the cell. When tumors make too much of this pump, drugs lose their punch and the disease can grow again.

The authors explain how the pump drives drug resistance and how it links to changes in cell energy use and stress damage. They then survey new ways around it, such as plant compounds, polymer carriers, and tiny drug packages built with nanotech. Some newer cancer drugs are also less prone to being pumped out. The team hopes these paths can restore the power of treatment for patients whose cancers resist drugs.
pmc-13360308:
Artorn Anuduang and co-authors tested Thai shallot extracts in obese mice in a 2026 study. Shallots hold natural compounds that may ease high blood sugar and poor blood fats. The team made two extracts, one plain and one treated with enzymes to change a key compound, quercetin, into a form the body absorbs more easily. Both were fed to mice raised on a high-fat diet.

Even though the enzyme version held more of the easy-absorb form, both extracts helped in much the same way. Blood sugar and blood fats improved, cell damage from stress fell, and less fat built up in the body and liver. No harm to major organs was seen. The authors say either extract could suit low-cost health foods, so the simpler method may be enough.
pmc-13360608:
The Cells Editorial Office issued this 2026 expression of concern about a 2022 review by Tokunaga and co-authors. The review covered how heat shock transcription factors regulate the cell cycle, and it appeared in the journal Cells. After it came out, readers raised doubts about the validity of one figure, Figure 2C. The journal contacted the authors and asked them to explain.

The authors sent no reply, so the doubts could not be settled. The editorial board reviewed the matter and judged that the issue does not change the paper's overall findings in a major way. The board planned no further action at the time, but left the door open if new information arrives. The notice stays attached to the paper so readers know about the open question.
pmc-13362808:
Huanyu Zhang and colleagues describe a 2026 study that makes glucovanillin, a sugar-linked form of the vanilla compound vanillin, and tests its promise against type 2 diabetes. An enzyme built the compound in the lab from vanillin and a sugar donor. Computer network tools then mapped its likely body targets, and gene data from patients helped narrow the list to a few key players.

Seven core targets emerged, two of which sorted patients from healthy people with good accuracy in data tests. Lab assays showed the compound slows alpha-glucosidase, a gut enzyme that frees sugar from food, more strongly than plain vanillin, and cell maps tied the targets to immune cell talk. The dual action makes it a lead worth animal tests.
pmc-13363308:
Howard R Selden, Rebecca Y Lai, and Ryan A Riskowski describe a 2026 device study on making strong radio-frequency magnetic fields inside very small spaces. Their generator stacks paired coils printed on circuit boards, replacing bulky wire solenoids. The team measured the pair's electrical response near 330 kilohertz, a band used to heat magnetic nanoparticles, and modeled how even the field is across a five-millimeter test square.

The modeled field matched bench readings closely, and the field strayed from its average by only a small margin across the test area. The compact stack cuts size, sample volume, and power needs versus standard coils. Such pairs could suit nanoparticle heating rigs for cancer and drug delivery research, plus remote control of chemical systems.
pmc-13363908:
Yong-Hua Li and colleagues present a 2026 study on pulling polysaccharides from Siegesbeckia orientalis, a traditional herb, with help from low-temperature plasma. These plant sugars show wide health promise, but hot water extraction is slow and low-yielding. The team tuned the plasma dose with structured trials, then purified the top fraction and mapped its sugar makeup and chain shape with standard tools.

The plasma route yielded notably more sugar than hot water, since the discharge roughens the plant surface and frees the contents. The clean fraction was built mostly of galactose with rhamnose and arabinose, folded in a triple helix with a highly branched core. The authors offer the method for food and herb processing.
pmc-13364108:
Michael N Getz and a large team present a 2026 study on making silicon photodiodes, precision light sensors, survive deep ultraviolet exposure. Their induced-junction design relies on charge in a glassy coating to form the sensing junction, but UV drains that charge and the signal collapses. The team tracked the decay, then tested shallow implanted junctions of arsenic and antimony, plus a strip-and-regrow step for the surface oxide.

Plain devices lost photocurrent fast at the test wavelength and some died outright. Implanted junctions steadied at most of their starting output through heavy doses. With the regrown oxide, output stayed nearly unchanged through the longest exposure. The authors show the fix frees the sensor from leaning on fragile coating charge, a step toward UV-grade radiometry.
pmc-13365508:
Andrea Farini and others studied whether gut bugs upset shapes defence and muscle disease in dystrophin-lacking mice, in 2026. Duchenne muscle wasting is a growing, severe muscle-wasting disease caused by dystrophin changes, leading to loss of muscle function with cardiac and breathing failure and early death. Infiltrating swelling cells sense wasting muscle, and gut microbes can cause immune upset.

The team asked whether intestinal germs support the muscle immune response in wasting mice, linking gut microbial communities to muscle pathophysiology. The study connects microbiome, defence, and muscle degeneration in a mouse model of Duchenne disease. Teams gain evidence that gut microbes may shape muscle disease beyond the muscle itself.
pmc-13370708:
Beaumont and colleagues review experimental models of cerebral small vessel disease, a disorder of the brain's tiniest blood vessels, in 2026 neurology research. The disease is the second leading cause of dementia after Alzheimer's, accounts for about 20 percent of strokes, and underlies half of vascular dementias. Because the vessels are small and deep, progression is hard to watch in living patients, so models carry the research burden for understanding mechanisms and testing therapies.

Rodent models reveal blood-brain barrier leakage, white matter injury, and vascular dysfunction, but rodent brains differ from human ones in anatomy and disease course. Lab systems using vascular cells in three-dimensional cultures and microfluidic chips offer control but mature too fast to mimic decades of slow disease. pmc-13372008:
Sara Almaradweh and co-authors share a blood clot case in a 2026 report. A woman aged 40 with sugar disease and a smoking habit lost blood flow to her right leg after hours spent with legs crossed. A first surgery cleared the clot, and she went home on blood-thin pills and aspirin.

Two weeks later the leg lost flow again, with clots in more than one spot. She had the surgery again, plus a fix to a foot artery. Blood tests pointed to a clotting fault that can strike on its own. Her team switched her to a drip drug, then to a long-term pill plan.
pmc-13373008:
Faris Abushamma and co-authors detail a hard kidney cancer surgery in a 2026 case report. A healthy man aged 59 had a large right kidney tumor. A clot of tumor, nine cm long, grew up the main vein toward the liver.

On one day the team blocked the kidney's blood flow, blocked the tumor clot's flow, and placed a soft balloon in the vein for control. Then they took out the kidney and the clot through a wide cut under the ribs. Work of this sort takes heart, vessel, and scan teams at once. The case lays out the steps for teams that face the same hard task.
pmc-13374208:

The Burst-Drift-Control model holds that short genomic bursts, such as extrachromosomal DNA amplification, chromosome shattering, or whole-genome doubling, create new heritable states.

Those bursts are followed by drift-dominated intervals where weak selection lets many lineages persist, creating time-limited vulnerabilities. Clinicians might then steer, or control, the tumour during those windows. The model reframes reactive heredity, where bursts transiently alter what is inherited, as a therapeutic opportunity. It offers a framework for timing treatment to the tumour's own evolutionary tempo.
pmc-13374308:
Marek Wiśniewski and colleagues review heart ultrasound findings in children and teens with anorexia nervosa in a 2026 systematic review. Anorexia carries the highest death rate among psychiatric disorders, and heart complications are common. The team searched MEDLINE to late November 2025, keeping studies where anorexia was the main eating disorder, average age was 18 or younger, and echocardiography findings were reported.

Twenty-three studies covering 1,246 patients were eligible, with 19 providing data for synthesis. The most common abnormalities against controls were lower left ventricular mass and related structural and functional changes. Two reviewers screened independently under PRISMA rules. The review gives clinicians a consolidated picture of which heart changes to watch in young patients with anorexia.
pmc-13374808:
Hamid Abbasi and co-authors counted wound germs after a new spine fix in a 2026 review. The fix joins spine bones through a side path with a scope, which cuts less flesh than open work. Germ growth in the wound is a grave harm that can mean more surgery and long ward time.

The count held 2,069 cases of the new fix and its add-on steps. Past counts for open spine joins are well logged, but this path lacked a large count. A firm rate helps surgeons pitch the new path's risks in true terms, and helps wards set germ guard steps for it.
pmc-13378308:
Tomohiko Sunami and co-authors published a 2026 study on why some early bowel growths grow faster than others. Such growths, called colorectal adenomas, can turn into bowel cancer over time as gene changes build up. The team grew mini versions of patient growths in the lab, called organoids.

Within some organoids, single cells differed in how fast they grew, and that difference was not explained by genes alone. A protein called IGF2BP3 stood out between fast and slow growers. It raised or lowered levels of another growth protein, keeping fast growth without killing the cells. In mice, it also affected whether growths formed tumours.
pmc-13380808:
Alaa Hassouneh, Rajinder Singh, Laveena Castelino, and Babatunde Campbell present a 2026 study of dialysis access surgery in patients aged seventy and over, and whether frailty predicts failure. The preferred access, a fistula at the wrist, joins an artery to a vein so it can mature for dialysis. Outcomes in older patients are debated.

The study reviewed 52 patients treated over twelve months at one centre. Frailty was scored on a standard scale, and failure meant the fistula never became usable. Failure was common overall and more frequent in frail patients. Each step up the frailty scale raised the odds of failure, which may help surgeons counsel older patients.
pmc-13383808:
Boulton and colleagues show that a leukemia-linked protein, MLLT3, binds chromatin marks and an RNA molecule, in 2026 biology research. Tests revealed the domain gripping 7SK, a nuclear RNA, with high affinity for its stem-loop structures.
