Putting mutations into MLLT3 skewed production toward the lymphoid lineage, destroyed its leukemia-driving power in a fusion form, and reduced its self-association. Profiling showed transcription initiation blocked when RNA binding was lost. Boulton concludes RNA binding is not decoration but a part of how MLLT3 controls development and, when fused wrongly, leukemia.
pmc-13383908:
Ion Bogdan Codorean and co-authors detail a modified all-inside knee ligament rebuild that joins synthetic and tendon grafts in 2026 work. Anterior cruciate ligament surgery is common, and hybrid grafts aim to add strength and speed recovery. Their construct threads the gracilis tendon through a tubular synthetic device to form a 4 by 2 strand graft.

Step-by-step guidance covers graft building, tunnel placement, and fixation on suspension loops at both ends. The graft is soaked in antibiotic solution before placement, and tunnels are sized to the graft width. The authors present the method as a bone-sparing option suited to professional athletes and other high-demand patients.
pmc-13384908:
Alessandro Serretti benchmarks a fully local AI pipeline for screening paper abstracts in 2026 work. The system ran an open-weight model on a desktop machine, avoiding cloud services and their governance worries. It combined fixed metadata filters, AI screening, and structured extraction against three published reviews.

On a ketamine imaging review, the pipeline kept every study the original team included. Recall was lower on two clozapine topics, where blank or thin abstracts caused most misses. Extraction of audited fields showed no detected errors, and the maps matched the reviews' main themes, which supports local tools for evidence work.
pmc-13385908:
Zhiming Mao's team found PD-1 restrains latent killer-cell maturation of thymic CD8 T cells, in a 2026 study. Durable cancer immunity depends on fresh killer CD8 T cells, and thymic output tracks with better prognosis, yet whether killer potential arises in the thymus was unclear. The team showed thymic single-positive CD8 T cells undergo latent killer maturation after selection, under PD-1 control.

PD-1 limited how much thymic output shaped the tumor T cell receptor range for tumor watch. Blocking PD-1 expanded peripheral killer CD8 cells, but those cells gradually lost antitumor activity inside tumors through faster burnout without PD-1. The findings complicate PD-1 blockade: it boosts killer supply while hastening their burnout.
pmc-13386508:
Yuhang Gao and colleagues spot fast waves carrying real energy in the Sun's polar corona in 2026 work. Heating the corona and driving the fast solar wind are long-standing puzzles, and one model family needs high-frequency waves. Solar Orbiter's sharp, rapid imaging finally caught such waves in coronal plumes, the team reports.

Over a third of the tracked kink waves cycled in under 100 seconds in their counts. Those fast waves carried substantial energy flux that slower sampling had badly understated. The results give wave-heating models long-missing observational support and stress the value of high-cadence solar imaging.
pmc-13387008:
Fan Zhang and colleagues trace tomato spotted wilt virus into pepper seeds through flowers in a 2026 study. The virus causes heavy crop losses and was reported as seed-borne, but its entry route into seed stayed murky. Microscopy found virus particles spread through floral tissues, including anthers, pollen, ovaries, and ovules.

Protein signals ran strongest in anther walls, vessel bundles, and ovule coverings in their images. Cross-pollination tests passed the virus through pollen alone and through infected mother tissue alone. Self-pollinated infected plants gave the highest seed and seedling infection rates, which maps the risk for growers.
pmc-13389408:
Changxing Zhao's team used a meta-analysis of 2,100 site-years of root and germ respiration across 163 sites to ask how global change shifts belowground seasonal timing. Aboveground phenology is well tracked, but root and microbe calendars remain poorly characterised.

Root and germ seasons usually shifted asymmetrically, except for a symmetric advance of season onset under warming. Heat plus nitrogen lengthened root seasons, while germ seasons lengthened with warming and drying but shortened after partial vegetation removal. Warming-driven germ extension alone could raise global heterotrophic respiration by about two and a half petagrams of carbon yearly, a flux Earth system models should now represent.
pmc-13390008:
Joao A Pinto and Ana Dourado audit, in 2026, how often laboratory tests are repeated too soon in a Portuguese health network. Repeat testing outside advised minimum intervals wastes money and staff time and can harm patients through needless follow-up.

The retrospective study covered three hospitals and fourteen primary care centres in northeast Portugal, reviewing requests for 77 blood markers across 2023 and 2024. Each repeat was classed as suitable or unsuitable against advised minimum intervals. Laboratory managers gain counted proof of where overuse clusters. They also get an estimate of what hard-stop rules in ordering systems could save. A general concern about overtesting becomes a target that managers can act on directly.
pmc-13390408:
Ingrid A Worth's team checked whether lightly handled diets meant to ease low mood might by chance worsen tangled eating. pmc-13390508:

pmc-13391808:

pmc-13392208:

pmc-13392408:

pmc-13392508:

pmc-13393508:

pmc-13393608:

pmc-13394108:

pmc-13394808:

pmc-13395308:

pmc-13395908:
Martine Mussies re-reads, in 2026, two amphibians that never grow up: the axolotl and the cave-dwelling olm. Both keep larval traits for life and breed in that state. pmc-13396108:

pmc-13396308:

pmc-13396408:

pmc-13396508:

pmc-13396608:

pmc-13397708:

pmc-13397808:

pmc-13398208:

pmc-13398908:

pmc-13399408:

pmc-13399808:

pmc-13400008:

pmc-13400208:

pmc-13400308:

pmc-13400408:

pmc-13400608:

pmc-13400708:

pmc-13401308:

pmc-13401408:

pmc-13401708:

pmc-13401808:

pmc-13402708:

pmc-13404008:

pmc-13404108:

pmc-13404408:

pmc-13404508:

pmc-13404908:

pmc-13405108:

pmc-13407408:

pmc-13407708:

pmc-13408008:

pmc-13408508:

pmc-13408908:

pmc-13409008:

pmc-13409708:

pmc-13409908:

pmc-13410708:

pmc-13411308:

pmc-13412108:

pmc-13415808:

pmc-13418208:

pmc-13418708:

pmc-13419208:

pmc-13419308:

pmc-13419408:

pmc-13420208:

pmc-13420308:

pmc-13420708:

pmc-13421108:

pmc-13421808:

pmc-13422808:

pmc-13422908:

pmc-13424208:

pmc-13424308:

pmc-13424608:

pmc-13424908:

pmc-13426008:

pmc-13426208:

pmc-13426408:

pmc-13426708:

pmc-13427408:

pmc-13428308:

pmc-13428608:

pmc-13429108:

pmc-13430008:

pmc-13430608:

pmc-13431008:

pmc-13432508:

pmc-13433008:

pmc-13433508:

pmc-13435508:

pmc-13435608:

pmc-13435708:

pmc-13436008:

pmc-13436408:

pmc-13437508:

pmc-13461908:

pmc-13463008:

pmc-13465608:

pmc-13466508:

pmc-13467708:

pmc-13468208:

pmc-13469308:

pmc-13469408:

pmc-13470808:

pmc-13471308:

pmc-13471608:

pmc-13471808:

pmc-13473008:

pmc-13473108:

pmc-13473508:

pmc-13473608:

pmc-13474008:

pmc-13482608:

pmc-13483408:

pmc-13485008:
Luca Elizabet Kosik films the tail fibers of the T7 virus at molecular speed to see how it hunts for a bacterial foothold. Published in 2026, the study combines high-speed atomic force microscopy on isolated fibers with computer simulation and X-ray scattering. Six bent fibers, each about 40 nanometers long, handle first contact and help inject viral DNA.

A kink midway along each fiber works as a hinge, allowing large bending sweeps. Partial unwinding and rewinding inside the fiber's triple-helix base adds rotation and twisting motion. Together the two flexible zones let fibers flex and stretch quickly over a wide area, searching topologically for an anchor point. Because many viruses likely hunt the same way, tuning fiber motion could fine-tune engineered phage therapy.
pmc-13485608:
Colton D Brown pools case reports on surgery in people whose body tissues stretch too much and tear with ease. The group of diseases is called Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. Their 2026 review follows standard search rules across five databases to September 2025. From 1,816 records, 52 studies with 77 cases in plastic surgery made the cut.

The loose-joint type led the set, then the classic type, then the vessel type. Most patients were female, and mean age was near 32 years. Repair work drove most operations, with looks-based work a small share. Craft tips that recur are soft handling of tissue, care for blood vessels, and layered closure with no pull on the wound. Strong trial proof is thin for this group, so pooled case wisdom stays the guide.
pmc-13486408:
Peiling Tsou and Chang-Jiun Wu survey loose DNA circles that amplify cancer genes in head and neck tumors. Published in 2026, the analysis runs a dedicated detection pipeline on whole-genome data for 153 tumors from a public cancer atlas. A panel of 38 candidate cancer genes is checked for circle-based amplification, then tied to survival.

Circles appeared in 68.0 percent of tumors, an unusually high share among cancer types. Shapes ranged from simple linear pieces to heavily rearranged structures, with circles proper in about one quarter. Frequency did not vary by tumor site or by sex. One amplified gene, CCND1, anchors the survival story promised in the study title, with full outcome curves in the report. Loose DNA may quietly drive both aggression and drug resistance in this cancer.
pmc-13486908:
Anne Bouthillier and co-workers reply in 2026 to notes on their past call for a health-first plan for stimulant-linked psychosis. Experts across lands now agree on the weight and tangle of this harm, the reply says. Health systems, diagnosis habits, and drug markets still vary by place. Split care paths and thin proof recur in each account.

Rapid checks on new harms and fast shared learning top the joint plan. New lab-made stimulants can outrun clinic guides, so watch systems must move fast. Care should span mind, body, and social needs over years, not stop at the acute phase. Global team work to scale shared lessons gets clear backing. The reply maps where views now meet and where systems must go next.
pmc-13488408:
Sara Mateo, Jannis Wenk, John Chew, and Antonio Exposito study electric cleaning of microplastics from water in a 2026 laboratory investigation. Electrocoagulation uses a dissolving iron electrode to form clumps, called flocs, that trap particles for removal. Polystyrene and polyethylene particles across several sizes were treated in a batch reactor, with cameras tracking floc growth and lab tests probing surface charge and chemistry to reveal how each plastic sticks.

Removal reached about eighty percent for both plastics at their best sizes in the reported runs. Polystyrene was swept into growing flocs, while polyethylene removal relied more on charge neutralization, giving different energy needs. Floc shape differed by plastic, compact and elongated for one, spongy and rounded for the other, and flocs grew with particle size.
pmc-13489708:
Qi, Wang, Fang, and Wei examine when combining data types hurts a prediction model in this 2026 study. Their test case is predicting whether a T cell receptor binds a given peptide, where protein language model embeddings are strong but structure-based graphs, built from predicted folds, are noisy. Simply fusing the two views destabilized training and could drag accuracy below using sequences alone, especially with little training data.

Their framework, TRACE, encodes each partner with parallel sequence and graph towers. It aligns the two views of the same molecule before letting them interact. The alignment uses a contrastive method borrowed from image-text models. On a carefully leakage-controlled benchmark where all methods scored near chance, TRACE achieved the best mean discrimination, about 0.58 averaged across five folds in the evaluation. Alignment prevented collapse when labels were scarce or graph edges were corrupted.
pmc-13491808:
Marian Shaker, Adel Zaki, Sara Lofty Asser, Iman El Sayed and Mohamed Moustafa Azmy published this 2026 study on using deep learning to flag drug-resistant urinary tract infections early. Resistance here means standard antibiotics may fail, so quick prediction could guide treatment sooner. The team worked with patient data from a hospital in Egypt, a clinic in the Philippines, and a laboratory in Yemen.

The authors compared ways of turning patient records into model inputs, then tested a deep learning classifier against logistic regression and gradient boosting. Their fractional discrete cosine method gave the strongest inputs. With deep learning it reached an accuracy of 97.4 percent on the Egyptian data, and 99.1 percent and 98.2 percent on the other two datasets. They propose the model as a support tool inside antibiotic stewardship programmes, the hospital schemes that police antibiotic use, rather than a replacement for clinical judgement.
pmc-13492108:
Manju Narwal, Yeonoh Shin, and Katsuhiko S Murakami solve in 2026 the structure of one of the largest single-protein copying machines known. It is the RNA polymerase that bacteriophage N4 smuggles into the bacteria it infects. The virus carries its own enzyme so it can start copying genes before the host machinery wakes. Frozen-electron microscopy captured the full-length enzyme alone and caught in the act of starting on a promoter.

Alone, the enzyme sits locked, with its tail domain pressed against the working core and a plug blocking the slot where building blocks enter. Grabbing promoter DNA springs the lock open and swings the tail away. The front domain stayed too flexible to image, fitting its suspected role in squeezing through the narrow tail channel during injection. The structures explain how the phage keeps the enzyme silent until the right moment.
pmc-13493908:
Tarafdar and a large Bangladeshi team characterise a purple bacterium pulled from sediment in Bijoypur Lake, in the Netrokona district. The strain, named SAM215, belongs to Chromobacterium amazonense and makes violacein, a violet pigment with possible medical uses. Their 2026 characterisation mixes bench tests with a full genome readout. It paints a tough organism: the strain tolerated very salty water, resisted common antibiotics, shrugged off metal ions, and built strong biofilms, the slimy sheets bacteria live in.

Its genome ran to just over four million letters and carried about 4,100 protein-coding genes, including equipment for metal tolerance, stress survival, and enzymes that attack fungal walls. Shaking that broke up biofilms sharply cut pigment output, tying production to settled growth. Worrying genes also appeared, covering antibiotic resistance and possible virulence, and a small mouse test hinted at harm at high doses. The authors flag both the promise and the caution.
pmc-13494008:
Henrik Mäkinen, Heikki Suhonen, and Simo Huotari address in 2026 a failure mode of dark-field X-ray imaging, a technique that reveals microscopic fibers and pores invisible to ordinary scans. When a sample scatters too strongly, the signal saturates, retrieval math breaks down, and three-dimensional reconstructions fill with artifacts. Their fix filters the raw projections adaptively, strengthening only the regions where the signal nears saturation.

Filtered projections improved markedly in exactly those trouble spots. Reconstructions that previously failed became possible even with strong scatterers inside the sample. The method rides on the standard grating interferometer setup used with ordinary X-ray tubes. Lung imaging and mammography, the field's flagship medical hopes, both involve the kind of fine structure that saturates, so the repair widens what clinics might eventually scan.
pmc-13494208:
Raitis Bobrovs and others review the aryl hydrocarbon dock, a gene copying factor once known only for mediating dioxin toxicity. In 2026, the review traces how this dock, activated by diverse endogenous, germ, dietary, drug, and pollutant ligands, now appears as a broad controller. It governs swelling, immunity, barrier integrity, fuel use, and cancer. Its effects depend heavily on context and cross-talk with other pathways.

Healing progress covers an approved agonist, tapinarof, for scaly skin and atopic skin rash, plus emerging blocker plans in cancer immune care, supported by structural studies of ligand binding. Remaining challenges include ligand promiscuity, feedback control, and long-term safety. The review maps mechanisms, functions, and drug design prospects for this complex target.
pmc-13494508:
Gan and colleagues investigated a sugar-binding protein called Lgals3 in brain injury that follows restored blood flow after stroke, in a 2026 mouse study. Restoring circulation saves tissue but triggers inflammation and cell death, worsening damage. Mining gene-expression data flagged Lgals3 as increased after this ischemia-reperfusion injury, and the team confirmed the rise in mice whose cerebral artery was blocked.

Gan delivered a virus carrying a silencing sequence against Lgals3 into the mice weeks before the artery blockage. Silenced mice developed smaller brain regions of damage, scored better on neurological tests, and lost fewer neurons to cell death. Brain levels of three inflammatory messengers fell while a messenger rose. The team showed Lgals3 binds TLR4, an immune alarm receptor, and that silencing quieted the signaling chain running from that receptor to the inflammation switch. They propose Lgals3 as a drug target for limiting reperfusion damage after stroke.
pmc-13495208:
Muhammad Jamil and colleagues run, in a 2026 field study in Pakistan, a two-season trial on nitrogen fertilizer for winter forage cereals grown without irrigation. Barley, oat, rye, and triticale feed livestock, and farmers need to know which crop, dose, and harvest stage give the best silage. The trial crossed four nitrogen doses with two harvest stages and tested molasses and formic acid as silage additives.

Oat won on bulk, yielding far more fresh biomass than the rest at the top dose, and it used both fertilizer and water most thriftily at every level. Rye trailed on yield yet gave the cleanest fiber profile and the highest feed value at the top dose. Oat silage also reached the highest protein when fed the top dose with additives. The authors recommend oat cut at the early stage with molasses for protein-rich silage under rainfed farming.
pmc-13495508:
Shiva Maleki and colleagues pool, in a 2026 review and dose-response meta-analysis, studies linking the triglyceride-glucose index to kidney stone disease. The index, built from blood fat and sugar, offers a cheap read on insulin resistance, which may prime stone formation. The team searched six databases under a registered plan and graded the proof.

Fourteen studies covering over a million adults qualified. Each one-step rise in the index went with about a third higher odds of stones, and the highest index group carried about half again the odds of the lowest. A dose-response model fit a straight line: no bend where risk suddenly jumps. Wide disagreement between studies, though, held the authors back from urging the index as a screening tool. They frame it as a risk marker that belongs inside broader heart and metabolic checks.
pmc-13499408:
Kimi Iinuma and colleagues present in 2026 a deep learning system that sorts pigmented skin spots into eight categories from ordinary clinical photographs taken in Japan. Sorting such spots by eye is hard, especially where a magnified skin exam tool is unavailable. The system was trained and checked on 979 photographs gathered from dermatology centres, covering harmless marks such as moles and freckles alongside two skin cancers.

Data were split by patient so no person's images leaked between training and test sets, keeping the check honest. On the held-out test set the model classified most images correctly, reaching accuracy in the mid-ninety percent range in the reported figures. Every melanoma in that small test set was caught, though the authors caution the set was too small to prove cancer safety, and mistakes clustered between look-alike harmless and cancerous growths.
pmc-13499508:
Barbara E Ainsworth, Haili Tian, and Zhenghua Cai comment in 2026 on new United Kingdom Biobank evidence about light physical activity, the gentle movement of daily life below brisk exercise. Light activity has been tied to lower early death risk, yet how much per week helps most was unclear. The study under discussion tracked 69,492 adults aged 43 to 78, measuring movement with wrist sensors worn for seven days and following health records for a median of about eight years.

Compared with the least active quarter, adults reaching at least roughly four hours of light activity a day showed lower risks of overall and cardiovascular death in fully adjusted models. Cancer death benefits appeared only at the two highest activity levels, needing around five or more hours daily, while gains for developing disease were smaller. Everyday movement, not only formal exercise, emerges as a measurable public health lever.
pmc-13500408:
Sheikh Abdullah and co-authors write to the editor in 2026 about a blood cancer that changed identity twice in one patient. Lineage switching, where a lymphoid leukaemia returns as a myeloid disease, is a recognised escape route after immune therapy. A stepwise path through a defined intermediate cancer is rarely documented in adults. Their patient was a 69-year-old woman whose B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia passed through chronic myelomonocytic leukaemia before becoming acute monoblastic leukaemia.

Serial molecular profiling across her treatment course from April 2024 to August 2025 tracked how mutation levels shifted with each phase. One RAS-family mutation persisted at low level during remission, surged as the intermediate disease emerged, and fell with treatment, while new mutations appeared at the final transition. The pattern favoured a two-lineage RAS-driven process over a simple single-clone switch, a distinction the authors argue matters for monitoring similar patients.
pmc-13500508:
Min Wu and colleagues assess in 2026 public services within the fifteen-minute community life circle in Nanchang, China, the planning idea that daily needs should sit within a short walk of home. Their closed-loop framework measured distribution, access, and coordination of 28,082 facilities across the city's six districts and three counties, covering 24 categories of service. The diagnosis then fed a location allocation model proposing where to add or move provision.

Supply was spread unevenly, with strong spatial variation in access between neighbourhoods in their analysis. Overall coverage efficiency ran low, and quality differed sharply by facility type, while supply often mismatched where people live. The authors convert those findings into targeted fixes for the worst-served areas, offering city leaders a template for renewal decisions elsewhere.
pmc-13501308:
Noto and colleagues showed that a simple linear model can predict drug-target interactions as well as complex black-box systems, in a 2026 study. The study tackles a perennial drug discovery problem: most drugs' target sets remain unknown. Their model, LI-DTI, borrows from recommender systems, the technology behind product suggestions, and expresses each prediction as a transparent weighted sum of drug-drug and target-target similarity measures.

Noto showed the model recovers interactions for drugs or targets with no previously known interactions, the hard cold-start case, across several validation designs. It kept performing when the team deliberately reduced chemical and sequence similarity between training and test cases to counter bias. In a prospective test, training on interactions known by 2011 and predicting those added through 2022, it reached state-of-the-art accuracy. A public web tool lets users inspect individual predictions and the evidence behind each one.
pmc-13501608:
Nur Duman leads a three-author team reporting a 2026 survey of midwifery students in Turkey on whether handedness makes learning episiotomy harder. An episiotomy is a cut made in childbirth that later needs careful repair, a fine motor task. Teaching materials and instruments are usually designed for right-handed learners. The sample covered 769 third- and fourth-year students in the 2022 to 2023 academic year. Students completed an information form and the Edinburgh Handedness Inventory, which measures how strongly one hand dominates.

Right-handed students made up 82.4 percent, left-handed students 7 percent, and ambidextrous students 10.6 percent. Left-handed students reported significantly more difficulty with both the cut and its repair, in the laboratory and in clinical practice alike. Regression analysis flagged trouble during clinical practice and lab repair sessions as predictors of left-hand use. The authors recommend adapted equipment, practice conditions, and mentoring for left-handed trainees.
pmc-13501708:
Ann S. W Irungu and others study access to sexual and reproductive health services among women with disabilities in Murang'a South, Kenya. In 2026, the one-time study surveys 325 women aged fifteen to forty-nine, treating at least one service visit in the past year as access. Family planning was the most used service, while HIV testing, mother care, post-abortion care, and cancer screening lagged far behind.

Overall access reached about sixty-eight percent, rising with age, tertiary education, marriage, Protestant affiliation, and sexual action, while stigma, restrictive norms, and gender power shifts sharply reduced it. Facility communication, privacy, physical access, distance, and inclusive information also mattered. The authors call for disability-inclusive training and safer, more private medical environments.
pmc-13502308:
Ana Virginia Silva Vilela leads a seven-author team reporting a 2026 multicentre case series of six teeth with apical periodontitis. The bone-destroying inflammation gathers at a root tip when the canal stays infected. Large lesions harbour complex bacterial communities in side channels and tubules, so root canal treatment often fails. Every case began the same way: chemomechanical cleaning irrigated with 2.5 percent sodium hypochlorite, agitation of the fluid, and calcium hydroxide dressing, with cone-beam CT guiding planning and review.

Four teeth healed on that nonsurgical regimen alone. Two kept leaking pus and maintained open sinus tracts despite rounds, a failure defined in advance. Those two went to periradicular surgery with a retrograde seal at the root tip, a tooth-preserving last step. Follow-up imaging showed healing in all six teeth. Because the series mixes approaches, the authors credit individualized judgement rather than any single protocol.
pmc-13502608:
Wei Zhang leads a nine-author team reporting a 2026 light study pinning down why bending a dye molecule kills its glow. Perylene bisimides, a family of strongly coloured pigments, can be made with steadily increasing bend. Flat members emit almost perfectly, while bent ones dump their absorbed energy silently, and nobody knew whether the energy gap or the shaking was to blame. Fast light tests ruled out triplet paths and pointed to internal conversion as the main escape route.

Raman tests then watched the shaking directly. Bending muted the backbone ring mode that couples to the light jump, scrambled the low-frequency shaking pattern, and sped up dephasing, the loss of synced motion. In other words, a bent molecule sits in a setting that drinks the excitation quickly. The authors generalize the lesson: loss of synced motion and shaking losses, not gap shrinkage, govern silent decay across such systems.
pmc-13503708:
JaeBin Sung and five colleagues propose a way to pick the best inputs for medical prediction models, in a 2026 paper. The test case predicts whether a patient in intensive care can come off a breathing machine with success. Wide data tables carry noise that can hurt such models.

Their method merges the rankings of three tools that explain model choices, then reorders the list with signals from cases the model got right. On records of 19,567 ventilated patients, the model scored well and used a small, clear input set. The top inputs matched known signs that a patient is ready to breathe alone. Tests on seven more medical data sets gave gains on most tasks.
pmc-13503808:
Martina Magni leads a team that chemically read the resin mixes on an ancient Egyptian burial set, in a 2026 study. The set belonged to Kha and Merit, from the New Kingdom age, and sits in a Turin museum. Such mixes had both holy and practical roles, yet their exact make-up stayed partly unknown.

Two lab methods scanned residues from bandages, coffins, and a small jar. The mixes proved resinous, with no trace of bitumen. Plant markers ruled the profiles, and body gear differed from coffin coats, which hints at recipes tuned by use. Two finds stood out: a marker from liquorice root and one from pine nut oil. The liquorice find is the earliest proof of its use in a burial of that age.
pmc-13504208:
Angie Lorena Medina Bolivar and two colleagues compare stomach gland disease in horses, donkeys, and mules after death, in a 2026 study from Colombia. The glandular form of equine stomach disease is poorly mapped, and its causes are still murky. Post-mortem checks give a clean look at how common it is.

They examined 300 stomachs, one hundred from each animal type, taken right after slaughter. Signs of the gland disease showed in about 68 percent overall, but rates split sharply: lowest in horses, higher in donkeys, and highest in mules. Sores clustered in the lower stomach zones. Other finds included broad stomach swelling in most animals, blockages in some, and parasites in a share. Mules showed a distinct swelling pattern in the gland layer.
pmc-13504808:
Grace Sanyu leads a team measuring drug resistance in Ugandans whose HIV stays low but detectable on first-line therapy, in a 2026 study. Such low-level virus can precede full treatment failure. Resistance data for this group in Uganda were scarce.

Plasma samples came from 444 people with two detectable but low viral loads and strong reported adherence. Gene reading succeeded in only 67 samples, a known hurdle at low virus levels. Resistance showed in nearly two thirds of those read, most often against the older drug class that anchors first-line care. Higher low-level loads and age under 25 raised the odds. The authors urge resistance testing for this group and better deep-reading tools, plus youth-focused HIV programs.
pmc-13505108:
Yu and colleagues test inhaled nitric oxide in the sickest breathing patients: forty adults on ventilators with moderate-to-severe ARDS, where inflamed lungs fill with fluid and blood passes through unaired regions. Nitric oxide gas widens blood vessels only where air reaches, which should reroute blood toward working lung. Their 2026 randomised study used electrical impedance tomography, a belt of electrodes imaging air and blood flow breath by breath, to watch matching between ventilation and perfusion over 24 hours.

Patients given the gas improved their air-blood matching significantly more than controls, with both wasted ventilation and shunted blood falling further in the treated group on the imaging measures. Blood oxygenation roughly doubled its efficiency ratio in the nitric oxide group, a gain significantly larger than the control group's. Yet the gas did nothing to systemic inflammation markers, echoing large earlier trials.
pmc-13506108:
Leonidas E Mastrokostas and colleagues used a national United States hospital database to ask how mental illness affects outcomes after neck spine surgery. They covered elective posterior cervical decompression and fusion admissions from 2016 to 2022, about 167,000 weighted cases in all. Roughly 32,500 admissions had depression and about 5,800 had a psychotic disorder.

Patients with depression faced higher odds of heart and mechanical complications and were more often sent to a place other than home. Psychotic disorders carried still stronger risks, including more than double the odds of dying in hospital. Hospital stays grew longer step by step across the three groups, and costs rose in the same order, topping forty-two thousand dollars with psychotic disorders. The authors urge routine mental-health screening before this surgery and discharge planning that starts early for such patients.
pmc-13507308:
H Yoshimochi leads a 2026 team that reports a large magneto-optical Kerr effect, a twist in reflected light's polarization, arising from collinear antiferromagnetic order in a room-temperature insulating crystal. Textbooks long held that antiparallel spin arrangements cancel out and cannot twist light, since they carry no net magnetization. Careful optical measurements on the crystal told another story.

First-principles calculations matched the measured twist's size and color pattern closely, pinning it on the antiparallel order itself rather than stray magnetism. The crystal also flips between two spin layouts with temperature, each obeying different selection rules. Optical readout of antiferromagnetic memory, prized for speed and density, gains a concrete physical basis.
pmc-13508408:
Mingkang Chen and four co-authors follow knee replacement patients to see whether kneecap joint wear, leg alignment, or implant position shape results, in 2026 work. The operation replaces only the inner half of the knee and remains debated when the kneecap joint also shows wear. Records covered 69 Chinese patients with 79 treated knees from 2017 to 2020. MRI graded kneecap joint disease before surgery. Leg alignment after surgery and implant angles were classed against target ranges. Function was scored with several standard scales over about five and a half years.

Function improved markedly overall, with no loosening or revision surgery seen. Kneecap disease grade or spot did not change final function scores. Alignment mattered more: straight or mildly angled legs scored better on function and symptom scales than strongly angled ones. The study supports offering this partial replacement despite kneecap wear, while respecting alignment targets.
pmc-13508808:
Kaewtha and colleagues report a 2026 study using machine learning to predict how long hip fracture patients stay in hospital after surgery.  Records of 3,118 surgically treated patients, with demographic and perioperative details, were split into training and test sets. The team built a two-stage approach and compared it with a standard one-stage model.

The first stage sorts patients into short-stay or long-stay groups. The second stage then predicts the number of days within each group, a task that suits each half better than one model fitting all. Standard accuracy measures were reported for both stages.  Sharper forecasts help hospitals plan beds and staffing.
pmc-13509608:
Thai Hau Koo, Rishi Chowdhary, Kirti Arora, Kelly Chun Lynn Lai, and Andee Dzulkarnaen Zakaria review blood tests for leftover cancer DNA after colon or rectal cancer surgery, in 2026 work. Fragments of tumor DNA in the blood clear within hours after full removal, so any signal found later points to tiny amounts of disease that scans cannot see. The review traces the field from early watching studies to recent large trials.

One major trial showed that test-guided care cut chemotherapy use in stage two colon cancer while survival without return of disease stayed equal. Other large trials found that stronger chemotherapy for test-positive patients did not improve outcomes, and one drug given at the first blood signal also fell short. The authors conclude the test predicts risk well, yet proof that acting on it helps patients is still catching up.
pmc-13509908:
Serav Koç and seven co-authors test whether an ultrasound stiffness measure can predict which women with a tubo-ovarian abscess will need surgery, in 2026 work. This abscess forms near the ovary and fallopian tube and is treated first with antibiotics, with surgery held for cases that fail to settle. Thirty-four women had stiffness readings of the abscess wall and its contents taken at admission.

Women who went on to surgery stayed in hospital longer and had larger abscesses with stiffer walls. A wall stiffness cut-off gave fair prediction on its own, while abscess size predicted surgery more strongly. When factors were combined, only size held up as an independent predictor. The authors say stiffness readings may add context at admission, yet size remains the measure to trust most for planning.
pmc-13510108:
Ben Amor and colleagues used ultrasound to extract phenolic compounds from the peel and pulp of horned melon, a fruit grown in Tunisia. They tuned the process with a statistical design that varies three factors at once: extraction time, temperature, and solvent-to-solid ratio. The aim was to maximize total phenolics, flavonoids, and antioxidant power measured by two assays.

Ben Amor found the best pulp conditions near sixteen minutes at about fifty degrees with roughly thirty milliliters of solvent per gram. Peel settings were similar, with the pulp yielding higher phenolic and flavonoid totals. Profiling found gallic, chlorogenic, and caffeic acids as the main phenolics, with chlorogenic acid dominating the peel. The extracts showed dose-dependent anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial effects in lab tests. The authors present the process as a sustainable route for industry to turn this fruit, including its waste peel, into antioxidant ingredients.
pmc-13510708:
Andrew J. Zillgitt and six co-authors review how magnetic brain mapping strengthens planning for implanted electrode studies in hard-to-treat epilepsy, in 2026 work. When drugs fail to stop seizures, surgery may help, and many centers now place electrodes inside the brain to find the seizure source. Good placement depends on a strong early guess built from how seizures look and feel, called semiology.

Magnetic mapping, which tracks faint magnetic fields from brain activity, adds noninvasive evidence that few other tests can match. The review shows how mapping results sharpen the placement plan alongside seizure signs, and two detailed cases make the process concrete. Surgical outcomes from evaluations that included mapping are also weighed. The authors argue the pairing matters more as implanted studies spread to more centers, since a better opening guess can mean fewer electrodes and clearer answers.
pmc-13510908:
Schecter and colleagues reported in 2026 a case of late-infantile Krabbe disease found through newborn screening. This inherited disease destroys nerve insulation when an enzyme called GALC fails, letting a toxin called psychosine build up. Screening flagged the baby, whose gene carried two copies of a mixed haplotype. A haplotype means a set of variants carried on one gene copy. It included a so-called pseudodeficiency change plus a modifier that can amplify harm.

Schecter describes how the child developed normally at first, yet scans showed growing white matter damage by age three and three-quarters. Psychosine in red blood cells also rose well above the control range. Doctors then gave a cord blood transplant, after which enzyme activity normalised, toxin levels fell, and scans stayed stable with no loss of skills by age nine. The case shows screening results need gene, toxin, enzyme, and scan evidence read together.
pmc-13512208:
Qi Liu, Bowen Yang, Tianbao Li, Raven Garcia, Shengtong Han, and Victor X. Jin test whether a signature chemical mark on DNA packaging also steers how genes are spliced in a rearranged form of acute myeloid leukemia, in 2026 work. The mark is placed by an enzyme called DOT1L and defines this leukemia subtype. The team profiled the mark and gene activity in samples from 24 rearranged-form patients, a few normal-form patients, and healthy donors.

Skipped gene segments clustered at marked spots in the rearranged samples. Blocking the enzyme reshaped skipping patterns, and many switched segments lost their local mark at the same time. Partner proteins included core splicing machinery, and about two thirds of shared switches overlapped a mark peak. A splicing score built from the switches split patients by survival in a large public cohort. The authors link the subtype's core lesion to splicing control.
pmc-13518108:
Abdel-Rahman Zakieh, Judy Teran, and Subhashis Mitra report a brain infection traced to a dog bacterium in a 2026 case study. Staphylococcus pseudintermedius lives harmlessly on dogs but rarely infects people. A seventy-two-year-old man with a household dog had skull surgery to drain a traumatic blood collection, then returned with worsening decline. Repeat surgery found pus filling the space under his skull lining.

Nine separate cultures grew the same germ, in its methicillin-resistant form. Surgeons cleaned the space and long courses of intravenous vancomycin followed, with scans improving. The man still died, from the severe brain injury beneath it all rather than uncontrolled infection. Zakieh's team believes this is the first documented case of its kind. Their point for clinicians: when post-surgical fluid collections puzzle, ask about pets and culture widely, because the culprit may commute from the family dog.
pmc-13518308:
Kaveh Karimadini and Sharareh Pourebrahim run a fair fight between forecasting models for environmental change in a 2026 benchmark study. Long-range prediction across space and time is hard, and flashy graph-attention networks are not automatically best. Every contender trained and tested through one shared pipeline on annual satellite data from 2000 to 2023, holding 2024 fully unseen, and scored on the usual error measures.

A neighbourhood-augmented LSTM with helper variables won, scoring an R-squared near 0.95 and staying stable. Its cellular-automata style window over the surrounding pixels did the heavy lifting. A graph-attention model with a feed-forward block placed second; stripping parts made rivals wobble or degrade. Vegetation and water measures predicted most readily. The authors' engineering verdict: strong time modelling plus good side information beats fancy spatial attention for this job.
pmc-13518808:
Yiling Zhang and colleagues examine in 2026 how plant seed storage proteins fold into amyloid fibrils, the tightly ordered protein fibers best known from brain disease. Animal amyloids have been mapped atom by atom, while plant versions stayed largely unexplored. The team tested oat 12S globulin, soybean 7S globulin, and rice glutelin under harsh cooking-like acidity and heat.

Oat and rice proteins formed fibrils both purified and inside whole-seed extracts, while soybean protein formed them only when purified. Cryo-electron microscopy revealed the oat fibril core at 3.9 angstrom resolution, a compact triangular shape held by dense hydrophobic and aromatic packing. Food scientists gain a structural starting point for plant-based amyloid materials.
pmc-13519008:
Muhammad Syamsul Hazry Yahya leads an eight-author mapping study in 2026 on where dengue cases cluster across housing types in Kuala Selangor, Malaysia. Dengue control is often applied uniformly, yet mosquito risk may differ between terrace houses, high-rises, and traditional rural homes. Georeferenced case records from 2020 to 2024 fed a geographic analysis.

Terrace housing showed the strongest, most continuous clustering, tied to dense building plus nearby vegetation. High-rise cases clustered tightly inside heavily built zones, while rural cases spread broadly but weakly across mixed landscapes. The edge where buildings meet vegetation emerged as a key risk zone. Yahya and colleagues urge control tailored to each housing setting rather than one blanket program.
pmc-13520308:
Zhongxing Jiang and colleagues build in 2026 computer models that predict serious heart events within five years for people with coronary artery disease. Their models use routine hospital data and include plain-language explanations of which factors drive each prediction.

A group of 705 hospital patients was split into training and check sets, and 221 people had a major event during follow-up. Eleven predictors were kept, including heart pumping strength, a blood marker and low mood. A random survival forest model sorted risk best in training, with weaker sorting in the check set. Calibration and benefit checks suggest possible clinical use, pending wider testing.
pmc-13520408:
Zhang Liu, Yi Shen, Juan Zou and Weiqin Huang examine in 2026 whether a pre-surgery inflammation index predicts stubborn low oxygen after repair of a torn aorta, a life-threatening emergency. The index combines platelet, neutrophil and lymphocyte counts into one number.

Among 490 surgical patients from 2018 to 2024, about one third developed the lung complication. Index values were far higher in those patients, and each doubling of the index raised adjusted odds in the main model. Added value beyond standard clinical and lung measures was checked with discrimination and reclassification tools. A cheap blood-count score could help teams flag high-risk patients early.
pmc-13520608:
Kimberly W Lu, Samantha S Sattler and Jordan B Slutsky present in 2026 an 81-year-old man with deep scalp skin cancer. The cancer ate through skull into the brain lining. Such deep growth is rare and very risky. The tumour grew in a scar from past surgery for a related skin growth.

His history held several skin cancers and sun-damaged scalp skin. Staged surgery cleared the first growth with checked margins. The wound reached down to skull and took a graft cover. A nearby sore patch that would not heal drew care team notice. The authors stress close wound watch after scalp surgery. Fast joint care from several fields matters when healing stalls.
pmc-13520908:
Ao Zhang and colleagues reviewed tiny carbon particles made from natural medicines as a greener path to new therapies. Published in 2026, the review covers carbon dots, particles just one to ten nanometers wide with glowing, tunable surfaces that suit imaging, sensing, and drug delivery. Older recipes relied on chemical precursors that left toxic byproducts, limiting medical use.

Natural sources such as plants, animals, minerals, and their extracts offer abundant, renewable starting material, and the resulting particles keep some of the source medicine's own activity. The review maps how these particles form, how heat and added atoms tune their behavior, and how they apply across seven disease areas. Ten open opportunities and hurdles close the survey. Readers get a bridge between traditional remedies and modern nanomedicine, with its limits stated.
pmc-13521008:
Maria Aman and colleagues report a man with lasting alpha-gal syndrome who regained partial tolerance to red meat through a graded food ladder. The syndrome is a meat allergy sparked by tick bites, with reactions that start hours after eating.

The patient, a 26-year-old insect scientist, developed the allergy after years of fieldwork tick exposure and strict meat avoidance. He climbed a bacon-based ladder, eating slowly rising amounts, until most red meats no longer triggered symptoms. Fried pork skin still set off reactions, so his tolerance stayed partial rather than complete. Aman presents the ladder as a workable path for patients whose allergy does not fade with avoidance alone.
pmc-13523208:
Halil Uğur Hatipoğlu, Cevher Kızılırmak, and Murat Elevli measure a stress-related peptide in children with fever in a 2026 exploratory study. Copeptin was measured in blood and spinal fluid of children who had fever seizures, fever without seizures, or meningitis, and blood levels were also taken in healthy controls. All patient groups had undergone spinal tap in the emergency department for clinical reasons.

Blood copeptin was significantly higher in the fever seizure group than in the fever-only group and in healthy controls. Blood and spinal fluid levels correlated weakly, and two routine measures independently predicted spinal fluid levels. Spinal fluid testing added nothing over blood testing for telling the groups apart. The authors caution that the meningitis group was very small, so those findings need careful interpretation.
pmc-13523508:
Zahra Bastani Nejad and others explore, in a 2026 qualitative study, what helps and hinders internal review at an Iranian medical sciences university. Internal review is a structured self-review through which staff examine teaching, research, and administration. Faculty sit at its center, yet evidence from resource-limited settings was thin.

Sixteen faculty members at Fasa University of Medical Sciences were interviewed between January and October 2025, with sampling continued until saturation. Analysis produced three categories, covering how faculty understand review, what facilitates it, and what blocks it. Helpers included personal motivation, training, structural support, infrastructure, and a learning-oriented culture. Barriers included resistance to change, workload, limited resources, inefficient procedures, negative attitudes, and tension between departments. The authors argue review succeeds only when cultural and organizational conditions support it.
pmc-13524008:
Alshreef and colleagues published a 2026 systematic review of cooling therapy for newborns starved of oxygen at birth. The condition, hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, injures the brain, and cooling the baby is now standard care. What remained unclear was how development unfolds years later, past the usual toddler checks.

Searching four major databases, Alshreef kept ten studies covering 1,134 babies with moderate to severe injury. Between fifty-two and eighty-one percent of cooled survivors developed normally or with only mild problems by eighteen to thirty-six months. Delayed cooling, high lactate, severe brain wave changes, and abnormal scans each predicted worse outcomes. Problems could also appear at school age, so the authors back follow-up well beyond two years.
pmc-13524208:
Valeria González Quiroz and colleagues present a 2026 case that shows how a rare leukemia fusion can hide a diagnosis. Chronic myeloid leukemia is usually driven by the BCR::ABL1 fusion making a p210 protein. The variant in this patient made the smaller p190 form, more typical of a different leukemia, and standard tests missed it.

A 48-year-old woman with two years of unexplained anemia showed blood and marrow packed with maturing myeloid cells and 35 percent blasts carrying myeloid markers. Her chromosome study looked normal, while a targeted probe found the fusion and a qualitative test identified the rare e1a2 transcript after the usual quantitative test returned negative. She received acute leukemia induction chemotherapy. The authors stress that atypical features should prompt broader molecular testing.
pmc-13524908:
Marta Miszczuk-Cieśla and colleagues evaluate, in a 2026 prospective single-center study, training inhaler technique with a feedback device called Vitalograph AIM in patients with asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Correct technique is essential for inhaled medicine to work, yet many patients use inhalers wrongly and training guidance is unclear.

The study enrolled 121 patients, 82 with asthma and 39 with lung disease of the obstructive type, most using two or more inhaler types. At baseline, correct technique appeared in only six point six percent of metered-dose inhaler users and 43 percent of dry powder users. After device-guided training, correct use rose substantially, reaching about half of metered-dose users and nearly two thirds of powder users overall. Gains were largest for the metered-dose group, supporting device-based training.
pmc-13525508:
Sherwani and colleagues wrote a 2026 clinical comment warning that hidden breast filler injections may be the missing history behind stubborn breast abscesses in young women. The women affected have never given birth. Writing from a large breast hospital in Pakistan, the authors describe a surge of infections after filler injections in clinics with no oversight. Patients conceal the injections because cosmetic breast work carries social stigma.

Sherwani explains that filler forms a foreign-body pocket where infection persists despite antibiotics, sometimes involving hard-to-treat mycobacteria that need prolonged culture-guided drug mixes. Cure often requires surgical cleaning. Because patients disclose the history only under repeated, asking, the authors urge doctors to ask one gentle, private question about past breast injections at the first visit. They also urge sending cultures that include mycobacterial testing. Spotting it early, they argue, prevents repeated failed treatments and worse complications.
pmc-13525708:
Chloe Veilleux, Alison Omsberg, Janelle Richard, and Aurora Quaye present a narrative review, published in 2026. It covers intrathecal morphine. This is morphine given into the spinal fluid. It controls pain after surgery. The authors review twenty years of trials. Observational studies, reviews, and guidelines are also covered. They assess how well it works. They also assess how safely it can be monitored.

Across surgical groups, the treatment lowered pain scores. It reduced the need for other opioids after surgery. At modern doses, slowed breathing was uncommon. Its rate was similar to intravenous opioids. Events tied mostly to patient risk factors. These include age, obesity, and sleep apnea. This supports monitoring matched to each patient's risk.
pmc-13526308:
Pushpaleela and colleagues report a 2026 case of acquired hemophilia A in a 93-year-old man taking clopidogrel, a blood-thinning drug. The rare autoimmune disorder makes antibodies that attack factor VIII, a protein needed for clotting, and it can cause sudden heavy bruising and bleeding in older adults.

His tests showed a prolonged clotting time, low factor VIII activity, and factor VIII inhibitors, confirming the diagnosis. Hematology specialists directed treatment, but his course grew complicated and he died. The authors weigh whether clopidogrel or age-related autoimmunity triggered the condition. They urge doctors to suspect acquired hemophilia A quickly in older patients with unexplained bleeding, since delays raise the risk of death.
pmc-13527508:
Crisan and co-authors described a 2026 case report of a severe skin drug reaction in a man with mycosis fungoides, the most common skin T cell lymphoma. He was sixty-nine and receiving durvalumab, an immune therapy antibody, together with lenalidomide, a drug that reshapes immune responses. The pair was hoped to strengthen attack on the lymphoma.

The man developed a delayed eruption resembling erythema multiforme, a reaction pattern with target like spots and blistering risk. Crisan details how staging scans, blood tests, and skin biopsies confirmed his lymphoma stage while the new eruption emerged on treatment. Telling a drug reaction apart from lymphoma spread is hard in such patients, the authors note. Immune therapies often cause skin side effects, and some force treatment to pause or stop.
pmc-13527908:
Mousa Ghelichi-Ghojogh, Mohammad Hossein Rajaei, and Abdurrahman Charkazi surveyed 339 adults who smoke in Golestan Province, Iran, for a 2026 study of how much lung cancer risk smokers believe they face. Participants filled in questionnaires covering smoking history, nicotine dependence measured by the Fagerström test, readiness to quit, and their personal sense of risk.

Average perceived risk came to about 7.3 on a scale of twenty, a low to moderate level. People with stronger nicotine dependence rated their risk higher, with each added dependence point lifting the score modestly, while age, years smoked, and readiness to quit showed no clear link. The authors recommend education and support that raise risk awareness and reduce dependence, and they call for larger studies that follow smokers over time.
pmc-13528008:
Srijana Paudel and eight colleagues survey people with HIV in Nepal's Gandaki Province for a 2026 study of other illnesses and quality of life. Participants were drawn from the treatment center at Western Regional Hospital in Pokhara. In total 337 people took part. The team measured health-related quality of life with a standard score.

Just over half reported poor quality of life. About twenty-eight percent had at least one added illness. High blood pressure was the most common, then diabetes, then tuberculosis. Hepatitis B and C were less frequent. People with added illnesses had higher odds of poor quality of life. Many social factors also mattered, from education to travel costs. The authors recommend care that treats HIV and daily-life needs together.
pmc-13528908:
Nicolas Roy and four colleagues test whether flickering light can dull pain in a 2026 study. Brain rhythms sync to rhythmic sights and sounds. Earlier work hinted alpha-rate flicker eases laser pain. Two experiments delivered rhythmic visual stimulation at varied rates and lengths. Brain responses were read with EEG. Pain came from heat, laser, and electric pulses.

The flicker did entrain the brain as expected. Frequency-matched responses rose clearly in the EEG. Pain ratings, though, did not budge. No rate or duration changed how much the stimuli hurt. The null held across all three pain types. The authors report the negative result plainly. Entrainment alone seems too weak to move felt pain. Their work trims hopes for simple light-based pain gadgets.
pmc-13531508:
Roger Esteban-Fabró and colleagues tested whether pay bonuses and feedback helped Catalan primary care recover after COVID-19. Published in 2026, the long-run study tracked 37 quality measures across 287 practices serving over five million adults, month by month from 2019 through 2024. Pandemic disruption had cut care quality, and bonuses were paused in 2020 before a staged return.

Thirteen measures rejoined pay-for-performance in 2021, while 24 waited until 2023. Early-bonus measures recovered faster, with about five sixths back to pre-pandemic levels by late 2024 against half of late ones, and early bonuses doubled the odds of recovery before 2023. Yet many practices also recovered late measures on feedback alone. Smaller practices rebounded faster and rural practices fell less. The authors back tailored bonuses plus timely feedback for resilience.
pmc-13531808:
Rujira Nonsa-ard and co-authors survey fall prevention habits among 1,256 older adults in rural Thailand during 2026 reporting. Many participants still farm for a living, which shapes home hazards. Questionnaires plus walking and knee tests measured risk, while statistical grouping sorted prevention habits into five families.

About a third had fallen within six months. Safer home setup and house management habits linked to clearly fewer falls even after adjustment, as did safe movement habits. Clothing and footwear habits helped before adjustment only. The authors rank home environment work as the sturdiest lever for rural fall prevention.
pmc-13531908:
Bang-lin Xie and colleagues dissect in 2026 the rare disaster of spinal infection after a cement injection procedure for collapsed vertebrae. Their hospital counted just three infections among 6,328 procedures over a decade. A pooled group of 39 treated patients, mostly referrals, supplied the clinical detail.

Every patient had back pain, about half had fever, and germs were seldom grown in culture. Eight cases were actually spinal tuberculosis mistaken at first for simple fractures. Surgery patients ended with less disability than conservatively treated ones, though groups differed at start. Careful partial cement retention worked in eight chosen cases.
pmc-13532308:
Yuanyuan Tang and colleagues report in 2026 on mocravimod, a drug first used for other care, as a possible tool against Staphylococcus aureus. The germ causes skin harm, lung illness, and blood infection, and drug-resistant forms are hard to treat. Films of germs called biofilms add more protection against drugs.

Tests on lab isolates showed the drug killed both drug-sensitive and resistant germs and slowed new biofilms. It also cut live germs in mature films and harmed the germ cell wall. Readers see lab proof for a new use, with a clear note that safety and benefit in people still need study.
pmc-13532508:
Jingyuan Chen and colleagues introduce in 2026 light-driven particles that act as tweezers for tiny objects. Small grains coated to absorb visible light move on their own and gather inside shaped light fields. Tests and models show a round light spot forms a trap whose hold can be tuned by grain and spot size.

Shifting light patterns reshaped groups, sorted grains by colour of light, and built lattice forms that could change back. Single grains and groups also pushed cargo larger than themselves and drove small joint machines. Readers see a low-power way to move tiny loads without direct grip.
pmc-13534208:
Elzbieta Czembor, Lukasz Stepien, and Jerzy H Czembor search in 2026 wheat genes for adult-plant resistance to several fungal diseases. Wheat feeds about 40 percent of the world, and leaf fungi cut yields each year. The team scored 411 wheat lines from many origins in 2018 and 2019, then scanned their DNA.

Regions on several chromosomes linked to resistance against rusts and blotch diseases. Some markers held up in both years, and shared regions offered resistance to more than one disease. One region on chromosome 7D looked new for leaf rust. Breeders gain fresh targets for durable resistance.
pmc-13536608:
Masato Matsuura and colleagues test in 2026 whether variants in sodium channel genes track chronic nerve damage from the cancer drug oxaliplatin in Japanese patients. Such gene links were unclear in this group. Seventy-six patients with colorectal cancer who had oxaliplatin-based treatment gave samples and symptom scores.

One variant in the SCN4A gene linked to lower symptom burden both at treatment end and six months later. Another variant showed a weaker, short-lived link the other way. The authors call the lead variant a candidate marker, pending checks in larger groups.
pmc-13538608:
Sedat Arslan and colleagues relate nutrition knowledge to eating attitudes and body satisfaction among Turkish adults in a 2026 online survey. The survey gathered 1,457 adults aged 19 to 64 years, who completed scales for nutrition knowledge, eating attitudes, rigid healthy eating scores, and body satisfaction. Adjusted layered models tested each link while holding background, health, and lifestyle traits steady.

Nearly half of respondents scored low on nutrition knowledge. Stronger knowledge tied to fewer disordered eating symptoms and higher body satisfaction. Knowledge also tied to the rigid eating scale, though the authors warn that scale runs in reverse, with lower scores flagging greater risk, so the direction needs care. They advise teaching that pairs accurate knowledge with flexible attitudes, and call for follow-up studies with updated tools.
pmc-13539908:
Zhao and colleagues reviewed in 2026 the causes of pancreatic cancer pain and the move toward pain relief aimed at those causes. Pancreatic cancer is among the deadliest cancers, and its pain is common, crushing, and linked to shorter survival. Pain was once blamed on the tumor's bulk alone, but the authors show a far more tangled picture centred on two-way talk between tumor and nerves.

Zhao explains that cancer cells invade the space around nerves, building a niche where tumor, support, and immune cells trade signals that reshape nerves and inflame them. This sensitises pain fibres, and the spinal cord and brain then amplify the signal into lasting pain. Standard pain drugs and nerve-blocking procedures often give partial, short relief. Newer plans target the shared signals directly, with molecular blockers, nerve modulation, and precision nano-scale drug carriers.
pmc-13540908:
Warut Aunjitsakul and six colleagues survey, in a 2026 study, how psychiatrists in Thailand feel about psychotherapy, the talking treatments whose value is well evidenced yet unevenly used. A very long questionnaire, 190 items, covered attitudes, use, access barriers, and hopes for training and digital tools.

Seventy-four professionals replied, almost all fully trained psychiatrists. Attitudes were broadly positive, and most respondents folded therapy into daily practice, usually beside medication. Cognitive behavioural therapy, supportive therapy, and mindfulness approaches led usage. Lack of time was the biggest barrier, ahead of system limits and self-doubted skill. Appetite for further training ran high, which the authors say should guide national planning.
pmc-13541608:
Benjamin Dudouet and colleagues built a hands-on way to grade fairness in fishing management. Published in 2026, the study defines fairness through a three-layer frame rooted in the fisheries social contract, plus a scoring system for judging it. Fair shares of fishing rights shape whether rules win support and work, yet fairness was rarely measured.

The team tried the method on French and Spanish sharing rules for Bay of Biscay hake, a case where access rules decide who fishes and how much. The side-by-side showed why fairness must sit beside green and money goals in fishing rule-making. Readers get a usable yardstick for scoring fairness in other fisheries, plus a worked case for reform talks.
pmc-13541808:
Esen, Taş, and Eroğlu measure the muscles of people with fibromyalgia with instruments rather than questionnaires, testing whether the widespread pain condition leaves a physical signature in tissue. Thirty-one patients, nearly all women, and 31 matched healthy controls had three muscles probed: a neck-shoulder muscle, a forearm muscle, and a calf muscle. A handheld myotonometer tapped each muscle to read its tone, stiffness, and elasticity, while a pressure gauge found how much force triggered pain.

Patient muscles ran tenser and stiffer than controls' at all three sites, with the strongest effects in the shoulder muscle, while elasticity showed no difference between groups in the 2026 results. Pressure pain thresholds were significantly lower in patients, confirming their hallmark tenderness with an objective dial. They conclude fibromyalgia involves measurable passive muscle change, and suggest relaxation-targeted therapy deserves testing alongside pain control.
pmc-13543608:
Amy M Loviska and colleagues tested whether mixed-sex friendships and teen drinking drive each other over time. Published in 2026, the study tracked 1,021 teens aged just over 12 on average across six time points. Teens with mostly other-sex close friends drink more on average, yet whether friendship mix and drinking push each other was unclear.

Friendship mix and drinking each held fairly steady, with other-sex friendship share building more at later time points. The model found no same-time or time-lagged links within teens, ruling out a back-and-forth process inside persons. Yet teens with a higher other-sex share drank more on average, a between-person link. The authors conclude that friend-sex effects on drinking run between teens, not within them, changing theory.
pmc-13543908:
Yin and colleagues published a 2026 review on Nipah virus, a deadly virus carried by fruit bats that can spread to people. The review weighs how likely the virus is to cause a pandemic, drawing on how it harms the body and how it jumps from animals to humans.

The Malaysian strain reached people through pigs, while the Bangladesh strain can pass directly between people. Death rates in past outbreaks ran from 40 percent to over 75 percent in the worst cases. No licensed vaccine or drug treatment exists yet. The authors argue that deforestation and climate change push bats closer to towns, and they urge One Health surveillance that links human, animal, and environmental health.
pmc-13544708:
Sibari and colleagues reported a 2026 case series on brown tumours of the jaw, rare bone lesions caused by too much parathyroid hormone. The hormone excess, called hyperparathyroidism, slowly dissolves bone and can leave expanding lumps that mimic other jaw diseases. For some patients the jaw swelling is the first sign of the hidden hormone problem.

Sibari reviewed three women, aged twenty-two to sixty, treated during 2022 and 2023 for painless jaw swellings. Scans showed lucent or mixed lesions that expanded the jaw bone, and tissue tests found giant cells in a fibrous, blood rich bed. Two women had primary hormone excess and one had the secondary form while on dialysis. Removing the parathyroid gland shrank the lesions in the primary cases.
pmc-13546708:
Mohammad H. Gharaibeh and colleagues reported in 2026 the first DNA-based identification of Leptospira bacteria in animals in Jordan. Leptospirosis spreads from animals to people and kills tens of thousands worldwide each year, yet Jordan had only blood antibody evidence before this work. Blood and urine samples came from 82 animals suspected of infection between January 2020 and May 2021, mostly cattle.

A sensitive two-step DNA test found the bacterium in three samples, and sequencing confirmed it in pooled urine from imported calves and in blood from a dog. Both sequences were deposited in a public gene bank. The authors urge clinicians and vets to consider leptospirosis in fever cases and to strengthen monitoring.
pmc-13547408:
Galen Cobb and colleagues surveyed bee viruses in 2026 across wild bees and honey bees living side by side in north-central Florida. They tested whether viruses simply spill from managed hives into wild species. Four common viruses were measured for presence, amount, and co-occurrence across seasons in wild bees from 23 genera. Nearly every honey bee carried at least one virus, against about three in five wild bees.

Two viruses fit the spillover story, dominating honey bees first. A third, Israeli acute paralysis virus, appeared more often and at higher levels in wild bees, especially sweat bees, and persisted in wild bees through spring when honey bees showed none. The authors conclude some viruses circulate on their own within wild bee communities, complicating one-way blame on beekeeping.
pmc-13548608:
Sophie Fox and Daniela Munteanu describe a 2026 case of invasive pneumococcal disease spreading through the body of a healthy fifty-six-year-old woman. Pneumococcus usually threatens the very young, the old, or people with weakened defenses, yet this patient had no predisposing condition beyond obesity. She arrived after ten days of fevers, shaking chills, and several hot, swollen joints.

Blood cultures and joint fluid both grew the bacterium. Scans then revealed infection in the sacroiliac joint bone and at several levels of the spine. Small abscesses sat beside the spine, deep in the pelvis, and along the psoas muscle. None of them could be drained. Eleven weeks of intravenous antibiotics brought a full recovery. The authors use the case to urge quick joint aspiration whenever septic arthritis is possible and to remind readers about vaccination.
pmc-13548708:
Yan-chao Hu and colleagues uncover a partnership between two sugar-burning enzymes that helps hepatitis B related liver cancer grow and helps the virus copy itself, in a 2026 laboratory study. Tumors rewire their metabolism, and both enzymes, ENO1 and PKM, sit in the core energy pathway. The team measured them in virus-infected cancer cells and mouse tumors, then tested whether the proteins physically meet.

Both enzymes ran high in infected cancer tissue. Binding experiments confirmed they interact directly. Raising ENO1 sped cancer cell growth, movement, and invasion, and tumors grew faster in animals. Higher levels of both proteins also boosted virus replication, feeding the cycle that drives the cancer. The authors propose breaking the ENO1 and PKM partnership as a metabolic treatment strategy for this virus-linked cancer, pending drug development.
pmc-13550608:
Ithipri Emonena, leading seven colleagues, published a 2026 study on predicting machining quality when only a little experimental data exists. Using 27 Taguchi-designed trials, the team varied material, tool angles, speed, feed, and cut depth for polyamide workpieces. Eight outcomes mattered, from surface roughness and cutting force to tool wear and noise.

Five learning models were trained, and three optimization methods each chose the same three strongest models to combine. The crayfish-inspired optimizer reached its best weighting faster than genetic or swarm methods, giving more weight to two of the models. The blended predictor, named CrayStack, beat every single model across all eight outcomes in material-stratified cross-validation.
pmc-13551208:
Angela Cheng, with four colleagues, published a 2026 retrospective study of how much laboratory work breast cancer specimens need after drug therapy given before surgery. Such neoadjuvant therapy can blur the tumor bed, making assessment harder. The single-institution team compared 241 treated specimens from 2019 to 2025 with a matched set of untreated specimens.

Treated cases needed a median of 20 tissue blocks against 13 for controls, and far more often required extra sampling or a pathologist's review. Reports took a median of 17 days rather than 15 for treated specimens. Pretreatment clinical stage predicted whether the tumor bed could be seen at gross examination, and the authors urge health systems to plan laboratory capacity as such therapy spreads.
pmc-13551808:
Jorge Antonio Aguilar Estrada, leading a large Cuban research group, published a 2026 observational study of the Abdala COVID-19 vaccine in pregnant women. Pregnant women are usually excluded from vaccine trials, leaving safety evidence thin. The ESPIRTA study followed one cohort across five Havana maternity hospitals, mixing retrospective and prospective records from first dose through delivery and the newborn period, with 2020 hospital data as context.

A subgroup at one hospital gave blood for antibody measurement against the virus's receptor-binding domain, testing both maternal response and passive transfer to newborns. The design tracks vaccine-related events for mother, fetus, and neonate together. The authors present the study as filling a population-specific evidence gap for a protein subunit vaccine already used in the general population.
pmc-13551908:
Luke E. Grzeskowiak and thirteen colleagues set out SUMMIT, a trial protocol for domperidone dosing in lactation insufficiency after preterm birth. Mothers of preterm infants often struggle to build and keep up milk supply during long hospital stays. Domperidone beats placebo for this problem, but the best dose is uncertain. Their 2026 paper designs a multicentre, double-blinded randomized trial comparing 60 mg per day with 30 mg per day.

The trial targets mothers of infants born before 34 weeks, 7 to 28 days after birth, with lactation insufficiency. One hundred women will be split evenly into the two dose groups. The main outcome is daily expressed milk volume over 24 hours on day 21 after randomization. Mothers and infants will be followed until term corrected age or discharge from the neonatal unit, whichever comes first.
pmc-13553708:
Felix Holm and colleagues introduce ProtoFlow, a method that models surgical workflows in a way surgeons can inspect and trust, publishing it in 2026. Detailed workflow recognition could power AI help in theatre, but labelled surgical video is scarce and most models hide their reasoning. ProtoFlow learns dynamic scene graphs, structured maps of tools, tissues, and their changing relations, then distils them into prototypes that stand for recurring patterns of interaction.

Tested on a fine-grained surgical scene-graph dataset, the method beat standard graph baselines and stayed strong when trained on very little data, even a single video. Its prototypes also picked out distinct sub-techniques and flagged workflow departures and rare complications in plain view. The work points toward AI support that explains itself in training, live guidance, and review.
pmc-13554208:
Mohammad Mousaei Ghasroldasht and colleagues engineered tiny vesicles to protect ovaries from chemotherapy damage, publishing the study in 2026. Cancer treatment saves more young women than ever, yet drugs such as cyclophosphamide can wipe out the finite egg reserve and cause early ovarian failure. The team copied chemical signals between umbilical cord stem cells and ovarian support cells to craft enhanced exosomes, then tested them in cells, mice, and cultured human and rat ovarian tissue.

Treated mice kept far more resting follicles than chemotherapy-only controls, and breeding improved markedly, with seven pups versus one at first mating and later pregnancies only in the treated group. Human tissue showed a doubled marker of follicle health. The work supports engineered exosomes as a possible fertility-preserving option for young cancer patients.
pmc-13554308:
Michael J Patetta leads a five-author team reporting eight cases of stand-alone prone side-approach spine fusion in a 2026 series. Patients lie face down while the surgeon fuses a spinal segment from the side, saving a position change. All eight had earlier multi-level fusions and mid-range anaesthesia risk scores. Cages with built-in side plating supported the fused segment without back screws.

Surgery ran between eighty and 194 minutes, with tiny blood loss and stays of one to three days. Disc and channel heights grew as hoped, and spinal curve measures improved. Three patients, though, needed fresh surgery: two after the cage sank, one for leftover numbness. The authors call the approach workable for chosen patients, with sinking the main worry.
pmc-13554508:
Wissam Zam and three colleagues test which simple body measure best flags insulin resistance in Syrian women in a 2026 study. Seventy women aged seventeen to forty-six attended a clinic in Homs. Three measures were compared: a waist-to-height ratio, a waist-to-hip ratio, and the standard body mass index. Insulin resistance was scored from fasting blood values by a standard formula.

Body mass index barely tracked insulin resistance, and the link missed statistical firmness. Waist-to-height ratio tracked it most closely by a wide margin. In accuracy tests it also beat both rivals at picking out resistant cases. The authors recommend the waist-to-height ratio as a cheap clinic screen for this group, while noting that men still need their own study.
pmc-13555908:
Kashika Mendiratta and three colleagues profile simple bedside breathing tests in North Indian children in a 2026 hospital study. Standard lung testing is often impractical for children, yet early impairment can stay silent. Their study enrolled 190 children aged seven to eighteen at an outpatient clinic. Three simple measures were taken: single-breath counting, breath-holding time, and peak flow rate.

All three measures rose with age, and peak flow peaked around age thirteen. Counting and breath-holding each tracked peak flow closely. Height and age strongly shaped peak flow in the models, with breath-holding also a firm predictor. The authors propose the simple tests as practical helpers for spotting breathing trouble where spirometry is scarce, not as replacements for it.
pmc-13556008:
Vini Mehta and five colleagues gathered in 2026 the systematic reviews that test probiotics against oral candidiasis, a common mouth infection caused by Candida yeast.
