The condition clusters in people with weak immunity, denture wearers, older adults, and heavy antibiotic users, and resistance to antifungal drugs is a growing worry. Their umbrella review searched four databases for reviews published up to the end of January 2026.

Seven reviews met the criteria, five of them with pooled analyses. Across those analyses, probiotic products tended to lower Candida counts in the mouth, though the size of the benefit varied widely between studies. Differences in strains, delivery forms, and treatment length made the reviews hard to compare. Quality checks with standard tools temper the message: probiotics look promising as an add-on, but firmer trials are still needed.
pmc-13557008:
Job J Herrmann and co-authors examine whether a patient's fluid habits before a trial change the effect of fluid advice in chronic heart failure. Their 2026 paper is a subanalysis of the FRESH-UP trial, prespecified in advance,, which randomised 504 patients to liberal fluid intake or restriction to 1,500 millilitres per day.

Before the trial, 269 patients restricted fluids and 235 drank freely. After three months, health status scores differed by switching pattern. Patients who moved from restriction to liberal intake scored higher on a heart failure questionnaire than those who moved the opposite way. That latter group also reported the most thirst distress. Reported intake followed the assigned advice in both strata, and deaths and hospitalisations did not differ. The authors conclude routine fluid restriction is unnecessary in stable heart failure.
pmc-13558508:
Zuzanna Pawlus and four colleagues described in 2026 a case of necrobiotic xanthogranuloma, a rare skin disease tied to abnormal blood proteins, and reviewed one of its treatments. Their patient was a 58-year-old woman with spreading yellow-orange plaques. Close-up skin imaging showed irregular vessels and bleeding dots, while confocal microscopy revealed the large fatty immune cells and ring-shaped giant cells that mark the disease under the microscope.

Testing also uncovered a monoclonal blood protein and a slow-growing B-cell lymphoma, associations typical for this condition. Treatment with intravenous immunoglobulin plus steroids brought partial improvement. Pooling sixteen published cases with follow-up, the authors find immunoglobulin therapy often works fast and sometimes clears the disease, though stopping it can invite relapse. They call for individualised, sustained management of this multisystem disorder.
pmc-13558608:
Fatima Zahra Bouchachi and six colleagues weighed in 2026 whether cannabis smoking links to lower chronic pain in men on haemodialysis. Pain is common in this group and hard to treat safely, which pushes interest toward alternatives. Their cross-sectional study enrolled 186 men, measured pain on a standard numeric scale, and used inverse probability weighting to balance smokers and non-smokers on the background factors that might distort the comparison.

After weighting, cannabis smokers reported pain scores roughly one and a half points lower than non-smokers on average. Adding painkiller use to the sensitivity check softened the gap only modestly. The authors are careful about limits: only men were studied, the design captures a single moment, and unmeasured differences could still explain part of the gap. They call for prospective work with detailed exposure records before any clinical conclusion.
pmc-13558708:
Dong-Gun Kim and four colleagues identified in 2026 a histone variant that acts as a brake on lung adenocarcinoma spread. Metastasis drives most deaths in this cancer, yet no recurring mutation explains it, pointing suspicion at epigenetic control. The variant, H2A.J, sits in the spools around which DNA winds, and the team found it sharply reduced in these tumours, with low levels tracking poor survival.

Restoring the variant in cancer cells curbed their invasion and metastatic behaviour. The mechanism traced to one target gene, TMEM158, whose promoter collects H2A.J; there the variant reshapes local chromatin packing and quiets the gene, which otherwise supports spread. The authors propose H2A.J both as a prognostic marker that flags dangerous tumours and as a therapeutic idea: restoring an epigenetic brake rather than blocking a mutated accelerator.
pmc-13560108:
Ahmed Hamdi and colleagues report national data on kidney transplant evaluation and waiting times in Qatar. Their 2026 retrospective cohort covers 1,201 adults with end-stage kidney disease referred to the national transplant center between 2003 and 2017. A multidisciplinary process judged suitability, and listed patients were followed to transplant, death, or continued waiting.

Of those referred, 835 completed evaluation, and 95.4 percent of them were deemed suitable; advanced age and cardiovascular disease caused most rejections. Living donor surgery served 361 patients, while 436 joined the cadaveric waiting list. Only 84 of the listed patients, 19.3 percent in the reported share, received a deceased-donor kidney, after a mean wait under two years. Fifty-nine died waiting, and the rest remained listed. Peritoneal dialysis patients were likelier to be transplanted, a link the authors attribute to patient differences rather than the dialysis method itself.
pmc-13560308:
Supriya Samal and colleagues show how Helicobacter pylori strips an adhesion protein, L1CAM, from stomach lining cells and the vesicles they shed, clearing a path for cancer. Their 2026 study examines infected biopsies, cell cultures, vesicle preparations, and mouse xenografts. The bacterium is a major gastric cancer risk factor, yet its vesicle-mediated effects were largely unexplored.

Infection cut full-length L1CAM sharply in cells, secreted vesicles, cancer tissue, and patient plasma vesicles. The enzyme ADAM10 did the cutting, leaving fragments behind. Vesicles from infected cells made healthy stomach cells grow and migrate more, and boosted tumor growth in animals, while vesicles from uninfected cells calmed those traits. Losing the protein also flipped cells toward a mesenchymal state and lowered a specific integrin partner. The authors name a three-part signaling axis behind this cancer-promoting shift.
pmc-13560408:
Narendra Kumar and colleagues review animal models of Long-COVID, arguing the Golden Syrian Hamster best captures the disease's lung-brain-immune tangle. Their 2026 article synthesizes preclinical evidence across species. Long-COVID spans over two hundred reported symptoms, with unresolved lung inflammation and immune dysregulation suspected of feeding brain problems.

Hamsters catch SARS-CoV-2 naturally, without genetic modification, and mirror human acute disease: strong viral replication, lung damage, and inflammation. Past the acute phase they develop lingering faults along the same axis, including poor alveolar repair, fibrotic remodeling, brain inflammation, viral persistence, and behavior changes. Mice and primates each offer different trade-offs in relevance, cost, and feasibility. The hamster's gaps include scarce immune reagents and weakly validated behavior tests. The authors still judge it the most balanced platform for testing Long-COVID therapies.
pmc-13562208:
Hajek and colleagues report a 2026 German study of relationship quality in the oldest old, people aged 80 and above.  The team used a national ageing survey wave from 2022 to 2023, with 810 people aged 80 or more living at home. 

High relationship quality with family showed no clear statistical link to either loneliness or depressive symptoms. High relationship quality with friends, in contrast, went with lower scores on both measures. The split is striking: at very old age, chosen bonds with friends may carry more weight for mood than family ties, which can mix support with duty and strain. The results argue for protecting friendships too, through transport and meeting places.
pmc-13562508:
Hajira Imran and seven colleagues map how quinoa, a naturally salt-loving crop, organises its defence against salty soil. Salinity threatens food supply worldwide, and quinoa copes far better than most crops, for reasons still partly hidden. The 2026 study put eight advanced quinoa lines through growth, physiology, chemistry, gene-activity, and metabolite testing under rising salt. Three survival styles emerged: a short burst of high output, best performance under stress, and steady conservative growth.

A gene family called universal stress proteins sat at the centre of the response, switching on by tissue and stress level. Tolerant lines protected their light-harvesting machinery, raised their antioxidant enzymes, and moved protective compounds into place. Roots turned on salt-exclusion genes at 300 millimolar salinity. One variety, Q-33, stood out for its coordinated chemical reshaping. The authors present salt resilience as a whole programme, not a single trick.
pmc-13563708:
Beini Zhang and seven colleagues test a two-part recipe for helping potatoes through drought: humic acid in the soil plus magnesium oxide sprayed on leaves. Drought is a standing threat to the world's fourth food crop. Their 2026 trial crossed two watering regimes, full watering against 40 percent of soil capacity, with humic acid at zero or a set dose and four spray strengths. Growth, leaf chemistry, tuber quality, and soil enzyme activity were measured.

Drought stunted the plants, drained their chlorophyll, and raised damage markers, while cutting tuber starch and protein. The strongest spray, 60 milligrams per litre, combined with humic acid, reversed much of that: leaves kept their green, antioxidant enzymes rose, and osmotic balance steadied. Tuber yield and quality under drought improved, without matching the well-watered plants. Soil enzymes also livened up. The authors present the pairing as a sustainable drought shield worth field testing.
pmc-13563808:
Hamide Rezaeizade and six colleagues ask a question: if thyroid blood tests are corrected by levothyroxine, why do patients still feel worse than healthy people? Their 2026 cross-sectional study enrolled 220 participants, half of them hypothyroid patients on the replacement drug and half healthy controls, matched in having equivalent hormone levels on paper. Everyone completed the World Health Organization's quality-of-life questionnaire, covering physical health, mental health, social life, and environment.

The treated group scored lower on every subscale, and on quality of life and general health, despite the matched blood work. Regression singled out three predictors of the score: being a patient dragged it down steeply, while education and the active hormone T3 lifted it. The authors conclude that normalising the blood numbers does not restore lived health. They press for care that asks patients how they feel, and for research into the T3 gap.
pmc-13563908:
Qiuyi Wang and five colleagues build a forecast model for emergence delirium, the confused, agitated waking that strikes some older patients after spine surgery. Their 2026 study enrolled 430 elderly patients having spine surgery at Shanghai Changzheng Hospital during 2024. Predictors were gathered across five windows, from background through anaesthesia to early recovery, while delirium was scored in the recovery unit. A shrinkage method distilled 38 possible features to nine, including age, education, pain after surgery, and exposure to a sedative.

Six machine learning models competed on held-out patients. Logistic regression won, with an area under the curve of 0.832, specificity 0.858, and sensitivity 0.610. Importance plots ranked education, age, and midazolam as the strongest global signals, while heavy bleeding and long operations drove personal risk, each worsening the other when combined. The authors offer the model as an adjunct for flagging patients who deserve waking watch, not as a stand-in for doctors' judgement.
pmc-13569508:
Duha N. Gide and co-authors interview, in a 2026 Australian study, twenty-eight health workers about pharmacists using medication reviews to screen older adults for depression. Participants included community and hospital pharmacists, geriatricians, and general practitioners. Their views were sorted with an acceptability framework.

Five themes covered how the service should be delivered, home visits as a screening setting, resources needed, timely follow-up, and benefits. Late-life depression often goes missed, and pharmacists already meet older patients often over medicines. The study gives service designers a practical sense of what colleagues would accept and what must be in place before screening starts.
pmc-13569608:
Jessan A. Jishu and colleagues query, in a 2026 study of a large United States health record network, how often collapsed lung follows thyroid or parathyroid surgery and what it predicts. Among 228,340 adults operated on between 2000 and 2025, only 237 developed the complication within a week, about one in a thousand.

Those patients faced far higher one-year risks of death, pneumonia, swallowing trouble, vocal cord paralysis, ventilator use, readmission, and emergency visits. The complication is rare enough to be known mostly from case reports, yet its shadow is long. Neck surgeons get population-scale numbers for consent talks and for vigilance when breathing problems appear after surgery.
pmc-13571308:
Keča and colleagues report in 2026 two mechanical failures of carotid artery stenting, the procedure that props open a narrowed neck artery with a metal mesh tube. One failure struck during the operation itself; the other arrived years later.

In the first case, the protective filter device used to catch debris became hooked on the freshly placed stent and could not be pulled out. In the second, the stent had fractured and a clot had formed inside it, producing symptoms. Both patients were rescued with open surgery: the surgeons removed the stent-bearing segment of artery and replaced it with a six-millimeter synthetic graft. Both grafts were still open at a mean follow-up of eight years. The authors stress that mechanical complications are commoner than believed and need immediate surgery when they occur during the procedure.
pmc-13572508:
João C. Ferreira and Pedro Faria present a 2026 proof-of-concept system that scores patient awareness from video. The AVPU scale grades a patient as alert, or as responding to voice, to pain, or not at all. Scores guide triage, yet busy staff record them unevenly, and forms fragment across services.

Their platform, Consc.ia, reads face marks, eye state, arm moves, and voice replies on a local device, so no raw video is stored. A clinician checks each call before it enters the record as a standard FHIR entry. The team built 136 staged videos from 58 health workers and mapped three rollout settings, from ambulances to wards. Adoption models project slow spread, near half of mid-level wards by 2037. No accuracy scores are claimed yet; tests on real clinical footage come first.
pmc-13573408:
N Wielens, with five colleagues, sets out a 2026 protocol for a trial of looser movement rules after open-heart surgery. Most such surgery at the Twente centre opens the breastbone, and patients then face strict limits on lifting and pushing. North American work hints those limits may be harsher than needed, at a cost to mood and mobility.

The trial assigns patients at random to standard strict rules or to the T-REX rules, which let patients lift and push as long as arms stay inside a set tube zone. The main outcome is change on a quality-of-life scale before rehabilitation starts. Activity levels and fear of movement are also tracked. Pain, wound healing, and complications are watched to prove no harm. The study runs at one Dutch centre through mid 2026.
pmc-13575108:
Nayab Asim and five colleagues build a hybrid system for spotting faults in factory sensor data in a 2026 paper. Predictive maintenance needs early warning of faults, yet fault examples are scarce and factory conditions keep changing. Their design mixes a generative model, transformer blocks that read time patterns, and classic statistical checks.

Tests ran on two public benchmark sets and on real current data from cranes with no labels. On the machine failure set the system reached 84.09 percent accuracy, and on the water treatment set it reached 92.25 percent accuracy. For the crane data, a weighted fusion of methods agreed on 14 high-confidence faults. The authors argue the combined design beats any single method alone.
pmc-13575208:
Qiaoling Pei, Yayu Guo, and Yuan Yu build a model that predicts how deep building excavations deform over time, in a 2026 paper. Foundation pits for underground construction can shift in complex ways that threaten nearby structures. Accurate forecasts of that movement support safer building work.

Their model pairs a bidirectional memory network, which reads data forwards and backwards, with an attention step that weights the most telling moments. Dropout and a combined penalty in the loss function were added to keep the model general. Tested on a real excavation project in Guangzhou, the model settled after about 30 training rounds. Its mean error was 0.311 millimetres, beating rival models on the measures used. The authors see promise for engineering safety management.
pmc-13575408:
Ahmed Alshawi and four colleagues test whether the brush used to apply dental adhesive changes how strongly a filling sticks to dentin, in a 2026 lab study. Adhesive dentistry depends heavily on technique, so small tool choices may matter. The team used 42 extracted molars cut into disks.

One universal adhesive was applied for 20 seconds with either a bristle brush or a microbrush, then set with light. Small tubes of flowable composite were bonded on top and sheared off to measure strength. The bristle brush group failed at a mean stress of 49.09 megapascals, well above the microbrush group's 37.20 megapascals in the same units. Nearly all microbrush samples failed at the glue line. The authors advise using a bristle brush for this step.
pmc-13576108:
Sang-Suk Choi leads a 2026 study of how high blood pressure and diabetes vary across levels of urbanisation in South Korea's Gyeonggi Province. Head counts by city and countryside can miss the in-between zones of modern settlement. The team used a United Nations degree of urbanisation scheme with three bands: urban, urbanised, and rural.

Survey data covered 41,983 adults in 2020. Raw rates ran highest in rural areas, at 29.4 percent for blood pressure and 13.4 percent for diabetes, against much lower urban figures. After adjusting for age, sex, schooling, and habits, the rural gap shrank to borderline levels. Trends from 2008 to 2023 were also traced. Checks using only towns whose class never changed showed stronger rural effects. The authors argue fine-grained settlement classes reveal gaps that blunt labels hide.
pmc-13576208:
Armen Zohrab Yeretsian leads a 2026 study of how home cleaning methods change the surface of clear dental aligners. Aligners made of PET-G plastic are worn nearly all day, so daily cleaning is routine. The team compared mouthwash, cleansing tablets, and brushing with toothpaste against an uncleaned control.

Eighty samples were cleaned once a day for 14 days. Large-scale roughness differed across groups overall, driven by the mouthwash group sitting higher than control. At the nanoscale, every measure differed clearly between groups. Chemically cleaned samples looked smoother and more even under the atomic force microscope. Brushed samples showed tiny scratches and uneven patches from abrasion, without a matching change at the larger scale. The authors conclude cleaning effects depend on the scale you measure.
pmc-13578208:
Arun Kumar Arigela and colleagues present a 2026 method for judging depth from event cameras, sensors that log brightness changes with very fine timing. Such cameras suit fast, hard scenes, yet depth methods often need hand-checked depth maps for training. The team set out to learn depth with no ground truth at all.

Their system pairs event streams with normal frames in one transformer model, a type of network that weighs links across a whole scene. Attention across mismatched frame rates ties the two feeds together over time. Training leans on how well rebuilt images match the real ones, plus smoothness and timing checks. On a standard test set the method beat earlier deep learning systems on the main error scores.
pmc-13579208:
Nag and colleagues reported in 2026 on a layered crystal, LiInP2S6, whose optical power grows when it takes in water. Moisture normally ruins optical crystals, which soak up water and degrade. Here, water slipping between the layers changed the crystal's symmetry. It created a new polar phase, a state with a built-in direction of charge. Tiny shifts in the lattice hold that phase in place.

Nag measured a strong second-harmonic response, where light comes out at twice its entry frequency, in the wet phase at a wavelength used in telecom systems. The values were up to twice those of known materials with similar light gaps. Computer theory matched the new polar mode and the large response. Warming and drying reversed the change, confirmed by several tests. The team sees water-driven switching as a way to create and erase tunable optical parts on demand.
pmc-13579808:
Elaheh Azadian and Mahdi Majlesi read the hidden shape of body sway to chart how balance matures in children, in a 2026 study. Standard sway measures count wobble but miss its pattern. The group enrolled 460 healthy participants, children aged seven to twelve plus young adults. Each stood through eight tasks that varied sight, stance width, and mental load. A force plate traced the pressure point underfoot all the while.

A shape analysis tool turned each thirty second trace into loop diagrams, scored four ways. Children showed richer, longer lived loops than adults, a sign of looser, more wandering control. Closing the eyes and standing on one leg swelled every shape score. A thinking task shifted most scores too. The authors pitch the method for spotting odd balance growth early in clinics and schools.
pmc-13579908:
Yayun Xu and colleagues ask whether better sleep and calmer inflammation move together during antidepressant care, in a 2026 study. Seventy four adults with major depression, all new to such drugs, took duloxetine for four weeks. Full sleep lab recordings ran before and after, and blood was drawn for six inflammation signals.

Sleep time and sleep efficiency rose, while time spent awake in the night fell. Four of the six inflammation signals dropped clearly across the month. At the start, patients who slept less or less soundly carried higher levels of some signals, knotting the two problems together. The authors read the twin gains as a hint that part of the drug's help may flow through cooling inflammation, a link worth testing in larger, controlled work.
pmc-13582708:
Yiying Huang and colleagues test taurine, a protective nutrient, against muscle aging in mice and muscle cells, in a 2026 study. Fast aging mice and their slow aging cousins drank taurine water from five to ten months of age, then ran a rotating rod test of endurance. The fast aging mice tired sooner, as expected, and taurine stretched running time in both lines.

Gene reads from the calf muscle flagged a handful of shifted genes under taurine. In dish grown muscle cells, a sugar treatment faked aging: more cells stained as senescent, and tube like fibers failed to form. Taurine cut the aging stain, restored fiber building, and lifted a key growth protein the sugar had pushed down. The authors read a guard role for taurine in aging muscle.
pmc-13584408:
Rongji Yu and colleagues map how age and sex shape the body chemistry of Père David's deer in this 2026 study. The deer is extinct in the wild and survives only in captivity, so keepers need fine detail on how it grows. The team combined three kinds of molecular readouts, covering gene activity, proteins, and small body chemicals, in male and female deer at several life stages.

Clear split patterns emerged. Young males leaned toward ion handling, while females nearing adulthood leaned toward fat use. Many of the shifting chemicals and proteins tied to immune defense and inflammation. A gene-based age clock read the youngest deer as youngest, as expected, and immune cell mixes moved in step with growth. The work gives carers a molecular baseline for this rare species.
pmc-13586408:
Basic, Begeer, and Ziermans evaluate in 2026 a sixteen-item screening questionnaire for early psychosis signs in autistic adults. This group faces elevated risk, and early symptoms can hide behind autism's own features. The tool had never been properly checked in this population.

Using the Netherlands Autism Register, the team analyzed 1,686 autistic adults with an average age of 46. About a third scored above the questionnaire's cutoff, a far higher share than in non-autistic groups. Higher scores tracked independently with stronger autistic traits and with more depressive symptoms. Among 361 participants with follow-up data, five reported a new schizophrenia-spectrum diagnosis, just over one percent. Every one of them had scored above the cutoff at baseline screening in this cohort. The authors weigh what that pattern means for screening practice.
pmc-13587108:
Thomas Frisell, Sebastian Hedberg, and Fredrik Piehl compare two B-cell drugs for multiple sclerosis using Swedish national records. Both drugs, rituximab and ocrelizumab, strip out B cells and control the disease well, yet they raise infection risk, and rituximab is far cheaper because it is used off-label. Their 2026 study followed close to seventeen thousand treatment rounds started between 2014 and 2025.

Both drugs carried higher rates of serious infection, hospital-treated infection, and antibiotic use than other MS therapies. Relapses, meanwhile, were much rarer on either drug. Head to head, infection and relapse risks looked much the same for the two. The authors say the cheaper drug does not appear to cost patients extra safety, a point that matters for health systems weighing the two.
pmc-13587508:
Xiang Liu and colleagues survey what shapes toddler development inside Shanghai families. Early childhood development covers language, movement, problem solving, and social growth in the first three years, when most brain building happens. Their 2026 study sent an online questionnaire to caregivers across the city between 2022 and 2024 and kept 534 valid replies, framing the answers inside a family ecosystem model.

About one child in six showed a delay in at least one area. Risk ran higher for boys, for children born early who needed oxygen, and where homes held few children's books. Strained marriages, rare shared parent-child activities, heavy maternal screen use with signs of neglect, and weak overall family functioning also raised the risk. Language and social areas were hit most. The authors call these family factors measurable targets for early spotting and help.
pmc-13591508:
Daisuke Kanda, Nobuhiro Ito, and Mitsuru Ohishi describe, in 2026, a stepwise fix for a hardened lump blocking a heart stent in a 67 year old woman. She had kidney failure, diabetes, and severe obesity, and access through the leg was hard, so the team worked through the arm. Scans showed a large off center calcium nodule inside the stent of her right coronary artery.

A spinning burr first shaved the lump, yet it followed the wire and cut too little. By steering the guide tube and wire, the team aimed the burr at the lump and ground it down in stages. A cutting balloon barely helped, so shock wave pulses from inside the vessel cracked the rest. A drug coated balloon finished the job, leaving a wider channel.
pmc-13592308:
Jun Hu leads a 2026 team using carbon dioxide as a courier gas in a light driven reaction that turns plant derived alcohols into light alkanes. The change needs two clashing steps: stripping hydrogen from the alcohol, then cutting a carbon bond and adding hydrogen back. Carbon dioxide ferries the reducing power between steps without ending up in the products, the team shows. Isotope tags and radical traps back that reading.

Under visible light the catalyst first turns alcohols into aldehydes, then clips them into shorter alkanes. The courier role also curbs wasteful hydrogen gas release and keeps the catalyst cycling. Hu and the team present redox shuttling as a way to marry clashing steps inside one photocatalytic loop.
pmc-13597308:
Christopher A Martin leads a twenty-three-author longitudinal study of COVID vaccine booster responses in healthcare workers, asking whether ethnic differences seen after first doses persist. Participants in the BE-DIRECT cohort gave blood before a booster, a few weeks after, and around six months later, with antibodies and T-cell responses measured at each point in the 2026 report.

South Asian participants mounted substantially higher antibody levels right after boosting than White participants. The gap held after accounting for prior infection, vaccine type, and starting levels. It closed by six months, though. Levels waned at similar rates in both groups. T-cell boosting did not differ, yet the later decline of spike-specific T-cell responses ran slower in South Asian participants. The authors say booster programs should understand this uneven durability, since headline antibody peaks and lasting cellular protection tell different stories.
pmc-13598308:
Yi-Ling Tseng and co-authors tested an eight-week multicomponent group exercise program for older adults. The sites were community care sites in central Taiwan. The design was quasi-experimental. A comparison group kept its usual activities. Eighty participants were assessed before and after in 2024 on physical performance and sleep.

The exercise group improved in walking speed, upper limb strength, sleep quality, and heart rate recovery after exertion. Head-to-head at the end, the exercisers beat the comparison group on arm curls, grip strength, and sleep quality. The authors present group exercise that mixes strength, endurance, and other components as a practical community offering, noting that peer support, suitable equipment, and motivation help older adults stick with it. They recommend implementation in community settings while acknowledging the design cannot fully exclude other explanations.
pmc-13599708:
Kenza Latrèche leads a ten-author team asking parents what they noticed during an intensive early autism program. The 2026 study followed 104 autistic children aged about 1.3 to 3.5 years through six months of the Early Start Denver Model, a one-to-one play-based therapy. Standard tests measured each child's development at the start and after six months. Parents then answered an 18-question survey covering twelve areas of progress, plus their own skills, well-being, and family life.

Parents reported gains across every area, and setbacks were rare. Their answers grouped into three themes: social communication, nonverbal social engagement, and a positive parental experience. Parents' views matched standard test results closely, above all for social communication. Feeling more skilled tracked with parental education and family size, not the child's measured gains. Parent perspectives, the team argues, deserve a formal place beside test scores.
pmc-13604908:
Yao Zhao leads a seven-author team studying where the Eurasian water shrew chooses to live in China's Lesser Khingan Mountains. This semi-aquatic mammal hunts in streams yet shelters on land, and its habitat needs in northeastern China were poorly known. The team compared 44 used plots against 44 control plots across winter and spring, measuring water-side and land-side features separately before combining supported predictors into one model.

Shrews used sites closer to water and favored still water over fast flow. They largely avoided upper slopes, preferring lower slope positions. The combined aquatic-terrestrial model beat either single-side model and discriminated used from unused plots well, surviving repeated cross-validation. Judging habitat from water features alone, or land alone, misses the point, the authors conclude. Conservation assessments should treat the water-land interface as one unit.
pmc-13612208:
Mohammed Alshehri leads a ten-author team asking how long a urine culture result stays useful for choosing antibiotics. Doctors pick empiric therapy before new results arrive, often leaning on past cultures, but resistance memory must decay eventually. Using twelve years of urine cultures at a Saudi tertiary hospital, the team formed consecutive same-species pairs within each patient. They asked how often a resistant first isolate was followed by a resistant second one.

From 8,045 patients, 3,380 evaluable pairs entered the persistence analysis. Memory was strong but faded. In E. coli, fluoroquinolone resistance persisted in 96.8 percent of pairs within thirty days and 79.9 percent after a year. Cephalosporin resistance fell much faster, from 90.0 to 48.2 percent. Klebsiella pneumoniae showed the same pattern at slightly different rates. Every decay model pointed the same way with time. The authors advise treating a past result as time-stamped guidance, specific to species and drug class.
pmc-13613008:
Ziwei Song, Pyoung Jik Lee, Li Bin, and Thomas Hampton compare hearing between nurses who work in an intensive care unit and nurses who work elsewhere in a hospital in Chongqing, China. Intensive care units are loud places, filled with alarms and machines, and long exposure to such noise can harm hearing. In total, 93 registered nurses, 45 from intensive care and 48 from other areas, took full hearing tests.

Intensive care nurses had worse hearing, mainly at high pitches between 4 and 8 kilohertz. About one in five of them met the study's mark for hearing loss. Tests covered both pure tones and speech heard against background noise, and the analysis hunted for traits that raised the risk on their own. The results make a practical case for noise control and hearing checks for staff in the loudest wards.
pmc-13614208:
Reza Karimpour, Matteo Gori, and Alexandre Tkatchenko review how quantum field theory, a framework that treats fields as quantum objects, can be brought to bear on chemical systems. Standard quantum chemistry rests on famous equations for particles and works well, yet it struggles with huge molecular groups because accurate calculations cost too much. It also misses effects that arise when light and matter fields act as quantum players themselves.

The review covers fresh work on bonds within molecules and weaker forces between them, in empty space, in solvents, and inside optical cavities. Confining light in a cavity can steer reactions and change the weak forces that hold molecules together. The authors point toward methods that may one day handle systems of millions of atoms, opening a path past the size wall that limits chemistry computing today.
pmc-13614308:
Jiaqi Guo leads a team watching, at several scales at once, how a designer peptide assembles inside and around cancer cells and pushes them toward a non-standard form of death. The peptide switches on in response to an enzyme and forms tiny structures, yet which shapes actually do the work inside cells was mostly guesswork. The team paired detailed imaging with chemical tests to follow one peptide, named NBD-L4pY, from plain solution to the cell surface.

In solution the peptide formed mixed thread shapes that depended on its strength and history, including a tube about 7 nanometres wide. At the cell surface that tube form took over. The pictures trace a path from disturbing the cell membrane to scrambling the actin skeleton that gives cells their shape. Such direct views help designers build peptide drugs that strike cancer cells on purpose.
pmc-13615308:
Qin Qian and Ling Yin present a case report of a 68-year-old man. Hours after he received a left ventricular assist device, his heart tracing showed a warning pattern. The device is a pump implanted for end-stage heart failure. The pattern, called the spiked helmet sign, lifts one segment of the tracing into a dome with a spike, and it usually points to inflammation around the heart. In this setting it meant something else.

A bedside ultrasound found a small, localised blood collection, just 6 millimetres, pressing in the sac around the heart, an early step toward the dangerous squeeze called tamponade. His heart injury marker peaked on day one and then fell, and careful watchful care succeeded without more surgery. The authors urge teams to treat this tracing after pump surgery as a trigger for an instant ultrasound check.
pmc-13616608:
Arvendi Rachma Jadi leads a team charting the arteries that supply the pig thyroid gland. They dissected 212 pigs from three breeds. The breeds were Landrace, Large White, and a cross of the two with a third line. The thyroid is richly supplied with blood, yet the pig's pattern was poorly documented, a gap for a species central to farming and to medical research. Glands fell into three shapes: pear-shaped, butterfly-shaped, or partly separated.

Supply to the front of the gland came from four possible arteries, and the rear drew on five more sources, mixing neck and chest vessels. Breed differences were clear, with the crossbred pigs differing from both pure breeds in parts of the pattern. Surgeons and researchers working on pig necks gain a map of what to expect and where variation will ambush the unwary.
pmc-13616708:
Polona Rus Prelog, Matija Zupan, and Senta Frol comment on a study of 78 survivors of acute ischemic stroke. It followed them for six months. The aim was to predict who would develop depression, thinking problems, or both after stroke. The original study found three predictors: a lesion in the right half of the brain, higher early depression scores, and lower early thinking scores. The commentators welcome the joined view of mood and cognition as one burden.

Their caution centres on measurement: both outcomes were defined by brief screening scales rather than full diagnosis. Short scales can blur the line between low mood and poor cognition, since each can inflate the other's score. Risk labels built on screens may misdirect support. The piece asks the field to sharpen its tools before sorting survivors into risk groups that guide real care.
pmc-13616908:
Malipeddi Saketh and twelve colleagues report a 2026 study of non-duality, the state where the felt line between self and world dissolves. They compared advanced meditators from the Isha Yoga tradition with novices and with people who had never meditated. They watched their breath or did a thinking task while the team recorded brain activity and asked about their experience.

Advanced meditators reported stronger non-dual experiences during breath watching than the other groups. Brain signals showed that intrinsic neural timescales, the windows over which brain activity stays linked, lasted similarly during inner and outer attention for the advanced group. That similarity tracked how strong their reported non-duality was. The authors propose this timescale pattern as a neural signature of the non-dual state.
pmc-13617308:
Ammar Ismail and four colleagues report a fatal case of stubborn hepatic encephalopathy, the brain failure that liver disease can trigger through ammonia buildup. The patient had received a TIPS shunt to relieve liver pressure. The sixty-nine-year-old, whose cirrhosis came from fatty liver disease, developed a small bowel obstruction soon after a shunt revision. Standard gut treatments could not get through the blocked bowel.

He arrived with severe confusion, seizures, and brain swelling confirmed on imaging. Continuous dialysis-style blood filtration cut his ammonia level from 447 to 160 micromoles per liter, a strong biochemical improvement. The brain injury nevertheless became irreversible, and he met brain death criteria. The authors argue that blood filtration should start proactively in such high-risk patients and that new ammonia-lowering strategies are needed when gut decontamination is impossible.
pmc-13618808:
Yue-Xuan Mu and two colleagues examine physical activity and mood in young-old adults in China, asking whether digital life changes things. Data came from China Longitudinal Aging Social Survey waves of 2020 to 2023, covering five thousand six hundred forty-three adults. The team modeled activity volume and exercise guidance against depressive symptoms. They tested whether internet use frequency and self-rated digital skill altered the links.

More activity and more guidance tracked with fewer depressive symptoms, though the activity link wobbled by subgroup. Frequent internet use tracked with lower symptom scores. It connected more consistently to guidance than to activity itself, and the activity-internet interplay showed among rural respondents. Among users, feeling digitally proficient came with fewer symptoms and a clearer guidance effect. The authors suggest mental health support for this age group should pair activity promotion with guidance and age-friendly digital help.
pmc-13620108:
Shakera Khatoon, Amna Javed, Qaiser Khan, and Kaleem Abbas describe a leaner way to make terbium-161, a radioactive isotope gaining ground in targeted cancer therapy, in a 2026 study. Their reactor ran on enriched gadolinium-160 targets prepared two ways: standard oxide powder and a new thin-layer chloride film. A day of neutron bombardment in Pakistan's research reactor produced the isotope for testing.

Thin-layer targets used neutrons far better because less material shielded itself, reaching more than double the specific activity of bulk oxide in side-by-side batches. A resin separation in hydrochloric acid recovered most of the product and yielded a chloride form ready for direct use, skipping steps that other chemical routes demand. Purity cleared very high marks, and tagging cancer-targeting peptide carriers succeeded at high rates. The authors pitch the workflow for labs working with limited reactor resources.
pmc-13620408:
Chunfeng Xiao and five colleagues followed families through the death of a terminally ill relative to map how grief moves before and after the loss. Sixty adult family members, mostly adult children of the patients, joined the pilot cohort at a Beijing hospital in late 2023. They answered grief, depression, anxiety, and stress scales monthly before the death and quarterly for six months afterward.

Two paths appeared before death: most relatives stayed low, while a small group climbed steadily. After death, four paths emerged, from low and falling to high and stuck. By the final visit, about a sixth of participants met criteria for prolonged grief disorder, and anxiety disorders touched nearly a third. People on the climbing path before death and the stuck-high path after it carried the most illness. The authors stress the study is exploratory and needs a larger confirming cohort.
pmc-13621508:
Laxmidhar Das reviews, in 2026, how refined versions of the PSA blood test could sharpen prostate cancer diagnosis. The standard test flags many harmless enlarged prostates and misses some real cancers, driving waves of unneeded biopsies. Das surveys the derivatives built to fix that weakness and a newer biochemical clue: the sugar coating on the PSA molecule itself.

PSA comes in several measurable forms, and their ratios and related markers separate cancer from benign enlargement better than the total level alone. The sugar chains attached to PSA also change shape as cancer advances, in patterns that differ between healthy and malignant tissue. Combining derivative measurements with these sugar signatures in multi-marker panels, Das argues, could cut pointless biopsies and catch aggressive disease earlier. Such panels could also spare slow tumors from overtreatment and help track response and recurrence after therapy.
pmc-13621808:
Chandrasekar Praveen and colleagues present a chemistry method that builds a family of compounds called quinolines, ring-shaped molecules found in many medicines and natural products. Their route starts from simpler building blocks known as 2'-aminochalcones and uses a gold salt as a catalyst, meaning a helper that speeds a reaction without being used up. Microwaves supply the heat.

In the reaction, an alcohol serves both as the liquid medium and as a reacting partner, so no extra oxidant is needed. Straight, branched, ring-shaped, and plant-derived alcohols all worked, giving products in fair to good yields. The route also made two natural alkaloids in one step and could be steered toward related ring systems. Early tests of how the reaction proceeds suggest the gold catalyst drives two steps in a row, which helps explain the clean results.
pmc-13623108:
Marco Zanotti and Flavio A Ziegelmann ask whether combining many retail forecasting models is worth its computing cost. Retailers forecast demand for huge product ranges, and blending model outputs, called ensembling, usually improves accuracy. Bigger blends, though, burn far more computer time, and the trade-off is rarely measured.

The pair tested ten base models and eight blend designs on two large retail data sets, scoring both single-value and probability forecasts at several retraining schedules. Blends did forecast better, above all for probability forecasts, but the largest blends cost much more to run. Retraining less often cut costs sharply with little accuracy loss. Small blends of two or three models usually came close to the best scores at a fraction of the cost. The authors frame their guidance as a path to forecasting that is both scalable and lighter on energy use.
pmc-13623808:
Todd Bertoch leads the authors of a 2026 phase three trial of a fast-absorbing meloxicam pill for pain after bunion surgery. Meloxicam is an anti-inflammatory painkiller, and this new formulation aims to work faster for moderate-to-severe pain after operations, when opioid sparing matters. The trial compared the pill with a dummy pill and with tramadol, an opioid-like standard.

Four hundred ten participants with clear pain after surgery were randomised, and nearly all finished the study. Over forty-eight hours the new pill beat the dummy on total pain relief by a margin, and it beat tramadol in an exploratory comparison. Patients on the pill reached relief sooner, needed less opioid rescue medicine, and more of them stayed opioid-free. Side effects were mild or moderate, and opioid-type side effects ran below the tramadol group. The authors call for confirmation in other surgical settings.
pmc-13624308:
Zhengjun Yan and colleagues tally how much of the carbon farm plants capture from the air travels below ground, and in what form. Soil carbon storage is a major climate lever, and roots feed it two ways. Plants grow root tissue, and they leak sugars and other compounds, called rhizodeposition, that slip into the soil during life. The split between those routes was poorly measured.

Combining 746 isotope-tracing observations from around the world, the team found that about seventeen percent of captured carbon goes below ground, and leakage accounts for a third of that input. Legumes favour the leak route while cereals and grasses invest more in root mass. Leakage rose with soil carbon up to a point, then ebbed. Warming cut underground input, while drought raised the leak share. The authors supply crop-by-crop coefficients so climate and soil models can stop guessing this hidden flow.
pmc-13627208:
Matthias Buntru and co-authors turn marigold cells into a factory for useful proteins. Plant cell cultures can brew recombinant proteins, yet many hosts chew the product up with their own proteases. The team grew a suspension culture from young marigold roots. Its broth, they confirmed, carried very little protease activity. The cells were then engineered with two production cassettes. A red fluorescent reporter stayed inside the cell. Brazzein, an intensely sweet protein, was sent outside.

Seven engineered lines were measured with precision mass spectrometry. The best made brazzein at a solid concentration in the broth, while the red protein piled up to over a third of all soluble protein inside the cells, a striking yield. The authors pitch their marigold line as a serious rival to the tobacco cells that dominate this niche.
pmc-13627908:
Writing in 2026, Yasser Fakri Mustafa reviews coumarins, a family of natural and lab-made compounds, as possible tools against cancer. His focus is two systems inside cancer cells: autophagy, the process by which cells break down and recycle their own parts, and the PI3K/mTOR signaling pathway, which drives cell growth.

Mustafa gathered preclinical studies from major databases, keeping only work on cell or animal cancer models. The evidence shows coumarins can switch autophagy up or down depending on context, often by acting on PI3K/mTOR signaling, and that this affects whether cancer cells survive, die, or resist chemotherapy. He concludes that better drug design and patient selection are needed before such compounds reach the clinic.
pmc-13632008:
François Tyckaert and twelve colleagues published this 2026 paper presenting a lab system for studying how cancer cells invade different organs. Spread to distant organs kills most cancer patients, yet common lab tests lack the real tissue scaffolding that shapes invasion. The team cleaned mouse lung, liver, and intestine tissue until only its natural matrix remained. They then cut thin slices and placed them inside standard microfluidic channels for microscope study.

The clear scaffolds kept each organ's structure, stiffness, and chemical character. A non-invasive breast cancer cell line could not enter any of the scaffolds. A strongly invasive line entered lung and liver scaffolds but failed in intestine scaffolds, matching how organs differ in welcoming spread. Gene activity readings showed distinct programs in invading cells. The system offers a cheaper, animal-sparing way to test what drives organ-specific spread.
pmc-13633108:
Jemma G. Gasperoni and five colleagues studied a gene called plag1 in developing zebrafish. The gene's human counterpart is linked to Silver-Russell syndrome, a growth disorder that often includes delayed development and face shape differences. The team lowered the gene's activity in fish embryos using a blocking molecule. They then checked brain structure, motor nerve growth, face skeleton formation, and how the young fish answered sensory triggers.

Brain structure and motor nerve patterns looked largely normal. Movement problems appeared clearly when fish were kept in groups, yet vanished when each fish was tracked alone, which points to a social or sensory role rather than weak muscles. Jaw and skull cartilage showed subtle flaws matching the human syndrome. Responses to light and sound also changed, and the fish hugged the walls of their tank more. The authors propose the fish as a new model for the syndrome.
pmc-13636608:
Amin Javidanbardan and three colleagues published this 2026 study measuring how thick concentrated messenger RNA solutions become. Makers of mRNA medicines must concentrate their product to reach useful doses, and thick fluids fight back during filtering and filling. No published numbers existed for such solutions. The team tested two model molecules: a standard reporter mRNA and a much longer self-amplifying RNA, across a wide range of concentrations and flow speeds.

The long molecule thickened dramatically faster. At the top concentration tested, its solution ran more than ten times thicker than the shorter one's. Both fluids thinned slightly under faster flow. The team matched their data against existing physics models to understand the behavior underneath. For factory design, the message is blunt: molecular length, not just concentration, sets how hard an mRNA product will be to process, so equipment and filtration plans must budget for it early.
pmc-13637108:
Zhemin Fu and six colleagues published this 2026 cohort study of how movement and sleep shape depression risk. The pair of habits are usually studied apart. The team followed over three hundred twenty thousand depression-free UK Biobank adults for a median of thirteen years. Participants reported activity levels on a standard questionnaire, and the researchers built a quality score from six sleep traits. New depression cases came from linked health records.

About seventeen thousand participants developed depression during follow-up. Low activity paired with poor sleep carried the highest risk by far, quadruple that of active, good-sleep peers. Too much vigorous activity with poor sleep also ranked near the top, a U-shape worth noting. Activity's protective edge shrank badly when sleep was poor, while poor sleep hurt at every level. The authors conclude sleep quality sets the stage on which exercise can or cannot protect mood.
pmc-13639008:
Henghui Zhang and eighteen colleagues present a 2026 preclinical study of an mRNA vaccine for esophageal squamous cell carcinoma, a cancer with few options once immunotherapy stops working. The vaccine, called IPM514, carries pieces of proteins commonly found on these tumors.

Its fifteen fragments come from nine tumor antigens chosen from large datasets and checked in samples from 132 patients. In cell tests the vaccine expanded T cells that killed cancer cells, and in mice it slowed tumors and extended survival. Adding a PD-1 blocking drug strengthened the effect. The authors propose the vaccine as a new immunotherapy strategy.
pmc-13642408:
Jessica Fanelli led a 2026 survey of the traits that go with orthorexia nervosa, a rigid focus on eating healthily that can impair daily life. Orthorexic patterns look like both eating disorders and obsessive-compulsive symptoms, yet which links belong to which sides was unclear. The team surveyed 300 Italian adults, averaging about twenty-four years old, with validated measures of orthorexic tendencies, eating disorder symptoms, perfectionism, emotion control, and food attitudes and motives.

The strongest links were to eating disorder symptoms, especially dieting concerns, and to perfectionism, especially high personal standards and worry over mistakes. Links to emotion control were weak overall, though the problems side tied to not accepting emotions and loss of control. Obsessive-compulsive symptoms added little once other factors were counted, while eating disorder symptoms, perfectionism, and food motives together explained 44 percent of variance.
pmc-13643608:
Jonathan A Golding and five colleagues present a 2026 observational study of frailty and blood sugar control in older adults living with type 1 diabetes. Guidelines borrowed from type 2 diabetes push frail patients toward looser targets to avoid low blood sugar, which can cause falls.

Eighty-three people over sixty-five wore blinded glucose monitors for ten days while frailty was graded by strength, walking speed, and activity measures. Frail participants were older and had higher long-term sugar averages and lower thinking scores. Yet no monitor measure, including time spent low, differed across frailty levels by any grading method. The authors note these patients managed successfully despite frailty.
pmc-13650408:
Sarah A Shaw and ten co-authors describe how three community-based groups in King County, Washington worked to offer whole-person services alongside HIV care. Such groups serve under-resourced communities well, yet they need workable plans for joining medical care with help for housing, food, and other social needs.

In a partnership between the groups and academic researchers during 2021 and 2022, staff brainstormed plans in structured group sessions, then rated each for feasibility and likely impact. The process yielded 118 plans that staff judged highly impactful, though only moderately feasible on average. Most aimed at restructuring the groups, giving staff better access to knowledge, improving communication, and engaging clients and partners. Plans that were both easy and strong often concerned knowledge and engagement, while structural fixes lagged. The paper maps the plans onto established implementation frameworks to guide similar efforts elsewhere.
pmc-13650708:
Matthew DiGiuseppe and two colleagues test whether calling a chatbot politically biased blunts its power to correct false beliefs. Politicians increasingly portray large language models as ideologically rigged, and the team wondered if that framing alone changes how people respond in conversation.

In a preregistered experiment, 2,144 American participants chatted through three rounds with ChatGPT about an economic misconception each person personally held. Conversation corrected beliefs in every condition. A short warning that the model was biased against the participant's own party shrank the correction by about a quarter and lowered trust and willingness to use AI. Most of the persuasive effect survived even so. Transcript comparisons showed the warned participants pushed back more and listened less receptively rather than quitting. The authors frame perceived bias as a user-side lever that weakens, but does not erase, AI persuasion.
pmc-13651708:
Ran Chen and five co-authors tune a terahertz detector with nothing more exotic than infrared light. Their device, a photoelectric tunable-step detector built on a two-dimensional electron gas, senses far-infrared waves through an in-plane photoelectric effect prized for its sensitivity.

Shining infrared illumination exploits a memory effect in the semiconductor sandwich: the light persistently raises the electron density and mobility of the conducting channel. The change sticks after the light is gone. With that knob, the team optimized responsivity for different operating modes and swung the detector's output impedance across roughly a tenfold range. The paper explains the physics of how the illumination reshapes the quantum detection process. The authors pitch the approach as in situ tunable optoelectronics, marrying infrared control to terahertz sensing inside one device for future communications, imaging, and testing hardware.
pmc-13659208:
Anton Osnytskyy and colleagues review modern treatments for vaginal dryness and atrophy in a 2026 survey spanning hormone, energy-based, injectable, and hormone-free options. Dryness affects women of all ages, most often around and after menopause, but also younger women with hormone disorders, gland disease, infections, drugs, or smoking. The authors trace causes including low estrogen, lining inflammation, surface thinning, and microbe imbalance, then assess each treatment's evidence and uses.

Energy-based options such as laser, radio waves, focused ultrasound, and tiny ultrasound show promise for restoring hydration and elasticity, especially after menopause and in cancer patients. Injectable hyaluronic acid, platelet-rich plasma, and collagen support local repair, hormone therapy remains standard for estrogen deficiency, and moisturizers relieve symptoms when hormones are unsuitable. Clinicians get a case for tailored, sometimes combined or staged therapy matched to cause, hormonal status, and patient factors.
pmc-3483008:
Cane, O'Connor, and Michie test the validity of the theory domains framework for behaviour change and rollout research. The framework gathers theory about why behaviour happens into a set of domains, such as knowledge, skills, and setting. It had already been used in a wide range of clinical cases.

Their study asks experts to judge whether the framework's structure holds up. Sorting sample behaviours into domains checks whether the groups are clear and complete. A validated framework gives intervention designers confidence that they are spotting behaviour problems with a sound map.
pmc-4201108:
Italiani and Boraschi wrote in 2014 about how monocytes become macrophages of different kinds. Monocytes are blood cells that move into tissues and mature into macrophages. These tissue guards keep organs sound by clearing damaged cells and matrix, and by repairing harm.

The authors contrast two lenses on this change: what the cells look like and what they actually do. In one mode, often called M2-like, macrophages calm inflammation and promote healing. In another, they attack and inflame. The authors argue that function matters more than surface labels. That view helps immune studies describe these flexible cells with more honesty.
pmc-4516908:
Burgess, Scott, Timpson, and their co-authors gave a blueprint in 2015 for Mendelian randomization with published data. Finding individual-level data for a well powered analysis can be hard. At the same time, large research groups were publishing more and more summarized genetic association data.

Using those public summaries is an attractive option, and the paper shows how to do it efficiently. It sets out how to identify causal risk factors from data already in the open. That lowers cost and speeds work, since no new samples must be gathered. The blueprint helped teams turn public genome data into causal evidence for prevention and drug targets.
pmc-5383908:
Bakdash and Marusich presented repeated measures correlation in 2017, a statistical technique for a common design. Many studies measure the same people on two or more occasions, for example before and after training. Simple correlation is often applied to such data, but the observations are not independent, which breaks its assumptions.

Repeated measures correlation, shortened to rmcorr, finds the common within-individual association between paired measures. It asks whether, as one measure rises within a person, the other tends to rise too. That focus fits psychology and health data, where each person serves as their own baseline. The method gives a cleaner answer than pooling all points as if they were strangers.
pmc-6030908:
Jean-Paul Concordet and Maximilian Haeussler presented CRISPOR, a web tool for CRISPR guide choice, in 2018. CRISPR editing needs a short guide RNA that matches the target DNA. A poor guide can cut at the wrong places or barely work.

CRISPOR searches a pasted sequence, lists candidate guides, and scores each for off-target risk and likely activity. It covers many genomes and offers primer designs for checking the edit. The plain layout suits bench scientists who do not code. Careful guide choice at this stage prevents wasted weeks of lab work later.
pmc-7054408:
Manli Wang, Ruiyuan Cao, Leike Zhang, and coauthors tested two existing drugs against the new coronavirus in early 2020. The virus had just emerged, and no proven treatment existed. Screens of known drugs offered the fastest hope.

In cell culture, the antiviral remdesivir and the malaria drug chloroquine both blocked the virus at low doses. Remdesivir had already been through human safety testing for other viruses. The authors urged clinical trials to follow at once. The short report helped launch the first wave of treatment trials in the pandemic. Both drugs had published human safety records, which made rapid trials ethically plausible.
pmc-7547708:
Juliane Winkler and co-authors set out key concepts in 2020 for how tumors reshape the material around them as they grow and spread. Healthy tissue is held in a scaffold called the extracellular matrix, and cells constantly talk with that scaffold in both directions. Tumors exploit this remodeling, loosening and rebuilding the matrix into surroundings that favor their own growth.

The authors explain the main ways tumors rework their scaffold, and how those changes help cancer cells break away and seed new sites. They also discuss the enzymes and signals involved, several of which are drug targets. Their framework helps readers see metastasis not just as rogue cells, but as a whole neighborhood remade for escape.
pmc-7778908:
The UniProt Consortium described in 2020 the state of UniProt, the universal protein knowledgebase, as it stood entering 2021. The knowledgebase aims to give anyone free access to protein sequences paired with rich notes on what each protein does. It is one of the most heavily used reference resources in all of biology.

The article reports the significant updates made over the previous two years, covering new data, improved annotation, and better ways to search and download. It explains how the consortium keeps quality high while the flood of new sequences grows. For many researchers, UniProt is where a question about a protein starts, so these updates describe infrastructure that quietly supports work worldwide.
pmc-8116208:
Stephen Nayfach and co-authors presented CheckV in 2020, a pipeline for judging the quality of viral genomes recovered from metagenomes. Environmental sequencing had uncovered millions of new viral sequences, but those fragments vary greatly in completeness and accuracy. A partial genome can mislead studies of what a virus is and what it can infect.

CheckV automatically spots genomes that are complete, estimates how complete each fragment is, and trims away host DNA mistakenly attached to viral sequences. The authors test it against known references to show how well the estimates hold. With virus discovery running far ahead of manual checking, an automated quality gate like this keeps large catalogs honest.
pmc-8482308:
Kathryn Skivington and colleagues presented in 2021 a new framework for developing and evaluating complex interventions in health research. Complex interventions, such as programs that change clinician behavior or whole care pathways, cannot be tested like a single pill. Guidance from the United Kingdom's Medical Research Council had shaped this work for years, and this document replaces it.

The framework was commissioned jointly by two major British research funders and reflects recent advances in methods and thinking. It guides researchers through developing an intervention, testing whether it can be delivered, evaluating it, and putting it into practice. The authors stress context and the involvement of those affected. Trials of health programs worldwide are designed against this guidance.
podcast-joerogan-EoFniMSMj08:
Conservationist Paul Rosolie joins Joe Rogan for episode 2441 to defend the Amazon rainforest. Rosolie has spent years in the Peruvian jungle protecting wildlife from poachers and loggers. His books and films brought the fight to a wide audience, and Rogan is a keen listener.

Rosolie tells tales of giant snakes, jaguars, and the armed patrols that guard the forest. He explains what is lost each time another stretch of jungle falls. Rogan asks how outsiders can help without ruining what they save. Green and brave listeners get a modern jungle defender's stories from the front line.
podcast-joerogan-SmGbhtyfY08:
Jackie Gleason's UFO house is the hook for a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience on the ongoing alien fascination. Gleason, the great TV comic, was a serious UFO collector who built a home shaped like a flying saucer. Rogan uses the tale to open a wider subject.

The talk moves from Gleason's library of saucer books to the stars and soldiers who shared his obsession. Rogan asks why the subject draws such unlikely believers. The segment is light on its feet but real in its detail, a reminder that UFO culture was built by famous, curious people long before podcasts.
podcast-tuckercarlson-cxe_Da7OF08:
Commentator Matt Walsh joins Tucker Carlson as fights split the American right. Carlson praises how Walsh has handled the drama as a man. Walsh knows most of the figures involved in person.

The title says Walsh refuses demands to disavow his allies. The pair discuss how a civil war inside a movement can end. They weigh loyalty, honesty, and public pressure. Carlson leaves room for views that differ from his own. The episode offers a calm, personal take on a feud that plays out daily in angry posts online. Walsh stays even-toned while the feud rages on.
podmore-naturalisation-of-the-supernatur:
Frank Podmore was a lead hand in the Society for Psychical Research. His Naturalisation of the Supernatural came out in 1908. Podmore spent years at seances and in the hunt for fraud. The book is his calm sum of what the whole field had found.

Ghosts, spooks, and knocks all get a fair but hard test here. Podmore finds fraud, self deceit, and tricks of the mind in most tales. A few hard cases stand fast at the end of his sieve. The book is the great cool sum of the field at its prime.
popol-vuh-spence-1908:
Long before print, the K'iche' Maya of Guatemala kept the tale of how the world was made. The Popol Vuh, in Lewis Spence's English rendering of 1908, gives that book of creation in full. Spence's version is the classic public-domain rendering of the Maya text.

The gods shape the earth, fail with mud men and wood men, and at last make men of maize. Then the Hero Twins dive into the dark land of the dead and outwit its lords. No native book of the Americas stands higher than this one. Its tales still anchor Maya pride and study.
punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-159-19:
Charivaria heads the Punch of September 8, 1920, in volume 159, with short jokes on drink, hats, trains, and husbands. The column keeps its habit of finding the absurd side of plain news items.

Rumours of prohibition in Scotland draw the warning that a dry Scotland will also go south. The Food Controller frees rice from all limits, which the column calls a timely blow against weddings. The Daily Mail offers one hundred pounds for the best new hat for men. A Chichester horse is run down by a train, and a Massachusetts wife offers her husband for sale at twenty thousand pounds.
rasmussen-people-polar-north-1908:
Knud Rasmussen grew up in Greenland and spoke its tongue, and this book of 1908 was his first great Arctic tale. He wrote from trips among the Inuit of the far north. The text came out with drawings by Harald Moltke. His mixed roots gave him a rare place in both worlds, Danish and Inuit.

Rasmussen tells of hunts, camps, and long dark months, told close to the people who lived them. He gives much space to shamans and to the spirit world as the Inuit knew it. Few books of its time show Arctic life from so near at hand.
recollections-of-the-private-life-of-nap: In the pages at hand, the eighth volume of Constant's Private Life of Napoleon Bonaparte has a publisher's header for its only front matter. The header states the title, gives Constant as author, and marks the text as English. No memoir prose, contents list, or opening chapter is printed after it here. A reader learns the part's number and its maker's name, but learns nothing of the scenes, people, or years that the eighth volume itself contains.
richard-carvel-volume-08:
Winston Churchill's Richard Carvel closes in an eighth volume, opening with Farewell to Gordon's after Mr. Swain's death. Richard cannot bear to recall his misery of mind, he writes. One hope had lightened all the years of his servitude: that Dorothy still loved him, and letters from Comyn said she was still free.

Yet Patty Swain, whose father took him in when homeless, grieves in crape at church, and conscience binds him where his heart does not. The volume's chapters promise how the gardener's son fought the Serapis, discoveries, and good come out of evil. Its last title brings the teller to his own again.
royce-philosophy-loyalty-1908:
Josiah Royce published The Philosophy of Loyalty in 1908, his best-known work of ethics. Royce defines loyalty as devotion to a cause larger than the self. A good life, he argues, is built by choosing such a cause and serving it fully. Yet causes conflict, and bad causes can claim loyalty too.

His answer is loyalty to loyalty itself: choose causes that let others be loyal as well. The beloved community is his name for a world bound by shared devotion. The book offers a uniquely American moral philosophy. It influenced thought on community, service, and identity. Its central idea still sparks debate.
scheible-das-kloster-vol08:
Cells twenty-nine through thirty-two fill band eight of Das Kloster, issued in 1847 under Johann Scheible's editorship. The set had become the place where lost German print came back to light. Scheible bought, borrowed, and reprinted texts that most scholars of his day had never seen.

Folk magic leads again: grimoires, conjuring books in the Faust line, and the dreaded Höllenzwänge. Folk charms for house, field, and body keep company with chapbook tales. Taken as a whole, the band reads like a fair stall of the old print world. Its value lies in breadth: high sorcery and kitchen lore preserved in one binding.
schoetensack-unterkiefer-homo-heidelberg:
Otto Schoetensack, a German scholar, published his monograph on the Mauer jaw in 1908, in German. A workman had found the massive jawbone in sand pits near Heidelberg in 1907. Schoetensack named its owner Homo heidelbergensis.

He describes the jaw's size, teeth, and primitive features in careful detail. The fossil was then the oldest human remain known in Europe. It proved that humans had deep antiquity on that continent. Later finds across Europe and Africa filled out the species Schoetensack announced. The Mauer jaw still anchors the species name in museum collections and textbooks today.
shahnama-warner-vol-3-1908:
Volume 3 of the Warner brothers' Shahnama of Firdausi appeared in 1908, the third of nine volumes in the first complete English version. Firdausi wrote the Persian Book of Kings around 1000, drawing on older chronicles and oral tales. Arthur and Edmond Warner turned the long poem into English verse and prose summary.

Heroes, kings, and demons move through battles and feasts as the epic's early ages unfold. The translation notes names, places, and variant tales for careful readers. Taken with its companion volumes, this part keeps the long chain of Persian kings unbroken in English. It shows the scale of the task the Warners took on and sustained for two decades.
shahnameh-warner-vol3-1908:
English verse by the Warner brothers carried Ferdowsi's Shahnama to new readers in 1908. Their version was the first full one in English verse. Book three holds the mid part of the vast poem. Persia's kings, both famed and flawed, march through its pages.

Old tales tell of quests, duels, and courts where fate turns on a word. The poem blends myth with what looks like early past fact. Ferdowsi aimed to keep the Persian tongue and its old glory alive. The Warners' steady verse lets the long tale hold an English reader to the end.
shakespeare-king-lear-1608:
William Shakespeare's King Lear first reached print in 1608. Many call it his bleakest tragedy, a tale of madness and ingratitude. Old Lear divides his realm by which daughter claims to love him most.

Cordelia, the honest one, is cast out, and the flatterers take all. Lear ends up mad on a storm-torn heath, stripped of power and kin. Gloucester's plot mirrors Lear's, with a loyal son and a false one. The end is stark, yet love and service shine in the wreck. The storm scene alone secures its place on any stage in the world, even now, for new crowds.
simmel-soziologie-1908:
Simmel's Sociology, published in German in 1908, is his masterwork, subtitled studies on the forms of association. Simmel spent years as an underpaid lecturer in Berlin while his fame grew across Europe and America. The big book gathered the essays and lectures in which he had built a new way of seeing society.

He analyzes the forms of social life: the stranger who is near and far at once, the secret society, the pair and the trio, rule and subordination. Content varies endlessly, but the geometry of relations repeats, and that geometry is his subject. The book founded formal sociology, the branch that studies patterns of interaction rather than institutions. Its chapters on the stranger and the metropolis are still assigned wherever sociology is taught.
southey-chronicle-of-the-cid-1808:
Robert Southey published Chronicle of the Cid in 1808, the first English version of Spain's national epic tradition in full. The Cid, Rodrigo Díaz, was a Castilian warrior of the 1000s, famed in poem and chronicle. Southey, poet and historian, gathered the Spanish sources into one English narrative.

Exile, battles against Muslim and Christian foes, and the winning of Valencia fill the chronicle. Southey mixed the epic Poem of the Cid with later prose accounts and ballads. His preface and notes explained Spanish history for English readers new to it. The book fixed the Cid in English imagination and helped spark British interest in Spanish literature and history.
spr-proceedings-vol22-1908:
Part fifty seven stands alone as volume twenty two of the Proceedings, dated 1908. The Society for Psychical Research devoted single parts to its largest inquiries. Mediumship investigations dominate this era of the journal. Sittings are reported with sitters' names, dates, and tests against fraud or guessing.

Telepathy work continues in the background of society business. Apparition cases, checked against death records and letters, appear in support. The society's critics, inside and outside, get their say in print. Volume twenty two is a focused sample of the archive at work. It shows how one year's evidence was built. The file remains open to any reader's judgment.
state-of-the-union-addresses-1790-2008:
Yearly addresses from 1790 to 2008 stand in one long set, parted by three stars. The contents run in order of office. George Washington leads, with addresses from January 8, 1790, through December 7, 1796, eight in all. John Adams follows with four, the last on November 11, 1800, and Thomas Jefferson with eight, from December 8, 1801, to November 8, 1808.

James Madison comes next in the list, opening on November 29, 1809. The run of names and dates forms a plain spine for the whole set: each president in turn, each December or nearby date in turn. A reader can trace the office year by year from the first Congress to the last address named, and dip into any single year without hunting through the rest.
steiner-way-of-initiation-1908:
Steiner's Way of Initiation, in this 1909 edition, is his practical manual on attaining knowledge of the higher worlds. Where his other books describe the unseen, this one tells the student how to train for seeing it. It became the working handbook of Anthroposophy.

He gives exercises in attention, reverence, and the control of thought, with warnings against haste and vanity on the path. The student is told to keep ordinary duties faithfully while the inner senses slowly open. Followers of Steiner still use the book as their first guide to his meditative discipline. His counsel is strict: slow growth, clean motives, and no hunger for power.
stronsa-beast-wernerian-society-1808:
A great carcass came ashore on Stronsa in the Orkney Islands in the autumn of 1808, and men argued over it for years. Doctor John Barclay told the Wernerian Society of Edinburgh what the sworn witnesses had seen and measured. His account, with its affidavits, appeared in the years 1808 and 1809.

The beast was long, maned, and finned, by the tales told of it, and some called it a sea serpent. Later study of the bones and form named it a basking shark, huge and rotten past knowing. The papers show science at work on a monster in the open. Error and care sit side by side in the record.
suess-face-of-earth-vol3-sollas-1908:
